->PROLOGUE<-

# Preface of Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to his letters. Salutations in the first book to Julian de' Medici: The Great-Souled.

## MARSILIO FICINO SENDS MANY GREETINGS TO JULIAN DE' MEDICI, THE GREAT-SOULED. <note>original: "S. D." for "Salutem Dicit," a standard Latin greeting.</note>

Cosimo the Great, your grandfather and my patron, O great-souled Julian, often had that Platonic saying on his lips: that nothing is more suited for accomplishing great things than the goodwill of prudent and learned men. He held that there is no certain proof of justice or prudence if such friends are present, nor of injustice and imprudence if they are absent. This was a golden precept of our Plato. Cosimo proved this in reality even more than in words throughout his entire life; he was a man certainly rich in money beyond others, but far richer in men, and richest of all in prudence and justice. And—what is most rare and wonderful—he left his son and grandsons as heirs to all this treasure. Thus it is that in my Julian, I recognize that old man upon whom, second only to God, my well-being depended. There is no one, therefore, whom I more desire to be well than Julian. Indeed, I pray and beseech God for this daily. However, so that I might declare the vow and affection of my soul to you more certainly, I have decided to dedicate the first volume of my letters to you, the king of friends. By this, all my friends may be referred back to one principal friend, and you, in reading them, may understand that as often as you read a greeting, Julian is being greeted by Marsilio.

### Concerning the desire for happiness.

Cosimo de' Medici sends many greetings to Marsilio Ficino the Platonist.

<margin>c</margin> I took myself yesterday to the Careggi estate, <note>Careggi was the site of the Medici villa where Ficino's "Platonic Academy" met.</note> not for the sake of cultivating the field, but for the sake of cultivating the mind. Come to us, Marsilio, as soon as possible. Bring with you our Plato's book *On the Highest Good*, <note>original: "de summo bono."</note> which I believe you have already translated from the Greek language into Latin, as you promised. For I desire nothing more ardently than to know which path leads most conveniently to happiness. Farewell, and come—and do not forget your Orphic lyre. <note>Ficino was famous for performing "Orphic hymns" on a lyre as a form of musical therapy and meditation.</note>

### What the path to happiness may be.

Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to Cosimo the Great.

<margin>♥</margin> I shall come to you as soon as I can, and most gladly. For what is more pleasing than to dwell in Careggi—that is, the "Field of Graces"—together with Cosimo, the father of the Graces? <note>Ficino is making a pun on the name of the villa, *Charegium*, and the Greek word *charis*, meaning grace.</note> Meanwhile, accept in a few words what the Platonists hold to be the most suitable path to happiness. And though I think a path ought not be shown to one who has already almost reached the finish line, I nevertheless decided that your desire must be obeyed, both in my absence and presence. All men wish to do well—that is, to live well. Moreover, they will live well if they possess as many "goods" as possible. These things are called goods: wealth, health, beauty, strength, noble birth, honors, and power; also prudence, justice, courage, temperance, and above all others, wisdom, which indeed [contains] all power...

<meta>This page continues the text from the previous leaf, following the sub-heading "Concerning the desire for happiness." The opening word completes a sentence describing what the study of philosophy encompasses.</meta>

encompasses happiness. For happiness indeed consists in the successful attainment of a desired goal. Wisdom provides this in every individual skill. If indeed skilled flute-players best achieve whatever the use of flutes requires, and learned grammarians achieve what pertains to both reading and writing letters, so too do wise pilots <note>original: "gubernatores," referring to ship captains or navigators</note> reach a prosperous harbor of navigation before all others. Likewise, a wise general manages more safely what belongs to military service, and a wise doctor better brings the body to its desired health. For this reason, wisdom in every individual human work makes us masters of our wishes to the best of our abilities. It neither wanders from the path nor is it ever deceived. Otherwise, it would not truly be wisdom. Since wisdom is truly the cause of attaining one's goal, it is necessary that it has total power in leading us toward happiness.

Furthermore, only those who possess many "goods" are called blessed. These people, however, are not blessed until the goods present to them actually benefit them. Nor do they ever benefit them unless they are used. For possession alone, without use, has no importance for happiness. Nevertheless, even use is not enough. For one can use things badly: from which it happens that one is harmed rather than helped. Therefore, just as we add use to possession, so it is fitting to add rectitude <note>original: "rectitudinem," meaning rightness or moral correctness</note> to use. Let us not merely use things, but use them rightly; and only wisdom provides us with the ability to use individual things rightly. 

Indeed, one can see this in the arts. Only those who are skilled in an art use both the materials and the tools rightly. By the same reasoning, wisdom ensures that we rightly use wealth, health, beauty, strength, and the other things that are called "goods." Wherefore, in every possession, use, and operation, knowledge is the cause of acting prosperously and well. For he who lacks a mind <note>original: "sine mente," implying a lack of intelligence or rational direction</note> and yet possesses many things and uses them, is harmed all the more because he possesses more things to abuse. Truly, the more a foolish man acts, the more he errs. By erring less, he acts less wickedly; and by acting less wickedly, he is less wretched. He certainly acts less if he is poor rather than rich, if he is weak rather than strong, fearful rather than bold, lazy rather than vigilant, slow rather than fast, and dull rather than keen. 

Therefore, none of those things which were previously called "goods" are good in themselves. For if ignorance <note>original: "inscitia"</note> presides over them, they are so much worse than their opposites, insofar as they can more abundantly supply a wicked leader with the means for crimes; but if prudence and wisdom preside over them, then finally they are better. Yet in themselves they are neither good nor bad; to a wise man, both adverse and prosperous circumstances finally turn out to be useful because he uses both rightly, whereas for the foolish man, it is the opposite. Therefore, of all our concerns, wisdom alone is a good in itself, and foolishness alone is an evil in itself. 

Since we all wish to be happy, and happiness cannot be had without the right use of things, and knowledge provides that right use, everyone ought to strive—leaving all other things aside—with both fullness of spirit and the study of piety to become as wise as possible. For in this way our soul becomes most like God, who is wisdom itself. Plato <note>Plato’s concept of "homoiosis theo" or "becoming like God" was a central pillar of Ficino’s Neoplatonism.</note> believed that the highest degree of blessedness consists in this very likeness.

->Imitation is more useful than reading.<-

<vocab>happiness, wisdom, Plato, blessedness, foolishness, rectitude</vocab>

<summary>Ficino argues that happiness is not found in the mere possession of "goods" like wealth or health, but in their right use, which only wisdom can provide. He concludes that wisdom is the only inherent good because it directs all other things toward a virtuous end, ultimately making the soul like God.</summary>

# BOOK ONE
A 2

### Marsilio Ficino sends greetings <note>original: "S.D." for "Salutem Dicit," a formal Latin greeting</note> to the Magnificent Amerigo Benci.

<margin>a</margin>Today I received in your name the Greek dialogues of our Plato: a truly magnificent gift, worthy of your spirit and most pleasing to mine. I give you great thanks. May the celestial Graces <note>the three Charites of mythology who personify charm and gratitude</note> someday return immortal grace to you. In this act, as in most others, I believe you wished to imitate the great Cosimo <note>Cosimo de' Medici, Ficino’s primary patron and the ruler of Florence</note>; for in days past, he adorned my library with a Greek Plato. Amerigo, I indeed praise your house and I approve of this imitation. For imitation is a path better suited to virtue than reading. Truly, just as a harmony affects us more powerfully while it is present and flowing into our ears than when it is merely remembered from the past, and as a battle moves us more sharply when it is watched than when it is narrated, so the distinguished works of living Heroes inflame one more ardently toward virtue and form one’s character more exactly than the words of ancient philosophers disputing about morals.

->A theological dialogue between God and the soul.<-

### Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Michael Mercati of San Miniato, his beloved fellow philosopher.

<margin>f</margin>We have often philosophized together about moral and natural things, beloved Michael. More often still about divine things. I remember, however, that you were frequently accustomed to say: moral things are to be acquired by practice; natural things are to be sought by reason; and divine things are to be requested from God by prayer. I have also read in our Plato that divine things are revealed because of a purity of life rather than being taught through doctrine and words. Therefore, when I was carefully considering these and similar matters, I began at some point to grieve in my soul—as one who now distrusted reason and did not yet trust in revelation. From this was born a certain intimate dialogue between the soul and God. Hear this, if you please, although I think perhaps you already speak to God more closely than we do.

**GOD:** Wretched one, why do you grieve so much, my soul? Put an end now to your tears, O daughter. Behold, I, your father, am present for you. I am present as your medicine and your salvation.

**SOUL:** O, would that my father might breathe upon me! Ah, if I thought such a great gift could fall to me, ah, how I would be driven mad with joy! But now I do not see by what means that can happen; for he who is present to me only from the outside <note>original: "extrinsecus"</note> is not my highest father. For that Architect of nature, as I believe, fathered me, His offspring, even more inwardly than His own nature. Nor is he who is only within me <note>original: "intrinsecus"</note> my highest father; for He is greater than I, yet whoever is inside me is undoubtedly lesser than I. But how anything can be both inside and outside me at the same time, I do not know. This, stranger, whoever you are, this deeply distresses me: that I do not wish to live without my father, and I despair of being able to find Him.

**GOD:** Put an end to your tears, O daughter; do not afflict yourself. It is no stranger who speaks with you, but a member of your household, more familiar to you than you are to yourself. Indeed, I am present for you and in you at the same time. I am present for you because I am in you; I am in you because you are in me. For unless you were in me, you would not be in yourself; indeed, you would not exist at all. Put an end to your tears, O daughter; behold your parent. Your Parent, who as much as He is the smallest of all in physical mass, is that much greater in power...

<summary>This page contains a letter of gratitude to Amerigo Benci for a Greek Plato manuscript and the beginning of a mystical dialogue between God and the Soul. Ficino argues that God is more intimate to the soul than the soul is to itself, existing both "inside" and "outside" the person.</summary>
<keywords>Marsilio Ficino, Amerigo Benci, Plato, Cosimo de' Medici, Michael Mercati, Neoplatonism, soul and God, revelation, divine light, Florence</keywords>

[nearest] of all: and because it is the narrowest: it is within all things. Because it is the most ample, it is outside all things. Behold, I am present to you both inside and outside; the greatest narrowness: the smallest amplitude. Behold, I say: do you not see? I fill, penetrate, and contain heaven and earth. I fill, but am not filled, because I am fullness itself. I penetrate, but am not penetrated: because I am the power of penetrating. I contain, but am not contained: because I am the faculty of containing. I am not filled, lest I should be unworthy, because I am abundance itself. I am not penetrated, lest I should cease to be, I who am Being itself. I am not contained, lest I should cease to be God, I who am infinity itself. Behold, do you not see? I enter through all things without being mixed with them: so that I might also be able to surpass them, I who am excellence itself. I surpass all things without being separated from them: so that I might simultaneously be able to enter into them: to enter deeply and to unite them, I who am the union itself through which all things are made, through which they stand firm, and which all things desire. Why do you despair of finding your parent, O mad one? It is not difficult to find where I am: since in me, from me, and through me all things are preserved, always and everywhere. And by infinite virtue, I am amplified across an infinite interval. Indeed, there is no way to find where I am not, since through me this very "where" exists and is spoken of everywhere: I am the leader; I act as the light: and whatever anyone seeks, and wherever they seek it, they seek through me. Nothing is desired anywhere except the Good; nothing is found anywhere except the Truth: I am all Good: I am all Truth. Seek my face and you shall live. But do not be moved in order to reach me, since I am stability itself; do not be distracted by varied things in order to apprehend me, since I am unity itself. Still your movement. Collect your multitude <note>the fragmented thoughts or desires of the human mind</note>. You will follow me immediately: for a long time now, you have followed me from within.

**SOUL.** Why do you desert me so quickly, O my salvation? Why do you so suddenly desert your thirsty daughter? Go on, proceed further: proceed, I pray, venerable divinity. Speak, I beseech you by your majesty, more clearly if it pleases you: ah, make it so that it pleases you. Speak, then, because it has pleased you to speak more clearly: why are you not my father so that I may be revived? What are you, again, my father, so that I may live?

**GOD.** I am not the parent of your body's nature, my daughter. For you are better to the degree that you more greatly obey your parent: you are moreover more excellent to the degree that you more greatly oppose the body. It is good for you to be with your father; it is bad for you to be with the body. No mere spirit <note>original: "animus," referring here to a lower or individual mind/spirit</note> generated you, O Soul. Otherwise, you would think of nothing beyond the spirit and you would stop your step in the very mutability of the spirit; nor would you demand a completely stable nature. No multiplex intellect created you: for then you would not reach the highest simplicity. And the attainment of that intellect would be enough for you; but now, by understanding and loving, you ascend toward life itself, toward essence itself, toward absolute Being itself above any intellect. Nor is understanding enough for you unless you understand both "well" and "the Good" <note>Ficino distinguishes between the act of knowing and the "Good" (God) which is the source of all value</note>. Indeed, the Good itself is undoubtedly enough for you: for you do not seek anything for any other reason except that it is good. Therefore, the Good itself is your procreator, O Soul: not a good body, not a good spirit, not a good intellect, but the Good; the Good which indeed consists in itself, infinite beyond the limits of any subject. And it grants you infinite life: either from age to age, or at least from a certain beginning into eternity. Do you desire to gaze upon the face of the Good? Behold the entire universe full of the light of the sun; behold the light in—

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Theological Dialogue" where God explains the nature of reality to the Soul. Having previously described His omnipresence, God now uses the metaphor of light and the sun to explain the hierarchy of existence from raw matter up to the Divine essence. The Soul then responds with a prayer-like expression of mystical ecstasy.</meta>

### FIRST BOOK

The <term>matter</term> <note>original: "materia"</note> of the world is full of all the forms of all things and is constantly in flux. Subtract the matter and leave the rest. You then have the <term>soul</term> <note>original: "anima"</note>, which is an incorporeal light, containing all forms but still subject to change. Remove change from this, and you have attained the <term>angelic intellect</term>, which is an incorporeal light, containing all forms and remaining immutable.

Remove from this that diversity by which any form is distinct from the light or is infused into the light from elsewhere. Imagine instead that the essence of these lights and forms is the light itself, and that this light forms itself so that it may form all other things. This light shines infinitely because it shines by its own nature; it is neither tainted by being mixed with another thing nor is it limited. It is through all things because it is in no specific thing; it is in no specific thing so that it may shine equally through all things. It lives of itself and provides life to all. Indeed, its shadow—which is this light of the sun—is the only thing that gives life to physical bodies. 

The light perceives all and bestows sensation. If its shadow excites all the senses in all creatures, it surely loves individual things, especially since they are its own. Therefore, what is the light of the sun? It is the shadow of God. Therefore, what is God? **God is the Sun of the sun.** <note>This "Sun of the sun" metaphor is a hallmark of Neoplatonism, suggesting that just as the sun illuminates the physical world, God illuminates the world of ideas and the mind.</note> The light of the sun is God within the "body" of the world. God is the light of the sun above the angelic intellects. Such is my shadow, O soul, that it is the most beautiful of all physical things.

How great then do you think my own light is? If my shadow shines so much, imagine how my light gleams! You love light everywhere above all else; indeed, you love light alone. Love me alone, O soul, for I am the only infinite light. Love me, and in me you will shine infinitely and be delighted infinitely.

**THE SOUL.** Oh, wonderful thing that exceeds wonder itself! What unusual fire burns me now? What new sun is this for me, and from where does it glow? Who and from where is this great and sweet spirit that now pierces and soothes my very marrow? It bites and licks, stimulates and tickles—what a <term>bitter sweetness</term> <note>original: "amara dulcedo," a common phrase in mystical literature to describe the overwhelming, sometimes painful intensity of divine love.</note> this is! 

Who could even conceive of it? A bitter sweetness that melts me within and pours me out. By comparison, those things which have been taken away from me now seem bitter, even if they once seemed the sweetest. How sweet is the bitterness that joins me back together and restores me after I have been torn apart! Through it, even the most bitter things become sweet to me. How necessary this <term>will</term> <note>original: "voluntas"</note> is, since I cannot *not* want the Good itself. I can avoid or delay anything else more easily than this greed for the Good. For even if I wished to avoid it, I would only try to do so because I judged that very avoidance to be a "good" thing. Thus, this is a voluntary necessity, since nothing is more voluntary than the desire for the Good. Because of the Good, I desire everything—or rather, I desire the Good in all things everywhere. I desire it so much that I wish to be unable to *not* want it. 

What a living death this is! Who could conceive how I die to myself yet live in God? Through this, I die to death and live to life; I live as life itself and rejoice in joy. Oh, pleasure beyond sense! Oh, gladness beyond the soul! Oh, joy beyond the mind! I am indeed now "beside myself," yet I am not mindless, because I am *above* the mind. I rage with a holy frenzy, yet I am not cast down because I am raised on high. I exult now everywhere; I flow away, yet I am not scattered, because God—the **Unity of unities**—gathers me to Himself and lives within me as He lives in Himself. Rejoice therefore now with me, all you for whom God is exultation; my God has come to meet me.

The God of the universe has embraced me. The God of gods now flows into my very marrow. Now, God himself nourishes all of me; he who sired me now regenerates me. He who had sired the soul now transforms it into an <term>angel</term> <note>In Ficino’s Neoplatonic hierarchy, the "angelic" level is a state of being above the human soul, characterized by direct, unchanging intellectual vision.</note>; he converts it into a god. What thanks shall I return to you, O grace of graces? Teach me yourself, O grace of graces; teach me, I pray, and provide for me. Finally, let God himself be your thanks; you, O God, be your own reward.

## Law and Justice.

### Marsilio Ficino to the learned men Otto Niccolini and Benedetto of Arezzo, and to the knights Piero Pazzi and Bernardo Giugni: Greetings.

<margin>p</margin>You have persuaded me to translate Plato’s Greek laws into Latin; the great <term>Cosimo</term> <note>Cosimo de' Medici (1389–1464), Ficino’s patron and the de facto ruler of Florence.</note> also urged me to do the same. And so I have now done it, and all the more willingly because I judged that a city has more need of excellent, learned men than of good merchants or doctors. Indeed, Minos <note>A legendary king and lawgiver of Crete.</note> was as much more beneficial to the Greeks than Galen <note>The most famous physician of antiquity.</note> as the soul is more excellent than the body or the <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus". In Renaissance medicine, the "spirit" was a subtle vapor that connected the soul to the physical body.</note>, and as eternal life is more excellent than temporal life. For trade seems to be the body of the city, medicine its spirit, and law its soul. And although there may seem to be many laws in a city, there are not many souls of the city. For just as many arts and various ranks of citizens do not make many cities but a single one—if they advance toward the same end by a similar reason—so, although there may be many constitutions of magistrates in a city, there is nevertheless only one public Law: namely, the common rule of living rightly, leading toward public happiness.

To this Law, God and nature prepare us. Constitutions encourage us, but the one God ultimately forms us. For from the divine law proceeds both the law of the stars and the law of men. For this reason, all lawgivers—partly imitating <term>Moses</term> <note>original: "moïsem". Ficino, like many Renaissance thinkers, believed that ancient pagan wisdom was ultimately derived from or parallel to the Hebrew tradition of Moses.</note> like apes, as he was the truest author of divine laws, and partly compelled somehow by the truth—affirmed that they received their laws under various stories. Osiris, the lawgiver of the Egyptians, claimed they came from Mercury; Zoroaster among the Arimaspi from a good divinity; Zalmoxis among the Scythians from Vesta; Minos of Crete and Solon of Athens from Jupiter; Lycurgus the Spartan from Apollo; Numa, King of the Romans, from the nymph Egeria; Muhammad, King of the Arabs, from the angel Gabriel. Our own Plato begins his books on laws with God, whom he says is the common author of all laws.

He also confirmed this in the dialogue titled *Protagoras*, saying that those arts which pertain to physical survival were handed down to us by Prometheus—that is, by human providence. However, the Law of living well and happily was granted by Jupiter—that is, by divine providence—through Mercury, which signifies angelic inspiration. I cannot, my best friends, help but admire the power of Law. Indeed, some order and harmony of law is necessary in the elements of the world, in the fluids of a living creature, and in the life of brute animals. It is present even in a band of thieves; for they cannot live together without a certain just order. What shall we say to this: that although there is no other virtue among those in the <term>Underworld</term> <note>original: "inferos", referring to the classical afterlife.</note>, Law and Justice are not absent there, so that they may punish the wicked according to their deserts. And since those moral virtues are no longer necessary among the blessed—those which serve to calm the <term>disturbances</term> <note>original: "perturbationes". Catchword: bati.</note> of the body and the senses...

<summary>Ficino introduces his translation of Plato's Laws with a letter to Florentine dignitaries, arguing that Law functions as the "soul" of a city and originates from Divine Providence, citing historical lawgivers from Moses to Muhammad as evidence.</summary>
<keywords>Marsilio Ficino, Plato, Laws, Justice, Divine Providence, Moses, Minos, lawgivers, political philosophy, Neoplatonism</keywords>

### On Divine Madness.

->Marsilio Ficino to his other self, Peregrino: Greetings.<-

On the twenty-ninth of November <note>original: "Tercio chalendas decembres". The Roman calendar counts backward from the Kalends (the 1st) of the following month.</note>, my father, Ficino the physician, brought me two letters in your name. One was written in prose, the other in verse. By reading them, I am indeed moved to congratulate our times for producing such a youth whose fame and glory might illuminate them. Truly, my sweetest Peregrino, when I consider your age as well as those things which proceed from you daily, I not only rejoice in such great gifts for a friend, but I also marvel at them vehemently. And I do not know—to omit these more recent men—which of those ancients whose memory we venerate made such progress at the age you are now. I attribute this not only to art and study, but much more to that **divine madness** <term>divine madness</term> <note>original: "divinus furor". A Platonic concept where the soul is "possessed" by a higher power, leading to poetic, prophetic, or religious insight.</note>, without which Democritus and Plato deny any man was ever great. That you are, so to speak, inspired and thoroughly seized by this is proven by those more agitated movements and most ardent affections which your writings express. The ancient philosophers intended this very agitation, which occurs through external movements, to be the primary evidence that there is a certain divine power in our souls. 

But since I have mentioned madness, I will recount in a few words—and with the brevity an epistle requires—the opinion of our Plato on this matter: so that you may easily understand what madness is, into how many parts it is divided, and which god presides over each madness. I trust this will be of both the greatest pleasure and utility to you. He judges, therefore, that our soul, before it fell into bodies—as Pythagoras, Empedocles, and Heraclitus had also previously argued—existed in the celestial seats. There, as Socrates says in the *Phaedrus*, it was nourished and rejoiced in the contemplation of truth. And since those philosophers I mentioned just now learned from **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: "Mercurio Trismegisto". A legendary sage of ancient Egypt believed to be the author of the Hermetic Corpus and a precursor to Plato.</note>, the wisest of all Egyptians, that the highest God is a certain fountain and light in which the archetypes of all things (which they call **Ideas** <term>Ideas</term> <note>The eternal, unchanging patterns or forms of all things existing in the divine mind.</note>) shine forth, they thought it necessary that the soul, assiduously contemplating the eternal mind of God, should also behold the natures of all things more clearly. The soul, says Plato, saw justice itself; it saw wisdom; it saw harmony; it saw a certain wonderful beauty of the divine nature, and all these he calls both Ideas and divine essences. Then he names the primary natures which exist in the eternal mind of God, by a certain perfect knowledge of which the minds of men are happily nourished as long as they dwell there. But when, due to the thought and desire for earthly things, the souls are weighed down into bodies, then that which was previously nourished by ambrosia and nectar—that is, by the knowledge of God and perfect joy—is said, in its very descent, to have drunk from the **River Lethe** <note>original: "flumen Letheum". The river of forgetfulness in Greek mythology.</note>, which is the forgetting of divine things; nor does it return to the upper realms from where...

### BOOK

<note>original: "LIBER"</note>

...worldly thoughts had fallen by their own weight, they begin to fly back and to reflect upon those divine natures whose memory they had lost. That divine philosopher <note>referring to Plato</note> believes we attain this through two virtues: specifically, the one pertaining to morals and the one pertaining to contemplation. He calls the former by the common name "justice" and the latter "wisdom." Therefore, he says that with these twin wings—at least in my opinion—the perceiving souls fly up to the heavens. Socrates discusses in the *Phaedrus* <note>One of Plato's dialogues concerning love and the soul.</note> that we achieve these through the two parts of philosophy, namely the **active** and the **contemplative**. Hence, he says in that same *Phaedrus* that only the mind of the philosopher recovers its wings. In this very recovery of wings, the soul is drawn away from the body by their power; filled with God, it is pulled toward the heavens and strives vehemently. This withdrawal and striving Plato calls **divine madness** <term>divine madness</term> <note>original: "divinum furorem". A state of being possessed by a higher spiritual power.</note>. He divides this madness into four parts; for he thinks that men never remember divine things unless they are excited by certain shadows and images of them which are perceived by the bodily senses.

Therefore, Paul and Dionysius <note>Saint Paul and Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian whom Renaissance thinkers believed was a direct disciple of Paul.</note>, the wisest of Christian theologians, assert that the invisible things of God are understood through those things which have been made and are seen here. Plato, for his part, maintains that human wisdom is the image of divine wisdom. He considers this very harmony which we create with voices and musical instruments to be the image of divine harmony. Furthermore, he judges that beauty—which is produced from the most fitting arrangement of the body’s parts and members—to be the image of divine beauty in its grace and loveliness. 

However, since wisdom is present in no men (or certainly in very few) and is not grasped by any of the body's senses, it follows that the likenesses of divine wisdom among us are very scarce, and indeed remain hidden from our senses and utterly unknown. Therefore, Socrates says in the *Phaedrus* that the likeness of wisdom can in no way be seen with the eyes; but if it were seen, it would stir up marvelous loves for that divine reality of which it is an image. 

But we do see the likeness of divine beauty with our eyes, and we note the image of harmony with our ears. Plato considers these two senses to be the most perceptive of all that operate through the body. Thus it happens that by those images which exist in bodies—drawn into the soul through the physical senses—we remember in some way those things which we knew before, when we were situated outside the **prison of the body** <note>original: "corporis carcerem". A common Platonic metaphor for the physical world.</note>. By this recollection, the soul catches fire and, beating its wings, it gradually cleanses itself from the thoughts and filth of the body. It becomes utterly affected by divine madness, and through these two senses I mentioned a moment ago, two species of madness are excited. For by the appearance of beauty which the eyes offer, we recover a certain recollection of true and intelligible beauty, desiring it with an ineffable and hidden ardor of the mind. This, finally, is what Plato calls **divine love**, defining it as: a desire, arising from the sight of a physical likeness, to return again to the contemplation of divine beauty. Furthermore, it is necessary that he who is thus affected not only desires that celestial beauty...

rare: but also to be greatly delighted by the sight of that which is open to the eyes. For nature is so constituted that whoever desires something is also delighted by its likeness. But he <note>Plato</note> considers it a trait of a duller mind and a corrupted nature if someone lusts only after the shadows of that true beauty, and admits nothing beyond that appearance which is offered to the eyes. For he holds that such a person is affected by that love which is a companion to insolence and lust, defining it as an **irrational and immoderate desire** for the pleasure perceived by the senses regarding the form of the body. He defines this love in another way: as a heat of the soul that is, in a certain sense, dead in its own body but living in another's. 

Hence he says the soul of the lover leads its life in a foreign body. Imitating this, the **Epicureans** <note>Followers of Epicurus, who believed the world was made of material particles and that pleasure was the highest good.</note> define love as a certain striving of little bodies, which they call **atoms** <term>atoms</term> <note>original: "athomos". In this context, the Epicureans believed physical attraction was caused by the literal flow of atoms between people.</note>, to pour themselves deeply into the one from whom the images of beauty were drawn. Our Plato says that love of this kind is born from human illnesses and is full of care and anxiety. It belongs to those men whose minds are so shrouded in darkness that they think of nothing lofty, nothing excellent at all, nothing except the fragile and fleeting image of this little body; nor does the mind look back to the heavens, shut away in darkness and a **blind prison** <note>A common Platonic metaphor for the physical body.</note>. 

But those whose intellect has been drawn away and freed from the "mud" of the body are of such a kind that when the form and charm of some body is presented to them, they are drawn away at first sight as if by a likeness of divine beauty. Truly, from this image they immediately recall that divine beauty which they admire above all else, and which they truly long for, and by whose most burning desire they are snatched up toward higher things. And this first attempt at flying away, Plato calls **divine alienation** and **madness** <term>divine madness</term> <note>original: "divinam alienationem furoremque".</note>. 

These things now seem sufficient regarding that madness which we said occurs through the eyes; through the ears, however, the soul drinks in certain harmonies and most sweet rhythms. By these images, it is reminded and excited to consider **divine music** with a sharper and more intimate sense of the mind. Moreover, among the Platonic interpreters, divine music is twofold: they believe one kind consists in the eternal mind of God, while the other is in the order and movements of the heavens, by which the celestial spheres and orbits produce a certain **wonderful harmony** <note>Often called the "Music of the Spheres," the ancient idea that the movement of planets creates a perfect, mathematical song.</note>. They hold that our soul was a participant in both of these before it was enclosed in bodies; but in these shadows, it uses the ears as if they were little cracks or narrow openings, and through these, it receives the images—as we have often said—of that incomparable music. 

By these images, the soul is led back to a certain intimate and silent memory of the harmony it enjoyed before, and it burns entirely with desire; it longs to enjoy true music again and to fly back to its own home. And since the soul understands that it can in no way achieve this as long as it is hedged in by the dark dwelling-place of the body, it strives at least to imitate as best it can that music which it cannot possess here. This imitation among men is twofold. For some imitate celestial music with rhythmic voices and the sounds of various instruments; these we certainly call light and almost common musicians. Others, however, [pursue] more serious...

# BOOK

...ds. With a certain firmer judgment, imitating the divine and heavenly harmony, they arrange the senses and notions of their innermost reason into rhythmic feet and numbers. These are the ones who, inspired by a divine spirit, pour out—with a **round mouth** <note>original: "ore rotundo" – a classical idiom meaning eloquent, polished, or well-rounded speech.</note>, as they say—most grave and noble poems. **Plato** calls this the "graver music" and "poetry": a most effective imitator of heavenly harmony. For that lighter music, which I mentioned shortly before, charms only by the sweetness of voices. 

Poetry, however, because it possesses the quality of divine harmony, expresses certain very grave and—as a poet might say—**Delphic meanings** <note>original: "delphicos sensus" – referring to the Oracle at Delphi, meaning prophetic, profound, or divinely inspired wisdom.</note> more ardently through the rhythms of voices and movements. Thus, it does not merely flatter the ears, but it also provides a most sweet food for the mind, very much like **heavenly ambrosia** <note>The food of the gods in Greek mythology, granting immortality.</note>. For this reason, it seems to approach closer to divinity. 

He <note>Plato</note> considers this **poetic madness** <term>poetic madness</term> <note>original: "poeticum hunc furore" – also known as *furor poeticus*, the state of divine inspiration where a poet is "possessed" by the Muses.</note> to arise from the Muses. He judges that whoever approaches the gates of poetry without the instinct of the Muses—hoping that he might become a good poet through mere art—remains himself uninitiated, and his poetry is for naught. Those poets who are seized by heavenly inspiration and power frequently bring forth senses so divine and inspired by the Muses that they themselves, once placed outside that madness, understand less of what they have produced. 

And as I believe, that divine man <note>Plato</note> intends for the **Muses** to be understood as **heavenly songs**; therefore, they say they are called "canorous" and "camenae" from "song" <note>original: "canoras & camenas a cantu" – a traditional etymological link between the name of the Muses (Camenae) and the Latin word for song (*cantus*).</note>. Whence, by the Muses—that is, by the heavenly deities and songs—divine men are stirred to meditate on poetic modes and rhythms in imitation of them. 

Thus, in the *Republic*, when Plato was treating the rotation of the heavenly spheres, he said that **individual Sirens** sit upon the individual orbits, signifying that a song is offered to the deities by the movement of the spheres, as a certain Platonist says. For "Siren" is correctly expressed in Greek as **"one singing to a god"** <note>original: "siren deo canens græce" – the author is providing a Greek etymological interpretation of the word Siren.</note>. The ancient theologians also held that the **nine Muses** are the musical songs of the eight spheres, plus one greatest harmony which is composed of all of them. 

By this reasoning, poetry proceeds from divine madness, madness from the Muses, and the Muses from **Jupiter**. For the Platonists often call the **Spirit of the Whole World** "Jupiter," who nourishes from within the heaven, the lands, the flowing fields, the glowing globe of the moon, and the Titan stars; and, infused through the limbs, he moves the whole mass and mingles himself with the great body. 

From this, it follows that from Jupiter—the spirit and mind of the whole world, since he moves and rules the heavenly spheres—the songs of those same spheres also arise, which they call Muses. Wherefore, that most famous Platonist said: **"From Jupiter is the beginning of the Muse; all things are full of Jupiter."** Since that spirit which is called Jupiter flourishes everywhere and fills all things, he produces heavenly harmony by "striking the heaven like a certain lyre," as **Alexander of Miletus** <note>A scholar and geographer from the 1st century BCE.</note>, the Pythagorean, says. Thus the divine prophet **Orpheus** says: 

"Jupiter is first, Jupiter is last, Jupiter is the head, Jupiter the middle. All things are born from Jupiter. Jupiter is the foundation of the earth and the starry heaven. Jupiter came forth as the male, Jupiter the incorruptible bride. Jupiter is the spirit and the form of all things. Jupiter is the root of the sea, Jupiter is the unwearied..."

# BOOK I VI

...the movement of fire: Jupiter, the Sun, and the Moon. Jupiter is the king and prince of all, hiding his light; then, through the work of his thoughts, he sends it forth again from his nourishing heart. From this, it is understood that Jupiter, infused into all bodies, contains and nourishes all things. Thus, it is not without merit that it was said: **Jupiter is whatever you see, whatever you are moved by** <note>original: "Iupiter est quodcunque vides quodcunque moveris." A famous quote from the Roman poet Lucan, used here by Ficino to illustrate the Neoplatonic idea of God's omnipresence in the universe.</note>. Following these are the remaining types of divine madness, which he <note>Plato</note> divides into two parts: one concerning the **mysteries** <term>mysteries</term> <note>Sacred rites or hidden religious truths revealed only to initiates.</note>, and the other concerning the outcome of future events, which he calls **prophecy** <term>vaticinium</term>. 

He defines the first madness as a more vehement stirring of the soul in performing those things that pertain to the worship of the gods, religion, expiation, and sacred ceremonies. However, he calls that affection of the mind which falsely imitates this kind of madness **superstition**. The final nature of madness, in which he places prophecy, he considers to be nothing other than a foreknowledge inspired by divine breath. We call this, with a more specific term, **divination** and **prophecy**. If the soul burns more sharply within that very divination, he calls it madness, for then the mind is drawn away from the body and stirred by divine instinct. However, if someone foresees the future through human skill and shrewdness rather than divine infusion, he judges that such a foreknowledge should be called **providence** or **conjecture**. 

From all this, it is now clear that there are four types of divine madness: **Love, Poetry, the Mysteries, and Prophecy**. That other common and utterly insane love falsely imitates divine love; a lighter music (as we said) imitates poetry; superstition imitates the mysteries; and conjecture imitates divination. In **Plato**, Socrates attributes the first madness to **Venus**, the second to the **Muses**, the third to **Dionysus**, and the last to **Apollo**. 

Furthermore, I chose to be longer in describing that madness which pertains to divine love and poetry for two reasons: because I recognized that you are vehemently affected by both, and so that you may remember that the things written by you do not proceed from yourself, but from **Jupiter** and the **Muses**, by whose spirit and divinity you are filled. Therefore, O my guest, you will act justly and piously—as I believe you have done until now—if you recognize that neither you nor any other man is the author and principle of the greatest and best things, but rather the immortal God. Farewell, and be persuaded that nothing is dearer to me than you. 

From Figline. 
December, 1457. <note>original: "Klis. D. M.cccclvii" – referring to the Kalends of December, 1457.</note>

### On divination and the divinity of the soul.

Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to his fellow philosopher, Matteo Corsini. Greetings. He says:

<margin>a</margin> My mother Alexandra was born to her father Giovanni and her mother Angela. <note>Alexandra was Ficino's mother; Giovanni was from the town of Montevarchi, and Angela was from Florence.</note> This Angela wrote to Giovanni and Alexandra saying she was doing well and would return the following day. After they had read the letters and night had fallen, both saw Angela at the same hour while they slept. She appeared to Alexandra in the entryway of the house; and when the daughter congratulated her mother as if she were returning, the mother, evading her daughter's embrace, said: "Farewell, and see to it that the priests pray to God for me." To Giovanni, however, she said: "Oh, how much I grieve for your fortune, my Giovanni! Farewell, and command that prayers be offered to God for me." Suddenly, both were awakened by these visions and cried out, judging her to be dead. They sent word to Florence, and it was reported back that she had departed from this life that very night. You may marvel at these things, Corsini.

Hear also another thing equally marvelous: my mother handed over her son, immediately after he was born, to a rural nurse. On the seventeenth day thereafter, while sleeping at midday, she seemed to herself to be weighed down by a great anxiety of the heart, and to be comforted by her own mother, who had died long ago. Her mother said: "Do not be distressed, daughter." The following day, the country folk brought her son back to her, who had been suffocated by the nurse. I pass over how, while dreaming, she foresaw the future fall from a horse of her husband Ficino the physician, including the place where he was to fall and every detail. I pass over many other things as well; let it suffice for the present to have recounted those two instances above.

From these, two things especially seem to be confirmed: one, namely, that the souls of men—which on account of a balanced temperament, purity of life, and the abstraction of sleep are in a way separated from the body—**divine** <term>divination</term> <note>The ability to foresee the future or perceive hidden truths through spiritual or divine influence.</note> very many things, as they are divine by their very nature; and when they return into themselves, they exercise their own **divinity** <term>divinity of the soul</term> <note>The Neoplatonic belief that the human soul contains a spark of the divine and can act independently of the body.</note>. The other is that the souls of the deceased, once released from the chains of the body, care not a little for our affairs and human concerns. This is what Hesiod sang, and what our Plato confirmed in the *Laws*. All antiquity used to call these spirits **heroes** <term>heroes</term> <note>In this context, "heroes" refers to semi-divine beings or elevated souls that mediate between the divine realm and the human world.</note>. Farewell.

### A way of praising without flattery.

Marsilio Ficino to Francesco da Castiglione <note>original: "Francisco Castiliolonensi," a priest and Greek scholar who was a close associate of the Medici and Ficino.</note>, the theologian. Hearty greetings.

<margin>1</margin> I have read your expositions concerning the **mysteries** of the prophet David. I desire to exclaim, Francesco: just as God found David to be a man after His own heart, so have I found you to have found David to be a man after your own heart. But where a suspicion of flattery might be imagined, it is better to remain silent than to explain. Give my greetings to Giorgio Antonio Vespucci <note>The uncle of Amerigo Vespucci and a learned canon of the Florence Cathedral.</note>, a man distinguished for his kindness and learning. Farewell.

<meta>Continuity: This page follows a series of letters regarding the nature of the soul and the divine. ### The utility of the solitary life.

Marsilio Ficino to his fellow priest, Gregorio Epiphanio. Greetings. <note>original: "S. D." stands for "Salutem Dicit," a standard greeting meaning "sends greetings."</note>
God is stable unity and a unique state of being. These matters are subtly debated by our Platonists, as you well know. Whoever, therefore, wishes to reach God should avoid multiplicity and movement to the best of their ability. Let us, then, my Gregorio, retreat into a single and stable watchtower of the mind. There, as Plato says, an invisible light will immediately shine upon us. Truly, so that we may more conveniently achieve and continue this in these times, I have decided to dwell for a while at that Mount Vecchio <note>original: "montē uecbium," referring to the Montevecchio estate</note> given to me by the Great Cosimo <note>Cosimo de' Medici (1389–1464), the wealthy banker and patron who founded the Platonic Academy in Florence</note>. You shall be there with me. You have heard that proverb: the possession of no good thing is pleasant without a companion. For my part, I do not know what companion I could have who would be more pleasant than you in these times. Farewell, and fly to us.

### On modesty in writing.

Bessarion, Cardinal of Sabina <note>Basilios Bessarion (1403–1472), a Greek scholar and Roman Catholic cardinal who was instrumental in bringing Greek philosophy to Italy</note>, to the Platonist Marsilio Ficino. Greetings.
Observe, learned man and our friend, our work labored over in previous letters and recently published. We promised to send to you our *In Defense of Plato* <note>original: "In defensionem Platonis," referring to Bessarion's famous work "In Calumniatorem Platonis," written to defend Plato against the attacks of George of Trebizond</note>, both on account of your own genius and your exceptional study of Platonic doctrine, and so that you may perceive and read what we have drawn from that fountain. If anything of eloquence or knowledge of the liberal arts has shone forth in this industry of ours—if we have ever been anything—we willingly allow and desire it to be thought that we either received it all from him <term>Plato</term> or that he himself supplied it while defending himself. For it seems to pertain not a little to his praise that he pleaded his cause by his own strength and his own greatness. He did not lack the help of others; he left for his advocate only the space for a voice and for devotion. We have given this book to you through those who handle their affairs here from the house of the Medici <note>original: "ex medicis," a play on words referring to the Medici family as the "physicians" who managed the delivery</note>. By sending it, we believe we have satisfied our promise and your own studies and spirit toward Plato. Farewell. Let us know if you have received the book. From the City <note>Rome</note>, on the 13th of September, 1469.

### In praise of the Platonic interpreters.

Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Bessarion, the Greek Cardinal of Sabina. Greetings.
Our Plato, venerable father, as you well know, disputed subtly and at length about beauty in the *Phaedrus*. He called the beauty of the soul—which is wisdom—a most precious gold granted by God. This gold, granted to Plato by God, shone most clearly in the Platonic breast, as if in the purest of places. However, although he was most brilliant in words and letters, the gold turned out to be somewhat obscure, wrapped in the darker thoughts of the mind. Overgrown, as it were, by a certain earthy covering, it remained hidden from those men who did not possess lynx-like eyes <note>A common Renaissance metaphor for exceptionally sharp or penetrating vision</note>. For this reason, some rather petty seekers of glory, deceived by the outer crust because they could not penetrate to the inner depths, used to despise the hidden treasure. But that gold was cast into the workshop first of Plotinus, then of Porphyry, then of Iamblichus, and finally of Proclus <note>These were the primary Neoplatonic philosophers who interpreted and expanded upon Plato's original works in late antiquity</note>, where it was tested by the most exquisite fire and the dross was shaken away—

It highlights the intellectual network of the Medici circle and the Renaissance effort to "refine" and interpret ancient Greek wisdom.</summary>

...it shone out to such an extent that it filled the whole world with a wonderful brilliance. Indeed, certain owls or eagle-owls <note>original: "noctue siue bubones," birds that see in the dark but are blinded by the sun, here symbolizing critics of Plato</note> were apparently so offended by such great rays that they began not only to despise that sacred treasure of our Plato—as some once did—but, oh the shame! <note>original: "proh nefas"</note>, they began to condemn it, which was a much worse error than the first. But Bessarion <note>Cardinal Basilios Bessarion (1403–1472), the Greek scholar who defended Plato against Aristotelian critics</note>, the light of the Academy, immediately applied a most healthy remedy to their dull and dim eyes, so that this gold might be not only pure and brilliant, but also manageable for the hands and harmless to the eyes. Plato prophesied to King Dionysius that this time would come after many centuries, when the mysteries of theology would be purged like gold in fire through the most exact discussion. Those centuries have come, Bessarion; those times are now here, in which let the spirit of Plato rejoice, and let all of us, his family, be greatly glad. Farewell.

---

### An exhortation to knowledge.
### Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Antonio Pacini. <note>original: "S. D." stands for "Salutem Dicit," a standard greeting</note>

<margin>l</margin>Lorenzo de' Medici <note>The de facto ruler of Florence and Ficino's patron</note> praises two things in you above all others: your magnificence and your sharp intelligence. I praise them too; but Antonio, while you can compare yourself to others in the use of magnificence, in the exercise of sharp intelligence you must compare yourself to yourself. If you devote as much study to learning as you have long indulged in generosity, I do not doubt you will soon be the most learned of all, just as you are now the most magnificent of all. Come, I pray, my sweetest Antonio, commend yourself to yourself just as you have others commended to you. Our Lorenzo says you are not only magnificent toward the learned, but also abundantly learned yourself. I believe it and I am glad. But you will not have satisfied me until you excel as much in knowledge as you do in greatness of soul. If the most erudite men please you above all, see to it that you please yourself above others. What then? Order prevails most in all things—rather, it is everything. I pray you, set aside four hours daily for study; give the remaining hours to your friends as you please. Farewell. But do you wish to fare well? Speak well and learn today, I pray. He who learns tomorrow never learns. November 8, 1473.

---

### Consolation on someone's death.
### Marsilio Ficino sends consolation to Sigismondo della Stufa.

<margin>i</margin>That which is greatest within us is truly what each of us is; that which remains always the same is what we ourselves grasp. Certainly, the soul is the man himself; the body is but the man's shadow. Anyone so delirious as to think a man's shadow is the man himself will, like Narcissus, dissolve miserably into tears. You will cease to weep, Sigismondo, when you stop seeking your Albiera Albizzi <note>Albiera degli Albizzi (1454–1473), a celebrated Florentine beauty whose early death prompted many elegies</note> in her dark shadow, and begin to follow her into her own white light. For then you will find her as much more beautiful than you were accustomed to, as she is further removed from the deformed shadow. Retreat into your own soul, I pray. There you will possess her most beautiful soul, so dear to you. Indeed, from your own soul, betake yourself into God. There you will contemplate the most beautiful Idea <note>Ficino uses "Idea" in the Platonic sense: the perfect, divine blueprint of a person</note> according to which the divine craftsman had created your Albiera. And as much more beautiful as she is in the form of the Creator than in herself, so much more blessedly will you embrace her there. Farewell. August 1, 1474. Florence.

### In praise of brevity.

Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Angelo Poliziano, the Homeric poet.
<margin>c</margin>Certain letters, as you say, are being circulated in my name that are, as it were, Aristippian <note>Referring to Aristippus of Cyrene, a philosopher who emphasized sensory pleasure; Ficino is distancing himself from hedonism</note> and in some part Lucretian <note>Referring to the Roman poet Lucretius, whose Epicurean views were often seen as materialistic or anti-religious</note> rather than Platonic. If they are mine, Angelo, they are not of that sort. If they are of that sort, they are certainly not mine, but were forged by my detractors. For from my tender years, I have followed the divine Plato, which no one is ignorant of. But you will easily distinguish our writings from those of others by this sign: in my letters, some sentiment is always present—by the strength of character, or morals, or nature—or it is theological. If there is sometimes something of an amatory nature within them, it is truly Platonic and honorable, not Aristippian and lewd; and if there are praises, they are true and such that they may exhort and admonish rather than flatter. Almost no words are superfluous; for I determined from the beginning of my studies to always write as briefly as possible. For in such great brevity of time, to speak superfluously is the mark of a philologist <note>Here used in the sense of one who loves talk or grammar for its own sake</note> rather than a philosopher. And since there are very few people to whom many things are known, those who speak much often speak either falsehoods or superfluities, or both. All these things are foreign to the dignity of a man and most foreign to the profession of a philosopher. Farewell.

---

### How useful it is to support the learned.

Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to the magnanimous man, Lorenzo de' Medici.
<margin>d</margin>Almost all other wealthy men nourish the ministers of their pleasures; you nourish the priests of the Muses. I pray you continue, my Lorenzo. For those others will turn out to be the slaves of pleasures, but you, truly, are the delight of the Muses. Homer, the supreme priest of the Muses, has come into Italy under your leadership. And he who until now was a wandering beggar has at last found a sweet lodging open to him at your house. You nourish in your home that Homeric youth, Angelo Poliziano, so that he may express the Greek persona of Homer in Latin colors. Indeed, he expresses it now; and what is wonderful in such a tender age, he expresses it in such a way that unless one knew Homer had been Greek, one would doubt which of the two was the natural Homer and which the painted one. Continue to delight in these "painters," Medici, as you have begun. For other painters decorate their pictures for a time; these, however, illuminate the inhabitants for eternity. Farewell.

---

### The praise of the craftsman comes not from words but from the work.

Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Lorenzo and Giuliano de' Medici.
<margin>a</margin>Receive with a joyful spirit, Medici, the poem of Naldo of Florence <note>Naldo Naldi (1436–1513), a humanist poet and friend of Ficino</note> and the declamations of Benedetto Coluccio of Pistoia <note>Benedetto Coluccio (1438–1505), a noted orator and teacher</note>. The former is the delight of Phoebus <note>Apollo, god of poetry</note>; the latter is the companion of Mercury <note>God of eloquence and rhetoric</note>. I do not care to praise them sparingly, since they seem to be worthy of praise beyond measure; yet it is not permitted for me to praise them much, lest by praising my own favored ones I should seem to be extolling myself. I shall therefore remain silent. Examine the virtues of these painters <note>Ficino frequently uses the metaphor of "painting" to describe the art of writing or composing poetry</note> in the panels yourselves. The pictures will speak. When a painter speaks [of himself], he speaks poorly. When the picture speaks, it speaks well. Vain is the craftsman who expects honor from another rather than from the work itself; the virtue of the work does not depend on the judge, but the work commends the artist to the judge. Farewell.

### On the civil, purgative, and exemplary virtues of the purified soul.
**Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Francesco Lapacino and Melchior Cresci.**

<margin>i</margin>Those who seek God do so by the straightest path: first, through the **civil virtues**, they prune away the excessively flourishing passions of the soul; then, through the **purgative virtues**, they cut them back almost to the quick; thirdly, through the **virtues of the already purified soul**, they root them out with all their might. Once these passions have been eradicated as far as is humanly possible, they are finally shaped by the **exemplary virtues** which reside in God. For these three types of virtues are certain steps by which we gradually approach the divine virtues. Moreover, every natural movement is capable of reaching its end at some point, and every preparation naturally ordered toward a form is eventually able to attain that form itself. <note>Ficino is describing the Neoplatonic hierarchy of virtue: 1. Civil (social/moral behavior), 2. Purgative (cleansing the soul from the body), 3. Purified (the state of the soul after cleansing), and 4. Exemplary (the divine archetypes of virtue in God).</note>

---

### On the wise and happy man.
**Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to his companion Antonio Seraphico of San Miniato.**

<margin>f</margin>I consider that man wise and happy who, since he depends on God alone, lives joyfully in the midst of calamities. He is one whom fear does not deprive of spirit, nor pain torture, nor pleasure corrupt, nor lust inflame. He is the one who gathers soft and beautiful flowers from among the thickest thorns; who digs out and uncovers pearls from the dung; who sees in the deepest darkness; who, though weighed down by shackles and bound by chains, runs about as if free and unhindered. He is one, finally, upon whom the heavenly spirit has breathed. Therefore, continue as you have begun to imitate Pythagoras, Socrates, and Plato, who philosophized no less by acting than by disputing, even when fortune was unwilling. <margin>Prudence<br/>Justice<br/>Fortitude<br/>Temperance</margin> <note>The margin notes list the four cardinal virtues, suggesting the "acting" Ficino refers to is the practice of these virtues.</note> They cherished with their whole heart that philosophy which many others only hold on their tongues. It is in vain that a man is wise, O Seraphico, if he is not wise for his own benefit. <note>original: "Frustra sapit... qui non sibi ipse sapit." A common Latin proverb suggesting that knowledge is useless if it does not improve the life of the one who possesses it.</note> Farewell, and persevere in your ways.

---

### It is better to write good things than many things.
**Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Angelo Poliziano, the Homeric poet.**

<margin>q</margin>Why do you so often ask for the titles of my books, Angelo? Is it perhaps so that you may praise me in your poems? Yet praise lies not in the number but in the selection; the "good" lies not in quantity but in quality. Or is it rather so that you may have everything of mine with you? Since among friends all things are common, receive what you asked for, however it may be. From the Greek language into Latin, I have translated: the physical and theological elements of **Proclus the Platonist**; four books of **Iamblichus of Chalcis** on the Pythagorean sect; the mathematics of **Theon of Smyrna**; the Platonic definitions of **Speusippus**; the Platonic epitome of **Alcinous**; the book of **Xenocrates** on the consolation of death; the *Golden Verses* and *Symbols* of **Pythagoras**; the book of **Hermes Trismegistus** on the power and wisdom of God; and all the books of **Plato**. I have also composed: a commentary on the **Gospels**; a short commentary on Plato’s ***Phaedrus***; a commentary on Plato’s ***Philebus*** regarding the highest good; a commentary on Plato’s ***Symposium*** regarding love; a work on **physiognomy** <note>The study of a person's character or fortune from their outward appearance, especially the face.</note>; the *Declarations of Platonic Discipline* addressed to Cristoforo Landino (which I later revised); and a compendium on the opinions of the philosophers concerning God and the soul...

## Exhortation to Knowledge.
### Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to Niccolò Albitii:

<margin>2</margin> You have heard that proverb, my Niccolò: "nothing is sweeter than profit." But who among men truly makes a profit? It is he who obtains that which is destined to be his own. What we know is truly our own; all other things belong to fortune. Let little men envy the wealthy whose treasure chests are rich but whose souls are not. You, however, should emulate learned and good men, whose minds are like God’s. Admonish your fellow students to beware of **Scylla and Charybdis** <note>In Greek mythology, two sea monsters on opposite sides of a narrow strait; here used to represent the twin dangers of vice and ignorance.</note>—that is, the allurements of pleasures and the pestilential inflammations of the mind of one who merely opines rather than truly knows. Let them remember that the highest pleasure for them will one day be that which is perceived in the highest part of the soul, drawn from the supreme treasury of Truth itself, once they have set aside the shadows of empty pleasures for the sake of knowledge.

The tree of knowledge—even if its roots seem somewhat bitter—nevertheless bears the sweetest fruits. Remember, besides, that what is never enough can never be done too much. He has not yet learned enough who still doubts anything. Yet we doubt as long as we live. Therefore, we must continue to learn as long as we must live; we must imitate that wise man **Solon**, who even while dying strove to learn something. He was one who was nourished by the food of truth, and for him, dying was nothing other than coming to life again. He who feeds on immortal nourishment can never die.

**Socrates** was first called the wisest of all by Apollo <note>Referring to the Oracle of Delphi's pronouncement.</note> only when he first began to proclaim to the common people that "he knew nothing." **Pythagoras** commanded his disciples to look at themselves in a mirror not by the light of a lamp, but by the light of the sun. For what is the spark of a lamp but a mind as yet little educated? And what is the light of the sun but a mind that is most highly educated? Therefore, when someone desires to behold the form of his own soul, let him compare himself not with the unlearned, but rather with the most learned; for thus he will more clearly discern how much he has gained and how much remains to be done. 

In feeding the soul, we ought to imitate gluttons and misers, who always focus their minds on what is left over rather than what has been consumed. What more? The teacher of life <note>Jesus Christ; reference to Luke 9:62.</note> says: "That plowman is not worthy of reward who turns himself backward." You have heard also that she <note>Lot's wife (Genesis 19:26), who turned into a pillar of salt for looking back at Sodom.</note> for this very reason was turned from a living being into a statue. You have heard again that **Orpheus** lost **Eurydice**—that is, the depth of judgment—at the moment he looked back. A hunter is lazy and vain who goes backward rather than forward. Farewell.

BOOK I.

### Invitation to write.

**Lorenzo de' Medici sends many greetings to Marsilio Ficino the Platonist.**
<note>original: "S.D."; abbreviation for *Salutem Dicit*, a standard Latin greeting meaning "he says health" or "sends greetings."</note>

When I returned here from there, my most delightful Marsilio, I discussed it with you and obtained your promise that we would not have to miss your letters for any longer during our absence. You undertook to do this; however, although four days have already passed since my departure and your letters have not yet been delivered—even though many letters from other friends and close associates have reached us—I both wonder at and grieve over your slowness in writing. For I truly thought that if equal goodwill flourished in both of us, an equal zeal for writing—which is the duty of love—would not be lacking.

I first began to make an excuse for you to myself, and I said to myself on your behalf: "Perhaps the studies of philosophy, which demand the whole and complete man, are the reason why Marsilio's letters are not delivered to us." Our almost incredible love for you caused me to make the most honorable excuse possible on your behalf. This excuse had such weight with me that the wait of a few hours did not seem at all difficult. But when I saw that what I thought should be measured in hours had to be measured in several days, no room was left for excuse. 

And I, who had taken up the care of your defense, began to think with all my soul of the ways in which I might accuse you, as many came to mind. I find so many types of offenses against you that even if you were to obtain Demosthenes <note>The most famous orator of ancient Greece (384–322 BCE).</note> and our Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman statesman whose letters and oratory were the gold standard for Renaissance humanists.</note> as patrons for your cause, I hold it for certain that you would still be found guilty. If you do not repent of your deed—for I desire no other sign of repentance than your letters—know that you will undergo the judgment of our shared love. For Love commands you to plead your case before such a judge, and we find none who could be fairer or more just, or who could be a truer witness to our soul. 

He [Love] grants you a space of only three days for writing. Once these have passed, he promises you will be found guilty unless you have written. But you will say: "What shall I write to Lorenzo? I have nothing about the republic, nothing about domestic matters." I expect neither from you. Since you neglect both in yourself, I know you are no more curious about other people's affairs than your own. What, then, should you write? Whatever comes into your mind. Nothing proceeds from you that is not good; you think nothing that is not right; therefore, nothing can be written by you that is not useful and pleasant to us. 

And what makes me desire your letters beyond measure is this: that in your letters, charm <term>charm: (Latin: *lepos*) - a quality of wit and elegance highly prized by Renaissance humanists.</term> is so mixed with gravity that if they are considered for their charm, everything is full of charm; if for their gravity, they seem so weighty that nothing could surpass them. Therefore, as soon as the opportunity for writing is given to you, I ask that you do not delay any longer. Nor should you allow us to long for your letters for so long. Farewell, at Pisa.

->Love Letters<-

### Lorenzo de' Medici to Marsilio Ficino the Platonist, Greetings.

<margin>c</margin>I believe now, most learned Marsilio, that the opinion of Plotinus <note>Plotinus was the 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism, whose works Ficino translated.</note> regarding the soul is true—if I remember correctly—which you placed in your book on theology: <note>Refers to Ficino's masterpiece, the *Platonic Theology*.</note> namely, that our souls are everywhere at the same time. For what is proved by many arguments in that book is now more clearly established by the reality itself. Indeed, I had scarcely sealed another letter to you when your most longed-for letter was delivered to me; its sweetness made me realize how wonderfully I had missed you. I believe, in fact, that you, though absent, both read my letter and perceived from where you are my accusation of your slowness in writing; and being warned by this, you did not delay any longer in sending a letter to us. But whatever the case may be, it does not please me now to inquire into the causes of the letters; it is enough for me to have received them, than which nothing is more pleasing or more delightful to me. I see—what was already clear to me before—that nothing is done by you rashly. For the longer expectation made the sweetness itself somehow sweeter, as usually happens to those who are very thirsty. As I read your letter, I find nothing that is not "Marsilian" <note>characteristic of Ficino’s style</note>—if those expressions of gratitude were removed from the letter. For this kind of thanks does not seem to suit either our friendship or a man who has so totally given himself to me that he has left nothing of himself for himself. Even if you were of such a great physical size as that Saint Christopher you mention is painted, there is nothing left of you that is not mine. So you once willed it. So it once pleased you. I truly have both accepted such a noble gift with a willing mind and, having accepted it, I rejoice and congratulate myself. Now, therefore, you do not belong to Marsilio, but to your Lorenzo—no less yours than your own. In which matter, if you wish yourself to be returned to you, know that it will be on this condition: that you can have no account of yourself without having an equal account of me at the same time. For "those whom immortal God has joined, let no man separate." <note>original: "Quos enim immortalis deus coniunxit homo non separet," quoting Matthew 19:6.</note> You, therefore—to return to the matter of thanks—do not use this kind of writing with me anymore. For if the thanks you give are not yours...

->God, not man, is the author of wonders.<-

### Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to the high-minded Lorenzo de' Medici.

<margin>q</margin>What I should do in your presence I do not know, Lorenzo. Your marvelous letters compel me to wonder in a marvelous way; yet my philosopher’s modesty forbids me to cry out. Your singular humanity and magnificence urge me to give innumerable thanks, but your letter again dissuades me. Allow me at least, I pray, my Lorenzo, to give thanks to the highest God, who has established in our times, in a fortunate citizen, the humblest affection alongside an exalted mind; in a private youth, prudence with power; in a powerful man, restraint with liberty; and in the busiest man, wisdom joined with eloquence. These are great things in you, Lorenzo; without doubt, they are great. And lest anyone should suspect the vice of flattery—which ought to be most foreign to a man who is both a philosopher and a very dear friend—I have said these "great" things are *in* you, not *from* you. For only Almighty God performs wonders. You are an instrument of God, O good man; I know well what I am saying: you are fit for the performance of magnificent things. You will therefore happily carry out wonders for as long as you obey the divine Artisan. Believe me, you will obey Him perfectly if you pray to Him often, so that He may show you the way in which you are to obey. He will certainly show the one who asks; He who even before you ask, stimulates you to ask, and shows you both what and in what manner you are to ask. Farewell happily, hope of our fatherland; but before I make an end, I beseech you, my Lorenzo, both for the sake of the Academy which flourishes through you <note>The "Platonic Academy" of Florence, an informal circle of scholars supported by the Medici.</note>, and for this your fatherland—the land which is dear to you above all others—that you take care of your good health. For unless you are well, I do not think either the Academy or the fatherland can be well in these times. January 21, 1473. Florence.

### Wonderful praises of Lorenzo de' Medici.

### Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to the true man, Niccolò Michelozzi. <note>Niccolò Michelozzi (1447–1527) was the dedicated secretary to Lorenzo de' Medici and a close associate of the humanists.</note>

<margin>o</margin>How difficult it is, my Niccolò, oh how difficult it is now not to be struck by envy. Perhaps, Niccolò, if Lorenzo’s qualities were not also mine, I would not be able to avoid envying so many and such mature virtues in a young man. Tell me, friend, I ask: who speaks more elegantly? Who proves a point more sharply? Who soothes more sweetly? Who rouses more vehemently? You poets have long since yielded to the Laurel <note>original: "lauro," a pun on Lorenzo's name (*Laurentius*) and the laurel wreath of poets.</note>; you orators have just now yielded; and now, let us philosophers yield. By Jupiter! Idle veterans are surpassed so quickly, so easily, and so greatly by that most busy young recruit. If others are envious of what belongs to another, let them burst with consuming jealousy. I, for my part, marvelously rejoice in and enjoy what is mine: for Lorenzo is mine because of his incredible kindness...
