->Letters on Friendship<-

### Lorenzo de' Medici sends many greetings to Marsilio Ficino, the Platonic philosopher.

<margin>o</margin>
My judgment of you was false, and that common proverb is true: that distance of places, just as it separates us from the eyes, so it separates us from the thoughts of friends. But who would have believed this? I myself barely believe it, even though I have seen it for myself. I sent two letters to you. You sent barely one to us, and it was of so few words that if you were to remove the opening greeting and the final note of the place and date, almost nothing would be left. Perhaps it is not fitting for a philosopher to be talkative; yet it is also not fitting to be mute. Indeed, Terence <note>Publius Terentius Afer, a Roman playwright.</note> teaches us what he is said to have received from the Greeks: "nothing in excess" <note>original: "ne quid nimis," a famous ancient Greek aphorism translated into Latin.</note>. But even from these circumstances, I see what the cause is for why I am absent from your thoughts. Since you always have before your eyes Saint Christopher, to whom your house is dedicated <note>Ficino's home was near the church of San Cristoforo a Novoli.</note>, his body is of such great size that it completely takes away your view of all other things. And in a way, he creates a kind of eclipse between you and us. I wonder at this, and yet I have finally found the words with which to accuse you. For there is no word so harsh or so insulting that your "Marsilian silence" is not much worse, by which you have failed both your promise and our friendship. I grieve not a little that you have broken your word and brought such an injury to our friendship. But what is even more troublesome to me is this: while you have frustrated our love, you have so alienated us from the goodwill of other men that no one remains whom I seem able to trust hereafter. For nothing seemed so perfect, so constant, and so true as our friendship, which had grown so much through your virtue and the length of time that if it has somehow failed, none remains in which we can safely trust. Therefore, know that we are wonderfully angry with you. Yet not so angry that if a very pleasant letter...

### On Matters of Love: How each person is to be loved and how they should be praised.

Marsilio Ficino to the Magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, sends greetings.

<margin>q</margin>That you love me, Lorenzo, I have known for a long time by many very clear proofs. That you love <note>original: "ames"; Ficino distinguishes between "diligere" (to esteem/value) and "amare" (to love passionately).</note> me has recently been shown by this one thing above all: that like a jealous lover, you grow slightly angry over the slightest and most false little offenses. Be angry as you please; be angry like a jealous lover; as long as you meanwhile grow warm with love. The fire of anger and of love is similar. For I, when I am slightly angry with you—which I often do—am then burning most of all with the fire of love. You also burn no small amount; I know what I am talking about. But if we ever seem to grow lukewarm, then even this lukewarmness of ours burns more fervently than the heat of others, and our hatred—by Jove!—is more loving and lovable than the love of others. Behold now, my Lorenzo, this anger of yours seems gentler to me than the mildness of others; this bite of yours is sweeter than a kiss. Oh, how sweetly you bite! How sharply you kiss! You mix a wonderful sweetness with bitterness, and bitterness with sweetness, as nature is accustomed to do in the most pleasant flavors. And as often as your bitterness turns more sour, it gives off a scent sweeter than sweetness itself, like Malmsey vinegar <term>acetum maluaticum: A high-quality aromatic vinegar made from Malvasia wine</term>. But what do you accuse me of, you sharp accuser, you most sharp lover? Brevity? But you are the cause. For that I am brief is due to your business. That I seem very brief to you is caused by the magnitude of your love toward me. You accuse me of silence, suspecting it comes from forgetfulness, and forgetfulness from absence. You ought to remember that Marsilio is not absent from there if Lorenzo is not absent, in whom Marsilio dwells. If the soul is everywhere at the same time? Which you yourself confirmed in your letter the other day. What then does Saint Christopher <note>Ficino is punning on the name of their mutual friend, the scholar Cristoforo Landino</note> hinder me from seeing you? Especially since he is "diaphanous" and transparent; and in Christopher himself I see Lorenzo, since through Lorenzo himself I seem to see and embrace Christopher. Finally, do you want me to tell the truth? It is not the opposition of Christopher that causes an eclipse through which I might go blind or fall silent. On the contrary, you compel me to grow dark, to be stunned, and to fall completely silent by your flashing and your thunder. Wicked youth! Ah, you rejoice too much in a victory, however honorable it may be. What more is left for you or for the rest? For you, indeed, it is to conquer yourself. For the others, it is to suffer being conquered with a calm mind. I certainly—to speak of myself first—rejoice in being surpassed by you almost as much as you yourself rejoice in surpassing me and the others. But what shall I say of the others? The morning sun gathers the mists. The midday sun scatters them. Youthful virtue excites envy; mature virtue calms it. He finally tames spite who has first conquered all opinion. You have now turned almost all envy into admiration. Many praise you openly who until now were envious. But although almost no one lies when praising Lorenzo, nevertheless to no one except the Platonists...

BOOK I

...rightly praise. The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, who emphasized observation and systematic study.</note>, seeing Lorenzo professing each subject so successfully, praise him in all things. The Platonists, on the other hand, praise everything in him. Truly, when they consider how suddenly he comes forth as a master of every art, they believe these arts were not sought through labor, but were both provided by nature and infused by God. I, therefore, esteem <note>original: "diligo"; to value or hold dear.</note> your person in me, and love <note>original: "amo"; to love passionately.</note> my person in you. I praise you in art. I approve of art in you. In nature, I honor you. I admire nature in you. I worship you through God. I venerate God through you. To God alone, therefore, be all glory from all people, from age unto age. Farewell.

### A playful invitation to Giovanni to return, through pretense.
->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his Unique Friend.<-

I had decided late last night to write to you this morning: "Return, hero. Hurry, I beg you; fly here, I implore you." But then, considering more maturely, it seemed better to hide this desire of mine. For it would be that you return more quickly if you thought I were a little angry. Behold, I am a little angry! What then? Will indignation move him whom love did not move? I think not. Therefore, I know not where to turn: to prayers, or to quarrels? But now I have found where to take refuge. I will trust in your heroic heart <note>Giovanni Cavalcanti (1444–1509) was Ficino’s beloved friend and patron; Ficino frequently refers to him as his "hero."</note> which is accustomed to run more rightly of its own accord than by the use of spurs. But in the meantime, how shall I restrain myself? Since I can hardly bear it for even a little while—O, you who are too forgetful of me! But I will hold back my reproaches; and lest it weary you to hear these same old songs too often, I shall move on to greater things. I shall write about public affairs. You ask what is being done in the city? Grave matters are being discussed—listen, but reveal it to no one. Many great citizens say: "O Marsilio, why are you so long alone in the city?" Because he wants me to walk alone now, he who never allows me to be alone. "Has he not returned yet?" Not yet. I have nothing else at hand to write to you. I have written to you of urban business; you write to me of rustic things. Alas, I have erred: I do not want you to write, but to speak. If we talk, my hero, we speak of the same things; while we write, we write of different things. I write of memory; Giovanni writes of forgetfulness. But do not say that. My Giovanni has not forgotten me, nor himself. Indeed, he comes now, having yielded to me; behold, he comes! Run to meet him, my fortunate feet. Receive him, happy arms <note>The OCR "vltiæ" is likely a misreading of "ulnae" (arms/embrace).</note>.

### A genial letter concerning heroes.
->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his Unique Friend.<-

I received a letter from Carlo Marsuppini <note>A Florentine humanist and diplomat.</note>. When I first set out to reply to it, and wished to write the heading "Marsilio to Carlo," my guardian spirit <note>original: "genius"; in the Platonic tradition, a personal spirit that guides an individual's destiny and creative impulses.</note> suddenly bent my pen so that I wrote "to Giovanni" instead of "to Carlo." Accept, therefore, this "genial" letter <note>Ficino plays on the word "genialis," meaning both "pleasant/festive" and "pertaining to one's genius/guiding spirit."</note>. God thought it a sin for me, while absent, to write to anyone before writing to my hero. I believe the gods favor heroes. Since, as Plato suggests, heroes are born from the love of the gods, I have experienced in reality that philosophers are reborn from the love of heroes. Farewell. 1 May 1473.

### That which is given freely is more pleasing than that which is owed.

## Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his Unique Friend.

<margin>n</margin>The hand cannot guide the pen unless the hand itself is moved by the soul. In these times, Marsilio could not write to the Hero <note>original: "Heroem"; Ficino often uses elevated, quasi-mythological titles for his close circle.</note> unless he were first invited by the Hero. But one thing troubles me above all others: you write to me because you promised to do so. Therefore, I credit this to a bargain rather than to love. I ask for letters of love, not of trade. Are you mine only by contract? Since I am yours, I want you to be mine through love. Farewell. January 5, 1474.

### A provocation to write.

## Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his Unique Friend.

<margin>q</margin>Why have we been competing in silence for so long, my friend? In the end, what gain will go to the victor, and what loss to the defeated? Indeed, in this stubbornness of silence, I decided it was better to be defeated by you, so that I might be the victor in a contest of speaking. Thus, from now on, the first prize in keeping quiet is given to you; the first prize in speaking is given to me. Will you always need spurs in the race? Will you never run of your own accord? Why are you so harsh with me? Perhaps I seem to joke too sharply with you, my dear Giovanni. But you act most sharply; answer most sharply too, if answering pleases you; but if it pleases you less, remain sweetly silent. Be assured that beneath this sharpness of my words lies a heart-felt affection sweeter than honey. Farewell, and stay away only as long as your business requires. For it is enough for me when your business is being taken care of. October 7, at Careggi <note>The location of the Medici villa where Ficino did much of his work.</note>.

### That letters are necessary among friends.

## Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his Unique Friend.

<margin>q</margin>Since I thought you would return to Florence shortly, I sent you no letters, hoping soon to hear your actual voice and to speak back to you. But now this perpetual serenity of the sky—if I may call it so—threatens me with your longer delays in the Trebbian hills. But who would not be captured by the sweetness of Trebbia? Certainly Bacchus <note>The Roman god of wine, referring to the famous vineyards of the Trebbia region.</note> loves these hills. My Giovanni has been twice captured. This is certainly the reason why I have not written until now. But why do you write nothing? "I have nothing to write," you will say. Write at least that very thing—that you have nothing to say—although a friend is never lacking a subject for letters. For what is dearer to a friend than a friend's life? Therefore, one must often indicate, in turn, how one's health is. I cannot declare my health to you unless you first declare your own. Indeed, I am well if you are well; or rather, if I understand that you are well. Farewell, from Careggi. October 13.

### The loss of time is a living hell.

## Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his Unique Friend.

<margin>o</margin>The care of both my own and my father’s body <note>original: "paterni corporis"; likely referring to the physical health or medical needs of his father, Diotifeci d'Agnolo, who was a physician.</note> is a burden to me. Your absence is a burden. Both must be endured with a level mind, lest they become heavier through impatience. If you have any humanity, do not press me with a double load, nor burden me with a third weight on top. You burden me too much unless you send the books back to me. For the loss of time <note>original: "Temporis... iactura"</note> drives me to demand them more often. There is no loss more grievous than that of time. Alas, I demand more boldly things which perhaps I would not wish to receive. Whom I would truly wish to receive... <note>The sentence is interrupted by the page break.</note>

### Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his Unique Friend.

<margin>q</margin>
What then shall I do? Shall I write to you first? Or shall I wait for your letters? Indeed, since I usually never write to others unless provoked, I am nonetheless compelled to come to meet you and enter the contest first. It is no longer possible for you to allow these matters to remain silent. For you cannot remain silent without causing me to languish. An immoderate heat <note>original: "estus"; this could refer to physical summer heat or an emotional fervor.</note> has driven me to this, as you well know. An intolerable wind pulls me back toward that place, so much so that I can hardly contain myself today from flying immediately back to the city. Truly, you alone can hold me here for some few days with your letters. For while I am entirely focused on reading your letters, I feel neither the blasts of the winds nor do I fear the lightning and thunder. Thus it happens that words are able to calm the winds and drive away the storms. Greet your Ugolino Verino <note>A contemporary humanist poet and friend of Ficino.</note>, a priest of the Muses. Farewell. August 30, 1473. From Careggi <note>original: "Marciniani"; the site of the Medici villa where Ficino often stayed.</note>.

->No one should be slandered because God takes vengeance.<-

### Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his Unique Friend.

<margin>b</margin>
Homer is said to have been deprived of his eyes because of his disparagement of the divine Helen; because he never recognized that he had erred, it is said he never saw again. For the same reason, Stesichorus <note>A Greek lyric poet who, according to legend, was blinded for insulting Helen of Troy in his poetry.</note>, having lost his sight, understood his error. Hence he sang a "palinode" <term>palinodia: a poem or song retracting a previous statement</term>—that is, a contrary song—saying: "That story was not true; you did not go upon the high-decked ships, nor did you reach the towers of Troy." Having said these things, he immediately recovered his lost sight. Furthermore, when Socrates had disparaged the god of Love, he was seized by a familiar spirit <note>original: "demone"; referring to Socrates' *daimonion*, a divine inner voice or guiding spirit.</note> while crossing the river Ilissus. Before any misfortune could occur, he purified himself and again praised the Love he had previously disparaged. Thus he escaped unharmed. So, Stesichorus was wiser than Homer, but Socrates was wiser than both.

Certainly, I have been more careless than Socrates; I hope I am not more unfortunate than Stesichorus. What is the point of this? Specifically, on the Nones <note>In the Roman calendar, the 5th or 7th day of the month.</note> of this month, I wrote a letter to you in the morning to reproach your long silence, in which I accused you of being untameable and nearly the hardest of all men. By evening, I was overcome by ill health, and I have not yet recovered. Therefore, fearing lest some misfortune hang over me because of my disparagement of the Hero <note>original: "heroem"; a term of endearment Ficino frequently uses for Cavalcanti.</note>, I have decided to write a palinode, however brief, for the sake of expiating my crime. I assert, therefore, not that the Hero is hard, but rather that I am soft, and that a constant man often seems fierce to a soft man. Let this be my palinode; let it be a song contrary to the previous one, and let it also be a contrary request. For I was asking that you send me the sharpest letters, if it pleased you, rather than none at all. Now, on the contrary, I ask for none rather than sharp ones; for my soul needs consolation, not goading. Farewell. Florence, October 15, 1468.

# BOOK VI

-> Man is the soul. The soul of the lover is in the beloved. <-

### Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his Unique Friend.

<margin>e</margin> I, Giovanni, have often sought myself. First, I touched my chest with my hands. Then, I often gazed at this face in the mirror; but I could never assert that I had touched myself there, nor seen myself here. For when I seek myself, I certainly do not seek anyone other than that very person who is seeking, where Marsilio is entirely the same as both the sought and the seeker. Who then seeks? He who desires to find. Who indeed desires this? He who judges that it must be sought. Who judges? The soul <note>original: "animus"; in Ficino's thought, the *animus* is the rational part of the human spirit that constitutes our true identity.</note> alone judges. Therefore, I seek the soul alone when I seek myself, inasmuch as I myself am only the soul. I am certain that this soul can be neither touched nor seen. Indeed, we would not have doubted its nature for so long if it were open to these physical senses. Therefore, I have at times withdrawn the sharp edge of the mind into itself, if perhaps in this way I might see myself. But even so, I did not entirely achieve what I desired. Indeed, by this inner gaze of mine, I am neither sufficiently delighted nor do I find rest. But he who obtains what he investigates immediately rejoices and rests; therefore, I do not find myself within myself. But if I am to seek myself in another, by what means shall I seize myself? If I do not possess myself—through whom alone I am able to grasp whatever I can grasp. Return, therefore, and give yourself—no, give me—back to me. Since I cannot do it myself, return today; do not always postpone it to future hours. I beg you, do not allow more days to be marked by us with a black pebble <note>original: "nigro numerari lapillo"; a Roman metaphor for an unlucky or unhappy day, as opposed to a white stone for a lucky one.</note>. For however many sunny days you spend there, just as many cloudy and black ones do we spend here. Farewell.

-> Serious matters for Giovanni. The soul understands after death, and much more clearly than in the body. <-

### Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his Unique Friend.

<margin>f</margin> I have written several letters to you, best of friends, in which I attempted a somewhat amorous style of writing. This indeed seems to suit our intimacy and is not foreign to that honorable freedom of Socrates and Plato. Now, however, in the manner of the Platonists, after these amorous jests (for such are the Platonic introductions <note>original: "prooemia"; referring to the way Plato's dialogues often begin with light conversation or themes of love before moving to deep metaphysics.</note>), let us come to serious matters. Hear now what I once discussed concerning the mind with Bernardo del Nero <note>original: "Bernardo iunio"; a Florentine politician and friend of Ficino.</note> and Bartolomeo Fortini <note>original: "Bartholomeo fortino"; a prominent citizen and member of the Platonic Academy.</note>, citizens excellent in justice. Among mortals, there are two principal doubts concerning the mind: The first is whether the intellect can be separated from the body and, once the body is laid aside, live and operate. The second is: if it then understands anything, whether it understands clearly or not? We shall respond to these for now as briefly as we can. For these and similar matters are discussed most extensively in our *Theology on the Immortality of Souls*. We grant that the intellect thinks of many incorporeal things: namely, God, angels, souls, virtues, the proportions of numbers, and the Ideas and universal reasons of things. Just as we cannot see invisible things through sight, so we can neither think of incorporeal things through any bodily instrument; nor, through a nature restricted to body, place, and time, can we seek, search for, find, or preserve things that are absolute <note>meaning free from or independent of physical constraints.</note> from matter, place, and time. <meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s philosophical exploration of the soul’s nature. While the previous page focused on the soul as the seat of human identity and its connection to others through love, this page shifts to a technical argument from his *Platonic Theology* regarding the independence of the mind from the body and the superiority of intellectual vision over physical sight.</meta>

<page-num>14</page-num>
<header>BOOK ONE 14</header>

If the mind <note>original: "mens"; the highest, intuitive part of the soul.</note> sometimes, even while it rules the body, so collects itself within itself that it contemplates certain things by its own power, it follows that once it is separated from the body, it will be able to contemplate by itself much more easily. If it can operate by itself, it will also be able to exist and live by itself. And to descend more clearly to the second question: the mind will then discern whatever is offered internally to be understood just as the senses now discern what is offered externally to be felt. And it will do so at least as much more clearly as sight is sharper and faster than hearing and the rest of the senses; and also as much as the mind is more excellent than the senses, and the object of the mind more excellent than the object of the senses.

No one who uses the powers of the mind doubts that it is more excellent than the senses. For one sees that the mind is the judge of the senses. And, as something more precious, it is granted to fewer people, and is exercised more slowly and more rarely. That the objects of the mind are more sublime than the objects of the senses is shown by the fact that the former are universal, broad, and eternal, while the latter are particular, narrow, and mortal. 

<note>Ficino uses "universals" to refer to abstract, timeless concepts (like "Beauty" or "Justice") as opposed to "particulars," which are individual, temporary things (like a single beautiful flower).</note>

Added to this is the fact that the more the outer sense is focused, the more the inner sense is relaxed, and vice versa. For he who looks or listens very attentively can hardly imagine anything in the meantime; and he who imagines intensely hardly sees or hears what is then being offered from the outside. The same proportion exists between the imagination and the intellect.

The soul in this body has two greatest obstacles of all. The first is that it is distracted into many different operations and disturbances; however, varied operations hinder and weaken each other, for it is most difficult to apply oneself to different things at the same time. The second is that, both because of the condition of this lowest dwelling <note>Referring to the physical body.</note> and because of the physical service assigned by God to humans for a time, the soul exercises lower demands far earlier, more attentively, and more often than the higher ones. From this it happens that when we wish to contemplate incorporeal things, we for the most part work weakly; we perceive them obtusely and as if in a certain mist. 

But when the actions of nourishing, growing, sensing, or imagining are either omitted entirely or greatly relaxed, then the gaze of the mind will be sharpened to such an extent that whatever it sees, it discerns more clearly than this [physical] light. Truly, the soul will then see through itself; it will see that intelligible light <note>The "intelligible light" is the divine truth that illuminates the mind, just as the sun illuminates the physical world.</note> more clearly than it now sees this sensible light through the glass windows of this body and prison. For it will gaze calmly, through its own clear and most sharp serenity, upon the most excellent objects in the light of the divine sun—a light so clear that the light of our sun is like a shadow compared to it. And because that light is the brightest, it is most hidden from impure eyes, but most manifest to pure ones. 

It will not look upon these things as if they were painted images, but as true things, of which all other things are merely images. When, during sleep, the operations of movement and the external senses cease, the imagination—which feeds on the remains of the senses—is strengthened to such a degree that it paints images internally, representing them as if they were true things. What, then, will the intellect do—being far more effective than the imagination—when it has escaped, free from obstacles, much more than the imagination of a dreamer? In the highest truth and reason, it will behold the true reasons <note>original: "rationes"; here meaning the divine blueprints or "Forms" of things.</note> of all things. It will then, of course, depict within itself all true things most exactly...

<summary>Ficino argues that the mind's ability to think independently of the body proves its immortality, suggesting that once freed from physical "distractions," the intellect perceives divine truth far more clearly than the eyes see the sun.</summary>
<keywords>immortality of the soul, intellect vs sense, universals, allegory of the cave, divine light, Marsilio Ficino, Platonic Theology</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes a discussion from Book XV of Ficino’s *Platonic Theology* regarding how God, the "Light of Lights," illuminates the human mind. It then transitions into a famous polemical letter addressed to his close friend Giovanni Cavalcanti. The letter attacks the "Monopsychism" of the philosopher Averroes—the theory that all humans share a single, communal intellect. Ficino argues for individual immortality and the personal nature of the human soul.</meta>

<header>BOOK XV.</header>

...will be painted from elsewhere. But by whom most of all? By the mind, from the Mind, by the light of lights <note>original: "lumine luminum"; a Neoplatonic metaphor for God as the source of all truth and visibility, just as the sun is the source of physical sight.</note>. And how easily will it be done? Most easily indeed. For suddenly, because of a certain natural kinship, the visible light illuminates the physical transparency [of the eye] as soon as it becomes clear and pure. And it shapes it with its own form, through which it conveys its form to the forms of all visible things. Similarly, the intelligible and more-than-intelligible light—that is, God—shapes the intellectual transparency [the mind] as soon as it has emerged clear. It shapes it, I say, with His own form, that is, the divine form, through which it conveys that form to the forms of all intelligible things. And immediately it affects it with as much vital heat and joy as it has already affected it with brilliance. And thus it hands over a life free from death, just as it pours in a light foreign to darkness. And it pours this light into the mind beyond any limit of time, by which the mind now ascends from the changing nature of time to the state of eternity. Moreover, He feeds it with goodness according to its desire always, and by filling it, His beauty lures the appetite; and He fills it by luring it. There, there is fullness without satiety, where there is good without evil; through which the infinite good creates an infinite capacity as well. Therefore, the infinite good and beauty—the fountain of innumerable good and beautiful things—lures and fills the mind equally forever.

### Against Averroes: that there is not one single intellect for all humans.
### Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to his unique friend, Giovanni Cavalcanti.

<margin>a</margin>Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher from Spain whose interpretations of Aristotle were highly controversial in the Renaissance.</note> was of the opinion that there is one single intellect for all men, and that all people understand whatever they understand through that same intellect. Some people, more greedy for new things than true ones, say this opinion is quite natural. And I confess it: but I call it "natural" only because, just as natural things are wont to be, it is highly changeable and is destroyed by its own opposite. For by the very fact that someone affirms the contrary, Averroes's opinion is suddenly undermined. Since, indeed, contraries cannot exist in the same thing at the same time, if the intellect in a certain Averroist philosopher and in a Platonist philosopher thinks contrary things about itself at the same time—while in the former it says it is one, but in the latter it says there are many and not one—it clearly follows that there is not one intellect in them, but many. Is there not the greatest diversity among men at the same time in those things that pertain to the intelligence and the will? For at the same time, some affirm and others deny; some want and others do not want. What, moreover, shall we say about the conflicting habits <note>In this context, "habits" refers to acquired qualities or skills, such as knowledge or moral character.</note> of the intellect? One person is most learned, another unlearned; in this one it is just and upright, in that one unjust and wicked; happy in this one, miserable in that one. Therefore, there cannot be the same intellect in all. If the intellects are diverse, the souls are much more diverse. Add to this that if the intellect is one and always has been, as Averroes says, it is not likely that it is so ignorant of itself that in almost all men—except for Averroes alone!—it has always thought and still thinks that it is multiple in number. What is more natural to the mind than knowledge of itself? Why then, when the mind thinks about Averroes's opinion, can it never or hardly grasp it, unless because it is a false opinion? Finally, as often as we contemplate the unity of the mind, we are accustomed to hate it and to desire a plurality of minds, if only we desire to survive. That same mind would only hate itself if it were able to hate unity...

<summary>Ficino describes God as the divine light that grants the mind eternal joy and then argues against Averroes's theory of a single collective intellect, asserting that individual differences in thought and morality prove each person has their own soul.</summary>
<keywords>Averroes, Giovanni Cavalcanti, unity of the intellect, individual soul, divine illumination, light of lights, immortality, Platonism</keywords>

<header>BOOK ONE XV</header>

...its own: which alone is able to know itself. It is not likely, however, that a thing so eternal and indeed divine should always despise its own nature, and reject and hate it. Why do I draw out my speech further? You rule sufficiently and more in this field of yours <note>original: "in agro tuo regnas"; a complimentary metaphor suggesting Cavalcanti is a master of these philosophical topics</note>. I and you have debated these things in turn, while Marsilio, a guest first here and then at your home, was composing that great volume of theology. Farewell. April 16th, Florence.

->Theologians are awake. All others dream.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, sends greetings.

<margin>m</margin>
Some wonder why we follow Plato with such devotion, as he always seems to be occupied with paradoxes and portents. But they will cease to wonder, I believe, if they consider that only those things which are divine truly exist: because they are neither infected by the contagion of an alien nature, nor do they ever change from their state. Corporal things, however, are by no means truly real, but only seem to exist, since they are infected by contraries and change perpetually. Therefore, they are not true things, but images or shadows of true things. While almost all other philosophers, dedicated only to the study of natural things, were dreaming in these as if in images of true things, our Plato, leaning upon divine matters, was alone—or most of all—awake. Thus I think it is as much better to follow Plato the theologian rather than other philosophers as it is better to commit oneself to awake pilots rather than sleeping ones. Farewell.

->Truth is the splendor of God; beauty is love.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, sends greetings.

<margin>b</margin>
This was the principal study of the divine Plato—as the dialogue *Parmenides* and the *Epinomis* indicate—to show that there is one principle of things, which he named "the One" <note>original: "unum"; the Neoplatonic concept of the Monad or the ultimate source of all existence</note> after an earlier title. He also willed that there is one truth of all things. Namely, that the light of this very One, which is God, is infused into all minds and all forms; it offers forms to minds and joins minds to forms. Therefore, whoever wishes to profess Platonic study must worship a single truth: a single ray of the one God. This ray passes through angels, souls, the heavens, and the rest of the bodies. And as we discuss in our book *On Love*, its splendor shines in individuals according to the nature of each, and is called grace and beauty. And where it shines more fittingly, there it especially allures the beholder, excites the contemplator, ravishes and occupies the one who approaches, and compels him to venerate such splendor above all others as if it were a divinity; and to strive for nothing else than that, having laid aside his former nature, he himself might become that splendor. This is evident from the fact that when a lover is not content with the sight or touch of the beloved person, he sometimes cries out: "This person has I-know-not-what that burns me, and I do not understand what I desire." Where it is clear that the soul is burned by the divine glow which shines in a beautiful person as if in a mirror, and is secretly seized by it and drawn upward as if by a hook <note>original: "hamo"; a favorite metaphor of Ficino for how God "fishes" for souls through the bait of beauty</note> so that he may turn into God. Therefore, anyone must be considered insane and miserable who, while being provoked by God through sight toward sublime things, instead drowns himself in the mud through touch; and when he could have become a god from a man by contemplating divine beauty itself through human beauty, he instead reduces himself from a man into a beast.

<summary>Ficino argues that Plato is the only "awake" philosopher because he focuses on eternal divine truths rather than the "dreams" of the material world. He explains that human beauty is a divine ray meant to draw the soul back to God, warning that focusing on physical lust (touch) rather than contemplation (sight) turns a man into a beast.</summary>
<keywords>Marsilio Ficino, Giovanni Cavalcanti, Neoplatonism, Divine Light, Beauty, The One, Parmenides, Epinomis, contemplation vs. lust</keywords>

### That Ideas, according to Plato, exist in the Divine Mind

### Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to his unique friend, Giovanni Cavalcanti

<margin>p</margin>
Our Plato, in his *Timaeus*—imitating and confirming the views of Timaeus the Pythagorean—asserts that the world was born from God. He introduces a threefold cause for this creation: the efficient cause <note>the 'agent' or creator</note>, the final cause <note>the purpose or 'end'</note>, and the exemplar cause <note>the pattern or model</note>. He intends for the world to have been brought into being by the power of God, by the grace of His goodness, and according to the model of divine wisdom. 

And just as in the mind of an architect there are models for an entire building and its various parts, so too in a certain divine intelligence above the world there exist the models of this entire universe and its parts. He calls that world "intelligible" <note>perceivable only by the mind</note> and eternal, but this world he calls "temporal" and "sensible" <note>perceivable by the senses</note>. He calls the models of this world that exist in that higher world "Ideas." The likenesses of those models here in this world he calls "images" and "shadows." 

For this reason, it is both possible and pleasant to laugh at certain envious people who commonly preach so clumsily and unfairly that Plato proposed "Ideas" and the universal "reasons" of things were separate from both physical bodies and the divine intelligence—as if they were like little clouds scattered through the air by the wind. But since we have brought many arguments against those people in the books we composed at your estate in Regnano, let it suffice now to bring forward only the testimony from Plato’s *Timaeus*. 

"First," he says, "let us consider what is usually investigated before all else in a question about the universe: whether this universe has always existed without any beginning of its generation, or whether it was born, taking its start from some beginning. It is surely seen and touched, and it is a body. All such things move the senses. Those things which move the senses are perceived by 'opinion' through sense; and it is established that such things are of the kind that are born and have been generated. We have asserted that whatever is born must necessarily be born from some cause. Indeed, to find the maker and father of the world is difficult, and even when you have found him, to speak of him to the common people is impossible."

"Again, we must consider whether the craftsman of the world looked toward an eternal model—that which is always one, the same, and similar—or toward that which we call 'generated' <note>something created in time</note>. If the world is beautiful and the maker of the world is good, he surely preferred to imitate the eternal model. If it were otherwise—which is not even lawful to speak of—he would have followed a generated model instead of an eternal one."

<margin>Note here that the craftsman of the world is the supreme God.</margin>
"Since the world is the most beautiful of all things generated, and its author is the best of all causes, there is no doubt that he followed the eternal model. Thus, it was generated and brought to effect according to that which can be understood by reason and wisdom alone and which remains immutable. From this it follows that it is necessary for this world to be the likeness of another." 

And a little later: "Let us say for what cause that author of things established generation and this universe. He was good. And the good is never touched by envy regarding any matter. Therefore, since malice was most alien to him, he willed that all things should become as much like himself as possible."

<summary>Ficino explains the Platonic concept of "Ideas" not as abstract concepts floating in space, but as divine blueprints within the Mind of God used to create the physical world. Quoting the Timaeus, he argues that the beauty of the universe proves it was modeled on an eternal, divine pattern rather than a temporary one.</summary>

<keywords>Plato, Timaeus, Ideas, Divine Intellect, Giovanni Cavalcanti, creation, efficient cause, exemplar, intelligible world, sensible world</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s letter to Giovanni Cavalcanti, moving deeper into the specific arguments from Plato's Timaeus regarding the world as a "living creature" and the nature of divine Ideas.</meta>

# BOOK ONE

...concluded. If anyone accepts this principal cause of the world's generation from wise men, he will surely accept it most correctly. And a little later [Plato says]: We must say that this world is a living creature <note>original: *animal* — in Platonic thought, the universe is not a dead machine but a living, breathing, and conscious entity</note>; and that it was truly established as an intelligent being by divine providence, once we assume what follows. 

To the likeness of which living creature did God establish the world? We do not think He made it similar to any one specific species of animal. For if it were made similar to an incomplete animal, it would certainly not be beautiful; rather, we consider it most similar to that [divine] living creature of which all other animals, both individually and by their kinds, are parts. For that [divine model] embraces within itself all living things that are perceived by the mind alone <note>original: *sola mente percipiuntur* — referring to the 'Intelligible World' of Ideas that exists beyond physical sight</note>, just as this physical world contains us and the other animals that are seen. 

Therefore, God, wishing to make this world most similar to the most beautiful and perfect of all things that can be understood, made it a single living creature, subject to sight, containing within its own boundaries all animals suitable to its nature. Did we say correctly that there is one world? Or would it be more correct to say there are many or countless? One, certainly, since it was formed according to the likeness of the One. 

For that which contains all intelligible living things cannot have another companion. For if there were another, there would have to be yet another living creature that contained those two, and those two would merely be parts of it; and then this world would be more correctly called a likeness of that third one. Therefore, so that this world might be most like the perfect living creature in being unique and one, for that reason neither two nor countless worlds were created; but one world was made, "only-begotten" <note>original: *unigenitus* — Ficino uses this term, often reserved for Christ, to describe the unique and singular nature of the created universe</note>, as it is and shall be. 

But hear Timaeus the Pythagorean <note>a philosopher from southern Italy whom Plato credits as the speaker of the dialogue named after him</note>, who was Plato’s teacher and who, in similar words, placed the Ideas in God. He says the world is the best of those things that are born. Since it was begotten by the best author, who looks not at man-made models, but at the "Idea" and the intelligible substance <note>the non-physical essence of a thing that exists in the divine mind</note>. According to this model, what is made is perfectly beautiful and beyond reproach. It is always perfect according to the things of the senses: since that model of it, which contains all intelligible living creatures within itself, left nothing else outside; for it is the most absolute limit of intelligible things, just as this world is the limit of sensible things. 

So he says. We have heard that the Ideas of all things exist in a certain living and eternal model which is the most excellent of all intelligible things: and so perfect in every way that nothing intelligible exists outside of it. This can be nothing other than God. But what could be clearer than this? Plato, when he had said that God made all sensible things in the likeness of intelligible ones, added that He made all things similar to Himself—as if the model and God were the same. 

Truly, just as many species of created things as there are in this world, there are at least as many Ideas in God. That is, they are the "intelligible reasons" through which all things are created. These created species, because they exist in matter which does not live by itself, either do not live or barely live. But the Ideas live because they are in God, who lives through Himself. Therefore Plato says in the same book: "As many and of what kind the mind beholds Ideas in the living creature itself, just as many and of such kind he thought to fashion species in this world." 

This is what Plato felt, Giovanni <note>Giovanni Cavalcanti, the recipient of the letter</note>, as you hear. This is what the predecessors and successors of Plato felt. Believe Marsilio: He who feels otherwise dissents from the truth.

<summary>Ficino uses Plato's Timaeus to argue that the universe is a single, living creature modeled after the "Ideas" within the divine mind of God. He asserts that the world is unique (one) because its divine archetype is one, and that all physical life is a shadow of these living, eternal divine patterns.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Timaeus, Marsilio Ficino, Giovanni Cavalcanti, Divine Ideas, Intelligible World, Only-begotten, Neoplatonism, Macrocosm</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the collection of letters by Marsilio Ficino. # BOOK ONE
The cause of sinning. Hope. The remedy.

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend. Sends greetings.

<margin>c</margin>
Since souls are divine, why do they live so profanely? It is because they inhabit a profane house and region. Some fall into error through negligence or ignorance. This is hardly surprising, so long as we are occupied with this murky dross of the physical world. Others sin because of an excessive love for the body; nor is this surprising, for the body is the companion and the offspring of the soul. Others sin because they lack faith in either immortality or divine mercy. And what wonder is that, when they lead their lives in a place of death and malice? Still others sin because they trust more than is proper in divine mercy or in the hope of tomorrow’s self-improvement. Both a lack of confidence and an excess of it are dangerous: the former torments, while the latter deceives. Therefore, the highest wisdom is to always use the present moment as best as we can. Our only refuge is to frequently commend ourselves to God. It is a most excellent thought, when you have done these things, to remember that it is not hidden from God how harsh and dangerous a province He has handed to us to inhabit and manage. Infinite goodness far surpasses finite evil. He has established various degrees of either correction or punishment, and indeed directed them toward a good—either for the individual or for the common whole. However, He has established many more, and far more fruitful, degrees of reward.

->Those whom God has joined in character, He will join in happiness.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend. Sends greetings.

<margin>b</margin>
Yesterday in the fields of Novoli <note>A district in the northwest of Florence where the Cavalcanti family had property</note>, we celebrated the sacred feast days of Saint Christopher and Saint James. I said "sacred" only, Giovanni; I would certainly have added "festive" if you had been present, for without you nothing is a festival to me. See, therefore, how dear you are to your Marsilio, to whom not even heavenly things—if it is permitted to say so—are dear without you. And rightly so: for He who joined James and Christopher in the sacred rites, the same joined Marsilio and Giovanni in life. Likewise, the same spirit—or certainly one very similar—presides over both of us. God has, I believe, ordained that we live on earth with the same will and similar characters, and that we shall live in heaven under the same Idea <note>In Ficino’s Platonic thought, an "Idea" is the divine eternal pattern or archetype of a person or thing</note> and with equal degrees of happiness. Farewell, you who are the Achates <note>The loyal companion of Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid; a synonym for a faithful friend</note> of our voyage, and finally, the harbor and the seasoning of my life.

->A maker of laws is more excellent than a sophist.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend. Sends greetings.

<margin>m</margin>
The Greeks once marveled at Carneades <note>A Greek philosopher known for his incredible rhetorical skill and for arguing both sides of an issue with equal force</note> for his power of speech, his memory, and his sharp wit. Let your companions, as you say, praise these same qualities in Giovanni Guidi. Because of a certain similarity, they often nickname him "Carneades." You, however, call him an imitator of Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta, credited with establishing the city's communal and virtuous way of life</note> because of his skill in the invention of laws. You ask, furthermore, which is the more excellent praise: to be like Carneades or like Lycurgus. Carneades introduced disputes through his arguing. Lycurgus, however, dissolved them. The cleverness of Carneades was more often useless than useful; or if useful, it was so only to a few, and rarely in any one place. The discipline of Lycurgus is always useful, everywhere, and necessary to everyone. Finally, just as it is better to live well than to speak well, and better to be happy than merely to seem so, so the faculty of Lycurgus is more excellent than that of Carneades. But hear from Herodotus <note>The Greek "Father of History"</note> how great is the excellence of a lawgiver. For he writes that when Lycurgus first entered the temple of Apollo, the Pythia <note>The priestess and oracle at Delphi</note> poured forth these verses...

# BOOK ONE
<page-num>XVII</page-num>
<header>FIRST</header>
<sig>C</sig>

Beloved of ethereal Jove <note>original: "ioui" (Jupiter)</note> and all the dwellers of heaven, Lycurgus: <note>Lycurgus was the legendary lawgiver of Sparta; Ficino uses this name to address a person of great wisdom or legal authority.</note> you who come to our rich temples. I am uncertain whether to prophesy you now as a man or a god; I hope for you rather as a god, Lycurgus. Read this letter to our friend, the elder Prealdolfino; I know the nature of the man. I know he will confirm these things. Farewell, and persevere in the goodwill of Giovanni Guidi.

->The legitimate limit of love is intimacy.<- <note>original: "consuetudo," referring here to the shared life of the mind and senses through conversation and sight, rather than physical union.</note>

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend. Sends greetings.

<margin>i</margin> You ask what cause chiefly induced me to devise certain love letters. There are very many people, Giovanni, who, when speaking or writing about matters of love, wander far from the law of love. An error of this kind is as harmful as right love is useful; it is also as manifold as there are many who love. Indeed, all men love—I said *men*, Giovanni, for he who does not love a human is not a man. Therefore, not only in the book I composed *On Love*, but also in my letters, I have fixed a limit for lovers to which they may proceed. He who transgresses this limit, since he is a true enemy to himself, cannot be a true friend to others. Only he will preserve the legitimate limit in speaking or writing who has first preserved it in thinking. He will preserve it in thinking if he recognizes what true beauty is, and what is not truly beauty but merely a resemblance of it.

The legitimate limit of loving is intimacy; this consists of three things: thought, sight, and hearing. For, as all philosophers define it, love is nothing other than the desire for beauty. The beauty of the body consists not in the shadow of matter, but in the light and grace of form; not in a dark mass, but in a certain luminous proportion; not in a sluggish and unfit weight, but in a fitting number and measure. We reach that light, grace, proportion, number, and measure only through thought, sight, and hearing. To this point, therefore, the true affection of a true lover extends. But the appetite of the remaining senses, since it carries one away toward the matter, the mass, the weight, and the deformity of the form—which is contrary to love—is not love, but a certain unfit and burdensome itch, and altogether too deformed. But why do I consult the common crowd for so long in the manner of our Socrates and Plato, rather than myself? Perhaps the more I strive to prevent the common crowd from loving basely, the more that insane and ungrateful crowd will suspect that I love too much; which is said to have happened even to those divine heroes, our leaders Socrates and Plato. Therefore, let enough and more than enough be said of these things. Farewell.

->Medicine cures the body, music the spirit, and theology the soul.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Musano of Cesi. Sends greetings.

<margin>c</margin> As soon as the tertian fever <note>A fever that recurs every third day, often associated with malaria.</note> was expelled by our medicines, you, together with Giovanni Aurelio, greeted our Academy as if it were your physician; you requested the sound of the lyre and the singing of hymns from us, and you obtained them. Then, you read many things scattered throughout our *Theology*. Do not wonder, Francesco, why we mix medicine and the lyre with the study of theology. ### Neither love without religion nor religion without love is praised

### On Enduring Injury
#### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend. Sends Greetings.

You say that one of your household was recently affected by insult and injury from certain insolent people. He who does an injury, Giovanni, does it to himself. For it disturbs his own mind and stains it with the mark of a bad habit. Hatred, danger, and inconveniences follow into the soul. He who receives an injury receives it not from the one inflicting it, but from himself. For the rational mind itself, which is the "good" itself, is not offended unless it considers that injury to be bad for itself. An assessment of this kind is placed in our own judgment. Since therefore no one is harmed except by himself, no one ought to complain about another more than about himself. Therefore, let him who complains think not how he might punish another, but how he might punish—that is, chastise and correct—himself. Have you ever seen certain puppies who bite a stone thrown at them, even if they were not hit by it? These, since they were not harmed by the stone, harm their own teeth by biting it. Foolish men do the same. For often, having been kicked by an ass, they strike the ass—or rather, they strike themselves with their own fist. Indeed, foolish people take many injuries upon themselves through their own opinion, which by their nature usually bounce back like balls toward the thrower. You will say perhaps that it is difficult not to desire revenge. Do not doubt: even if men ignore the act, shortly after, the most just God will take vengeance. What is more advantageous, what more glorious, than to have God as one's protector and avenger? And to deserve at least as much good from Him by waiting as the other person wished to inflict evil; and in this way, to convert evil into good. Oh, what a precious good is tolerance! Socrates, the wisest of the Greeks, practiced this alone. Christ, the teacher of life, practiced this above all other virtues; for He is said to have descended to men almost for the sole purpose of practicing this. So blameworthy is impatience...

...through which patience is to be praised. Let us set aside other things: impatience disturbs the mind, deletes past goods, and infects the present. It hinders the future. Nor should the ears be offered to the rumors of the low rabble if it invites one to vengeance; for the rabble is a <term>Polypus</term> <note>original: "Polyppus." Referring to an octopus or similar creature, used here as a metaphor for the fickle, many-headed, yet mindless nature of the common crowd.</note>, that is, a multi-footed animal without a head. It is the mark of a great soul, by its own greatness, to consider small those things which are small. All temporal things are small and very brief; that which is past is no longer; that which is future is not yet; that which is present is indivisible, and begins at the same moment it ends. He is not brave who succumbs to injuries, but he who overcomes them. He overcomes, however, who so resists that he is not moved from his state by their impact. Read these things to your friend; tell him also to seek a remedy from reason, rather than waiting for time. For Time is a harmful doctor; daily, by the expectation of the future, he deceives the sick man, and before he expels old pains, he adds new ones to the old. Daily he accumulates so many evils that he leads one to death by the false hope of life. One must live today; for he who lives for tomorrow never lives. If you wish to live today, live for God, in whom yesterday and tomorrow are nothing other than today. Farewell. 30 March 1474.

->On acquiring constancy against fortune.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his Unique Friend. Sends Greetings.<-

<margin>f</margin> Socrates, in the book by Plato titled <term>Theaetetus</term> <note>A dialogue concerning the nature of knowledge</note>, arms his friend Theodorus the geometer—who had been subjected to the blows of fortune—to bravely repel them, not with iron weapons as most are accustomed to do, but with golden ones in this manner. He says, "Theodore, it is impossible to completely uproot evils. For it is necessary that there always be something contrary to the good. Among the gods above, evils cannot exist. But they necessarily circle this mortal nature and the lower region. Therefore, one must strive to fly from here to there as quickly as possible." We say that to "fly" is to make oneself as similar to God as possible, according to one's strength. Wisdom, holiness, and justice make a man similar to God.

Now, you shall hear in brief how this divine precept of our Plato should be understood. Just as God is the creator and governor of our souls, so the world is the parent and governor of our bodies. Since the mind is a son of God and the body is a member of the world, our mind is led by God as by a father, through the laws of providence, mercifully and sweetly. Our body, however, is dragged from the body of the world by the forces of fate, like a small particle from its whole mass, by a certain violent impact. The force of fate does not penetrate our mind unless the mind itself first voluntarily immerses itself in the body which is subject to fate. Therefore, let no one trust so much in his own counsel and strength that he hopes he can entirely avoid the diseases of the body and the loss of things. Let each soul recover itself from the plague of the body and collect itself into its own mind. Then, fortune will exhaust its force upon the body, but it will not pass into the soul. The wise man will not fight in vain against fate, but will rather resist by fleeing. Adversities cannot be chased away, but they can be fled. Therefore, we are commanded by Plato to fly "from here to there"—that is, to flee from the love of the body and the care of external things to the cultivation of the soul and of God; for otherwise, evils cannot be avoided. He adds that...

...most swiftly. For this reason, I think it right that we begin from a tender age to separate the soul from its commerce <note>original: "commercio," meaning the distracting business or entanglement of the soul with the physical world</note> with the body, before it is submerged by long habit. Through this "flight," the soul is not undeservedly rendered similar to God; for indeed, it escapes like a god when it is free from the contagion of the body. We achieve this kind of freedom primarily through three virtues: Prudence, Justice, and Holiness. Prudence recognizes what we owe to God and what we owe to the world. Justice gives the world its due. Holiness attributes to God what is His. Thus, the prudent man leaves his body—a member of the world—to the world’s own revolution, to be tossed about wherever it may happen. The soul, however, the child of God, he separates from the commerce of the body and commits to divine providence to be governed at its discretion. If we follow this golden precept of our Plato, my sweetest Giovanni, then while this whirlpool of fortune rages, we shall sail safely and unharmed to the port, aided by the breath of a heavenly wind. Farewell.

->That stable friendship which is forged by God.<-
->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his Unique Friend.<-

The Platonic philosophers, my dearest Giovanni, best defined friendship as a stable union of the lives of two people. We believe that there is truly one life in those men alone who walk together with one effort toward a single end, as if toward the same finish line of a journey. We also consider that their society will only be stable when that thing which they have proposed to pursue—through a certain shared duty between them—is not only one, but also stable and firm. However, since every human pursuit and commerce always tends toward that which is thought to be good, and there seem to be three types of goods for mortals—goods of the soul, the body, and external things—men seek either the virtue of the soul, the pleasure of the body, or an abundance of riches. Of these, the first is certainly fixed and perpetual. The other two are fleeting and mortal. Therefore, a stable union of life, which is true friendship, can only exist among those who strive with shared zeal and the full heat of the mind to capture and cultivate the one stable virtue of the soul, rather than to accumulate riches or fulfill the lusts of the body, all of which are flowing and perishable. Our leader and the master of all philosophers, Plato, wished for the virtue of the soul to be called <term>Sapientia</term> <note>Wisdom. Ficino uses the Latin term to denote a specific kind of spiritual knowledge rather than just cleverness.</note>; indeed, he judged wisdom to be the knowledge of divine things. In his books on the Republic, he demonstrates that divine things cannot become known to our mind unless God illuminates us—just as the forms of bodies are not seen by the eyes unless the sun illuminates those eyes. Therefore, God is the very thing we desire to see: He who illuminates the edge of the mind so that we may perceive; He who finally shows Himself to the clear mind; and by showing Himself, He brings delight. God is at once the way for us, the truth, and the life. He is the Way because He turns, leads, and carries us to Himself by His own rays; He is the Truth because He reveals Himself as true to those who have turned to Him; and finally, He is Life because He perpetually feeds and delights our soul, the contemplator of Him, with that blessed vision. If we seek this perennial fountain of all wisdom...

...perceive, as all must who desire to taste the most sweet liquids of wisdom. Indeed, it is necessary that all who wish to attain virtue of the mind pursue wisdom. From this it follows that whoever undertakes to cultivate their own mind is compelled to worship God. In the preceding passages, we defined friends as those who strive toward virtue with a similar and equal zeal, and who cultivate their minds through mutual favor. The cultivation of the mind consists of virtue alone; and virtue is wisdom. Wisdom is the knowledge of divine things, and divine light grants us knowledge of this kind. Therefore, the cultivation of the soul is the worship of God himself. Since friendship, with the consent of two people, strives to cultivate the soul through virtue, it seems to be nothing other than the highest concord of two souls in worshipping God. Moreover, whoever worships God with a pious mind is loved by God. Therefore, it is not merely two, but necessarily three who are always friends: namely, two humans and one God. God, I say—Jupiter the god of hospitality, Jupiter the god of friendship, Jupiter the preserver of human life <note>Ficino uses the name "Jupiter" here in the Neoplatonic tradition to refer to the divine Providence or the supreme Godhead who governs human interaction.</note>. This is the one whom Plato always worshipped, whom Socrates always honored; this is the light of life for men. He joins us into one; he is the indissoluble knot of friendship and its perpetual guardian. The ancient theologians, whose holy memory we venerate, pass down the tradition that they entered into the holy bond of friendship with this God as their reconciler. Among the Persians, Zoroaster is said to have chosen Arimaspes as his constant companion in the mysteries of religious philosophy, with the divine spirit breathing upon him. Hermes Trismegistus among the Egyptians likewise chose Asclepius. Orpheus chose Musaeus in Thrace. There also, Aglaophemus chose Pythagoras. The Athenian Plato chose Dion of Syracuse first, and then, after Dion had died, he chose Xenocrates. To such an extent did these wise men judge that both God as a leader and a man as a companion were necessary to complete the heavenly journey safely and peacefully. Although I have little confidence that I can follow their footprints impressed upon the high regions of heaven, I seem to have already achieved this one thing abundantly: that I do not lack the helpful and pleasant company of the best of men for practicing the studies of sacred philosophy and investigating virtue and truth. For I believe the intimacy between Giovanni Cavalcanti and Marsilio Ficino should be placed in the number of those friendships I mentioned just before. With God as our leader, who fortunately established and forged <note>original: "conflauit," suggesting the melting and joining of metals</note> this bond, it will greatly benefit both of us in conducting our affairs, in achieving tranquility of life, and in the investigation of divine things.

->Care for country, family, and friends.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Tedaldi. Sends Greetings.

<margin>b</margin> Bartolo Tedaldi, your uncle—a learned and prudent man—often had that Socratic saying on his lips: "Two things must be cared for above all other human affairs: namely, one’s country and one’s family." And rightly so; for of what country is the family not a member, or the body of the father? Why then, our Francesco, why do you travel abroad for so long? In this way, you neither serve your country nor do you sufficiently cultivate your family. You must not think so much about leaving many goods to your sons, as much as leaving them very good. One you can perhaps achieve outside your country; the other you can certainly achieve within it. I believe you trust in the diligence and honor of your son Lactantius. Nor indeed do I myself lack confidence in him; but what shall I say of your friends? You ought to yield to them sometimes if you wish them to yield to you; yield to your friends—indeed to yourself—today. Yield tomorrow to your enemies, if you have any; I pray that you have at least some care for me, to whom you are indeed as dear as that which is dearest. Farewell. March 5, 1474.

->Who should be called a true man.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Bartolomeo Fonzio and Alessandro Bracci, students of the Muses. Sends Greetings.

<margin>ſ</margin> If you wonder why I call Niccolò Michelozzi <note>Niccolò Michelozzi was a prominent Florentine statesman and secretary to Lorenzo de' Medici.</note> by the specific title of a "true man," I answer that I find nothing effeminate in that man, nothing savage, nothing deceitful, nothing that does not display the power of virtue and dwell within itself. From where do you think this proceeds? That no one can be found anywhere who takes anything away from Niccolò, even in excess. Why is he praised without exception? Because he is loved without pretense; and from where does that come? Because he loves without pretense and lives without a lie. Farewell, and take care that Niccolò does not read this letter. I decided to praise him while he was absent, lest I might seem to praise a "true man" with perhaps less than the truth. Greet our Pietro Cennini <note>A noted Florentine scholar and calligrapher.</note>, a man adorned with piety and letters. April 6, 1474.

### On Humanity.
**Marsilio Ficino to the humane man Tommaso Minerbetti sends greetings.** <note>Tommaso Minerbetti was a Florentine nobleman and a close associate of the Medici and Ficino; he served in several high diplomatic offices.</note>
<margin>c</margin>
Just as children tend toward greater cruelty than the elderly, the insane more than the prudent, and the dull-witted more than the gifted: this is because they are, so to speak, "lesser men" than the others. For this reason, those who are cruel are called "inhumane" and "feral." Indeed, those who are far removed from the perfect nature of man—whether due to a defect of age, a vice of the soul, a disease of the body, or an adverse disposition of the stars—usually loathe or neglect the human species as if it were something foreign and alien. Nero was not a "man," if I may speak thus, but rather a certain monster covered in skin resembling a human. <note>original: "nero: sed monstrum quoddam pelle homini simile." Ficino uses the Emperor Nero as the ultimate historical example of a man who abandoned his human nature for animalistic cruelty.</note> For if he had truly been a man, he would have loved other men as members of the same body. Since each individual man exists under one "Idea" and within the same species, they are all one single man. For this reason, I believe, the sages gave the name of man himself to that one virtue among the many: <term>humanity</term> <note>original: "humanitatem." For Ficino, this is not just a trait but a specific virtue that recognizes the shared essence of all people.</note>, which loves and cares for all men as brothers born in a long succession from one single father. Therefore, most humane of men, persevere in these duties of humanity. Nothing is more pleasing to God than charity. There is no surer sign of madness or portent of misery than cruelty.

->Grace. Love. Faith. Friendship.<-

**Marsilio Ficino to the poet Naldo Naldi sends greetings.** <note>Naldo Naldi (1436–c. 1513) was a humanist poet and a member of the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note>
<margin>v</margin>
I used to call you, Naldo, the "delight of Phoebus," <note>Phoebus is another name for Apollo, the Greek god of music and poetry.</note> and I used to pursue your poetry with many praises, as is fitting. But it occurred to me that it is hardly becoming for a Muse to be celebrated except by a Muse, or for songs to be celebrated except by songs. However, I am utterly unable to remain silent about your qualities. What provokes me to speak? Love and faith. Therefore, I shall praise love and faith. Grace moves love; love procreates faith; faith fosters love, its own father. And with this nourishment, it generates friendship from love. Finally, once friendship is born, that same faith nourishes and increases it daily, and preserves it deep within as something indelible. Why do we think it happens that while other things weaken as they grow older, friendship itself becomes more robust the older it gets? Is it because many favors are exchanged back and forth? Not at all. For since the will is free, it "buys" a free will with its own will, not with a price. Therefore, faith proven over a long time confirms a friendship; and it is through faith alone that goodwill becomes both most ancient and most robust at the same time. I am pleased to celebrate this above all others. For the learning of any individual belongs to one person alone; but faith belongs to at least two. For he who is wise is wise for himself; but you are "faithful" both to yourself and to me. Farewell, you who are to me more faithful than faith itself, and the oldest of all my friends. And persevere in your intimacy with Bernardo Rucellai, <note>original: "Bernardi oricellarii." Rucellai was a wealthy patron, son-in-law to Piero de' Medici, and owner of the famous Oricellari Gardens where humanists met.</note> a learned and virtuous man. Remember that as often as we have together envisioned either a law-abiding citizen or a happy man, we have been accustomed—with Marsilio's agreement—to place Rucellai ahead of a hundred thousand men. Again, farewell. April 8, 1474.

### The Folly and Misery of Men.
**Marsilio Ficino to his fellow philosophers Riccardo Angelerio of Anghiari, Oliviero Arduini, and Antonio Seraphico sends greetings.**

--- Page 44 ---
<meta>This page continues the philosophical letters of Marsilio Ficino. Following his discussion on "Humanity," he now shifts to a classic Renaissance theme: the contrast between human folly and human misery, illustrated by the famous figures of the laughing and weeping philosophers.</meta>

BOOK
q
v

Why did Democritus laugh so much? Why did Heraclitus mourn? One, I believe, laughed at the **folly** of men; the other wept for their **misery**. Folly seems laughable, while misery seems pitiable. What else is folly but a corruption of judgment? And what is misery but an affliction of desire proceeding from that same corruption of judgment? Who will deny that men are fools? They care for the affairs of others and neglect their own. They magnify things that are distant and new, while they value little that which is present and familiar. Oh, the constant craving for the future! They do not enjoy the present. And when motion ought to be stopped so that they might rest, they are forever starting new and various movements just so they might eventually find rest. Thus they accumulate riches as if they were never going to die, yet they abuse pleasures as if they were going to die tomorrow. Let us set other matters aside for now, for infinite material occurs to us here. 

I cannot help but judge this as the most foolish thing of all: that many people most diligently feed their own "beast"—or rather, a noxious and untamed wild animal—which is the **body**, but they allow themselves—that is, the **soul** itself—to perish from hunger as much as they are able. And we wonder why we live, or rather why we die, in such misery for so long, as if we could reap anything other than what we have sown. Misery is the fruit of folly. But how? Since we foolishly feed the body too much and neglect the soul, the former becomes fat and robust, while the latter becomes thin and weak. From this it happens that, because of the soul's own thinness and imbecility, bodily things appear to it both large and strong. Those things which seem large, it greatly desires; those things which seem strong, it fears exceedingly. Thus, like a wretch, the soul is agitated partly by the heat of desire and partly by the horror of fear. 

I beseech you, let us nourish and increase the **spirit** with spiritual food. Thus, once it has become great and begins to value bodily things as if they were tiny, it will not be knocked from its seat in any part by the onset of the body. Let us ascend into the high watchtower of the mind, leaving behind the lowly dust of the body. Then we shall look upon divine things more closely and human things from a distance. The former will appear greater than they used to, and the latter smaller. Therefore, by cherishing the former and neglecting the latter, we shall no longer be fools nor wretches, but wise and blessed. Farewell.

### The Folly and Misery of Men.

### Marsilio Ficino to Pietro Vanni, Cherubino Quarquagli, and Domenico Galletti, sends greetings. <note>Pietro Vanni, Cherubino Quarquagli, and Domenico Galletti were members of Ficino’s inner circle of students and friends in the Platonic Academy of Florence.</note>

You have seen the sphere of the world painted in my academy <note>original: "gymnasio." In this context, Ficino refers to his "Platonic Academy" at the Villa di Careggi, where he taught.</note>, and on either side of it, Democritus and Heraclitus. One is laughing, while the other is weeping. Why does Democritus laugh? Why does Heraclitus mourn? They look at the common people—that monstrous, insane, and miserable animal. Mortals daily ask God for "good things," but they never ask to use them well. They wish for fortune to follow their desires, but they care nothing for their desires to follow reason. They strive to make even their smallest household items as beautiful as possible, but they almost never strive to make the soul beautiful. They diligently seek out remedies for bodily diseases, yet they neglect the diseases of the soul. They think they can have peace with others, yet they constantly wage war with themselves. For there is a battle between the body and the soul, between sense and reason...

<summary>Ficino explores the relationship between human folly and misery, arguing that neglecting the soul in favor of the body leads to a distorted perception of reality. He uses the imagery of the laughing Democritus and weeping Heraclitus to illustrate the two reactions to this human condition.</summary>
