<meta>This page concludes the previous letter discussing the dichotomy between the body and soul before beginning a new letter to Cristoforo Landino. It continues the theme of human inconsistency and the necessity of divine guidance over mere human reason.</meta>

# BOOK I
# XXI

...perpetual. They trust they can acquire a faithful friend from the number of others, yet none of them keeps faith with themselves. They reject what they once approved. What they wanted, they now do not want, and vice-versa. They arrange the parts of buildings with the utmost precision, and they tune the strings of a lyre <note>Latin: *lyria*, a stringed instrument often used as a metaphor for cosmic or psychic harmony</note> to perfection. Yet they never attempt to bring the offspring and movements of the soul into harmony. They make stones look like living beings, but they treat living beings like stones. The "wise" themselves they despise, yet they venerate the statues and names of the wise. They profess to know the affairs of others while they are ignorant of their own. What more shall we say to this, friends? Magistrates forbid homicide, yet everywhere they permit the manufacturing of instruments for the slaughter of men. They hope for a harvest of the best men, yet they do not sufficiently cultivate the "seed" of men—that is, childhood. Men always live poorly today, hoping to live well only tomorrow. For the sake of **ambition**, they contend with one another through malicious deeds. It would be a more convenient path to **glory** to compete through mutual benefits. While they always speak ill, they hope to hear good things. While they act wickedly, they expect to receive good. We proclaim ourselves the authors of good, but God the author of evil. We cast our own faults upon the stars. Where will you find someone who values a human being as much as money? Who tends to themselves as they tend to their fields and other possessions? Who educates their household with as much diligence as many train their horses, dogs, and birds? Who considers how heavy a loss of time is? In spending money, we are most stingy; in the expenditure of time, we are prodigal beyond measure. How many people will you find who recognize the poverty of their own soul? Everyone thinks they abound in wisdom but lack money. Alas, we seek the greatest things in the smallest; the lofty in the lowest; good in evil; rest in fleeting things; peace in discord; abundance in poverty; and finally, life in death. Let us seek, friends, I beseech you, these same things we already seek, but let us no longer seek them where we have been seeking. He is far too insane and wretched who trusts he will find a thing in its opposite. Farewell.

->The Folly and Misery of Men.<-

Marsilio Ficino to Cristoforo Landino <note>A celebrated humanist, poet, and commentator on Dante, who was a close associate of Ficino in the Platonic Academy</note>, a man of singular goodness and learning, sends greetings.

<margin>Aristotle</margin> Aristotle introduced problems regarding the nature of things. I now raise problems with you regarding the nature of men. Tell me, I pray: why do men boast that they are **rational**, and yet they live by chance? They desire or fear many things before they sufficiently know whether they should be sought or feared, or the reverse. They prefer the shortest and smallest things to the eternal and immense. Why do they wish neither to obey a man nor to submit to a wise one? Yet they most willingly serve beasts and vices. Why do we strive to rule over others when we do not rule ourselves? Why, in our zeal for ruling, do we fall daily into servitude? And we strive to obtain **honors** <note>Latin: *dignitates*, referring to high social or political rank</note> more than we strive to be worthy of those honors. Furthermore, since we see that beasts cannot be rightly guided without the care of a human, how on earth do we think that men can be happily governed by a man without the counsel and aid of God? What is it that makes us, in such a superfluous abundance of things, so complaining and needy? What makes us envy many people when the condition of mortals [requires] mercy...

# BOOK I
# XXI

...worthy of pity rather than envy. Why do we so easily forget good things, but never the bad? And since opposites are expelled by their opposites, why do we attempt to cure evils with more evils? Why do we often hope to reach glory through infamy? We admire virtue in another, yet we strive to *appear* admirable rather than actually knowing how to be so. Another person’s vice displeases us, yet we hardly consider how we might avoid being displeasing to ourselves and others. We close our ears to the truth, yet we open them wide to lies. What shall I say of those who, captured by the love of some person or thing, value others more than themselves? They desert themselves to pursue something else. O madmen! O wretched souls! Since you cannot grasp external things except through yourselves, how can you ever grasp the external if you have lost your internal self? Why do you wanderers seek good things far away when they are near—indeed, when they are within you? 

I often marvel at this too, Landino <note>Cristoforo Landino (1424–1498), a prominent Florentine humanist and close associate of Ficino</note>: why do we fear only one death—specifically that which is the final end of dying—but not our daily deaths? For at every moment the balance of the body changes, and past life ends. Finally, as it seems to me, because we practice virtues falsely but practice vices in earnest, we will end up—as far as it depends on us—falsely happy but truly miserable. Democritus laughed at these things; Heraclitus wept for them <note>A common Renaissance reference to Democritus as the "laughing philosopher" and Heraclitus as the "weeping philosopher" regarding human folly</note>; Socrates wanted to cure them; but only God *can* cure them. O, what a wretched animal is man, unless he somehow flies up above humanity—that is, unless he commends himself to God. Let him love God for God’s sake, and everything else for His sake. This is the only solution to those problems and the only rest from evils. Farewell.

## Exhortation to modesty and the study of literature.

->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to the great-hearted Giuliano de' Medici.<-

<margin>e</margin> Even if my love for you is such that I cannot be a perfect judge in your affairs—or rather, *our* affairs—I will nonetheless tell you what I feel, Giuliano <note>Giuliano de' Medici (1453–1478), the younger brother of Lorenzo the Magnificent</note>, since you ask. First, I praise your prudence: you do not rely solely on your own wit, but you consult an elder. For you know how much everyone pleases themselves because of natural self-love. Next, in your letter, I praise a certain natural sweetness. You seem to me like certain painters: just as you always express the beauty of your eyes and the charm of your mouth through your gaze and your speech, so you have now expressed them with your pen. Proceed then, Giuliano, sweetest of all men. Proceed, I pray. Diligently survey the Tusculan gardens <note>Referring to the "Tusculan Disputations," a famous work of Cicero; the "gardens" represent a place of philosophical study</note> as you have begun. For if you graze upon the Tullian flowers <note>A metaphor for the eloquent rhetoric of Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> with year-long practice, you will at last pour forth nectar-like honey. If it were permitted to recommend your own people to you, I would most highly recommend Andrea Cambini <note>A Florentine historian and notary close to the Medici family</note>. Farewell.

## That a friend exists within a friend.

But you will ask, "Why did you not summon me when you could?" Even if I had thought you were away from there, I would not have come, lest I be a burden to you. But in truth, my great love for you...

# BOOK I
## XXII

my mind has for a long time now impressed your image upon itself. And just as I sometimes see myself reflected outside of myself in a mirror, so I very often gaze upon you within me, in my own heart. Moreover, your brother Lorenzo was present then—your second self in both nature and will. Therefore, since I perceived this Julian <note>Giuliano de’ Medici (1453–1478), the younger brother of Lorenzo the Magnificent</note> of mine so clearly both inside and out, I could not imagine him to be absent from that place. It was not, therefore, through any negligence, but through an excess of love that it happened: that I did not call upon you then to handle affairs, nor did I later inform you of what had been done. You wish to be called upon at other times, sweetest Julian; you must strive to be loved less. This is an arduous task—perhaps even an impossible one. For you would first have to labor not to be Julian. You will only strip off my love when you strip yourself of who you are. What then shall I do in the future? Shall I call you at other times? Not at all, I think. For a long time now, Desire has sufficiently called us both to each other and to himself. Farewell.

->A friend’s greeting to a friend.<-

### Carlo Marsupini to Marsilio Ficino the Platonist, sends greetings.

<margin>s</margin>Greetings, you who are my only health <note>original: "salus," which carries the dual meaning of "health" and "salvation"</note>. For I am only healthy and safe as long as I am with you. Indeed, I seem to truly live only when I live with you. As often as I am away, so often have I perished. See to it then, my Marsilio, that you do not lose a man or kill a friend by deserting me. You are always running about, here and there. Now you care for bodies below <note>referring to Ficino’s practice of medicine</note>; now you guard souls above <note>referring to Ficino’s work in theology and philosophy</note>. Meanwhile, I, your soldier, perish. If you have such great charity—which you certainly do—why, I ask you, do you not care for your dear Carlo by staying here? For my mind is sick from your departure and my body is ill; the only health is for you to return. This is now the fourth day since you left. When you have doubled your promises <note>likely referring to an eight-day absence or a specific commitment</note>, keep them. Farewell.

->A divination concerning a friend.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to his dear Carlo Marsupini, greetings.

<margin>t</margin>And to you, greetings three and four times over. This morning at dawn, while sleeping, I seemed to be reading a certain very brief speech, in which the arrangement of words and thoughts was such as I have always strived to observe. Therefore, I was uncertain whether I was reading my own work or another's. Shortly after rising from bed, your letter was delivered to me. From this, I suddenly knew by the facts themselves what I had argued in my book *On the Immortality of the Soul*: that morning dreams often contain no small amount of prophecy. Today, Marsupini, I saw a Marsilio in your pupil <note>referring to the reflection in the eye</note> more beautiful than Marsilio himself. But let us set these matters aside for now. In short, your letter is of such a kind that it compels me to respond with my feet rather than my hands, and with my voice rather than with letters. Greet Taddeo Ugolini <note>A Florentine priest and close associate of the Platonic Academy</note>, a religious man.

...they think of contemplation as something more distant. Therefore, how much you love me you have declared especially by your letters, in that you called the silence of a single day a "long silence" and you called my letters—which flew to you very swiftly—"most long-awaited." How much I, in turn, love you, let this now declare: I wish that your letter, though I have already read it ten times, appears so short to me that in almost the same moment it bids me both to be well and to be gone. 

These two things are contradictory in love. Others, when they are told "farewell," are understood to be "well." Lovers, when they hear "farewell" <note>original: "vale," which can mean both "be strong/well" and "goodbye"</note>, hear it as a bad thing; indeed, as an evil. You cause me to rejoice when you say "greetings" <note>original: "salue"</note>. At the same time, you cause me to grieve when you command "farewell." You seem to command both to me at once. I would certainly write more, and perhaps even better things. But, distracted by these conflicting emotions for your sake, I can neither write more at present nor better. Be well <note>original: "salue"</note> and farewell <note>original: "vale"</note> at the same time. March 21, 1474. Florence.

## It is better to praise goodwill than genius.
### Marsilio Ficino to Angelo Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494) was a brilliant humanist poet, dramatist, and scholar under the patronage of Lorenzo de' Medici</note>, the Homeric poet, sends many greetings.

<margin>a</margin> I had taken up my pen, Angelo, to extol that Homeric Muse of yours to the heavens with wondrous praises as much as I could. But suddenly, Desire <note>original: "cupido"</note> interrupted me: "What are you doing, foolish Ficino? Will you always be occupied in praising the Muse? Praise me instead, if you wish to praise without the suspicion of flattery. If you celebrate the Polizian Muse, you celebrate Angelo alone. If you celebrate Desire, you celebrate Angelo and Marsilio together. For I am the love common to you both. I cherish both; I am cherished by both." These things that god said to me, Angelo; but I said to him: "Poliziano's Muse is truthful; she never compelled me to lie. But you, perjured Love, you force me to lie every day. For yesterday I so loved Poliziano’s delights that I would have sworn I could not love them more vehemently in the future; yet today I love them so much again that I would swear I did not love them enough yesterday; and at the same time I affirm I cannot love more ardently tomorrow than today. That 'tomorrow' deludes me similarly every day. My love is always full-grown—who would believe it?—and yet it is always growing. Let it grow as it pleases, provided it does not grow old. But listen, Cupid. Venus is not the mother of this love, but Calliope <note>The Muse of epic poetry</note>. The Muse fosters him diligently. He grows steadily; let him grow continually with this nourishment, and let him be a perjurer <note>Ficino plays on the idea that Love "lies" because it constantly outdoes its own previous limits</note>. This is not a vice in love. Thus, Angelo, I both ought to and wish to cherish our common love and your Muse together. You, adore the Muse herself, the mother of love and glory. March 21, 1474.

## Whom love may deceive and whom it may not.
### Marsilio Ficino to Niccolò Michelozzi <note>Niccolò Michelozzi (1447–1527) was a confidential secretary to the Medici family and a close friend of Ficino</note>, a true man, sends many greetings.

<margin>f</margin> I have written letters to Lorenzo de' Medici and Angelo Poliziano today, Michelozzi, which were somehow so full of love <note>original: "amatorias"</note> that it is no wonder if they seem rather foolish. For love is foolish. Do you wish me to be foolish a third time? You wish it, and I am willing—but in few words. I have nothing greater, Niccolò, than that I love. Nothing better than that I am loved, and by men most worthy of love. Because of love, I may perhaps sometimes speak less than the truth; but about love, I can only speak the truth. Yet love does not deceive me where I have judged before I loved. Love [follows] judgment...

### A recommendation based on need and merit.

-> Marsilio Ficino to Matteo Palmieri <note>Matteo Palmieri (1406–1475) was a Florentine humanist and politician, best known for his poem *Città di vita*, which Ficino refers to here as "theological poetry"</note>, the theological poet. <-

<margin>e</margin> Even though I know for certain that learned men do not need a recommendation to obtain the palm of the Muses <note>A metaphor for poetic or scholarly excellence</note> from you, Palmieri, yet so that I may fulfill the duty of friendship, I commend to you most highly Luca of San Gimignano, my former teacher. I recommend him along with my grammar; I owe him as much as speaking with skill is more excellent than pouring out empty words by chance. You ought to favor him for two reasons: because he is in need, and because he deserves it. Doing good to the needy is the duty of the merciful; doing so for the deserving is the duty of the just. I know that you are accustomed to being both merciful and just. Farewell.

### Since all things are well-ruled by God, all things should be taken for the better.

-> Marsilio Ficino to Bishop Campano <note>Giannantonio Campano (1429–1477), a distinguished humanist and Bishop of Teramo</note>, the poet. <-

<margin>n</margin> Campano, do you ever laugh at the arrogance of mortals? I often laugh at it, and I refute it as a wealth of folly. Neither the plans of the elderly reach the understanding of boys, nor the thoughts of the wise reach the rustics. Yet <note>Indented text with missing initial, likely intended for a decorative 'T'</note> the terrestrial animal [man] dares to track the reason of divine nature more proudly than is fitting, and to guess at its end. And what is worse, mortals of any age—even amidst feasts and harlots—treat divine mysteries quite loosely. Regarding these matters, Pythagoras rightly prohibited speaking without divine light. No one perceives divine things, Campano, unless he is divine. For the apostle Paul rightly said: "No one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God" <note>1 Corinthians 2:11</note>. Again, no one lies more about divine matters than the one who lies "to the fingernail" <note>original: "ad unguem," an idiom meaning "perfectly" or "precisely," suggesting those who claim exact knowledge of God are the greatest liars</note>. For thus God says in Isaiah: "I will catch the wise in their own craftiness" <note>Ficino here attributes a quote to Isaiah that is found in Job 5:13 and quoted by Paul in 1 Corinthians 3:19</note>; and elsewhere: "The Lord knows that the thoughts of the wise are vain." Therefore, it ought to be enough for a man to know that this most beautiful machine of the world <note>original: "mūdi machinam," a common Renaissance metaphor for the universe as a divinely constructed mechanism</note> depends on and is governed by one most wise Architect. And from Goodness itself, nothing can proceed except what is good; and those things proceeding from Him cannot be governed by Him otherwise than well. Thus, all things are to be taken for the better. He who thus understands and loves divine things is divine by nature, good by art, joyful in hope, and happy in reward. Farewell, and be happy.

...we are too foolish and unjust. We try to change God, not our own character. We want to persuade others of good things, yet we must persuade ourselves. We carry good on our lips, but evil in our hearts. Speaking of virtue, we are like a lute: we do not hear our own sound. And you will say that this is too difficult. It will not be difficult in the manner of Panaetius <note>Panaetius of Rhodes was a Stoic philosopher whose work on duties heavily influenced Cicero; Ficino suggests that living virtuously is easy if the will is directed toward it</note>, if you desire to live well as greedily as you desire to live.

-> Praise of Liberality and Praise of Almsgiving <-

-> Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, sends greetings. <-

<margin>d</margin> I will tell you, my Lorenzo, what I feel, even if by chance it seems a shocking thing to say. But in truth, what is true is not shocking. For nothing is more sacred than truth. I will say what I feel freely. God, Lorenzo—God himself is for sale! But with what coin is God most especially bought? With that which He himself buys others: that is, by a certain liberal charity toward the poor. For God, out of immense love, bestows everything on everyone freely, and gives to the poor alone. For all people, however wealthy they may seem, are altogether destitute before God; therefore, we buy God with this virtue alone, because by this alone do we most truly imitate Him. Let no wise or brave or temperate man boast that he emulates God. These virtues are shadows of divine virtues, or rather images. Only the man who is liberal toward the poor imitates Him exactly. For the manner of giving is the same for a liberal man as it is for God. O, what a truly happy merchant! One who, for a small price, redeems himself from his enemies—that is, from his vices—and at the same time "buys" both men and God. He will never be poor who is rich in men and in God. He is one who often considers, amidst the greatest riches, what it is to be poor. He who, established at the highest point, mercifully looks down upon the lowest things will never end up as the lowest. A small man never accomplishes anything better than when he humbly ascends to the heights. A great man does nothing greater than when he magnificently descends to the bottom. Other virtues for the most part benefit only the person practicing them. Liberality profits both the giver and others; and as it spreads its duty more widely than the remaining virtues, it is judged more excellent. For a good is more divine the more widely it is shared. And if doing evil is the worst crime—because it is against the nature of good and the society of the human race—then we necessarily judge doing good <term>beneficium</term> <note>literally "a good deed" or "benefit"</note> to be the best thing. Other virtues can sometimes stir up envy. This one alone always both kindles love and utterly extinguishes hatred and envy. Indeed, it performs its duty most of all when it helps a man, both on account of misfortune when he is needy, and on account of virtue when he is well-deserving. Sow, therefore, my Lorenzo, sow, I say, like a happy farmer—just as you began long ago—with a good spirit into this dry human soil. It will at last flow for you not only with common crops, but truly also with milk and honey. Although "human" is said to come from the soil <note>original: "homo dicatur ab humano" - Ficino is playing on the Latin etymological link between *homo* (human/man) and *humus* (earth or soil)</note>, yet the method of sowing is different for a man than for the ground. He who throws seeds into the poor ground makes a loss of seeds. But he who...

April 12, 1474. Florence.

### No virtue is more lovable than kindness.

-> Marsilio Ficino to Niccolò Michelozzi <note>Niccolò Michelozzi (1447–1527) was a close friend of Ficino and a devoted secretary to the Medici family</note>, a true man, sends greetings. <-

<margin>f</margin> To weep is the mark of a woman, Michelozzi; I confess that I am more womanly than others, for a soft nature has given such traits to us <note>Ficino often referred to his own melancholic and sensitive temperament as "soft" or "moist," terms used in Renaissance psychology to describe the scholarly disposition</note>. But our "Laurel" <note>Laurus: a frequent pun on the name of Lorenzo de' Medici</note> has made me the softest of all. Indeed, I weep with a certain tender joy or some other strange affection whenever I consider—and I consider it often—how pious our Lorenzo is toward God, how merciful toward the poor, and how beneficent toward everyone. 

Truly, the more beneficent he is to others, the more "maleficent" <note>original: "maleficus"; Ficino is playing on words—while Lorenzo does good (beneficus) for others, his goodness makes Ficino "suffer" from missing him</note> he is in a way to his own Marsilio. If indeed by these benefits—or rather "malefits"—of his, he fascinates and ensnares me, poor as I am, in wonderful ways every day. And while he moves others to tears of repentance, he moves me to tears of longing. When he is loved more ardently by me, then he departs further away. Advise that most beloved man, our Laurel, that he should love the things he once loved. And as soon as it is allowed, let him approach as near in his presence as he has approached in my love. April 12, 1474.

### A true friend does not need absence to increase his longing.

-> Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous Giuliano de' Medici <note>Lorenzo’s younger brother, later killed in the Pazzi Conspiracy of 1478</note>, sends greetings. <-

<margin>c</margin> When in previous days, in a certain moral speech during the night services, you provoked your friends to repentance and tears for their sins, some wailed aloud, while others beat their breasts with their palms. It is said that Antonio, the Tuscan poet <note>Antonio Pelotti, a poet in the Medici circle</note>, fell down as if bloodless and lifeless. Shortly thereafter, you suddenly betook yourself to the mountains of Mugello <note>The Medici family’s ancestral home and site of several of their villas north of Florence</note>, so that just as you had almost destroyed that Antonio by your presence, you might destroy this Marsilio of yours by your absence. 

Ha! This is hardly dutiful, my friend. Once, you spared your most cruel enemies; yet you do not spare this friend. Perhaps you have decided to live in the country for a few days so that you might return to us more greatly desired, and appear more "urbane" <note>original: "urbanior"; a pun on moving from the country back to the city (urbs)</note> after your stay in the rustic lands. To be sure, you know that appetite usually arises from lack, and admiration from novelty. But there is no need for this medicine, O astute "Medici" <note>Ficino frequently punned on the family name "Medici" (meaning "doctors" or "physicians")</note>, for either you or me. For what can seem more urbane than your urbanity? What, if I may say so, more longed-for than this longing? 

Dismiss these remedies, I pray—they are very troublesome to the sick and unnecessary for the doctor. Let those people be desired more because of their absence who, because of their long presence, are desired less day by day. But for us, this thirst of ours is not so much extinguished by your "liquor" as it is inflamed by it. At least while you linger there with our Angelo <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the famous humanist poet and tutor to the Medici children</note>, let the name of your Marsilio roll upon your lips. Either lick this Marsilio, Giuliano, or chew him. I would rather be bitten by Giuliano than spat out. Farewell.

### Who is the unjust rich man and who is the just.

### Marsilio Ficino to Angelo Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494) was a brilliant humanist poet and scholar under the protection of the Medici; Ficino calls him "Homeric" in recognition of his translations of the Iliad</note>, the Homeric poet, sends greetings.

<margin>d</margin>God willed the whole water to be common to every aquatic creature, and the earth to all land creatures. Only man, that unhappy animal, has separated what God had joined together. He has constrained his empire, which by nature was vast, into a narrow space. He introduced "mine" and "thine" into the world—the beginning of all the malice of discord. For this reason, not without justice did Pythagoras decree among friends, and Plato among citizens, that all things should be held in common.

Therefore, those rich men must be considered entirely unjust who, out of pride, forget God, the giver of all riches. They make themselves masters of the poor as well; they call themselves the possessors of money, when in truth they themselves are possessed by money. On the contrary, those are truly just and happy who, though situated amidst the greatest riches, consider themselves the ministers of God, the guardians of the poor, and the distributors of wealth. 

You are a fortunate young man indeed to have recently found such patrons. I have enjoyed such patrons for a long time. And you will wonder, Angelo, if I say that I am most sorrowful because of the absence of my Giuliano <note>Giuliano de' Medici (1453–1478), the younger brother of Lorenzo the Magnificent</note>. Truly, unless Matteo Franco <note>Matteo Franco (1447–1494) was a priest and poet famous for his sharp wit and humorous exchanges with Pulci</note> were now seasoning me with his wit—me, who am as if tasteless <note>original: "insipidum... salibus"; Ficino plays on the double meaning of "sal" as both salt and wit. Without the "salt" of his friends, he feels flavorless</note> because of Giuliano's departure—I would either not smell quite right to myself, or I would certainly fly back immediately to the sweetest flowers and scents of Giuliano's presence. In any case, Poliziano, I shall hardly contain myself here for three days.

#### The goodness and dignity of the legal scholar.

### Marsilio Ficino to Angelo Nicolini <note>Angelo Nicolini (1450–1525) later became a prominent diplomat and cleric; here, Ficino addresses him as a student of law following in his father’s footsteps</note>, the distinguished son of the distinguished legal scholar Otto and heir to his father’s art, sends greetings.

<margin>p</margin>A painter who uses his art wrongly is not necessarily a bad painter because of this, but rather a bad man. Therefore, a good painter and a good man are not one and the same, for there is a great difference between goodness and the skill of painting. The same holds true in the other arts. 

But truly, a legal scholar <term>iurisconsultus</term> <note>A technical term for a jurist or expert in the law who provides legal opinions</note> who uses the law illegitimately is both a bad legal scholar and a bad man. Therefore, a legitimate legal scholar is a good man and a legitimate citizen. So great is the affinity between skill in civil law and a man's virtue. 

As you know, he who counterfeits a coin—a truly worthless thing dug from the bowels of the earth—is punished with the severest judgment by human law. How much more rigidly then will he be punished by divine law who counterfeits the law itself, which is a most precious thing sent from heaven? I approve of you, therefore, my Angelo, for using the law legitimately. 

Go on, I pray. Despise threats and allurements with a high mind; Almighty God, the author and teacher of the law, its end and reward, will not desert you. Go on, friend, do not doubt; you will pile up incorruptible riches with God. Great also is the dignity of the legal scholar among men. He is the public patron of citizens, the common oracle of the city, and the interpreter of the divine mind and will. Farewell.

#### The dignity of the priest.

### Marsilio Ficino to Pace, a priest and professor of canon law, sends greetings.

<margin>s</margin>Often I and Riccardo Angelleri, a distinguished theologian, discuss together the dignity of the priest. We concluded at last that, just as there is nothing better than a good angel after God, and nothing worse than a bad one, so nothing on earth is more beautiful than an honorable priest, and nothing more foul than a shameful one.

One man is the salvation of religion, the other its plague. What is a legitimate priest? Nothing but a mind dedicated to God. An angel acting in God's place among men. A living temple of God. ### Marsilio Ficino to Mariano, Bishop of Cortona <note>Mariano Salvini, a relative of Ficino's who served as Bishop of Cortona</note>, sends greetings.

Our cousin Sebastiano Salvini <note>original: "Bastianus saluinus"; Sebastiano was Ficino’s cousin, a translator and priest who helped disseminate Ficino's works</note> comes to you to request the third mystery of holy orders, and, as I believe, to receive them. You, however, who do not know the man and know that "holy things should not be given to dogs," <note>A reference to Matthew 7:6</note> will perhaps say: "Marsilio, it is necessary that he who is to perform such a great office be literate, pious toward God, and just toward men. Who will testify or stand surety that this young man will be such a person?" I respond to you, venerable father, with that saying of Socrates: "Just as the vessel is known by its ring, so a man is known by the sound of his voice." Therefore, to a certain person who met him and remained silent, he said: "Speak, stranger, so that I may see you." <note>This famous Socratic anecdote suggests that speech reveals the soul, which is the true essence of a person</note> This is because he judged the soul alone to be the man. Furthermore, if you possessed the art of Zopyrus <note>Zopyrus was a physiognomist in ancient Greece who claimed he could judge a person's character from their physical appearance</note>, you might perhaps apply it to consider his natural character. But the Master of Life <note>A reference to Christ, specifically John 7:24</note> forbids a man to be judged according to his face. You seek a guarantor? You have Marsilio. Do you wish for one even more substantial? The Bishop of Volterra <note>Antonio degli Agli (1400–1477), a humanist and prelate</note> stands as surety. The young man was educated at the homes of both.

->No harmony delights more than that of the heart and the tongue.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to the Magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" (1449–1492), the de facto ruler of Florence and Ficino's primary patron</note>, sends greetings.

Bastiano Foresi <note>A Florentine poet and friend of the Medici</note> sends to you his poem, *The Triumph of Virtues Against Vices*, a work worthy of such a great title. Read the poem, Lorenzo, and choose the poet; for in his soul, too, the virtues triumph over the vices. No dissonance offends more, nor does any harmony delight more, than that of the heart and the tongue.

->On the duty of a citizen.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Pietro Nero <note>original: "Petro Hero"; Pietro Nero was a student and friend of Ficino</note>, sends greetings.

Tell me, Pietro, why is it that when a fever invaded your uncle Bernardo, it suddenly set me on fire as well? Is it perhaps because we are such close neighbors that the "Dog Star" <note>the star Sirius, associated with the "dog days" of summer and the spread of fever</note> could not vomit its flames onto one without reaching the other? I hope he recovers quickly so that Marsilio may recover—or rather, so that Florence may be in better health. If the city always had such doctors as she has in him, she would never be seriously ill. For these men rightly perform the duty of a citizen, without which the good health of the fatherland is not preserved. It is the duty of a citizen to consider the city as a single living animal, composed of citizens as if they were its parts. And the part ought to serve the whole, not the whole the part. For when only the benefit of the part is sought, the benefit of both—the part and the whole—is utterly lost. But when the good of the whole is sought, the good of both is preserved. Therefore, a citizen ought to remember that nothing, whether good or evil, can happen to any member of the city without affecting the whole, because of their connection.

Therefore, let no one in this urban family say, "this is mine" and "that is yours," for all things in this great animal are, in a certain way, common. Finally, let him know that the best place in the heavenly homeland is reserved for him who, to the best of his ability, has arranged the earthly homeland according to the heavenly model. For to the Ruler of the common world, nothing is more pleasing than the common good. ### What it is to live well.

->Marsilio Ficino to his friend Girolamo Pasqualino, sends greetings.<-

You ask what it is to live well. Nothing more useful can be asked. To live well is to understand the truth; to deliberate well; to will the good; and to do good things. The first belongs to wisdom. The second to prudence. The third to justice. The fourth to perseverance. The first comes from God. The second from the first. The third from God and man together. The fourth comes from the third. Those who live thus, live as men. Those who live otherwise, live as animals. Farewell, and live as a man.

### Vows are not to be despised.

->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Marescalco of Ferrara, his excellent fellow-philosopher, sends greetings.<-

I have not yet finished the book *On the Christian Religion* <note>original: "de christiana religione"; one of Ficino's major works, defending Christianity through philosophical reasoning</note>, Francesco, because while I was correcting it this August, I fell into a fever and diarrhea. Perhaps Saturn threatened this for me this year, since from the beginning of the year it was in Aquarius, the ascendant of my birth, and at this time it is in Cancer, the sixth house of my nativity <note>In traditional astrology, the Sixth House governs illness and physical health. Ficino, a physician and astrologer, frequently diagnosed his own "melancholic" temperament as being influenced by Saturn</note>. Let us now set aside celestial things—for there are those who think little of such matters—and come to super-celestial things. Listen, then, to what happened to me in this illness: I fell into such weakness, Marescalco, that I almost despaired of my health. I meditated, therefore, on whatever great things I had read over thirty years, to see if anything might occur to me that could console a sick soul. Human writers, with the exception of the Platonists, contributed nothing at all; however, the works of Christ consoled me much more than the words of philosophers. Moreover, I made vows to the Blessed Mary and asked for some sign of health. Suddenly I breathed...

...then I received a clear and manifest message of health in my dreams. Therefore, I owe a cock <note>A reference to the final words of Socrates: "Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius." Asclepius was the Greek god of medicine. Ficino is Christianizing this famous deathbed request.</note> not to Aesculapius, but my soul and body to Christ and his mother. Everything must always be taken in the best light, Marescalchi <note>Domenico Marescalchi, a close friend and correspondent of Ficino.</note>. What if God wanted to warn me with this sign during my illness so that hereafter I might confirm the doctrine of Christ with sharper wit and study? Especially since a few days later I was also freed from a burning in the urine <note>Likely a urinary tract infection or kidney stones, which Ficino suffered from frequently.</note> by a similar vow. Listen, if you please, to another wondrous and true thing. 

<margin>Pr m</margin> My father, Ficino the surgeon—a man unique in Florence in his age—was once led by a certain peasant named Pasquino to treat his son Tomma, who was very severely wounded in the head. After inspecting the incurable wound, the doctor, thinking the boy would undoubtedly perish shortly after, departed from there as if not to return. The parents of the sick boy, abandoned by the doctor, suppliantly begged the Blessed Mary for the health of their son. Therefore, at the same hour that they were praying, a certain woman of very venerable appearance appeared to Ficino—who was either yawning or certainly sleeping very lightly under an oak tree on his journey—addressing him thus: "Why are you ungrateful toward God, Ficino? Those things which you have received freely from him, do you not give freely?" He replied, "I give bread daily to beggars." She added, "Give the gifts of your art also abundantly to the needy." After three days, that peasant returned to the doctor, praying that he would return to treat his son. Ficino was indeed greatly amazed at this, for he thought the boy had died. He went there for free, admonished both by the past dream and the vow of the parents. For the peasant told him what vows he had made and at what hour. Finally, the boy emerged healthy, beyond the doctor's hope or the skill of healing. From that time on, Ficino often made vows to Mary for the health of those committed to his care, and he succeeded happily. For which reason, warn your friends: let them not despise vows. For not even Aristotle [overlooked this] in his work on general disease. Contemplated on the 6th of September, 1474, Florence.

### The Nobility, Utility, and Use of Medicine.
### Marsilio Ficino to Tommaso Valori, Distinguished Physician, Greetings.

<margin>I</margin> Read in Homer: *For a physician is a man worth many others* <note>original Greek: "ΙΗΤΡΟΣ ΓΑΡ ΑΝΗΡ ΠΟΛΛΩΝ ΑΝΤΑΞΙΟΣ ΑΛΛΩΝ"; from the Iliad, book 11.</note>. And rightly so. For the sacred Hebrew scriptures teach that the faculty of healing is a gift of God rather than an invention of men: *Honor the physician, for the Most High created him because of necessity* <note>A reference to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 38:1, a common justification for the dignity of medicine.</note>. Furthermore, the Gentiles hold that the authors of this art were gods. This same person [Homer] followed Apollo, Aesculapius, and individual physicians with divine honors; for they dedicated shrines to Chiron, Machaon, Podalirius, Hippocrates, and Hermagoras. Hippocrates confirmed these things in his letters to the Abderites, saying that medicine is a gift of the gods and should be free, and that he never accepted a fee for its use. Also, in a letter to Philomenes, he says: "Medicine is close to prophecy; for Apollo is the single parent of these two arts, who is indeed our progenitor; he predicts future diseases...

<sig>C 2</sig>

<summary>Ficino recounts a miraculous healing involving his father and a vision of the Virgin Mary, then begins a letter to Tommaso Valori arguing for the divine and prophetic nature of the medical profession.</summary>
<keywords>medicine, miracles, Virgin Mary, Asclepius, Marsilio Ficino, Tommaso Valori, divine gift, healing, Apollo, Hippocrates</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the divine nature of the medical profession, likely following the anecdote of Ficino's father and the miraculous healing of the boy Tomma. It shifts here into a broader philosophical defense of medicine as a sacred art practiced by prophets, kings, and the greatest philosophers of antiquity.</meta>

# BOOK

...and he cures those who are affected by ill health. For this reason, it is said that Pythagoras, Empedocles, and Apollonius of Tyana <note>Apollonius of Tyana was a first-century Greek philosopher and reputed miracle-worker often compared to Pythagoras.</note> cured diseases not so much with herbs as with incantations. He <note>Likely referring to Pythagoras or a similar sage</note> believed the soul of the sick person must be purged with sacred reasons and rites before the body, because an art of this kind is both received from the divine and practiced divinely. Since the soul depends on God, and the body depends on the soul, do not the Hebrews maintain that the Archangel Raphael <note>The name Raphael literally means "God heals" in Hebrew.</note> practiced the work of this art? 

Let us pass over the others; Christ himself, as the physician of the human race, cured the sick and as many as were brought to him, and he handed down the power of healing to his disciples. Therefore, kings once did not disdain to study and practice this art as the most noble of all—kings such as Sabor and Ginges of the Medes, Sabid the King of the Arabs, Mithridates the King of the Persians <note>Mithridates VI of Pontus was famous in antiquity for his study of poisons and antidotes.</note>, and Hermes the King of the Egyptians <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Hermetic philosophy, to whom many medical and alchemical works were attributed.</note>. There was also Mesue, the nephew of the King of Damascus. Some even wish for Avicenna <note>The famous Persian polymath Ibn Sina; Ficino here notes a tradition claiming him as a prince of Córdoba.</note> to have been a prince of Córdoba. The most illustrious philosophers—Democritus, Timaeus Locrus, Plato, and Aristotle—wrote on this art, as did countless other noble philosophers. 

How great the nobility of medicine is has been said almost as much as this letter allows. We can see how great its utility is from this: that the arts directed toward living well seem to be of little use without its help. For we cannot live well unless we are alive, nor can we make much progress in any faculty during this very brief span of life unless we are in good health; nor can we easily deserve much from men or God unless we live long and sober lives. Diligence in medicine supplies every faculty of this kind. 

However, one must use this art with the highest piety toward God and charity toward men, just as Luke the Evangelist <note>Tradition holds that Saint Luke was a physician.</note> and the divine physicians Cosmas and Damian <note>Twin brothers and Christian martyrs who practiced medicine without charging fees.</note> taught us by their example. For God is the author of all good things, and a legitimate physician is like a certain god among men, for he restores them to life from death. He is even honored as a god by kings and wise men when they are sick. 

Everyone confesses that a physician needs sharpness of doctrine and experience. No one doubts that gravity and diligence in deliberation are also required. But once a decision has been maturely reached, Hippocrates of Abdera <note>Ficino likely means Hippocrates of Cos, though he connects him here to Abdera, the home of Democritus.</note> says that delay can harm no art more than this one. Nevertheless, it is no less—indeed more—dangerous, as Galen says to Glaucon, to anticipate or impede nature. For he says that many are lost daily through this error—that is, the rashness of doctors who either hinder or hurry nature. He who does not rely solely on his own wit will more easily avoid this error. For Hippocrates wrote to Democritus that even though he was established in old age, he had not yet reached the end of medicine. Galen also said that when he was ninety years old, only then did he truly grasp the nature of the pulse. 

Above all, the physician must remember that God is the author of health, and that nature is the instrument of God for producing and preserving health. The physician is the servant of both; he prepares not the strength, but the material for the craftsman, and he removes impediments. If he should wish to move or stop the material at an improper time, he often does both poorly and hinders nature, which [works] well...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical defense of medicine, transitioning from a discussion of ancient sage-physicians to the specific advice of Plato regarding the treatment of the body and the preservation of health through natural means rather than harsh drugs.</meta>

# FIRST BOOK XXVII

...both should be followed. But let us hear our divine Plato speaking on this matter in the *Timaeus* according to the mind of the Pythagoreans: "Of all motions, the best is that which occurs within itself and from itself. For it is most closely related to the motion of the mind and of the universe itself. But that motion which comes from another is inferior. The worst motion, however, is when a body lying down and at rest is moved by others in its individual parts. For this reason, among all purifications and seasonings of the body, that which happens through gymnastic exercise is the healthiest. Closely following this is easy transport, whether by ship or any other vehicle. A third species of movement is useful only when extreme necessity compels it, but otherwise should by no means be undertaken by a man of sane mind: that medical purgation <note>In this context, "purgation" refers to the medical practice of clearing the body of "humors" through laxatives or emetics.</note> which is usually done with drugs, that is, with dissolutive medicines. For diseases, unless they are extremely dangerous, should not be provoked by drugs."

For every constitution of diseases in animals is in some way similar to the nature of the animals themselves. Indeed, the composition of animals from the very beginning of their generation is limited by certain cycles of time. Both the genus as a whole suffers this, and every individual animal contains within itself from birth a fated span of living, except for necessary passions <note>Here "passions" refers to external accidents or injuries rather than emotions.</note>. For the triangles <note>original: "trianguli" — In the *Timaeus*, Plato posits that the four elements are composed of microscopic triangles; the strength and "fit" of these triangles determine the health and lifespan of the body.</note>—that is, the proportional qualities possessing power from the very beginning of each individual—cohere sufficiently for the use of life up to a certain time; beyond that, life is extended to no one. The same mode of constitution applies to illnesses. If anyone tries to cut these short with drugs before their fated course of time, great illnesses usually emerge from small ones, and many from few. Therefore, diseases must be corrected and governed with diligence of diet as much as leisure allows, nor should a difficult and troublesome evil be goaded with drugs.

These are the words of Plato. The Florentine people often commend our Galileo <note>This refers to Galileo Bonaiuti, a famous 14th-century physician and ancestor of the later scientist Galileo Galilei.</note> who used this rule. I also highly praise Lorenzo Marcellino, a true physician, for this reason. I would also praise Tommaso Valori greatly, if I were not writing to him. Farewell, and give my best regards to Antonio Benivieni <note>Antonio Benivieni (1443–1502) was a pioneering Florentine physician often considered the founder of pathological anatomy.</note>, a good doctor. Our companion Girolamo Amati, who is very delightful in the study of both medicine and the cithara <note>A stringed instrument similar to a lyre; Ficino was famous for using "spiritus" and music as a form of therapy.</note>, also greets you.

->Time must be spent sparingly.<-

Marsilio Ficino to the Magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, Greetings.

Greetings a thousand times, my health after God. I thought it a sin, as soon as my hand could guide a pen, to write to anyone else before my sole patron. What then should I write most of all? I would certainly write to you now in a more serious style than is my custom, for "not always do the orchards and humble tamarisks flourish" <note>original: "non semper arbusta viuant humilesque myricae" — A reference to Virgil's Fourth Eclogue, suggesting that the writer is moving from lighter to weightier subjects.</note>. But what prevents me, Marsilio, from doing so at present? Especially since you are writing to him who not only permits it but even long ago commanded it of you in his letters. Lorenzo, in this illness of mine, nothing afflicted my mind more sharply than the memory of time spent uselessly; on the other hand, nothing remained that could comfort me even a little...

# BOOK

...he might be comforted, except for the memory of those things I had learned—and who has not learned much? For truly the divine mind is delighted, nourished, and increased by the divine food of truth alone. Other delusions of fleeting trifles do not fill the immortal mind, which, by a certain natural instinct, demands things that are eternal and immense. I beseech you, therefore, my dearest patron, by the heavenly God, that you spend even the smallest amount of this most precious and briefest time sparingly and wisely, lest you ever repent in vain for a loss that is unrecoverable and wasteful. 

<margin><image-desc>a pointing hand (manicula) directed toward the text</image-desc></margin>
The loss of time frequently brought Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle</note>, when he was eighty years old, to tears. The loss of time often forced the great Cosimo <note>Cosimo de' Medici (1389–1464), the grandfather of Lorenzo the Magnificent and Ficino's original patron</note>, when he was more than seventy years old, to sigh heavily in my presence. 

Oppose, I pray, to empty cares, superfluous games, and unnecessary business, that Socratic saying: "Go far from here, sacrilegious enemies! Depart immediately, thieves of my soul, lest I be forced to depart from myself." These things steal you from yourself little by little, and they lead captive a great man, a man born to command. Redeem yourself, I pray, from this wretched captivity while you can; but you can only do so today. Today, for the first time, be your own master. Believe me, it is not the mark of a wise man to say "I shall live"; a life tomorrow is too late—live today. 

<margin><image-desc>a pointing hand (manicula) directed toward the text</image-desc></margin>
What I ask is easy, Lorenzo. It is not difficult to spend one hour rightly and usefully. I pray, use one hour well every day—that is, to nourish the mind with liberal studies <note>The "liberal arts" or "humanities," intended to free the mind for higher thought</note>—and for that tiny bit of time, live happily for yourself. Spend the rest, if you wish, for others; for, as you know, you must often live for others if you wish to live for yourself. But do both by the grace of God. Indeed, you were created first for the grace of God, and then for the sake of yourself and others. Indulge rarely and little in games and jokes, for I know—and I know what I am talking about—that God has prepared you for greater, or rather, the greatest things. 

Such false delights vanish as quickly as a lightning flash, so that while they seem to arise, they turn into their opposite. But do not promise me "tomorrow" any further. You promise what you neither have nor know you will have. If you only eat or drink tomorrow, will you not perish in three days, my friend? Let that "tomorrow" <note>original: "cras"</note> perish today; let it perish as soon as possible, lest you perish yourself. Nothing is more deceitful than that "tomorrow"; it has deceived every person the earth has brought forth. 

Alas, what are you doing, foolish Ficino? <note>original: "ficine" — The author, Marsilio Ficino, addresses himself in a moment of self-correction</note> Look, will Lorenzo knit his brows, or will he laugh? Either is bad. No, both are good. For I know the character of doctors. From a good man comes nothing but good. But with this letter, I am not warning Lorenzo so much as Marsilio and all other mortals. We all labor most seriously under this disease. That "tomorrow" will happen. We hardly possess the present time; for we possess it so lightly that we are unable to retain it for even a moment. But the future is nothing; therefore, no one possesses the future. O madmen! O wretched ones! We cast our hopes into nothingness, and we always abuse the treasure we possess. Yet we wish to use rightly that which we least possess. Thus, we are all sick almost to the point of destruction. 

Therefore, we must not seek Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon, the most influential medical writer of antiquity</note> or Hippocrates <note>The legendary "Father of Medicine"</note>, but Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of healing</note> and Apollo <note>The god of light, music, and prophecy, often invoked by Ficino as a healer of the soul</note>. Fare well today; if you fare well tomorrow, you will never fare well. But I wish with this seal...

# BOOK ONE

...seal this letter; neither ever listen to flatterers nor give ear to any detractors, with whom every great house abounds. The former try to tear out the eyes of your mind; the latter try to cut off your hands—that is, <note>Latin: "i." (id est)</note> your friends. ->A human without religion is unhappier than the beasts.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Benedetto Colucci of Pistoia, Rhetorician. Greetings. <note>Benedetto Colucci was a humanist educator and friend of Ficino from the Pistoian school.</note>

<margin>b</margin> You urge me to persevere diligently in the defense of religion, just as I have begun. I shall indeed endeavor to do so to the best of my strength, Benedetto. Not because religion stands in need of such defenders—for it stands firm against its enemies, with God always ruling, who wills to be honored among all nations—but because I seem to myself to live happily, or rather, only then to live at all, when I write, speak, or think about divine things. Indeed, I believe that if divine worship were removed, the human race would be unhappier than all the animals. I set aside the constant and manifold care of this defenseless, weak, and ever-ailing little body; even the very inquiry of reason, which seems to make us superior to the beasts, would undoubtedly render us more wretched than them if divine hope were taken away—on account of our regret for the past, our fear of the future, our anxiety for the present, our knowledge of evils, and our insatiable desire for innumerable things. Blessed are the heavenly beings who know all things as if in light. Secure are the beasts who, as if in darkness, understand nothing at all. Anxious and miserable are humans, who dwell in a kind of middle mist, stumbling and vexed. Only the divine light, by the merit of piety and the gift of mercy, can bestow upon us truth and blessedness.

### Lorenzo de' Medici to Marsilio Ficino, Platonic philosopher. Greetings.

<margin>p</margin> Your letter was most pleasant to me. It so reproved the loss of past time in us that our leisure does not seem to have been entirely useless. For it has happened, by the private loss of a small amount of time, that these precepts have flowed from you, which are able to benefit not only us, but all those who labor under the same disease. You had indeed often declared your mind toward us. But to me, revolving this letter of yours more often in my mind, you seem to have surpassed every other duty of friendship—whether because you hold the first place in love toward us and far excel others in friendship, or because you are able to provide those gifts of friendship abundantly which others cannot. For others who follow us with goodwill can help either with riches, honors, or pleasures; all of which are so placed in the power of Fortune that we have nothing more firm or more constant than their weakness and volatility, as you have often taught and we have even more often experienced. But you abound in these precepts, and you deal with us with that kind of friendship, so that it easily appears that just as you yield to none of your friends in virtue, so you surpass the rest in love. You do this indeed by a natural...

# BOOK ONE

...by that certain beneficence of yours. You do, moreover, what does not escape you: that virtues were given to humans by the immortal God on this condition: that they should be lived by as many people as possible; nor can you be induced to abuse this divine liberality. I rejoiced in a wonderful way that you have recovered your former health. I would rejoice much more if I might attain through your letters that my former health of mind were restored to me. I certainly do not despair of this, both because of your most weighty precepts and because, as you know, I wander <note>original: "deliro"; implying a state of mental distraction or folly</note> not out of malice but rather out of a certain lightness of nature and habit. 

Indeed, your part is the same as the Apostle's: that you argue, rebuke, and beseech <note>Reference to 2 Timothy 4:2: "Preach the word... reprove, entreat, rebuke."</note>; and since you understand that I am moved by things of this kind, do not cease to use all those spurs with us, by which you think our more prostrate mind can be raised. This one thing I strive for and expect from you, which no one desires more willingly or advises more wisely than you. I congratulate you again, and myself, that the immortal God has restored you safe and sound to us; nor was I less warned than you by the danger to your life. For the same fate would have snatched away both darkness from your eyes and light from ours; for nothing can illuminate our life more than your most weighty and loving admonitions and your most pleasant company. If these were extinguished, a full half of our life would be utterly extinguished—and indeed that part, outside of which whatever exists is nothing. Warned by this danger, I shall enjoy your company more willingly and more often. And since the human condition is such that it is moved more by examples than by reasons, I shall use both you and time by this law: time, as if I were to have no tomorrow; and you as a man for whom not even a moment of time remains free from the fear of death. Farewell, and take care of your health. Florence, September 22, 1474.

->To no one who is rightly willing is the way to the good entirely closed.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Niccolò Michelozzi <note>Niccolò Michelozzi (1447–1527) was a chancellor of the Florentine Republic and a dedicated secretary to Lorenzo de' Medici.</note>, a true man, sends greetings.<-

<margin>s</margin> Those who refute someone, Michelozzi, are accustomed to doing so in no other way than by contradicting them. But our friend Lorenzo de' Medici, even when he agrees with me most, then refutes me most. For while he most artistically praises my letter in which I rebuke his loss of past time, he shows that not even a point of his age was spent unprofitably by him. But if our patron Lorenzo is such a man in his negligence that he seems to have been diligent, what kind of person do you think he will turn out to be if he wishes and is able to be more diligent? I pray that he indeed wills this; and I beseech God that he may be able. Indeed, there is not so much need to beseech God that he may be able as that he may will it. This is both because the way to the good is never closed to anyone who is rightly willing, and because God hears an honorable will rather than the prayers of words. Farewell; and exhort Lorenzo to diligence, so that in a short time he may surpass the Latins <note>Ficino refers here to the "Latini," the contemporary humanists writing in Latin.</note> in learning as much as he surpasses his fellow citizens in authority without controversy.

->FIRST<-

<margin>for</margin> Just as harmony, while present, glides into our ears and affects us more vehemently than when it is merely thought of in the past; and just as a battle moves us more sharply when it is witnessed than when it is narrated: so the outstanding works of illustrious men inflame us more ardently toward virtue and form us more exactly than the words of orators and philosophers disputing about morals. For it is so arranged by nature that things themselves have much greater power than their names. Indeed, the very truth of things moves the soul more effectively than that which is merely probable or false. For this reason, the imitation of Socratic character <note>original: "socraticorum morum"; referring to the lifestyle and ethical conduct of Socrates</note> has instructed more people more truly toward virtue than Aristotle's discipline concerning morals. And Christ alone, by his example, has benefited more people more greatly toward an honest and holy life than all the orators and philosophers have with their words. Therefore, I praise you, my Lorenzo, because you do not despise moral reading; yet you far prefer imitation to reading, as if it were a living thing. Especially since you have for a long time proposed to yourself that old man to be imitated—he who was judged by a decree of the senate to be the Father of his Country <note>original: "patrem patriae"; a title bestowed upon Cosimo de' Medici posthumously in 1465</note>. I speak of the great Cosimo, your grandfather, my patron: a man prudent before all others toward God, pious toward men, just and magnificent, temperate in himself, exceedingly diligent in family matters, and much more accurately circumspect in the republic; he who lived not for himself alone, but for God and his country. In his soul, nothing was more humble among men, yet nothing was more exalted. Lorenzo, I philosophized happily together with him for more than twelve years; he was as acute in disputation as he was prudent and brave in governing. Truly, I owe much to our Plato; but I confess I owe no less to Cosimo. For that **Idea** <term>Idea: In Platonic philosophy, the perfect, eternal form of a virtue or object of which earthly examples are mere shadows</term> of the virtues which Plato showed me once, Cosimo acted out every day. I pass over now the other good qualities of this man. Cosimo was as miserly and stingy with his time as Midas was with his money. And since he spent his days most sparingly and counted his hours intensely—as a man most greedy for moments—he frequently lamented the loss of hours. Finally, imitating Solon the philosopher, though he had philosophized excellently throughout his whole life even in the highest business, he philosophized most of all in those days when he migrated from this shadow toward the light. And so, after we read Plato’s book *On the One Principle of Things and the Sovereign Good* <note>Likely referring to the Parmenides or the Philebus</note>—as you know, who were present—he departed shortly thereafter, as if he were already about to possess in abundance that very Good which he had tasted in disputation. Farewell; and just as God formed the world according to the Idea <note>the divine pattern</note>, so may you yourself shape your life, as you have begun, according to the Idea of Cosimo.

### The divinity of the soul from invention.

<margin>H</margin>itherto, I have spoken with you most religiously, most religious Lorenzo, in a certain temple of yours of the Christian religion <note>Ficino refers to his recently completed work, "De Christiana Religione," which he had dedicated to Lorenzo</note>. And I spoke so much about God that I did not notice any need for a letter. Today, for the first time, having completed the sacred discourses and departed from the temple, I recognized that I now require the help of a letter. Arise then, my letter: arise. Approach God: today you must carry greetings to Pisa, to him through whom Florence is safe.

## Marsilio Ficino to his Lorenzo de' Medici, Greetings.

### A truly marvelous thing.

<margin>O</margin>r rather, even too foolish. From where does this come, best Lorenzo? I began a little while ago, appearing quite fine to myself. Now, suddenly after the greeting, all invention <note>original: "inuentio"; the rhetorical skill of finding or creating arguments</note> fails. Perhaps, Marsilio, this is the highest health <note>original: "salus"; a wordplay on "salus" meaning both "health/safety" and "a greeting"</note>: to find nothing at all beyond health itself. But truly, I do not think it is health to be deprived of invention. Will you then, poor letter, carry nothing further with you? Nay, I want a few more words with you. For behold, in the meantime, I have found something else to be carried, though perhaps this itself is ridiculous: why I find nothing. Halt your step, letter, and receive this as well. I find a third thing: that I just now recognized invention to fail because I am usually accustomed to finding many things. But do not hurry. Receive first, if you please, a fourth: that from abundance, lack is often recognized, just as a privation is recognized from a habit <note>a reference to Aristotelian logic where one understands a lack only by knowing what the full state should be</note>. Do you want a fifth? Turn the dialectical scales: that from lack, as if from a privation, the appetite for abundance arises and grows as if for its own habit. But look, somehow a sixth thing sprouts in my presence: that appetite, since it draws its natural origin from lack, is always poor. Yet never—which can be called the seventh—is the human soul poor, for it generates abundance even from lack, and weaves an invention from the privation of invention. From the dark boundaries of the earth it digs out the whiteness of silver and the brilliance of gold; this is surely the land of the living in which they see the goods of God: the land into which souls are eternal, whose fruit is never-failing and whose motion is perpetual. Let us therefore cultivate this land, my soldier, the letter asks; this will provide us with the most fertile, incorruptible, and sweetest fruits. But I do not wish to press the little back of this small letter with a heavier burden. Farewell now, bold letter. And after the greeting: O Medici, bid him be well and happy, and ask him to return.

This letter to Lorenzo, both as it was being born and immediately after it was brought forth, flattered me excessively, as is usually the case. But a little while later, upon consideration, it pleased me less. Yet, whatever its quality may be, it belongs to doctors <note>Ficino often uses medical metaphors for his philosophical work, viewing himself as a physician of the soul</note>. I, however, like a just man, return to each his own: if anything of the worst sort from the writings of schoolmasters has come into your hands in these years, read it to Lorenzo. Then, soon after, you shall read my letter to him, so that when compared to the worst, it may cause less offense. But, look here, I pray you to read it elegantly: partly with a sweet voice, and partly with a "round mouth" <note>original: "ore rotundo"; a classical reference to a polished, eloquent style of speaking</note>; thus, perhaps finally deceived by its flavor <note>original: "suco," literally 'juice' or 'sap,' referring to the vitality of the prose</note>, he will praise it a little. Or certainly he will say: "At least Marsilio sent something; I prefer inept servants to lazy ones, and lazy ones to none at all." I gladly accept that you commend Giovanni Pietro of Padua to me. For philosophy also commends him to me, since he seems to be a philosopher as much by nature as by study. Farewell.

### On perseverance.
-> Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Altoviti, Greetings. <-

Those who grab us by the neck or the hands pull the body. Those who capture the senses through the eyes, or the soul and mind through the ears and hearing, pull the person. You have just now captured our soul by the ears. For so many and such great reports concerning your elegance and constancy have sounded in my ears through the words of our friend Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Ficino's closest friend and frequent messenger</note> that I could not, nor would I wish to, restrain myself from greatly esteeming and loving you. Let this letter be a sign of our love for the present; it confirms your constancy and exhorts you to perseverance. For the one cannot exist without the other. Nor does a man seem worthy of approval among the wise whom fortune has not yet sufficiently tested. Nor has he been sufficiently tested by fortune unless he has persevered until the very end. How great a good perseverance is, is indicated by this: that while other virtues promise good things, perseverance provides them. Indeed, the more difficult it is, the more praiseworthy it is compared to the rest. But do not let difficulty terrify you. For all the labors of human virtue are very brief, while the reward is eternal. Add to this that the burning purpose of a clear mind illuminates the obscure, warms the cold, softens the hard, and tames the untameable. Farewell.

### It is the mark of a wise man to desire nothing except the health of the soul and the good health of the body.
-> Marsilio Ficino to his friend Andrea Cambini, Greetings. <-

There are many mortals, Andrea, who are so greedy that they desire many and diverse things daily—indeed, they desire countless things, like the insatiable. My Cambini, as one who is wise and moderate, desires, I believe, nothing other than the health of the soul and the good health of the body. Therefore, be saved and be well <note>original: "Salve igitur simul & Vale"; Ficino puns on 'salve' as both a greeting and a reference to salvation/health, and 'vale' as both 'goodbye' and 'be strong'</note>.

# BOOK
<header>FIRST [BOOK]</header>

...and refer it back. They think that medicine proceeds from Jove, and music from Mercury and Venus. Our Platonists, however, refer both to one god: namely, Apollo. The ancient theologians considered him the inventor of medicine and the king of playing the lyre <term>cithara: a stringed instrument similar to a lyre, used in ancient Greece for formal recitals</term>. In his book of hymns, Orpheus believes that this god grants health and life to all with vital rays and drives away diseases. Moreover, he believes that with tuneful strings—that is, by his own motions and powers—Apollo tempers all things: with the *hypate* <note>original: "hypate," the lowest-sounding string in the ancient Greek musical system</note> (that is, the low voice), he brings winter; with the *nete* <note>original: "neate," the highest-sounding string</note> (that is, the high voice), he brings summer; and with the Dorian modes <note>original: "dorionibus"</note> (that is, the middle voices), he produces spring and autumn.

Since, therefore, the same being is the leader of music and the discoverer of medicine, what wonder is it that both arts are often practiced by the same men? It is added that the soul and body resonate with each other by a certain natural proportion. Furthermore, the parts of the soul resonate among themselves, as do the parts of the body. Indeed, the harmonic cycles of fevers and humors <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were the bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that determined health and temperament</note>, as well as the motion of the pulse itself, seem to imitate this resonance.

As Plato and Aristotle assert, and as we ourselves have often experienced, serious music preserves and restores the resonance of the parts of the soul, while medicine preserves the harmony of the bodily parts. Since, therefore, the body and soul agree within themselves (as we have said), it can easily be within the power of the same man to cultivate the harmony of the parts of the soul and the parts of the body. Hence, Chiron <note>The centaur of Greek mythology, teacher of Achilles and a master of both music and healing</note> practiced both faculties; and hence the prophet David is said to have cured the soul and body of the raving Saul with the Lyre.

Democritus and Theophrastus affirmed that this could also be achieved in other diseases of both body and soul. Pythagoras, Empedocles, and the physician Asclepiades even demonstrated it through practice. Nor is that wonderful. For since song and sound proceed from the thought of the mind, the impulse of the imagination, and the affection of the heart—and together with the "broken" and tempered air, they strike the aerial spirit <term>spiritus: in Ficino's philosophy, a subtle vapor that acts as the "knot" or bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul</term> of the listener—they easily move the imagination, affect the heart, and penetrate the innermost recesses of the mind.

It also stops and moves the humors and limbs of the body. Timotheus showed this when he excited King Alexander to fury with sounds, and then restrained him. I pass over the miracles of Pythagoras and Empedocles, who suddenly restrained lust, anger, and fury with more serious music, and conversely excited sluggish minds with other melodies. I also pass over what is told of Orpheus, Arion, and Amphion.

But to return to the purpose: the first music consists in reason; the second in imagination; the third in speech (song follows this). Song follows the movement of the fingers in sound, and sound follows the motion of the whole body in gymnastics or dancing. We see, therefore, the music of the soul brought down step-by-step to all the limbs of the body. Orators, poets, painters, sculptors, and architects also imitate this in their works.

Since there is such great communion between the soul and the body, what wonder is it that both the body and the soul are tempered by the same man? Finally, he who has learned from the Pythagoreans, Platonists, Hermes, and Aristoxenus that both the soul and the body of the world—and of individual animals—consist of musical ratios; and he who has received from the sacred letters of the Hebrews that God disposed all things in "number, weight, and measure" <note>A reference to the biblical Book of Wisdom 11:20</note>, will neither wonder that almost all animals are captivated by harmony, nor will he accuse Pythagoras, Empedocles, or even Socrates (who played the lyre even in his old age). Instead, he will accuse the poorly learned Themistocles, who [refused?] the lyre...

<summary>Ficino argues for the shared divine origin of music and medicine under Apollo, explaining how musical harmony can heal the body and soul because they are linked by a "spirit" that responds to mathematical proportions.</summary>
<keywords>music therapy, Apollo, harmony, spiritus, soul and body, Pythagoras, David and Saul, musical ratios, ancient medicine</keywords>
