<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s discussion on the medicinal and spiritual utility of music, transitioning from ancient Greek theories of harmony into personal letters where he applies these philosophical principles to his friendships and his duties to the Medici family.</meta>

...that he would admit he refused the one offered to him at the banquet. Indeed, in the dialogue *Alcibiades* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the nature of man and the need for self-knowledge</note>, our Plato shows that music belongs to the learned who are worshippers of the Muses, saying that the Muses are the leaders of music and that music is named after them. However, Plato everywhere rejects melody that is plaintive or frivolous, because it renders the mind either broken, or lascivious and angry; he chooses only the grave and constant melody as the most healthful medicine for the spirit, soul, and body. I, however—to say something to your Marsilio—frequently apply myself to the more grave strings and songs after the study of theology or medicine with the intention of entirely neglecting other pleasures of the senses; thus I expel the troubles of the soul and body. I raise my mind to sublime things and to God to the best of my ability, relying on the authority of Mercury <note>The Roman name for Hermes, often associated by Ficino with the "Hermetic" tradition of ancient wisdom</note> and Plato, who say that music was granted to us by God for the taming of the body, the tempering of the soul, and the praising of God. I know that David <note>King David of the Bible, famous for playing the harp to soothe King Saul</note> and Pythagoras <note>The Greek philosopher who discovered the mathematical ratios of musical intervals</note> commanded this before all others, and I believe they attained it. Farewell.

### The truest praise is that which is worthy of praise.

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Aurelio of Rimini, Greetings.<-

<margin>For the greatest praise is that which is worthy of praise. Farewell.</margin>
Aurelio, you praise our lyre with songs worthy of praise. I, in turn, will praise your songs with the lyre. But I shall do so as things worthy of praise, so that you may speak the truth and I may truly speak of things usually considered empty <note>original: "vanam." Ficino likely means he will treat "empty" or worldly things with truth</note>. Let each of us praise most truly.

### He is happily loved who is loved by a man most worthy of love.

->Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo, Orator of the Venetians, Greetings.<-

I used to think, Bernardo, that I loved Marsilio <note>Ficino often speaks of himself in the third person when discussing his soul or his public persona</note> in such a way that I could never love him more, since everyone, for their own sake, loves each thing—and themselves in each thing—and loves themselves most of all. But yesterday this opinion of mine most happily deceived me. For then I first began to love myself more brightly <note>original: "argentius," literally 'more silverly,' implying a more refined or pure self-regard</note> than I was accustomed, as soon as I most certainly recognized that I was ardently loved by you, a man above others most worthy of love. Indeed, I attribute so much to Bernardo that I value myself as much as I understand I am valued by him. Who, therefore, can ever please me more than he through whom I please myself more daily? I wish that I may always please you, Bernardo, so that I may displease none of the prudent. Therefore, what gratitude shall I return for this love of yours toward me? Love. Other things are for the most part purchased at another's price. But since love is born spontaneously in free will and is therefore free, it is never bought or sold at any price, except by itself. Farewell, be happy. 7 March 1474. Florence.

### On law and justice.

->Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous man Lorenzo de' Medici, Greetings.<-

<margin>Because I wish to write at present what I ought. It is just to keep a promise...</margin>
I promised, if I remember correctly, on the Nones of March <note>March 7th</note>, to Lorenzo as he was returning from Pisa to Florence (while at another time he was traveling into the Pisan territory), that I would write something to him. Therefore, I who am always accustomed to write to friends...

...to keep. Thus it is commanded by law. Receive, therefore, a just and lawful letter. Or rather, to speak more correctly, as often as I wish, I also ought; but by the law of love, conversely, when I ought, then I also wish, but through the love of the law. Whence you shall receive today a letter both just and voluntary. To separate the voluntary from the just, or the just from the voluntary, is neither permitted to anyone, nor is it pleasing to friends. 

Behold, Marsilio, you both ought and wish now to write something to the Medici <note>original: "medicem". Ficino is likely addressing Lorenzo de' Medici or another member of the ruling family of Florence</note>. But what will you write above all, and relying on what divine power? 

O salvation of men, O Justice, queen of the world, you have long since given me the cause for writing. Now, I pray, suggest the matter, so that I may happily fulfill, with your help, what I had freely promised you by God’s command. 

That divine law by which the world exists and is governed kindles in our minds, while they are being created, the inextinguishable light of that **natural law**, to which the examination of good or evil is referred. From this natural law—which is a certain spark of the divine—proceeds the **written law**, which is a ray of that same spark. 

Moreover, these three laws—the **divine**, the **natural**, and the **written**—teach every person what justice is, so that almost no place for excuse is left for those who sin, as if they might seem to have failed entirely because of ignorance. Truly, to the eyes of the mind, these three lights show that justice is nothing other than a habit of the will, so directed and strengthened by reason that, having despised both threats and allurements, it resolves to act no differently than divinity, nature, and civility <note>original: "civilitas", referring to the duties of a citizen and social conduct</note> shall have dictated. 

For what does divinity command, except that we refer back to God—from whom we have everything—the whole edge of our thought, the movement of our will, the power of our operation, and the merits of our works? What else does Nature teach but this: that we subject money to the body, the body to the soul, the soul to reason, and reason to God? Finally, civility seems to advise that individual citizens remember they are certain members of the state. And therefore, it is fitting to love one’s country as the whole body, and the citizens as members of that same body. 

Wherefore, he will without controversy be held a just man who worships God as father and lord with incomparable piety. He will most diligently moderate his own affections and impulses. He will love men with brotherly charity; he will love himself in God, and men in himself; he will cling to God with all his strength; and he will join others with himself to divinity as far as he is able. 

Furthermore, it is the duty of the just man to render to each what is his own: to his superiors, honor and reverence; to his equals, a certain familiar intimacy; to his inferiors, help and counsel. Moreover, when he is established in the magistracies <note>Positions of high government office</note>, he should always have the law itself before his eyes like God. He should consider himself not the master of the law, but its faithful interpreter and diligent servant. In administering it, he should punish offenses with a certain equity and without agitation. He should return rewards to virtues according to merit without envy; nor should he think of his own interest, but the common good. Nor should he trust in his own intellect, but consult pious and prudent elders in all things. Let that also remain stored deep in his mind <note>original: "alta mente repostum", a classical allusion to Virgil's Aeneid</note>:

> You to whom the ruler of sea and earth has given the great right of death and life: set aside your proud and swollen expressions; whatever an inferior fears from you, a greater Lord threatens against you. <note>This verse is from the Roman philosopher Seneca the Younger’s tragedy "Thyestes", warning rulers that they too are answerable to a higher power</note>

every kingdom is under a weightier kingdom <note>original: "omne sub regno grauiori regnum est." This is a reference to the Roman playwright Seneca, implying that even earthly kings are subject to God’s justice.</note>. Enough has been said regarding what justice is, who is just, and what the duty of a just man is. Furthermore, how great the fruit of just action is can be clearly declared from this: that neither a household, nor a city, nor an army, nor any commerce whatsoever—whether among good men or bad—can stand without that just distribution which is made according to merit. Indeed, if justice is so necessary to the **machine of the world** <note>original: "mundi machinae." A common Renaissance metaphor for the universe as a complex, divinely designed structure.</note> that, were it removed, the world would immediately fall into ruin, then certainly it cannot be said how necessary it is for the life of men. Truly, if it is lacking to men, they quickly destroy one another if they are gathered together; or, if they live apart, they will be torn to pieces by wild beasts. 

O perpetual bond of the human race! O most healthful medicine for our diseases! O public soul of the city: **Justice, the blessed life.** Justice, the heavenly life. Mother and queen of the Golden Age. Sublime **Astraea** <note>In Greek mythology, Astraea was the goddess of Justice who lived among humans during the Golden Age but fled to the heavens to become the constellation Virgo when humanity became wicked.</note>, you who inhabit the starry thrones: we pray that you do not abandon your earthly seats to Diana <note>This may be a metaphorical reference to shifting from the light of justice to the "night" or "wilderness" represented by Diana as a huntress.</note>, lest we wretched ones slip into the **Iron Age**. Dwell with us, we pray, dwell forever, O heavenly divinity, so that we, the citizens of the heavenly fatherland, may imitate the life of the celestials as much as we can in the present, and fully attain it in the hereafter. Farewell.

### On the soul.

->Marsilio Ficino to his friend Francesco Tedaldo, greetings.<-

<margin>1</margin>
Lactantius Tedaldus <note>The son of Francesco Tedaldo and a student/associate of Ficino.</note>, a companion as dear to me as he is a son to you, has delivered to us in your name a small work in which the debates of Western philosophers concerning the soul are reviewed. At last, he asks what I think on this matter. While it is not my place to settle such great disputes among them, I will nonetheless say what I feel, since they ask. The books **On the Immortality of Souls** <note>Ficino refers here to his masterpiece, the *Platonica Theologia de immortalitate animorum* (Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls).</note> composed by us, which I hope will be sent to you shortly, will explain this most extensively. Meanwhile, I shall respond very briefly to that part of the dispute which they most especially desire. 

<margin>Marsilius Ficinus</margin>
First, I know indeed that my soul is a **substance** <note>In philosophy, a "substance" is something that exists in itself, whereas an "accident" is a quality (like color or height) that can only exist within a substance.</note>. Otherwise, I could not perfectly comprehend and define "substance." I would not be able to be anything more excellent than an **accident**, nor could I judge and measure how much an accident falls short of a substance. I know it is not corporeal and mortal. For I would not grasp incorporeal and immortal things, nor would I discern them from corporeal and mortal ones. I know it is **rational**. Otherwise, I would not know how to bring forth reasons concerning it and other things. 

I know that although the soul is a participant in **reason**, it is not—as some think—reason itself. For in assigning the reasons for things, souls are able to wander from the truth, and in doing things, they can wander from reason; therefore, he who affirms that the soul *is* reason wanders further from reason than he who denies it. Furthermore, reason is either a substance or a quality. If it is a substance, reason according to its essence is the highest, absolute, and utterly infinite thing. Such a thing is not the soul, but God alone. If it is a quality, it is seen to be an accidental virtue of the soul rather than the soul itself. Truly, since the soul freely dominates the substance of the body by forming it, moving it in contrary directions, and bringing it to a halt, and can take on contrary qualities in turn, no one would dare to affirm that it is a mere quality or accident. For in what way can it be called a falling or "accidental" thing, when it remains so...

# BOOK ONE

it moves equally through the genera and species of both substances and accidents. It is also reflected back into itself, both by affection and by cognition, and for that reason also by life; for it belongs to itself and not to a bodily subject. Without a bodily instrument, it acts as often as it touches and chooses incorporeal things, and it correctly distinguishes them from the corporeal. It often resists bodily inclination. Nor does it find rest in the body. Finally, the further it removes itself from the body, the more effectively it understands, and the better and more happily it conducts itself. 

The soul, therefore, is an **incorporeal, rational, and immortal substance** suited for governing the body. Many among the **Platonists** <note>Followers of Plato, who generally argued that the soul exists before it enters a physical body.</note> believe that the soul precedes the body. The **Peripatetics** <note>original: "Peripatetici." The followers of Aristotle, who generally viewed the soul as the "form" of the body, meaning they are created or exist together.</note>, on the contrary, think otherwise. However, I think those "Western" philosophers whom you praise—even if you do not declare it—are Peripatetics. For, as you say, they disputed about the soul after their banquets, like poets who thought the body should be refreshed before the soul is produced. Even if I produced the "little soul" <note>original: "animulam." A play on words referring to both the soul and the "spirit" or essence of this short letter.</note> of this short letter before my own meal, I nevertheless agree with them regarding the order of creation. Farewell. And see to it that you are frequently present at these disputes; for in this way, you will cultivate both body and soul at the same time. Our friend **Giovanni Cavalcanti** <note>A close friend and student of Ficino, often the recipient of his philosophical letters.</note> commends himself to you. You, in turn, commend me to those philosophers of yours.

->Consolation on the death of a friend.<-

Marsilio Ficino of Florence to **Bernardo Bembo** <note>A prominent Venetian diplomat and father of the famous poet Pietro Bembo.</note>, Ambassador of the Venetians, sends many greetings.
<margin>d</margin>Come now, Bernardo, tell me, if it is permitted: why do you mourn at the death of a friend? Is it for Death itself? Or for the dead man? If for Death, Bernardo, mourn your own. For just as you are certain that he has died, so you are certain that you will die—or rather, that you are dying already. For at every moment, the life that has passed perishes. If you mourn for the dead man: was he evil or good? If he was evil, it is a good thing for you to have lost such an associate. You ought not to grieve for your own good. If he was good—which I rather believe, since he was loved by a good and wise man—it is certainly good for him to live apart from the **continuous death of the body** <note>Ficino, following Platonic thought, often describes physical life as a kind of "death" or imprisonment for the eternal soul.</note>. It is not right to envy a friend for such great blessings. 

Perhaps you grieve because you will no longer see your friend as you were accustomed to do. Was your friend not simply the one who loved you? And who loved you but the soul itself, which knew you? You saw that soul then no differently than you see it now, and you see it now no less than you saw it then. Perhaps you will blame his absence. But since souls do not fill a place, they are made present not so much by location as by thought. When you do not think of him, you cannot grieve. But when you do think of him—which you can do at your own will—you immediately call him back into your presence. Therefore, you should never complain of absence; unless perhaps you object to us that the companionship of that liberated soul is not suitable to your soul, which is now shut within a body. Separate your mind from the body, Bernardo, if you can. Believe me, it will suddenly be suitable. If you cannot do so now, have no doubt that a little later—whether you wish it or not—it will be suitable. For the fact that we live, if compared to our own will, is very brief; if compared to the age of the world, it is a point; if compared to the age of God, it is even less than a point. Farewell, and live for God; who, since He alone is infinite life, alone drives death and the sorrow of death far away from His worshippers.

<header>FIRST BOOK</header>

### Marsilio Ficino to Pierfilippo of Perugia, the illustrious legal consultant, sends greetings.

<margin>I</margin>Astronomers attribute the power of kings to Jupiter and the Sun, for nothing in the heavens is more beautiful than they. What, therefore, is more beautiful on earth than a just interpreter of equity and the laws? Conversely, what is more foul than an unjust one? I believe you desire to look upon the likeness and the character of a legitimate legal consultant. O, what a beautiful sight! How wonderful is his soul: the worship of God. His spirit: the care of the laws of his fatherland. His brain: a clear judgment. His eyes and tongue: his learning. His chest: a tenacious memory. His heart: a righteous will. His hands: the fulfillment of that righteous will. His feet: perseverance. The whole of him: equity and gravity. But why do I fashion the ideal <note>original: "ideam." Ficino uses the Platonic concept of an "Idea" or perfect form.</note> of a legal consultant in words? While Pierfilippo—that painter of morals—paints himself in the person of his disciple Francesco Soderini <note>Francesco Soderini (1453–1524) was a Florentine diplomat and later a Cardinal; he was a student of both Ficino and Pierfilippo.</note>, he will achieve a true likeness of that very Idea in reality. Indeed, even if the suspicion of flattery forbids me from asserting that Pierfilippo is such a man, the truth nevertheless compels me to confess it. His teacher strives that Soderini will also be such a man. The character and the beginnings of the disciple indicate it. His father, the most famous knight Tommaso Soderini, ardently desires it. Our friend Girolamo Amati, who is most fond of him, undoubtedly promises it. Marsilio Ficino hopes for it and prays to God for it.

->That which is ardently desired is quickly acquired.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Altoviti, sends greetings.

<margin>c</margin>Your soul ardently desires, as you write to us, to fly to us. If it does not have wings, it can neither fly nor should it desire what it cannot do. If it does have them—which is what I believe instead—it flew here as soon as it desired to. Indeed, with eternal and spiritual wings, neither time nor place can stand in the way. Therefore, you already possess what you were seeking with your whole mind, unless my reasoning fails me. It follows that what you possess is as great a thing to me as it is to you: it is easy for me, who compares it, and dear to you, who possesses it. Thus, Marsilio possesses it in reality no less than Giovanni does in his estimation. Farewell. Our friend Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Ficino’s closest friend and the man he often called his "unique friend" (unicus amicus).</note> commends himself to you.

->We ought to seek the sources rather than the streams.<-

### Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Giovanni Pietro of Padua, sends greetings.

<margin>f</margin>There are many in our times who are not "philosophers" <note>original: "phylosophi." Literally "lovers of wisdom."</note> but "phylopompi" <note>original: "phylopompi." A pun combining the Greek roots for "love" and "procession" or "pomp." Ficino is calling them "lovers of ceremony" or "lovers of show."</note>, who too proudly profess that they hold the views of Aristotle. Yet, they have heard that Aristotle himself speaks only very rarely and briefly—and even then, not expressing his own thoughts in Greek, but rather babbling the thoughts of others in a barbaric tongue <note>Ficino is criticizing Scholastic scholars who read Aristotle in poor Latin translations rather than the original Greek.</note>; for this reason, they have understood very little. When these men chatter among boys in the marketplace, they seem to the common people to know something. But if you were to question them prudently at home, you would find they know little of physics, less of mathematics, and very little indeed of metaphysics. Men of this sort are still "boys" even in the seventieth year of their lives, lacking not only eloquence but even basic grammar. They do not think deeply upon natural or divine matters, but rather obsess over certain barbaric terms which they ineptly mix and confuse with one another. Whence these trivial sophists bring before the public things worthy of a circle of children rather than a crown of men. They speak in such a way that you would despise philosophy based on their speech; they live in such a way that you would despise philosophy based on their lives...

### A Peripatetic <note>A follower of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> seeks money not as a philosopher, but as a man.
### Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" (1449–1492), the de facto ruler of Florence and Ficino’s primary patron.</note>, sends greetings.

<margin>O</margin>I would recommend Oliviero Arduini, the distinguished Peripatetic, to you in no small measure, were it not that his own Aristotle recommended him to you most highly. If Aristotle—who judged money to be necessary for happiness—could have composed his books without coins, then this Peripatetic too could interpret the Aristotelian works without coins. You understand, therefore, what Oliviero wants: he is a Peripatetic, not a Cynic <note>The Cynics were a school of philosophers known for their extreme poverty and rejection of material comforts. Ficino is jokingly explaining that Arduini, as an Aristotelian, believes some material wealth is necessary for a good life.</note>. But you will say, "It is not the part of a philosopher to desire these things." Let it be so, indeed. Truly, he does not ask for these things insofar as he is a philosopher, but insofar as he is a human being. Whether it is indeed the part of a philosopher to seek money, we shall dispute after you have granted it. Farewell. Lorenzo Bonincontri of San Miniato <note>A famous humanist poet and astronomer (1410–1491).</note>, that astronomical poet and poetic astronomer, sends you his greetings.

### A recommendation by way of once-happy fortune, innocence, and knowledge.
### Marsilio Ficino to Donato, son of Carlo <note>Donato Acciaiuoli (1428–1478), a Florentine scholar and statesman.</note>, sends greetings.

<margin>C</margin>I recommend the Marsuppini family to you as much as possible; they were men once fortunate enough, but now, alas, too unfortunate. I believe they are unjustly so. Above all others, his father Carlo <note>Carlo Marsuppini (1399–1453), a famous humanist and former Chancellor of Florence.</note>, the poet, recommends the young Carlo from on high. Listen for a moment, if you please, and if you can, grant a hearing. Look, he implores you, both through your wisdom and humanity and indeed through divine mercy, at least not to abandon this learned and deeply innocent youth, today the only likeness of his father. It is not fitting for the Muse to become a beggar, nor for innocence to be made miserable. Bring help, therefore, patron of the Muses, to a foster-son of the Muses who is bound to perish without your aid. April 14, 1474. Florence.

### Precepts for memory.

### Marsilio Ficino to Banco the Mathematician <note>Banco was a Florentine associate of the Medici circle, often involved in financial and mathematical matters.</note>, sends greetings.

If you desire to have a strong remembrance of good things, strive to forget the bad. It is worth the effort to submerge worthless things in the River Lethe <note>In Greek mythology, Lethe is the river of forgetfulness in the underworld.</note> so that you may retain the precious. Flee, Banco, from the force of disturbances; flee the tumult of manifold business and thoughts. Do you wish to think usefully? Think of very few things, and those which very few people think of. This is that saying of Pythagoras: "decline the common paths; go by the side-ways." Why do we wander aimlessly? There is a need for sagacity and selection. The joyful thing lies hidden in a small plot; evil lies open everywhere; that which is good is reduced to a narrow space. 

Do you wish to excel in the memory of good things? Take diligent care that you understand the certain **reason** <term>ratio: the logical underpinning, cause, or system</term> of what is to be learned. For **reason** is the unbreakable bond of truth and memory. Because of this, perhaps, our Plato says that what is once well understood can never be entirely surrendered to oblivion. Those things also should be committed to memory which are not only useful but also pleasant. For the nourishment that brings the sweetest flavor passes more easily into our nature and is converted into us. And what is swallowed more greedily is retained for a longer time. 

Add to these what Aristotle and Simonides <note>Simonides of Ceos was a Greek poet credited with the invention of the "method of loci," a mnemonic system using mental architecture.</note> think should be strictly observed: that a certain order be either present in the things to be learned or at least devised. Order consists in a certain proportion and connection. In those things which are arranged in an ordered series, if you take up one, the rest follow immediately by a certain necessary continuation of either nature or art. Furthermore, the very intention of the mind—if it is directed toward one thing or toward a few things as if they were one—acts more vehemently than if it is distracted by many things. For every continuation and order of parts into a single thing induces both the whole itself (which is composed of them) and the mental focus. 

It must be observed, moreover, that we should meditate often on what we have learned; in this way, the nourishment of the mind is "digested" and, as it were, converted into the soul. It also helps a great deal if someone frequently reviews what they have committed to memory with elegant speech and sweet song. For pleasure is the seasoning of things and the "bait of love"—the delight of genius, the food of the will, and the strength of memory. Wonder <note>original: "admiratio"</note> also contributes much: for because of this, the mind is made more attentive and brands the marks of things deeper into its inner chambers. For this reason, children, since they wonder more because of the novelty of things...

### Definition, Duty, and the End of the Virtues.
### Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to Antonio Calderino <note>Antonio Calderino (1448–1500) was a Bolognese scholar and a correspondent of Ficino within the humanist circle.</note>.

You have often asked me, Antonio, to define the virtues for you. Perhaps you expect from me those very minute divisions of the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, known for their detailed classifications.</note> and the Stoics. Our Platonists, Calderino, are not accustomed to doing it that way. Certainly, the power of virtue consists in union rather than in division. Therefore, the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who associated numbers with metaphysical qualities.</note> thought that unity pertained to the good, and multitude to evil. I shall, therefore, define it very briefly, especially since it is better to practice the virtues than to know them.

Virtue is a habit of the soul that, through choice, contributes to happiness. There are two types of virtues. Some reside in the intellect. Others reside in the appetite, whether it be the rational or the irrational appetite. The former are called speculative <note>theoretical or intellectual</note> virtues; the latter are called moral virtues. The speculative are so named because they are acquired by contemplating <note>original: *speculando*</note>, and once acquired, they are occupied in the act of contemplating. The moral virtues, however, are so named because they are acquired through habit <note>original: *more*</note> and custom. Once acquired, they consist in the character and the practice of works. 

In the intellectual category are: wisdom, which is the contemplation of divine things; science, which is the knowledge of natural things; prudence, which is the knowledge of things to be managed correctly both privately and publicly; and finally art, which is the correct rule for performing works. 

In the other category <note>the moral virtues</note> are: justice, which spontaneously gives to each person their due; furthermore, fortitude, which, being more ready for honorable works, casts away from us the impediment of fear; and finally temperance, which repels the softness of lusts—the other impediment to honorable things. Liberality and magnificence are the companions of justice, and other virtues are similarly companions of others. To put it briefly, speculative virtue is nothing other than an acquired clarity of the intellect. Moral virtue is nothing other than a steady fervor of the appetite, ignited by the clarity of the intellect. 

One must remember, however, that nothing in human virtues is more precious than the power of choice. Plato, in his books *On the Republic* <note>original: *de Re.p.*</note>, judges that all other things should be sold [exchanged] for it. For all things hinder the person who does not know how to distinguish the good from the bad and separate the bad from the good. 

Do we wish to attain the faculty of choice? Let us consult older and more proven men in all things. Let us, therefore, consult Time above all others. For what among temporal things is older or more proven than Time? We will consult Time if we frequently and deeply consider the events of the past. For the past is the teacher of the present and the future. Also, the consideration of the future teaches us about the present. For it is most difficult to manage the present correctly unless you have considered the end and the outcome of every action. Think as much as is proper. Leave the rest to God. Approve whatever follows as if it were done by God. For he who [submits to] the divine...

### The nature and duty of the soul, and the praise of history.

Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Jacob Bracciolini, son of Poggio the orator <note>Poggio Bracciolini (1380–1459) was a famous humanist and chancellor of Florence known for recovering lost classical manuscripts.</note> and heir to his father’s art.

The ancient Platonists renewed the urban celebrations of Plato's birthday every year. The "New Platonists," however, Bracciolini, have celebrated both urban and suburban ones in our times. The suburban ones, indeed, held at the home of the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici in the countryside of Careggi, are all recounted in our book *On Love* <note>original: "de amore" — Ficino's famous commentary on Plato's Symposium, which describes a banquet held in 1468.</note>. But Francesco Bandini, a man excelling in genius and magnificence, celebrated the urban ones in Florence with royal expense. There you, and Bindaccio Ricasoli, and our Giovanni Cavalcanti, and many other academicians reclined to dine. I also was present.

And from the many and various topics we debated in that banquet, I often meditate on one in particular, and I will gladly recount it to you today: what we concluded before the feast regarding the nature of the soul. For nothing pertains more to man than what is debated concerning the soul. In this way, that Delphic precept "Know thyself" <note>original: "noſce teíp̄m"</note> is fulfilled, and all other things—whether above the soul or below the soul—are investigated more sagaciously.

For in what way can we grasp other things abundantly unless we first grasp the soul itself, through which all other things are perceived? Does one not misuse the soul if they do not strive to look upon that through which, and for whose sake, they desire to look upon all things? The rational soul, as we all agreed there, is placed on the "horizon"—that is, on the boundary of eternity and time—since it occupies a middle nature between eternal and temporal things. Being in the middle, it possesses rational powers and actions that rise toward the eternal, but it also has powers and operations that decline toward the temporal.

Rightly so, since different inclinations are born from different natures; by the very fact that we see the soul turning both to eternal and temporal things, we recognize that it is constituted from both natures. Our Plato located that superior part of the soul in the kingdom of Saturn—that is, in the realm of the mind and providence—but the inferior part in the kingdom of Jupiter—that is, of life and fate. Therefore, the soul now seems to have a twin face like a two-faced Janus <note>original: "bífrontí" — a reference to the Roman god Janus, who looks both forward and backward.</note>, namely a golden one and a silver one. With the golden face, it looks upon the things of Saturn; with the silver, the things of Jupiter.

By looking, it judges and desires. It is better to love eternal things than to judge them. They are judged well only with great difficulty. They can never be loved poorly, provided they are loved ardently, for they are never loved too much—indeed, not even enough. It is better to judge temporal things in moderation than to love them. They are usually judged quite well, but they are usually loved basely. Indeed, the judge transfers the form of the thing to be judged into himself; the lover, however, transfers himself into the form of the beloved. It is better to lift lower things up to us by judging them than to cast ourselves down to them by loving them. It is better to raise ourselves to higher things through love than to bring them down to us through judgment.

Farewell. But before I make an end, I ask you, my Bracciolini, that you do not desist from your begun study of composing histories. For historians praise the style of your writing. And the matter itself is for life; not only a delight...

...but it is also most necessary for the instruction of morals. For indeed, those things which in themselves are mortal attain immortality through history; things that are absent become present through it; old things become young again. ->### Three guides of life: and the one best way of life.<-
->#### Marsilio Ficino to Lorenzo Francesco. Greetings.<-

<margin>t</margin>There are three guides of human life. The first is reason, long and diligently examined. The second is experience of things, confirmed by long-standing habit. The third is the authority of the ancients—namely, of those who are such that they could not easily be deceived by another, nor do they themselves seem to have wished to deceive others. For more attention should be paid to what each person has done than to what he has said; to speak well is the lot of many, to act well is the lot of few. The best way of living is indeed this: that you think and strive as much as you can to live according to the mind <note>original: "secundum mentem" — referring to the higher intellect or rational soul</note>. For this is to live always and happily. Since indeed stability and tranquility are found in the mind, he who falls from the mind slips down to the lower depths. Do not strive too hard to live long in the body. For in bodily things, "long" is nothing if you compare it to eternity. Add to this that in the life of the body itself we are surpassed by many and most lowly creatures. The life of the body is a punishment and should be called the death of the soul; strive for this one thing above all others which our Plato commands in the *Gorgias* <note>A dialogue by Plato focusing on the difference between true justice and mere persuasion</note>: that you live as well as possible during that time which is assigned to you here by God. Thus the punishments of eternal misery are avoided, and the foundations of an eternal and happy life are laid with a certain divine help.

->### The method of teaching, praising, and blaming.<-
->#### Marsilio Ficino to Lorenzo Lippo the Rhetorician. Greetings.<-

<margin>q</margin>Since you have read the Greek and Latin rhetoricians, I judge that you so instruct your students that they always remember that the audience should be persuaded not of what is pleasing, but of what is lawful. For he who persuades toward what is just persuades more easily and more successfully; since indeed he has justice as a patroness in his cause. Let them remember that they must be just themselves. For if a man's life is not approved, his speech is rejected. Deeds move more vehemently than words. He moves others most who is himself moved most; but he altogether offends the ears who sings one way with his mouth and strikes the lyre another way. Divine music is the upright harmony of thoughts, words, and actions. Let them remember when they are about to praise or blame someone that the nature of things, places, and times is most vast; and so no one can be so wise and good that another wiser and better person cannot be found. Conversely, no one is so foolish or evil that there is no room for someone more foolish and worse. Therefore, one should praise sparingly, but blame even more sparingly. Furthermore, in praising, let them exhort and move the listener. No murderer is more pestilential than a flatterer, who, as much as lies in him, kills the soul. Let them therefore praise the virtues, and God...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s letter to Lorenzo (likely Lorenzo the Magnificent or a close associate) regarding the duties of a teacher, followed by a new, famous short address to the entire human race on the subject of self-knowledge.</meta>

...of virtues, and rather their givers than the persons themselves. For that is the mark of a pious philosopher; the other is the mark of a flatterer. Let them censure vices, not individuals. The former is the way of a friend, the latter of an enemy; let them hate not the person, but the faults. Therefore, let them consider not how they might harm a person, but how they might dissolve their vices. Let them strive more to be good than to be learned. For knowledge <note>original: "scientia" — in this context, technical or academic knowledge</note> breeds envy, but goodness kills it. Goodness is both more useful to humanity and more pleasing to God than mere knowledge. It is also more stable; for we more quickly forget something that we learned in a short time than we lose the character and habits we have acquired through laborious and long-lasting practice. Learning by itself contributes little for a short time. Goodness lasts into eternity and leads toward the attainment of God.

Therefore, advise your students that, in the Socratic manner, they should use human teachings to drive away the mists of the senses and to clear the soul. For then, a ray of truth from the divine sun will shine upon the mind; otherwise, it never will. This is the only true study. He who acts otherwise labors in vain and in misery. In this way, your "bleary-eyed" <note>An allusion to those who are spiritually or intellectually short-sighted</note> students will honor you. It was not books but disciples that made Pythagoras and Socrates famous as divine teachers. Or rather, the books are alive; for a disciple without a soul is a dead book, but a disciple is a living book.

Lorenzo, those things which you have learned freely from God—the master of all truth—teach freely in return. It is a crime for knowledge, which is by nature free, to become mercenary. I praise the man who has learned much without the blush of shame, and who teaches those things without envy. Whatever overflows in the disciples reflects back upon the teacher. Teach, I beg you, with a willing heart. For we have as many "sons of the soul" as we have disciples. If biological parents beget children of the body with pleasure, why should the learned not also procreate sons of the soul with joy? 

Present yourself as an example of good character. Holiness of life makes one's teaching venerable; younger men easily "drink in" the habits of their elders. Those who infect the minds of the young—or indeed anyone—with their words or behavior are to be considered sacrilegious. Finally, imitate Pythagoras and Apollonius of Alabanda, who, following the custom of the Indian philosophers, did not admit just any young men into their discipline, but only those who were fortunately born and excellently raised. For it is not fitting for the Muses to become either the servants of lust or the weapons of iniquity. Farewell, and greet Albertino of Cremona <note>A contemporary philosopher and associate of Ficino</note>, a true philosopher—that is, a model of learning and integrity.

### Knowledge and reverence for oneself is the best of all things.
### Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to the Human Race: which is to say, 
### he speaks of the knowledge and reverence of oneself.

<margin>K</margin> Know yourself <note>The famous Delphic maxim "Nosce te ipsum"</note> as a divine race clothed in a mortal garment. Strip yourself bare, I beg you. You will immediately see pure gold once the filth of the earth has been set aside. You will see clear air once the clouds are scattered. <meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s philosophical exhortation on the nature of the soul. The previous page discussed the importance of inner goodness over mere academic learning. Here, Ficino moves into a profound meditation on self-reverence and the soul's celestial origin, followed by a personal letter to his friend Francesco Bandini.</meta>

...and all things lie open before Him. Nothing of yours is hidden from the ever-living mind of God, who lives everywhere. If the venerable sight of an ancient king produces a sense of shame <note>original: "verecundiam" — here meaning a respectful awe or modest restraint</note> in you, then you should always and everywhere revere the marvelous presence of God the King, the ruler of all minds and bodies. Rightly, therefore, did the divine Pythagoras command: **revere yourself.**

He who does not blush to think of base things in his own presence, and who allows his soul—which is divine by nature—to serve its servant, the body, and who plunges this divine pearl into the mud: such a person certainly seems to be ignorant of his own value. Nor has he considered that divine oracle: *You have made him a little lower than the angels,* <note>Psalm 8:5</note> and those words which follow; and again: *I have said, "You are gods, and all of you are children of the Most High."* <note>Psalm 82:6</note> Alas, our minds are too ignorant! Alas, our hearts are blind! Rise up now, I pray, from this deep sleep. Come to your senses, <note>original: "resipiscite" — literally "recover your wisdom" or "return to a right mind"</note> I beseech you. For if you come to your senses, you will breathe happily again.

Why do you look at the ground for so long? Look up at the divine heaven, you who are citizens of a heavenly fatherland but inhabitants of the earth. A human being is indeed an earthly star surrounded by a cloud. A star, conversely, is a celestial human. You are a great thing, O soul, if small things do not satisfy you. You are also the best, if evil things displease you. You are most beautiful, if you shudder at what is base. You are eternal, if you value temporal things little. Since you are such a being, if you desire to find yourself, seek yourself, I beseech you, where such things are. 

Great things are truly found only where no place imposes a limit or an end. The best things are where nothing adverse happens. The most beautiful things are where nothing is out of harmony. Eternal things are where there is no failing. Therefore, so that you may both seek and find yourself outside this world, fly "outside." Or rather, look "outside." For you are already "outside" while you encompass the world itself. But you think you are in the lowest place of the world because you do not perceive yourself flying above the heavens; instead, you see your shadow—the body—in the lowest place. 

It is just as if some boy, standing over a well, should think himself to be at the bottom of the well because he does not turn his gaze toward himself, but sees only his shadow at the bottom. Or as if a bird flying in the air should believe it is flying on the ground while it sees its shadow on the earth. Therefore, leaving behind the narrowness of this shadow, return into yourself. For thus you return into the vastness. Know that in the spirit there is an immense vastness, but in the body there is—so to speak—an infinite narrowness. 

You can see this from the fact that numbers, which approach the spiritual nature, increase without end, yet they do not decrease without end. <note>Ficino refers to the mathematical principle that you can always add 1 to a number (spiritual growth), but in division, you eventually reach the unit (1), which cannot be divided further in his metaphysical system.</note> Physical magnitude, on the other hand, is the opposite: it has a limit to its growth, though it has no limit to its decrease. <note>A physical object can only grow so large, but can be divided into smaller and smaller pieces infinitely.</note>

### On the divinity of the mind from religion.
### Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Bandini, <term>S.D.</term> <note>Latin "Salutem Dicit," a standard greeting meaning "Sends Greetings."</note>

Others, when they are about to write to Marsilio Ficino and Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Ficino's closest friend and "unique contemporary"</note>—his unique contemporary—write two letters, thinking that where they see two bodies, two wills must also exist. But Bandini, who looks inward with "lynx-like eyes," <note>original: "linceis oculis" — a common Renaissance metaphor for exceptionally sharp or penetrating insight, referring to the legendary sight of the lynx.</note> so to speak, wrote a single letter to a single person. In it, he calls Marsilio immortal and divine, as one who does not fix his gaze upon the fleshy garment of this man, but looks upon the inner man: the soul itself. For the soul, which was granted to humans by God, is immortal and divine. Oh, how sharp-sighted you are, Bandini, to perceive with a sudden intuition what I first investigated through long windings for ten years, and then composed on this subject...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s philosophical discourse on the soul’s immortality. Having previously urged the reader to "revere yourself" and recognize the soul's divine origin, Ficino now references his major work, the *Platonic Theology* (composed of eighteen books), to explain why human life would be the most miserable of all without the hope of an afterlife. The page then transitions into personal correspondence: a letter of consolation to the Bishop of Volterra and the beginning of a sharp rebuke against a detractor.</meta>

# BOOK ONE

...eighteen books. Their beginning—concerning the divinity of the soul, which I think you are already beginning to perceive—he begins to signal gradually with these words: "Since the human race, on account of the restlessness of mind, the weakness of body, and the need for all things, leads a harder life on earth than the beasts; if nature had assigned the same end of living to him as she did completely to all other animals, no animal would be unhappier than man. But since it cannot be that man—who through the worship of God approaches God (the author of blessedness) more closely than all other mortals—is altogether unhappier than all, and since he can only be made happier after the death of the body, it seems necessary that some light <note>original: "lucem aliquam" — referring here to the light of divine life or the soul's survival</note> survives for our souls as they depart from this prison." <note>prison: "carcere" — a standard Platonic metaphor for the physical body which "imprisons" the soul</note> 

But enough about these things. You, however, proceed, Bandini <note>Francesco Bandini, a member of the Platonic Academy and a close friend of Ficino</note>; look as deeply as you can into individual things, as you are doing. For in this way you will never be deceived. He who looks only at the surface sees only shadows and dreams. The center is the hinge and substance of things. You promise to honor us as soon as you can. For a long time now you have magnificently honored the divine Plato and his followers. Now you honor them even while you promise. For a truth-telling man like Bandini fulfills his duty when he promises. Farewell.

### Consolation on the death of someone.
### Marsilio Ficino speaks divine consolation to Antonio Agli, Theologian and Bishop of Volterra.

<margin>s</margin> If it were permitted to console him who can and is accustomed to console others, I would write to you now a consolatory letter on the passing <note>original: "migratione" — literally "migration," implying the soul's journey from this world to the next</note> of your brothers. Therefore, I will not console Antonio, but I will pray. I beseech you, venerable father, by God Himself—the life of the living—that you do not think so much of the earthly death of your kin as of their heavenly life; nor follow your own will so much as the divine will. Indeed, to agree easily with this is the only true piety, true wisdom, and the highest happiness. For those things which happen to others as necessary and adverse become voluntary and prosperous for him who agrees with the will of the Governor of all. 

But why do I, unskilled, offer medicine to Hippocrates? <note>Hippocrates: the famous ancient Greek physician; Ficino is using a proverb to say he shouldn't give advice to someone more expert than himself</note> Physician, heal thyself; or rather, commit yourself to God to be healed. For there is no remedy, as you best know, against the poison of earthly death except the fervent love and frequent consideration of both the celestial and super-celestial life. Farewell. April 28, 1474. Florence.

### Against liars and impious detractors.
### Marsilio Ficino sends greetings.

You know your brother is a great disgrace to you because he is held by all to be a liar and unstable. I cannot deny that he is a liar—he who exercises a poisonous tongue and pen so impiously and insolently against the Divine Majesty, which is infinite truth. Therefore, people say nothing truer about him than that he is a liar. But why I should call him "unstable" I do not find, for he is so persistently stable in his purpose that he has now grown old in his very instability and malice. Either correct your brother’s vices if you can—though to cure such an old disease is very difficult, and such a nefarious vice is perhaps impossible. For the demon <note>original: "demon" — a reference to Lucifer</note> never rose again who, when he had rebelled against God, is said to have fallen once and for all. Or at least bear it with an even mind, since even God...

# BOOK XVII

...endures insults. Perhaps because God knows this man does not know what he babbles. A brother’s vices do not obscure your virtues, my friend; they illustrate them. For your whiteness shines more brilliantly because of his blackness. Do not, therefore, be less stable in good character than your brother is in bad; so that you may do good as well as he does evil.

### Against lying and impious detractors.

->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to the distinguished Bernardo Rucellai <note>Bernardo Rucellai (Oricellario), a prominent Florentine politician and scholar, and a member of the Platonic Academy</note>.<-

<margin>N</margin>o not be overly disturbed, Bernardo, if that man barks so shamefully against everyone. For that dog barks according to his nature and habit. Such a brawler <note>original: "rabula" — a term for a low-class, noisy, or deceptive orator</note> will only stop barking when he stops living. Unless perhaps he even accompanies Cerberus <note>Cerberus: the three-headed dog of Greek mythology who guards the gates of the Underworld</note> with his barking after death. But tell me, I pray, Bernardo, what harm can his barking do to anyone? On the contrary, it makes men more vigilant and more cautious. And since it is widely known that he always tends to disparage upright men—either through envy or because of their difference from him—the man whom he most disapproves of will be considered the most proven. I certainly would prefer to be criticized by the words of the wicked rather than by the reality of my own actions. However, an unjust man actually criticizes the one he praises in words, for he is then judged to be a friend and similar to him. Every detractor necessarily disparages himself before everyone else, for he undergoes the crime of envy and slander. 

Oh, how greatly one abuses the tongue who uses it for evil! Let the slanderers pollute their own mouths with curses; let us not, in turn, pollute ours. If we loathe foul smells, we ought to know that nothing smells worse than evil in the mouth. Filth is not to be wiped from the clothes so much as from the mouth; foul speech is a sign of a putrid mind. One must therefore take diligent care not to be infected by the contagion of the wicked. We should not care what "little men" <note>original: "homunculi" — a dismissive term for people of small character or intellect</note> say about us, but what "men" <note>original: "viri" — meaning true men of character and gravity</note> say, nor even what men say so much as what Truth itself speaks. If some falsehood is thrown at you, despise it, trusting in the truth. If something true is said, use the enemy's insults for your own improvement. 

Do not be turned in any direction by the lightest breeze of common whispering, whether favorable or adverse. A divine soul ought to depend on nothing other than God. But you strive in vain to correct that ruined man; for as a madman he neither listens to nor hears reason. That impious man, who never spared God, will never spare upright men. How can a madman who hates God love any humans, who are images of God? You ask me to correct him with whatever reasons I can. You are commanding me to "plow the shore" <note>original: "Litus arare" — a classical idiom meaning to perform a useless or impossible task</note>. No one attacks divine matters more hostilely or more foolishly than this little man whom you ask me to correct. This Thersites <note>Thersites: a figure from Homer's Iliad known for his ugliness and foul-mouthed insolence toward leaders</note> should be punished rather than rebuked. 

Oh, the shame! He has vomited many invectives from his poisonous mouth against God without punishment. But with what mouth? One that was created by the grace of God to praise God. I have nothing for which to accuse this age of ours, Bernardo, except that it produced this impious little monster. It is told that a glorious war was once declared against Jove by the Giants; in these times, an ignominious one is declared against the highest God by Pygmies. You commend this miserable little monster to my teaching. And certainly, if he had a brain and strength, he would be very harmful to the human race. Hercules would have passed this by out of contempt; Marsilio rejects it because of the stench. Farewell, be happy, and command lighter things another time.

<header>BOOK ONE</header>

### What happiness is: that it has degrees: and that it is eternal.

## Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to the Magnanimous Man, Lorenzo de' Medici.

<margin>c</margin>Since you and I recently debated many points concerning happiness back and forth in the fields of Careggi <note>The Medici villa at Careggi was the primary meeting place for Ficino’s Platonic Academy</note>, we finally reached the same conclusion, guided by reason. In that discussion, you discovered through subtle reasoning certain new arguments for why happiness consists in the act of the will rather than the act of the intellect. It pleased you then that you should fulfill your part of that debate in verse, while I should write it in prose. You have already fulfilled your duty with an elegant poem <note>original: "eleganti poemate" — referring to Lorenzo’s philosophical poem 'L’Altercazione'</note>. I, therefore, with God’s breathing spirit, shall now carry out my task as briefly as possible. Three kinds of human goods are numbered: namely, the goods of fortune, of the body, and of the soul. The goods of fortune are money, honor, favor, and power. And to begin with the first: money is not the highest good, as Midas <note>The mythical King Midas, whose touch turned everything to gold, leading to his ruin</note> believed. For it is not sought for its own sake, but for the sake of the comforts of the body or the soul. Nor are honor and favor the highest good, as Augustus <note>The first Roman Emperor</note> was accustomed to say. For these are subject to the judgment of another; they are often not felt by us; and very often they are hindered or lost despite our merit.

Nor is power the highest good, as Caesar <note>Julius Caesar</note> maintained. For the more people we rule, the more we are tormented by sharp cares. We undergo more dangers. We serve more men and more businesses. We have more enemies. The goods of the body are strength, health, and beauty. Strength and health are not the highest good, as Milo of Croton <note>A famous Greek wrestler known for his incredible strength</note> seems to have thought. For we are made subject to even the smallest injuries. Nor is beauty the highest good, in which the skeptic Herillus <note>Herillus of Carthage, a philosopher who was a pupil of Zeno, though Ficino here associates him with the value of beauty</note> gloried. For no one lives contented simply by the fact that they are very beautiful; and beauty is often a good for others rather than for the beautiful person themselves. The goods of the soul are divided: some belong to the irrational part of the soul, others to the rational part.

To the irrational part belong the sharpness of the senses and their pleasures. Aristippus <note>A Greek philosopher and pupil of Socrates who founded the Cyrenaic school, which taught that sensory pleasure is the supreme good</note> judged the highest good to be in both. We believe that happiness consists in neither. Not in sharpness of sense, both because we are surpassed in this by many beasts, and because a sharp sense tends to trouble us no less than it helps us. Nor does it consist in the pleasures of the senses. For a burning desire precedes them. Suspicion accompanies them, and repentance follows. One brief pleasure is purchased by many long pains. And the intensity of such pleasure lasts only as long as the deficiency of the body lasts—for example, the sweetness of drink lasts only as long as the thirst. Every deficiency is, in truth, a kind of distress. Therefore, because sensory pleasure is often mixed with its opposite—that is, pain—it is neither a pure nor a true pleasure, nor is it sufficient. And if anyone should say that there are some sensory pleasures that do not follow a deficiency, I respond that they are so weak that no one would place their blessedness in them. Nor would anyone dare to place blessedness in a certain habit composed of sharp senses and sensory delights. For such a habit is deceptive, fleeting, and restless. Vile delights do not fill the soul, which seeks higher things by a certain natural instinct. Other goods of the rational part of the soul are called "natural," such as wit, memory, and a ready boldness of the will. Happiness does not consist in these. For though they are used well by the good—

<meta>This page continues the letter to Lorenzo de' Medici concerning the nature of happiness. It transitions from discussing external goods of fortune to the internal goods of the soul, contrasting various philosophical schools like the Stoics, Epicureans, and Peripatetics with the Platonic view.</meta>

<header>BOOK</header>

...[goods of fortu]ne are good, but when used badly they are truly evil. Others are the acquired goods of the rational soul, such as the **moral** and **speculative** virtues. But is happiness found in moral conduct? The <term>Stoics</term><note>A school of philosophy that taught that virtue is the only good and that humans should be indifferent to pleasure and pain.</note> and <term>Cynics</term><note>Followers of Antisthenes who emphasized living a life of virtue in agreement with nature, often rejecting social conventions.</note> think so. By no means; for the operations of the moral virtues, such as temperance and fortitude, are busy and laborious. In labor, however, there is not that end which we seek, but rather in rest. For we do business so that we may have leisure, and we wage war so that we may live in peace. Furthermore, morals are never sought for their own sake, but are referred to as a kind of medicine for the purgation and tranquility of the mind. Yet the ultimate end is not found in <term>Epicurean</term><note>Refers to the followers of Epicurus, who sought "ataraxia" or freedom from fear and bodily pain.</note> tranquility. For tranquility of the mind is directed toward the contemplation of truth, just as the serenity of the air is directed toward the light of the sun.

Is happiness, therefore, found in the speculative virtues, such as the contemplation of truth? Certainly it is in these very things. But there is one kind of contemplation, so to speak, of earthly things <note>original: "subcoelestium" — literally "under the heavens."</note>; another of the celestial; and another of the super-celestial. <term>Democritus</term><note>A pre-Socratic philosopher known for his atomic theory; here associated with the study of the physical world.</note> placed the end in the first kind of study. <term>Anaxagoras</term><note>An early Greek philosopher who focused on the heavens and the mind (Nous).</note> did not wish to rest in that, because celestial things are more excellent than earthly ones; he wished to be content with the contemplation of the celestial. Hence he said that he was born for the contemplation of those things, and affirmed that the sky was his homeland. Aristotle certainly rejected this, because the consideration of super-celestial things <note>Things beyond the physical heavens, referring to divine or metaphysical realities.</note> seems much more worthy. And happiness is the highest act of the highest power concerning the highest object.

Truly, there is one kind of consideration of these things which the soul can achieve while enclosed in the body, and another when it is released. <term>Aristotle</term> thought that the man who possesses the first kind is happy. Our <term>Plato</term> denied it. For the consideration of divine things in this life always has the ambiguity of the intellect and the anxiety of the will mixed in. For this reason, according to Plato, true happiness belongs to the soul separated from the body, contemplating divine things.

In the genus of divine things are placed the angels and God. <term>Avicenna</term><note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant thinkers of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> and <term>Algazel</term><note>Al-Ghazali, a major Muslim theologian and philosopher.</note> seem to affirm that the soul will be happy in the contemplation of the angels. The Platonists refute this for two reasons. The first reason is this: this condition is innate to our intellect, that it seeks the cause of every thing, and again the cause of the cause. Therefore, the inquiry of the intellect never ceases unless it finds that cause of which there is no cause, but which is itself the cause of causes. And this is God alone. The second reason is such: the affection of the will is satisfied by no good so long as we think another good remains beyond it. It is satisfied, therefore, only by that good beyond which there is no good. What else is this but God? 

Wherefore, the inquiry of the intellect and the affection of the will can rest in God alone. In God alone, therefore, does the happiness of man consist. This indeed happens because no thing can rest anywhere except in its own cause; and because God alone is the proper cause of the soul, therefore the soul rests in God alone. But we have discussed these things more broadly in our theology on the immortality of souls.

There are two acts of the soul regarding God. For it sees God through the intellect, and it rejoices in the God it has known through the will. Plato calls this vision <term>ambrosia</term> and this joy <term>nectar</term><note>In Greek mythology, ambrosia and nectar were the food and drink of the gods, granting immortality.</note>. He calls the intellect and the will the "twin wings" by which we fly back to God as if to our father and our homeland. Therefore, when pure souls have flown up into heaven, they feast at the divine table on ambrosia and nectar. Joy in that happiness is more excellent than vision. For to the extent that we deserve more in this life by loving God than by inquiring about him, so much greater is the reward in that life...

<summary>Ficino argues that human happiness (beatitudo) cannot be found in earthly goods or moral labor, but only in the eternal contemplation and enjoyment of God, which satisfies both the intellect and the will.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument regarding the nature of the "supreme good" and human happiness. After dismissing external goods and moral virtues as the ultimate end, the text now explores whether happiness is found primarily in the intellect (knowledge) or the will (love), arguing forcefully for the superiority of love and the joy it produces.</meta>

<header>BOOK ONE XXXIX</header>

is attributed to **love** rather than to **inquiry** <note>original: "inquiſitõni" — the active, rational search or investigation into truth.</note>. We deserve much more by loving than by investigating for many reasons. First: because no one in this life truly knows God. However, one truly loves God as he is known when he scorns everything else for the sake of God. Second: just as it is worse to hate God than to be ignorant of Him, so it is better to love Him than to know Him. Third: we can use the knowledge of God badly—namely, for the sake of pride. We cannot use His love badly. Fourth: he who perceives God grants nothing to God on that account alone. But he who loves Him grants both himself and whatever he possesses to God. Therefore, God rewards the one who loves Him more than the one who scrutinizes Him. Fifth: by scrutinizing God, we barely make a little progress over a long time. By loving, we progress the most in the shortest time. For this reason, love joins the mind with divinity more quickly, more closely, and more firmly than knowledge, because the power of knowledge consists more in **distinction** <note>original: "diſcretõē" — the intellectual act of separating and categorizing concepts.</note>, while the power of love consists more in **union**. Sixth: by loving God we not only perceive a greater pleasure than by scrutinizing Him, but we are also made better. By these reasons we can conclude that the reward which is owed to love is greater than that which is granted to human inquiry. It is fitting for the lover to enjoy and rejoice in the thing loved. For that is the end of love. But for the inquirer, the end is to see. Therefore, joy in the happy man surpasses vision.

Furthermore, we seek to see so that we may rejoice. We do not seek to rejoice so that we may see. We can assign a reason why we wish to see; but we cannot assign any reason why we wish to rejoice other than joy itself. It is as if it is desired for its own sake. We do not desire to see Him simply, but to see such things and in such a way that we may rejoice.

Nature itself never rejects any joy. Yet it sometimes rejects a certain knowledge—indeed, even life itself—if we judge it will be very troublesome. Thus delight is the seasoning not only of knowledge but also of life; when it is removed, all things seem tasteless. Joy is fuller than knowledge. For not everyone who knows also rejoices at the same time. But whoever rejoices necessarily also knows. Just as nature considers it worse to suffer than to be ignorant, so it is better to rejoice than to know. And just as it always and everywhere flees pain for its own sake and flees all things because of it as the supreme evil, so it follows pleasure for its own sake and other things because of it as the supreme good. Since the power of knowledge, as we said above, consists in a certain distinction, while the power of love consists in union, we are joined more closely to God through the joy of love—which transforms us into the beloved God—than through knowledge. And just as it is not he who sees the good, but he who wills it who becomes good, so the soul becomes divine not because it considers God, but because it loves Him. This is just as matter becomes fire not because it catches light from the fire, but because it takes on the fire’s heat. This reasoning is confirmed by this: since the soul is not the Good itself, and therefore the Good must be sought outside its own nature, it follows that the turning of the <term>will</term><note>original: "volũtatis" — the faculty of choice and desire.</note>—which reaches out to the object—enjoys the Good more truly than the notion of the <term>intellect</term><note>original: "intellectus" — the faculty of understanding and logic.</note>, which remains within. For the intellect captures the object in a certain imaginary way <note>In the sense of creating an "image" or mental representation of the thing, rather than reaching the thing itself.</note>. The will strives to transfer itself into the object by an essential instinct. The appetite is founded in the essence, and is most broad and perpetual...

<summary>This page argues that the highest human happiness is found in the love of God rather than intellectual inquiry, because love unites the soul with the divine and produces a joy that is the ultimate end of all human desire.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous section, specifically focusing on the hierarchy between the intellect and the will. Having established that love (the will) deserves a greater reward than investigation (the intellect), the author now explains the psychological and metaphysical reasons why the soul is "expanded" by love but "contracted" by mere knowledge.</meta>

<page-num>XIX</page-num>
<header>BOOK</header>

is. For whatever exists always desires something. Knowledge acts through received **images** <note>original: "imagines" — in medieval philosophy, these are the mental representations or "species" of external objects that the mind perceives.</note>. It belongs to only a few people and is intermittent. Therefore, the possession of the Good through the nature of **desire** <note>original: "appetitus"</note> is more substantial than the intuition of knowledge. If God were to separate the mind from the will and preserve each nature on its own, the mind would perhaps seem to retain its prior form, for it would still be a kind of rational form. The will, perhaps, would change its form, for it would be a kind of desire lacking the choice of reason. But the mind would enjoy no further good at all; it would be like an animal without the sense of taste; nothing would please it; it would approve of nothing, nor would it assent to any other thing or even to itself. The will, however, would still enjoy its own certain goods through its own powers. Therefore, the enjoyment of the **supreme good** <note>original: "summo bono"</note> seems to belong to the will rather than to the intellect.

The end of movement—that is, **happiness** <note>original: "fœlicitas"</note>—rightly belongs to the will, since the beginning of movement pertains to it. For when the intellect knows things through the nature of things, because it understands the things themselves through its own nature, it seems to draw those things to itself in a certain way, and therefore it is not properly said to "move" the soul. The will, because it desires to follow things in the way they are in themselves, draws the soul toward external things; therefore, the will is the beginning of movement. Moreover, the end of universal movement is external. This end finally joins itself to the soul like a form. The soul enjoys this end most through the will, because a reward is owed to the one who labors. Indeed, the care and the stimulus regarding the attaining of good or the avoiding of evil reside in the **affection** <note>original: "affectu" — the emotional or volitional state of the soul.</note>. The will enjoys God more, not only because it is more deserving than the intellect in the sight of God, but also because the distinction of **blessedness** <note>original: "beatitudinis"</note> belongs to it. For the more ardently one loves, the more blessed one becomes; therefore, the very substance of happiness belongs to the will itself.

What shall we say to the fact that since many more people can love God ardently than can clearly know Him, the "way of love" is both safer for human beings and far more suited to the **Infinite Good**—which wishes to impart itself to as many as possible? Therefore, the attainment of this Good pertains to the will. What, again, shall we say to the fact that the movement of rational souls is free? And because it is free, proceeding beyond any finite limit, it can progress in merit to such a degree that it can even surpass the blessedness of some angels. We are able to surpass them by loving and rejoicing rather than by understanding. 

Accordingly, by **knowing** God, we contract His greatness to the capacity and concept of our own mind. But by **loving** Him, we enlarge the mind to the immense breadth of the divine goodness. In the former, we almost cast God down into ourselves; in the latter, we truly lift ourselves up to God. For we know only as much as we ourselves can contain. But we love both what we perceive and how much we prophesy of the remaining divine goodness that exists beyond our clear intuition. Where we perceive the abyss of divine infinity weakly and obscurely, we nevertheless love intensely and ardently, and we similarly rejoice. **Vision** is not, as some think, the measure of joy. For one who sees little can love much, and vice versa.

Finally, that is the supreme good of the soul by which the soul is content. However, it is not content with its own vision of God. For the vision which in the seeing soul is sufficient...
