<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into why the will, rather than the intellect alone, is the faculty that experiences ultimate fulfillment. It builds on the previous argument that the intellect is limited by the mental images it can hold, whereas the will can reach out to the infinite reality of God himself.</meta>

<page-num>XL</page-num>
<header>BOOK ONE 40</header>

[per]ceived is a created thing and is finite in its degrees of perfection, just as the soul itself is. However, the soul is never satisfied with any created and finite good. Therefore, **vision** <note>original: "visio" — here referring to the intellectual "seeing" or understanding</note> is not the highest good. Rather, the soul is satisfied by God having been seen, more so than by the [mere] act of the vision of God. The **enjoyment** <term>fruitio: the joyful possession or use of something for its own sake</term> of the good in the senses does not consist properly in the fact that the good moves the sense, but in the fact that the sense reflects, turns itself toward, and pours itself out into that good which has been offered.

This spiritual turning and pouring out is nothing other than **pleasure** <note>original: "voluptas"</note>, as we discussed in our book *On Pleasure*. Thus, while the mind itself is inseparable [from the process], so to speak, the enjoyment of God does not properly consist in the fact that God shows Himself to the mind. For this is an act of God rather than an act of our own; instead, it consists in the fact that the mind turns itself toward God, which is joy. Nor should it be thought that the soul turns itself into its vision of God so that it may rest in the vision itself, but rather it rests in God who is seen. For it desires the vision for the sake of the One who is seen, because He is also joined to the soul as its very form. Just as taste does not expand into the act of tasting a flavor, but rather into the flavor that is tasted; for it desires the act of tasting for the sake of what is tasted.

No **desire** <note>original: "appetitus"</note> seeks an imaginary thing, but a substantial one. Otherwise, memory and imagination would be enough for someone desiring a good that is absent. However, the vision of God within us is an imaginary thing and, as I said above, it is finite. Therefore, the act of the will—which is a turning toward and a substantial pouring out into the infinite God—possesses the character of infinity more than the act of understanding, which is merely a certain notion of God according to the mind's capacity. Therefore, the **supreme good** is God. **Happiness** <note>original: "beatitudo"</note>, however, is the enjoyment of God; we enjoy Him, therefore, through the will. For through the will, by loving, we are moved toward God; by rejoicing, we are expanded and turned into God. Moreover, different souls enjoy different virtues and **ideas** <term>ideis: the eternal archetypes or divine patterns in the mind of God</term> of God. For each person possesses primarily that virtue which they loved above all others in this life and imitated according to their strength. Yet all enjoy the whole of God. For He is whole in every single idea. But those who behold Him in a more excellent idea possess the whole of God more excellently. Since indeed each person both possesses the whole of God according to their capacity and enjoys Him in the manner in which they had loved Him, therefore, as Plato says, "envy is absent from the divine choir." <note>original: "liuor abest a diuino choro" — a reference to the *Phaedrus*, meaning that in the divine realm, there is no jealousy because everyone is perfectly satisfied.</note> For since it is the most pleasant of all things to possess the thing loved, anyone possessing what they loved lives content and full. Truly, if two lovers should become masters of their delights, each will rest in the possession of their beloved, nor will they have any care whether another possesses a more beautiful beloved. Add to this that although some there are more capable than others, nevertheless each overflows to the peak of their own capacity, which results in them requiring nothing further. Add also that, through a certain amorous affection, everyone there most willingly yields to the will and distribution of divine justice.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Furthermore, a blessed soul can never be removed from God. For it must not be said that this can happen by force. For from where could violence be brought against a soul held fast by the infinite power of God? Nor can it happen by choice. For since the will is not moved toward anything except by the reason of the good, after it has <unclear>given itself</unclear> <note>original: "sesebeſerit" — likely "sese adhibuerit," meaning to apply or unite oneself</note> to that in which the whole reason of the good resides and recognizes it, it is never moved from there toward anything else. And because the nature of the good is to apply to itself the force of desire, it follows that the soul applies itself to the infinite good without end. Again, because the will rests in something only insofar as it is thought to be good, it rests without end in the infinite good. And if the soul, while it was engaged in the movement of the body, chose a happiness void of all change, it will do so much more when it is above movement. Nor can the lower parts of the soul turn away from there...

->A Theological Prayer to God.<-

Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Bernardo Rucellai <note>original: "Bernardo oricellario" — a Florentine statesman and humanist</note>, an outstanding man and sweet friend.

Nothing is sweeter to me above men than to speak with God. Nothing is sweeter to me among men than to speak with you. What I speak with you, God—the leader of life and the mediator of our friendship—always hears. What I often speak with God, you yourself will now hear. I use this prayer to God daily, O Rucellai, so that God may shine upon my mind and favor my will. You too should use it sometime, unless perhaps you have something better. For there is no one for whom I more desire God’s favor than for you. I have sometimes heard our Lorenzo de' Medici singing some things similar to these to the lyre, stirred by a certain **divine frenzy** <term>divino furore: a state of inspired madness or poetic ecstasy described by Plato</term>, <margin>I pray</margin> as I believe; but now hear the prayer itself. O immense light seeing yourself: seeing all things in yourself; O infinite vision shining by yourself, illuminating the universe; O spiritual eye, by which alone and whom alone spiritual eyes see; O immortal life of those who see; O every good of those who live. O Good that completely fills the desire of lovers: you alone, O God, kindle in us the desire for the whole good, you who alone are the whole good. I beseech you, O most pure light, by yourself: purge, I beseech you, the dim-sighted gaze with which I may discern you, you who inflame the cold heart by which I thirst for you. Enlarge the narrow eye by which I may behold you, you who raise the humble pupil so that I may look up. For you penetrate my innermost parts, O depth of depths; you also lift up my highest parts: O loftiness of all lofty things. What penetrates my innermost parts? What raises my heights? Certainly the wondrous rays of your wondrous goodness and beauty, wonderfully diffused everywhere through minds, through souls, through bodies. By these, therefore, you affect me even when I am unaware; by these, I say, you entice me, you compel me, you burn me. O how great is this singular beauty! Behold, now, behold, I hasten to you, panting, O unique beauty. But he limps, ah, too much this lover of yours limps, alas, wretched man! Stretch out, I pray, your pious hand to the limper, O my hope. Lead, I pray, him whom you entice. Receive him whom you compel; cool the things which you burn; delight the things which you distress. You will now, I hope, delight this [servant] of yours wonderfully; O wondrous joy, O fountain of all joys! I know indeed that in you alone—nay, that you alone *are*—whatever we desire. If this good pleases us, if that good pleases us: it is not because it is "this" or "that," but because it is "good." Surely we desire the quality of goodness in individual things. If the healing liquid diffused everywhere through individual things flows from a single fountain of goodness—which flourishes in itself, overflowing above all things—then without a doubt we long to drink from the fountain of goodness itself. O perennial fountain of all goods: you, you we thirst for everywhere. And therefore [this thirst] is not extinguished if—

# FIRST

...not so much this good or that for us, nor again this one and that one together, insofar as we rightly prophesy that the Good itself <note>original: "bonū ipsū" — the Platonic concept of the Absolute Good</note> is above this good and that good. Therefore, You, our God, You alone will extinguish this burning thirst. You, I say, the Good of every good: lest You have forced all Your own to thirst so much and for so long in vain. O First Wisdom, far from all madness; O First Wisdom without any folly, from whom nothing is hidden of those things which You wisely bring about. You who despise nothing of the things You create by Your benevolent will—and You create all things. Do You not care for even the smallest of earthly things, which do not care for You? Do You care for the smallest things? These You both feed and fill. Yet do You despise us alone, we who alone on earth do not despise Your majesty? Do You permit us alone, I say, to wander always restless, we who alone trust that we can find rest in You alone? Let evil ingratitude be far from supreme beneficence. Let deception be far from supreme truth. You deceive us, certainly You deceive us—alas, wretched ones—if, wounded by Your stings <note>original: "aculeis" — referring to the sharp, painful goads of divine desire or the "stings of love"</note>, You compel us to sigh for You anxiously every day and yet never heal us; if You command us to abandon temporal things in favor of worshipping You, and yet You do not grant eternal things in exchange for the temporal. If You have decreed that these diligent worshippers of Yours lead a life on earth more wretched than the beasts, and You do not preserve for them a more blessed life hereafter. 

But You do preserve it for us, as we all constantly hope: O Savior of the world, O unique salvation of the human race, the refuge for each one, in whom is every good for man and without whom there is no good. Truly, just as Your clear intelligence and burning charity illuminate and kindle our intelligence and will toward gazing upon and loving You, and shape them into Your own and unite them to Yourself, so Your eternal life perpetually brings our life to life within itself. And to those to whom the understanding of immortal things is granted—a capable will that commands mortal things—immortal life belongs much more and much sooner. Indeed, by the virtue of this life joined to eternity and separated from the passions of time, the eternal mind grasps as much as its affection dominates over temporal things. For thus every act of the soul reaches eternity in its own way: the will by willing, the intelligence by understanding, the life by living. And eternity itself, which communicates itself to the later acts of the soul, has already communicated itself to the prior act, which is life itself. 

Therefore, O best Father, You will one day make us partakers of Your bliss by hereditary right as well as by the gift of Your blessedness. Make us, we pray, partakers moreover in the present; do this also if it pleases You; do it, we pray. But if this does not yet please You because we do not yet deserve it, grant at least that we are neither ensnared by the deceptive charms of this world nor succumb to its threats and blows. Have mercy on us, most indulgent Father, have mercy on Your children: cherish Your own, we pray, cherish Your own, and recreate those whom You have created. For from You alone are we born, since You alone can fill our intellect and affection with Your whole truth and goodness. Therefore, have mercy on Your children who are exiles far from the celestial homeland <note>original: "patria" — the soul's true home with God</note> in this forest <note>original: "silua" — the material world, often described in Neoplatonism as a dark "forest" of matter</note> full of miseries. Have mercy on Your own, we ask, who everywhere, day and night, sigh for You as for both Father and Homeland. Where the homeland is, there is rest; there is the true good. Where exile is, there is restlessness; there is false good; there is true evil. But then we live in life only for a little while and removed from evils: and go[od]...

...unless we seem to taste something of true reality and rest for ourselves when we cling to You for a short while, whether by the focus of the mind or the feeling of devotion. Drive far from us, therefore, O nourishing Father, whatever separates us far from You: lack of faith, despair, and lukewarmness. Let us rejoice happily without end, with You, without any limit to our desires. Let us love Your infinite beauty infinitely and without anxiety. Let us enjoy the infinite Good again forever without any satiety.

### That one must trust and serve virtue and God alone.
#### Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Salviati, greetings.

<margin>f</margin>If anyone thinks the reason for my long silence has been forgetfulness, they are wrong. For I confess I owe you so much that I could no sooner forget you than forget myself. I knew indeed it was not fitting to write about trivial matters to a man occupied with so much business; I was therefore hoping for some great success in your affairs, and I was waiting for it daily, as a reason to write a letter of congratulation to you. I do not yet see anything having happened that is worthy of my wish and your merit. Have confidence, Salviati; I know you were not born for small or mediocre things. Therefore, be of good—and as you usually are—great spirit. For you will have already achieved great things if you possess a great spirit. Moreover, the most merciful God does not frustrate the hope of those who came before. Why should I weep for the death of our Cardinal Pietro? <note>Likely referring to Cardinal Pietro Riario (d. 1474), a powerful papal nephew and patron</note>. Immortal God will certainly not desert us, even if a mortal man has. But the younger Pietro died in prosperity, in my opinion, so that he would not perhaps die more miserable in old age. A long life, though it is sometimes an opportunity to improve one's character, is often the undoing or lessening of past success. He has lived long, Salviati, whoever has earned much from men and most from God during the time he lived. He who has not yet made enough progress in character <note>original: "ingenio" — natural talent or character</note> and virtue—even if he fulfills a hundred years—has not yet lived enough. Finally, to be brief: no one lives long and happily except the one who lives for eternal bliss <note>original: "beatitudini" — the state of supreme blessedness</note>. Farewell, my Francesco, always mindful of what God has often warned you: that one must not trust or serve fortune or man, but only Him who serves no one; who never wishes to deceive and cannot be deceived. To whom nothing is lacking and who never allows His own people to lack anything. Farewell again; our Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Ficino's closest friend and fellow philosopher</note> sends his regards.

...and you have fulfilled the judgment of physiognomy <note>The Renaissance practice of judging a person's character or future based on their physical features</note>. From that physical judgment, you can indeed approach the deputy of God <note>original: "deivicariā" — likely referring to the Pope or a high earthly ruler</note>; but from this spiritual state, you can approach God himself. As his letters and character declare, the epistles of Paul the Apostle have instructed him sufficiently. Farewell, be happy.

### The Praise of Philosophy: Oratorical, Moral, Dialectical, and Theological.

->**Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo <note>Bernardo Bembo (1433–1519) was a Venetian statesman, diplomat, and father of the famous Cardinal Pietro Bembo. He was a close friend of Ficino and the Medici</note>, legal consultant and knight,**<-
->**distinguished in learning and authority, Orator of the Venetians, sends greetings.**<-

<margin>q</margin>You ask why, although I have praised many things and arts here and there, I have never pursued the praise of Philosophy, the study to which I am devoted. My friend Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Ficino's closest friend and frequent correspondent, often called his "unique friend"</note> asked the same thing a few days ago. I reply, first, that the inventions of men can sometimes be praised by men according to their worth. But Philosophy, a discovery of God, far surpasses human eloquence. Second, I reply that in celebrating individual things and arts, I *have* celebrated Philosophy—the inventress of all things and the mistress of the arts. Indeed, we cannot worthily praise individual things except by her strengths and reasons; and we judge a faculty to be worthy of praise only insofar as it participates in philosophical virtue and dignity. But since this mother and nurse of ours seems by the best right to demand a specific declamation from us, let us now begin here, if you please.

### The Oratorical Praise of Philosophy.

<margin>o</margin>O Philosophy, leader of life! O seeker of virtue and expeller of vices! What could not only our life, but the life of all humanity, have been without you? You gave birth to cities. You called scattered men into a community of life. You joined them together, first in homes, then in marriage, and then in the sharing of letters and speech. You were the inventress of laws, the mistress of morals and discipline. But where have I impertinently strayed? I was beginning a sort of oratorical and Tullian <note>original: "tullianamq;" — referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman master of eloquence</note> melody. This kind of melody is certainly sweet. However, since we ought to sing of Philosophy—which is the rule for every song as well as for the thing being sung—in no other way than *philosophically*, let us repeat this exercise from another beginning.

### The Moral Praise of Philosophy.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s correspondence and philosophical treatises addressed to the Venetian diplomat Bernardo Bembo. <header>BOOK ONE XLIII</header>

**P**hilosophy is defined by everyone as the love of truth and wisdom, and the study of them. However, truth and wisdom itself is God alone. It follows that legitimate philosophy is nothing other than true religion, and legitimate religion is nothing other than true philosophy. If the proper meaning of words is derived partly from the nature of things and partly from the nature of concepts—as Plato, Aristotle, Varro, and Aurelius Augustine <note>St. Augustine (354–430 AD), the influential Christian theologian who integrated Neoplatonism into Christian thought</note> most subtly argue—then certainly philosophy, the seeker of things and inventor of concepts, gave birth to Grammar as the rule for speaking and writing correctly. If philosophy alone, or most of all, understands the nature of souls, the power of actions, the form of works, the arrangement of places, and the opportunity of times, it is this that taught orators what, by what reasoning, to whom, and when they should persuade. It taught poets how to describe things, move the emotions, and delight minds. From this, it also follows that historians could not preserve their dignity without her help. She <note>Ficino uses "Næc," likely a transcription for "Haec" (This one/She), referring to Philosophy</note> gave a soul to cities when she refined earthly and human laws according to the likeness of celestial and divine laws. Nor did she fail to create and increase the body of the city, since she provided agriculture, architecture, medicine, military skill, and all other faculties pertaining to sustenance, decoration, or defense. Finally, she removes misery from mortals above all else and bestows happiness. Since she distinguishes good from evil, she shows how we can either cautiously avoid evils so they do not harm us, or bravely endure them so they harm us less. Furthermore, she shows how we may more easily attain good things, and by what reasoning we should rightly use goods—whether given by nature and fortune or acquired through industry—so that they may be beneficial. I wanted, my best Bernardo <note>Bernardo Bembo (1433–1519), a Venetian statesman and father of Cardinal Pietro Bembo</note>, to put an end to this letter here, so that for now I would not be more long-winded than usual. For you yourself know how much prolixity <note>Excessive wordiness</note> displeases us, except in our Plato, that source of celestial eloquence. But look, the divine lady <note>Philosophy personified as a noble woman, a tradition famously established by Boethius in the 6th century</note> whom we venerate above all others, cries out against it. Therefore, if it pleases you, hear what speech she still demands of us—or rather, what she offers to us.

->The Praise of Dialectical and Theological Philosophy.<-

**P**hilosophy uses dialectical instruments <note>The tools of logic and formal reasoning</note> fashioned by her own hand to investigate the true in the contemplation of things, the honest in the use of things, and the good in both. From this, she hands down many principles for contemplation, many precepts for action, and many institutions common to both. Among the common principles, this seems to me the most important to bring forward: The "End" <note>The final goal or purpose</note>, like a master, is more excellent than those things which are referred to the end as mere servants. And those things which are more excellent are always the ends of the rest. Therefore, it is right and fitting that external and mortal things serve the body; the body serves the soul; the senses serve reason; active reason serves contemplative reason <note>original: "speculatiūæ" — the higher intellectual function of "looking" at divine truths</note>; and contemplation serves God. From this, it follows that all arts pertaining to external things, the body, the senses, and action, ought to yield and be subject to contemplation as if to a queen. And rightly so, for this kind of operation is proper to God. He does not need...

...fense, or to tool, or to place. It does not serve external things. It is the most continuous of all things; indeed, it is perpetual. Its object is eternal and present everywhere, embracing everything everywhere at its own discretion. And if life is a certain act, and where there is more action there is more life, surely the act of contemplation—as it excels all others in both dignity and perseverance—is a certain greatest and most eminent life. Add that it is the sweetest of all. For it does not borrow impure, false, and fleeting delights from the external images of things, as the senses do. But possessing within itself in abundance the true and eternal reasons and natures of things, it feeds and rejoices purely, truly, and stably upon things that are pure, true, and stable. It rejoices in the infinite, deeply and infinitely; for what is greatest is that this kind of life is closest to the life of God and is transformed into His most exact image. God, therefore, is both the light and the eye of human contemplation. Contemplation, however, is the light and the eye of action. And if such an eye seems to be at leisure <note>original: "otiosus," meaning at rest or contemplative rather than lazy</note>, nevertheless without it, all things are badly idle, or most wickedly busy, and entirely dark and miserable. At its command, however, we perform each task happily.

Wise philosophy shows mortals this life—placed at the very summit of things and unquestionably most blessed—through both her own eye and the finger of her dialectic <note>the art of logical discussion and investigation of truth</note>. She also leads us to it, I believe, by four principal steps: Ethics <term>Moralibus: the study of right conduct and the soul's purification</term>, Natural Philosophy <term>naturalibus: the study of the physical world and elements</term>, Mathematics, and Metaphysics. The divine Plato thinks that the celestial and immortal soul in a certain way dies when it enters the earthly and mortal body. It comes back to life when it departs. However, it departs through a certain study of meditation before it departs by the law of nature <note>referring to physical death</note>, when philosophy—the medicine for human diseases—purges and revives the little soul buried in the pestiferous filth of vices with ethical remedies. Then, lifting it from the lowest depths by certain natural mechanisms through all things composed of the four elements, she leads it through those four elements all the way to heaven. Then, by mathematical ladders, she provides a gradual ascent to the highest spheres of heaven for the senses. Finally—and what can be said that is more wonderful?—she lifts the soul on metaphysical wings beyond the peak of heaven to the very Maker <note>the Creator or Demiurge</note> of heaven and the entire world.

There, by the gift of philosophy, the soul not only turns out to be happy, but since it becomes—so to speak—a god, it becomes happiness itself. There, all mortal affairs, arts, and business cease. Of all things, holy philosophy alone remains. There, true happiness is nothing other than true philosophy. Indeed, since philosophy is defined by the wise as the "love of wisdom" <note>etymological definition: philo (love) + sophia (wisdom)</note>, we believe that the highest happiness there consists in a certain affection of the will, which is the love and joy regarding divine wisdom.

Moreover, we infer that by the benefit of philosophy, the mind can eventually become a kind of god from this: that while under her guidance it gradually comprehends the natures of all things with intelligence, and thoroughly takes on the forms of those things which it apprehends, it further enjoys each part with its will and even rules over them in a certain way...

<summary>Ficino describes the soul's ascent through four stages of philosophy (Ethics, Physics, Mathematics, and Metaphysics) to reach a state of divine contemplation. He argues that this contemplative life is the highest form of human existence, allowing the soul to transcend the body and mirror God.</summary>
<keywords>contemplation, Neoplatonism, Plato, soul's ascent, ethics, mathematics, metaphysics, happiness, divine wisdom</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the contemplative life. Having established that contemplation is the highest form of human existence, Ficino now argues that the human intellect is "divine" because it can replicate the logic of God’s creation—specifically citing the mechanical and mathematical genius of Archimedes as proof of our shared nature with the "Celestial Architect."</meta>

# BOOK I

XLIIII
F 4

...everything. And while in this manner he gradually becomes all things, God—who is the source and lord of all—is brought to fulfillment. Indeed, God completes the universe both within Himself and outside Himself. The mind of a man who philosophizes rightly, like a certain god, also conceives within itself the true and eternal notions of all things.

But shall we say that the human mind is able to create individual things outside itself? To pass over how the philosophical intellect, through thought, words, and letters, manifests the hidden works of almighty God and imitates and expresses them perfectly <note>original: "examussim," meaning according to a level or rule; with extreme precision</note> with various instruments and materials, I believe this one thing especially should be noted: that not just anyone can discern by what logic and in what manner a most skillfully constructed work of a clever artisan was built, but only one who possesses nearly the same artistic genius. For no one could discern how that philosopher Archimedes <note>Archimedes (c. 287–212 BCE), the Greek mathematician who famously constructed a mechanical planetarium or "sphere" that mimicked the motions of the sun, moon, and planets</note> constructed bronze spheres and gave them movements similar to the movements of the heavens, unless he were endowed with a similar genius. And because he discerns this through a similarity of intellect, he could certainly construct those same things once he understood them, provided he did not lack either the instruments or the material.

Since, therefore, the philosopher has seen the order of the celestial spheres—from where they are moved, where they proceed, and by what measures, and what they produce—who would deny that he possesses nearly the same genius as the Author of the heavens? And that he himself is able in a way to create the heavens and the things within them if he obtained the instruments and celestial matter—seeing as he creates them now, albeit from a different material, yet through a similar order.

O exceedingly wonderful intelligence of the celestial Architect! O eternal Wisdom, born from the head of the supreme Jupiter <note>original: "summi Iouis," here used as a classical poetic name for God the Father, referencing the myth of Athena (Wisdom) being born from Zeus's head</note> alone! O infinite Truth and Goodness of things, sole Queen of the whole world! O truth-telling and kindly light of intelligence! O saving ardor of the will! O beneficial fire of our heart! Enlighten us. Enlighten us to such a degree and inflame us, we pray, that we may be utterly burned with the love of your light—that is, the love of truth and wisdom. For this alone, O almighty God, is to be truly wise; this alone is to live most blessedly with God and as a god.

Whoever wanders far from your rays, since they never discern anything clearly, are everywhere deceived and terrified by the deceptive shadows of things; they are wretchedly harassed everywhere as if in certain horrific dreams under perpetual night. Whoever lives diligently with you—since they alone perceive, love, and embrace true, eternal, and immense things beneath your rays—they judge whatever is confined by time or place to be but a tiny shadow of a dream. Thus it happens that they cannot be cast down from the high citadel of celestial happiness by either the desire for or the fear of earthly things.

I think enough has now been declaimed by your Marsilio, my Bernard <note>Likely Bernardo Bembo, a Venetian diplomat and close associate of the Platonic Academy</note>, as far as a letter allows. Farewell then happily, patron of philosophers, and as you have done until now, continue to live in the blessed arms of holy philosophy. Live also, I pray, constantly mindful of Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Ficino’s "unique friend" and a central figure in his social and intellectual circle</note>, who is of the Marsilian heart.

Greetings, dearest Arsilius <note>Michael Arsilius (Michele Arsie) was a close friend and student of Ficino, often acting as a secretary or intermediary</note>. ### Expression of Gratitude

Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Francesco, Cardinal of Siena <note>Francesco Todeschini Piccolomini (1439–1503), who later briefly became Pope Pius III</note>. In return for an immortal gift, he sends immortal greetings.

<margin>c</margin>When I, together with my parents, read your happy letter in which you indicate that the grace of the Jubilee has been obtained for us from the Pope, we were affected by no less joy than those who are about to hear that most blessed voice:
> "Come, you blessed of my Father." <note>A reference to Matthew 25:34, describing the invitation to heaven at the Last Judgment</note>
Therefore, my father <note>Diotifeci d'Agnolo, a physician to the Medici and Marsilio's father</note> suddenly exclaimed before the others:
> "Now, Lord, let your servant depart in peace, according to your word." <note>original: "Nunc dimittis..."; the Canticle of Simeon from Luke 2:29, often said when one's life's purpose has been fulfilled</note>
But you, who are so magnificent a giver, seem to be just as fair and prudent an exacter: you grant eternal things, not temporal ones. You do not demand temporal things from us, but eternal ones. Indeed, you command that we pray to God for your health. You certainly command most justly. For we ought to do even more than you command. You also command most prudently; for before you commanded us to pray, you took care that we should not pray in vain <note>Ficino implies that by obtaining the Jubilee indulgence for them, the Cardinal has purified their souls, making their prayers more effective before God</note>. We shall therefore do what you command, venerable father, as long as we live. And undoubtedly as gladly as you yourself have bestowed this singular and divine gift, and as we have received it. Know that we consider and openly confess: to whom we owe eternal life, we owe much more our temporal life and all temporal things. Farewell, and be happy in God, the author of happiness.

### The Utility of a Life of Leisure

Marsilio Ficino to Andrea Cambino, guardian of the fortress. Sends greetings.

<margin>c</margin>While I was walking in the forum together with our distinguished friend Francesco Casati, your elegant letter was delivered to me, in which you signify that you have now established a life of leisure <term>otium</term> <note>In the Renaissance, "otium" did not mean laziness, but rather productive leisure or "holy rest" dedicated to study and contemplation</note> in the guarding of that fortress. And you say that in that state of life, all other things are present to you, but divine things alone are lacking. Therefore, you ask that we give our work *On the Christian Religion* to the son of Francesco Berlinghieri <note>Francesco Berlinghieri was a Florentine geographer and member of the Platonic Academy</note>, a young man adorned with letters and character, to be sent to you. First, I indeed approve of what you say: that you have found leisure at the summit of the fortress. Truly, only in the highest watchtower of a serene mind is that Elysian and happy tranquility found. The lowest valley of the senses is tossed on every side by the waves of Acheron, Styx, Cocytus, and Phlegethon <note>The four rivers of the Greek underworld, used here by Ficino as metaphors for the turbulent passions and distractions of the material world</note>. However, as to what you add—that in such leisure human things are supplied to you in abundance, but divine things not at all—this I cannot help but wonder at. For other things, as you know, since they are placed both outside of us and only in specific places, are acquired through movement, business, and labor. But divine things, since they are both within us and everywhere, are grasped through rest, leisure, and tranquility. Therefore, if you are truly at leisure as you say, you possess nothing less than human things, which are all too full of business; conversely, you possess nothing more than divine things, whose immense light is everywhere.

...shining, it reflects into the clear and perceptive eye of the mind as often as the mind is rightly turned toward it. It turns toward that light by its very nature, as if it were something divine, as soon as it is no longer turned away from it by the disturbances of human affairs. Perhaps, indeed, for a divine being to be turned toward the sun is nothing other than to not be turned away from it. 

Why then, my dearest fellow-godfather <note>original: *compater*. This term signifies a close spiritual bond, often through the sacrament of baptism, and was used by Ficino to denote intimate friendship</note>, do you ask about our religion? You are already religious enough, I think, if through your leisure—freed from the cares of the lowest things—you are bound by nature to the tranquility of the highest. 

But look, while I am writing, it occurs to me what my friend desires. No one is ignorant of the reason why beautiful people delight in mirrors more than the deformed. Therefore, our friend Cambinus <note>Giovanni Cambini, a member of the Platonic Academy in Florence</note>, since he has already emerged as abundantly religious, seeks my book treating divine matters as if it were a mirror, in which he may gaze upon his own piety as if it were his own beautiful form. I will send this mirror of mine as soon as I am able. Or rather, to name it more correctly, I shall direct this "pupil" of mine toward you <note>Ficino plays on the word *pupilla*, meaning both the pupil of the eye and a minor under guardianship, suggesting a deep, reflective intimacy</note>. Looking into it, you may clearly discern yourself and me at the same time. For those who live with one heart see also with one eye. They are even seen within a single pupil. But let me not be much longer at present than is my custom. Farewell. 

Yet I see that you, as someone most dear to my son <note>Likely referring to a younger student or protege shared between them</note>, do not wish to say "farewell" so quickly so that you may "fare well" even longer. Do you desire a letter a little longer still, as those who love from a distance usually do? Therefore, receive a greeting from our common friend, by which you may fare even better. Paul of Saxia <note>Paolo da Saxia, a learned contemporary and friend of Ficino</note>, a man of great learning, bids you greetings. And so, now, fare you well.

### On Perseverance

->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Soderini, greetings.<-

<margin>d</margin>
Tell me, my sweetest Soderini <note>Francesco Soderini (1453–1524), a Florentine diplomat and future Cardinal who was studying law at this time</note>, what should I write? Shall I praise your talent, your character, and your learning at great length? Not at all: for in a matter manifest to everyone, there is no need for witnesses. Shall I perhaps exhort you more vehemently to the most precious studies of civil law? Not even that: for he who spurs one already hurrying of his own accord does not, I think, provide a command, but rather pushes him headlong. Therefore, I will not urge you to run faster, but rather I will pray that you continue. 

Certainly, the prize for runners is not located in the starting gates, but at the finish line <note>original: *calce*. Literally the "lime" or "chalk" line that marked the end of a racecourse in antiquity</note>. To begin the race belongs to anyone, even the most lazy; but to reach the end belongs to very few. At the start of the sowing, thorns and rocks threaten; in the middle, the most charming flowers smile; at the end, the sweetest fruits are gathered. It is not the one who sows, but the one who tends and reaps the corn who should be called a happy farmer. 

I believe our Soderini will shortly be a happy farmer. The hard labor of sowing has long since passed for him, as has the harsher winter. For a long time now, a flowery spring has been underway. The fruitful summer approaches by the day. Therefore, since you are doing so well in health, may you be most sweetly able to eat the sweet fruits of your agriculture. Farewell. 

But why do I write so little at present to him whom I love so much? Because even while we seem to be absent from one another, we converse much with each other day and night because of our mutual love. Furthermore, Girolamo Amati <note>Hieronimus Amatius, a scholar and friend</note>, who is yours, and because he is yours is therefore mine...

### Only the divine physician can cure diseases of the soul.
## Marsilio Ficino to Francesco, Cardinal of Siena, sends greetings. <note>original: *S.D.*, abbreviation for *salutem dicit*. Francesco Todeschini Piccolomini (1439–1503), the recipient, later became Pope Pius III</note>

<margin>n</margin>Recently <note>The initial 'V' in the printed text is a printer's error for 'N', as indicated by the guide letter 'n' in the margin; the intended word is *Nuper* (Recently).</note>, Venerable Father, I was being weighed down by heavy grief due to the loss of a certain excellent friend. Neither could Calliope <note>The Muse of epic poetry and eloquence</note> with her lyre provide solace to my mourning—though she has often been a sweet relief for my labors at other times. Even Minerva <note>The goddess of wisdom</note> had somehow abandoned me. For unless she had for a little while moved her unyielding shield aside, the weapons of either harsh Saturn or cruel Mars <note>In Renaissance astrology, Saturn was associated with melancholy and Mars with strife or sudden pain; Ficino suggests his mental defenses were down</note> would never have wounded my miserable self. 

Only Phoebus <note>Apollo, the god of both healing and light</note> remained—that is, the divine physician who seemed able to cure a disease of the soul. To what end is this? Truly, Venerable Father, as if divining this unfair lot of mine—for you could not have known it otherwise—you sent a letter to your Marsilio at a most opportune moment, full of love and grace. In it, you forbade thanks to be given to you for the greatest benefits I have received from you. To speak further: it was not a letter you held out, but rather a most healthy and divine medicine—manna, nectar, and ambrosia. Indeed, whether by this medicine or rather by this nourishment, my soul was restored; it lived again, breathed again, threw off the sickness, and recovered its strength. 

Therefore, from now on, you shall be my Phoebus. My lyre shall always sing of you as the singular author of my soul's tranquility. The philosophers of Democritus's school <note>Ficino refers to the followers of Democritus, who identified "tranquility" or *euthymia* as the highest human good</note> valued this tranquility so highly that they placed both divine and human happiness in it alone. And yet, this tranquility is usually least present in those who perform great deeds, because they are "least" within those great things. But to my Phoebus, the harbor of my tranquility, both great things are fitting and the greatest things await him, since he is greatest even among the great.

### Where the reciprocity of love originates.
## Marsilio Ficino to Amerigo Corsini, sends greetings. <note>Amerigo Corsini was a Florentine nobleman and a member of the Platonic Academy</note>

<margin>p</margin>That proverb, Corsini—"If you wish to be loved, love"—from where do we think it receives its greatest power? If we ask Love himself for the reason behind this proverb, perhaps he will answer that he is so free and precious that he neither wishes nor is able to be bought or sold for any price other than himself. 

But if we ask a man who is a true lover and friend, he will answer, I think, in this way: "Whoever loves vehemently somehow takes himself away from himself and gives himself to the beloved." Now, therefore, the beloved—provided he is of sound mind—cares for the lover just as he would his own property. For one's own possessions ought to be most dear to everyone. He also knows that for a human being to be repaid in kind, a human must be given for a human, and for a will—that is, a heart—a will must be given. Added to this is the fact that he who loves carves the image of the one he loves into his own soul. Thus, the soul of the lover becomes like a kind of mirror in which the image of the beloved shines back. Therefore, when the beloved recognizes himself in the lover...

...[he recogni]zes that he is compelled to love him. If we seek the truth of that proverb from nature, she will perhaps teach us thus: likeness always procreates love. Likeness, moreover, is a certain nature that is the same in several people. For if this person is like that one, that one is also necessarily like this one. Therefore, the same likeness which compels this man to love that one also leads that man to love this one. For a similar tuning, whether in twin strings or in two lutes, has the effect—as we experience daily—that whenever one is struck, the other moves as well. If teachers of this kind either do not satisfy us or perhaps explain too little, let us turn now to the philosophers, my dear Corsini <note>Amerigo Corsini (1452–1501), a Florentine nobleman and student of Ficino</note>, and let us hear what cause they primarily offer for this mutual affection. Astrologers believe there is mutual goodwill between those in whose birth charts <note>original: *genesi*</note> there was an exchange of the luminaries—that is, the Sun and the Moon. For instance, if at my birth the Sun was in Aries and the Moon in Sagittarius, and at your birth the Sun was in Sagittarius and the Moon in Aries. Or for those whom the same or at least a similar sign was rising, or the same or a similar planet was in the ascendant. Or if the "benefic" planets <note>Usually Jupiter and Venus in Renaissance astrology</note> looked upon the angle of the Orient in a similar way; or if Venus was positioned in the same house of the birth and at the same degree. The Platonists add: those whose life is guided by the same or certainly a similar "demon" <note>original: *demon*; in the Platonic sense, this refers to a personal tutelary spirit or guardian angel assigned at birth</note>. But the natural and moral philosophers do not want the cause of similar affection to be a likeness of temperament <note>original: *complexionis*, referring to the balance of bodily humors</note>, nutrition, education, habit, or counsel. Finally, where more causes concur, there a more vehement mutual goodwill is found. Where all causes are present, there the affection of Pythias and D<gloss>a</gloss>mon, and of Pylades and Orestes <note>Famous pairs of legendary friends from Greek antiquity known for their inseparable bonds</note>, rises again. Why say more? A reason of this kind has for a long time joined Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Ficino’s closest friend and "unique friend," to whom he dedicated many works</note> and Marsilio Ficino in a certain divine love. The same reason now also happily joins Amerigo to us. What shall I say of Bernardo Bembo <note>A Venetian diplomat and father of the famous Pietro Bembo; he was a close associate of the Medici circle</note> the Venetian? Not only a reason of this kind, but even divine providence has joined him to us.

<margin>p</margin>Our Plato, in the dialogue titled *Ion*, considers only those poems to be divine which are infused into poets by the music of the Muses and by a divine frenzy <note>original: *furore*; referring to *furor poeticus*, a state of divine inspiration that transcends rational thought</note>; these, when they are sung as human music, stir both the singer and the listeners into a frenzy in some way. My lute will soon prove to many listeners that the poems of Alessandro, written yesterday to Marsilio, are of such a kind; Giovanni Battista Boninsegni <note>A scholar and close associate of the Platonic Academy</note>, our friend and a man exceptionally learned in Latin and Greek letters, also proved this shortly thereafter. ### Marsilio Ficino to Piero Soderini, most distinguished in letters and character, sends greetings.

<margin>v</margin>I have often wished, my dearest Soderini, to send my very own original manuscript <note>original: *archetipum*</note> to those who requested my letters. But this book of mine immediately objected with the greatest complaint: "I pray you, do not send me where you yourself are not, my father." However, when I just now commanded it to go to Piero, it raised no objection at all; for it seemed to understand that when it set out for Soderini, it would not be leaving Marsilio. Go then, my book, go happily to this man, without whom I go nowhere. But I see you now ask for some "travel provisions" <term>viaticum: funds or supplies for a journey; here used metaphorically for a companion</term>. At present, I find no provision more precious than Paolo Antonio, the dearest brother of both Piero and myself. Therefore, carry his sweet name with you as your provision. And whenever he happens to look upon you in his home, bid him greetings many times in the name of Marsilio.

### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Federico, Duke of Urbino, ever-undefeated, exceptionally wise and merciful, sends greetings.
<note>Federico da Montefeltro (1422–1482), a celebrated condottiero and patron of the arts who commissioned one of the greatest libraries of the Renaissance.</note>

<margin>c</margin>When I was distinguishing my letters, collected from all quarters, into books, I decided to separate those which pertained to Platonic theology above all others—being "divine" by their very subject matter—from the other "human" letters, and to bring them together into one volume. And since I wished to place a truly divine head upon this body, which is divine in its matter, I most gladly assigned it to Federico, Duke of Urbino. His divine virtue—to speak in the Platonic way—has fulfilled from God the <term>Idea: In Platonic philosophy, the perfect, eternal form of a thing</term> not only of a perfect man but also of a consummate prince. If that famous Diogenes <note>Diogenes the Cynic, who famously mocked Plato's theory of Ideas by saying he could see a table but not "tableness."</note> were to behold him, he who used to deny that Ideas could even be conceived would undoubtedly confess that they can now not only be understood by the mind, but even perceived with the eyes.

# The Second Book of Letters by Marsilio Ficino the Florentine.

## Five questions regarding the mind.
1. **First:** Whether its motion is directed toward a specific and certain end or not.
2. **Second:** Whether the end of its motion is further motion or a state of rest.
3. **Third:** Whether it is something particular or something universal.
4. **Fourth:** Whether it is able to eventually achieve its desired end.
5. **Fifth:** Whether, after it has attained its end, it ever departs from there.

### MARSILIO FICINO sends greetings to his fellow philosophers.
Wisdom—born from the supreme head of Jupiter, the creator of all things—commands her lovers, the philosophers, that if they ever desire to possess the thing they love, they should always seek the highest "heads" <note>original: *capita*. Ficino uses "head" both as a literal reference to the myth of Athena being born from Jupiter's head and as a metaphor for the primary principles or sources of things.</note> of things rather than their lowest footprints. For Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom.</note>, that divine offspring, is sent down from high heaven: *She herself dwells in the high citadels that she also founded.* <note>original: "Altas ipsa colit quas & condidit arces." A poetic line emphasizing that Wisdom resides in the highest intellectual realms.</note> 

She shows, moreover, that we cannot reach the highest sources of things unless we first ascend into the "head" of the soul—that is, the **mind**—having left behind the soul's lower parts <note>In Platonism, the soul is divided into parts; the "mind" (mens) is the highest, most divine faculty, while the lower parts deal with physical sensations and emotions.</note>. Finally, she promises that if we gather ourselves into this most fertile head of the soul, we shall there, without doubt, by means of that very head (which is the mind), beget **Mind** itself: a Mind that is both a companion of Minerva herself and the ward of supreme Jupiter. 

Therefore, my excellent fellow philosophers, I shall now bring into our midst that "mind" which I recently created with my own mind during a certain night-study <note>original: *lucubratiõne*. This refers to study or writing done by lamplight at night.</note> on Mount Coelano. I do this so that you—who are far more fertile than Marsilio—might be provoked by a certain emulation <note>A friendly competition in intellectual creativity.</note> to one day give birth to an offspring even more worthy of the sight of Jupiter and Pallas.

***

**The natural motion of every species, because it is conducted according to a certain order, is therefore known to be directed from a specific principle toward a specific end.**

<margin>o</margin>
Every motion of any natural species <note>original: *species*. In this context, it refers to the specific "kind" or "nature" of a thing, like the nature of a bird to fly or a stone to fall.</note> proceeds by a certain reason. For one species moves in one way and another moves differently; yet any given species always maintains the same tenor in its motion. It progresses from one point to the next, and from that point to the one after, in a most fitting manner, always moving forward and returning. 

We must ask from where such an order of motion is primarily received. According to philosophers, there are two limits to motion: the point *from which* it flows and the point *into which* it flows. From these two limits, motion gains its order. For this reason, motion does not wander aimlessly from the uncertain and disordered into the uncertain and chaotic; rather, it is directed from a certain and ordered nature toward a certain and ordered end that agrees with the nature from which the motion began. 

Everything runs back toward what is its own, rather than toward what is foreign. Otherwise, dissimilar species of things would sometimes move in the same way, and similar species would often move differently. The same species would be driven at different times in different ways, and different species would often be driven in the same manner. Furthermore, if this were not so, we would lose that succession of motion by which a thing is formed step-by-step through many fitting and proper degrees—flowing out at a certain time and flowing back in certain cycles of time. Finally, if this order did not exist, no motion would be directed toward a specific region, quality, or substance rather than toward any other.

### The highly ordered movement of the world is directed toward a certain end by divine providence.

If individual movements are carried out in a certain wonderful order, certainly the movement of the entire world itself does not lack the perfection of order. For just as individual parts exist from the whole and for the whole, so they receive their order from the order of the whole and are referred back to it. In this very common order of the whole, all things—however diverse—are brought back into one by a certain harmony and reason. Therefore, all things are led by a single Ordainer who is full of reason. Indeed, a primarily rational order flows from the highest reason and wisdom of the Mind, in which the individual ends toward which He directs individual things are necessarily prescribed. A common end for the entire universe is also prescribed, toward which the individual ends are led.

### What boundaries the movements of the elements, plants, and irrational animals have.

We have no doubt what boundaries the movements of the elements, plants, and irrational animals <note>original: *brutorum*. In Renaissance philosophy, "brutes" refers to animals that lack human reason.</note> have. Some elements descend toward the center of the world by a certain weight <note>This refers to the Aristotelian concept of "gravity," where heavy things like earth move to the center of the universe.</note>. Others ascend by lightness to the hollow of the higher sphere <note>This refers to "levity," where light elements like fire move upward toward the lunar sphere.</note>. The movement of plants, perfected by the power of nourishing and generating, ends in the sufficient nourishment of the plant itself and the generation of a plant similar to it. The same happens to that power which we and irrational animals have in common with trees. The movement of irrational animals, which properly pertains to sense, proceeds from a sensible form and from need—as it proceeds from nature—through those things which they perceive externally to satisfy the body's needs. The same happens to that nature which we ourselves have in common with all animals. All these motions we have just described, since they tend toward something particular, are known to come from a particular force. And they find sufficient rest within these boundaries we have mentioned, and are perfected as much as their nature requires.

### Five questions concerning the movement of the mind.

It remains for us to inquire about the movement of the human mind: **First**, whether it tends toward any end or not. **Second**, whether the end of its movement is further movement or a state of rest <note>original: *satus*, likely a typographical error for *status*, meaning a state of permanence or completion.</note>. **Third**, whether this good is something particular or universal. **Fourth**, whether it is able to eventually attain its desired end, that is, the highest good <note>original: *summum bonum*. This is the ultimate goal of human existence in Platonic and Christian thought.</note>. **Fifth**, whether, after it has attained its perfected end, it ever departs from it.

### The movement of the mind looks toward a certain end.

If other things do not wander aimlessly by foolish chance, but are directed by a certain rational order toward something most appropriate and fitting—by which they are also thoroughly perfected—how much more so is the mind, which is the receptacle of wisdom? The mind understands the order and ends of natural things; it daily orders its own affairs rationally toward a certain end; it [is the guide] for others...

<meta>catchword: others</meta>

SECVNDVS XLVIII

In all things that we have previously said, it is much more perfect insofar as it regards a certain end ordered by a natural instinct, so that it might be brought to its desired fulfillment. Especially because, just as the individual parts of life—that is, <term>deliberations</term> <note>original: *consultationes*</note>, <term>choices</term> <note>original: *electiones*</note>, and <term>facultates</term> <note>meaning the powers or abilities of the soul</note>—are referred to individual ends (for each of these regards its own specific end as a good), so too is the whole of life directed toward a universal end and good. Since any parts serve the whole, it follows that the order which exists among the parts is for the sake of their relationship to the whole itself. Again, the order of those parts which looks to particular ends depends upon a certain common order of the whole, which especially contributes to the common end of the whole. Indeed, if every mover moves for its own sake, it is fitting that the Mind leads its various parts to their own ends for no other reason than to contribute to the common end and good of the Mind. Finally, who is so lacking in mind as to think that the mind strives, both by nature and by purpose, to exhibit an order for individual and diverse things toward a single thing, unless it also possessed an order of its own toward the One? Truly, since the ultimate and common end everywhere moves the rest—for it is the first thing desired, for the sake of which other things are desired—it is no wonder that if this ultimate and common end were entirely absent, the others could not exist. For unless the absolute form of the entire building is prescribed to the <term>architect</term> <note>original: *architecto*</note>, the various servants will never be moved to their diverse tasks in an order that serves the whole. Indeed, they will in no way be sent to their pre-defined duties by one who does not himself first have the common goal of the entire work defined.

->The end of intellectual motion is not movement, but a state of rest.<-

If the end of <term>intellectual motion</term> <note>original: *motionis intellectualis*</note> is movement itself, then surely it moves so that it may move; and moves again so that it may move thereafter, shifting without end. From this it would follow that, persevering perpetually in motion itself, it would never cease to be moved. And therefore, it would never cease to live nor to know. Perhaps this is that perpetual motion of the soul by which the soul is thought by some <term>Platonists</term> <note>original: *platonicis*. This refers to the followers of Plato who argued the soul is "self-moving" and thus immortal.</note> to always be in action and life. The proof of this is that the mind profits more in a state of rest than in motion. Again, because its familiar objects are the <term>eternal reasons</term> <note>original: *rationes eterne*. In this context, these are the unchanging, divine blueprints or "Ideas" of things.</note> of things, not the shifting passions of matter. ### The object and end of the mind is the universal truth and good.

But is it a certain specific truth and good that is called the end of the intellect and the will? Or is it the universal? Certainly the universal. Since the intellect conceives a certain very broad notion of that which philosophers call <term>being</term> <note>original: *ens*</note>, truth, and goodness, under which it thoroughly understands whatever either exists or can exist. The <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle, who famously taught while walking about the Lyceum</note> believe that this very thing which is called being, truth, and goodness—containing all things—is the common object of the human intellect. Because just as the object of sense is the "sensible" (that which can be felt), the object of the intellect itself is called the <term>intelligible</term> <note>meaning that which can be understood by the mind, rather than perceived by physical senses</note>. Moreover, the intelligible, in its vastness, encompasses all things. Again, the intellect is naturally inclined to grasp the entire breadth of being; and in its notion of being, it perceives all things, and conversely, in the notion of all things, it looks upon being itself. Furthermore, it understands everything under the aspect of truth and desires everything under the aspect of goodness. The Peripatetics refer both of these back to the nature of being. Whether the good is truly broader than being—as the <term>Platonists</term> <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy</note> believe—or not, seems to have no bearing on the question at hand. Let us therefore use these three names for the present, if you please—namely, being, truth, and goodness—as if they signified the same thing. For we have discussed these matters more carefully in our commentaries on [Plato's] *Philebus* <note>original: *philebi*</note>.

First, it seems necessary to ask whether the intellect can clearly reach whatever is included under being; it certainly can. For it divides [being] into the ten <term>most general categories</term> <note>original: *genera decem generalissima*; referring to Aristotle's list of the primary ways something can be said to exist, such as substance, quality, or quantity</note>; and again, it divides those ten categories into many subordinate types step by step. Then it places certain final species under these subordinate types. Finally, it subjects individual things to these species, so to speak, without end. If the intellect can describe being itself as a whole and divide it gradually into all its "limbs," and most diligently compare those parts both to each other and to the whole, who does not see that this mind is by nature capable of grasping the being of the universe itself? For he who sees the whole in its form and observes its boundaries and the stages through which it spreads everywhere, can undoubtedly grasp the individual things contained within those boundaries.

I pass over the fact that, since among the Platonists one can conceive of the "One" and the "Good" as being above and beneath being, the mind will be all the more able to traverse its entire breadth on every side. Certainly, after the notion of being—a word we have now repeated quite often—the mind also thinks at will of that which can be imagined as most different from it: that is, non-being. If it can traverse from being to non-being, which is infinitely distant from it, it can much more easily pass through whatever intermediate things are contained under it. Hence Aristotle says: just as matter, which is the lowest of natural things, can take on all bodily forms—and in this way all things become bodily—so the intellect, which (so to speak) is the last of supernatural things and the highest of natural things, can receive all spiritual forms of all things, and become all... <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing the Aristotelian idea that the soul "is in a way all things."</note>

...to surrender. Just as the universe, under the rationale of being and truth, is the object of the intellect, so under the rationale of the good is it the object of the will. What does the intellect seek? Nothing but to transform all things into itself by depicting everything in its own way. What, on the other hand, does the will lose itself in? Nothing but to transform itself into all things by enjoying everything in the manner of all things. The former [the intellect] strives so that the universe may become, in a sense, the intellect; the latter [the will], however, so that the will may be the universe. To this, therefore, the natural effort of the soul inclines, just as <term>Avicenna</term> <note>original: *Avicenna*; a Persian polymath (c. 980–1037) whose work on metaphysics deeply influenced medieval and Renaissance philosophy</note> says in his *Metaphysics*: that the soul itself, in its own way, should become the whole world. For we see that every soul, by a natural instinct and continuous effort, strives to know all truths through the intellect and to enjoy all goods through the will.

### The origin and end of the mind is only the infinite truth and good

<margin>m</margin>
Indeed, one must remember that the universe itself, which we call being, is the goal of the mind, and it is entirely infinite. For we consider the primary and proper end of anything to be that which the thing itself properly desires above all else as its highest good; for the sake of which it seeks and does everything else; and in which it finally rests completely, so that, without the further sting of nature or desire, it is finally at peace. This condition is innate to our intellect: that it seeks the cause of every thing, and then the cause of that cause. Therefore, the inquiry of the intellect never ceases until it finds that cause which has no cause, but is itself the cause of causes. That is God alone, the boundless. Likewise, the affection of the will is satisfied by no good as long as we believe another good remains beyond it. It is satisfied, therefore, only by that good beyond which there is nothing good. What else is this but the boundless God? Therefore, whatever truth or good is offered that has limited degrees—no matter how many—the intellect still seeks more and the will desires further. Thus, you can never rest except in the boundless truth and good, nor can you reach your end except in the infinite. Since every thing rests in its own origin—the source from which it is made and where it is perfected—and since our mind can only rest in the infinite, it follows that only that which is infinite is its proper origin. This should properly be called infinity and eternity itself, or rather something eternal and infinite. Since an effect closest to its cause becomes most like that cause, it follows that the soul is, in a way, an infinite and eternal power. Otherwise, it would never properly incline toward an infinite end. This is certainly why no humans live contentedly under the sky or are ever fully satisfied by temporal riches.

### The mind can eventually reach its desired end and good.

<margin>p</margin>
The rational mind can, at some point, attain its perfect end. For if things that are quite perfect in nature achieve their natural perfection by reaching their sought-after goal, how much more should the mind, which is both most perfect and the goal of all things in nature...

...if those things which prescribe an end neither to others nor to themselves <note>original: *Si quæ finem neq; aliis neq; sibi ipsa præscribunt*; referring to inanimate objects or lower forms of life that act according to natural laws without conscious intent</note> sometimes attain a suitable end, how much more so the mind: which catches sight of its own end and, having found it, establishes ends for many other things. It foretells the ends of many, and sees the end of all. If natural power in even the smallest things is not in vain, certainly it is not in vain in the soul; which exists as something so great from God that it can precisely measure the distance by which the smallest things are exceeded by the greatest. It follows that the soul would by no means naturally follow a certain end unless it were also able to reach it. For by what other power is it moved toward that end, if not by that power which can also actually arrive there? Furthermore, we see that when the soul strives intensely, it progresses much in a motion of this kind. By the very virtue through which it progresses, it is at some point perfected. Finally, we see it move more and more vehemently by degrees. Just as any element, the closer it approaches its natural limit, the faster it moves. Therefore, just as with a physical element, so too the mind does not always progress in vain from one thing to another without a limit. But it eventually reaches the desired end for its own sake. 

There are, moreover, in natural and human things and actions, certain principles <note>In this context, "principles" refers to the starting points or fundamental origins of things</note> and there are ends. It is against nature itself and the logic of a principle to ascend from one principle to another forever without a [first] principle. It is against the logic of an end to descend from end to end successively without an [ultimate] end. Every action takes its origin from a supreme agent. Every desire <term>appetitio</term> <note>original: *appetitio*; the natural inclination or "appetite" of a thing toward its proper good</note> takes its origin from a supreme end. For whatever things are such-and-such for the sake of another are necessarily reduced to that which exists as such for its own sake. Therefore, if both supreme points are missing, neither will any action begin at all, nor will any desire be stirred up. Finally, since a mover moves for its own sake, where there is a supreme mover, a supreme end is likewise found. This is true in any specific order of things, and it is similarly true in the order of the universe. 

But it is helpful to explain the above reasoning about the mind somewhat more broadly. If anyone should ask us which of these is more perfect: the intellect or the sense? The <term>intelligible</term> <note>things that can be understood by the mind, like geometry or justice</note> or the <term>sensible</term> <note>things perceived by the five senses, like colors or sounds</note>? For we all use our senses continuously, and we use them most greatly and intensely. Thus, I now respond to that earlier question of yours in this way: the intellect is at least as much more perfect than the senses as its power is more widely and perfectly spread through its actions. The senses, as you yourself were showing, can recognize neither themselves, nor the intellect, nor the objects of the intellect. But the intellect knows both. There is, in addition, another degree of perfection: for when the intellect compares itself, the senses, and other things regarding their degrees of perfection, it already holds the highest form of perfection itself before its eyes, as it were. By comparing both to this form, it judges that whichever comes closer to it is the more perfect. If the intellect reaches this highest form of perfection, it undoubtedly does so because it shares a certain supreme proportion with it. Therefore, the intellect is not only more perfect than the senses, but is itself almost "supremely perfect" after perfection itself.

I see, moreover, a third degree of perfection in the intelligence. For while it seeks and judges itself, it is certainly reflected back upon itself. Whatever is of such a nature also exists and remains within itself; it is, furthermore, entirely **incorporeal** <note>Having no physical body or material form</note> and simple. Finally, since it proceeds from itself back to itself in a **circular motion** <note>original: *motu circulari*; a Neoplatonic concept where the mind "rotates" from its source back to itself, indicating its self-sufficiency and immortality</note>, it can certainly move eternally—that is, it can always act and always live. 

I shall pass over the fact that the intellect, being more perfect, is shared by fewer beings; it is exercised later in life and more rarely, and is granted as a final goal after the use of **growth** <note>original: *vegetationis*; referring to the "vegetative soul" responsible for nutrition and physical development</note> and the senses. It gives the senses their rules and laws and prescribes their end. It leads itself to act according to its own will when it reasons and deliberates. The senses, however, whenever reason does not resist them, are always driven by natural instinct. I shall also pass over how reason often chooses differently than what the senses and the needs of the body require. This is because the principle of choice clearly does not depend on the body; otherwise, its goal would always be focused on the body. 

Certainly, one can see that reason is by no means subject to physical bodies in its motion, because in its contemplation it transcends bodies altogether; in its deliberation, it extends itself to diverse and opposite things; and in its choices, it often resists the body's inclinations. Therefore, it is much less subject to any bodies in its essence and its life. Consider this: the senses seem to grow dull as one ages, but the intellect does not. It can, however, be turned away from its goal of contemplation when it is too occupied with caring for and tending to the physical body. Consider also: whenever the object of a sense is too intense, it suddenly harms that sense; after such an encounter, the sense cannot immediately discern weaker things. Thus, an excessive brightness offends the eye, and a violent noise offends the ears. 

The mind, however, is the opposite: it is never harmed or confused by its most excellent object <note>God or Universal Truth</note>. In fact, once it has known that highest object, it discerns lower things more clearly and truly at the same time. This signifies that the nature of the mind is highly spiritual and excellent. <summary>Ficino argues for the superiority of the intellect over the senses, noting that while the senses are limited by the body and can be overwhelmed by intense stimuli, the intellect is self-reflective, incorporeal, and strengthened by contemplating higher truths.</summary>
