<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument regarding the superiority of the human intellect over the animal senses. Having established that the intellect is more perfect because it can judge both itself and the senses, Ficino now explains how the intellect handles universal truths and why reason is unique to humanity.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>BOOK</header>

according to its essence and life, the intellect is not submerged in matter. It separates bodily forms from the passions <note>In this context, "passions" refers to the passive states or physical changes that matter undergoes.</note> of matter. It also distinguishes those forms which are entirely within the body from bodily things themselves, precisely because the intellect itself is separated from the passions of matter and from the conditions of the bodily form. Furthermore, the senses are content with particular objects alone. However, the familiar objects of the intellect are the **universal and eternal reasons** <note>original: *rationes*; these are the underlying principles or "blueprints" of things</note> of things. The intellect cannot reach these in a familiar way except through a certain special proportion to them; from this, it appears that the intellect itself is also absolute and eternal. This is especially true because it reaches reasons of this kind through certain **mental forms** <note>original: *species*; the conceptual images or archetypes the mind uses to understand the world</note> which it both creates and receives. It is necessary for these forms to be free from the passions of matter. Otherwise, they could not represent those eternal reasons and ideas. Moreover, unless the intellect itself existed free from the passions of matter, it could neither create nor receive forms of this kind in this way.

<sig>r</sig> **The Mind, more than the senses, can reach its desired end.**
**Reason** is indeed proper to us. For God did not infuse it into the beasts. Otherwise, He would have given them speech as the interpreter of reason. Furthermore, He would have given them the hand as the servant and instrument of reason. Moreover, we would see in beasts some signs of consultation and variety. But instead, we see that they never act otherwise than by the impulse of nature, driven only by the necessity of the body. They all weave their webs <note>Ficino likely refers to spiders or birds building nests</note> in the same way; they neither learn to weave, nor do they improve in their weaving over any length of time. Finally, there would appear in the brutes certain signs of **religion** and works manifest to all. For where the intellect is present—which is like an eye established to see the light of the mind—there also the intelligible light, which is God, shines, is looked up to, is loved, and is worshiped.

Just as the intellect is more perfect than sense, so at least man is more perfect than the brute. And from this very fact, he is more perfect because he possesses something proper to himself and not common to the beasts. Therefore, he is judged more perfect only because of his intelligence. This is especially true since, through the gift of intelligence, he approaches that infinite perfection which is God through affection, contemplation, and worship. Now, the chief perfection of anything consists in the possession of a **fitting end** <note>original: *conuenientis finis*; the ultimate goal or purpose suited to its nature</note>. The attainment of this end is easier and fuller the more abundant the innate perfection is. For where that formal perfection which is born within from the start prevails, there, by the order of nature, that final perfection is granted more abundantly, easily, and happily. Indeed, the former serves the latter. It does not happen that the latter serves the former. From this, it is concluded that reason can attain its fitting and desired end much more easily than sense, and man much more easily than the brute.

**The immortal soul in a mortal body is always wretched.**
<sig>e</sig> We experience within ourselves our "beast"—that is, the senses—reaching its end and its good very often; for instance, when it is completely satisfied by the attainment of its sufficient object. But we do not experience our "human"—that is, reason—attaining its desired end. For in...

<vocab>essence, bodily forms, intellect, reasons, mental forms, Mind, Reason, consultation, brutes, religion, intelligence, immortal soul</vocab>

<summary>Ficino argues that human reason is unique because it contemplates universal truths and God, whereas animals are driven by fixed instincts and lack religion or progress. He concludes that because humans have a higher innate perfection, they must have a higher ultimate goal, though this goal is not fully realized in our mortal bodies.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the relationship between the human intellect and the divine. Having argued that the intellect is eternal and separate from matter, Ficino now compares the light of the mind to the light of the sun, warning against the pride of philosophers who rely solely on their senses.</meta>

<page-num>LV</page-num>
<header>SECOND BOOK</header>

...we would see. We certainly understand nothing other than the light of the highest **intelligible** <note>In Platonic philosophy, "intelligible" refers to things that can only be perceived by the mind or intellect, such as mathematical truths or divine ideas, rather than by the physical senses.</note> which is full of the reasons <note>original: *rationibus*; the underlying logic or blueprints of creation</note> of every intelligible thing. Just as we do not see anything except the light of the sun, which is depicted with the colors and shapes of all things. 

And do we still doubt whether immense goodness loves us or provides for us? This goodness fosters us without a mediator, as if we were its own children, and it embraces us everywhere and always. And do we still doubt whether we distinguish the sublime rays of forms from the lowest shadows of matter by some lowly and bodily spark, or rather by an incorporeal and heavenly light? 

Let us argue for higher things; let us everywhere refute lower things. Let us measure how small earthly things are, how great heavenly things are, and how immense **super-celestial** <note>The realm beyond the physical heavens, often identified with the divine mind or the dwelling of God.</note> things are. No one seems to lie more everywhere than he who settles for measuring the greatest things with the tiny finger of bodily sense, rather than measuring them with the greatest measure of the mind. No one slips more deeply into the shadows—whether secretly by himself or cast down against his will—than he who becomes so proud toward himself and so ungrateful to the heavenly Sun that he claims to see light without the light of Him from whom all light comes. It is as if someone believed he could see the heavenly lights by the ray of his own eye alone, rather than by heavenly splendor. 

Here **Paul the Apostle** <note>Referring to the biblical passage in Romans 1:21-22.</note> cries out against certain prouder philosophers: "Who, when they had known God, did not glorify Him as God, nor did they give thanks. But they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened; and thinking themselves to be wise, they became fools." 

The mind of these men seems to have suffered an **eclipse** <note>original: *eclypsim*; Ficino uses this astronomical term to describe the soul losing its connection to the divine light.</note> when it too proudly turned away from God. Indeed, it turned away most miserably from itself. For we ourselves unhappily desert our own being when we foolishly desert Him without whom we cannot exist in any way. Alas, whoever miserably leaves this Protector does not leave Him entirely. For at the same time, he falls back into the hands of the same Being, but as a Punisher. Alas, whoever scorns the Father while He shines kindly will meanwhile experience Him as a Judge who burns. Thus, in the same light where he neglected to venerate his own infinite Good, he may eventually feel his own infinite evil because he neglected what he neglected. And because of the impurity of his eyes, he may forever grieve under the ray of that light, he who did not purify his eyes and lift them up so that he might always rejoice in the whole light. 

When the mind of impious philosophers imprudently falls away from God, then the senses in them impudently fall away from the mind. The body, though willingly, followed the senses powerlessly. From this arise certain most monstrous opinions. From this have sprung the most savage customs of all. From this comes a life miserable on all sides. 

But on the contrary, there are no opinions more probable, no customs more proven, nor any life more blessed than the life of those who are legitimately—that is, piously—approved. This is the study of knowledge and truth when joined with a religious and always true piety. This seems to be nothing other than a refusal to separate the love of honoring the truth from the love of finding the truth.

->**The Hierarchy of Stability**<-

The **elements** move in a changeable way. 
The **celestial spheres** move in a stable way. 
**Souls** stand in a changeable way. 
**Angels** stand in a stable way. 
**God** is stability itself. <note>Ficino presents a hierarchy of existence: physical matter is purely mobile, the stars move predictably, human souls have a foot in both change and permanence, angels are fixed in their state, and God is the unchanging foundation of all.</note>

<summary>Ficino argues that human reason is a reflection of divine light and warns that prideful philosophers who ignore God suffer a "mental eclipse." He concludes with a hierarchical scale of existence ranging from the moving elements to the absolute stability of God.</summary>
<keywords>divine light, Paul the Apostle, pride, eclipse of the mind, hierarchy of being, stability, piety and truth</keywords>

## Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Giovanni Francesco Ippolito, 
## most distinguished doctor of both laws and Count of Gazzuolo, gives greetings.

<margin>♥</margin> We see that the elements, from the earth even to the heavens, are moved changeably. Changeably, I say: because they seem to be moved away from the strictly straight rule of motion at times, either due to an impediment or some other cause. But the celestial bodies are indeed moved, yet they move **stably** <note>Ficino distinguishes between the "changeable" motion of earthly elements (which can be blocked or diverted) and the "stable" motion of the stars and planets, which never deviate from their orbits.</note>. For they persevere continually in their natural motion. Hence, a state of rest is judged much more perfect than motion. For motion necessarily requires a state of rest, but the reverse is not true. Wherefore, if motion appears to us to be gradually more perfect as we ascend from lower to higher things—and that motion is more perfect which is more stable—then much more must a state of rest itself appear to be gradually more perfect than other states of rest. Thus, just as stability increased from the elements into the heavens to such an extent that a mode of "standing" (which is called stability) has been found, much more must it increase above the heavens so that a certain substance of rest itself is discovered. There, therefore, will be something that always stands, even if it does so "changeably." These are the **rational souls** <note>In Platonic philosophy, the soul is the "mean" or middle point. It is unchanging in its essence (substance), but its thoughts and feelings (actions) are always moving from one thing to another.</note>: whose substance is always the same and does not suffer any change, but whose affection and action are varied.

Since indeed any change signifies a certain lack, on account of which that which is moved usually runs toward that which it does not have, it is necessary that above that which is lacking there exists something which is full. By this full thing, mobile things are sustained and ruled, and to it others return to be filled. Therefore, above souls are the **angels** <note>Ficino places angels at the top of the hierarchy of created beings because they possess "intellectual constancy"—they don't need to "think through" a logic chain; they understand all truths simultaneously and eternally.</note>: who both stand always and stand stably. This is because both their substance and their action are always the same in them.

Bodies are but shadows of spirits. Spirits, on the contrary, are the lights of bodies. Indeed, there are three types of bodies. Therefore, there are three types of spirits: A body composed of the elements changes from its state both in its whole and in its parts. The spheres of the elements, even if they are changed in their parts by turns, nevertheless remain incorrupt as wholes. Finally, the celestial spheres persevere as indissoluble both in their parts and in their whole. Spirits void of reason <note>Ficino likely refers here to the "animal spirits" or the vital breath that animates physical bodies but lacks higher intellect.</note> perhaps change entirely. But **rational spirits** <note>Human souls.</note> remain the same in their whole substance and primary action, although they are changed by a certain alternation according to certain "particles"—that is, their lowest powers and actions. Angelic spirits consist as the same and stable in both substance and action.

Nay rather, to express it more properly: if many bodies are found which, although they change in disposition, always remain the same in substance—and these are indeed those whose proper movement is the **circuit** <note>original: *circuitus*; the circular motion of the heavens, which returns to its starting point and thus mirrors eternity.</note>, that is, the celestial bodies—much more are there many spirits who, even if changeable in a certain disposition, are nevertheless inwardly immutable in substance. Such indeed are those who, endowed with reason, perform a certain rational circuit from themselves back into themselves internally when they notice and cherish themselves. They act externally, however, by deliberating from the end of things to be done back to the principles and vice versa; then by moving from certain propositions to conclusions and back; then by speculating from the effect to the cause and again from the causes to the effect. Again, this happens when they resolve particulars into universals and, in turn, universals into particulars.

<summary>Ficino outlines a hierarchy of existence based on stability, moving from the volatile earthly elements to the stable celestial orbits, the semi-stable rational soul, and finally the perfectly stable angels.</summary>
<keywords>Marsilio Ficino, celestial spheres, rational soul, angels, hierarchy of being, motion vs stability, Neoplatonism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the human soul. Previously, he discussed the hierarchy of motion and stability, moving from the physical elements to the celestial spheres and eventually toward the divine. Here, he shifts focus to the psychological and existential tension within the human being: the conflict between bodily senses and the insatiable nature of human reason, using classical myths to illustrate the soul's restless search for its source.</meta>

# BOOK SECOND

Even in the highest physical pleasures, when the sense itself is completely filled as far as its capacity allows, reason is still intensely agitated and agitates the senses in turn. For if reason chooses to obey the senses, it always suspects there is something more. It devises new delights. It continually seeks I-know-not-what beyond. Or, if it strives to resist the senses, it makes life laborious. Therefore, in both cases, not only is reason itself not happy, but it thoroughly disrupts the happiness of the sense itself. Even if reason has already subdued the senses and gathered itself into its own center, then—driven by its own nature—it searches for the reasons and causes of things. In this search, it often finds what it did not want, or fails to find what it did want. Or perhaps it does not comprehend as much as it desires and is capable of grasping. It is certainly always in doubt, wavering, and anxious. Since, therefore, reason is never at rest, it is certain that as long as it is in this state, it neither attains its own desire nor allows the sense to enjoy its own goal <note>original: "fine" - referring to the 'telos' or ultimate purpose of a thing</note> even when that goal is present. 

Indeed, nothing more irrational can be imagined than that man—who through reason is the most perfect of animals, indeed of all things under heaven—should, for that very same reason, be the most imperfect of all in regards to that final perfection <note>Ficino distinguishes between "formal perfection" (our biological/intellectual design) and "final perfection" (our ultimate fulfillment or happiness). He finds it paradoxical that our highest gift, reason, makes us the most miserable creature on earth.</note> for the sake of which our initial perfection was granted. This man seems to be that most unhappy Prometheus: who, instructed by the divine wisdom of Pallas <note>Athena, the goddess of wisdom</note> and having obtained the celestial fire—that is, reason—is judged the most miserable of all for this very reason. He stands on the highest peak of the mountain—that is, in the very stronghold of contemplation—suffering the continuous bite of a most rapacious bird—that is, the sting of restless inquiry. He remains so until he is carried back to that same place from which he once received the fire; so that just as he is now constantly stimulated toward the Whole <note>The Divine or the Absolute</note> by that one little ray of heavenly light, he may then be completely filled by the entirety of that light.

->How difficult it is for man, placed outside his natural state, to pursue happiness;<-
->yet how easily he attains it when restored to his natural state.<-

The arguments concerning the ease of human happiness brought forward by us earlier seemed clearly to show the truth itself in a certain natural order. Why is it then that—as experience teaches—such great difficulty is opposed to us as we strive for blessedness? We seem to roll that great stone of Sisyphus <note>In Greek myth, Sisyphus was condemned to roll a boulder up a hill for eternity, only for it to roll back down each time.</note> up the steep parts of the mountain. And what wonder: we seek the highest summits of Mount Olympus, yet we inhabit the abyss of the lowest valley. We are weighed down by the burden of a most heavy body. While we pant toward the heights, we often slide back suddenly into the precipice, as much by our own weight as by the jagged rocks on every side. Furthermore, many stumbles and obstacles hold us back from one side, while from the other, the harmful allurements of certain meadows <note>A metaphor for worldly distractions and sensory pleasures.</note> delay us. Thus, alas for the wretched! For those thus banished from their sublime homeland to the lowest depths, nothing is ever encountered that is not extremely difficult. Nothing occurs that is not miserable on all sides. What shall we answer to such an ambiguity? On the one hand, reasoning promised the highest ease; on the other, experience likewise shows the highest difficulty.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument regarding the human soul’s perpetual restlessness. While the previous page established that reason is never at peace in the physical world, this page seeks a theological and philosophical explanation for this condition. Ficino transitions from the internal experience of dissatisfaction to the external authorities of Scripture and ancient philosophy to explain why humanity feels "out of place" in the natural world.</meta>

->-># BOOK [SECOND]<-<-

Finally, only the <term>Mosaic law<note>The Torah or the first five books of the Bible, attributed to Moses.</note></term> will settle such a great dispute for us: we have been placed outside the order of our first nature. Alas, we act and suffer outside the order of nature. Just as easily as the first man—having turned entirely toward God at first—was able to receive happiness, so easily thereafter did he lose that ease by turning away from Him. Therefore, all the offspring of that first parent, being placed with such difficulty outside the order of their former nature, receive blessedness as difficultly as they would receive it easily if they were restored to that same order.

But what will the philosophers say to these things? The <term>Magi<note>The priest-sages of ancient Persia.</note></term> indeed, followers of **Zoroaster** and **Hostanes**, assert something similar. For they say that because of a certain ancient infirmity of the human mind, all things happen to us as weak and difficult. And if anyone were to restore the balance <note>original: "temperationem" - a harmonious mixing of qualities</note> of the soul, all things would then be set in order. This is also not in disagreement with the teachings of the **Pythagoreans** and **Platonists**: namely, that the soul is afflicted by so many evils in the sensible world because, being too much enticed by the greed for sensible goods, it imprudently lost the goods of the <term>intelligible world<note>The realm of pure ideas and spiritual truths, as opposed to the world of physical objects.</note></term>. 

The **Peripatetics** <note>Aristotle’s followers, named after the "peripatos" or covered walkways where they walked while teaching.</note> perhaps will say that man, more than the beasts close to him, goes astray because he is moved by <term>free will<note>original: "libero arbitrio"</note></term>. Whence, here and there, as he uses various conjectures in deliberation, he is able to transgress. However, an irrational animal is not led by itself, but is directed toward its appropriate end by the never-erring providence of nature itself, like an arrow directed toward a target. 

But that error and transgression of ours—since it does not come from a defect of nature, but from the variety of reason and the crookedness of counsel—by no means destroys our natural power; rather, it disturbs the will. And just as in a physical element placed outside its own proper place, a natural force and inclination toward its own proper goal <note>original: "terminum" - a limit or final resting place</note> is preserved along with its nature—by which it can one day return to its own region—so too they think that in man, even after he has wandered from the right path, there remains a natural power to seek again both the path and the goal. 

Finally, the most exact examination by the theologians briefly concludes the whole matter thus: No inclination toward any motion can be greater than the mover that causes it. Since, therefore, the inclination of the soul leans primarily toward the infinite, it clearly depends solely on the infinite. For if it proceeded immediately from some determined cause acting as the soul's mover after God, it would lean only toward a limited end. For although the power of moving is infinite in the infinite beginning, it is nonetheless limited in the subsequent cause which is determined. And the motion follows the quality of the immediate mover rather than the remote one. 

Wherefore, the very mover who properly turns the soul toward the infinite is itself solely an **infinite power**: This power moves the mind, in accordance with the nature of free will, in a certain way to choose paths with the greatest freedom. Again, by the infinite power of the mover, it incites the soul toward desiring the end to such an extent that it cannot help but desire it. If a motion of this kind cannot reach the place where it is directed, certainly no motion can. Where infinite power flourishes, there also infinite wisdom and goodness reign. And these move nothing in vain, nor...

<summary>Ficino explains the human condition of "unnatural" suffering and error through both the biblical Fall and classical philosophy, arguing that our desire for the infinite proves we are moved by God alone.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the soul's destiny. Having established that the human soul is currently "out of place" and restless in its earthly state, Ficino now argues that this very dissatisfaction proves a future state of perfection where the soul and a perfected body will be reunited in eternal happiness.</meta>

SECVNDVS
G 4

...does not withhold any good from anyone that can and should already be received. Therefore, since man—both through the use of reason and contemplation (approaching the most blessed angels) and through divine worship (approaching God, the fountain of happiness)—comes much closer than the beasts do, it is necessary that he will eventually be much more blessed in the possession of his desired end. For one who is more like the higher beings <note>original: "supernis"</note>, both in the fire of his will and the light of his intelligence, should likewise be more like them in the happiness of his life. Indeed, from the strength of life comes the power and excellence of understanding and willing. 

But now, in this body, man is far more miserable—partly because of the weakness and frailty of the body itself and the lack of all things, and partly because of the constant anxiety of the mind. Therefore, however difficult it is for the celestial and immortal soul to pursue its happiness in an earthly, imbalanced <note>original: "intemperato" - refers to an imbalance of the four bodily humors.</note>, and decaying body, it will just as easily attain it when either freed from the body or residing in a balanced, immortal, and celestial body. Furthermore, a natural end <note>The ultimate purpose or "final cause" of a thing's existence.</note> does not seem to exist except in a natural state <note>original: "habitu naturali"</note>. Now, the most natural state for an eternal soul seems to be this: that it lives in its own body, which is then made eternal. From this, it is concluded by necessary reasoning that the soul's immortality and brightness can and must eventually shine forth into its own body. In this state alone is the highest happiness <note>original: "beatitudo"</note> of man completed. And indeed, this opinion of the prophets and theologians is confirmed by the <term>Magi<note>The priest-sages of ancient Persia, whom Ficino considered part of a "perennial philosophy" leading to Christianity.</note></term>, the <term>Mercurial philosophers<note>Followers of Hermes Trismegistus, also known as Hermeticists; Ficino translated the Corpus Hermeticum.</note></term>, and the **Platonists**.

### The mind, once it has attained happiness, never loses it.

<margin>q</margin> When the soul reaches an infinite end, especially because it reaches it by the same reason through which it is moved, drawn, and led there, it certainly reaches it without end. If it could rise from a certain infinite degree (which is infinitely distant) to the immense, it can also remain infinitely within that immensity itself. This is especially true because the same infinite power that drew the soul so far toward itself now holds it closer than can be explained. In the infinite good, no evil can even be imagined; and whatever good can be imagined or desired is found there in full. There, then, is eternal life, the clearest light of intelligence: a state free from change, a condition <note>original: "habitus"</note> devoid of lack, and the secure, safe possession of every good. Joy is full on every side.

## End of the five questions concerning the mind.

Above the senses is the intellect. Above the sensible <note>Things perceived by the physical senses.</note> is the intelligible <note>Things understood by the mind alone.</note>. Above our minds are other minds. Above bodily forms are incorporeal <note>Non-physical or spiritual.</note> forms.

## Marsilio Ficino the Florentine, to his fellow philosophers, sends greetings.

<margin>a</margin> Every day, through reasoning and consultation, we seek and find what might be truer or better in both natural and human affairs. In this discourse, we use certain common and incorporeal rules of truth or goodness, and we refer those things being discussed to an incorporeal, universal, and supreme good of truth...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul’s current misery in the body proves it is meant for a future, eternal state where it will illuminate a perfected body. He concludes his "five questions on the mind" by asserting that the soul's ultimate happiness, once reached, is permanent and infinite.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*. Having argued that the soul’s restlessness in the body suggests a future state of perfection, Ficino now shifts to an epistemological proof: the superiority of reason and the intellect over the senses, arguing that the soul must be incorporeal and eternal because it perceives eternal truths.</meta>

# BOOK
## SECOND

...or we refer to it by comparing it to the form of divinity <note>The text begins mid-sentence; "nitatis" is the end of "divinitatis" (divinity).</note>. So that whatever thing among others seems to approach closer to its own degree is judged to be truer and better than the rest. However, we do not do all this by sense, but by **reason** <term>ratio: in this context, the human faculty of logical thought and judgment</term>. For in men, reason alone is that which assigns the reasons <note>original: "rationes" — here meaning the underlying principles or essences</note> of things. And by reasoning, it compares individual things to a common form according to common rules. From here, two things especially are concluded. 

First, that **reason** exists in a truer and better manner than **sense** <note>original: "sensu" — the faculty of physical perception</note>, since this alone in us brings itself to the highest truth and goodness, as much by discourse <note>logical progression of thought</note> as by affection. And when the truth and goodness of sense itself is dealt with—of whatever kind that may be—this very thing is performed by no means by sense, but by reason. 

Second, that by as much as reason is truer and better than sense, by at least that much are the objects called "objects of reason" truer and better than the objects of sense. Especially because whenever the truth or goodness of sensible things is investigated, this itself can neither be tracked down nor found except by a certain power and light of **intelligible reasons** and forms. Wherefore these intelligible things, which are called the **objects of the intellect**—that is, the incorporeal reasons and forms of things themselves—are absolutely truer and better, being free from the "passions" <note>disturbances or limitations</note> of matter; and therefore they seem to exist more in the nature of things than the forms of bodies which are offered to the senses. 

To these is added that, just as the sensible moves the sense, so in a certain way the intelligible moves the intellect. If we cannot perceive those things which are below us <note>Physical, material objects.</note> unless we are in some way moved by them through certain **appearances** <term>species: the mental images or "likenesses" of objects that the mind perceives</term>, much less can we conceive anything above us <note>Metaphysical or divine truths.</note> unless we are so moved by it that the mind, pregnant with its seed, brings forth from there an offspring similar to a more excellent substance. For the mind, by its own power alone, would never bring forth anything except what is either inferior or equal to itself. 

Therefore, when the mind rises to the **intelligible** itself—which is both truer than the sensible and often more excellent than the mind itself—it is necessary that the mind be completely raised to it, above itself, by the power of that intelligible object. Unless this very thing existed more truly than the sensible, it certainly could not move the intellect more truly than the sensible moves the sense. But now it moves the intellect far more truly, since it leads more toward the truth as well as toward the reason of any truth. For what is true in its own reason, and what the reason of truth is itself, and conversely the truth of reason, we perceive not by sense but by reason. 

But if anyone should say: that the mind is not moved to understanding by foreign or external things, but that it conceives its own appearances and its own objects for itself by its own and a certain wonderful power, we shall say that from this it follows that the mind is entirely incorporeal and eternal; if it is moved in no way by another but by itself, and by its own power conceives incorporeal and eternal appearances or reasons. For the true reason <note>The essential definition or "Idea" in the Platonic sense.</note> of anything, since it cannot at any time be otherwise, is of an everlasting nature. 

Furthermore, we shall add to these: if there is not lacking to the mind a certain most simple and most perfect form—nay, rather it is present—through which and toward which it speaks concerning the simplicity and perfection of all things, and concludes that it itself is simpler and more perfect than many things, and also that many things are simpler and more perfect than itself. If, I say, such a form is not lacking to the mind but is present, by much less...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human intellect is superior to the senses because it can perceive incorporeal, eternal "reasons" or forms. He concludes that if the mind can grasp or produce these eternal truths, it must itself be incorporeal and eternal.</summary>

...is lacking to the universe. Indeed, it is present much more; and the **mind** <term>mens: the highest part of the soul, the intellect</term> receives from that One the power by which it is moved toward those forms. We will add, furthermore, that the human mind is indeed at the summit of the genre of natural forms, since it conceives or receives purer and truer perfections, in comparison to which natural things are of no weight. However, it is not at the summit of the order of minds, because it is not "most true"—that is, supremely truthful—since, due to the fault of the harmful body, it often doubts and is deceived. But that Mind <note>Referring to the Divine Mind or God</note> is seen to be most true which never admits anything false, and nothing at all ambiguous. Because, in truth, whatever is truer is also greater and more powerful in its existence, it follows that above our mind there are other minds: ones that are truer in their manner, being further removed from falsehood than ours. And finally, above all others, there is a certain supreme and truest Mind. In this Mind, the "mind" is not one thing and "truth" another; understanding is not one thing and being another; acting is not one thing and willing another. Since this Mind is most fertile—indeed, it is **fertility** itself—it produces, preserves, and illuminates many minds thereafter, like daughters.

But truer minds possess truer **reasons** <term>rationes: the underlying spiritual principles or "blueprints" of things</term> of things. The truest Mind possesses the truest reasons. From this, it is concluded that the incorporeal reasons of things—which are thought of by human reason at its will—are not mere figments. This might seem to be the case to those who live and judge things by their senses rather than by reason. On the contrary, above us, in a certain divine mind—as if in a **heavenly sun**—the truest lights of all these "reasons" shine most clearly. From there, the rays of the true reasons are sent down into other minds (which seem to be intermediaries between that Mind and ours, like superior and somehow unchangeable stars) and even into our own mind, which is like a changeable moon.

**The mind is everlasting because it uses the ray received from above to reach for eternal things.**

<margin>Q</margin> Because the "eyesight" of the mind does not act through such rays—that is, it does not see and desire—in any other way than the substance of the mind itself has received them, we therefore conclude by the clearest light of true reason: to all degrees of minds, even the lowest, **eternity of life** has been granted by the first Mind, or rather, by the supreme Light of minds. This is evident since a certain recognition, desire, and veneration of natural eternity is granted to them all.

->The mind is understood as a created thing by the **reflected ray** of God; it understands the Creator by the **direct ray**.<-

<margin>L</margin> This "moon" of ours—that is, our mind—is varied by a diversity and succession of light and certain shadows, according to how it is turned toward or away from its Sun <note>God</note> in more or less different ways. It is never deprived of the total capacity for receiving light. Yet, it never shines totally on every side; for the part that lacks **reason** <note>original: "ratione cares"—the non-rational or animal part of the soul</note>, being somewhat "denser" (that is, less fit), does not reflect the light. I say that this "moon" of ours perceives the rays by which it looks up at the super-celestial stars (that is, the **angels** <term>angelos: spiritual beings who, in Ficino's Neoplatonism, act as higher intellects</term>) and discerns that they are, by certain reason, far more excellent than the physical stars of heaven. It loves and worships them more vehemently. I say it receives such rays from those very celestial stars, which do not extend their understanding or affection any higher than to itself...

...[they] can perform. It <note>The human mind.</note> cannot have had these things on its own. It can, however, have received them from the **angelic stars**—or rather, from the super-celestial sun through the angelic stars: for all light of the stars, as common opinion holds, comes from the sun and returns to the sun. Every light of minds comes from God and returns to God; and this moon of ours <note>Ficino likely uses the moon here as a metaphor for the human soul, which reflects divine light.</note>, when it looks toward the divine sun so that it sees clearly that he is infinite and in what way he is so: and because he is infinite, it asserts that he precedes the angels by an utterly infinite interval. It considers those angels as nothing in comparison to him, receiving a ray of such a kind that it progresses infinitely even above the angels and holds them almost as nothing.

Certainly, the mind did not receive this from the angels. Nor, again, did it receive it from God himself *through* the angels. For while a ray passes through a limited angel, the ray itself is limited; for this reason, the mind could not raise its sight or its love toward the truly **immense** <term>immensum: that which is immeasurable or infinite</term>—insofar as it is immense—through such a limited medium. For an inherently infinite power is needed for that movement which, truly verging toward the infinite, proceeds without end in such a way that it can only reach its end in an infinite limit. Therefore, it is a pure ray of the immense God alone by which we recognize that God is immense; unless we knew this, we would always seek further beyond. It is also seen to be a flame of the immense God alone, by which we burn for the infinite in such a way that no liquid except the infinite can extinguish—or rather, to speak more correctly, fulfill—our thirst.

Perhaps it will be worthwhile to explain that **Platonic simile of the sun**—just as we have explained it most extensively in the book *On Love* <note>original: "de amore"; referring to Ficino's *Commentary on Plato's Symposium*</note> and in the *Theology*—here also somewhat more broadly than above. Among all the instruments of the senses, the eye is the purest; among all the powers of the soul, the **intellect** <term>intellectus: the higher rational power capable of grasping abstract truths</term> is the purest. In the visible world, the sun is the supreme visible thing. In the intelligible world <term>mundus intelligibilis: the realm of ideas and spiritual reality that exists beyond physical matter</term>, God is the supreme intelligible.

Therefore, just as sight relates to the visible, so the intellect relates to the intelligible. Sight discerns all visible things (that is, colors) in the brightness of the supreme visible thing (that is, the sun). The intellect perceives all intelligible things and all truths in the light of the supreme intelligible and of Truth itself. And any intellect needs such light so much more than sight needs its light, as much as every intellect and any intelligible thing depends more on the supreme and infinite intelligible than sight and any visible thing depend on the sun itself—which is finite and is produced and preserved by higher causes. 

Whatever is seen—whether by the eyes of certain animals that see at night by some **innate little ray** <note>Ficino refers to the ancient theory of "extramission," the belief that the eye emits its own light to see.</note>, or by others by the light of fire or stars—all of this is seen by the splendor of the sun itself. For just as everything hot is made and preserved by the supremely hot, so everything bright is made and preserved by the supremely bright. It is "preserved," I say, because even if equal causes (that is, those in the same species as the effect) are necessary in the creation of an effect but not in its continued existence, nevertheless, higher causes are necessary even in the preservation of an effect. By the same reasoning, whatever is understood—whether by some innate and natural light (like a familiar little ray of the eye), or by the rays of the lower angels like fire, or by the lights of the higher angels like stars—this whole thing is understood by the rays of that infinite and intelligible sun. Especially because a sun of this kind flourishes everywhere as a whole and fills all things from within; and more so from there all things both in...

...preserving them, which depend on their birth just as images in mirrors depend on bodies. Through a ray of the sun reflected everywhere through other things, we can see those other things. But the sun itself we cannot look upon except through a certain direct ray of its own, and by directing our sight straight toward it. 

And because of this ray, which flows out beyond the sun—and is therefore mixed and diminished in some way—the eye cannot discern how pure and how great the sun actually is. If we acknowledge its purity and size, it is not the eyes that do this (for they are greatly deceived), but we measure it by **reason** <term>ratio: the human capacity for logical thought and measurement</term>. It would have been necessary for the eye to be so constituted by nature that it adhered most closely to the solar sphere itself, so that it might perceive its own purity and size. 

In the same way, the ray which, emanating from God, is infused into created things, shows us created things alone in their proper sense. But it is the ray directed into the **mind** <term>mens: the highest part of the human soul</term> itself—truly directed toward God—that shows God himself to us more clearly. Nevertheless, because he is perceived by the mind according to the mind's own quality and capacity, this ray cannot fully show the purity and infinity of God. Therefore, through this ray alone, we could never think of God as a completely **pure act** <term>actus purus: a philosophical term for a being that is fully realized and perfect, with no mere potential to be something else</term> and infinite. 

We have nothing inside ourselves above the mind that is able to refute the mind's deception. Yet, by a certain reason, we consider the abyss of divine purity and infinity; we notice the "reason of infinity" and, in turn, the "infinity of reason." When we also think about how, even above the highest angels, through innumerable degrees of perfection progressing more and more step by step, the divine act infinitely transcends a progression of this kind, which is itself almost infinite. 

Therefore, not only is a ray of the **Divine Sun** <note>Ficino's term for God as the source of all intellectual light and truth</note> present in the eye of the mind, but the Divine Sun himself is present under the very reason of his own infinity (if I may say so), through which the mind may see and desire both the truest reason of infinity and the infinity of reason itself. He is present, I say, everywhere; and he is present always. 

Since everywhere, as often as minds are unburdened and apply themselves more attentively to this work, they consider the divine act to be infinite by this reason: because it is not confined by any limits of any subject, nor is it stained by the mixture of any quality. It is not surpassed by the excellence of a higher cause; it is not exceeded by intervals of time or the spaces of places; it is not terminated by any number of degrees of power, however many; nor, perhaps, is it terminated or surpassed by the mind, which proceeds without end beyond any number and limit, both in imagining and in desiring. 

The mind sees that beneath the infinite act of God there lies an infinite **passion** <note>original: "passionem" — here meaning receptivity or the potential to be acted upon</note> of matter, so to speak. It sees time as a kind of interminable motion, a space equal to the **immense** <term>immensum: that which is immeasurable or infinite</term> (if I may speak thus), and a kind of perpetual succession of generation, and the tireless wandering of the mind. It sees that **pure nothing** <note>original: "purum nihilum"</note> can be considered infinitely by denying it; and it sees an immense evil being thought of there. 

It sees **pure being** <note>original: "purum ens"</note> (as I might say) being infinitely affirmed through reasoning, and that it is an entirely immense good, because it is an **immense power** <term>virtus immensa</term>. For any power is one thing; number and measure are another. And any power is prior, in a certain order, to that by which it is measured. Therefore, whenever number or measure is added to power...

Therefore, he who completes all things with **number** and **measure** does not possess number or measure himself. The Platonic philosophers believe that wherever the highest visible thing is, the highest sight exists there as well. For this reason, they attribute not only life to the sphere of the sun, but also the most sharp and certain power of seeing. In this, they seem to imitate Orpheus <note>original: "Orpheum"; Orpheus was a legendary Greek poet and musician whom Ficino believed was a founding father of ancient theology</note> above all others, who calls the sun the "eye of the world," through which and by which the eyes of all see. <margin>P</margin> <note>This "P" likely marks the beginning of the discussion on the **Peripatetics**</note> The **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetici: the followers of Aristotle, who traditionally emphasized logic and natural philosophy</term> think that the highest intellect and the highest **intelligible** <term>intelligibile: an object that can be understood by the mind, as opposed to a "sensible" object seen by the eyes</term> are completely the same. Indeed, the highest intellect possesses the highest mode of understanding; therefore, in understanding, it does not look outward, but inward. Nor does its intelligence depend on anything other than itself. Moreover, that the highest intelligible is also the highest intellect is clear from this: there must be a certain greatest proportion between the intellect and the intelligible. Since that which is furthest removed from the passions of matter becomes most intelligible, that which is most **abstract** <term>abstractum: here meaning "separated from physical matter"</term> is most truly and greatly an intellect. Finally, the highest intelligible would not be such unless it were also an intellect to itself; and it is understood by itself. Furthermore, if "intelligible" signifies a certain excellence over common intellects—for it moves, illuminates, forms, and perfects them—then nothing is found in an intellect by **participation** <note>participation: the philosophical idea that things have qualities (like beauty or intelligence) only because they "share" in the essence of a higher, perfect source</note> or **form** that is not found in the highest intelligible itself by way of its cause and acting power. Therefore, rational souls are said to be intellects by participation. Angels are considered intellects by form. The highest intelligible—that is, God—is intellect **by cause**. He is an intellect, I say, above all thinkable intelligence—an intellect infinitely more excellent than any other intellect. If the light of the sun, by which the eye sees the sun, had an eye itself, then surely while our eye saw it, it would also—and much more clearly—look back at our eye in return, since all clarity flows from it. And do we still doubt whether that divine eye—by which and through which the eyes of our minds see everywhere—sees our eyes in turn? Unless he himself saw us, who by continually seeing us always illuminates us, and by illuminating us grants us the power and act of seeing, certainly nowhere [would anything...]

they divide by composing. Indeed, every force directed toward a revolution <note>original: "circuitum"; referring to circular motion, which was considered the most perfect and eternal form of movement</note> is considered natural and eternal: both because it does not withdraw from itself through its own center, and because, if necessary, it returns to itself through its own circumference; and at any given point, it always begins its start from the end. This is especially true where a spiritual revolution occurs. For there, the circumference is joined to the center. And a simple substance of this kind reflects its power back into itself and increases it by this very reflection. Leaning upon itself, it preserves itself. 

It is necessary to remember that where the discourse of reason <term>discursio rationis; the step-by-step process of logical thinking</term> occurs, there are certain innate, stable principles of reasoning—that is, certain common and manifest notions <note>original: "communes quasdam manifestasque notiones"; these are innate ideas or "seeds of truth" that Ficino believes are implanted in the human mind by God</note> from which, starting out as if with rays, we seek things that are more unknown. And by comparing them to these same principles, we shall judge. 

It is fitting, moreover, to remember that because those principles are necessary and eternal, the power of the soul, which is the subject of those principles, is likewise eternal. We possess that discourse as something proper to our nature. But the foundations of discourse are common to us and the angels. In that part, we are celestial; in this, we are super-celestial <note>original: "supercaelestes"; Ficino suggests that human intellect shares a rank above the physical heavens, participating in the divine realm of angels</note>. 

There are two extremes of the worldly body: the Earth and the Empyrean heaven <term>coelum empyreum; the highest, unmoving heaven in medieval cosmology, believed to be the dwelling place of God and the angels</term>. Both seem immobile, but for different reasons. The Earth, because it has not attained any power for revolution; the Empyrean heaven, because it has already attained all the power of bodies. The middle spheres, however, through a certain eternal but mobile power, require something further—I know not what—that is permanent and eternal. What we have said regarding these three levels, understand as being said fully regarding sense, reason, and mind. Again, understand it as being said of beast, man, and angel. 

Because the elements are not only bodies but are also composed of the lowest matter, they are restlessly agitated. But celestial things, because they lack such matter and are almost like non-bodies, therefore move steadily and equally; and by their order, they seem to restrain the errors of the elements. Yet because they are carried by opposite and contrary motions, if they were carried by their own [physical] natures, it would be necessary for contrary natures to be within them. Nevertheless, there is no dissonance of contrary qualities where all destruction and all transgression is absent. They move, therefore, by a certain tempering by which the superior cause itself rules powerfully and leads them sweetly. 

Nature is "uniform" <note>original: "uniformis"; having one form or essence</note> because it brings so many things into one; it is also "omniform" <note>original: "omniformis"; having all forms</note> because it reduces those things to all-form boundaries and effects. It is not, however, a bodily form. Otherwise, it could not be uniform and omniform at the same time. And everything bodily, while it moves, is necessarily changed. Therefore, it cannot be the most perfect mover. And because it does not remain stable while moving, it cannot by its own power alone maintain a permanent course in motion. 

For this reason, the celestial globes are moved by a certain spiritual and rational substance. And that substance indeed possesses an eternal and indefatigable power by which it can roll such great masses so equally and quickly for so long, and produce a wonderful, rational, and most beautiful order. They are called rational souls <note>original: "Rationales animae"</note> because they are in no way...

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the nature of the soul. Note: although the previous page was identified as Book II, this page is headed as Book VI of Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*. <header>BOOK VI</header>

...bodies, but they already incline toward bodies by a certain natural effect. For this reason, they remain indeed eternal in essence and life, but as it were, in a mobile manner. They are moved, in truth, by an innate and proper power. Angels, however, since they are neither bodies nor incline toward enlivening bodies, both stand and do so stably, as we have argued in the previous sections. Just as all moving things are led back to one motion and a first time, so all stable things are necessarily reduced to one first state and eternity, as if to a hinge or center. Upon this hinge, whatever stands leans according to its strength, and whatever moves revolves around it. Through the union of this center, things so many and so diverse give birth to a single harmony. 

Motion and time are almost the same thing. Rest and eternity are entirely the same. For those things which appear separate in the lower realms are marvelously joined in the higher ones. Whatever is said to "stand"—whether in itself or in another—stands first of all by rest itself. Then, it takes on a certain composition in some way. But above that which is in some way composite, there necessarily exists something most simple <note>original: "simplicissimum"; in Platonic philosophy, simplicity refers to being non-composite and indivisible, the ultimate source of all things</note>, upon which all other things depend, and by which they are united and composed. 

Especially because that which is first in nature—since it receives nothing from elsewhere beyond its own first being—cannot be conceived as composite in any way. Thus, therefore, above the sluggish nature of the mobile thing, let there be a more constant motion above wandering motion. Above a stable condition, let there be a stable substance with a certain mutable condition. Above this, let a nature that is entirely stable be placed. Above stable nature, let there be rest itself, the simplest of all things. Where there is the highest simplicity, there is the highest unity; therefore, a single God exists. He is, in truth, absolute unity; and as the Platonists <note>original: "platonicis"; referring to the followers of Plato, particularly the Neoplatonists like Plotinus whom Ficino studied deeply</note> hold, He is also in a way the unity and hinge of the Mind, just as the Mind is the hinge and unity of the Soul, and the Soul is the unity and hinge of Nature. Finally, Nature is the hinge of bodies. 

Just as God is pure rest <term>status; a state of unchanging permanence</term> lacking all change, so He is pure unity, free from imperfect multitude. Because His rest is pure, He is therefore swifter than all motion. For already from eternity He is in Himself all that which, in some minimal part, universal motion scarcely and gradually achieves through the whole of time. And whatever the divided motion of a divided nature performs in a divided interval of time, all that the indivisible state of rest accomplishes in an indivisible moment of indivisible eternity, as it wills. For where the most constant power <term>virtus; here meaning 'inherent power' or 'efficacy' rather than moral virtue</term> dominates, there the swiftest action of all is produced. But where an unstable nature wavers, the motion becomes slower. 

Again, since God is pure unity and the principle of infinite multitude, He is therefore infinitely more powerful than any infinite multitude of things. If an innumerable number can emanate from Him through eternal time, He is already in act an innumerable number—or rather, an infinite unity and immense power. And whatever things are infinitely dispersed are, so to speak, infinitely weakened; but He, by His immense unity, powerfully gathers them into the immense. Since, truly, no difficulty of action is present where the measure of power is absent <note>original: "unde mensura virtutis abest"; literally "from where the measure of power is absent," implying the power is infinite or unmeasurable</note>—a power which a measured nature cannot resist—for that reason God perfects all things infinitely more easily and more blessedly than can be imagined; so much so that if he should stand...

<summary>Ficino explains the metaphysical hierarchy where God exists as absolute unity and rest at the center of all things. He argues that this divine rest is paradoxically more powerful and swifter than any motion, serving as the source and "hinge" for souls, angels, and nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book VI of Ficino’s *Platonic Theology* regarding the ontological hierarchy of being. Having established that all things depend on a single, simple center, Ficino now distinguishes between the four levels of existence: Body, Soul, Angel, and God, specifically focusing on their relationship to motion and division.</meta>

<page-num>LVII</page-num>
<header>SECOND [PART] LVII</header>

...that He may preserve all things at once, He who is all things at once: from whom and toward whom, as if from a center and toward a center, individual things depend like lines and points, so that by one stable command <note>original: "nutu"; literally a 'nod,' implying an effortless exercise of divine will</note> He may cause each thing to move according to its own nature.

Corporeal form is divided and moved by another. The rational soul is not divided, but moves by itself. The angel is neither divided nor moved but is filled from elsewhere. God is a single, simple, immense plenitude.

->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Nicolaus, Bishop of Vác, and Francesco Bandini.<-

<margin>f</margin>A form which, by itself and primarily, exists as such-and-such a thing in its kind, must be most fully that thing. For that which by itself and primarily is hot and shines, is hot and shines in the highest degree. Therefore, a corporeal **FORM** that is not perfectly such a thing depends on some other higher thing. Every form that is divided along with matter or dimension and is changed by another is the most imperfect of all forms. For it requires the support of the subject or the dimension itself, since it does not exist by itself, given that it is not either in itself or with itself. Nor is it primarily born from a subject, which by its own nature is judged to be formless; nor again from quantity, which does not act through itself but through quality. Furthermore, because of extension and dispersion, that form becomes weak. Finally, because of its motion, it appears needy. Therefore, it neither acts nor is moved by its own power, since it does not possess its power whole; and it is neither sustained nor does it subsist by its own power.

**SOUL**: For this reason, it depends on a certain more excellent form which can consist in itself without a subject and with itself without dimension—that is, the soul. Although the soul is moved by itself in a certain way (because it precedes qualities that are entirely changeable), it is nevertheless not divided in any way by matter or quantity. This is especially evident because it clearly distinguishes indivisible forms from divisible ones and joins them with itself, and also because it turns back into itself, which a divisible form cannot do. For where one part is distant from another, a turning of the whole into itself has not yet occurred. That the rational soul moves freely by itself appears most clearly when it understands corporeal things in its own way rather than in the way of the things themselves. And against their impulse, it often chooses by its own judgment what it has decided to provide. It issues its motions into many and opposite parts continually, as one that is not drawn by a determined quality of nature or an object, but is led rather by the variety of its own counsel.

**ANGEL**: However, since it is moved in a certain way and for that reason is judged as if "unworthy" <note>the soul is "unworthy" of perfection in this context because motion implies a search for something not yet possessed</note>—since no thing is accustomed to seek through motion what it already possesses—there is therefore above the soul the immobile angel. I say "immobile" because it is already full in every respect.

**GOD**: Just as one ascends from that which is by no means entirely full to that which is most full, so one ascends to Fullness itself from the "most full." This is because a descent occurs in a certain order from Fullness to the less full through that which is "most full." Truly, the intention of every cause in acting is something...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book VI of Ficino’s Platonic Theology regarding the ontological hierarchy of being. Having established that all things depend on a single, simple center, Ficino now distinguishes between the internal and external actions of God, moving from the generation of the Divine Word to the creation of the cosmic hierarchy.</meta>

<header>BOOK</header>

...to generate something most similar to itself according to its own powers. And the more powerful a cause is, the more and more easily it achieves this. <margin>**GENERATION within God. Creation by God.**</margin> From this it follows that from that cause—than which none more powerful can be conceived—something is generated so similar to itself that nothing more similar could be thought. Such a similarity is found nowhere else unless the substance of the generator and the generated is entirely the same. <note>Ficino is here using Platonic logic to explain the Christian Trinity: "Generation" refers to the Son being of the same substance as the Father, while "Creation" refers to the making of the world, which is of a different, lesser substance.</note> But let us set aside for now the fact that God generates within Himself. Let us consider those things He procreates outside of Himself. For here too it is consistent that God procreates certain things most similar to Him, and then progressively less similar things, so that no rational order of stages can be contemplated by us that has not first been both contemplated and fulfilled by the highest Reason. Truly, it is from such a divine order that natural causes preserve a similar order in producing their effects; likewise, minds, in their reasoning, maintain a skillful order and discover both the natural and the divine. To what end is all this? So that I may conclude that above souls—which are not yet most full—there already exist angels who are most full. And above the angels who are being filled, there is a fountain from whose waters <note>original: "liquoribus"; literally 'liquids' or 'fluids,' a common Neoplatonic metaphor for divine grace or being flowing from the source</note> they are filled. <margin>**GOD is one and simple.**</margin> Many things can and indeed must be "most full," so that in God’s most perfect work, perfect parts may abound everywhere. However, that plenitude <term>plenitude: the state of being completely full; in this context, the absolute fullness of Being</term> itself is simple, and it is through it that all full things are filled; and because they are filled, they are called "composite" <note>In this philosophical system, anything created is "composite" because it consists of its own nature plus the "fullness" or "being" it receives from God.</note>. Plenitude in its highest form can only be one. If someone were to propose two highest plenitudes, we would ask whether they differ from each other entirely or agree in every respect. Or rather, do they partly agree and partly differ? If both were similarly "plenitude," they could not differ entirely. If they are said to agree entirely, they are one—and thus not two, which is what we are currently discussing. If they coincided in one part and differed in another, first, each would be composite and dependent on parts and some simple composing element. Secondly, neither would be that very plenitude we are seeking. For that by which one differed from the other would not be found in the other. Add to this that in the highest plenitude there ought to be nothing that is (so to speak) not full. But if it had diverse parts, no part would be the same as any other, nor the same as the whole. Thus, no part would be most full. Therefore, to repeat myself once more: plenitude must be unique and entirely indivisible. Add also: it is infinite. <margin>**GOD is infinite.**</margin> Indeed, just as in that which we call a pure vacuum or emptiness itself, nothing can be imagined to be present; so in pure plenitude—which must exist as the direct opposite of pure vacuum—nothing into infinity can be imagined that is *not* present. From where else do the first matter of the world, the entire course of the universe, and the discourse of every mind derive this quality? For they naturally strive to be filled beyond any limit, which they would not do unless they were drawn by that very Plenitude which both overflows beyond all limits and allures minds, the world, and matter above every boundary.

### Compendium of the Platonic Theology of Marsilio Ficino the Florentine.
### The Ascent from Corporeal Substance to the Incorporeal: namely to Souls, Angels, and God.

### Marsilio Ficino to his fellow philosophers, greetings. <note>original: "S.D." abbreviating *Salutem Dicit*, a standard Latin greeting meaning "sends health" or "sends greetings."</note>

Since substance is the foundation of every accident <note>In philosophy, a "substance" is a thing that exists in itself (like a tree), while an "accident" is a property that exists only in something else (like the greenness of the tree).</note>, it is prior to the accident by a certain order of nature. Because it is prior and does not lack the power of form, it can exist somewhere without an accident—especially a corporeal accident, which, when added to the common nature of substance, brings not so much progress as defect. Indeed, if a substance exists without a corporeal accident, it will be truer because of its purity, and more powerful because of the simplicity and unity of its indivisible nature. For this reason, there is already some substance in act <note>Existing fully and currently, rather than just as a possibility.</note> apart from the division of quantity and the mixture of corporeal quality. This must be so lest that potential, which is so rational and so good, should always be in vain within the universe. Otherwise, that nature which is esteemed to be truer and more powerful than any corporeal substance would be either entirely false or completely weak.

The FIRST stage of incorporeal substance is a certain life; that is, the soul. Moreover, that incorporeal substance seems to be the same as a certain life. This is because the proper characteristic of life is a certain power—quite miraculous—for penetrating, uniting, and moving the body. Such a power belongs primarily to a substance that is entirely incorporeal. Lives of this kind already exist in the order of things. For a living body depends more on the life joined to it than the life depends on the body. For the body is formed, sustained, ruled, and moved by it. Therefore, just as below this union of body and life certain bodies are found—namely stones and metals, and others of the same kind—which can remain without life: so also, and much more likely, there perhaps exist many lives that can sustain themselves without any support from a body. These are partly rational souls and partly angels. Angels are ABOVE souls. But is it necessary for angels to exist above bodies and souls? It is indeed necessary: for certainly the nature of the intellect itself, insofar as it is intellect, seems to be such that it rather...

<meta>This page continues the "Compendium of Platonic Theology" by Marsilio Ficino. It follows the previous page's introduction of substance and accidents, now moving specifically into the nature of the mind and its relationship to the body, ascending through the hierarchy of human, angelic, and divine intellects.</meta>

<header>BOOK</header>

the mind lives apart from the body rather than within it. It understands through a certain abstraction of forms from the individual experiences <note>original: "passionibus," referring to the sensory inputs or "passions" that the body undergoes</note> of bodies. And the more it is abstracted from these, the more clearly it discerns, and the more effectively it acts and lives blessedly. It is as if that state were the most natural habit of the mind; indeed, to join the mind to the body is perhaps nothing other than to separate it far from its own origin. Moreover, that which is more natural exists for the most part in the very order of things. Therefore, above those intellects which are present in bodies—that is, rational souls—there are surely minds which are entirely sequestered from the commerce of bodies.

Just as the property of pure intellect is to live apart from the body, so it is the nature of pure sense to be with the body. Therefore, the spirit in which there is only sense with life lives, as it seems, only in the body. However, the spirit in which there is only intellect conducts its life entirely outside the body. But where intellect and sense are joined—which is the case for a human being—a spirit of this kind is endowed with such a nature that it can live both in the body and outside it. Yet, because the intellect in this state is a certain part within the soul (which contains other parts as well), it is ambiguous; it runs about by a certain spiritual motion, understanding by moving from one thing to another. For this reason, there must exist above it a more perfect mind: one that is neither contracted to the capacity of a soul, nor mixed with lower parts, nor distracted by time in its action, but is absolute in itself, pure and clear on all sides, performing its action not by running about <note>Ficino uses "discurrendo" to describe "discursive" thought, where the mind moves step-by-step, unlike the "intuitive" or "static" thought of higher beings.</note>, but by remaining still.

Above the mind in the soul is the mind in itself. Above that is God.

<margin>c</margin> That Platonic reasoning <term>Platonic reasoning</term><note>Marsilio Ficino was the central figure in the Renaissance revival of Plato. Here he uses "Platonic reasoning" to describe the theory of Participation: the idea that if many things share a quality (like intelligence), they must all be drawing it from a single, perfect source.</note> contributes to the same point. If the soul, according to its own form and reason, were intellect, then certainly the entire soul would be intellect—and an absolutely pure intellect at that. Every soul would then appear to be fully possessed of intelligence. But since the matter stands otherwise, it is clear that the soul possesses intelligence not according to its own primary form, but through a certain participation. Just as there are many minds above the minds of souls (which are said to be such by participation) who are minds according to their form—namely, the angels—so above minds that are such by form, there is one Mind who is mind according to cause and effective power: that is, God.

Many are the human intellects, many the angelic, but the divine is one.

<margin>q</margin> That there are many intellects according to participation is evident from the fact that rational souls are numerous. Furthermore, in the minds of different men, at the very same moment, there appear opinions, emotions, and habits <note>original: "Affectus habitus," referring to internal dispositions or moral characters.</note> that are utterly conflicting among themselves. We have already declared that there are also many intellects according to form among the higher beings, when we said that it belongs more to the nature of the mind itself to live apart from the senses and the body than with them. We prove that above all minds which are such by their very form, there is a single intellect according to cause by this: since the spiritual multitude of individual minds is more ordered and united than the multitude of bodies, it is necessary that a union of this kind proceeds from one single cause.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument in Book II of "Platonic Theology." Having established the distinction between intellect and body on the previous page, he now argues for the necessity of a single, supreme "Unity" (God) that governs both the material and spiritual realms to prevent cosmic chaos or infinite regress.</meta>

# BOOK TWO LIX

For diverse things, whether they are indeed corporeal <note>physical or bodily</note> or incorporeal <note>spiritual or non-physical</note>, cannot work together toward a single task, order, or end by the very reason that they are diverse. Rather, they do so only insofar as some "one thing" is common to them. And this very thing which is called "common" to all is not properly contained within the order of any one of them; for if it were, it would be the property of that one alone, or at least of a specific few, and not equally common to the whole. Nor does that common quality arise from the collective, varied power of the things themselves. For things that are diverse, as we have said, do not produce union insofar as they are diverse. 

But could it be that the nature which is common to all exists entirely of itself? Not at all. For it is a greater thing to exist *from* oneself than to consist *within* oneself. Since, therefore, a nature of this kind does not consist in itself but in a multitude, it certainly cannot exist from itself. Therefore, from a certain Unity which consists in itself above the number of all things, that union of all things proceeds. And because that sublime Unity is the property of no single thing, just as the numerical unit <note>the number "one"</note> is present everywhere in all numbers, and the point is present in all lines, so too that Unity, remaining indivisible, is present everywhere to all spirits and bodies alike, and it binds the universe together in equal measure. These things, by this very fact of a certain mutual agreement, are led toward the One because they are led *by* the One. Just as all the bodies of the world are reduced to one supreme body that contains and moves all things, so all spirits are reduced to one supreme Spirit that embraces all; through this, the Spirit gives life and motion to the spirits and bodies subject to it.

->Things are neither confused in a circle, nor are they reduced to several equal principles, nor do they proceed upward without end.<-

<margin>b</margin>Thus, as it seems, three primary errors are excluded. The first is of those who say that all things depend on each other in a circle, so that just as "this" depends on "that," so "that" in turn depends on "this." In this way, the same thing compared to itself would be both cause and effect, as well as prior and posterior, superior and inferior. The second error is of those who introduce several principles <note>starting points or first causes</note> side-by-side. For then there would be a certain number of principles composed of a common nature and individual properties. None of them would then truly be a "principle," because none would exist as a simple entity, and they would all proceed from a higher Unity that binds them individually. The third error is of those who always ascend upward from one principle to another without end. But while these people seem to pursue innumerable principles quite busily, they never reach any principle at all, since they never find a "first." Indeed, they ought to consider that whatever depends on another depends by its own nature; and unless it is sustained by something else that does not depend on anything further, it must utterly collapse. Therefore, if all things depend on others without end, everything will collapse everywhere. It would be as if liquids were to cling to liquids and were never solidified by something that could hold them. There will be no stability in things, no order, no cycle, no perseverance, and no restoration. One thing will not be more excellent than another, since where no "highest" is given, other things cannot be closer to the highest than others.
