XII
# BOOK

...they do not approach. Indeed, we clearly see some things in nature act, while others are acted upon; the former certainly precede in dignity, while the latter follow. Furthermore, a multitude and breadth of causes produce a corresponding number and magnitude in their effects. Therefore, if one were to ascend from causes to causes without limit, one would similarly descend through a limit to effects from effects. There would be no extremes <note>no beginning or end</note>. Instead, everything would be an intermediate, and everything would be infinite. If indeed any thing received its powers from innumerable predecessors and were able to give powers to innumerable successors, there would be an infinite number of innumerable things. This is absurd. Every thing would appear equal to every other thing. No human judgment considers this anything but absurd. Nowhere would be found the lowest body, which is earth. Nowhere would be found the lowest matter <note>referring to "Prime Matter," the most basic, formless substance of the universe</note>, which is a single, pure potentiality capable of receiving forms. 

This must be so unless there is a supreme spirit throughout; unless there is a supreme Form, a "pure act" <note>original: "actus purus" — a philosophical term for a being with no unfulfilled potential, namely God</note>, and a fountain of all forms. Otherwise, no effects would ever begin to happen, because no intermediate causes would ever begin to act. For these causes do not act unless they are first moved by all those above them; and if the beginning of motion were expected from an infinite number of things across an immeasurable interval, it would never be received. There would be no knowledge of any effect, because there would be no comprehension of innumerable causes. Why say more? Individual movements in human and natural affairs are directed toward certain ends precisely because they are ruled by a certain principle; for unless they were ruled from that point to this, they would never be so directed. Since, therefore, the movement of the whole world is more ordered than the individual movements that relate to its order, it directs itself all the more toward a certain end—that is, toward the good and beautiful common to all. It is necessary, then, that it proceeds from one certain principle: that is, from Goodness itself and Supreme Beauty.

### Truth is above the mind.

But lest, while we strive to prune away this infinite progression, we ourselves foolishly wander by an almost infinite interval from the very purpose of our discussion, let us now return to the mind, if you please. What the eye is in the body and sight is in the eye, the intellect is roughly the same in the soul. Furthermore, what the light of the sun is to sight, the light of Truth is to the mind. The sun’s light is one thing, the eye another. Similarly, Truth itself is one thing, and the intellect another. Otherwise, every mind would be entirely truthful, and any true thing would likewise be a participant in intelligence. Because your eye is a part of something else—that is, the body—it neither sees all things clearly nor all its own things at once. If your whole body were made into a single eye, it would see all things from every side at once. Yet, even then, the eye and the light would not be the same. Similarly, because your mind is a part of the soul, it understands neither all things clearly nor at the same moment. If your entire soul were to turn into a single intellect, the soul would then become an angel <note>original: "angelus" — here meaning a pure, disembodied intelligence</note>; it would perceive all things clearly, and would no longer hunt for this or that through the passage of time, but would behold all things clearly and simultaneously. Yet even then, Truth itself would be one thing, and the mind itself another.

...it will be nothing other than a spiritual eye for perceiving that very light of truth and heat of goodness through the intellect and the will.

### Truth and goodness are the same.

<margin>v</margin> It seems we must examine the nature of Truth. Is it not the case that truth and goodness are one and the same? Let us set aside what those dialectical arguments <note>original: "dyaletice machinentur" — referring to the technical logical disputes of the Scholastic philosophers</note> might devise. If, in the order of things, the false and the evil do not actually differ from one another—for to exist falsely and to exist evilly are the same—it follows that in that same order, the true and the good do not truly differ; that is, to exist truly and to exist well are the same. Therefore, above the order of all created things, truth and goodness are the same in substance. This is especially true because the empire of goodness extends as far as the empire of truth, and vice versa. For whatever is found to participate in truth is also a participant in goodness, and the reverse is also true. Yet, this very thing which is called truth and goodness transcends every mind. For the mind finds rest not in its own nature, but in the possession of the true and the good. Indeed, the traces of truth and goodness spread further than those of intelligence. For even where no function of intelligence appears, some element of the true and the good seems to lie hidden <note>Ficino means that even inanimate objects have a "truth" (their reality) and a "goodness" (their utility or existence), even if they lack a mind</note>. What then shall we say? God places all things according to the pattern of His art <note>original: "artis exemplar" — the divine ideas or blueprints</note> in a certain proper and pure form; then, according to the pattern of His bounty, He kindly distributes to all things a certain order and use toward an end. In the first act, He makes all things **true**; in the second, He makes them **good**. Again, when God shines upon the intellect, He is called **Truth**; when He warms the will, He is called **Goodness**. In the former, the intellect is enlightened and grows; in the latter, the will is gently drawn and fulfilled.

### God transcends the mind by an immense interval.

<margin>m</margin> Furthermore, let us measure—if it can be measured—how great a distance God transcends the mind. Ah, what immense madness it is to attempt to measure the immeasurable! For He stands as far above the mind in dignity as the space that lies open to the mind’s journey as it runs step by step from what is clear to what is clearer, or as the will strives from what is better to what is even better. This path lies open until we encounter something that is utterly immense, which by its own infinity sets a limit to our own "infinite" progress.

### God is certainty itself and joy itself.

<margin>q</margin><margin>lo</margin> Although it seems the height of madness to wish to comprehend with the mind that which insurmountably surpasses the mind and its stimulus (that is, the will), it is by no means the act of a madman to wish, at the very least, to be fully comprehended by Him. For perhaps to "comprehend" what is incomprehensible is nothing other than to be happily comprehended by Him. What then? Do we not wish to be most clearly comprehended by that supreme and uncreated Form which has, until now, embraced us in secret? That is, to be grasped in such a way that this fact is not hidden from us? Let us apprehend, as much as we are able, among the various kinds of created forms...

XI
->BOOK<-

the highest things occur to us. Among these, the highest are those which can turn themselves without a medium <note>original: "absque medio" — meaning directly, without an intermediary step or secondary cause</note> toward the highest and uncreated form, for the very reason that they proceeded from that same form without a medium. All species of minds appear to be of this kind. Since they all are able daily to seek, consider, and worship the highest divinity—not only in other things, but even after setting all other things aside—in its very excellence itself, so to speak. Therefore, the highest things in the universe, after the highest principle of the universe, are minds, acting as mirrors of the highest. Let us take the highest things in the mind, namely the intellect itself and the will. Again, consider what is highest in the intellect and the will. In the former, the supreme act is to understand; in the latter, to will. But what is the supreme point further in understanding? What again in willing? In the former is highest clarity, that is, the most exact certainty of all true things. In the latter is the fullest joy, that is, the complete and secure enjoyment of all good things. We can neither imagine nor desire anything further. What then is God? Certainly, as much as he shines back in the mirror of the mind itself: God is the clearest and most certain truth, the source of all true things. He is also the truest clarity of clarities. Again, he is infinite goodness which, while it delights in itself, delights in innumerable goods. He is also immense joy, good in himself; through which, by making himself, he causes other things to be good in which one can rejoice. This certainty or clarity is the same as the joy itself.

<margin>q</margin> When we say God is clarity or joy, we do not place clarity in an intellect or joy in a will, but in themselves. Nor do we wish clarity to differ from joy there, where truth does not differ from goodness. Thus, there is a rejoicing clarity and a clear joy. I say clarity rejoices not as if in another thing, but in itself. Joy is clear not by another clarity, but by itself.

->Just as light does not need the eye, so truth does not need the mind.<-

<margin>a</margin> The eye is one thing; a certain little ray <note>original: "radiolus" — a technical term in Neoplatonism for the "inner light" or the power of the soul that reaches out to meet external light</note> inborn in the eye is another; and the most ample light of the sun is yet another. That little ray is the eye’s own clarity and is located within the eye. But that light [of the sun] is the common clarity of all things; a clarity not needing the eye, which was established to perceive it. Similarly, the mind is one thing; its own clarity—that is, the ray implanted in it from the beginning—is another. God is another: the pre-eminent clarity of clarities. A clarity not properly needing the mind, which seems created to perceive it. He is the joy of all joys which are felt by any will: a joy not needing a will through which to rejoice. Indeed, every will rejoices only by that joy.

->To the highest certainty, nothing is uncertain.<-

<margin>s</margin> If the light of the sun were not only the cause of sight and the visible thing itself, but also the cause of all causes; and if sight itself were the most excellent and closest effect of the sun (since perfection cannot be given by a defect; rather, there is a need for a perfect sight to generate a needy one). Certainly, whatever appears in sight as especially good and desirable, all of that—and much more excellently—would be in the light. But the best and most desirable thing for the eye...

LXI
# SECOND #

10. So that light does not remain hidden from itself, nor cause offense when it is revealed; rather, let it be intensely delightful. Even if light did not possess an eye, it would nonetheless—in its own way, that is, by its very self as if by a more sublime sight—see itself clearly. It would behold all colors within itself as the fountain of colors. It would also see that it is that which all eyes see; and seeing all things through itself, it would see itself everywhere. I pass over for now the fact that the <term>Platonists</term> <note>original: "Platonici" — followers of the philosophy of Plato, who often used light as a metaphor for divine knowledge</note> believe that light sees all things with joy. God, however, is the total and <term>proximate cause</term> <note>original: "proxima causa" — the immediate or nearest cause in a chain of events</note> of the mind, and the mind is the highest work of God. Whatever, therefore, is most greatly to be desired by the mind as the "best," God already possesses this entirely, in a manner more excellent than can be described. For what is more desirable to the intellect than the certainty of all true things? Or to the will than the joy that rejoices in all goods? Ask the mind: it would not be enough for it to possess the whole of truth if that truth which it possesses remained hidden. Every good is not enough unless it occurs pleasantly and the mind rejoices in it all. Therefore, the divine clarity—although it does not strictly "use" an intellect—is by no means hidden from itself. Nor does anything anywhere remain hidden from it, since through it all things are open everywhere. Indeed, what could be certain to anyone if certainty itself, through which all things are made certain, were not certain of itself?

->Where the primary end of minds is, there also is their beginning.<-

<margin>S</margin>
But repeat the previous points in this manner: any effect, driven by nature, seeks its cause, so that it may be perfected in the same place from which it was produced. It specifically seeks the <term>proximate cause</term> if that cause is such that it collects within itself the functions of all the <term>remote causes</term>. For the mind receives its own distinct form from the proximate cause rather than from a remote one. Therefore, in that proximate cause from which it had its own principle <note>meaning: its point of origin</note>, it also places its own end <note>meaning: its final goal or fulfillment</note>. Just as fire reaches its natural limit in the <term>concave sphere of the moon</term> <note>In ancient and medieval science, fire was believed to rise to a "natural place" just below the sphere of the moon</note> rather than in the Sun or Mars; and air reaches its limit in the concave sphere of fire, not in Venus or Jupiter. Since every mind, led by nature, establishes its own primary end in that proximate cause—whether in that highest certainty of all things that rejoices supremely, or in that highest joy of all things that is supremely certain—who does not see that God himself, who is the proximate cause of minds, is that very highest point: the supreme certainty and supreme joy? I speak of a certainty not of something else, or in something else, or toward something else, but of itself in itself and toward itself. Otherwise, it would be neither pure nor simple, nor would it be the "highest of the high." Since it accepts no boundary or measure from any side, it is left as immense. For this reason, it admits nothing at all of the uncertain. Therefore, nothing—whether within it or outside it—can ever exist or be imagined that is uncertain to certainty itself. While it stands above all things, it is all things in a superlative way. It does not depend on anything else for its being or its acting; rather, all other things depend on it for both. In God, "being" itself is not different from "being certain"—indeed, he *is* certainty. Surely, while he belongs to himself, he is likewise certain of himself; or to speak more correctly, he is Certainty. And while he is certain of himself, he is certain of all things.

...embraces with wonderful power. It is certainly, beyond doubt, the certainty of all things; or rather, the certainty of everything. Therefore, whatever light is seen is nothing other than a certain expansion of a pure and effective <term>spiritual form</term> <note>original: "formæ ſpiritalis" — in Neoplatonic thought, "form" is the internal structure or essence that gives a thing its identity</note>. Where, then, the purity and effectiveness of form is least limited, there infinite light blossoms; from there, an altogether immense radiance flows forth. Indeed, what clarity is in bodies, insight is in spirits. Again, what visible light is in bodies, <term>perception</term> <note>original: "perſpectio" — suggests a deep, penetrating sight that understands the essence of what it sees</note> is in spirits. For this reason, bodies that approach it more closely shine more easily and abundantly. And conversely, those things that shine by themselves propagate a spiritual quality from within; therefore, from the highest spirit, light and the highest perception flourish. In Him, clarity and perception are the same thing.

I do not say that God is a certain power of perceiving that requires an act of perceiving; nor again do I call Him that which is simply named "to perceive," lest He seem to be either a straining toward something else or a composite being. But by the very word "act," I name God as <term>perception</term> <note>original: "perſpicientiam" — the state of being all-seeing</note> existing through itself, or perceiving by no other clarity than itself. But why did I just say "perceiving"? For who would not speak improperly if they said "vision sees" or "wisdom is wise"? Yet wisdom is not tasteless, nor is vision blind. Similarly, "Perception" itself should not properly be said to perceive anything; nor, on the other hand, can there be anything anywhere that is not transparent and perceived by it. For just as certain things are perceived by this or that specific perception, so all things are transparent and perceived by that highest and infinite Perception. There also joy abounds in the highest degree where the highest clarity flashes forth, which is the spiritual origin of joy. Indeed, clarity and joy are the same thing there. For neither in the eye, which appears most spiritual in the body, nor in the spirit itself, is cheerfulness anything other than clarity itself or a fitting illumination. For who doubts that all joy reigns where all good is? If indeed joy, as the best thing, is desired most of all; and it is both the splendor and grace of that surrounding good itself, and a certain expansion of the surrounding power around the good.

->God is the most joyful clarity and the clearest joy.<-

Where <note>The Latin text "Bi" is a common printer's shorthand for "Ubi," where the first letter was intended to be a large decorated initial.</note> therefore, when we wish to speak most correctly, we do not properly name God as the "intellect," lest He require an act of understanding; nor even as "intelligence" itself, lest He should reside within some intellect and be filled by some other light. Rather, [we call Him] clarity itself, wonderfully joyful, and the clearest joy. All intellects seek this, just as all the stars seek the sun. A clarity, I say, that sees all things by the rays of its own certainty, and makes things both see and be seen. Moreover, by the flames of His own joy—as if by the pleasure that is the mother of all things—He makes individual things. He also cherishes what has been made. By cherishing them, in turn, He brings them to life; He moves them by pleasant sense. Once moved, He draws them by reason. Having seized them, He then fixes them in the mind. Finally, He completely fills those who stand firm with His own truth and goodness.

BOOK TWO LXII

## God makes and moves things by willing rather than by understanding.

<margin>3</margin>But it delights me, I know not how, to ascend again by a certain likeness from what is most beautiful in bodies to the highest spirit. Therefore, just as the sun—a likeness of God—shines in itself with its own light and is warm by its own nature, it also illuminates and warms individual things with that same ray. However, it creates and moves things by warming rather than by illuminating. In the same way, God himself, the <term>archetype</term> <note>original: "exemplar" — the original pattern or model from which other things are copied</note> of the sun, is bright unto himself by his own clarity through his own way of understanding, and he rejoices within himself by his own way of willing. Furthermore, to speak in human terms, he understands and wills all things by the rays of that same clarity.

Yet, he does not procreate things so much by understanding as by willing. From this, it seems to have been granted to all animals and natures that they should generate things like themselves through a certain <term>appetite</term> <note>original: "appetitu" — a natural drive or inclination toward a goal</note> according to the nature of each, and even through pleasure. We must remember that just as God, by understanding himself, understands other things which are, as it were, rays of his own understanding; so by willing himself—that is, by rejoicing in himself—he simultaneously wills other things and rejoices in them, which are certain <term>dispositions of his own effect</term> <note>original: "affectus ipsius effectus" — a play on words suggesting that created things are the outward results of God's inner state of joy</note>. 

And this kind of action is voluntary because, being most perfect, it befits God, the most perfect of agents. For that which acts by free will acts more excellently than that which is driven to act by a necessary impulse of nature. Certainly, the happiest action is that in which the author is the master of his own action, so that he himself may prescribe the end, the manner, and the measure of acting; and that he may establish a proper purpose and certain paths for his works. 

Indeed, if God were to act by a natural quality just as fire warms by its heat, he would be the most composite of all beings. This is because he would produce innumerable things from his natural forms, which would be distinct from one another—especially those things that can only be produced by creation, namely matter itself and forms, whether they are separated from matter or separable. Furthermore, he would not distribute individual things with a certain order or turn, but would pour out everything at once—or rather, confound them. Add to this that, since his act is <term>infinite</term> <note>original: "immensus" — literally "unmeasured" or boundless</note>, he would compel all things suddenly; he would shake the spheres of the world in an instant. He would leave nothing in the universe to chance, and he would take away the freedom of deliberation. 

But now, since he effects all things by his will, he therefore makes, moves, and halts them by that specific measure which he wills. It is not difficult for him to understand the universe, for in him, to understand is the same as to be. It is not difficult for him to make and care for individual things, for in him, to make is the same as to already will that they be made. He understands all true things while he understands himself, who is all truth. He also wills all good things while he wills himself, who is all goodness. 

The logic of divine understanding and will is one thing; the logic of human understanding and will is another. A human truly understands the inner principles of things when he understands them primarily as they are. These things, however, are true because they are as God understands them, for he is truth itself, through which all things are both true and are truly understood everywhere. The human will desires individual things because they are good. But individual created things are good because God, who is goodness itself, wills them; and through this goodness, things are both good and we ourselves will them well.

### God provides for all things, especially for minds, because they are created most closely from him.

BOOK

<margin>v</margin>From this it is established that the first cause <note>original: "causam primam" — in Renaissance philosophy, this refers to God as the ultimate source of all movement and existence</note> provides for all things by the kindness of its own will because all things belong to it in the highest degree. Certainly, since it is the cause in the highest degree both in conserving and in perfecting, it is the cause just as much as in the initial making. Providence pertains especially to the highest good. This is nothing other than the diffusion and conservation of the good. It is established, furthermore, that following causes—while they receive the fertility and inclination for generating from the first cause—also acquire from the same source the diligence for providing for their own. Indeed, if anyone were to deny that the world is governed by both the most skillful reason and the most kind will, this person seems to me not to have considered the rational and most beautiful order of things in themselves, in relation to each other, and in relation to the whole; nor to have considered the wonderful convenience of individual things, everywhere serving each individual thing most aptly, and the mutual use of things. Truly, a comfortable dwelling moves the builder as an <term>end</term> <note>original: "finis" — the goal or purpose for which something is done</note> just as much as an acting cause: so that he devises a certain certain form of a house, for which form he again seeks certain material. Where the end moves the agent, the agent moves the form, and the form moves the material. The same happens in civil and military deliberations. From this it happens that the end is the cause of causes. Therefore, it precedes all causes. Moreover, all natural things are established for the sake of some certain end, since individual things are seen to lead most powerfully to individual uses. For instance, the little shoot of a vine-branch which they call a <term>tendril</term> <note>original: "capreolum" — literally "little goat," used here to describe the climbing vine's tendril</note> was born for this: to bind the vine to the nearest small tree. This act of binding is the cause for the tendril's birth. Because, however, that which in no way exists cannot be a cause of being for any inclination, nor is it possible for it to move all causes, it is necessary that an act of this kind existed both before the tendril and before all the remaining causes of the vine. However, it did not exist in bodies except most recently. Therefore, it existed in a certain incorporeal nature that directs bodies long before it existed in the vine-branch. Indeed, that nature—the "artisan" of the vine—for the sake of such an act, shaped the form of the tendril in such a material through its own form. But did an act of this kind precede in that nature according to the mode of nature, or according to a purpose of the will? Certainly, according to both. From the former, it was the same as a certain form of the agent and a <term>pattern</term> <note>original: "exemplar" — a blueprint or ideal model</note> of the effect itself; from the latter, it was the end. But where there is a purpose of a skillful will, there is mind. For this reason, the divine mind presides over all corporeal things; it embraces the forms of all corporeal things in an intellectual way. It directs individual things to their own ends: and finally, all things to the One. Most of all, however, God cares for and loves the minds of all—not only the angelic but also the human—as daughters created most closely from Himself. For since they are <term>indivisible</term> <note>original: "individuae" — things that cannot be divided into smaller parts</note> and separable from matter, or already separated, they cannot be made from a preceding part or material. To make something out of nothing—which is seen to be infinitely distant from "being" itself—is the work of <term>infinite power</term> <note>original: "infinitae virtutis"</note> alone.

they reach. Just as lines reach an indivisible center in no other way than through their own indivisible point: so we can reach an indivisible and hidden nature only through an indivisible and hidden power. To those to whom God granted temporal existence by bringing them forth, he provides temporal well-being by his providence. To those, however, to whom he granted eternal existence by his incorporeal generosity, he directs well-being not so much for a time as for eternity. Whence he disposes things in time so that even if they are not seen <note>that is, perceived as good</note> by those who do not see eternity itself, they are always best for those who are not ignorant of the way in which time serves eternity. Now we will briefly demonstrate from reason itself and from the light of reason—which is clearly visible—that he granted eternal life to minds. First, from reason in this way: If the reason of any thing, which is shown by its own specific definition, cannot be otherwise; whoever doubts whether that highest reason of reasons can be otherwise, either does not use reason or misuses it. Therefore, the highest reason is eternal, or rather, it is eternity itself. This insinuates itself into all minds everywhere, through which they can reason at their will wherever it pleases. And it grants a certain property of its eternity to this extent: that under the gift of reason itself—that is, through reasoning—the eternal reasons of things are captured insofar as they are eternal. And the eternity of reason is comprehended by the reason of eternity through its own definition. Then, from light in this way: No one doubts that the immense light of the divine sun is inextinguishable who notices that its shadowy image shining in the celestial sun is never extinguished. Indeed, in the highest and purest act <note>original: "actus" — in Aristotelian and Platonic thought, this refers to a thing in its state of complete realization or perfection</note> of any act, no suffering or deprivation can be imagined. Just as in the lowest potentiality <note>original: "potentia" — the capacity to become something else, often associated with matter</note> no act exists, or in mere deprivation no habit exists. That super-celestial light is widely diffused through all minds thinking upon super-celestial things, like stars according to the nature of each. It keeps its inextinguishable property to the extent that through it, that which cannot be extinguished is discerned from that which can be extinguished by a certain light of reason. And by what reason either this is extinguishable or that inextinguishable is shown. Truly, under the character of an inextinguishable property, that light is granted wherever the inextinguishable reason of any nature is perceived. And the fountain of that nature and light itself is sought, loved, and cherished by a certain natural thirst.

## Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, on the
## rapture of Paul to the third heaven: and the immortality of the soul.

My dear Giovanni, it is not permitted for us in these times, on account of the suspicion of the plague <note>original: "epidimiæ" — Ficino frequently wrote during outbreaks of the bubonic plague in Florence, using philosophy as a form of spiritual medicine</note>, to lead a life together in familiar intimacy on earth as we are accustomed. But what prevents us in the meantime from dwelling in heaven, where no fear of the pestilence causes anxiety? Therefore, friend, come now, let us flee into heaven. But you will perhaps ask: into which one among so many? Certainly into that one by whose rays we have been so inflamed that for a long time we have led a heavenly life together on earth. Do you not remember, Giovanni, when once that most esteemed man, our Bernardo Reneri <note>a member of Ficino's inner circle of scholars in the Platonic Academy</note>, was dining with us in your house, for what reason...

### A Dialogue between Paul and the Soul: which does not ascend to God without God; 
### and concerning faith, hope, and charity. MARCUS.

<margin>d</margin> Tell me, I pray, most blessed Paul—if indeed it is permitted for a man to speak of such things—how you ascended into heaven, and why specifically to the third heaven. PAUL. Far be it from us, far be it, Marsilio! Let such proud impiety be far from us, that we should say we *ascended* there. I do not wish to boast of myself in revelations of this kind. My whole glory is only that King of Glory: God. Therefore, I did not ascend, Marsilio, but I was *rapt* <note>original: "raptus," meaning snatched or caught up by a force outside oneself</note> into heaven. The heavy elements of the world do not seek the heights unless they are elevated by those on high. Dwellers of the earth do not climb the celestial steps unless a celestial force has drawn them. MARCUS. I beseech you, Paul, teach this also, by Him who snatched you up: whom indeed does He snatch up most of all from among all people? PAUL. Are you ignorant of this? For no one can be ignorant of what he either snatches or is snatched by. He snatches him whom he loves more ardently than the rest. He ardently loves the one who loves Him. That most kind Snatcher <note>original: "raptor"; used here in a positive, mystical sense to describe God's grace</note> wants nothing else from you by which you may be happily snatched by Him, except that you wish—even moderately—to be snatched; but even this you would never wish unless He had wished it first. Just as the moon does not shine back at the sun unless it was first lit by the sun, so you do not love Love itself unless you have been set on fire by Love itself loving and affecting you. Again, you do not call upon Him—like an echo—unless He is first calling you; you do not grasp Him, just as you do not grasp a place, unless He is grasping you. You can indeed grasp finite things for the most part, even if you are not grasped by them. But to grasp the Infinite is nothing other than to be grasped. And just as an image in a mirror does not look back at a face unless the face itself looks at it—indeed, even when the image seems to look at the face, this is nothing other than the image being looked at by the face. Again, just as our action and motion do not measure time for us unless time truly measures these very things; so the soul neither looks at God unless He looks at it first, nor judges unless He is judging. MARCUS. But come now, O one so greatly beloved by God, teach us thirdly: why you were especially elevated into the *third* heaven to see that invisible thing which is everywhere, just as it is in the third. For if it is everywhere, it is surely more in the highest [heaven] than in the third. PAUL. Not so, ah, too-earthly man! Celestial things are not grasped in that way. Lay aside the subtleties of the second heaven <note>the sphere of Mercury</note> invented by Mercury <note>the god of logic, commerce, and cleverness</note>. Lay aside the laws of the sixth heaven <note>the sphere of Jupiter</note> established, as you say, by Jupiter. Lay aside the philosophy of the seventh <note>the sphere of Saturn</note> given to men, as they say, by Saturn. These do not reach the Truth itself, the mother of Mercury, Jupiter, and Saturn. Do you wish to reach the sun running in the fourth heaven, in which that King of the world placed his tabernacle? Come then, climb the back of the third heaven which is next to the fourth. There Venus <note>the planet associated with the third heaven in the Ptolemaic system; Ficino associates this with Divine Love</note> will immediately bestow upon you what others could not provide. Venus is commonly said to give "vulgar love." But certainly, an angel <note>specifically the hierarchy of Principalities associated with the third heaven</note> increases excellent charity <term>charitatem: the highest form of Christian love</term> in excellent men. Charity, I say, flowing from the triple super-celestial heaven into both the third heaven and its angel, and into our own mind. For the Holy Spirit of God first burns this into the Seraphim <note>the highest order of angels, whose name means "the burning ones"</note>. It...

He aligns the biblical "third heaven" with the sphere of Venus to illustrate that love is the primary vehicle for mystical union with the divine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between St. Paul and the soul (Marcus). Here, Paul explains the mechanism of this ascent through the three theological virtues—faith, hope, and charity—and the various spheres of the heavens.</meta>

<page-num>64</page-num>
<header>SECOND BOOK</header>

...in the second [rank], the Principalities <note>The Principalities are the seventh of the nine traditional orders of angels; they were thought to guide the transitions of power on Earth.</note> enjoin the principal mystery and service of this work. These, ruling the third sphere, approach the angel of Venus. From there, the charity implanted in us by God is continually nourished, grows, and is perfected. What more? Do you wish, having set aside all circumlocutions, to reach the Sun of suns <note>God, as the ultimate source of light and truth.</note> by a shorter path? 

First, let your heaven be **faith**. By which you firmly believe that He is to be loved by you above all, from whom you also have this very thing: that you are able to love whatever you may love, and that the things which are loved possess the very quality of being lovable. Second, **hope**. Through which you undoubtedly and ardently expect to be loved in return by Him; for you could not love Him unless you were first loved by Him. Third, **charity**: which compels you both willingly and necessarily allures you—having set aside all other things—to embrace Him, for if He alone is set aside, you possess nothing. If you possess Him alone, there is nothing among all things that you have lost; without His arms, you are able to embrace neither yourself, nor other things, nor Him. 

Here, O soul too prone to wandering, here alone have I penetrated the most precious inner chambers of God. Which are not seen unless they are opened by the Master of the house. Moreover, the house of almighty Olympus <note>A common Renaissance humanist term for the Christian Heaven.</note> is not opened except to minds seeking this very thing through faith, asking through hope, and knocking through charity. Charity, however, is the end of the others and the perfection of all: by whose sparks Elijah was once kindled and snatched up to heaven in a fiery chariot. By whose flames I also was snatched to heaven. Finally, let this remain stored deep in your mind: Cold depends on darkness; darkness depends on death. Heat, however, depends on light; light depends on life. Therefore, cold leads to darkness, and darkness leads to death. Heat leads to light, and light leads to life.

->In the chariot of faith, hope, and charity, I ascended in vision into the third heaven. First indeed through the civil and purgatory virtues, and the virtues of the purified soul.<-

<margin>t</margin> In this first heaven, as if in a vehicle—that is, by right faith, firm hope, and most ardent charity—you will traverse the triple heaven in vision. First, by the merits of these three, three kinds of virtues will also be divinely granted to you: the **civil virtues**, the **purgatory virtues**, and the **virtues of the purified soul** <note>Ficino uses a Neoplatonic hierarchy of virtue: 'Civil' (social/moral), 'Purgatory' (internal cleansing from the physical), and 'Purified' (the state of the soul when it has reached divine contemplation).</note>. These indeed ensure that you do not know whether you are in the body or out of the body. Formed by these, you will finally reach the **exemplary virtues**, which are nothing other than God. For you will see yourself drawn by the Spirit of the Lord from glory to glory <note>original: "a claritate in claritatem"; a reference to 2 Corinthians 3:18.</note> in these three kinds of virtues, progressing more and more by degrees through the power of reason. You will recognize that this cannot happen except by a closer and then even closer access to the divine and supreme Idea of Virtue itself, so that you are transformed into that same image.

->Secondly, one goes into the third heaven through the region of the planets, through the starry heaven, and through the crystalline heaven.<-

...is movement and simple: There, "the waters which are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord." <note>A reference to Psalm 148:4, where the "waters above the heavens" were thought to be a spiritual or crystalline layer of the cosmos.</note> From the summit of this, immediately in the Empyrean <note>The Empyrean was considered the highest part of heaven, composed of pure fire or light, and the dwelling place of God.</note>—which is entirely a most healthy ardor—you will recognize that vital light of God: from whose overflowing goodness so great and healthy a heat is kindled there. You will most clearly see both the divine light and Truth itself dwelling in that heat—that is, in love—especially as if in the "tabernacle of the sun": <note>A reference to Psalm 19:4, comparing God's presence to the sun dwelling in the sky.</note> and that heat is born from and flourishes in light.

### Third, the third heaven is climbed through the visible world, the world of the imagination, and the world of the intellect.

<margin>third</margin>
Third, you will pass through the whole body of the world as if it were a single heaven manifest to the eyes. Then, you will betake yourself to its image painted in the imagination <note>original: "phantasticum," referring to the faculty of the soul that forms mental images of physical things.</note> as if to a second heaven. Finally, leaving behind both the universal visible body and the imaginary image of the body, you will proceed to the very nature by which it necessarily exists and the reason by which it is defined by the intelligence. This will be the third heaven for you in the mind, above sense and imagination. Here, suddenly, the divine intelligence shines within your own intelligence. For what else is the reason of the universe and its parts but that eternal art by which its architect <note>God, viewed as the Great Architect of the Universe.</note> disposed it? For if you subtract the matter from a physical craft, leaving the order behind, what remains is the mind of the craftsman, now visible to your own mind.

### Fourth, the third heaven is sought through irrational, rational, and intellectual spirits.

<margin>fourth</margin>
Fourth, let every spirit below your own be the first heaven to you. Let your own spirit be the second, by virtue of the gift of reason by which it judges irrational things—though it is not judged by them, being far superior to them. The third is the angel, who is a most bright eye; to whom things are known in a stable moment, which you hunt for through a kind of temporal discourse. <note>In medieval philosophy, humans learn through "discourse" (step-by-step logic over time), while angels possess "intellection" (instantaneous understanding of truth without the need for reasoning).</note> Continually behold God in the angel, as light in a clear eye, and eternity in a stable moment.

### Fifth, the crossing to the third heaven is made through the three angelic hierarchies.

<margin>fifth</margin>
Fifth, know that just as in you, who are a small world <note>The "microcosm"—the idea that the human being is a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</note>, there are three spirits: the natural in the liver; the vital in the heart; and the animal in the brain <note>In early medicine, the "animal spirit" (from *anima*, soul) was the refined fluid in the brain responsible for thought and sensation.</note> by which alone you perceive the finite light—so too around this larger world there are three armies of divine spirits, like three intelligible spheres revolving continually around a divine center. But some especially govern the region of the world subject to the moon. Others rule the celestial spheres. Others fly above the summit of heaven.

### Luminous darkness; dark light; pure light. The nine choirs of angels.

<margin>truth</margin>

I know that darkness cannot [sustain] itself...

...to illuminate, nor does light captured by darkness shine of its own accord; otherwise, it would thrive within itself and shine most purely and fully. I observe, therefore, that it shines from that light itself in which there are no shadows. Therefore, when it shines in the darkness, the darkness does not comprehend it. <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 1:5: "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it."</note> This is absolute Goodness itself in itself, constrained by no limits of subject, cause, degree, place, or time. Since all things by natural instinct seek the Good as their end—by which alone they are perfected—I conclude that the Good is the same Beginning <note>original: "principium"</note> from which all things are produced. Since this Good produces and perfects all things from itself and for its own sake, it certainly disposes all things toward the pattern of itself as a Middle. <note>original: "medium"</note> It is therefore the Beginning, the Middle, and the End of all things. And because it is entirely indivisible, the others are contained within any one of these three. Now, the End of an action moves the Beginning toward acting; the Beginning moves the pattern and form of the work. Toward this, all blessed spirits assiduously direct the eyes of their minds. Each one gazes upon these three, but different spirits do so in different ways. And in these, they behold the true reasons of all things that exist in the universe. The <term>Seraphim</term> <note>The highest order of angels, associated with burning love.</note> contemplate the End itself more closely and attentively than the others. The <term>Cherubim</term> <note>The second order, associated with divine wisdom.</note> see the Beginning in the End. The <term>Thrones</term> observe the Middle in the End. The <term>Dominations</term> behold the Beginning itself. The <term>Virtues</term> see the End in the Beginning. The <term>Powers</term> see the Middle in the Beginning. The <term>Principalities</term>, though they marvel at all things, look upon the Middle more closely and, so to speak, more gladly. The <term>Archangels</term> see the End in the Middle. The <term>Angels</term> contemplate the Beginning in the Middle. Happy souls—according to the various merits of a pious life and the similarity of their character to the different angels—follow the nine orders of angels in the nine spheres of the fatherland. I gladly omit the unhappy souls who, below the moon and beneath the darkness of the earth—where the ninefold-flowing <term>Styx</term> <note>The river of the underworld in classical mythology, used here to describe the boundaries of Hell.</note> binds them—accompany the nine crowds of malignant spirits.

## The light of God reflects in the heat of the Empyrean heaven.

<margin>c</margin> **W**hen I dismissed the spirits of darkness, suddenly an immense light flashed upon me from the highest watchtower of the shining spirits. I saw there the Seraphim burning with immense love. In this kind of heat, the infinite light of the Infinite Good reflected upon me. I had often thought before my rapture whether the Good itself is the object of the Will rather than the Intellect, so that the soul might enjoy the Good itself more through the burning of the Will than through the clarity of the Intellect. <note>This reflects a classic scholastic debate: is the ultimate experience of God an act of knowing (intellectualism) or an act of loving (voluntarism)?</note> I recognized there, in the moment of rapture, that I had thought truly: when I saw that it was not the knowledge of the Cherubim, but rather the charity of the Seraphim that is closest to God. Justly so, since it is the nature of all things to be desired; and the reason it is desirable is that it is good. Fervent love follows most closely upon the Infinite Good itself, and follows it immediately.

In the will, one proceeds and advances; there, following is nothing other than wishing to follow. Therefore, be of good cheer. Truly, if the end toward which you are moved—in a sense without end—is properly the Infinite Good, then the Beginning <note>original: "principium"</note> from which you are properly moved is necessarily also the Infinite Good. Since this Good exists from itself and for its own sake, and is the origin of all things, it certainly moves all things from itself and for its own sake. It moves the spirit especially and properly, as the spirit especially and properly desires this very thing. Your Father is so good that he did not give this to you in vain—that is, he did not give you the natural desire to follow such a good without also giving you the ability to eventually reach and attain it. In the order of things, as you know, all things are good. This is primarily because they are beautifully and usefully ordered, and they naturally desire the Good.

If all good things in the order of the world meet in a certain common nature of goodness—in which all good things are one single good—then necessarily, in the hands of the Orderer of things, one Good is all good things. Truly, that common and single nature which lies within and is contained by the multitude of all things emanates from a single Form which, in itself, is above all multitude and contains all things. But go further: if you think of something below the order of things as "infinitely evil," why do you not also confess that what exists above the order of things is "infinitely good"? If propagation belongs to goodness—for the more and the more perfectly things exist, the more they seem to be propagated—then without a doubt, infinite propagation exists within the Infinite Good. I speak of an inner propagation <note>The author is arguing that "goodness" by its nature must share or reproduce itself, leading to the concept of the Trinity.</note>. For nothing infinite truly exists outside of itself. Therefore, the Father and Son are there. In the Father, the Infinite Good, and the Son, the Infinite Good, an infinite love thrives. If each of the three is equally infinite, they are also equal to each other and most similar. Since an infinite nature and fullness leaves nothing outside itself and encompasses its whole self entirely, it can only be one: the substance of the three is one. Add also that it is most simple. If it must be most powerful, power consists in union, just as weakness consists in division.

Now, therefore, O soul—threefold and one, a single spirit consisting of intellect, will, and memory—you have ascended with me to the one ether and the unique, threefold heaven. Within the heaven, you saw three things in one sun, equal and similar to each other: Form, shape, and light. And you judged the sun in these three to be not triple, but single. Above the heaven, in the one nature of goodness itself, you found an eternal propagation and love. You did not recognize three natures in these, but a single one, continually propagating itself within itself and loving itself most fully and similarly; and what you have seen here divinely can never be spoken of by man in any other way than as three persons and one God.

-> The Trinity of the Creator is found in nine trinities of creatures. <-

<margin>d</margin>You will recognize the divine Trinity in all things when you consider within them nine trinities, which the nine orders of angels imitate: 
1. In the single machine of heaven: figure, light, and motion. 
2. In any spirit above heaven: substance, power, and action. 
3. In the whole number of spirits: three hierarchies. 
4. In each hierarchy: three orders. 
5. In any compound thing below heaven: matter, form, and virtue <note>term: "virtue" (virtus) here means the inherent power or specific quality of a thing</note>.

8. Furthermore: beginning, middle, and end. 
9. In yourself: memory, intelligence, and will.

## The Definition and Divinity of the Soul

<margin>b</margin>Thus, while you find God in things as if they were divine, you also find yourself. Indeed, if you find spirit in bodies, light in darkness, good in evil, life in death, and eternity in time; if you find the infinite in finite things, remember that you yourself are an incorporeal spirit—bright by nature, good, immortal, and capable of eternal truth, stability, and immense good. Let this be your first heaven, from the summit of which you have recognized both God and yourself in all things.

### That created things find their divine reasons and ideas in the Creator.

<margin>a</margin>Step forward, I pray, to the second heaven, so that from there you may inspect all things in God. One perceives all the works of God in God, just as one considers the arrangement and form of a house in the mind of the head of a family, a kingdom in a king, a craft in a craftsman, or the sciences in a wise person. Be mindful, however, that while humans meditate and act with time and labor, the Eternal Truth and that infinite power accomplishes all things in an instant, just as it wishes and with total ease—especially since in God, understanding is nothing other than being, and acting is nothing other than willing.

### Just as all natural forms exist in one matter, so all their divine reasons are gathered in one craftsman.

<margin>f</margin>And behold, I see a certain common mass in the machine of the world. I look upon the diverse forms in that mass. I know that one mass is formed, while another...

...that forms are formative: and because I understand this mass <note>original: "molem," referring to "primary matter," the formless "stuff" that precedes the creation of specific objects</note> as a foundation, I mentally separate this mass from the forms by a certain order. I imagine it either being dispersed into the abyss or being collected separately into a point. I preserve the forms as best as I can. But in what do I preserve them? In one single essence common to all things. For all things commonly agree in the fact that they exist. In this indivisible essence, I say, are the entirely indivisible forms. For we have already separated dimensions <note>physical measurements or spatial properties</note> from all of them. I wish, moreover, for one single form from every species of things to exist here. And just as all natural forms—which are such-and-such by a certain participation—are gathered together in one single subject that is inherently infinite in its capacity to receive (that is, in primary matter), so I wish and I see that all things which are such-and-such by their very essence (that is, the rational principles <note>original: "rationes," the archetypal ideas or "reasons" in the mind of God</note> of forms) are gathered together in one single fountain that is inherently infinite in its agency.

### God is the infinite life of lives and the light of lights.

If the act of being is infinite, it is also life, and indeed a life that is utterly infinite. <margin>❦</margin> Truly, life is the innermost and absolute act of essence. In infinite life, there is nothing that does not most perfectly assist. Therefore, that which was made by him was life itself. But where eternal activity and immense life flourish, there the light of intelligence is most absolute. Indeed, intelligence is the absolute reflection of life back upon itself. Therefore, this life is the light of men <note>original: "lux hominum," a direct reference to the Gospel of John 1:4</note>. This light also shines in the darkness, but the darkness did not comprehend it. The light of day is pleasant to healthy eyes, but most troublesome to those who are ill. The ray of God arrives as a kindness to a good mind, and is called "Father" and "Grace." But to a bad mind, he is a rigid judge and a fury. Through this true light, which illuminates every man coming into this world, you have just now seen all things in God, and God himself. For whatever is in the most simple God is God himself. That series of ideas which you understood in God is therefore the Divine Wisdom itself, which is the Word of God <note>original: "verbum dei," the Logos</note> with God, and God himself, through whom all things were made. Thus, God himself is found in all things, and all things are found in him.

### The mind finds its eternity in the eternity of rational principles and ideas.

<margin>i</margin> You have also just now discovered your own immortality. For in what way could you have separated mortal conditions from the forms of the world, and conceived of immortal principles from them? How could you have brought such principles back into the eternal life and intelligence of God—making that creative act, so to speak, present in your thought—unless you yourself were immortal and capable of the eternal life and intelligence of God? Therefore, let those most wicked men argue against their own immortality; their poor little souls <note>original: "animulæ," a diminutive and somewhat pitying term for the soul</note>, seeking life only in the region of death, have already been dead for a long time, buried in the filth of their vices.

### The four steps.

<margin>p</margin>
Surely you sense the eternity of reason when you judge that the rational principle <term>rational principle: the "ratio" or underlying logic and blueprint that makes a thing what it is</term> and definition of each species is so firmly established that it could never be otherwise. For instance, that "man is a rational animal" <note>original: "homo sit animal rationale"</note> and that "a circle is a figure turned back into itself, from whose center to the circumference all straight lines drawn are necessarily equal"—this was always, and always will be, true. You understand the meaning of eternity when you define its nature in this way: Eternity is a name for a state <note>original: "punctum," literally a "point"</note> that is always stable in itself; no point precedes it and none follows it; it is a measure of rest, just as time is a measure of motion. You recognize the truth of eternity when you prove that true eternity exists only in that which, of itself and in itself, rests without beginning or end. You perceive the eternity of Truth itself when you argue that truth never began nor will it ever cease. Otherwise, truth would have existed before itself and would exist after itself. For indeed, if it were said to have begun at some point, then before that point, it was true from eternity that truth did not yet exist—and it could not be "true" except by the existence of Truth itself. Likewise, if it were thought to end, it would then be true for all eternity thereafter that truth once existed—and it could only be "true" by that very same Truth.

->The immortality of the soul proven by its proportion to immortal things.<-

<margin>a</margin>
Attend, O soul thirsty for the eternal liquid! Remember that you could not reach an eternal object at all unless there were some proportion <note>proportion here implies a shared nature or a "fittingness" between the observer and the observed</note> within you to that object. Therefore, if you do not live *from* eternity <note>original: "ab euo," referring to having no beginning</note>, you at least live *unto* eternity <note>original: "in euum," referring to having no end</note>. You do not merely touch upon the fact that some things are eternal, nor do you only argue about what kind of things they are; rather, you even penetrate them through your own nature when you distinguish their intrinsic nature into certain parts and powers. Indeed, you even seem to comprehend them in a certain way when you define them. I set aside what might appear to some—that if the mind comprehends an everlasting principle, then the mind must be greater than that principle and therefore eternal; let it be enough that if the mind captures it in its own way, the mind must at least be equal to it in some manner. Whether the nature of the soul is already equal, or becomes equal by capturing these principles—constantly expanded by a certain silent love flowing from God, the fountain of all reasons—it is sufficiently shown that the mind is everlasting. In short, the soul was made from the beginning, in its essence and life, as an equal (so to speak) to eternal reason, since it daily renders itself as equal as possible in terms of intelligence and love. Finally, whatever power grasps something, it grasps it according to its own nature and draws it into its own way of being. If you were mortal, you would never conceive of eternal things as they are eternal, nor would you grasp the principle of eternity under the logic of eternity. But just as to red eyes all things seem red, and to a bitter tongue all things taste bitter, so to a mortal soul all things would be judged as mortal. Now, however, it is so far from the case that everlasting things are thought to be fleeting when properly contemplated, that the contemplating mind even separates the conditions of mortality from individual mortal things and perceives them under a universal principle. The mind could never separate matter and corruption from these things unless it were itself far more distant and separated from them. You grasp your own eternity, therefore, in this "second heaven" <note>referring to the intellectual sphere of existence</note> when you grasp, according to your strength, the eternity of every rational principle in God, the immense fountain of all reasons.

## The mind sees that God, in Himself, cannot be seen at all due to His excessive brilliance.

Furthermore, do you perhaps comprehend God Himself in Himself—that third heaven <note>The "third heaven" is a biblical reference to the highest realm of spiritual reality, mentioned by the Apostle Paul in 2 Corinthians 12:2.</note> remaining for you, in which I myself saw those secrets <note>original: "archana," meaning hidden or sacred mysteries</note> which it is not lawful for a man to speak? You look upon the light of the sun in the elements and look up at it in the stars, yet you cannot gaze upon it in itself. And yet, if you are wise, you are content that your sun is so great that it exceeds the capacity of the eyes. Similarly, you recognize the divine light in the things created by it and in the rational principles <term>rational principles: the "rationes," or logical blueprints, of created things</term> of those creations. But you cannot endure that light as absolute in itself. However, you rejoice that your treasure is entirely beyond numbering—beyond numbering, I say, not because you lack the skill of counting (which is there most full for you), but because that light surpasses the highest peak of art by its degrees of power. Yet you seem to have counted enough when, having enumerated all things that can either exist or be understood, you calculate by right reason that God Himself is "nothing" <note>By calling God "nothing," the author means God is not a "thing" or object that can be categorized like created beings; He is "no-thing" because He transcends all things.</note>; and then you understand how His power is beyond numbering. You see enough when you truly see how He is invisible. You comprehend enough when you comprehend that He is incomprehensible. For you never understand Truth itself more clearly than when you rightly understand how it is above understanding. Where the highest light is for you the deepest darkness, and the deepest darkness is the highest light. Hence nothing is better known than this, yet nothing is more unknown; nothing is more present, yet nothing is more absent; nothing is more visible, yet nothing is more invisible <note>The original uses a rhetorical paradox: "Nihil magis visibile. Nihil visibile magis." This suggests that God is both the most visible thing (source of all light) and the most invisible (impossible to see directly).</note>. From this David exclaims: *The night is my illumination in my delights.* <note>original: "Nox illuminatio mea in deliciis meis." A reference to Psalm 139:11, often used in mystical theology to describe the "divine darkness" where the soul meets God.</note>

## We speak more correctly of God by denying and relating than by affirming.

Truly, what you see in this heaven you cannot speak—that is, you cannot absolutely pronounce and affirm it. For whenever you deny other things of God, proceeding thus: "God is not any body, nor a quality of a body, nor a soul, nor an angel," nor anything higher that might be thought, you deny truly. Whenever you relate other things to God, comparing them thus: "God is the beginning because all things flow from Him; God is the end because all things flow back to Him; God is life and intelligence because through Him souls live and minds understand," you also relate truly. But if you were to affirm: "God Himself in Himself is absolutely this very thing which I have either found or thought," you would be greatly deceived. Indeed, if that highest author of all is greater than you, He cannot be that which is forced by your circumscribed intelligence to be a fixed limit. If He is the "Beginning of beginnings" and "End of ends," He is infinite; He is not any of those things which, having been discovered and comprehended by you, now appear finite.

## The blessed soul is content with this very fact: that its Good is incomprehensible. It would not be content if it were comprehensible.

What then? Do you live content, O soul, that you do not entirely comprehend or limit your life because it is infinite? Indeed, I know you rejoice in this very fact: that your life and your good are without end. It is enough for you to be happily encompassed by the Incomprehensible, and nothing is sufficient for you unless it is incomprehensible. For whatever of truth or goodness is offered that has certain degrees—however many there may be—you still seek more with your intellect and desire further with your will. Thus you can rest nowhere except in the immense True and Good, and find no end except in the Infinite.

You are able to do this. For you depend on the infinite alone; and from there you possess a power that is, in some sense, infinite, by which you incline and advance toward the infinite.

### The will enjoys God more than the intellect.

<margin>c</margin> <gloss>c</gloss> Behold, I see that where the intellect somehow falls short, the will suffices. See how love <note>original: "charitas," often translated as charity or divine love</note> penetrates where knowledge <note>original: "scientia"</note> cannot penetrate all things. Indeed, you look upon infinity, though not most clearly. You love this infinity most ardently; you rejoice in it most vehemently. You see, indeed, as much as is visible to you. You love both what you see and what you see as being beyond you—because it is too exuberant to be fully seen—and this very fact helps you most of all. Thus, without any anxiety or boredom <note>original: "satietate," meaning a sense of being "fed up" or overfilled</note>, you may enjoy the Good; since it is infinite, it is infinitely available to you and infinitely delights you. Here, even if the light of the intelligence does not discern the Immense by a completely infinite reason, the will is nonetheless affected by immense love and joy while it enjoys the infinite Good. If the will is full—and it is the nature of the will to be satisfied—then the whole soul is entirely satisfied.

### The mind, by its own immortality, measures its object which is without measure.

<margin>2</margin> <gloss>2</gloss> While the soul is in the third heaven, it measures how immense God is much more accurately than in the other realms (if I may speak this way). At the same time, it recognizes how much its own life exceeds the measure of nature and of any time. For the soul would not reach the underlying principle <note>original: "rationem"</note> of the infinite, or rather of infinity itself, if its life were destined to have some end. Nor would it be more delighted by contemplating an immense object than by contemplating limited ones, if it were merely one of the natural and temporal forms. The powers of such forms are not delighted by the greatest objects, but only by moderate ones that correspond to them by a certain proportion. If the power of life—such as the intelligence and the will—advances without end in understanding and loving beyond any degree of place or time offered to it as an end, then certainly that life itself is not constrained by the limits of place, nor exceeded by the boundaries of a specific time, nor overwhelmed by the degrees of an opposing quality. It is not filled up by the presence of a determined truth or good.

### Celestial light is perceived by celestial light; super-celestial by super-celestial.

<margin>d</margin> <gloss>c</gloss> Come now, by what light do you look up at celestial light? Surely by a celestial one. Tell me then, by what light did you just now see the super-celestial light? Surely by a super-celestial one. The light of the world, so manifest to the senses, is a single quality; therefore, different bodies do not receive it except through a certain nature inherent in them that is compatible with light. This kind of nature is called transparency <term>transparency: "perspicuitas," the quality of being see-through or receptive to light</term>. Truly, because transparency in the eye is more related to sensible light than in these other bodies (for there is a sensory transparency in the eye), the light, after it has been infused into the eye, is reflected back into itself, so to speak, when the eye perceives it. In this, the eye is seen not only to be acted upon by the light while it receives it, but also, in a way, to act upon the light, judging it in its own manner.

### The soul sees its own immortality when it sees the ray of intelligence being infused into it by God and reflected back to God.

<margin>e</margin>
By the same reasoning, spiritual light is a single entity; that is, it is truth itself <note>original: "veritas ipsa"</note>. Different spirits do not perceive this except through a certain innate spiritual clarity. Because the spirit endowed with reason is, by virtue of such clarity, more similar and closer to this light, it follows that these spirits not only receive that light but also judge it and are thus reflected back into it. Here it is seen that this spiritual light is also an "intelligible" light <note>An "intelligible" light is one that can be understood by the mind rather than seen by the eyes</note>: first, it flows into the understanding without ever leaving itself; then, it flows back into itself without abandoning the understanding. 

Just as the light of the sun is invisible while it remains in the sun, but becomes visible as it flows out from the sun into colors, and becomes "seeing" <note>original: "visiuum"</note> as it flows into the eye and becomes natural to it—and when it reflects from there back toward the sun, it is then made a "seer"—so too the light of God, insofar as it gathers itself absolutely within Him, is above all understanding. Insofar as it unfolds from there into the "reasons" <note>or "rational principles" of things</note>, it is intelligible. Insofar as it is infused into the intellect itself and becomes natural to it, it becomes "intellectual" <note>original: "intellectiva"</note>. But when it leaps back into God himself, it is "intelligent" <note>original: "intelligens"</note>. For this reason, a certain circle is formed here: wonderfully shining from the divine truth itself into the intellect, and from the intellect back into that same truth. The beginning and end of this circle is God; the intellect is the middle. If the first and last boundary of this circle is eternity, then insofar as it is eternity, the middle must certainly be eternal, as it participates in those boundaries. For in what way could the splendor flowing from eternity into the mind, and then flowing back from there into eternity through the intelligence—namely, through the intellect which seizes the object and through the will which passes into the object and is seized by it—unless it preserved its own power and eternity within the mind? By the same reasoning that the mind receives this light, it also acts through it. For it cannot act through it more excellently than it received it. Indeed, it acts through it in a certain absolute and eternal way; sometimes, when its rays are raised above place and time, it reaches the indivisible and eternal "reasons" of things and insinuates itself into eternity itself in wondrous ways.

## The mind is the mirror of God.

<margin>o</margin>
O most sagacious hunter, who investigates and finds the most hidden footprints of God in this deep forest of the world! O most sharp-witted reasoner, who finds the "reasons" <note>the underlying logic or patterns</note> of things in the supreme Reason of all! O most clear-sighted searcher, who penetrates the secrets of God and, in a certain sense, enters into Him! To put it briefly: in performing all these things, the mind contemplates God in itself as if in a mirror. It looks up at itself in God as if in the sun. O most divine mirror of the divine sun! Both illustrated by its rays and set ablaze by its flames! Truly, by the rays of Truth itself, it discerns the truth everywhere: both in all true things and, above all things, Truth itself. By the flames of the Good itself, it burns with love for and thirsts for all good things everywhere: both in all good things and, above all things, the Good itself.

<margin>v</margin>

Thus it is rightly said, "to the im..." <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing "to the image and likeness" on the next page.</note>

## Marsilio Ficino of Florence: Argument for the Platonic Theology, to Lorenzo de' Medici, Savior of his Fatherland.

### There are three levels of Platonic contemplation.

->Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to the high-minded Lorenzo de' Medici.<-

I have decided, high-minded Lorenzo, before publishing that great volume of *Platonic Theology* dedicated to your name—in which there still remains a little something needing examination—to publish, if it please you, this *Argument* <note>original: "argumentum," here meaning a summary or foundational outline</note>. I do this not so that you might come more prepared to "play" by practicing with this summary as a kind of prelude to the theology, since you seem to me to have already achieved the very prize of that game; but so that, reminded in the meantime by this pledge, you may remember—and that I may remember—that I owe you what I long ago rightfully promised, and that I wish to eventually pay what I know I owe. Especially since I do not owe this so much because I promised it, but rather I promised it because I owed you everything <note>Ficino frequently expressed his deep debt to the Medici family, who provided the resources for his translations and philosophical work</note>.

### The three levels of Platonic contemplation.

<margin>T</margin> Truly, there are three principal levels of Platonic contemplation. The first indeed ascends from the body, through the soul, to God. The second consists in God. The third, finally, descends back to the soul and the body.

Our summary also contains three levels. The first level of contemplation is: from the senses to the soul, the Angel, and God; and concerning the divine intelligence and love.

### The heaven is form without matter, as some believe.

<margin>C</margin> I was recently considering diligently that paradox of Aristotle: "the heaven lacks matter." I was also meditating on the reasoning of Averroes <note>original: "auerois," the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known for his influential commentaries on Aristotle</note> by which he proves the Aristotelian paradox. Specifically, that since matter is by its nature formless and therefore relates equally to any form—and can receive all forms in turn—it flows continually from form to form. This is why things made of matter can eventually lose their form. The heaven, however, cannot lose its own form, both because there is no contrary quality to it anywhere (just as no motion is found contrary to its circular motion), and because it has a motion that is always equal without any deviation, returning to its own starting point and beginning the start again where the end is seen. From these things, Averroes concludes that the heaven is a certain form existing through itself without matter. Although it does not require a subject of matter, it is nevertheless subject to quantity and local motion. He wants such a form to be a medium <note>A middle point or bridge</note> between physical forms and metaphysical forms. For natural forms exist with a certain quantity and within matter. But forms entirely above nature lack both quantity and matter. A certain medium...
