...he wants it to be a form so that one does not pass from one extreme to the other without a middle stage <note>Ficino uses the concept of a "mean" or middle ground to bridge the gap between physical matter and divine spirit</note>. Although it may have quantity and matter, he believes it does not have the same kind of substance as celestial bodies. Proclus the Platonist also thinks the celestial vehicle <note>The "astral body" or ethereal vessel that carries the soul</note> is the body of the soul, yet it has no matter.

### **Form can exist without quantity even more than it can without matter.**

<margin>b</margin> Using these steps from Aristotle, Averroes, and Proclus—which lead directly up to the heavens—I have tried with all my strength to ascend above the heavens. Indeed, since the genus of forms can somewhere free itself from matter, as it appeared to us just now in the case of the heavens, it can also somewhere release itself from quantity. This is even more likely. After all, if it depended on either one, it would depend more on matter (by which substantial form is often sustained) than on quantity (which substantial form perhaps sustains no less than it is sustained by it). This is most clearly seen in the heavens, as Averroes <note>Averroes was a 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to Renaissance thought</note> prefers, where such a form sustains the dimensions of quantity. Add to this that form agrees much more with matter than with quantity in a certain order of genus and nature. Therefore, if it can exist without matter, it can much more easily exist without quantity. This is especially true for that form which is a substance. For since substance precedes accident <note>In Aristotelian logic, a "substance" is a thing that exists in itself, while an "accident" (like size, quantity, or color) can only exist within a substance</note>, it can exist somewhere without quantity, which is an accident.

### **Form can exist without quantity even more than it can without mass.**

<margin>i</margin> Thus, the order of forms advances toward the better; just as it moves from the elements into the heavens while being freed from the shadow of matter, so too, above the summit of the heavens, it advances toward something far better when it is released from the mass of quantity <note>original: "mole quantitatis," referring to physical bulk or spatial extension</note> in souls and angels. Having cast off the weakness of division, it gains strength through the unity of an indivisible nature. Finally, it is perfected above those beings in the Best <note>referring to God</note>, when in God it is also freed from quality and the lack of an accident. However, it can be separated from quality more easily than from mass. For substantial form everywhere in nature itself sustains qualities. Truly, it is never sustained by them. Yet somewhere it seems to lie within quantity. This is clearly seen in the lowest forms of nature.

### **The heaven is either a certain visible life or a nature closest to life.**

<margin>c</margin> Indeed, since the heaven is without matter, it seems to the Platonists to be something spiritual in a certain way rather than corporeal. What, then, is the heaven? It is circular light and a luminous circle without matter, just as its opposite—the lowest part of the earth—is matter without light. Therefore, as the Platonists believe, the heaven is either a certain kind of life (not hidden by the soul, but made manifest to the eyes because of its dimension), or at least, since it is a nature closer to life than other bodies, it lives with a certain life more familiar to itself than others.

### **The difference of light in the heaven and the elements according to the Platonists and Peripatetics.**

<summary>Ficino outlines a metaphysical hierarchy where "form" gains power as it is stripped of matter, physical bulk (quantity), and eventually quality, ascending from elements to the heavens, then to souls, and finally to God. He describes the heavens as a spiritual, matter-less "circular light" that serves as the visible manifestation of life.</summary>

<margin>f</margin> But it is helpful to ascend step by step from light back toward light: We see in the elements <note>The four classical elements: earth, water, air, and fire</note> that where there is a less dense nature, light is more easily present; and once matter is ignited, the more it is thinned and rarified, the more purely it shines through. For this reason, since the heaven shines so greatly, it is proved to lack matter. And for this very reason—because it lacks matter—it shines most intensely. 

Now, if anyone should say that some parts of the heavens shine more than others because they are denser <note>A common medieval explanation for the visible stars compared to the transparent spheres</note>, the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato’s philosophy</note> will respond by reasoning that those parts do indeed shine more, but because of their extreme thinness and light, they cannot be seen. The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for walking—"peripatētikos"—while teaching</note>, on the other hand, respond that it is one thing to sparkle from oneself and another to sparkle from an outside source. Therefore, because the elements receive their brilliance from elsewhere, those that are thinner receive it more easily. But celestial things, which shine from within themselves, reflect more abundantly the denser they are. However, let us set aside questions of this kind. Let us leave the heavens for a moment, lest we be utterly dazzled by bodily splendor.

### When we purify celestial light, we first find the soul, and then the angel.

<margin>a</margin> Come now, leaving aside celestial nature, if you wish, subtract the dimensions of quantity from its light and motion. For it is permitted to subtract them in thought. Indeed, the light and motion of the heaven are one thing, and its dimension is another. The form that remains is a certain spirit, as much more lucid and swift than the heaven as the heaven is more lucid and swift than the elements. This incorporeal substance appears to be the **rational soul**. 

Now, subtract motion from this in turn. Leave only the light and the quality: for you are able to subtract it, since light and quality are one thing, and motion is another. The form that then remains is the **angel**, which is clearer and swifter in its own way than the soul. This is because the angel does not scatter its light through motion, nor does it distract its own action through time as the soul does.

### It is better to ascend to a substance in which power is nothing other than the substance itself.

<margin>c</margin> Furthermore, we do not yet seem to have sufficiently "purified" the nature of things. It remains for us still—unless my reasoning fails me—to separate the **accident** <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a quality or characteristic (like color or weight) that is not essential to a thing's core existence</note> from the **substance**. For even an angel possesses both substance and quality. 

Truly, we must first ask whether it is better for this separation to happen, and then whether it is possible. It is certainly better. For where substance is one thing and quality is another, a substance of this kind—being imperfect in its nature regarding forms—is formed and perfected from elsewhere. In receiving and sustaining a quality, it "suffers" or is acted upon in a certain way. Furthermore, that quality, because it is a certain form existing in another—that is, in a subject—cannot sustain itself, much less exist on its own. It therefore requires both a cause and a subject; it is not entirely whole and full since it is received according to the capacity of the subject. 

From this, it necessarily follows that there is a removal of form so that—<margin>lest we wander without end</margin>—it may be self-sufficient in itself, most full in itself, and be an everywhere-infinite power, since it is neither surpassed by something higher nor limited by anything receiving it. Add to this that everything composed of substance and quality is weakened in its power because it is divided into parts. And because it is composed, it depends both on its parts and on that craftsman who reconciled those parts into one; for since the parts are diverse, they would not have come together on their own. For this reason, since a composite of this kind is neither as to its parts nor as to its...

SECOND LXXI

Then it looks toward what is best. And something would be better if it were a substance <note>In medieval philosophy, "substance" is the underlying reality of a thing that exists by itself, while an "accident" is a non-essential quality, like being "tall" or "blue," which must exist in something else.</note> that is not distinguished from its own quality, and a quality that is nothing other than its own substance—so that finally a certain act might be found that is entirely pure and immense. <note>original: "actus... purus immensusq;" — "Pure act" refers to a being that is fully realized with no unfulfilled potential, traditionally identified as God.</note> Who could doubt that it is better for us to ascend from that which is composed of substance and accident toward that which is better?

### Many reasons why it is necessary that there be a pure and infinite act.

<margin>r</margin>
It is right, therefore, to ascend to this point; but is it possible? Why do you ask if it is possible? Indeed, that it already exists is as necessary as we have proved. But if you require another reason, it leads to the same conclusion through this logic: because substance is the foundation of accident, it is prior to the accident; and because that which is prior does not depend on the posterior, substance can exist somewhere without an accident. And this is better, as we have shown. Therefore, lest such a good potential at the beginning of things should exist in vain from eternity to eternity, it seems worthwhile that it should already exist in act. <note>Act (or actuality) refers to something being fully real and present, as opposed to "potency," which is merely the potential to exist or change.</note> Especially since where the highest act and highest perfection are, there power and act—the "ability to be" and "being" itself—are one and the same.

And if in lower and less good things—namely elements, mixtures, plants, and animals, regarding their parts and the rest—nature has provided that what is superior already exists, how much more in things that are better by far. At the summit of nature, whatever is proved to be better already exists, and exists more truly. Furthermore, whatever is better in the universe is judged to be better for no other reason than because it is truly consistent with reason; it contributes most to the order of things, and it especially befits the Ordainer of things. To say that such a thing is impossible or false is truly a wickedness. Again, power and truth are naturally desired as goods. And these things themselves either are goodness itself or come from goodness. Therefore, that which is more possible and truer in the nature of the universe is also better. And conversely, what is judged better for the universe is likewise more possible and truer. Also, what is better is more shared by man. Therefore, it is not impossible. For that which is impossible is judged to be a participant in no good. 

It follows that if the "pure and infinite act" which we have thought out through debate is infinitely better than an angel and the universe (of which the angel is a part, and which as a whole is limited), it is necessarily infinitely more powerful in existing, since power is a good and "good" is power. Indeed, since being truly and in act is a good, and nothing of the good is lacking in the immense good, the immense act already exists in act infinitely more truly than all other things. If infinite power, through infinite duration, has not yet come into act, no other power ever will. Indeed, if infinite act—which is the same as that power—is not always in act, certainly no other act will ever be. If there is always in act a certain potential which by its nature lacks all act and is infinitely passive—namely, matter—doubtless that power which is total act and is infinitely effective must always be in act; from this power, passive potential <note>term: passive potential (potentia passiva) — the capacity to be acted upon or shaped by an outside force, often associated with prime matter.</note> exists, is able to be acted upon, and is acted upon. But why do we search so curiously and foolishly whether it is possible or true that an immense good exists in the universe? For nothing is more possible or truer than that which nothing more powerful can be conceived. For it would not be...

<summary>Ficino argues for the existence of God as "Pure Act," reasoning that a being whose essence and existence are identical is logically necessary and superior to anything composed of parts or accidents.</summary>

...[im]mense good unless there were in Him whatever is judged better to be. Moreover, our mind would exceed the nature of the highest source in its thoughts and affections—through which it progresses without end through the levels of goodness—if it could think of any good that was not in Him, or if that good were not immeasurable. Why say more? If in the highest principle and end of all things, where it is found in the highest degree, whatever is desirable is the highest goodness—and that same highest goodness is exactly the same as the highest power and truth—it follows that whatever is judged to be better concerning Him is more possible, or rather, is already more truly so. Above all, however, one must remember that the potential <note>original: "potentiam"; in this context, the capacity or "possibility" for something to exist.</note> to receive some good is a real thing and is founded in some true reality. Furthermore, it depends on something else which already possesses that good in actuality. <note>original: "actu"; meaning "in reality" or "fully realized," as opposed to just being a possibility.</note> Again, that which possesses a good in actuality must proceed from something else that is itself the good in actuality, the very Act of every act.

### On the light of God, and the shadow of matter.

<margin>c</margin> Furthermore, it might perhaps seem to someone that a nature in which quality is not distinguished from substance exists without form and light. But let him remember that we have proven one must ascend to a "form existing in itself"; therefore, that substance is Form. <note>In this philosophical tradition, "Form" refers to the essential nature or "blueprint" that makes a thing what it is.</note> Indeed, just as in the lowest of things—that is, "prime matter"—to exist is the same as being formless and dark, so in the highest, to exist is the same as being beautiful <note>The Latin "formosus" implies both "having form" and "being beautiful."</note> and luminous. Indeed, Form is Light. For in the writings of Moses, matter is the abyss of darkness and the formless subject of forms. God is the Light, the abyss of lights, the Form and the source of forms. Matter is the infinite potential for being acted upon; <note>original: "patiendi potentia"; the capacity to receive impressions or changes.</note> God is the infinite power of acting—or rather, He is Infinite Act. Therefore, matter is the potential of all potentials that consist in being acted upon. God is the Act of acts. And just as in the service of truth it is said of matter that it is truly "matter" and is neither this form nor that one, so it is said of God in countless ways and most truly: God is this form and that one. One, matter, is the shadow of things, the lowest of shadows. One, God, is the highest light of lights. Matter is unknown because of its excessive darkness; God is unknown because of His excessive light. For if light is that which is more pure and more luminous, then surely God—since He alone is Pure Act—must be called the only true Light. If light consists in a certain form, or rather in a subject, and beauty consists in light, then true light is only where there is pure form without the stain of a subject. <note>The author argues that in God, "Form" isn't just a quality of a physical object, but exists purely on its own.</note> There alone is true beauty, where there is only light and true form. Therefore, every form and light that is either seen by the eyes or thought by the mind is a certain shadow compared to the form and light of God, because it is finite. Justly is God the Infinite Act, since He is not confined by the limits of a subject or a cause, as we have said. Hence, He is clearly an immeasurable light.

->As much as the light of God towers above the surface of the intellect, so much does the heat of God penetrate the center of the will.<-

<margin>c</margin> Since heat truly draws its origin from light, there is also an immeasurable ardor—an ardor in the infinite good that is infinitely beneficent. We reach this ardor through the ardor of our will, or rather through the "spark" of the mind. For as much as God towers above us by the light of His intellect, so much [does He tower above us] in goodness...

[He] burns Himself into us with such fervor that nothing is higher than God, yet nothing is deeper. The more ample His light is, the more unknown it is naturally to our intellect; yet the more vehement its heat <note>original: "ardor"; refers to the transformative "fire" of divine love.</note>, the more certain it is (so to speak) to our will. God is therefore, in the highest peak of intellectual cognition, a kind of "night" to the intellect. But in the highest love of the will, He is surely "day" to that will. This is why Orpheus <note>A legendary Greek poet and musician. Neoplatonists often cited "Orphic" hymns as ancient mystical wisdom.</note> calls God both "night" and "day." Nevertheless, when that divine splendor in the souls of the blessed is called "night," it arrives far more brightly than any temporal day. Indeed, by divine gift, it is nearly as much clearer as God is (to use the term) more radiant than the sun, and as the soul is purer and more serene than the air.

### Light in the elements, the heavens, the soul, the angel, and God

<margin>1</margin>
Light in the elements is easily perceived by the eyes, for the physical composition of our eyes is made from these same elements. Light in the heavens, although it is more ample, is nonetheless harder to see. This is because the quality of the eyes is too far removed from the nature of the heavens. Light in the soul is not seen in any way, just as the light of the sun is not seen by an owl <note>A classic philosophical metaphor: just as an owl is blinded by daylight, the human intellect is blinded by the "too-bright" light of the divine.</note>; this is because the light is too great, and the bodily senses have no proportion or scale to measure it. Instead, it is conceptualized through some logical discourse of the rational soul. Light in an angel is neither seen nor even conceptualized by discourse. For it is beyond the proportion of the senses and beyond the capacity of temporal, step-by-step reasoning. Nevertheless, it is understood through a flash of insight. For the soul aligns with the angel in its own capacity for stable intelligence, rather than through the shifting movements of thought. Light in God, because it exceeds even the limits of the intellect, is not understood at all by the natural intelligence of man, but is instead believed and loved. And once loved, it is seen as something freely poured into us. Truly, the soul ignited by this love shines more clearly the more it burns with fervor; it discerns more truly and enjoys more sweetly. Hence, Plato <note>The Greek philosopher; here the author argues that spiritual truth is gained through a pure life rather than just "pointing a finger" with logic.</note> asserts that divine light is not demonstrated by the "finger of reason" but is captured by the clear serenity of a pious life.

### What the heavens, soul, angel, and God are; and on the difference between visible and invisible light.

<margin>v</margin>
In order to gather the winding paths of our discussion into a few words: we say that the heavens are a certain kind of light that is, in a way, physical but without heavy matter. The soul is a certain light that is great but without physical size. An angel is a very swift light without movement. God is the best and most powerful light without any limiting qualities. We are imprinted by His heat through our will sooner, more certainly, and more vehemently than we are by His light through our understanding. In this way, invisible light differs most from visible light: visible light, whether in fire or in the heavens, comes from the outside and illuminates before it heats. Invisible light, on the contrary, acting from within, in some way heats the soul before it illuminates it. Therefore, in the case of visible light, we move from sight to touch; in the case of the invisible, we proceed as if from a kind of touch into sight. Human beauty is seen before it is loved. Divine beauty, however, is loved so that it may be seen. In the former, he who sees is miserably possessed by hope. In the latter, to see is nothing other than to possess happily. Therefore, whoever believes he will possess God without a singular love and worship of Him, or hopes to find Him before loving Him, labors in vain and acts against the very order of nature.

## The second stage of Platonic contemplation consists in God. The craftsmanship of the uniform and multiform depends on the uniform and multiform art.

<margin>c</margin> **T**he common opinion of all believes—and the diligent reasoning of the wise proves—that this craftsmanship of the world, which is skillfully and rationally arranged and driven according to its own nature and motion, is governed by a certain rational art and skillful reason. Truly, as much as can be gathered from craftsmanship of this kind, which is both one and universal, and which is established and driven everywhere throughout the whole and its parts by such marvelous reason that it can scarcely be followed by any logic, and no logic at all can imitate it: without doubt, together with Timaeus <note>referring to the speaker in Plato’s dialogue of the same name, which discusses the creation of the physical world by a divine Craftsman or "Demiurge."</note>, we argue that the art which created the world is a certain universal and singular Reason: uniform, so to speak, and multiform <note>original: "vniformē & omiformē"; meaning it is a single, simple principle that nevertheless contains the patterns for all diverse things.</note>. I say the Reason of the entire world, embracing in itself all the reasons of every part of the world.

## God is named art: reason: substance: nature: life: sense: intelligence: certainty.

<margin>f</margin> **I**f this Reason is the most absolute and the fountain of all reasons, from which all substance, nature, life, sense, and intelligence is produced inwardly; then no one ought to be so irrational as to deny that such a Reason is the most stable substance, the most fertile nature, eternal life, the most piercing sense, and the most lucid intelligence. I say "most lucid," meaning "most certain." For what light is to the body of the world—the light of both the luminaries and of those who see—certainty is to the Reason that created the world. This certainty is as much more lucid than physical light as it is more certain and more excellent; it is the certainty of each thing, a certainty that becomes sure of itself from within itself. Being certain in itself of all things, through its own power it makes all things clear and certain to serene minds.

## God is the truth of all true things, the fountain and cause of the truth of things and of the mind.

<margin>v</margin> **T**hence He is also named the highest Truth of every truth, from whom all true things are made. Through Him, true things are tracked down; in Him, they are truly perceived. For this reason, those who investigate things consult this Truth about true matters wherever they wish, according to their judgment. By His naturally implanted spark, they search out the truth. By His rays, poured out through all things, they distinguish truths found from falsehoods. By His examination, they compare truths already distinguished among themselves and judge them. And when they understand the species <note>original: "species"; the essential forms or "types" of things.</note> abstracted from individual things—in which the truth of each thing consists—they understand nothing other than Truth itself: that is, God, who is the gathering and fountain of all "abstracts," that is, of the Ideas <note>original: "idearum"; in the Platonic sense, these are the eternal, perfect blueprints of all things in the divine mind.</note>, just as the light of the sun is the source of colors.

## Common descriptions of God according to the Platonists.

<margin>q</margin> **W**hat then is God? The Reason of reasons, the Fountain and Craftsman of all things; the uniform and multiform Form. The immovable Substance moving all things. Stillness in motion, eternity in time. Containing all in space. Depth in the highest things, and the summit in the deep. Unity in multitude; power in weakness. The most fertile Nature of natures. The most natural fertility of fertilities, the eternal Life of living things and of lives. The Light of sensible things <note>original: "sensibilium"; things that can be perceived by the physical senses.</note> and the piercing clarity of the senses. The Sense that perceives the "marrow" of sensible things within their "husks," and the husks within the marrow <note>A metaphor for seeing the essential spiritual truth (marrow) within the physical exterior (husks), and vice-versa.</note>. Such an Intelligence that it is the very [intelligence] of things...

### Many reasons why the joy of the contemplative person surpasses the pleasures of the senses

<margin>g</margin> The joy, I say, which comes from the truest goodness and the best truth is itself the best and truest. From this, the divine Plato <note>Marsilio Ficino often refers to Plato as "divine" because he viewed Platonic philosophy as a precursor to and compatible with Christian theology.</note> says that from those things which are offered to the senses—because they come from the outside and do not truly exist, but are impure and brief—there arises a certain external titillation around the skin of the body and soul, a false pleasure mixed with pain and short-lived. But from those things which insinuate themselves deeply into the mind from within: because they are internal, true, pure, stable, and supreme, an internal, true, pure, stable, and supreme pleasure is poured into the very marrow of the soul. Furthermore, the sense and the sensible object <note>The physical thing being perceived, such as a physical color or sound.</note> are related to each other in such a way that, because of their density and weakness, they cannot entirely penetrate one another. But the intelligible object <note>A pure concept or truth that can only be grasped by the mind, not the eyes.</note>, by its fineness and marvelous power, glides into the inner parts of the intellect; and the intellect, by its own subtlety and virtue, penetrates the intelligible from every side. Otherwise, the mind would not be able to discern the nature of the thing to be understood from foreign things, nor distinguish it into its parts, nor compare its innermost parts with its outermost.

Thus it happens that the pleasure of the mind, if it is ever truly perceived through proper contemplation, is more internal and more vehement than the delights of the senses. If we are accustomed to be powerfully delighted when—concerning heat or cold, dryness and moisture, or the emptying and filling of the body—we have recovered the natural habit of the body (which was as if lost to its opposites) by means of those opposites—as when we are cooled after being too hot, and similarly in other cases: with how much pleasure do we think that man is flooded whose natural habit of mind, lost to darkness and malice, is even now recovered by light and goodness? And the whole of him is reformed according to his own Idea <term>Idea: In Platonic philosophy, the "Idea" is the perfect, eternal, and unchanging pattern of a thing. Here, it refers to the perfect version of humanity that exists in the divine mind.</term>. And if from things that are more and more suitable, a gradually greater and greater delight is born; and if nothing is more suitable to man than the Idea of humanity itself, which is the "true man," what could be sweeter than both embracing it within oneself by understanding it and being restored to it by loving it?

Furthermore, in loving all beautiful and good things, in truth there is perhaps nothing else involved than that we love beauty itself and goodness itself, from which and out of which individual things are beautiful and good. Just as if someone were to say that to a taste greedy for sweetness, the apple and the wine are pleasing not because they are apple or wine, but because they are sweet; and therefore, in these things nothing else is desired but sweetness itself, and in sweetness, goodness. Therefore, if it is the most pleasant of all things to possess the thing loved, what can be thought of as more pleasant than to possess Him <note>Referring to God as the source of all Beauty and Goodness.</note> who is Beauty itself and Goodness itself? For nowhere else do we possess the loved thing itself, but only its shadow. There, then, our Idea pleases us; for everyone is most dear to himself. There alone are we most fully delighted, where alone we most truly find ourselves. In our Idea all Ideas are pleasing. Beauty delights in all things, and all things fill us in goodness. And according to that specific form, we rejoice there in the very Idea of joy. By which it happens that there alone we rejoice in the total fullness of joy. If where there is a good thing, this or that person rejoices; surely where Goodness itself is, there is Joy itself. If no one truly lives or is wise except the one who properly lives by Life itself and is wise by Wisdom itself...

## The third level of Platonic contemplation. Why the soul in the body knows divine things with difficulty: and that it is immortal.

### The first obstacle of the mind in beholding the light of intelligible things <note>Intelligible things are truths or concepts grasped by the mind rather than the physical senses.</note>, because it is joined to the body.

> A fiery vigor and a heavenly origin belong to those
> seeds, so far as harmful bodies do not
> slow them down, and earthly limbs and

Let us see what our Platonic Maro <note>Publius Vergilius Maro, the Roman poet Virgil, whom Renaissance thinkers often interpreted as a philosopher-prophet.</note> intended in these verses. The soul, hedged in by the dark prison of this body, scarcely perceives the wonderful light of truth and the true things which shine wonderfully in nothingness <note>The author likely means they shine in a way that bypasses physical matter.</note>, because it has the smallest proportion to it. Now, the lack of such proportion arises from three causes. The first is: since the soul is a certain form joined to the body. But that light is a form entirely separated from the commerce of bodies. This is the point of what Aristotle says in the *Metaphysics*: Our intellect stands toward those things which are clearest in nature just as the eye of an owl stands toward the light of the sun. To the same point belongs what Avicenna <note>A famous Persian polymath and philosopher (c. 980–1037) whose work on metaphysics deeply influenced Western thought.</note> writes in the *Metaphysics*: Just as the tongue of a paralytic, oppressed by a certain humor, loses the certain taste of flavor, which it recovers once the tongue is purged; so the human intellect is like a paralytic because of its conjunction with the mortal body. That is, it is deprived of its natural sense for those things which are entirely incorporeal and eternal. And just as the humor of the tongue takes away the act of tasting but not the power (as appears in him who, once purged, recovers the act of tasting), so the body [takes away] the action of intel[lect...]

reading about incorporeal things <note>Non-physical or spiritual realities.</note> disturbs the mind but does not destroy its power. We gather this from the fact that the further the mind removes itself from the body—both through the cultivation of morals and the frequent practice of contemplation—the more clearly it discerns incorporeal things. And together with these, it also discerns itself; for the mind is itself incorporeal, since by its own action and a certain innate affection it sometimes transcends the order and power of physical bodies.

### The second obstacle to the intelligible light: that the mind is affected by the body.

The second cause which hinders the proportion we mentioned from the beginning is of this sort: because the soul is joined to the body, moving and acting naturally in the way it does here, it certainly turns its natural affection primarily toward physical things. This affection diverts the soul far away from the incorporeal.

### The third obstacle to the intelligible light: that the mind turns its gaze toward corporeal things.

The third is that it frequently turns the sharp gaze of knowing toward the senses and sensible objects, and their images stored in the **imagination** <term>phantasia: the mental faculty that stores and processes images received from the senses</term>. Indeed, these images are like clouds that shadow the mind's gaze to such an extent that it does not discern the wonderful light of intelligible things; while it looks upon their splendor, it does so for the most part not in the things themselves but in these clouds. Here, seeing itself as if degenerating and becoming almost physical, it sees neither the truth itself nor clearly, but rather sees things obscured by the darkness of images. This state of the mind seems similar to eyes suffering from **red ophthalmia** <note>original: "rubra obtalmia." An old medical term for an eye inflammation that was thought to tint the patient's entire field of vision with a reddish hue.</note>. To such eyes, the light is not clear as it actually is, but appears red; the colors within the light are also not seen as they are, but as red. 

There are also some whose mind is at times so obscured by the contagion of the body and the clouds of physical things that it nowhere sees the rays of spiritual things at all, much like an eye oppressed by a **cataract** <note>original: "chataracta."</note>. However, when these physical impurities are somehow washed away from the soul, they begin to see somewhat into incorporeal things. But when they are completely dissolved, suddenly the intelligible light—full of the rays of all intelligible things—pours itself entirely into the eyes of the intelligence. This light is indeed everywhere and, by its nature, illuminates the intellectual eye as soon as it has been purified, just as visible light illuminates our sight. And all sensible things shine much more clearly in this intelligible light—as if in their primary source—than they do in the physical light, which is in truth merely a shadow of that higher light. 

One must remember that the Soul—occupied as it is in building and governing the mass of the body and distracted by various actions—turns its gaze toward the rays of spiritual things either not at all or, most often, in a neglected and superficial way. Add to this that it looks "obliquely" <note>Indirectly or from a skewed perspective.</note>; for even when it looks a bit more attentively according to its strength, because it is joined to the body, it very often turns back toward the things it is joined to—that is, toward the clouds of physical things flying in the imagination. The imagination also clothes the rays of spiritual things with the likenesses of physical objects as soon as they begin to shine upon the mind. Therefore, the mind sees either not at all, or only with difficulty and obscurity. But when the mind is both separated from the body and cleansed from the body's stain, it turns with its whole intention to incorporeal things alone. In their abundant light, it shines back according to its desire. All things in it...

### Argument for the immortality of the soul from the fact that it understands incorporeal things without the instrument of the body. It reaches separated forms and separates those that are joined.

Regarding the fact that our soul can, according to its substance, be separated from the body and thereafter remain within itself: for the present, it should suffice to understand how the intellect acts. It acts without any bodily instrument whenever it runs through all the kinds and species of physical things and ascends from there higher to the order of spiritual things, distinguishing them into their own kinds and species. Indeed, through a bodily instrument—which would necessarily be limited to particulars—the soul could only comprehend physical and particular things. If it can act without the body, it can also live and understand apart from it. 

Add to this that, according to its action—which both comes from its substance and remains within its substance—the soul not only reaches those things that are separate and eternal (even when it reluctantly proves by the deceptions of the **imagination** <term>phantasia: the faculty that creates mental images from sensory input</term> that such things must exist in the order of reality), but it also, by its own power, separates forms from matter when it distinguishes the nature of each species from individual things in the natural world. **Plotinus** and **Proclus** <note>Neoplatonist philosophers who argued for the soul’s independence from the physical world.</note> say that since the essence of an action is both its beginning and its foundation, the mind—which calls itself away from the body by the act of abstracting—is therefore much more able to live according to its essence apart from the body. **Themistius** <note>A 4th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> considers it more difficult to separate natures that are joined together than to perceive forms that are already separate. From this, he concludes that the intellect can reach separated forms since it separates joined natures at its own will.

### Argument for the immortality of the soul from its proportion to separable forms and its access to separated ones.

Objects of this kind are natural and familiar to the human intellect as long as it inhabits this natural body. For it understands them continuously and by a certain natural instinct, by separating them from individual things. It is therefore necessary that there be no small proportion between the intellect and these forms. From this, one concludes that the intellect is joined to the body in such a way that it is separable—indeed, it is even now in a certain way separated, since its "domestic" objects are species that are joined to individuals, yet the intellect treats them not as joined, but as separable and distinct. 

Truly, this is the common mode of understanding: when the **imagination** pictures this or that specific man, the intellect then ignores the mortal accidents of that man—ignoring this specific place and that specific time—and turns itself toward humanity itself, which is common to all and flourishes everywhere and always; it does the same in other species. It appears most especially separated when it sometimes goes beyond the condition in which it lives here and resolves those species of natural things entirely into the very **reasons** <note>The rational principles or "logoi" underlying physical reality.</note> and **Ideas** that are above nature and completely free from all matter. And just as it previously proceeded from an image found in the imagination to a species by a certain natural intuition of abstracting, so it then proceeds by reasoning from the species to the entirely eternal reason of that species. ...it is necessary by nature that in many things a single form proceeds from one over a multitude.

-> The reason for the soul's immortality is that it understands something incorporeal; for the intuition of which a specific **mental image** <term>phantasma: a sensory-based mental image or representation</term> is sometimes not necessary. <-

<margin>p</margin> Indeed, since action proceeds from essence, the condition of acting is always the same as the condition of being, and vice versa. For this reason, because our soul is currently joined to the body in such a way that it may eventually be separable and remain separate, it begins its process of knowing from individual forms of things entirely joined to matter, regardless of the constraints of place. However, it then proceeds to **species** <note>In this context, "species" refers to the mental concepts or categories that group individual things together.</note> that are joined in their effect but are, by their own nature and the power of intelligence, separable. Third, by its own strength, having shaken off the images of the imagination, it moves toward **reasons** <note>original: "rationes" — here meaning the underlying formal principles or ideas of things</note> that are now separated from matter. The soul could never conceive of these reasons as existing absolutely in the order of things unless it expelled the clouds of mental images, at least for a very brief moment. But quickly, due to the nature and habit of this physical region, these clouds gather again and obstruct the clarity of heavenly things. From that sudden abstraction, however, metaphysicians conclude that the intellect is capable of understanding at some point without mental images. From this it also follows that it can live apart from the body and understand with total clarity.

-> The soul in the body, according to the Platonists, proceeds in knowing from individuals to species, and from species to ideas. Outside the body, it proceeds in reverse: namely, from ideas to species, and from species to individuals. <-

<margin>v</margin> But when the soul is separate, it proceeds differently than it does in the body. For in the body, the soul passes from individuals to species, and from species to reasons. When separate, however, it is the opposite. Naturally beginning its power among familiar things, it sees natural species through a natural intuition of divine reasons; and within those species, as if by a sudden (yet instantaneous) argumentation, it inspects individual things. From this, a circle is made by the soul from time to eternity, and from eternity back to time. Therefore, just as it was once so joined to matter as to be separable and eventually exist as a separate thing, so thereafter it exists as a separate thing in such a way that it may be joined again and at some point be bound. Powers proceed from natures; natures are indicated by powers. For the soul is ruled by infinite power, wisdom, and goodness. Therefore, natural powers are not in vain. The Platonists can perhaps use this argument to support the everlasting circuit of souls; the Hebrews, Christians, and **Muslims** <note>original: "Maumetenses" — a historical term for followers of Muhammad</note> can most truly use this same argument for the resurrection of human bodies.

-> How the soul understands incorporeal things obscurely in the body, but clearly outside the body. <-

<margin>p</margin> Therefore, while the soul leads its life in matter and, in a sense, under the conditions of time, it sees natural forms in the shadow of the lowest matter. It sees supernatural forms, however, mostly under the **eclipse** <note>The author uses the metaphor of an eclipse to describe how physical reality blocks the "light" of spiritual truths.</note> of natural things. But when it lives its life outside of matter and above time...

<meta>Continuity: This page follows the discussion on the soul's ability to abstract concepts from matter. It now transitions into the hierarchy of perception—from the physical senses to the "internal senses" of the imagination, and finally to the divine light where the soul sees the eternal "reasons" or blueprints of the universe.</meta>

BOOK

Then, indeed, the soul contemplates supernatural forms in the light of the highest form <note>In Platonic philosophy, the "highest form" usually refers to the Good or the Divine Intellect, which illuminates all other truths.</note>. While it gazes upon natural things, it does so under the rays of those supernatural ones. In that state, all things are clear; now, however, all things are obscure. For the soul perceives temporal things in no other way than through their images drawn from the senses and, as it were, purified within them. Indeed, there is no other proportion <note>A harmonious relationship or bridge</note> between these material things and the soul. Yet, as long as the soul is occupied by a mortal body, it turns toward eternal things with great difficulty and little success; and even when it has turned toward them, it is very often hallucinated and deceived by the intrusion of bodily images. Hence arises that mystery of our Plato in the *Phaedo* <note>original: "phedone" — a dialogue by Plato concerning the soul’s immortality</note>: the soul living in another—namely, in the body—through which it looks at something else—namely, through the windows of the senses and **mental images** <term>phantasmata: the sensory-based representations our minds use to think about the physical world</term>. Looking, he says, at those things which are in another—that is, both the specific types in individuals and the individual forms within matter—it discerns nothing clearly. But when the soul, living in itself, looks through itself, and looks within itself at those things which are in themselves—that is, the **reasons of things** <term>rationes rerum: the eternal archetypes or divine "blueprints" of all things</term> which exist in themselves while they are in the highest Reason of all—then it perceives everything most clearly. This is because those inner truths are both most intimate and most clear; they shine more brightly in themselves and to the soul than these material things do, just as they are purer, truer, and more powerful.

-> Perception is more excellent in the imagination than in sight; it is far more excellent in the mind than in the imagination. <-

But does the soul comprehend those things with the senses? Certainly, with certain senses: namely, the "sense of the senses." For besides those senses which the Platonists believe are exercised in the **ethereal vehicle** <note>In Neoplatonism, the "ethereal vehicle" is a subtle, celestial body that serves as a middle ground between the immaterial soul and the heavy, physical body.</note> of the soul, there are also several much clearer senses which the mind can use even without a body. To be sure, the five senses exercised in the nerves and spirits flow from those that flourish in the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasia"</note>. But within the imagination, those five senses are broader and more perceptive than the physical ones. Add to this that they are more stable, for the imagination preserves what the physical senses do not. Again, there is a sense in the mind that is just as much broader, more stable, and more perceptive than the one in the imagination as the mind is more excellent than the imagination. If it is broader, it surely extends beyond those categories of things grasped by the physical senses and imagination. If it is more stable, it also preserves things longer than the imagination. If it is more perceptive, it certainly sees more clearly and splendidly than they do. I say that it sees, at times through them and through the imagination, both images and individual things when it turns itself toward them. It sees through itself, stirred by the imagination, the **species** <note>The essential concepts or categories of things</note>, seeing them more clearly because it is closer to them. It inspects itself within itself when it reflects upon itself; and it can reflect upon itself if it loves, seeks, and understands itself. In this state, the soul appears first as indivisible and existing within itself. For a form that is either divisible or necessarily dependent on another can never reflect upon itself. Finally, it discerns the "reasons" most clearly when it looks from itself toward the highest Reason of all. In that Divine Reason, the sight of the mind sees the principle and power of light and of colors, which are as much more brilliant than this physical light and these colors as the "Idea" of light is more whole and excellent than light found in physical bodies. In that Divine Reason, the hearing of the mind also hears the principle of sounds with a more resonant harmony than all the sounds the ear can hear or the imagination can conceive. The same logic applies to the other senses of the intelligence.

It argues that the soul has higher, non-physical senses that allow it to see and hear divine archetypes directly.</summary>

### As the love is, so is the friendship.
### Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved Alamanno Donato, sends greetings. <note>original: "S.D." stands for "Salutem Dicit," a traditional greeting meaning "sends health" or "sends greetings."</note>

<margin>c</margin>Since friendship—as no one doubts—receives its power and its name from love: for friendship is nothing other than mutual love confirmed by a certain stable, that is, honorable, habit. It follows that whatever love itself is—from which friendship is drawn and named—such should the friendship always be. What then, Alamanno, shall we say our friendship will be? Certainly, since it began from nowhere else than from Platonic love, we shall never call it anything other than Platonic. Indeed, while recently explaining our commentaries on Plato's *Symposium* <note>original: "Convivium" — Plato’s famous dialogue on the nature of love.</note> concerning love, we began to love each other in such a way that we can now seem to have shaped and perfected within ourselves that very idea of true love which Plato envisions there. From this very Platonic love, a certain Platonic friendship is born, which is conceived, nourished, and increased in the nurturing lap of the Muse Urania <note>Urania is the Muse of Astronomy, often associated in the Renaissance with "celestial" or divine love as opposed to "vulgar" or physical love.</note>. Since it takes its origin from the Muses, it never smells or tastes of anything except what is musical, harmonious, and elegant. More trust should be placed in this one benevolence—as it is in Plato—than in any necessity or blood relationship. Why then do you doubt further, Alamanno, whether our Plato wanted there to be more than one soul in a single body? So far is it from there being many souls in one body, that the opposite often seems to happen: namely, when we perceive almost a single soul in the many bodies of friends, fused together by Platonic love. But enough of these things; I come now to those matters about which you ask.

### According to Plato, there is one soul in man and three powers in that one soul.

<margin>q</margin>You ask whether faith should be given to those **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle, who often differed from Plato on the structure of the soul</term> who do not hesitate to slander Plato, claiming he placed several souls in man: namely, the rational, the spirited, and the appetitive souls <note>These represent the three parts of the soul: reason, anger/courage, and physical desire.</note>. I respond indeed that there is only one soul, through which we do all these things by means of its several powers. Just as the body of a fire, being one, acts sufficiently in three ways through three qualities. For it shines with light and illuminates; it ascends quickly through its lightness; and it heats and burns with heat. And in any particle of fire, these three qualities flourish equally; they are in the same place together, yet distinct from one another by a certain property. So the substance of the soul, being one and the same, seems sufficiently able to perform three duties through its three powers: namely, by **reason**, as if by a kind of light, to discern the true and good from the false and evil; moreover, by **appetite**, as if by lightness, to carry itself most easily toward those things that please it; and again, by **spiritedness** and the ferocity of anger, as if by a kind of heat, to be carried away either in consuming or repelling those things which sometimes [hinder] it from those things it seeks...

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the discussion of the human soul, specifically transitioning from the concept of "Platonic love" and friendship discussed on the previous page into a detailed psychological analysis. It uses the fourth book of Plato’s Republic to explain how a single soul can possess multiple, sometimes conflicting, powers or faculties.</meta>

BOOK

[...they] seem to be able to prevent the pursuit. What prohibits there from being one soul fortified with three powers: which, although they differ from one another in their specific property, are nevertheless everywhere together in the same soul, wherever the soul is entirely present?
But it is worthwhile to hear Plato himself in the fourth book of the *Republic* disputing this matter, so that he may hold this as certain: namely, that the substance of the soul is one, but that there are several such powers together in the soul. For he says: One and the same thing can never do or suffer contrary things at the same time, in the same respect, and in relation to the same object. And if anything should seem to move and be at rest at the same time, it will either move in one part of itself while resting in another—just as if someone moves one hand while the other remains still. Or certainly it will move in one respect but not in others: just as a sphere <note>original: "spera" — a common medieval/Renaissance spelling of "sphaera."</note> is not changed in its upright position but meanwhile rotates in a circle while remaining fixed around its center. Therefore, while the center remains still, the circumference is rolled around. But let us now come to the nature of the soul. Insofar as a thirsty soul is thirsty, it desires nothing other than to drink, and it is driven toward that alone according to its thirst. If, therefore, anything meanwhile pulls back the thirsty soul, there will certainly be something else in the soul itself besides that power we called thirst, which pulls it away from the drink as if it were a beast. For as we said above, one and the same thing never performs contrary actions through the same part of itself regarding the same object at the same time. For in what way could the single hand of a single archer both draw and release a single bow at the same moment? Yet we see that some thirsty people sometimes do not wish to drink; therefore, the soul of these people has something in itself that drives it to drink, and something else again that forbids and hinders the drink. The former we are accustomed to call **concupiscence** <note>original: "concupiscentia" — the desiring part of the soul, which seeks physical pleasures like food and drink.</note>, and the latter **reason** <note>original: "ratio" — the rational faculty that governs choice.</note>. For this reason, concupiscence and reason appear to be distinct from one another. The powers of desiring and of being angry are also distinct from each other. For often reason commands certain things from which the appetite shrinks—as is apparent in taking medicines or undergoing labors and dangers—but the vigor of **irascibility** <note>original: "iracundia" — the "spirited" part of the soul (the Greek *thymos*), which provides the emotional drive for courage or indignation.</note>, once aroused (as if it then takes up arms on behalf of reason), eventually causes us, through indignation at the cowardly desire, to do and suffer what reason had commanded, even against the will of the desire. Furthermore, when reason commands us to fight for our country, appetite—provoked in the heat of battle by sleep, hunger, or thirst—calls us back from the battle to softness and banquets. But irascibility, while it charges against the enemy, drags us into battle despite the unwillingness of desire. But who, being of sound mind, could doubt that the power of anger is one thing and reason another? Indeed, in beasts there is anger but no reason. Again, in children almost as soon as they are born, anger seethes, but we use reason only later in life. Furthermore, anger often drives us to take revenge, but reason forbids it. Since both anger and **lust** <note>original: "libido" — used here as a synonym for concupiscence.</note> differ from reason, lust nevertheless seems to depart more from the dignity of reason than anger does; both because it twists us toward viler things, and because anger, often indignant against the vile impulse of lust, comes to the aid of reason. Lust, however, is never seen to favor reason against anger. Thus says Plato. From these points, it appears that Plato did not posit three souls, but three powers in the one soul of man.

BOOK TWO, SEVENTY-SEVEN

Angel: in God. To Phoebus Venetus, the most illustrious orator.

<margin>s</margin>Greetings always in the light of life, our Phoebus. Greetings, heavenly Phoebus, most illustrious not by external light but by that which is within. When, in recent days, the mind of your Marsilio <note>Referring to the author, Marsilio Ficino.</note>—pregnant with the rays of the Platonic sun as if with certain seeds of power—strove to give birth to a sun, it was unfortunately made too sterile by I know not what weakness of nature; it brought forth a moon instead of a sun, a moon in need of light from another. Therefore, I will dedicate this offspring of the Platonic sun, darkened as it is by my own shadows, first to the "Platonic Phoebus" <note>He is punning on the recipient's name, Phoebus, which is another name for Apollo, the god of light.</note> so that it might at least be illuminated by his rays. You, indeed, most illustrious Phoebus, receive gladly what is yours. And because they are yours by right, I pray you, make these things clearer with your own immense splendor.

**Each sense reaches only the object suitable to itself.**

<margin>o</margin>O gods, I greatly dislike the darkness of all things, through whose fault whatever displeases me does so—either because they exist within the darkness, or because, falling away from things, they slip back and are weighed down toward it. Above all things I love the light, for whose sake I cherish everything else—either because they exist with the light, or because, flowing from it, they flow back and are led back to it. Therefore, report to me, my senses, you who report almost countless other things. Tell me, I pray, what is light? Hearing responds: I am of the air; let it be enough if I report airy sounds to you. Smell also responds: indeed, I am not so bright. I am made of vapor; learn about vapors from me. Why do you seek foreign things from me? says Taste. Since I am born in liquid, I show liquids to you. Do not try to wrench from me what I cannot do, says Touch; I am corporeal <note>original: "corpulentus" — meaning heavy, fleshy, or material.</note>. I report corporeal things. Seek light higher up.

## Description of visible light.

Now, warned away from the lowest depth into which I had fallen, I shall ascend to the highest parts of my body, so that from there I may receive a light that is lighter and higher than all else. 
<margin>b</margin>Come now, my shining eyes, I pray you, by that light in which you delight more than all others—or rather, in which alone you delight—show our queen, Reason, what light is. Suddenly, the splendid Sight responds: I am spirit and I am spiritual splendor. Therefore, since you rightly demand my own duties of me, I grant as much as I have most willingly. Light is a certain spiritual, sudden, and most widespread emanation from the nature of bodies, occurring without any loss to the bodies themselves. It is a certain brilliance from "diaphanous" <note>original: "diaphanis" — meaning transparent.</note> things; but it is color when it comes from their opposites <note>i.e., opaque objects.</note>. It reports quantity, shape, and motion from all of them. Gather every kind of color into one genus. What will this whole be? Nothing but a certain "all-colored" light; or light made opaque when it is placed in the more solid and darker matter of the earth. Separate the earth mixed into it. What will be left? Nothing but a certain quality, or rather a clarity and an "act" of the transparent, just as color is the "act" of the opaque. Color, indeed, is opaque light. Light, however, is clear color, or rather it is a certain flower and vigor of the transparent body and of colors—as if it were of one color in its current state, but possessing the power of all colors.

## Nothing more clear than light and God. Nothing more obscure.

This is but a shadow, O my eyes, or rather a painting. I have never heard anything defined more obscurely. 
<margin>a</margin>O most wondrous thing! In what way can it be...

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the philosophical dialogue regarding the nature of light, moving from the physical senses to the "watchtower of the mind." The author explores the paradox of light—that it is both the clearest thing we perceive and the most difficult to define—as a way to understand the nature of God.</meta>

<header>BOOK</header>

it can be so: that nothing is more obscure than light. Than which nothing is clearer when, through it, all things shine and are made clear. I shall ascend, therefore, from here to the sublime watchtower of the mind so that I may at least see that thing from there, beyond which I can see nothing else anywhere. O mind, you who measure all things correctly, tell me: is God himself perhaps light? Than whom also nothing is clearer, and nothing more obscure. Nothing is clearer than that God exists, and that he is supremely powerful, wise, and good. For all things made by him proclaim this to our ears, so that no one is more deaf than he who does not hear the sound and noise of all things. On the contrary, nothing is more obscure than what God is, so that nothing is darker than he who imagines this to be most clear to himself.

## Intelligible light is the cause of intelligible things; visible light, the cause of visible things.

The mind responds: God is the father of lights. With him there is no change by which he might be extinguished or diminished. Nor is there any shadow of turning <note>original: "vicissitudinis obumbratio", a reference to James 1:17 in the Latin Vulgate, meaning God's light never fluctuates or fades.</note> by which he might alternately enter night or suffer an eclipse. It responds again that God is the light in which there are no shadows at all. Likewise, he is the form in which nothing is unformed. He is also beauty <note>original: "formositatem", a wordplay on "forma" (form); in Platonic thought, beauty is the perfect expression of form.</note> in which nothing is deformed. God surely—as the mind, which is his ray, demonstrates—is invisible light: infinite. He is the Truth of truth and the cause of all things. Whose splendor—or rather, whose shadow—is this visible and finite light, which is the cause of visible things. Since, indeed, the nature of light and truth is that it truly reveals other things to the rest, all things are truly and clearly visible to God through himself. It is just as if visible light, since it is the source of colors and visible things, were to look upon itself as all-colored and see within itself all colors and all sensible things.

## Visible, rational, intelligible, and divine light.

But the mind warns that we must not leap so suddenly to such sublime speculation, but must ascend step by step, lest we be forced into darkness and blinded by excessive splendor. Do not, O reason, trust in the senses. Sight does not report enough to you; the other senses do not report at all. Sensual sight is only light; it receives and gives a sensible splendor. And by this conversion—because it receives and gives sensible splendor—you recognize this to be a certain sensual light. But beyond that point, it is not permitted to proceed. But learn from me here: first indeed, that I—namely, Intelligence—am a certain intellectual light, since my object is intelligible light, which I both seek in seeking any thing and find when it is found. In fact, the light of each thing and its truth are the same. Truth is the innermost light; light is truth pouring itself out to the outermost parts. Learn next that you—namely, Reason—are a certain rational light and a shining reason, since you seek the reason <note>The Latin "ratio" means both "reason" and "the underlying account or cause."</note> for light as your origin with such greed through reasoning. But do you wish to attain the reason for light more easily? Seek it within the reason of anything. The reason for light is found where the reason for all things is: in the highest truth, which is itself the highest certainty and clarity; there you will find the truth and clarity of light. For the clarity and truth of this light which you seek are the same. What is light in God? It is the immense [truth] <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "vę", likely beginning "veritas" (truth).</note> of his goodness...

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the discussion on the nature of divine light, moving from the definition of God as light to how that light manifests as joy and vitality throughout the levels of creation—from angels to the physical stars and finally to earthly life.</meta>

...and the exuberance of truth. What is found in the angels? A certainty of intelligence that flows forth so greatly, and a profusion of joy within the will. What is in the heavenly bodies? An abundance of life received from the angels. An unfolding of power from the heavens. The laughter of heaven. What is in fire? A certain vital vigor implanted by the heavenly bodies and an effective power of propagation. Furthermore, in those things that lack the ability to feel, there is a grace poured out from the heavens. In sentient beings <note>Beings capable of perception, like animals.</note>, there is an exhilaration of the spirit itself and a vigor of the senses. In all things, in short, there is an outpouring of innermost fecundity <note>original: "fœcunditatis," referring to the internal power to create or produce life.</note>. Everywhere is the image of divine truth and goodness.

->**At the joy of the divinities, their celestial eyes smile with splendor and rejoice in motion.**<-

<margin>p</margin> After we see that from the rays of the heavenly bodies—which descend to us from the super-celestial realms through the heavens as if through pieces of glass—all things are given their perfection, life, sense, certainty, grace, and joy: it is necessary that light within the spirits above the heavens be the very perfection of their form. It is the fecundity of their life. It is the sharpness of their perception. It is the clearest and truest certainty of their intelligence, the abundance of their grace, and the overflowing of their joy. The splendor of the sky is an image of all these things; indeed, compared to their clarity, the sky is like a shadow, because the physical body of the heavens can no more exactly imitate the clarity of the spirit than the earth can imitate the brightness of the heavens. At the wondrous joy of the celestial spirits, the heaven—which is like their body, or rather like their eye (for Orpheus <note>A legendary Greek hero and poet; in this context, the author refers to the "Orphic Hymns" which were highly regarded by Renaissance Neoplatonists.</note> calls the sun the Eye)—smiles with splendor and exults in its motion. Just so, the earth, being the furthest removed from them, mourns in darkness and lies numb in its position and stillness. For it must not be thought that the heaven is moved by any external force or due to some lack. Its motion is perpetual by nature and it never leaves its natural place. Its substance is also most absolute, from which nothing of itself departs; rather, it moves from a certain excess of joy, which makes it so exultant that it does not know how to remain still. At the song of the joyful divinities, as the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed the universe was governed by mathematical and musical harmony.</note> believe, the spheres lead their dances. From this, they produce a marvelous harmony through their most orderly and varied movements. At the laughter of the stars—which is indicated chiefly by their rays—all things beneath the heavens and upon the earth laugh. At darkness, as if at sadness, all things mourn. For we are accustomed to rejoice with those who laugh and to feel sorrow with those who weep.

->**The laughter of heaven, proceeding from the joy of the divinities—that is, light—nourishes and delights all things.**<-

<margin>q</margin> That this light is the laughter of heaven proceeding from the joy of celestial spirits is indicated by human beings, who, whenever they are glad in spirit, are also seen to shine in their faces. Certainly, they are dilated <note>Expanded or opened up.</note> within by the spirit and are seen to shine in their faces, and especially in their eyes. The eyes are the most "heavenly" part of us, and in laughter, they perform a circular motion in imitation of the heavens. In those who mourn, however, the opposite occurs: all things are darkened, constricted, and become numb. Indeed, the rays from the "laughing" stars—directed most kindly and joyfully like the eyes of divine minds—cherish and generate all things within the "seeds of things," <note>original: "semina rerum," a Lucretian term referring to the fundamental building blocks of life.</note> not otherwise than the gaze of a brooding bird cherishes the egg. For by their power, natural heat is implanted in all things. From this, life arises, is nourished, and increases. Hence it happens that all things seek pleasure <note>original: "voluptatem," here meaning a natural, vital delight.</note>, because they are generated not only by earthly pleasure but also by celestial joy. Who then would deny that the divinities move and beget all things with a certain joyful affection? For we see that all things, whether by the nature of animals or by human art, are sought and perfected through pleasure.

<term>Spirit</term>: The vital breath or intermediary force connecting the soul to the body.

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the exploration of light as a spiritual substance. Having established light as the "laughter of heaven" and the source of vitality on the previous page, the author now distinguishes between light and heat and traces the hierarchy of light from God down to the human senses.</meta>

### BOOK

Light is one thing. Heat is another. And light precedes heat.
<margin>That</margin> it is clear that brightness is one thing and heat is another. For many things shine or glisten which do not grow hot, and many things are even cold. There are also many hot things which are dark. The heat of fire often penetrates where splendor does not pass; and splendor is propagated much further and faster than heat. Anyone who considers that even in spirits, the clarity of intelligence precedes the affection of the will in a certain origin, and that in the machine of the world <note>original: "mundi machina"; a common Renaissance metaphor for the universe as a divinely ordered structure.</note> the rays of the sun are the origin of the heat that follows, will find how heat comes from light.

Light is a kind of spiritual thing. And spirits are certain lights.
<margin>That</margin> light is something spiritual rather than corporeal is evident from the fact that it is propagated everywhere without time <note>meaning it moves instantaneously.</note>. It fills transparent bodies without any resistance. It pours itself around filthy things without being defiled itself. Furthermore, it bestows itself more easily upon those bodies which are furthest removed from bulky mass. From this, the purest bodies of heaven and fire—as the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato, likely referring here to the Neoplatonic tradition which saw light as a bridge between the physical and spiritual worlds.</note> believe—shine in themselves. Air and water shine from them. The interiors of the earth neither shine of themselves nor from them. On the surface of the earth, light is infused into the diverse mixtures of the four elements, especially the earthy ones, and takes on the forms of different colors: as if they were little bodies of which the sparks of light infused into them are like little souls. If you were to separate and preserve these sparks from those mixtures, perhaps you would see the nature of rational souls when separated from their bodies. For they are certain lights, once more confused in bodies, but now restored to their own nature and therefore most clear. For thus the body, which is most different from the soul, draws a kind of eclipse over it, just as the moon when joined to the sun; indeed, just as an earthly mixture, most foreign to heaven, renders celestial light opaque and creates colors from light, so the body around the soul turns intelligence into sense.

Light in God: In the angel: In reason: In the spirit: In the body.
<margin>But</margin> to return to where we digressed? Although the heaven shines and rejoices in itself, it does not do so from itself, but from the clarity and joy of the higher things, just as an eye reflects from the clarity of the spirit <note>term: "spiritus"; in this context, the "medical spirit," a thin, vaporous substance believed to connect the physical body to the immaterial soul.</note> and the joy of the soul. The spirit, moreover, rejoices most in its own clarity and that of the sun. The soul rejoices in the clarity of the spirit and the mind. It seems, however, that this light is the mind reflecting through a transparent body like glass, and from there it is made visible. But the mind itself is a light within itself, entirely invisible because of its extreme abundance and thinness. Next, light in the mind is truth rejoicing and true joy. Third, light from the mind in bodies is a certain declaration of the truth of sensible things. It is the flower of beauty; the delight of the sense. But to say it more correctly: light in the divine mind surpasses intelligence. From there, that same light infused into the angelic mind is rendered according to intelligence, but is above the limits of reason. This divine and angelic light in the minds of men now escapes according to reason, but it surpasses the imagination <note>original: "phantasia," the faculty of forming mental images.</note>. In the spirit it is according to the imagination, surpassing the senses. In the body, however, especially in the eyes—which are like the celestial stars of the soul—it becomes familiar to the sense, but not to matter. In all minds, light is exuberant life. Truth is clear and certain; full of joy. From there, in bodies, it is divine...

It outlines a hierarchy of light, showing how it descends from God through the mind, soul, and spirit until it manifests as color and sight in the physical world.</summary>
