# SECOND [BOOK]

...[Light] is the unfolding and outpouring of life. It is the declaration of the truth of things and the grace of the author of form; the incentive of pleasure. Empedocles and Zeno <note>Empedocles was a Greek pre-Socratic philosopher; Zeno was the founder of Stoicism. Both held "materialist" views of the soul and elements that Ficino here compares to light.</note> maintain that just as a flame is related to a coal, so in a certain way light is related to a flame. And that flame is like a dense light, while light is the rarest flame, and the life of all things. Plotinus and Proculus <note>Plotinus and Proclus were the primary architects of Neoplatonism, a philosophy that viewed the world as a series of "emanations" from a single source (The One).</note> consider light to be a certain vision and sight of the deities, sent forth from afar through the rays of celestial eyes. They see it as a certain divine spirit, which both sees all things and, as much as it is in itself, is seen by all things. They add that a spirit of this kind is never extinguished but follows the stars.

->Light is the shadow of God. God is the light of light.<-

<margin>d</margin> Finally, light is like a certain divinity in this mundane temple <note>original: "mundano hoc templo"; a common metaphor for the physical universe as a sacred space created by God.</note>, bearing the likeness of God. It is from God, just as our Plato, in the books of the *Republic*, named this the son of the Good itself <note>In Book VI of the Republic, Plato uses the sun as an analogy for the Form of the Good: just as the sun allows us to see physical objects, the Good allows the mind to "see" truth.</note>. For it is like God, to be venerated in appearance before all things; it is also a certain sudden and very wide expansion, overflowing its goodness and bounty to all things most willingly and most happily without any loss to itself. It is the cause, conservation, and arousal of all things that are born. Therefore, it lifts up other things toward life, truth, and joy, from whence it descends. Without its presence, all things seem to die. But by its presence, they seem to live again. And it reminds the human race of that which is best: divine worship. For the impious dare not deny that God exists, since nothing is clearer to the senses than His image; nor could the wicked trust they might hide from His eye or escape His hand, for His very image is clarity itself, and more swiftly than can be said, it spreads through all things in a moment. One God in all things and above all things. One light in all things and around all things. Light is a certain splendor of divine clarity in things made by God. And, if I may put it this way, it is God as if limiting Himself and accommodating Himself to the capacity of His works. But God Himself is an immense light consisting in Himself and through Himself, existing in all things and outside all things throughout the immense. He is that fountain of life in whose light, as David says, we see light <note>original: "Dauid"; referring to King David in Psalm 36:9: "For with you is the fountain of life; in your light we see light."</note>. He is also the eye by which all eyes see: and as Orpheus <note>The legendary poet; Ficino believed the Orphic Hymns contained ancient, hidden theological truths.</note> says, the eye that looks into all things in each particular. And truly He sees all things in Himself while He perceives Himself to be all things. Farewell, happy one, together with your divine senate, most illustrious Phoebus <note>A poetic address, likely to a high-ranking patron, using the name of the sun god Apollo.</note>. Greet Bernardo Bembo the Venetian—or rather, the Florentine and the darling of our people—in the name of Marsilio and all men of letters.

# BOOK [III]

### Preface to the third book.
### An exhortation to war against the barbarians.
### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine prophesies to Matthias, the most fortunate King of Hungary, security in peace, victory in war, and eternal glory in victory.

Our Plato, the father of philosophers, most fortunate King, whenever he saw that Xenocrates and Dion <note>Xenocrates was a student of Plato and later head of the Academy; Dion was a Syracusan statesman and Plato's friend. Both were known for their austere and stern characters.</note>—his beloved disciples and indeed holy men—were a little more severe and somber than becomes philosophers, he was often accustomed to warn them to "sacrifice most diligently to the Graces." He did this so that they might be rendered more gracious and pleasant. That which our Plato once had to do for his two disciples, I see I must now do for these twin books of my letters, which are like my own children. I seem to myself, like a pregnant ox—heavy with a certain "cold seed," if I may put it that way—to have given birth to children who are somewhat more severe than befits the character of letters. For who, in these iron ages and regions, could ever compose works of gold or silver? Therefore, in the Platonic manner, I now command them not only to sacrifice to the Graces <note>The Graces (Charities) in Greek mythology represent charm, beauty, and creativity. To "sacrifice to the Graces" meant to cultivate a more pleasing and polished style or personality.</note>, but even to vow themselves to them with their whole minds, so that they might emerge more gracious and sophisticated.

Behold, do you not see it now? Suddenly, seized by some divine power—I know for certain by some fortunate spirit—they take up their journey toward your lofty palace as if to the very home of the Graces. They hope, I believe, to be surrounded by the most pleasing splendor of the three Graces belonging to you alone: that is, [the qualities] of bountiful Jove, nourishing Phoebus <note>Apollo, the god of light and wisdom.</note>, and lovely Venus. When that somber expression is immediately changed, they may henceforth appear much brighter and more joyful to those looking upon them. I pray, most fortunate King, that you look upon these "Ficinian sons" with the joyful and vigorous rays of your eyes as they enter that house as suppliants to perform their rites, just as you are accustomed to look upon all other things. For in this way, they will owe it to me that they merely exist, but they will owe it entirely to the King and to the spirit that they are beautiful.

And so I shall seem to have satisfied my guide, the Platonist <note>Ficino likely refers to a specific Platonic ideal or a commentator like Plotinus.</note>, who commanded that one should only venerate that prince in whom excellent wisdom is joined with the highest power. I shall have satisfied not only Plato, through this veneration of the invincible King Matthias, but also the rest of the Greek philosophers—indeed, the poets, orators, and historians as well. Finally, I shall without doubt have satisfied everyone. For all these figures, who once sought nothing other than true glory and light with the greatest zeal, have at last—after many centuries of light—fallen into darkness under the cruel Turks (oh, the grief!). The stars, I say, have fallen into darkness under those savage beasts. 

Alas, the celestial lights of the liberal doctrines and arts have lain for a long time now in "Limbo"—indeed, in a place far more obscure than Limbo is. And just as those ancient holy ones <note>The "righteous dead" from the Old Testament who, in Christian theology, waited in the "Limbo of the Fathers" for Christ to descend and liberate them.</note> once lying in Limbo called out for the Messiah, so also these wise men call out to Matthias with a perpetual cry, as if to a "Messiah Matthias" <note>original: "Mathiam quasi messiam"; Ficino uses a clever wordplay on the King's name and the promised savior to urge him to lead a crusade against the Ottoman Empire.</note> who might restore them from Limbo, or rather from the underworld, back into light and life. Not only the learned men whom I have mentioned, but also many nations in Asia and Europe under the Turk...

<summary>This preface marks the beginning of Ficino's third book of letters, dedicated to King Matthias Corvinus. Ficino employs a messianic metaphor, urging the King to use his power and wisdom to liberate classical learning and oppressed nations from Ottoman rule.</summary>

[In the face of] such immense [evils], serving wretchedly like Jews under an impious Pharaoh, they cry out unceasingly to Matthias as if to another Moses: one for whom God might divide the Red Sea <note>A biblical reference to the Exodus, framing King Matthias as a liberator of Christians from Ottoman rule.</note>, and miraculously open every pathless way, to completely free the chosen sons of God from extreme servitude and misery. Just as you have often successfully arisen elsewhere. Arise, we pray, O victorious Hercules <note>original: "victor hercules"; Matthias Corvinus was frequently compared to Hercules in Renaissance court culture to emphasize his strength and labor against the enemies of Christendom.</note>, while time remains, against these dire and monstrous beasts that so wickedly depopulate the fields, destroy towns, and devour men. The disciplines of all laws and liberal arts, and—what is most wretched—holy religion, they not only impiously trample with their filthiest feet, but also, as much as is in them, they erase from all human memory. You have conquered, O Hercules, such monsters many times before by virtue alone, and you have tamed them. But now we know, without a doubt, what we are saying—or rather, what we are prophesying to you—a new victory is being sent down to you from high heaven. For you, certainly, who are about to fight bravely again for the whole race of men and for the sake of virtue, for God himself, the whole world will favor; the entire atmosphere will fight for you, and the winds will come in league at the sound of the trumpets. To you alone Almighty God has given empire without end. That highest God who established the sun in heaven as king of the stars and the sky, has also established Matthias as the only one under the sun to 'limit his empire by the ocean, and his fame by the stars.'" <note>original: "imperium occeano famam qui terminet astris"; a quote from Virgil’s Aeneid (1.287), originally referring to Augustus Caesar.</note> October 1st, 1480.

### That human prosperity is deceptive.

->Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo, most illustrious Venetian orator and knight, greetings.<-

<margin>s</margin>I have just taken up the pen, most illustrious Bembo <note>Bernardo Bembo was a Venetian diplomat and the father of the famous humanist Pietro Bembo; he was a close friend and patron of Ficino.</note>, on the condition that perhaps whatever first came into my mind, I should write to you. But perhaps this occurred to me first: that I should speak and wish true health to a friend and a man who is the truest of all. Moreover, I should judge the beginning of true health to be never to hope for true health from what is lying and false. Otherwise, dearest Bernardo, if we catch one of our servants in a manifest lie ten times, and yet we easily believe him again and again, will we not be judged worthy, on account of our own imprudence, to be deceived as many times as we place further faith in his words, to our great risk and loss? Two in particular, from the very beginning of things, have been perpetual liars: namely, the Evil Demon, that first rebel against the truth; and again, human prosperity, which is indeed a false happiness and a sharp hindrance to true happiness. But I cannot easily refute the lies of the Demon; yet I can show that earthly prosperity has already lied most aptly so many times to the human race...

# LIBER
### BOOK XXXI

...it is proven how many moments have flowed in the entire course of time from the beginning of the world until our own. Indeed, among the philosophers, moments of this kind are considered innumerable. Add to this that at any simulated point of time, with a fake smile, he <note>Referring to the personification of Fortune or worldly Prosperity.</note> deceives countless men everywhere with poisonous allurements, sorcerous charms, and false promises. Thus, the lies of such prosperity may rightly be said to appear infinitely more numerous than even infinite points of time. That which is of such a nature should no longer be called a liar, but rather must be named "Falsehood" itself, and most clearly so. 

Let us then believe rashly, let us still easily believe—as we are accustomed—in Falsity itself, so to speak. How truly wretched we are, who still place our trust in a most false happiness; we imprudently hold to a happiness, I say, that deceives the wretched infinitely more times than infinity itself. Who is so blind that they should not at last see clearly that this unhappy "happiness" of mortals is in truth most weak at the very moment it shows itself to us as most firm? 

Certainly, we do not call it "happiness" until it has reached the very peak of its course. But in that very moment in which it seems highest—and because it appears highest, it is judged to be happiness—it suddenly and without delay slips back into its opposite. So much so that what we call happiness is rather a certain beginning of unhappiness. And in truth, it turns into gall <note>original: "fel"; meaning bitterness or bile, contrasted here with "mel" (honey).</note> to our inner taste, though at first glance it appeared like honey through a certain likeness of color.

Perhaps someone will ask for what principal reason this is so arranged, whether by nature or by chance. Four causes of this matter are principally numbered among the philosophers: Divine, Celestial, Natural, and Human. 

First, **Divine Providence** established that earthly prosperity be volatile and most fleeting for this reason: lest it hold us too long far from divine blessedness, since not even a single moment of it can be truly held by us. And also that we might be compelled by frequent illnesses to remember more often the **Celestial Physician** <note>A common metaphor for God or Christ as the healer of the soul.</note>. We are to remember, furthermore, that we are not established in this restless region as if in our homeland, but are banished as if in a kind of exile. 

Then, the **fatal law of the stars** is so tempered by Divine Providence that in the perpetual course of the heavens—where all rest is absent—as soon as the planets reach the peak of either height or direction, they recede. Furthermore, they glide most swiftly from a **sextile** <term>sextile: an astrological aspect where planets are 60 degrees apart, considered harmonious and helpful</term> or **trine** <term>trine: an aspect of 120 degrees, also considered highly beneficial</term> aspect (which are considered healthy) into a **square** <term>square: a tense 90-degree aspect associated with obstacles</term> or **opposition** <term>opposition: a 180-degree aspect, often signifying direct conflict</term> (which are held to be harmful). 

After these, the **four elements** are arranged under the celestial bodies in a certain natural order; or rather, by the perpetual flight of the spheres, they themselves are continually swept along. Thus, when heat, cold, dryness, or moisture are stretched to the highest degree proper to their nature, then finite nature neither permits them to proceed further, nor does the condition of perpetual motion allow them to remain there even for a moment. Therefore, when qualities of this kind seem most intense, they are suddenly relaxed. The humors and temperaments of our bodies follow this swift change. Hence, as it is written in...

It explains this instability through four lenses: Divine Providence (to keep humans focused on God), Astrology (the movement of planets), Physics (the cycling of elements), and Biology (the changing humors).</summary>

# BOOK
### THIRD [BOOK] LXXXI

<margin>The false prosperity of Fortune</margin>
According to Hippocrates <note>The famous ancient Greek physician, often called the "Father of Medicine."</note>, the highest state of physical health is judged to be the most deceptive. Indeed, in the course of nature, descent almost immediately follows the ascent itself. And those things which flourished quickly also wither quickly. Finally, a richer breath of vain prosperity inflates the vain minds of mortals and renders them swollen and sick. Hence, like the sick and delirious, they now forget themselves, and thinking their fortune is higher than the human condition, they believe everything is permitted to them and that no danger looms; this is said to have happened almost exactly to King Alexander <note>Alexander the Great.</note>. Therefore, they become unrestrained within themselves through a looser license of behavior. They become quite negligent regarding their own affairs. Toward other men, they are proud, unjust, and insulting; others, in turn, spurred by hatred and envy against them, both plot snares and prepare for battles.

For this reason, for many causes which anyone can easily understand, our prosperity is very easily disturbed. And just as a stone thrown upward, when it seems to have reached its highest point, then suddenly descends without any interval of time, so Fortune, having raised someone to the highest peak of affairs, immediately and without delay either orders him to descend of his own accord as if from a mountain, or she herself casts him down. Indeed, a heavier fall threatens the great, and a deeper ruin threatens those placed on high. Very often, after mild breezes and sweet west winds <note>original: "zephiros"</note>, suddenly a screeching storm from the north wind strikes the contrary sail and lifts the waves to the stars.

Wherefore Philip, King of the Macedonians—on the day when he reported victory both in the Olympic games and in the military camp simultaneously, and also welcomed his first-born son Alexander—fearing not without cause a contrary wind in such a favorable breath of richer prosperity, said: "O divinity <note>original: "demon"; here referring to a guiding spirit or divine power</note>, repay such great good with the smallest possible evil." And a little while later, he was blinded in one eye by a certain arrow. We too, if we are wise, and if we wish to avoid grief, let us fear in like manner. Or rather, to speak more correctly, so that we may never be compelled to fear in such a way, let us not believe in lies, let us not hope in the wind, nor follow fleeting or flying things, nor love things hostile and harmful to us.

But let us at last believe in Truth, we who have believed in Falsehood so easily and for so long. Let us believe, I say, in Divine Truth which never lies, which does not deceive, which daily warns us in many ways never to trust in unfaithful Fortune, nor to follow her, who is blind, as the guide of our life. On the contrary, with all the strengths granted to us and preserved for us by the Infinite Good, let us pursue that same Infinite Good. This Good not only never flees, since it fills the universe with immense power, but it even comes to meet those who follow it with the immense kindness of its nature. And what is more, it even runs ahead of those about to follow, while it both makes all things and, by a certain natural instinct, always entices all things to follow it. And by the same virtue through which it commands us to follow it—because Wisdom commands nothing in vain—it also leads those who go and brings through those who persevere. It is the same Beginning, Carrier, Leader, Path, and End.

# BOOK
<meta>catchword: mi</meta>

You ask most elegantly, Fontius <note>Bartolomeo Fonzio (1446–1513), a Florentine humanist and close associate of the author.</note>, by whose command I am driven or upon whose authority I rely, that I should sometimes intersperse poetic modes and rhythms into prose <term>soluta oratio; literally "loosened speech," the standard Latin term for prose</term>. But to answer so sharp-witted a man briefly: heaven commands this of me. The heavenly Plato teaches the same. For if you look up at the heaven, you see there Mercury, the master of eloquence and at the same time the maker of the lyre. Therefore, if we were ever permitted to hear him speaking to us, we would frequently hear him mixing some melodies of his lyre with his words. Especially since he himself is always either deeply joined to or at least closely attached to both Phoebus <note>Apollo, the god of the sun and "serious" music</note>—the father of serious music, that is, poetry—and to Venus, the mother of lighter music. 

If you listen to the heavenly Plato, you immediately recognize his style, which, as Aristotle says, flows as a middle ground between prose and song. You recognize the Platonic speech which, as Quintilian <note>A famous Roman rhetorician.</note> says, rises far above prose and pedestrian speech, so that our Plato seems inspired not by human genius but by some Delphic oracle <note>The priestess of Apollo at Delphi, who delivered prophecies in verse.</note>. Indeed, such a mixture or tempering of style in Plato pleased Cicero so much that he said if Jupiter wished to speak in a human tongue, he would speak in no other language than the Platonic. 

I pass over how Moses, Job, Solomon, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, Ezekiel, and almost all the other prophets among the Hebrews did the same. Mercury also—the wisest of the Egyptians <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage to whom the Hermetic corpus is attributed.</note>—did likewise; as did Gorgias, Isocrates, Herodotus, Aristotle, and many others in Greece. Finally, among the Latins, occasionally Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note>, and frequently Titus Livy, Apuleius, Saint Jerome, and Boethius, that supreme philosopher, adorned prose with certain poetic rhythms. 

They did so with this intention: so that speech—partly because it is "loose" (prose), proceeding more often with a freer foot, might reach its destination more easily and quickly—and partly because it is rhythmic and poetic, might occasionally delight, charm, and captivate with musical harmonies and figures. For since all things, by a certain natural instinct, are born as musical beings, they are also wonderfully captivated by music. I prefer to follow these men with unequal steps rather than not to follow them at all. 

Therefore, you will forgive your Platonic (or perhaps inept) friend, and you will grant him this mixed style of speaking; for nature itself first implanted this in him. Then, the continuous reading of the poetic Plato increased it; furthermore, the frequent use of the lyre <note>Ficino was famous for singing "Orphic hymns" while accompanying himself on a lyre adorned with a picture of Orpheus.</note> confirmed it. Nor, however, do I break out into poetic sounds at random, but especially there where some poetic matter or form underlies the subject. For such a tone and such strings seem to be fitting. 

Indeed, all antiquity teaches us to mix poetic things with philosophical ones, which was done especially and always before Aristotle. They did this chiefly for this reason: so that the sacred mysteries of Minerva <note>The goddess of wisdom.</note> might be both venerable and beautiful to all, yet shared only by the few—and those indeed the pure. The Divinity itself teaches us the same, which, rejoicing everywhere in a certain poetic figure, adorned the heaven with innumerable lights just as a meadow is adorned with flowers. And it so modulated the various circuits of the spheres that they might produce a wonderful harmony and melody through congruent harmonies. Furthermore, beneath the moon, the same God, similarly delighted by poetry, arranged the discordant forms of things into a certain most beautiful harmony. Finally, the earth, which would have been the most deformed of all...

Indeed, it seemed as if He decorated it with wonderful figures and pictures of metals, gems, planets, and animals. He willed that the fruits of the earth be covered with leaves and adorned with flowers. What more? He tempered both the individual parts and the whole universe with musical numbers and poetic measures.

->He alone loses no dear one to whom all are dear in Him who is never lost.<-
<note>original: "Solus nullū carū amittit cui oēs in illo cari ſunt qui nō amittit." A famous sentiment from St. Augustine’s Confessions, Book IV.</note>

### Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to his unique friend, Giovanni Cavalcanti.

<margin>d</margin>
It cannot be said with how much weariness I am affected, my sweetest Giovanni, because by this suspicion of an epidemic <note>Likely an outbreak of the plague in Florence, which often forced the humanists to retreat to their country villas.</note> and by my father’s command, I am compelled to be without you for these few days. And yet, meanwhile, I am with you more constantly than can be imagined. By God, if I were not so with you in spirit, being without you would surely be unbearable to me. You alone are my care, Giovanni. You alone are my solace. I pray you, comfort your Marsilio with your most longed-for letters. Whoever brings them will undoubtedly be most welcome to us. I am writing this letter to you during the opposition of the Moon to the Sun, and in some manner involving Mercury and Saturn, and also under the quadrature <term>quadrature; an astrological aspect of 90 degrees, usually considered tense or unfavorable</term> of Mars to the Sun and Moon. At such a time, almost nothing is more unhappy according to the astronomers. Nevertheless, I know I shall write most happily. For it is not only by the conducive stars, but truly by God—the leader of the stars—who decreed it, that our friendship was joined from our earliest years. It pleases me now for a little while, as I often do both secretly and openly, to cry out together with our leader, that most divine Aurelius Augustine: *He alone never loses any dear one to whom all are dear in Him who is never lost.* My Giovanni, your thirtieth year <note>Since Cavalcanti was born in 1444, this dates the letter to approximately 1474.</note> is now passing, if I count correctly. Do not, therefore, be a prodigal in squandering that which is irreparable; rather, spend your days more sparingly each day, as fewer of them remain to be spent.

### Slanderers are to be despised.
### Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici.

<margin>I</margin>
The laws so greatly abhor infamy and hate slanderers that they even take rigid notice of those who speak ill of others regarding shameful matters. This has been seen and approved by us as a public observation in Florence twice, or even three times, in our age. However, I ask for no such thing from the laws today. For I do not wish to be loved for my own sake against public laws which may be suppressed at the first arrival of winter <note>A metaphor for the fleeting or seasonal nature of public favor or legal protection.</note>. Let it be permitted, therefore—let it be permitted among the people for those to touch your "anointed ones" <note>original: "x̃pos" (christos). Ficino uses this term to refer to himself or other scholars under Lorenzo’s protection, playing on the word "Christ."</note> with impunity, since it has long been permitted to touch Christ himself. Let the common crowd be the judge of doctrine, though it is scarcely known even to the very few. Let these little men, who have no fixed opinion, pass whatever judgment they please upon my life, which is known to God alone. I either care nothing for such things, following Socrates and Zeno, or certainly very little, following Aristotle and Theophrastus. Indeed, I have learned from Heraclitus and Thales that all mortal things, whether good or evil, seem to die even as they are seen to rise. I have learned from Pythagoras and Plato that the soul sleeps in the body, and that whatever we seem to do or suffer here is nothing other than dreams. I have learned from the Master of Life <note>A reference to Jesus or the Gospel authors.</note> that the whole world is set in the power of the evil one; yet for a good man, all things turn toward the good. Therefore, may the high walls of sacred philosophy protect you from all such trifles...

### Slanderers are to be despised.

Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous Giuliano de' Medici, sends greetings.

<margin>q</margin>**T**hat dog barks continuously against me, just as he has always been accustomed to do against good and learned men, and against the soul and God. I am not at all surprised, for he is so affected by nature and habit that he cannot help but bark; nor do I even care. For he is such a person that he can praise no one except by censuring them, nor censure anyone except by praising them. Let him bark both among those above and those below as much as he pleases, provided it is clearly understood that his barking does not please the Medici.

### Congratulation on taking office.

Marsilio Ficino to Pietro Nero, sends greetings.

<margin>p**A**</margin> great affection of mind and heart, my dear Pietro, bids me write many things. But what sort of things I am about to write at present, I do not know. For our domestic and more than familiar custom does not allow me to act too seriously; nor does the supreme dignity of the magistracy in which you have been placed now permit us to joke, as we often do together. What then shall I do? Certainly that which God especially advised and the matter itself most particularly demanded. Therefore, first, I pray and beseech the Ruler of Heaven, without whom nothing on earth is done happily, that He may direct your will to His own, and bring the outcome of the magistracy and the city to your desire. Then, I most greatly congratulate the magistracy itself, because it is conducted rightly by a pious and learned man. And I congratulate my Pietro, not so much because he has recently attained this dignity, but because he has long since been so established by God that he is worthier than any mortal dignity. Therefore, give thanks to Him diligently, and humbly commend yourself. Farewell.

### There is no sweet melody without a most sweet friend.

Marsilio Ficino to Sebastiano Foresi, sends greetings.

<margin>q</margin>**W**hat are you doing today, my Foresi? Are you playing the lyre? Take care not to play it without your Marsilio. Otherwise, if you break faith <note>original: "fidem." Ficino is making a musical pun: "fides" can mean "faith/loyalty" or the "string" of a musical instrument.</note>, the strings <note>original: "fides"</note> will sound completely discordant to you. Whenever I sing to the lyre, I sing with you; no melody is sweet to me without a most sweet friend. Commend me to Landino <note>Cristoforo Landino (1424–1498), a famous humanist scholar and commentator on Dante.</note>, my true friend. And what of the true Pietro? Greet him in my name as often as you see him. August 11, 1476.

...to be defended, not so much by the soldiers of Mars as by the priests of Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom</note>. He who attacks the attackers of truth with spears fights as best he can. But he who approaches with true reasons <note>original: "rationibus," referring to logical arguments or principles</note> always truly conquers.

### Venus Tames Mars; Jupiter Tames Saturn.

Marsilio Ficino to Rinaldo Orsini, Archbishop of Florence, sends many greetings.

<margin>P</margin>In recent days, Pietro Piacentino, the most distinguished commissioner of the Pope, was asked both through a letter and especially through words spoken in your name regarding whatever I had requested in the cause of a public burden. He very kindly not only promised but also wrote it down. Afterward, when I wished to thank you in person for the benefit designated on your account, a period of ill health detained me for several days. Finally, the day before yesterday, as I was trying more persistently to make the trip, my breath failed me in the middle of the journey so much that I could hardly return home on foot. Soon after, it was announced to me that this gift of yours had been disrupted. I wondered at this greatly and most diligently investigated the cause of the disturbance; when I could not find it on earth, I finally found it in the heavens. Do you wonder at this, venerable Father? Did not Thales of Miletus <note>original: "tales milesius," the Pre-Socratic philosopher famous for falling into a well while gazing at the stars</note>, having fallen on the earth, rise up in the heavens, so that he might inspect there what he had not seen here? I observed, therefore, what recently hindered my coming to you. I found that a malignant square aspect <note>an astrological term where planets are 90 degrees apart, usually indicating conflict</note> of Saturn to the Moon had caused it. From this I concluded that my benefit had been intercepted by the snares of some "Saturnian" man. At first, I almost lost all hope of a remedy, considering that Saturn is so strong, being the most powerful of the planets as well as the highest. But then it came to mind what the ancient sages fabled, not without the highest reason, regarding Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, and Venus: namely, that Mars is bound by Venus, and Saturn by Jupiter. This means nothing else than that the benevolence of Jupiter and Venus restrains the malignancy of Saturn and Mars. I think, therefore, that the wound perhaps inflicted by some Saturnian person can be cured most effectively by someone Jovial <note>Jupiter-like</note>. In whom, indeed, do I recognize the full image, power, and gifts of Jupiter at present, besides you? I find no one else in Florence. Perhaps someone here will mock a priest observing astronomical matters. But I, relying on the authority of the Persians, Egyptians, and Chaldeans, thought that while earthly things belong to others, celestial things belong to the priest alone—yet in such a way that a place is left for human counsel, and the supreme command is referred to the Ruler of heaven. But do you wish that we now set aside celestial things? Let us set them aside. What then shall I ask? This one thing: since in other matters you are superior to Caesar himself, do not allow yourself to seem inferior to Voluptas <note>Pleasure or Desire</note> in this one thing. Rather, may you wish that what was written by the commissioner's hands in your name from the beginning, while I was present in my case, remains so written. This, venerable Father, is what I ask for the sake of philosophical leisure <note>original: "philosophici gratia," likely referring to otium, the quietude needed for study</note>; nevertheless, let your will be done.

### Happy is he who is content with his lot.

Marsilio Ficino to Valerio Romano, scribe of the prince, etc., sends many greetings.

<margin>h</margin>**I**t is not easy for those to emerge whose virtues are obstructed by narrow means at home <note>original: "Haud facile emergunt quorum virtutibus obstat res angusta domi." This is a famous quotation from the Roman satirist Juvenal (Satire 3.164-165), reflecting on the difficulty of rising from poverty.</note>; certainly, it is much more difficult for those to emerge who are obstructed by having nothing at home. Those whom nothing obstructs are usually in want of nothing. Yet, our student who just greeted you is in want of everything for this very reason: because nothing at home obstructs him. Indeed, what shall I say about "everything"? An abundance of all things hinders the human race just as much as a lack does. A moderate possession of things and a temperate breeze of fortune is safer, more pleasant, and more stable; thus, it is better suited to Minerva <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare</note> and the Muses <note>The nine goddesses of the arts and sciences</note>. Just as we greatly approve of those poor men who are rich in that very poverty and sublime in their lowliest lot, so we greatly admire those rich men who live soberly even in the greatest abundance of things and are humble and prudent in high fortune. Many, since they seem to possess all things, think that everything is permitted to them; forgetting their human lot, they judge themselves to be something above men, when they are often less than men. Let them learn from Alexander the Great, from Caesar, from Nero, from Domitian; let them learn to attribute less to their guardian spirit <note>original: "genio," referring to one's innate nature or guiding spirit</note>, or to indulge their talent less, or to trust fortune less, or to despise men less. But while I speak many words about these men, I perhaps seem to make much of those whom, in truth, I think should be made little of. Fortunate is he to whom a moderate lot has fallen; happy is he who is content with his lot. November 1, 1474.

### The virtue of a lawful citizen.

Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, sends greetings.

<margin>c</margin>**S**ince you sent turtledoves <note>Symbols of Venus and romantic love</note> to us after the nightingales <note>Symbols of the Muses and poetry</note>, I promised too rashly and in vain that I would write about them another time. For nothing at all then comes to mind in this matter. But if turtledoves are far more comforting than nightingales, why did the latter give birth for us long ago—producing something—while the former produce nothing? Is it perhaps because the nightingale is consecrated to the Muses, but the turtledove to Venus? Our house, however, is not dedicated to Venus but to the Muses. But come, let us try for a little while if anything comes of it. At least Tommaso Minerbetti <note>A Florentine nobleman and member of Ficino's circle</note>, for whom an elegant wife recently bore a clever son, may produce something for us. Since Tommaso chose me as the godfather <note>original: "compatrem," literally "co-father," a significant spiritual relationship in Renaissance Italy</note> for the newborn, has he not made me his equal? It is a great thing, my Giovanni, to be made equal to great men. It is also the best thing to be compared to the best. How much I value the fact that Minerbetti thinks highly of us is not hidden from you, who know how much I have always valued his judgment. For that "Idea" <note>Ficino uses the Platonic term "Idea" to mean the perfect, eternal pattern of a thing</note> of the best citizen which we read daily in our Plato, we have already recognized in this man. To him, public cares are as much a concern as private matters are to others. In him, singular magnanimity and incredible gentleness contend with each other for equality. In him is both the most liberal prudence and the most prudent liberality. In him is such kindness combined with gravity that he delights as many as he sees, and he loves and cherishes as many as he knows. September 17, 1476.

<meta>This page continues the collected letters of Marsilio Ficino (Book III). The previous page concluded a letter to Valerio Romano and Giovanni Cavalcanti regarding the virtues of moderation and the humility required of both the poor and the rich. This page moves into personal correspondence with Antonio "Seraphicus" and Bastiano Salvino, focusing on the nature of true praise and the value of educating the youth.</meta>

<page-num>84</page-num>
<header>BOOK THREE 84</header>

**Marsilio Ficino to his fellow philosopher Antonio "Seraphicus" <note>Antonio Calderini, a student and close friend of Ficino, whom he nicknamed "Seraphicus" for his angelic or ardent nature.</note> sends many greetings.**

Other craftsmen, the smaller and lighter the work they undertake to fashion, the more easily and accurately they usually produce it. Add to this that their works are more highly praised the more their skill overcomes the material itself. On the other hand, the situation is quite different in these three respects for those skilled orators who occupy themselves with giving praise. Indeed, they praise great things more easily and truthfully than small ones. And among wise men, that praise is usually most approved which maintains such a balance that the praise seems, in a way, to be surpassed by the person being praised.

And why is there such a difference between the craftsman and the speaker? Is it not because a piece of work derives its power not from the act of crafting, but from the craftsman? For an action is powerful not when one approaches a massive machine, but where there is great virtue in the artist. Praise, by contrast, derives its virtue in truth not so much from the one who praises as from the person praised. And although praise often acquires a certain reputation for truth from the dignity of the person giving it, the praise will only be truly "true" if there is true virtue in the person we are praising. 

But I do not know by what unhappy negligence I am overlooking a fourth point here, my Seraphicus—and indeed the greatest of all—which even to omit for a moment is a matter of sacred duty <note>original: "religio"; here meaning a moral or conscientious scruple.</note>. Other craftsmen express what they propose exactly only when they look to nothing other than the form of the work to be made. Praisers, on the contrary, praise rightly only when they refer the excellence of the praised man to something else—namely, to God. From where do we think this proceeds? Surely because men derive their "well-being" entirely from the same source from which they derive their "being" altogether. And just as human art is revealed in some natural material, so all virtue and praise of both man and nature shines and is proven in the Divine Art.

Farewell happily, you speaker who is easy, truthful, proven, and upright. And if you wish to be praised by wise men always as you are now: just as you recently praised our friend Bernardo Nero <note>Bernardo di Nero Kaponi, a prominent Florentine citizen and member of the Platonic Academy.</note>, so from now on, whenever you find the opportunity, praise men like Bernardo Nero.

---

->Nothing is possessed on earth more precious than man.<-

---

**Marsilio Ficino to his cousin <note>original: "amitino", meaning a cousin on the father's side.</note> Bastiano Salvino sends many greetings.**

Greetings, our Salvino. Your letter has fulfilled our longing—not because it praises Marsilio, but because the letter itself seems worthy of praise to me. In letters, I desire clear brevity, elegant wit, and a charming seriousness. You write what was already known to me: that I carry much weight and authority with Tomma Minerbetti <note>Tommaso Minerbetti, a respected Florentine statesman and diplomat.</note>, a man outstanding in virtue. Indeed, I value having influence with a man of such great authority so much that I commend his noble children a thousand times over to your diligent care. 

Salvino, this is your own affair. There is no greater profit or more precious possession on earth than of men <note>Ficino implies that "possessing" or cultivating the friendship and minds of great men is the highest gain.</note>. You gain noble parents from God in their sons; you gain such noble sons through your teaching. Tomma's children are growing up for you, my Salvino, if they grow up in a liberal education <note>original: "liberaliter", referring to the "liberal arts" befitting a free man.</note>. 

From the countryside of Celle <note>Celle was a villa near Figline Valdarno owned by the Ficino family.</note>, 27 September 1476.

### The nature of the earthly banquet’s adornment; the splendor of the heavenly banquet; and super-celestial beatitude.

### Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, sends many greetings.

Today, my one and only patron, the sacred solemnities of the divine Cosmas return <note>original: "diui cosmi." This refers to Saint Cosmas, the patron saint of the Medici family. The feast day was used to honor the memory of Lorenzo’s grandfather, Cosimo "the Elder" de' Medici.</note>, <margin>r</margin> which we have been accustomed to celebrate every year for a full cycle of Saturn <note>Saturn takes approximately 29–30 years to orbit the sun; Ficino is marking a thirty-year tradition of these celebrations.</note>: first indeed under the great Cosimo, then under the pious Piero, and finally under the magnanimous Lorenzo. There, the beautiful lyre of Apollo <note>original: "appollochelim," referring to the *chelys* or tortoise-shell lyre of Apollo.</note> used to pulse sweetly; the Muses sang most delightfully. The Graces spoke most pleasingly. The playful nymphs used to frolic. Reckless Venus joked charmingly. Jupiter gave the laws. Mercury delivered his discourses. O happy Marsilio, too happy!—to whom it was granted by the kindness of the Medici <note>Ficino puns on the name "Medici," which means "doctors" or "healers," suggesting their kindness is a medicinal grace.</note> to recline at the banquets of the gods for so many years. 

But now, a certain pestilence—than which nothing, or almost nothing, more deadly moves upon the earth—the suspicion of a plague epidemic <note>Ficino refers to the outbreaks of plague that frequently disrupted life in 15th-century Florence, particularly around 1478–1479.</note>, disturbs that blessed banquet. Yet I see that what is now interrupted among mortals is being fully restored among those above. 

Look up now, celestial Lorenzo, look up at the heavens! There, in the Milky Way, the great Cosimo receives his familiar heavenly inhabitants at a banquet of nectar and ambrosia. Behold, the Galaxy provides them with perpetual milk, and he sets before them the fishes of Jupiter <note>The zodiac sign Pisces, traditionally ruled by Jupiter.</note> and the lunar crab <note>The sign Cancer, ruled by the Moon.</note>. To these he adds the wild goat <note>Capricorn</note>, the young bull <note>Taurus</note>, the lamb <note>Aries</note>, and the celestial birds <note>Signs like Cygnus or Aquila.</note>. For them, the mixing-bowls of Bacchus are tempered by the Water-Bearer <note>Aquarius</note>. Diana freely bestows her prey upon them. Most bountiful Ceres also distributes her fruits. Furthermore, Iris <note>The rainbow, messenger of the gods.</note> surrounds them on all sides with wonderful variety—Iris, reflecting the rays of Phoebus <note>The Sun</note> from the morning dew, shining among the stars of the zodiac and mixing sweet scents from the Elysian fields. A new song of celestial Sirens soothes them, and a lyre, sounding in harmony with the motions of the spheres and stars, delights them forever. 

O thrice and four times blessed are they, to whom heroic virtue alone has returned joy, and whom the harsh Fates <note>original: "parce," the Fates who spin and cut the thread of life.</note> now spare. Far from these storms of Aeolus <note>God of the winds</note> and the waves of Neptune, and the mists of Pluto, they feast in the Elysian fields upon the serene breeze of highest Jupiter. O happy banquet, Lorenzo, in which a single food is all food! Where greed is always satisfied, and satisfaction is always greedy for more. 

What a miraculous marriage! In which to love is the same as to enjoy. To see is nothing other than to embrace. To embrace now is the same as to embrace forever. What a just and joyful commerce! Where law instructs the will, and the will constructs the law. Nothing is pleasing unless it is permitted, and whatever is pleasing is always permitted. There, happiness is easier and fuller than can be imagined; there, every pleasure follows the will infinitely more easily and fully than our will follows pleasure here. 

O fortunate ones, whose fortune is already fulfilled! We are called from one fate to another. We wretches always follow Italy in vain as she flees from us <note>A reference to Virgil's *Aeneid*, where Italy is described as "ever-fleeing" the Trojan refugees.</note>. But if anyone follows a fleeing Italy in vain, it seems necessary that only he follows his "Italy" rightly and attains it happily who follows one that is not fleeing, but remaining. Remain, therefore, happy my Lorenzo, in the love of the ever-remaining God. I also pray that you love your Marsilio, who loves you uniquely, as you are accustomed to do.

->The wise man despises no one as being useless.<-

<summary>In this lyrical letter, Marsilio Ficino consoles Lorenzo de' Medici during a time of plague by imagining a celestial banquet where Lorenzo's grandfather, Cosimo, hosts the gods and virtuous souls among the stars. He uses astrological and mythological metaphors to describe the perfect joy of the afterlife in contrast to the instability of earthly life.</summary>

# BOOK THREE LXXXV

### Marsilio Ficino to Niccolò Michelozzi, a man of truth, sends many greetings.

<margin>v</margin> I have often wished, Niccolò, during this rural retreat of mine, to write something to the magnanimous Lorenzo, our one and only patron, as was only right. But I know not what faint-hearted and timid affection stood in my way until this very day. Yet today, during the sacred rites of the divine Cosmas <note>original: "diui cosmi." St. Cosmas was the patron saint of the Medici family; Ficino often associates the saint with the memory of Cosimo the Elder.</note>, the great Cosimo <note>Cosimo "the Elder" de' Medici (1389–1464), Lorenzo's grandfather and Ficino’s first patron.</note> provides from heaven a certain boldness and confidence such as he used to provide while on earth. This is chiefly because a good man is not to be feared, for he knows not how to harm anyone, and by the kindness of his nature, he always strives to be of use even to the ungrateful. Therefore, having cast out my timidity, I wrote to Medici <note>Lorenzo de' Medici.</note> today. 

Truly, in that letter, as it seems to me at least, he <note>Ficino refers to himself in the third person or his own spirit.</note> has somehow raved. Perhaps it is because I rashly put my sickle into another man’s harvest <note>A Latin idiom for interfering in someone else's business or field of expertise.</note> and, being unaccustomed to it, knocked at the doors of poetry. Indeed, all poetry, as Plato likes to say, is a kind of madness—albeit a divine one. Yet we had no need for poetic cups to reach madness, for Aristotle writes in his *Book of Problems* that those who philosophize are also, in a way, mad <note>original: "ph̃antes" (philosophantes). Ficino refers to Aristotle’s *Problemata* XXX, 1, which discusses the link between "melancholy" (the philosopher’s temperament) and genius or frenzy.</note>. 

But whatever the case may be, Niccolò, one should only demand from individuals as much as they are able to provide and know; the rest must be forgiven. God uses the prudent for governing, and the "insane" <note>In the Platonic sense of "divinely inspired" or "possessed" by the Muses.</note> for divining. A skilled craftsman uses various instruments as the matter requires; a worthy commander of war loves his knights but does not neglect his infantry. A prudent head of a household, who has gold, silver, and bronze vessels at hand, nevertheless scorns no small vessel, whether it be made of clay, or is fragile, or even humble. For he knows that almost nothing in a large house is entirely useless. A learned doctor collects diverse herbs, even the thorny and poisonous ones. For the grace of light, the painter necessarily makes use of black and dark colors. God uses formless matter for every form of nature; He uses deformed things—to pass over their certain number of ranks and necessary uses—for the sake of the ornament of comparison and variety. Finally, He even uses the evil demon for the good of examination, trial, and justice.

->To perverse minds, all things are adverse.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Antonio degli Agli, Bishop of Volterra, sends many greetings.

<margin>f</margin> Many report that the "freight of taxes" <note>original: "rez onerariā" (rem onerariam). This refers to the heavy tax burden or financial pressures placed upon the clergy.</note> against the priests is seething again and again, and that nothing can be found more boiling than this, since it seethes equally in frost and in heat. Some add that there is no need for it to boil any further, for the priesthood has already "boiled away" <note>original: "decoxisse." A pun: it can mean to boil down, to diminish, or to become insolvent/bankrupt.</note> completely long ago. They say they have seen this calamity of the Church depicted in the Apocalypse. Others assert the cause of this misery is Saturn in Leo and Jupiter retrograde in Pisces. Others are of the opinion that it is not the stars, but human minds that are "retrograde" in this matter. 

But what do we say? Truly, Antonio, we think that both the stars and the Lord are adverse only to those who interpret these things with a perverse mind. We believe that subjects are justly governed by just princes. We know that by the Infinite Good, all things are ultimately turned to good for good men. We have learned from Christ, the master of life, to pay tribute willingly. We have learned from Paul, the preeminent herald of Christ, to obey princes. 

But to come now to our own business: our fortune, venerable father, is thin and humble in the judgment of the common people—as it is usually the case for almost all who philosophize—

...but to my slender desire and humble spirit, it seems rich and sublime enough. If I do not commend this work to my ancient patron <note>Likely referring to the Medici family line, starting with Cosimo the Elder.</note>, I will perhaps seem to neglect the things entrusted to my care and custody. If I do commend it, I will seem to trust too little in the justice you show toward all and the benevolence you have for me. It will suffice, therefore, to mention one thing only: a long and continuous illness. Although at first it might appear light, nevertheless, in a frail physical constitution, it must be judged as most grave.

->The Graces and the Muses are from God: and they must be returned to God.<-

## Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo, Venetian knight and distinguished legal expert, sends many greetings.

You ask, my Bernardo <note>Bernardo Bembo (1433–1519) was a Venetian diplomat and the father of the famous poet Pietro Bembo. He was a close friend to the Florentine humanists.</note>, what our Academy is doing. It loves Bembo. What else? The Academy venerates Bembo. All the men of letters <note>original: "lꝛatī" (literati).</note> among us agree on this: that he is to be especially loved and venerated, for his breast is a temple of the Graces, and his mind is the fountain of the Muses. Rejoice, therefore, Bernardo, in your own blessings. Your "own," I say, because they are within you, not because they proceed from you. Surely, as it is not hidden from you, you hold each of these good things from the Goodness of all goods itself. Only he uses these successfully, and enjoys that Highest Good blessedly, who does not "enjoy" <note>Ficino uses "enjoy" (frui) in the technical Augustinian sense: to value something for its own sake, whereas "use" (uti) means valuing something for the sake of God.</note> these earthly things but uses them. Nor can one truly please himself who displeases the Truth. Nor can one truly rejoice in goods if, in loving them, he neglects the Good itself from which they come.

## Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his one and only friend, sends many greetings.

I cannot allow your people to return to you from the Figline marketplace <note>The marketplace of Figline Valdarno, Ficino’s home region.</note> empty of our wares. For I think it a sin <note>original: "Nefas."</note> that while they bring you the goods of others, they do not bring back your own. Therefore, they carry three letters from us. One corrects what I had hurriedly dictated to our boy <note>A servant or student acting as a scribe.</note> when my brother arrived; the others are copies of those I wrote long ago to Antonio Allio <note>A Florentine humanist and Bishop of Forlì.</note> and to Piero Nero <note>Piero del Nero, a dedicated student of Ficino.</note>. I did not have today’s letters at hand, so I gave them these external ones. "You are a rustic, Corydon; you send tasteless little apples to a sharp palate." <note>original: "Ruſticus es choridon..." A quote from Virgil’s *Eclogues* (2.56-57), where the shepherd Corydon laments his simple gifts.</note> Trust, however, that little Paul <note>Likely a servant or messenger.</note> or Alexis may taste them. For they are his own. It is common for their own fruits to please farmers more than those of others, even if they are less good. And perhaps no way seems more suitable for a certain human happiness than that one’s own things should mostly please him.

I said a "certain" happiness, Giovanni—namely, a shadowed one. For even if nature willed this to be a kind of solace for mortals, especially in a poverty of things and intellect, yet true happiness would not be found in this, since in these things that please us, we would displease the Truth. For he who does not please the Truth cannot truly please himself. Indeed, a little while later, he who already displeases the Truth truly displeases himself. But who among men is most loved by Truth if not he who loves Truth most of all? Where, oh friend, where is a lover of this kind? Let mortals be ashamed; let them be ashamed, I say, that while they love mortal goods for no other reason than that they are good, in loving them they neglect the eternal Good itself from which these things have their very nature as goods. All things are indeed good in themselves because they are from Him. They are good to us again insofar as they are referred back to Him. But they turn out bad and harsh for us—and not without justice—because with the greatest injustice we pursue these while abandoning Him, in whom these things necessarily exist and are preserved.

...from Him. Oh, how wonderful it is, my Giovanni, or rather how wretched, that those very things which are most intimately joined to Him should separate us from Him. These things could not join us to themselves unless they somehow reflected Him; if they were not in Him, they certainly would not exist in themselves, and would not exist at all. Farewell. But have you noticed us "riding" <note>Ficino often used equestrian metaphors for the movement of the mind or soul.</note>? Even I, to whom this just happened, hardly noticed. After I had said I had nothing from today to send you, suddenly something "of today" arose for us—sown, clearly, by Him for whom nothing is "tomorrow" and nothing is "external," and for whom whatever is a "moment" is the same as eternity. And therefore, He alone can sow and reap in the same moment; as often as He wishes, He reaps by sowing and sows by reaping.

No one is happy <note>original: "fœlix" (happy or blessed).</note> unless he truly rejoices. No one truly rejoices unless he rejoices in the truth.

->Marsilio Ficino to his unique friend Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Giovanni Cavalcanti (1444–1509) was Ficino's closest friend, student, and the "hero" of his *De Amore*.</note>, sends greetings of True Joy.<-

<margin>c</margin>
Since my brother said he would be passing by your way at this moment, and I could find nothing of mine to give him for you, I suddenly thought to give you this very thing, beyond which nothing else is to be found or sought. And even if all mortals seek it, no one who seeks it in a mortal way <note>That is, seeking eternal truth through temporary, physical means.</note> finds it. I was just now reading this definition of happiness in the *Confessions* of our Augustine, whose divine footsteps I follow as frequently as I can: "To live blessedly is nothing other than to rejoice in the truth." <note>original: "Beate viuere nihil est aliud q̄ veritate gaudere." See Augustine, *Confessions* 10.23.33.</note> And this very joy concerning the truth is happiness itself. Live happily, my dearest Giovanni. But so that you may live happily, rejoice truly. And so that you may rejoice truly, rejoice in the truth. Absolute truth is the light of God in itself. The truth of things is the splendor of God within them. Therefore, if you wish to rejoice in the truth, love, seek, and consider God for His own sake, and all other things for the sake of God.

He who loves the eternal form enjoys it as easily and securely as he who loves the temporal form enjoys it with difficulty and anxiety.

->Marsilio Ficino and Giovanni Cavalcanti to Giorgio Antonio Vespucci,<-
->a most learned man, send many greetings.<-

<sig>b</sig>
Your recent letter, dearest Vespucci <note>Giorgio Antonio Vespucci (1434–1514) was a Dominican friar, a distinguished humanist, and the uncle of the explorer Amerigo Vespucci.</note>, filled with affection and learning, brought us a long-lasting pleasure in a short time. For it declares how well you have been in your soul for a long time, and how beautifully you are now in your body. Our Vespucci is therefore happy, for he possesses what seems most desirable: a sound mind in a sound body. <note>original: "mēs sana in cor pore sano" (mens sana in corpore sano), a famous quote from Juvenal's Satires.</note> For him, the health of the soul depends neither on fickle fortune nor on the insane health of the body, which is lost daily against our will; rather, it flows from that fountain of life which is only lost when one lets go of it voluntarily. Whoever truly thirsts for this fountain seems already to have drunk from it. For the price at which this liquid is sold is the thirst itself; and the thirsty soul possesses what it thirsts for through a certain libation from Him, from whom he who drinks more deeply reaches a state where he thirsts for nothing else. He is a most fortunate hunter who, with all his strength, sets out to pursue the Sun of suns everywhere. Indeed, even before he seeks Him, he finds Him most easily, for he would not have sought Him unless he were already kindled by His heat. No, he would not have recognized Him when found, unless he were already illustrated by His light. Blessed is he who has enough...

It is followed by a brief exchange between Ficino and his close friend Giovanni Cavalcanti regarding astrology and personal disposition.</meta>

...loves with all his might that form which alone can never truly be loved enough. For this immense form is the measure of every other form; it is forever vast, shining everywhere. Out of the infinite love of goodness, it reveals itself to its true lover as both uniform and multiform, according to his soul's desire. And the lover, immediately by loving such a beloved, insofar as his arms can reach, embraces the One who embraces all things. Securely, he possesses his own possessor. Indeed, the wish of a man who affects anything besides love is often frustrated by events. But he who loves nothing besides love itself immediately attains what he desires, and in attaining it, always continues to desire it. 

Furthermore, just as no one can do anything without power or know anything without wisdom, so no one loves without love. That power, wisdom, and love are themselves fundamentally the same thing, and that this same thing is God, neither the powerful dare to deny, nor the wise fail to know, nor the lovers refuse to affirm. Add to this that just as nothing is beautiful without beauty, so there is no lover without love, as we have said. But among mortals, any finite beauty is one thing, and the desire for that beauty is another. Thus human love burns in one place, while beauty shines in another. However, because infinite Beauty suffers nothing foreign to exist outside itself, much less does it leave anything of its own outside itself. Therefore, it possesses its own love within itself. From this it follows, conversely, that wherever the fire of its love burns, that beauty must also necessarily shine. For just as extreme darkness is entirely consistent with extreme cold, so the highest light conspires with the highest heat. 

Perhaps, O excellent Vespucci <note>Giorgio Antonio Vespucci (1434–1514), a Dominican friar, scholar, and uncle to the explorer Amerigo Vespucci.</note>, we will seem to some to wander too far in these matters. Yet it pleases us to discourse at length about divine love with a man who is both pious and a most dear friend. For what limit can there be to immense love? Meanwhile, let some ridiculous fellow laugh at us for treating such things so often and so much. We, in turn, shall mourn for him while he laughs. Farewell.

->God, you turn all things to good for the good.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to his unique friend Giovanni Cavalcanti, sends greetings.

Write to me sometime, Giovanni, what you have done in those matters common to you and me, or what you wish me to do. If only you yourself knew at present what you want, my dear Giovanni! As for me, in these times I somehow do not know what I want. Perhaps I do not want what I know, and I want what I do not know. Nevertheless, I believe that through the kindness of your Jupiter <note>In astrology, Jupiter is known as the "Great Benefic," associated with growth, justice, and optimism.</note>, currently direct in Pisces, things are clear to you, which to me—due to the malignancy of my Saturn <note>Saturn is the "Great Malefic," associated with melancholy, restriction, and delay. Ficino famously attributed his own melancholic temperament to the influence of Saturn.</note>, retrograde in Leo during these days—are not clear. But as we are accustomed to proclaim frequently, thanks must be given to Him in all things, who through His infinite goodness turns everything toward the good.

->Evils are not properly from the stars, but from a defect either of matter or of judgment.<-

...you will change <note>The original Latin "mulabis" is likely a transcription error for "mutabis" (you will change) or "emollibis" (you will soften).</note> the malice of Saturn. By Hercules, the stars can do no evil to us. They are unable, I say, because they are unwilling. Furthermore, among the heavenly beings, to will and to be able are the same thing. For what reason would they, the children of the Highest Good, harm us? Especially since they are led by others who draw their very origin solely from the Highest Good. And those most blessed minds circle about entirely according to the reason of the Good itself. If an earthly father—who, compared to the Heavenly Father, can scarcely be called a father at all—loves his children as much as we see and as those who are experienced know, how much should we think the first and true Father loves us? In a wondrous way, certainly. Therefore, we shall never be harmed by those who live together in the prosperous house of our Father.

Beware, therefore, from this point on, of transferring your own fault to that supreme star <note>Referring to Saturn.</note> which has rendered you enriched with innumerable and greatest benefits. But—lest I try to enumerate every single thing in vain—did it not wish for you to be sent to adorn a flourishing city <note>Likely Florence.</note> now in its most flourishing part, and to look upon you with the same gaze with which it looked upon the divine Plato as he went to bring light to Athens? 

Answer me, I pray: from where does that wondrous genius come, by which you understand what Saturn is, recognize that it completes its journey in thirty years, and remain aware of what effects it produces on earth when placed in this location or that? Come, tell me, from where comes that robust and strong body with which you traveled through the trackless and untamed glades of all Greece and even penetrated into Egypt, so as to bring back those most wise old men <note>A reference to the recovery and translation of ancient Greek and Egyptian philosophical texts, such as those of Plato and Hermes Trismegistus.</note> to us upon your shoulders? It was certainly a daring deed. Posterity will owe you so much for this that it will be difficult to repay. Your undertaking did not fail you. You certainly brought back those whom no one else dared to touch, and you showed to the Western regions those whose names they had only heard before. Yet, they were greatly venerated, and you removed from them all the obscurity that surrounded them and wiped away all the mist from our eyes—so much so that their very heart can be looked into, unless we are utterly dim-sighted. In short, this age has gazed upon those whom Italy had never seen. All these things were given to you by that same star.

I would also like you to answer this: from where comes that memory, most capable of so many things and so tenacious that at any moment all things you have ever seen or heard are present to it? Nor does it only hold the facts, but remembers the times and places in which they were carried out. Will you then accuse Saturn, who wished you to surpass other men as much as he himself surpasses the other planets? Therefore, believe me, there is need for a **palinodia** <note>original: "palinodia"; a Greek term for a poem or song in which the author retracts something said in a former poem.</note> which, if you are wise, you will sing as soon as possible.

->Let all the praises of all things be returned to God, the beginning and the end of all.<-

->### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, sends greetings.<-

You command me, my Giovanni, to sing a **palinodia** to Saturn, about whom I was complaining loudly in previous days. And most justly indeed. For no one commands more justly than he who, in commanding just things, does himself what he commands. And although you command justly, you nonetheless send an unnecessary order. For truly, if my heart sings, the hollows of my chest necessarily echo; it follows that while you, my heart, sing, I shall sing along. You indeed seem to me [to sing] the **palinodia**...

...you sang in your letters of Saturn and the other stars—indeed, of the God who is the leader of the stars. Therefore, let your letter be a *palinodia* <note>original: "Palinodia"; a Greek term for a "retraction" or a song sung to take back a previous insult.</note> for your Marsilio. In this letter, he gladly accepts those praises of yours toward him on this condition: that they be attributed partly to your most burning love for him, and partly to the gifts of Saturn. However, let all praises of love and Saturn—and indeed of all things—be referred back to God, the beginning and the end of all. For my part, I praise Him in myself most especially for this: that by His eternal gift alone, I am not in the least bit greedy for mortal goods. But as for the fact that I am overly fearful concerning evils—which you sometimes rebuke me for—I blame a certain melancholic temperament <note>Ficino famously struggled with "melancholy," which he associated both with the planet Saturn and with the "divine frenzy" of philosophers.</note>. This seems to me a most bitter thing indeed, unless it were made sweet and somehow soothed for us by the frequent use of the lyre. Saturn seems to have impressed this nature upon me from the beginning, being positioned almost in the middle of my ascendant Aquarius, and receiving Mars in that same Aquarius; with the Moon in Capricorn, and looking upon the Sun and Mercury from a square aspect <note>A "square" is a 90-degree astrological aspect, often considered tense or challenging.</note> as they occupy the ninth region of the heavens. Perhaps Jupiter in Cancer and one other in Libra resisted this melancholic nature somewhat. But where have I rashly slipped away to? I see you will force me—and not without justice—to sing a second *palinodia* to Saturn. What then shall I do? Indeed, I shall turn back and say that either a nature of this kind (if you wish) does not proceed from him, or if it must proceed from another, I shall agree with Aristotle, who says that this very [melancholy] is a unique and divine gift.

->No one ascends to God except him into whom God himself has in some way descended.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, greetings.

<margin>e</margin> Even if I promised you three old letters a long time ago, nevertheless, because I think you would rather taste new wine <note>original: "mustum"; unfermented or new wine, used here as a metaphor for his latest writings.</note> these days than old, I am sending new ones. In these three days, I have composed three short theological works concerning the triple ascent of the mind to God. No one ascends to this point except him into whom He—who can be moved nowhere since external space is lacking to Him—has first in some way descended, filling all things entirely from within and infinitely encompassing them from without. I am sending the short preface of the third work, not yet corrected. October 28, 1476.

->The common crowd feeds on trifles.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, greetings.

<margin>a</margin> I shall go at this hour from our estate at Ceclano <note>A reference to Ficino's family property in the Val d'Arno.</note> to seek Florence. I am bringing with me five short theological works composed by us during this last period of our rural stay, concerning divine providence, the names of God, and the joy of the contemplative. Also: on the ascent from the matter of the elements to a heaven without matter; to the soul without quantity; to the angel free from change; to God, who is substance without accident. Also: on the rapture of Paul to the third heaven, and how the soul may see there the eternity of God and its own; on the hindrance of the mind by the body and its immortality; and on light—that in the divine spirits there is a rejoicing brightness and a bright joy, while in the machine of the world there is a certain reflection of the heavens...

...you will set out with the greatest joy. These words are indeed brief, as I clearly see myself. Whether they are also brief in thought, or perhaps long, others will have to judge—provided that those who once used to read my "leaves and flowers" <note>Ficino uses "leaves and flowers" to refer to his earlier, perhaps more poetic or lighter works, contrasting them with the "fruits" of his mature theological labor.</note> do not now disdain to gather these fruits, whatever they may be. But somehow, even if it is almost devoid of fruit, September arrives more pleasingly to mortals every year than other months. I am now heading to the city. Come too, Giovanni, so that we may at least be city-dwelling companions, since we were not rural companions this summer. Farewell, November 10, 1476.

But why have I said not a single word just now about this third girl recently born to you? Because you have said not a single word to me. Do you want me to confess the truth? I shall not say a word about this matter until I find out whether I should be offering congratulations or consolation <note>A characteristic bit of Renaissance wit; Ficino teases his friend about the birth of yet another daughter, reflecting the period's social preference for male heirs, before immediately pivoting to a more spiritual perspective.</note>. Nevertheless, rejoice, however it may be, in the gifts of the Great King. For nothing from the Great One is small or to be despised.

->True friendship is that which true religion has joined.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Antonio of Forlì <note>Antonio di ser Mario, a priest and one of Ficino's students and friends in Forlì.</note>, sends greetings.

<margin>n</margin>There is no true friendship among the religious <note>Ficino uses "religious" here to mean those dedicated to God or a spiritual life.</note> unless true religion has joined it. Therefore, I desire our friendship to begin from this. Your religion is indeed most bright. But as for mine, what sort it may be, this book which I am sending you will show. I fear that it may perhaps seem insufficiently beautiful. I only hope it is at least not bad. Then, finally, I shall consider it truly approved when I learn that it has been approved by Antonio, a man most approved by all.

->It is not the bark that anointed, but the marrow.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Filippo Sacramoro <note>A diplomat and professor of Canon Law who served the Sforza family of Milan.</note>, distinguished professor of Canon Law, sends greetings.

<margin>m</margin>I send our "Religion" <note>original: "religionem"; referring to his treatise *De Christiana Religione* (On the Christian Religion).</note> to you as a pledge of religious love. If by chance it seems very poor, remember that the Christian religion was founded in poverty. Remember, furthermore, that among us there are not "pressers" of books, but "expressers" <note>original: "non expressores librorum esse sed expressores." This is a pun on the newly invented printing press. Ficino suggests his circle doesn't just mechanically produce books, but "expresses" the inner spirit.</note>. If this work is loved by you, it will seem beautiful and rich enough.

->Wretched is he who depends on future and external things.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Lotterio Neroni <note>A Florentine nobleman and student of Ficino.</note>, sends greetings.

<margin>c</margin>I vehemently desire to be asked by you now why I read or why I write; why I learn or why I teach; and, in short, for what reason I either think, speak, or do anything at all. Imagine, therefore, my friend, that you have asked me. I answer immediately: I do whatever it may be for no other reason than that it delights me. Note what I say: I did not say *so that* it may delight. For that would be in the future. I do not wish to depend on a future and uncertain thing and be deceived; rather, I wish to stand in the present and the certain. But go further, if only this delights you now. If I do anything, I do it because it pleases me in the present and in eternity, not so that it might please me in a future time or for a time. Much less do I act to please mortals. For this is not only in the future and most brief, but it is also external and placed in the judgment of others. Indeed, I have often observed that whoever depends on external things always lives in worry and anxiety, and...
