...to be most deeply deceived. He alone lives truly peacefully and surely who lives his life not outside himself in mortal things, but within himself in eternal things. He alone is never poor who places his reward not in the finished work, but in the labor of the working. He alone is never unfortunate who does not expect his end to come after and outside the beginning, but places his end within the beginning. We do everything, therefore, for this very reason first: because it delights and pleases. We know, moreover, that we cannot be delighted by anything else except the Idea <note>original: "ydeam". In Ficino’s Neoplatonism, the "Idea" is the divine archetype or perfect form of a thing existing in the mind of God.</note> of delight itself—that is, God. Nor can anything please for any other reason than because it is good. From which we recognize that in the individual things that please us, nothing else truly pleases us but that divine Goodness itself, from which and through which all things are good. Therefore, setting aside all other things, my best friend, let us strive with all our strength to please this [Goodness] above all, without which it is impossible for either other things to please us, or us to please others, or for us to please ourselves in any way. Farewell—I had barely said "Farewell, my best friend," when suddenly your letter flew to us, sweeter to me than honey and more precious than gold. But I am not permitted to go further in this praise now, lest I seem perhaps too vain if I praise enough that letter which praises me more than enough. December 10, 1476.

->He who pursues everything achieves nothing.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Carlo Valgulio of Brescia <note>Carlo Valgulio (c. 1440–1498) was a humanist scholar and Ficino’s secretary, known for his translations of Plutarch.</note>, greetings.

<margin>q</margin> You ask what I am doing today, my dear Valgulio: what I did yesterday. You ask again what I think to do tomorrow: what I am doing today. Our Plato <note>Ficino refers to Plato as "ours" to signify his role as the leader of the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note> persuaded me that I will eventually achieve the greatest number of things if I always do the same thing. And not without reason. Surely he who pursues everything achieves nothing. Many things indeed get in the way of the One; however, the One contributes to the many. He who pursues many things is merely one of the crowd. He who pursues the One is truly singular. It is the mark of a childish and weak mind to attempt different things at every moment. It is also a sign of reckless ambition to profess many things every day. Pythagoras teaches us that unity looks toward the good, while diversity looks toward evil. Just as the natural power in the liver and the vital power in the heart <note>In Renaissance physiology, the liver was the seat of "natural" spirits (nutrition/growth) and the heart the seat of "vital" spirits (heat/life).</note> are weakened in both when they are distracted into two directions, so our animal power in the brain is not sufficient for diverse things. Furthermore, everyone performs that task more aptly for which they were better suited by nature. To one person, one thing is agreeable. One thing, therefore, is necessary. For many things cause turmoil. I say the "One" because it is honorable in itself and best suited to the one doing it. Finally, if God is always the same and does the same things, a person is further removed from God the more they are inclined toward diverse things. December 10, 1476.

Meaning kind, civilized, or refined in the humanist sense.</note> than others. Indeed, other goods usually provoke spite, but the highest goodness mitigates it. Or perhaps you desire to uproot all envy entirely? This work...

->Love all. Choose and love only one: Trust in God alone.<-

**Marsilio Ficino sends greetings <note>original: "S.D." for "Salutem Dicit," a standard Latin epistolary greeting</note> to a certain man.**

<margin>d</margin>I hear, as I am told, that you are grieving because you were deceived by a friend. Believe me, you could not have been deceived by *the* friend, but by "friends" <note>Ficino distinguishes between the singular "true friend" and the plural "common associates."</note>: the unique friend is another self <note>original: "alter ego"</note> who does not fail. However, many appear as if they were "me" who very often deceive. Therefore, if you are ever deceived, do not accuse *the* friend, but "friends"—or rather, do not even accuse those friends, but your own rashness. For you either loved before you judged with greatest diligence, or you loved too much, or you trusted too much in the human lot. Love all: Choose and love only one. Trust in God alone. December 10, 1476.

->I consider good deeds poorly placed to be misdeeds.<-

**Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Marsilio Ficino.**

<margin>b</margin>You think that good deeds poorly placed are misdeeds: And because you have done good to the evil and the ungrateful, you grieve that you have acted badly. I will not command you not to grieve; indeed, on account of a once-great error, you must be judged worthy of grief, and the greatest grief at that. And since you did a good thing badly, you are worthy of the bad. Therefore, grieve as you do, and be tormented by repentance as is fitting. But do not blame either the ingratitude of others or your own fortune, but rather your own imprudence. Men are justly ungrateful to you, to whom you yourself did not give justly. Furthermore, you yourself have at times been ungrateful toward another, whether toward a man or certainly toward God. Now, ingratitude is punished by ingratitude. Have you studied so many foreign things for so long under the mistress Philosophy only to unlearn your own? O wondrous thing! You philosophers, while you follow wisdom without enough wisdom, are often accustomed to act foolishly. What then? Should you have handed over nothing to anyone? Far be it, while you strive to escape the ingratitude of others, that you should be ungrateful to God, the giver of all things, from whom you have received everything for free. Far be it, while an evil person displeases you, that you yourself should either turn out evil or less good, and thus displease the good. Those who no longer sow seeds because the greatest part of the past harvest dried up are forced to perish by hunger. Therefore, you should have tested the character and life of the man with a long-lasting examination—at least fifteen years <note>original: "trilustri examine." A lustrum was a five-year period.</note>—before you gave him anything. Or, if by chance the matter was so urgent that you had to help more quickly, you should have done so at least in the manner of Aristotle: not giving to *this* man, but to *man* <note>Aristotle famously said he gave alms not to the character of the beggar, but to the human being.</note>; or better, in the manner of Plato: not giving to man, but to God. December 10, 1476.

### Marsilio's Irony against the adversaries of philosophers.
**Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to the Magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici.**

<margin>p</margin>Last night at your house, it was jokingly objected to a certain friend of ours that his disciples sometimes go mad. And because it was objected in a very pleasant way, he took it most pleasantly. But one thing was most bothersome to him: that he was not asked by you by what reason they were out of their minds. For he does not want them to be mad without a reason. Everything among those practicing philosophy, Lorenzo, is supported by some reason, so that they may even be insane with reason. And while they seem to be foolishly wise, they are certainly wisely foolish. But why did he not offer you the cause of this madness of his own accord, even though you did not ask? Because Pytha— <note>The text cuts off mid-word as it moves to the next page; it refers to Pythagoras.</note>

<header>BOOK THREE</header>

...in the manner of the Pythagoreans, to say nothing in the presence of great men <note>original: "heroibus"</note> unless asked. Suppose then, Lorenzo, that you have asked him. I respond on his behalf most willingly. You are often accustomed to say, Medici, that Christ fixed to the cross—through a certain marvelous variety of works by which he appeared to onlookers now as man and now as God—drove the demons into a state of delusion. Our friend also, with a nearly similar diversity, turns men toward insanity. But how? In Pythagoras’s school, there are four fountains of wisdom; in this man, there are four fountains of foolishness. This man, even if he never attains anything, nevertheless pursues everything, as you see. He is twice as bad as Attalus <note>Attalus III, the last king of Pergamum, was proverbially known for neglecting his kingdom to pursue eccentric hobbies like gardening with poisonous plants.</note>, because his affairs are managed neither well nor gracefully.

Therefore, when his companions see this Proteus <note>A shape-shifting sea god in Greek mythology; used here to describe someone inconsistent.</note> constantly changing forms, some, terrified by this chimera <note>A fire-breathing monster composed of different animal parts; here meaning a grotesque or baffling sight.</note>, are driven to rage. Others, struck with amazement, turn out even more dull. There are also certain monkeys who, while they strive to thoroughly emulate his versatile variety, are seized by dizziness and fall. Nor are there many little birds who, while they openly mock this owl or eagle-owl, are secretly caught by the fowler and perish. You have here, Lorenzo, the four-fold source of this madness.

What then will you, Apollo, do against this public plague—so to speak—of the city and the world? Will you never pierce this thing with your arrows as if it were the Python? <note>Python was the serpent-monster slain by Apollo at Delphi.</note> Not at all, I think. For a long time now, having taken up the lyre, you have laid down the bow and quiver. What then? Will you soothe him with the lyre and songs? Not even that. For there is no need for such great effort here. Hence, this man seems bad and wicked for so long only because certain malignant stars look upon him. Come then, most kind Phoebus <note>A name for Apollo as the sun god.</note>, look upon this man of yours only with your rays. Suddenly, he will appear good and beneficial to all. Farewell, and consider carefully this Socratic irony against the adversaries of philosophers. I commend to you our Angelo Poliziano <note>A brilliant humanist poet and close associate of both Ficino and Lorenzo.</note>.

->To each his own.<-

## Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Pietro Soderini.

<margin>v</margin>
I have often wished, sweetest Soderini, to send my very original manuscript <note>original: "archetipum"</note> to those who have requested my letters from me. But this book of mine immediately objected with the greatest complaint: "Do not send me there, I pray, where you yourself are not, my father." But when I just now ordered it to set out to Pietro, it objected not at all, as it seemed to understand that when it set out to Soderini, it would not be departing from Marsilio. Go therefore happily to this man, go my book, without whom I go nowhere. But I see you now ask for some travel provisions <note>original: "viatici," money or supplies for a journey.</note>. However, at present I find no provision more precious than Paolo Antonio, the dearest brother of Pietro and myself. Therefore, carry his sweet name with you as your provision. And as often as he happens to look upon you in his home <note>original: "laribus," the household shrines of Ancient Rome, here meaning the family home.</note>, bid him greetings as many times in the name of Marsilio.

->One must do good to a friend even if he is unwilling.<-

->There are three stages of Platonic contemplation.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to the Magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, sends greetings.

I have decided, magnanimous Lorenzo, before I publish that great volume of *Platonic Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his magnum opus, *Theologia Platonica de immortalitate animorum*, which sought to reconcile Platonic philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note> dedicated to your name—in which there still remains a fair amount that requires examination—to publish its summary <note>original: "argumentū." Here meaning an outline or introductory premise.</note>, if it pleases you. I do this not so that you might approach the work more readily to play—having been exercised by this summary as if by a certain prelude to theology—since you seem to me to have already almost attained the prize of the game itself. Rather, I do it so that, being reminded in the meantime by this token, you may remember both that I owe you what I had long ago rightfully promised, and that I wish at last to pay what I acknowledge I owe. Especially since I do not owe this so much because I promised it, but rather I promised it because I owed you everything.

->The three stages of Platonic contemplation.<-

There are indeed three primary stages of Platonic contemplation. The first, truly, ascends from the body through the soul to God. The second consists in God. The third, finally, descends back to the soul and the body. Our summary likewise contains these three stages.

->Where the foundation itself wavers, whatever you build on top will collapse.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Paulo of Florence, an outstanding priest and his fellow philosopher, sends greetings. <note>Paulo of Florence refers to Paolo Orlandini, a Camaldolese monk and philosopher in Ficino's circle.</note>

You ask, my Paulo, for what reason I write nothing to you. It is because where there is constant conversation, there is no need for letters. I speak with you, my Paulo, for as long as I speak with myself; I say "speak" because I love you. I do not love you because I speak. Friendship that stands only on letters and words falls with silence. That which is drawn together by a brief utility or pleasure is dissipated in a short time. Where the foundation itself wavers <note>original: "vocillat" (vacillat). Ficino uses a structural metaphor for the stability of friendship.</note>, whatever you build on top will collapse. For this reason, the knot of our benevolence is indissoluble. No light or brief cause connects it, but the arms of eternal philosophy bind it fast. The book on the providence of God which you seek, I shall send at that time when God has provided that I should send it. Yet I shall send it freely, because God has also provided that I would send it freely.

->Where charity glows, there God shines; there grace sparkles.<-

# BOOK

<margin>God is love</margin>God himself is love; he who remains in love remains in God, and God in him. <note>original: "Deus ipse charitas est..." quoting 1 John 4:16.</note> These things the almighty God sang through the divine mouth of John the Evangelist. Therefore, where love burns most strongly, since God shines there especially, the splendor of grace and the grace of splendor undoubtedly shine forth. Since, truly, nothing has ever been more pleasing to me than to be where this kind of grace shines, my heart has certainly lived in your heart for a long time. However, so that my mind might also live through discussion where my heart lives through loving, receive today—in the book I am sending—my mind as it discusses, to the best of its power, divine faith and hope. Justly, the vehicle of faith and hope—since it is accustomed to carry one toward love, as both philosophers and theologians believe—now carries my mind to your mind, which is both burning with love and shining with grace.

**All the good things of the world are bad for him who lives an unclean life in the world.**

->Marsilio Ficino to the human race, sends greetings.<- <note>The Latin "S.D." stands for "Salutem Dicit," a standard greeting meaning "sends health" or "wishes well."</note>

<margin>Why do you criticize</margin>Why have you criticized the world for so long, O man, as if it were utterly unclean and evil? Although the world is arranged and led most beautifully and excellently by a certain most beautiful and excellent Reason, it is nevertheless unclean and evil to you because you live uncleanly in the world, and evilly in the midst of good. The primary source of worldly evils for you is the excessive desire for worldly goods. You love the "small world" <note>Referring to the physical or material realm.</note> more vehemently than the "large." You also admire this world which you see more than the immense world which you understand—in which this visible great world is contained almost like a small thing within a large one. O celestial mind, you love your earthly shadow—that is, the body—more than your celestial splendor, more than the supracelestial light. Since, indeed, the principle of all motion—whether natural or animate—is love: therefore, while you ardently love the body, you desire or fear all things for its sake. By desiring you are distressed, and you grieve by fearing. Ah, why, O mindless mind, do you love these things with such passion? For they can be hindered as easily before you obtain them as they can be taken away after you possess them. Alas, why do you follow so anxiously those things that flee from you, while you yourself are fleeing? Miserable one, why do you try in vain for so long to hold these flying earthly things as if they were "goods"? These things can indeed keep you far from the Good; but they themselves cannot be held by you in any way. Why do you so rashly trust to plant your foot in the swiftest current? Why seek to be filled by a vacuum? Why try to clutch the wind in your fist? Do you wish to utterly extinguish this burning thirst that vexes you so much? While you are awake, drink true water, not the image of water seen in dreams. Know, however, that only those things exist as "true" which belong to <term>Intelligence</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, "Intelligence" or the "Intellect" (intellectus) is the faculty that perceives eternal truths, whereas the senses only perceive fleeting shadows.</note>, the judge of truth. Those things which belong to the senses—which are ignorant of truth itself—are only "lifelike" <note>original: "verisimiles." Literally "truth-like" or "probable." Ficino means they look like reality but are actually just shadows of the higher forms.</note>, not true. Do you wish to be rich in a short time? Strive now to take away as much from your desire as you have hitherto strived to add to your heap. Live, I pray, according to the law of nature, which is content with a few tiny things, and not according to opinion, which always compels you to be poor. Necessity is indeed enclosed within narrow limits; opinion has none. The things necessary for us are exposed and ready everywhere; but for superfluous things—

# THIRD BOOK

...we labor. Necessity provides a useful and convenient <term>viaticum|provisions for a journey</term> for the traveler. Opinion provides a useless burden and labor. If you desire quiet, do not seek it through movement, but seek quiet within movement itself. If you desire command, command yourself by reason. If you desire liberty, serve reason. If you wish to avoid pain, flee pleasure, the bait of evils. Scorn pleasure; pleasure bought with pain is harmful. That pleasure of the body especially gives birth to pain, which is seen as the greatest of all. The art of medicine and experience teach that no gall is made more from itself than from honey. The sweeter the foods are, the more bitter the bile they create. Why was it established by nature that by laughing profusely, we should often weep? Yet in weeping, we would least of all laugh; unless we were warned that there is truer pain in the senses than pleasure. Indeed, pain is felt in pleasure rather than pleasure in pain. If you desire to please yourself, see to it that you please not the common crowd but the wise, or rather wisdom itself. You will necessarily be displeased with yourself if you wish to please anyone beyond reason. If you wish to live prudently, remember that there is such an alternation of goods and evils that these good things ought not to be taken up without fear, nor these evils sustained without hope. Therefore, one must rejoice moderately in good things; but one must grieve even more moderately in bad things. Learn the present from the past. In present things, look around at each thing as much as you can. From each thing, look forward to the end. Do not ever approach present things, whether to be said or done, unless you have looked forward to the future according to your strength. Do not do or say anything for which you cannot give a probable reason. Finally, when in each thing you have humbly commended yourself to God, and have done each thing as much by the examination of reason as by the counsel of the prudent, live with a tranquil mind; and whatever follows, take it for the better.

-> What you have received for free, give for free. <- <note>original: "Quod gratis accepistis gratis date." Quoting Matthew 10:8.</note>

### Marsilio Ficino to Francisco Marescalco, his beloved fellow philosopher, sends greetings.

<margin>p</margin>Why indeed do you doubt, Marescalco, whether I gave you my book discussing divine grace for free or not? We are not, my Francis, Samaritans; as we have received, so also we have given. Let the price of this gift indeed be that it is pleasing to you; but let its fruit be that we are truly grateful for the act of divine grace.

...to be composed of body and soul. The body consists of one part that is coarser—that is, the limbs and the <term>humors|the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—thought to determine health and temperament</term>—and another part that is more subtle, consisting of certain vapors of the blood and the <term>spirits|refined substances that act as a bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul</term>. The soul, moreover, is composed of sense and reason. Just as the humor relates to the spirit, so sense relates to reason. Nor can anyone ever live contentedly in human affairs unless all these parts of the human being have been satisfied, at least for a little while. Other things held as "goods" among men seem to pertain to only one or two of these parts we have mentioned. Only the <term>convivium|a formal banquet or "living together," emphasizing intellectual and social fellowship over mere eating</term> encompasses them all. I speak of the "legitimate" banquet, which—to list its effects one by one—refreshes the limbs, restores the humors, recreates the spirit, delights the senses, and fosters and excites the reason. The banquet is a rest from labors, a release from cares, and food for the intellect; it is a proof of love and magnificence, a bait for benevolence, a seasoning for friendship, a fuel for grace, and a solace for life.

->The purpose of a banquet is the sweet communion of life.<-

<margin>c</margin> Furthermore, so that it may be clearer what constitutes a legitimate banquet, let us see what its purpose is, what its form is, and what its material is. The purpose of it seems to be what its name indicates: not <note>original: "comessatio"</note> "gorging" and not <note>original: "compotatio"</note> "heavy drinking" as the Greeks call it, but the sweet communion of life. Thus, just as we collectively feed upon the common nourishment of the body, we may also enjoy the same good of the mind and life through a common will.

### The form of the banquet consists of a decent number and quality of guests, conversation, and the lyre.

<margin>a</margin> To its form pertains especially the number and quality of the guests. In this matter, we strongly approve of that saying of <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE), a prolific Roman scholar.</note> Varro: that the guests should be neither fewer than the three <term>Graces|goddesses of charm, beauty, and creativity</term> nor more than the nine <term>Muses|goddesses of the arts and sciences</term>. From this "commerce" of Graces and Muses, it is also quite apparent what sort of people they ought to be. For it is necessary that they be gracious, musical, and literate. Care must be taken, therefore, that no one who is contentious or who flares up in anger quickly is easily admitted—unless by chance he is the sort who can be softened by the first cup of wine or a single little word. Let the profoundly melancholic and the bitter also be excluded from the gathering, unless they are like <note>Zeno of Citium, founder of Stoicism, and Xenocrates, a leader of Plato’s Academy; both were known for their severe, "dry" dispositions.</note> Zeno the Stoic and Xenocrates the Platonist, who, much like <term>lupins|bitter legumes that become sweet after being soaked in water</term> in water, would become sweet when drenched in undiluted wine. If any divine matters are to be treated, let them be deferred until they are sober; if they dispute natural matters, let it be after the table is cleared. During the feast, however, let the speech be varied, pleasant, and brief; let history be very brief, and a story be only slightly longer. Let them imitate Nature the craftswoman and the teacher of life, so that what she does in the sweetest flavors, they may achieve in their speech. Namely, let them mix the sweetness with sharpness, and wit with gravity—the <note>original: "Utile dulci" - a reference to Horace’s dictum that the best art combines the useful with the agreeable.</note> useful with the sweet. Let them be witty, sharp, and clever, but not annoying or bitter. A banquet can tolerate vinegar, but not <term>wormwood|a plant known for its extreme bitterness, used here metaphorically for an unpleasant personality</term>. We barely admit a buffoon, and then only if he is not too annoying; but we detest the obscene and the filthy exceedingly. For filth in the soul, the mouth, and the face is much more to be avoided than filth in one's clothes or equipment for a pru—

Therefore, let my lyre not sound out of tune, but let it be safe for me as I call upon you rightly: come, I pray, you who are the glory of Apollo and of the supreme feast, O shell <note>original: "testudo"; the lyre was traditionally made from a tortoise shell</note> pleasing to Jove, the sweet relief of our labors. Let long-haired Iopas <note>A musician mentioned in Virgil's Aeneid who performs at Dido's banquet</note> be present with his lyre at the table of the Graces and the Muses.

### The necessary material of a banquet: the fruits of Bacchus and Ceres.

<margin>q</margin>
**A**s for what pertains to the material of the banquet: First, we think sadness is the poison of life, and gloom is the poison of the table. The <term>thiriaca|a medicinal compound used as an antidote to poison</term> for sadness and gloom is sweet, clear wine. Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of medicine</note> equates its power to the strength of the gods. Our Plato also asserted that wit and strength are wonderfully fostered by the tempered warmth of wine. But lest I, like Homer, be accused of praising wine too much, I shall set Bacchus <note>The god of wine</note> aside and fly now to Ceres <note>The goddess of grain and agriculture</note> and the guardian of the gardens. We do not at all desire the fatty and overly greased feasts of Sardanapallus <note>A legendary Assyrian king synonymous with extreme luxury and decadence</note>. However, I would not wish to lack the "Pythagorean" fruits, herbs, and apples in any way. For no table is easier, and none more happy than that which most generous Nature prepares for you.

### The manner and seasoning of the banquet.

<margin>v</margin>
**W**e do not highly praise an altogether meager banquet, yet we utterly detest a luxurious one. For the latter is more like "dying together" than "living together" <note>A pun on the Latin "commori" (to die together) and "convivere" (to live together, the root of "convivium")</note>. We do not require the heights of elegant splendor, lest there be a servile difficulty where we seek an easy liberty. We certainly desire what is clean and pure; we abhor what is unclean and filthy. Finally, so that nothing among us is tasteless or dull, and nothing sordid or obscure, everything should be seasoned with the salt of wit and illuminated by the rays of the mind and character. Thus, just as was said of the dinners of Plato and Xenocrates, our banquet should "smell sweet" <note>In the sense of leaving a pleasant and lasting intellectual memory</note> even three days later.

### The authority of the banquet from philosophy, heaven, and God.

<margin>i</margin>
**I**f anyone should happen to wonder why I celebrate the banquet to such an extent, he ought to remember that Plato, Xenophon, Varro, Julian, Apuleius, and Macrobius the Platonic did the same. Did not Themistocles, Socrates, Empedocles, and many other philosophers frequently attend banquets? Do not the ancient heroes and the "heaven-dwellers" <note>the gods</note> often recline at the table? Even the Heavens have a "Milky" circle <note>the Milky Way</note>, and contain the mixing-bowl and the jar of Father Bacchus, as well as the Crab, the Fish, and the Birds. It even holds the Lamb, the Kid, and the Youth <note>A list of constellations: Crater, Aquarius, Cancer, Pisces, Cygnus/Aquila, Aries, Capricorn, and Ganymede/Antinous</note>. I pass over what kind of banquets Mohammed promises to the blessed. But who does not know that Christ, the Master of Life, frequently took part in banquets? He showed his first miracle there, when he is said to have turned water into wine. Furthermore, in that greatest assembly, he satisfied many thousands of men with a few loaves and fishes. What else does the honeycomb mean, or the roasted fish? Or the breaking of bread? Did he not sing the chief mysteries of divine things to his disciples at the Last Supper? And to this same purpose tends that wonderful Sacrament of the Eucharist.

...ment. To this also belong whatever things are often read concerning divine foods and drinks in the sacred Hebrew and Christian writings. Why so many words about the banquet? So that, evidently, we who live not without distress when apart from one another may live together most joyfully. And let us remember the true nourishment of man: that it is not so much plant and beast as it is man. Indeed, the complete nourishment of man is not so much man as it is God. By His nectar and ambrosia <note>In mythology, these are the food and drink of the gods that grant immortality; Ficino uses them here as metaphors for divine grace</note> alone, human thirst and hunger are continually excited and grow. ->How pleasing is the sight of a friend; how necessary; how voluntary is love.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to his unique friend Giovanni Cavalcanti, sends greetings.<-

Since I was forced to draw out long delays in bed today, and I was thinking of some remedy against the tedium of a longer confinement, the first—indeed the only one—to occur to me to meet this looming boredom was my Cavalcanti, my singular doctor. Hail, therefore, again and again, O my health! The driver-out of my evils. The seasoning of all my goods. You, my Giovanni, indeed declare many other things daily, but that Aristotelian point especially: that nothing in human affairs is more pleasing than the presence of an outstanding friend. I have already long since received the truth of this Aristotelian sentiment from you and have learned the reason. Truly, he who formerly by a longing for him, just as recently by the absence of his body, took me away from myself entirely, the same in turn gives me back by a certain mutual affection and presence of mind. It escapes no one how gladly everyone, even the lowliest little man <note>original: "homunculus"</note>, gazes at his own image in mirrors. But a friend does not look only at his own image in a friend, but at himself. I certainly, even if I am as if a handsome little fellow in myself—slender and short—yet in that heroic mirror from which I have loved for five lusters <note>A luster is a five-year period; Ficino is marking twenty-five years of friendship</note> now, I see myself as a noble among nobles, not a little man. 

Receive, therefore, a letter perhaps more necessary than voluntary. Indeed, to avoid tedium, as I said, I seem to have been compelled to dictate this. Alas, I have just sinned; I know not how, my Giovanni, I have sinned too much against the heroic genius and the Platonic divinity. Behold, now Plato from on high rebukes me more sharply, crying out thus: "Why, Marsilio, do you separate the voluntary from the necessary in a lover? A lover’s letter is as voluntary, O Marsilio, as it is necessary. No necessity is more voluntary, nor will more necessary, than that of love. For what is more voluntary than love? Which is the first, highest, and perpetual effect of the will. And it brings it about entirely that we do not wish *not* to love. What, again, is more necessary than love? Which is branded into the unwary heart by the hidden rays and flames of the celestial deities. And the lover experiences the flame already grown before he has felt the ray and the spark. He cannot help but burn; if heaven...

It cannot not burn: indeed, as long as it seeks refreshment, it always ignites the heat by this very drink in which it vainly trusts, in a certain way, to extinguish it. Why is there such a wonderful mixture of necessity and will? It is because God is both supreme necessity and supreme liberty. We all desire the highest good with the highest effort. Nor can we not want it; nor do we want to be able to not want it. Almost the same thing usually happens to this person: whoever is attracted by the warmer splendor of the divine rays—which shine wonderfully to us in beauty—is gently enticed, secretly snatched away, and vehemently ignited. January 30, 1476.

->Man is a wolf; to man he is not a man.<-

Marsilio Ficino to Jacopo Bracciolini <note>Jacopo Bracciolini (1442–1478) was a scholar and the son of the famous humanist Poggio Bracciolini; he was a member of Ficino's Platonic Academy</note>, a most learned man, sends greetings.

<margin>t</margin> A wolf is a sad thing for the stables. A little fox is a sad thing for the chicks in the hen-house <note>original: "Triste lupus stabulis... vulpecula pullis." This is an adaptation of a line from Virgil’s Eclogues (3.80), where nature’s threats are listed</note>. But more sad to men is man. For to men, man is both a lion and a wolf and a fox: just as he is the best of animals—if such a one is ever found—the best man; so the worst animal is the worst man. He is most prudent, my Bracciolini, who is most cautious. Most cautious of all is he who diligently guards against man. But here there is need for a Lynx and an Oedipus; here there is need for an Argus <note>Ficino cites three figures of legendary sight or insight: the Lynx for its piercing eyes, Oedipus for solving the riddle of the Sphinx, and Argus Panoptes, the hundred-eyed giant of Greek myth</note>. Only he will hold the nature and counsel of man who will always remember that it can be grasped either by no means, or certainly rarely and with the greatest difficulty.

->God never gave everything to anyone.<-

Marsilio Ficino speaks the knowledge of self to a fastidious man.

<margin>v</margin> Therefore, no one pleases you in every respect: this one is indeed sharp, but light and irritable. That one is grave, but either slower or puffed up with pride. This one is learned but lacks self-control; that one is self-controlled but unlearned. Another offends because he seems somehow deformed or inept or filthy. Another because he is too elegant and vain. Finally, lest I try to enumerate every single thing, in every individual there is something you do not approve of. To no one ever—as it is found in the writings of Homer and Plato—has God given everything. I want you to remember that you are a man among men: and while others displease you, you also displease others. Only the First Good <note>A Neoplatonic term for God, the source of all perfection</note> is that in which there is no defect. In heavenly things <note>The stars and planets</note> indeed some defect may appear, but not evil. In these things however which are subject to the moon <note>The "sublunary" realm, referring to the Earthly world characterized by change, decay, and corruption</note>, both defect and evil are found: all things besides the First Good, since they proceed from the Good, are in some way good. But since they are not the Good itself, they either seem not entirely perfect or they seem evil. Since therefore all things are mixed, he who collects the evil from each person finally turns out the worst; but he who chooses the good becomes the best. For such a person becomes whatever kind of food he feeds upon. Fare well. And just as others bear with you, bear with others.

# BOOK

...[Nature] gave us an instrument: namely, the faculty of speaking. Certainly, she warned us to use the service of learning so much more often than the gift of teaching, just as she handed down more instruments for learning <note>Referring to having two ears and two eyes but only one mouth</note> than for teaching. Therefore, no one who is wordy and talkative can be wise. For such a person has always taught, but has never truly learned. Furthermore, whoever lacks wisdom and letters is to be judged not only poor, but even blind and mute. I pray that you be swift and diligent in hearing and seeing; but slow to believe, slower to judge, and slowest of all to speak. So that you may be able to speak good things, hear good things; so that you may also hear good things about yourself, you also should speak well of others. For it cannot happen that he who speaks ill of others does not hear ill of himself. Moreover, in speaking, beware of a lie no less than a navigator avoids a reef. For the light of truth is immense, and its power is immense. It quickly detects a lie and betrays the liar. Remember that flattery is a slavish vice—indeed, even much viler than a slave's. For no one can flatter so aptly that he is not far surpassed by little dogs. Remember, moreover, that a rash or rigid rebuke is either dangerous or utterly useless. Our Plato <note>Ficino often refers to Plato as "ours" because he was the leader of the Platonic Academy in Florence and saw Platonic thought as a precursor to Christian truth</note> commands that we either speak the truth only where we are likely to be helpful, or we keep silent. But if anyone should be a disciple of the Apostle Paul <note>Saint Paul, whose writings Ficino frequently harmonized with Platonic philosophy</note> in prudence, life, and purpose, he alone will be able to persist as much out of season as in season. However, we must be entirely careful lest, while we rebuke the behavior of others with words, our own behavior meanwhile refutes our words. You have begun, as I hear; proceed well, therefore, on the path you have started. And so that you may make your journey successfully, you shall hold your horse—that is, your physical senses—and do not cease to restrain it with a bridle. <note>The horse is a classic Platonic metaphor for the passions or senses that must be steered by the rider, which represents reason.</note>

## The pursuit of revenge is nothing other than receiving an injury a second time.
### Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to a good man who is impatient with injuries.

<margin>a</margin>
You grieve at having received an injury, O friend; I grant you that indeed. But you seem to have been offended not so much because someone did something bad to you, but because you judged what he did to be "bad." To a bad person, indeed, all things, even good ones, are turned into evil. To a good person, however, all things—even those that seem the worst—are finally converted into good. You think of taking revenge: I warn you, be careful. For if you attempt to take revenge, you will suffer a second and a third injury. And in your zeal to destroy another, you destroy yourself. Even the smallest bees, when provoked by an injury, sting; and by stinging, they leave their life behind. I do not force you to forget at once. For perhaps it is worthwhile to remember, so that at least at other times you may guard yourself against malicious people. For he who has harmed once is usually never inclined to forgive. Forgive, I beg you, willingly, lest you both afflict yourself and allow him to harm you again and again. His own evils necessarily await him. For nothing does fortune leave untouched, nor does fortune leave anything unhurt, nor does God leave anything unavenged.

# BOOK THREE 94

<margin>v</margin> I see you, O friend, anxious to desire more than is fitting, handling not only your own business but even that of others, as if you had already properly settled your own affairs. Since we are deceived and wander astray at almost every moment, there is no way more suitable either for achieving tranquility or for avoiding errors than to think about a few, excellent things. To speak fewer, select words. To do very few things, and indeed only those that are as possible as they are honorable. Those who attempt to accomplish much by thinking, speaking, or doing many things err and labor greatly. But those who speak and do more than they have first thought through err most of all.

->**He whom his own craftsmanship always satisfies never satisfies Art.**<-
->Marsilio Ficino to a vain artist sends greetings.<-

<margin>s</margin> Whatever you have either said or done satisfies you greatly, O sluggish and over-busy craftsman. May I tell you the reason, with your kind permission? It is because your mind perhaps grasps nothing more than what your tongue or hands have expressed. O, what a tiny mind it is to which the tongue or hands are equal! Truly, wherever the mind—as is right—surpasses its instruments and its material, the work never satisfies the worker. Indeed, he whom his own craftsmanship <note>original: "artificium" refers to the technical execution or the specific product</note> always satisfies never satisfies Art <note>original: "arti" refers to the ideal or universal standard of excellence</note>.

->**Love is the unique guardian of life; but in order to be loved, love.**<-
->Marsilio Ficino to one seeking power over men sends greetings.<-

<margin>v</margin> Do you wish to live safe and secure? Beware that men do not fear you too much, or even see you as a threat to themselves. We have as many enemies as there are those who fear us, and as many as those who envy us. He whom many fear must of necessity fear many. He whom very many serve must also serve very many. Any subject serves one; the Master serves everyone. Love is the unique guardian of life; but in order to be loved, love.

->**The loss of money indeed seems serious; but the loss of people is the most serious of all.**<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Andrea Cambini <note>Andrea Cambini was a Florentine historian and associate of the Medici circle</note>, his excellent fellow countryman, sends greetings.<-

<margin>q</margin> What is truly remarkable in love? To not be loved in return. What is impious? To love for its own sake that which ought to be cherished for the sake of another; and conversely, to cherish for the sake of something else that which ought to be loved for its own sake. What is most shameful? To hate the one you had loved. In this we offend greatly: while we do not abandon other things, however trivial, unless compelled by a serious cause, we often both desert and even persecute a friend—that most precious treasure—induced by the slightest cause. Pythagoras <note>The ancient Greek philosopher whose followers placed a supreme value on the "harmony" of friendship</note> commands that we should not easily lose a friend for any reason whatsoever. Rather, let us endure as long as we can. And we can endure until we are forced, entirely against our will, to leave them. The loss of money indeed seems serious; but the loss of people is the most serious of all. Nothing in human affairs is either more rarely acquired, or more preciously possessed, or more unhappily [lost]...

->He should be trusted little who trusts too much.<-

## Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Salviati <note>Francesco Salviati (1443–1478) was the Archbishop of Pisa, later infamous for his role in the Pazzi conspiracy against the Medici family.</note>, Archbishop of Pisa. Greetings.

You ask, venerable father, why I trust some who live among us <margin>q</margin> so little. It is because, venerable father, these men trust too much. The logic of loving is very different from the logic of trusting; for we easily love someone a great deal who easily loves us a great deal. However, we will hardly place our trust in one who provides his faith too hastily to any man or any piece of evidence. Just as he who moves too quickly falls more quickly, so he who believes easily is easily deceived. But while it is reckless and dangerous to trust suddenly or too much in any person’s authority and words, or in some slight evidence, it seems equally dangerous and irrational to reject a probable argument without a more certain reason. Finally, it is so impious, wicked, and wretched to be unwilling to believe in God without the assertion of reason. For God is reason itself. There is no need for another reason by which we might first give our assent to Reason itself.

### On Duties <note>original: "De officiis" – Ficino invokes the title of Cicero's famous work on moral obligations, which was a cornerstone of Renaissance education.</note>

## Marsilio Ficino to Cherubino Quarquagli <note>A fellow humanist and frequent correspondent of Ficino.</note>, a most learned man. Greetings.

Although I am perhaps sometimes less dutiful <margin>e</margin> <note>original: "officiosus" – here meaning the performance of social and moral obligations</note> than is proper—as those occupied with the study of philosophy tend to be—I cannot contain myself at present from writing something about duty to a man who is the most dutiful of all. If I were as dutiful in discussing duty as you are in practicing it, neither the subtlety of Panaetius <note>A Stoic philosopher whose lost work on duty served as the primary source for Cicero.</note> nor the abundance of Cicero would be missed in this matter. I will act, therefore, with a "plain Muse" <note>original: "pingui Minerva" – a common Latin idiom meaning to speak plainly, using common sense rather than academic refinement.</note>, since I can do no other way now. And so that I may finally perform my duty, I shall send the duties of all people to the most dutiful friend of all.

Duty is the proper action of each individual, preserving what is decorous and honorable as the matter, person, place, and time require.

**The Priest's** virtue and duty is a certain wisdom burning with piety, and a piety shining with wisdom.
**The Prince's:** circumspect foresight, merciful justice, a humble highness, and a high humility.
**The Magistrate's:** to remember he is not the master of the law, but its servant, and the public guardian of the state. Furthermore, that he himself is judged by God while he judges men.
**The Private Citizen's:** to obey the commands of the magistrates so willingly that he seems led not by the compulsion of legal necessity, but by his own will.
**The Citizen's:** (whether he be a magistrate or a private person) a care for the public as diligent as his love for his own interests is great.
**The Knight's:** fortitude in war, but magnificence in peace.
**The Merchant's:** to nourish the city and himself with foreign provisions through truthful faith and diligence.
**The Artisan's:** to justly distribute the provisions received from the merchant to the individual members of the city.

Let merchants <note>The original OCR reads "Nercatores," a printer's error for "Mercatores."</note> and artisans and others seek money in such a way that they harm no one. For whatever rises from evil eventually falls back into evil. Let them save in such a way that they do not seem to save in vain, nor to have sought wealth only for the sake of saving. Let them spend in such a way that they can spend for a long time, and prove that they have spent both honorably and usefully.

<summary>Ficino discusses the dangers of excessive trust and provides a comprehensive list of moral duties for different social roles, emphasizing that God is the ultimate form of Reason.</summary>
<keywords>Marsilio Ficino, Francesco Salviati, trust, God as Reason, De Officiis, social duties, ethics, citizenship, merchant ethics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's discourse "On Duties" (De Officiis), addressed to Cherubino Quarquagli. The previous page defined the duties of priests, princes, and merchants; this page continues with farmers and moves through various familial and professional roles.</meta>

# BOOK THREE

**Farmers:** <note>original: "colæ/agricolæ"</note> they should consult the weather and elder farmers regarding the suitability of agriculture. Furthermore, they should offer the fruits of the field to their guests with as much faith and generosity as the field returns those fruits to them with interest. **Masters:** they must serve law and reason, so that they may rule over their servants legitimately and reasonably. They should consider that both servant and master are human beings. They must always mix humanity with dignity. **Servants:** they should consider their own life to belong to the master, and the master’s reason to belong to themselves. **Husbands:** they should love their wife as their own body and sense, and lead her with the greatest diligence. **Wives:** they should honor a prudent husband as their own soul and reason, and follow him most willingly. **The Father of the Family:** <note>original: "Patrisfamilias" – the head of a household who held legal and moral authority over all members.</note> he should cherish his sons as the literal offshoots of his own life, and rule them by his own best example as if they were his own limbs. **Sons:** they should follow the father as their root and head, and venerate him as a second god.

**Brothers:** they should feel toward a brother as if toward a second self. **Relatives:** they should love one another like the limbs of the very same body. **In-laws:** <note>original: "Affinium" – relatives by marriage.</note> they should remember that they are joined by law just as if by nature, so that they ought to share their wealth and their labor with one another. **Friends:** they should seek the truth through shared counsel and follow the good through shared help. **Teachers:** they should, through their own learning and goodness, produce a student who is learned and good, acting as a father to a "son of the mind." I desire to warn teachers, if I may, not to forget that Aristotle "kicked back" <note>original: "recalcitrasse" – a famous metaphor for Aristotle's intellectual rebellion against his teacher, Plato.</note> against the divine Plato.

**Students:** they should honor the teacher as a father of the intellect. However, they must take care not to secretly drink in the teacher's vices. **Legal Experts:** <note>original: "Iurisconsulti"</note> such a man should be the most serious of all people and should know that he who corrupts the sacred law should be punished with a harsher judgment than one who counterfeits money. **Doctors:** when approaching the sick, they should reflect that a life is at stake; they should dare to attempt nothing without reason, and nothing without consultation. **Orators:** they should already be persuaded themselves of the things they intend to persuade others of. **Poets:** so that they might be able to paint nature and character, they should have observed both. **Musicians:** they should imitate grace in sound, and in song they should imitate the elegance of speech. They must also remember that the movements of the soul ought to be much more harmonious than the voices. For a musician is out of tune and a stranger to the Muses if his mind is in discord while his voice and lyre are in harmony. David and Mercury <note>The biblical King David and the Greek god Hermes/Mercury were both associated with the creation of sacred music and the lyre.</note> command that, since we sing because God moves us, we should also sing *of* God. **The Philosopher:** he should seek divine things more diligently so that he may enjoy them; he should also examine natural things so that he may use them. He should be present for human affairs but not entangled in them. A singular philosopher is not compelled by Plato or Aristippus <note>Aristippus of Cyrene (c. 435–356 BCE) was a pupil of Socrates who favored a more worldly, hedonistic approach, contrasting with Plato's idealism.</note> to undergo the dangers of life for a homeland that is not his "true" one; this is pleasing to me as well, because a philosopher becomes a philosopher in spite of, and even against the resistance of, the city in which he is born. He is a son of heaven, not of earth. Add to this that it seems altogether impious and wretched for a man who sees all things to lose his life for the safety of the blind, who perhaps can never be saved anyway. **A man** should take care that he is not in any way womanly. **A woman** should strive to be, in a certain sense, manly, but above all modest. For as much as magnanimity <note>original: "magnanimitas" – greatness of soul or courage.</note> becomes a man, so much does modesty/chastity become a woman. **The Elder:** he should see to it that he is not childish; he should remember that he was once young. **The Youth:** he should take care to be like [the elders]; he should believe that he too can grow old, and he should honor his seniors. **The Native Citizen:** it is his duty to cherish the fatherland as a father, and the mother-city as a mother; and when dealing with foreigners...

...should act: and consider that he will one day go on a journey. <note>original: "peregrinaturum" – suggesting the transitory nature of life as a pilgrimage or travel away from one's true home.</note> **Inhabitants and foreigners:** they should know that they are alone; they should honor everyone. For we see the spring return the leaves to the trees which winter took away. **Man:** let him consider that since he can never live contentedly on earth, he is indeed a citizen of heaven, and merely a dweller on earth; let him think, speak, or do nothing that would seem unbecoming of a citizen of that heavenly fatherland.

He who is established at the peak never falls to the lowest depths if he looks down upon those depths both sharply and mercifully.

<margin>d</margin>While I was writing a certain philosophical letter regarding duties <note>original: "de officiis"</note> to our friend Cherubino Quarquagli, Cherubino himself—a man who is exceptionally dutiful <note>original: "officiosus" – Ficino is making a pun: the "dutiful" man arrived while Ficino was writing about "duty."</note>—stood over my shoulder unexpectedly. Behold, venerable father, a saving messenger bids Marsilio greetings again and again in your sacred name. Your messenger greeted us today with such good omens that he did not merely announce future health, but actually bestowed it. <note>The Latin "salus" means both "health" and "greetings."</note> Greetings, then, O my health! Greetings always under God, the eternal author of all health. You seem to me, indeed, to surpass Argus <note>A giant from Greek mythology with a hundred eyes.</note> in your eyes and the lynx in your vision (if I may put it that way), for you, being so sublime yourself, have looked upon Marsilio from so far off—Marsilio, who is so humble and so tiny. Would that, venerable father, you might see me as clearly as you perceive all things. Then I would be as well known to everyone as all things are known to you. But so that you and everyone else may see me clearly, I pray that you look upon me favorably, as you have already begun to do. For the astrologers say that through the benign aspect <note>A technical term in astrology referring to the favorable alignment of planets.</note> of a saving star, men are born fortunate and become illustrious. What thanks can I return for such a great favor? I have nothing else at present, except that after the duties of various individuals which I have described step-by-step according to my ability, I might add this: It is also the duty of Marsilio Ficino to love the Cardinal of Pavia ardently, as if he were a temple of the Graces, and to venerate him uniquely as a fountain of the Muses. And once I have performed this one duty, I shall consider that I have handled the subject of "duties" most dutifully. Furthermore, if you have ever heard anything from your high position regarding this lowly little man, you have heard this one thing above all: that Marsilio Ficino is the oldest foster-child of the Medici house. Therefore, the Medici—both Castor and Pollux, <note>A reference to the brothers Lorenzo and Giuliano de' Medici, likening them to the inseparable divine twins of mythology.</note> my patrons—humbly commend me to you. And they believe that as long as I am commended to the Cardinal of Pavia, I am commended to all great, upright, and learned men. February 8, 1476. Our Christopher Landino, <note>Cristoforo Landino (1424–1498), a leading humanist scholar and teacher in Florence.</note> a man of singular learning and goodness, commends himself to you.

<meta>This page continues the correspondence of Marsilio Ficino, transitioning from general moral advice to specific letters addressed to his inner circle, including the Florentine aristocrat Piero del Nero and Cardinal Jacopo Ammannati Piccolomini. <header>THIRD BOOK 96</header>

The difficulty of life follows the ease of vice. The ease of life follows the difficulty of virtue.

### Marsilio Ficino to Peter Nero, a most brilliant man. Greetings.

How much more difficult it is to walk by a certain reason than to wander by chance; to ascend than to descend. To attempt new things than to handle the familiar. To reach only the middle point of a circle than to run into any of the other points, which are innumerable. To strike the target <note>original: "scopon" — from the Greek 'skopos', meaning a mark or target for an archer.</note> itself—that is, the mark—with an arrow, than to hit the things that surround it. To keep to the path and the furrow than to transgress here and there. To hold a perfectly straight line <term>examussim: a mason’s rule or level used to ensure absolute straightness</term> than to slip into the oblique—by that much more is it difficult to act rightly than to sin, and to be good than to be evil. Indeed, the evidence of this matter is that we all err daily. However, rarely and few of us act honestly and justly.

Nevertheless, the divine law pays back two benefits for this difficulty of virtue. First, that the virtues are so connected to one another that he who attains one also attains them all. Vices, on the contrary, are so repugnant to each other that they cannot all exist in the same person at the same time. For in what way can someone be greedy and profligate at once? Or more bold and more timid? Second, that after that first difficulty of birthing virtue, a supreme ease and pleasure of life follows. And after a brief struggle, an eternal reward. 

But from the ease of vice, a miserable difficulty of life soon follows, and perpetual pain. Hence that Pythagorean symbol: *Do not touch an animal with a black tail.* <note>original: "Animal cauda nigra ne tangas." This is one of the "Symbola" of Pythagoras, which Ficino interprets allegorically.</note> This means: flee vice, which is followed by the blackness of the mind and the affliction of the will. Farewell, most brilliant Nero; and since you have already attained virtue through difficulty, and ease of life through virtue, so that you may achieve happiness from there, remember it is as arduous and as laborious to retrace one's steps from the vast precipice of vices and to escape to the upper air <note>A reference to Virgil's Aeneid, Book VI: "revocare gradus superasque evadere ad auras," describing the difficulty of returning from the Underworld.</note> that no one is able to ascend here unless he whom impartial Jupiter has loved, and whom burning virtue has carried from there to the heavens.

Just as beauty naturally begets love, so love, through opinion, regenerates beauty.

### Marsilio Ficino humbly commends himself to James, Cardinal of Pavia.

At the very moment when Cherubino Quarquagli <note>A poet and friend of Ficino.</note> greeted me in your name these past days, almost at that same moment, that letter of ours flew to you. For the most ardent affection of the heart, suddenly kindled by the rays and flames of your name, drove my hand to write before my mind could dictate what I was chiefly going to write. So it is no wonder if what we wrote so very quickly seems quite light. The logic of nature is one thing; the logic of speech is another. To be sure, in nature, those things which are lighter are also swifter. In speech, however, it is the opposite: that which is swifter is lighter. But remember, venerable father—I know what I am saying—that you recently received a letter from me that was the daughter not of counsel, but of love. Since, truly, I know you...

...be hidden: in no other way should anything that is sent be received. I believe you received it not so much by counsel as by love. Especially since you created it from the beginning with a certain immense love for me. Water gave birth to fish. Water catches them. A plant grows in the same moisture from which it sprouted. Our letter was born long ago from love. Your love, which created it, embraces it. In embracing it, it nourishes it wonderfully; in nourishing it, it regenerates its beauty for itself. Truly, just as beauty naturally gives birth to love, so love, in turn, through opinion, creates real beauty. But by what means do you think the writings of Marsilio were read with love rather than counsel by that man who is himself, so to speak, counsel itself? Because, clearly, if he is counsel itself, he is also love itself. As much as he looks into the things brought to him with the rays of his mind, so much does he penetrate them everywhere with the flames of his heart; however sharply and acutely he perceives, he always interprets just as sweetly and kindly. Just as cold accompanies darkness, so heat everywhere follows light. Again, sweetness follows heat surrounded by sharp flavor. In nature, sweetness overcomes what is perfected by heat; among men perfected in virtue, indulgence overcomes the judgment of severity. Hail, therefore, my counsel <note>original: "consilium" — Ficino often personifies abstract qualities like Counsel or Love when addressing his close friends.</note>. Hail again, my love. I pray you, consult your Marsilio freely where there is need; everywhere love your Marsilio. Consult him as an oracle in weightier matters; in every single thing, he will be venerated. February 19, 1476.

Not because I think there is need for these words for the pious—for he abounds in pious works—nor for this kind of faith of mine for a man who is strong in knowledge. <header>THE THIRD BOOK CXVII</header>

...there is a certain little Lenten declamation <note>original: "declamatiuncula... quadragesimalis" — a short rhetorical exercise or sermon intended for the forty days of Lent</note>, suited, perhaps, to these days. I only wish it would seem as elegant and mature <note>original: "compta barbataque" — literally "combed and bearded," a metaphor for something well-groomed and adult or serious</note> to you as you appear to me, beautiful both within and on the surface. How much more hideous is deformity in the face than in the hand, and a disease in the heart more pestilential than in the feet? So much more abominable and foul is the vileness and sickness in the souls of the impious and shameful than all the deformity and plague of all bodies. If we could see with our eyes or truly conceive in our mind the filthy and horrific image of a wicked soul, we would certainly sin very rarely and lightly; we would flee nothing more distantly than the sight of a bad mind. The comparison of the soul's beauty to the body's beauty is almost the same. For if that soul were seen, even for a moment, by the eyes or the mind, it would allure far more charmingly, seize more rapaciously, and delight more vehemently. Happy lovers! How much the singular appearance of the body makes lovers lost and wretched! Why did the wise men inscribe "Know thyself" <note>original: "nosce teipsum" — the famous Greek maxim from the Temple of Apollo at Delphi</note> on the temple of Apollo? Unless it was so that you might look up at the pure mind, as if at a ray of the true Phoebus <note>Phoebus is another name for Apollo, the sun god</note>, that is, the eternal ray of the super-celestial sun, surrounded by the cloud of the body. And so you may recognize that the brightness of the cloud comes from the ray, and the splendor of the ray depends on the sun. So that you may praise the body in the soul, but honor the soul in the body. Again, you should love and cherish the soul in God. Indeed, love and venerate God in the soul, but marvel and be astounded at Him in Himself. When our leader and teacher, Aurelius Augustine, had known himself and God in himself, he immediately exclaimed: "Late have I loved you, beauty so old and so new; late have I loved you" <note>original: "Sero te amavi pulcritudo tam antiqua et tam nova" — a celebrated passage from St. Augustine's Confessions</note>.

->Nothing is baser than he in whose possession everything is beautiful except the soul.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to the Human Race, sends greetings.<-

<margin>S</margin>
If any farmer, not only without any reward but even with his own greatest loss, should cultivate the fields of others while neglecting his own, he would undoubtedly be judged by everyone as most foolish and wretched. Therefore, those minds are excessively insane <term>insane: "dementes," literally "out of one's mind"</term> and miserable, which always spend all their effort on this: that the body and external things are kept in the best and most adorned state. But they utterly neglect that they themselves should be good and adorned. Oh, how bad is the man whose dog and horse are better than his soul! Oh, how hideous is he whose shoe, as much as it is in his power, is more beautiful than his soul! Nothing is truly good or beautiful to this man, in whose view everything besides himself—that is, besides his soul—seems good and beautiful. If some Cynic philosopher <note>An allusion to Diogenes the Cynic, who famously spat in a rich man's face because it was the only "dirty" place he could find in an otherwise spotless house</note> should enter such a man's highly decorated house and be compelled by some necessity to spit, he would certainly spit in the man's face. Because, clearly, he would see every single thing there clean and adorned except the man himself. Nothing is poorer and emptier than he whose granaries are full but whose soul is empty. We are accustomed to calling those who are positioned outside their mind "demented." But in what way can a soul be in a "demented" person, when for a long time it has been in the cooking pots? <note>original: "in patinis" — a classical idiom for being obsessed with gluttony and physical pleasure</note> Tell me, I pray, you unhappy mind, so curious about the things of others and so negligent of your own, tell me, I say. To whom...

<header>BOOK</header>

...for all things are healthy to men, unless they are not healthy themselves. Why then, out of your mind, do you wander so anxiously here and there outside yourself? And why do you labor so much and so much in vain? See to it that you are good and beautiful. Suddenly, all things will be good and beautiful to you. But truly, you will only achieve what I command if you desire to emerge as good and beautiful as much as you strive for even your smallest furnishings to be the best and to appear most ornate. If, while we feed the body and dogs and birds, we did not meanwhile let the man himself—that is, the soul—perish from hunger, surely everyone would live as contented and full as now no one lives contented. Indeed, to whom should it be a wonder if the soul is never filled, if it is always afflicted, when it deserts itself and its only care is to fill its beast <note>The "beast" refers to the physical body or the lower sensory appetites in Platonic philosophy.</note>? A beast which, in its very satiety, is continually more gluttonous; and, because of the master's negligence, it grows more savage and robust against its master, who is left utterly starving and bloodless.

To the wicked, indeed, good fortune is bad. But to the good, bad fortune is likewise good. To Cherubino Quanquaglio <note>A contemporary of Ficino, likely a student or associate to whom this aphorism was directed.</note>.

## Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Bernardo Bembo, the most illustrious Venetian knight, sends greetings <note>original: "S D" — abbreviation for "Salutem Dicit," a standard Latin epistolary greeting.</note>.

Tell me, steadfast man, for what reason Fortune hates and often suppresses the one whom the people rightly love? On the contrary, she more often loves and exalts the one whom the people, with some justice, hate. Is it perhaps because Fortune is not only opposed to reason, but has even been an enemy to the people from the very beginning of the world? Whence the people are always unfortunate and wretched. Perhaps she is also ambitious; so that any great deed we do may be ascribed not to the virtue or favor of men, but to her alone, she exalts in miraculous ways the one whom many men rightly wish to see brought low. But the one who is sublime, she casts down into the depths. What if she is blind, as they say, or a rival of nature? For Nature ordained that you live first as an animal before you live as a human. You feel before you understand. If Fortune affects to make some man great, she first makes him a huge beast, swollen with poisonous disdain. Whence a tyrant is born in character and countenance before he gains power over a tyranny. These men, established in dignities <note>term: dignities <gloss>high offices or positions of honor</gloss></note> beyond their worth, ensure that those dignities themselves are no longer worthy of upright men. They also cause it to be believed that neither divine providence rules the world, nor human prudence guides the human race, but rather chance. Yet divine providence sometimes suddenly hurls others down from the highest summit to the lowest depths against every favor of fortune. Others, against the malignant impulse of fortune, it wonderfully raises to the heights. If it allows the proud to stand for long or the humane to fall for a time, it also permits those proud ones to have a mind as dejected and wretched as their fortune is high; and those humane ones to have a mind as exalted as their fortune is humble and abject. To the wicked, indeed, good fortune becomes bad. But to the good, bad fortune becomes good. Indeed, if the choice were given to me, I would rather be Hercules than Sardanapalus <note>Hercules represents the virtuous hero who earns divinity through labor, while Sardanapalus was a legendary Syrian king synonymous with extreme luxury and decadence.</note>. As many monsters as the one crushed, so many was the other oppressed by; the one, having overcome wild beasts, emerged as a god; the other, overcome by beasts, was made a beast...

...more base and more wretched. Where there is the most wisdom, there is the least need for chance; where there is the least wisdom, chance dominates the most. And even if fortune sometimes joins itself to wisdom, they do not rule together at the same time. For either chance is by no means joined to reason, or it serves it. Wherefore chance, envious of upright men, resists them with all its strength, lest upright reason should rule everywhere—inasmuch as if reason were to rule, chance would lose both its glory and its empire. Chance often richly endows one whom nature or virtue has endowed little. Nor does it easily enrich those whom nature or virtue has consecrated. In certain ages, there are some great and powerful men, as if they were human gods and divine men; but they are rarer than phoenixes <note>The phoenix was a mythical bird that lived for centuries before being reborn from its own ashes; Ficino uses it here to mean something exceptionally rare.</note>, those whom not fortune, but divine providence makes great. These are distinguished by a certain sign: for they are such that they attribute nothing of their prosperity to luck, and very little to human virtue, but to divine virtue as much as possible. And they are as humane in their countenance toward all as they are divine in their mind above all others. If there is no health where there is swelling <note>original: "inflatio" — Ficino uses a medical metaphor; "inflatio" refers both to physical swelling and to the "puffing up" of pride.</note>, then certainly no one who is "swollen" with pride is not also insane. We cannot bear anyone who is both insane and supposedly sane at once. No one is divine who is not also humane. No one is most humane who is not also divine. A truly divine man certainly does not want fortune as his leader. For she is blind and often falls by accident. He does not rejoice in the promises of fortune, for she is unfaithful even to those whom she has raised to the highest peak of dignity beyond their merit. Truly, she delights in a reciprocal game between the highest and the lowest, and is pleased by alternating turns. The wise man does not fear the threats of fortune, for they are empty. Nor can she do anything more within us than what we allow ourselves to be capable of: "It is we, O Fortune, who make you a goddess and place you in heaven" <note>This is a paraphrase of a famous line by the Roman satirist Juvenal, suggesting that "Fortune" only has power because humans attribute power to her.</note>. No one is more wretched than he who places true happiness in fortune. No one is more fortunate than he who judges that accidental prosperity is not, in truth, happiness. He who either laughs at the ridiculous weeping of fortune along with Democritus, or weeps at her mournful laughter along with Heraclitus <note>Democritus and Heraclitus were known in the Renaissance as the "Laughing Philosopher" and the "Weeping Philosopher," representing two different but equally wise reactions to the absurdity of human life.</note>, is judged prudent by Hippocrates. He who tramples upon the childish game of fortune with Socrates is judged wise and divine by Apollonius. Finally, he who endures through hardships with Aeneas is the only one who, with Aeneas, preserves himself for favorable times. He looks up at the clear days after the rains, and at last possesses his longed-for Italy <note>Aeneas is the hero of Virgil's *Aeneid*; "Italy" here represents the final goal or state of peace achieved after long suffering.</note>. Therefore, my Aeneas: do not yield to evils, but go forth more boldly against them. Whatever it will be, every fortune must be overcome by enduring <note>original: "Quicquid erit superanda omnis fortuna ferendo" — a famous quote from Virgil's *Aeneid* (5.710).</note>. Farewell more joyfully, my Aeneas <note>Ficino is addressing his correspondent, Bernardo Bembo, as "Aeneas" to cast him as a heroic figure enduring the storms of political life.</note>: for you will one day enjoy as many good things, secure in the harbor, as the storms you have bravely overcome at sea.

->The soul of mortals is not filled because it seeks eternal things.<-

## Marsilio Ficino to Lorenzo de' Medici, the magnanimous man, sends greetings <note>original: "S. D." — abbreviation for *Salutem Dicit*.</note>.

If I were to recite to you now a certain little Lenten declamation, Lorenzo, which my mind declaimed to me this very dawn: behold, what would be the value of it? Perhaps only to move you to as much laughter at my silliness in the present moment as the most skillful preachers these days draw tears from the common people. I will recite it, however, as it seems right to me, Lorenzo. For I know that a man distinguished by piety—although he might perhaps occasionally laugh at words of piety—cannot, in truth, deride piety itself.
