<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s philosophical correspondence. The previous page concluded a letter to Bernardo Bembo about the struggle between reason and fortune. Here, Ficino uses the metaphor of thirst and the myth of Tantalus to explain why the human soul can never be satisfied by material things, concluding with a new letter to Francesco Guasconio regarding his work on the Christian religion.</meta>

# BOOK THREE

He who thirsts for Marsilio’s wine quenches his thirst, as you see, with wine. And even more so if he should drink two cups rather than one. To such a man, the image of wine—whether seen or thought of—incites rather than settles his thirst. For it is the nature of an image to entice, but the nature of a substance to nourish. Therefore, an image of wine nourishes thirst just as much as wine itself nourishes a thirsty man. Indeed, the punishment of Tantalus <note>In Greek mythology, Tantalus was punished in the underworld by being placed in a pool of water with fruit hanging above him, both of which receded whenever he tried to drink or eat.</note> reveals this to us. Or rather, our own punishment reveals it to us, for we are all Tantali. Indeed, we all thirst for true goods. We all drink in dreams. While we gulp down the lethal waves of the river Lethe <note>original: "lætei fluminis" — the river of forgetfulness in the underworld; Ficino suggests that by "drinking" from the material world, we forget our divine origin.</note> with full throats, we meanwhile lick a certain shadow-like droplet of nectar and ambrosia <note>The food and drink of the gods, granting immortality.</note> with the tips of our lips. From this, a gasping thirst continually overwhelms us wretched Tantali. If we were to take possession of such things as the mind naturally grasps, then certainly by possessing them the soul would at some point be filled, either entirely or for the most part. Since, however, the more we possess mortal things everywhere, the more the appetite of the soul is inflamed, it is sufficiently clear that the mind seeks not mortal things—which are but images of the eternal—but the eternal things themselves. Therefore, the soul is eternal and not perishable, since its true nourishment is eternal. Consequently, in a perishable body, the soul sleeps deeply and is sickly. In this state, drinking in dreams through the senses, it nourishes its thirst by drinking, rather than nourishing itself. Sickly also because of its passions, the wretched soul is never at rest. But in vain it wanders, restless, in every direction. Where it trusts it might lie down softly, it falls deeply. Where it hopes for a more healthful medicine, it drains a more deadly poison. O, wretched lot of mortals! A lot more wretched than misery itself. Where shall we poor wretches flee? Surely nowhere, unless we flee from the lowest things to the highest. Unless we flee to those things that never flee from us? What, then, must be done so that we may be both awake and well? Our life must first be turned in the opposite direction. We must unlearn what we have learned from the common crowd—by learning which we have, until now, remained ignorant of ourselves. We must learn what we have neglected; for while these things are unknown, we cannot know ourselves. We must love what we neglect. What we love, we must neglect. We must bear what we flee. What we pursue, we must flee. We must weep at the smile of fortune. The weeping of fortune must be laughed at. For in this way, neither the filth of the common crowd will defile us, nor will the neglect of the immortals harm us, nor the curiosity of mortals torment us. Neither shall softness cast us down, nor pleasure dissolve us. Fortune will not ensnare us when prosperous, nor kill us when adverse. But to the extent that we are purified, we shall be serene; and as much as we are serene, we shall be radiant. Then at last we emerge full of true forms <note>A reference to the Platonic "Forms" or Ideas, the perfect realities behind the physical world.</note> when first we are emptied of dreams.

->It is not the husk that nourishes, but the marrow.<-

## Things that are truly good are even better the greater they are.
## Marsilio Ficino to Lorenzo Bonincontri, astronomer and poet. Greetings.

<margin>d</margin> I cannot say, most illustrious Lorenzo, with what great pleasure I was moved upon reading your letter. In it, I certainly find nothing to blame less than that which you yourself excuse the most. But what did I just say, my Lorenzo? Rather, I blame nothing, since every single detail pleases me exceedingly. Therefore, to speak more correctly: nothing in your letter pleases me more than that which you perhaps suspect would please me less—I mean your prolixity, or rather, your sobriety. For those things which are truly good are even better the greater they are. You submit to us a most serious judgment between three divine powers: namely, Providence, Fate, and Liberty. <note>term: Liberty (libertas) — In this philosophical context, Ficino refers to human free will.</note> You have heard that once, in the presence of Paris, a judgment between three goddesses was proposed. But I would not wish to offend such great powers with such a distinction. "Stored deep in my mind remains the judgment of Paris and the insult to her scorned beauty." <note>original: "Manet alta mente repoſtum iudiciū paridis ſpretæqȝ iniuria formæ" — A quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (1.26–27), referring to the goddess Juno’s lingering resentment after the Trojan prince Paris chose Venus as the most beautiful over her. Ficino uses it here to jokingly explain why he avoids "judging" between different divine concepts.</note> Perhaps, however, no further danger remains. You yourself seem to have delivered a most cautious opinion regarding these matters. For you did not foolishly separate these divine powers, as some are accustomed to do, but joined them together most fittingly. We shall confirm your opinion more extensively in our book *On the Astrologers*. <note>Ficino refers to his work *Disputatio contra iudicium astrologorum*, where he argued that while the stars (Fate) influence the body, the human soul remains free under God (Providence).</note>

## Many cannot be firmly joined together in a thing that is itself mutable and diverse.
## Marsilio Ficino to Lotterio Neroni, his fellow philosopher. Greetings.

<margin>a</margin> I embrace your learned and pious letter, Lotterio, with a certain supreme joy. Especially in that part where you kindly embrace me in that Good which encompasses all things. You have often read that Peripatetic <note>term: Peripatetic — Referring to the followers of Aristotle, who famously taught while walking about the Lyceum.</note> principle: "Whatever things are the same as some third thing, are also the same as each other." But this seems to me to be fulfilled only when that third thing is entirely the same as itself; that is, when it is individual, simple, and permanent. Otherwise, it could not join to one another those things which return to it, nor could it first make them firm. But let us explain what we mean with a clear example. As long as lines remain in an indivisible and immobile center, they each consist within themselves as indivisible and immobile, and they are either entirely the same or joined to one another. But when they are drawn out from the center toward a divisible and mobile circumference, they gradually become more and more divided and mutable within themselves. Then they are rendered disjoined from one another. But if, in turn, they are folded back from that circumference into the center again, they will immediately be seen to recover their former unity and stability. Indeed, we ought to consider God in the center; the heavens and the elements in the circumference; and finally, souls and minds in the lines. Therefore, when the common people boast daily of a false benevolence: "I have already been entirely yours for a long time," says one. This other says in turn, "I shall always be yours." That one again dares to say: "You and I are first one and the same thing."

...men are fallible. Indeed, while they fall away from the stable unity of God and immerse themselves entirely in the changing, multifaceted, and divisible mechanism of the world, they lose their inherent stability and unity. Yet, in their madness, they shamelessly and foolishly promise to others that stability which they themselves have miserably lost. Therefore, let them stop professing mutual benevolence to one another: for one cannot become or remain "the same" <note>Ficino plays on the idea that true friendship requires two people to become "one" in spirit, which is impossible without God's unity.</note> as long as those who love are not the same [stable] people they boast to be, and as long as they love a thing that is itself unstable. Nothing ever gathers or steadies souls for themselves and others except unity itself—simple, immobile eternity, which most closely embraces all things as its own. In this unity, I most gladly embrace you, my Lotterio, who in turn most kindly embrace me.

### Marsilio Ficino to Domenico Galletti. Greetings.

If the love for you that daily spurs me to write, my dear Domenico, were matched by the inspiration provided by Maria's Muse <note>original: "musa mariae" — This likely refers to a specific source of poetic inspiration or a member of their intellectual circle.</note>, you would certainly read my greetings as often as you yourself wish to be well. But the subject matter that the envious Muse has long denied us is now provided by Giovanni Cavalcanti, <margin>s</margin> that sweet pupil of the Muses. He admits he owes you much because of our friendship, for I—having loved you first as the elder friend—learned from that experience how to love him ardently and steadily. Indeed, if my love were as powerful as it is great, you in turn would realize how much you owe Cavalcanti. Since he appears to us everywhere as your very image and is most loving of you, he ensures that in loving him, I do not forget how to love Domenico. 

Therefore, for Cavalcanti’s sake, that God <note>referring to Love/Cupid</note> commends him to you—the God without whom nothing is ever commended either quickly or successfully. Heavenly Cupid, whose soldier you yourself often are, often persuades before he even urges. He persuades much more vehemently even by remaining silent than Mercury does by speaking or Phoebus himself by singing. Why is this a wonder? For those others pour flying words into the ears at the gates of the soul. But he, within, brands the indelible marks of burning thoughts upon the heart itself. But I leave these amorous matters of the poet to you. I come to the matter common to our Giovanni and ourselves.

->THE END.<-

### The Fourth Book of the Epistles of Marsilio Ficino the Florentine.

> There is no one who can be envied by one who can see how much we are all agitated by furies, within and without. <note>original: "furiis" — In Ficino’s view, "furies" are the irrational passions and anxieties that disturb the human soul.</note>

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Lorenzo Francesco, son of Domenico, sends greetings.<-

<margin>m</margin>Pythagoras commanded his disciples not to eat the brain or the heart. That is, they should neither consume the brain with superfluous thoughts, nor burn the heart with immoderate cares. If all things happen by fortune <term>fortuna</term> <note>Ficino uses "fortune" to refer to seemingly random or accidental events.</note>, then those who trust they can fully define and arrange through certain reason things that occur beyond reason in innumerable ways labor in vain. If all things come by fate <term>fatum</term> <note>Fate refers to the fixed, inevitable chain of worldly causes.</note>, then whoever strives to avoid its inevitable necessity falls even more heavily into fate itself, for they add their own labor to the burden of fate. Finally, whether our affairs are said to proceed by fortune or by fate, divine providence <term>providentia</term> <note>The highest governing principle in Ficino’s philosophy, which directs all things toward the Good.</note> arranges irrational fortune into an orderly system through reason; it also most sweetly tempers harsh fate toward the good, so that all things turn out well and in double order for those who willingly consent to the divine will. For these people alone, internal and external things are in harmony. For all others, however, both are everywhere in discord. These [who follow God] alone make what is necessary into what is voluntary; what seems evil, they make good. Just as a pure mind rejoices in the universal good, so an impure mind is afflicted by all evils. Just as the greatest light draws all lights to itself, so the greatest evil on earth—that is, a bad man—draws all evils to himself from every side. And he inflicts much more upon himself than he receives from elsewhere. 

Just as we are insatiable for the good, so, in some unknown way, we are almost insatiable for evil. We do not so much feel present evils as we augment them; we repeat past ones and we anticipate future ones. We even invent those that will never be. I pass over the fact that we endure adverse things with a perverse mind; do we not also so abuse prosperity that our very happiness becomes most unhappy for us? The success of external things is nothing other than the excess of reason and law. And what is health of the body for us if not the insanity of the mind? Often, the beauty and strength of the body become the deformity and weakness of the soul. Oh, how deformed we are whenever we ourselves, in our deformity, rush into those things which God makes beautiful! Alas, how ungrateful we are to God, the giver of all goods, whenever we condemn the governance of his works. And the more our granaries abound with his good harvests, the more we produce thorns and weeds <note>original: "loliũ" — darnel or cockle, a common weed in wheat fields.</note> within ourselves, sowing them at home and abroad. And while we produce and bear evils, we are nevertheless surprised if we ever reap the worst from them; we do not blame our own cultivation, but rather the stars or God. There is no one, therefore, who can be envied by one who can see how much we are all agitated by furies, within and without. You could hardly discern who among others is happier in their homeland; it is even more difficult to discern who is more miserable abroad. The condition is nearly equal in both places. There, individuals rejoice to the utmost; here, we individuals grieve to the utmost. So that, unless we are altogether blind, we ought to see clearly from this: since our sowing is in such a poor state...

<summary>Ficino opens his fourth book of letters with a moral exhortation to Lorenzo Francesco, arguing that human misery stems from resisting the divine will and mismanaging the soul's internal state through excessive worry or "furies." He explains that Divine Providence harmonizes the chaos of Fortune and the necessity of Fate for those who align themselves with God.</summary>

->When you have satisfied reason and counsel, consider yourself to have satisfied all.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to his fellow philosopher.

<margin>t</margin>You are much disturbed, as I hear, because those things which you understand you have done with sound reason <term>ratio</term> <note>Ficino uses "ratio" to mean both the human faculty of logic and the underlying divine order of the universe.</note> are condemned by many. Do you hold yourself in such high esteem, my friend, that you wish those who do not spare even God to spare a man? What can be done that is more beautiful or better than those things which are done by God, who is the highest Reason? Yet divine works are slandered everywhere. We shudder at demons. We accuse the stars. We condemn the times. We even revile the forms and powers of plants and animals. We carp at men. We complain incessantly about our lot: those things which we have received so freely displease us, while those things which we ourselves have done ungratefully please us to such an extent that we displease God. 

Strive, I pray, that just as your new works suddenly charm you as if they were your own offspring, you may likewise obey reason and submit to your own counsel. Truly, after you have satisfied diligent reason and the approved counsel of the wise, consider yourself to have satisfied all men. For in this way, you have satisfied Truth itself, which is greater than all. But if those things which you have thought, said, or done by such reason are still disapproved of in some places, remember that it is a sign of good food to be displeasing to a bad palate. Moreover, it is proof of a bad thing to please a bad palate. Farewell; and once your will has followed right reason, do not be disturbed if anything happens thereafter contrary to your will.

->He is wise in vain who is not wise for himself.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to a moral philosopher who lacks morals, sends greetings.

<margin>q</margin>How absurd is a shoemaker with a garment torn everywhere; how useless is a doctor who is always sick; how annoying is a musician whose lyre is out of tune with his voice. Just so shameful is a moral philosopher without morals <note>original: "non moratus" — a play on words; a moral philosopher who does not practice the "mores" (morals/customs) he teaches.</note>. He indeed speaks well, but acts badly: such a man speaks good things in vain either to men who do not believe him, or seeks good things from the powers above who will not grant them.

->The medicine for worldly evils is the worship of the God above the world.<-

### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Bernardo Bembo, the most distinguished Venetian knight, sends greetings.

<margin>q</margin>Since the celestial Father of mankind has ordained that our homeland should be heaven, for that reason, while we inhabit the earth—a region most remote from our homeland—we can never be fully content. Moreover, a lot of this kind is common not only to men but indeed to all created things: they never find rest except in their own origin. And for the sake of rest, they strive to place their end where they had their beginning. Thus water and earth descend to the depths. Fire and air seek the heights. Thus moles and similar creatures hide themselves in the belly of the earth. Many others tread upon the back of the earth. Fish, born in water, swim in water. But the souls of men, by a certain common and natural instinct, continually yearn for heaven. And bey... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; "And beyond..." likely leading into a discussion on the soul's immortality or its ascent.</note>

# BOOK FOUR

...of the king of heaven from whom they are created. Since, truly, the natural appetite for God infused in us by God must not be in vain—lest the highest reason, which does nothing in vain, should have infused it in us in vain—it follows that the minds of men are eternal so that they might one day be able to reach the eternal and divine good desired by nature. From these things we have said, it follows that souls—since they are never filled by earthly nourishments, nor can they feed on celestial banquets while they gorge on earthly things in this life—should strive to cling to the king of heaven according to their strength. For they are stained less by the bitter flavors of the earth and refreshed more by the sweet liquids of heaven the more greedily they are moved by that super-celestial fountain of sweetness. The closer we approach the master of the world, the further we depart from worldly servitude. Furthermore, just as in our true homeland <note>Ficino refers to the celestial realm or Heaven as the soul's "patria" or homeland.</note> we are near Him by seeing and rejoicing, so outside our homeland we are near Him by loving and worshipping. Wherefore, no sufficient medicine is found anywhere against earthly diseases except divine love and worship. Nor indeed is this by mistake. For in any disease, when the medicine does not overcome the quality of the bad humor, the medicine itself is converted into that humor. It disturbs the body, diminishes strength, and increases the weight of the illness. Since, therefore, all our infirmity and adversity is corporal and worldly, whoever attempts to help such an evil with corporal and worldly medicines undoubtedly labors in vain. Believe me, a much stronger medicine is needed here. A medicine, I say, which is both spiritual and above the world, by which it may be able to expel corporal and worldly diseases. If we suffered from this languor alone, or perhaps that one, this or that physician might suffice for us. But our plague is every evil. Therefore, our theriac <term>thiriaca</term> <note>original: "tiriaca"; an ancient medical concoction used as a universal antidote against all poisons. Ficino uses it here as a metaphor for a spiritual panacea.</note> is every good. Our disease is an insatiable appetite and continuous disturbance. Our physician, therefore, is immense good and eternal tranquility. If anyone denies that our medicine is the true worship of God, no remedy for his evils remains, and all hope of health is taken away. But he who truly trusts in divine remedies recovers as soon as he trusts.

Is it what anyone gives? No, we ought to consider with what spirit he gives.

### Marsilio Ficino & Giovanni Cavalcanti to Giorgio Antonio Vespucci <note>Giorgio Antonio Vespucci (1434–1514) was a Dominican friar, a classical scholar, and the uncle of the explorer Amerigo Vespucci.</note>, a most excellent and learned citizen. Greetings.

<margin>d</margin> I give to you our volume *On True Piety*: not to instruct a man already distinguished in piety toward piety, but because I think that by this one gift I shall satisfy Piety herself more than by all my disputations. I shall also satisfy my pious friend (as I judge), who, since he always burns with pious affection, measures that very affection in all things rather than the effect. For he knows, in truth, that in external things there is nothing great; conversely, he knows that in a great affection, nothing is not great. He knows also that nothing great is ever given by one who never wished to give more than what he gave. On the contrary, nothing small is given by one to whom, compared to the will for something greater, whatever he bestows is small.

# BOOK FOUR

...He knows, finally, that one must look not so much at the hand as at the heart of the giver. And as much as the one desires to grant, so much the other confesses he owes. For even if it is not received by the hand immediately, it is nevertheless received by us in the soul as soon as it first became known to us: whatever the friend desired to hand over. He who can give new things every day never grants anything truly excellent. Only he has given the most excellent things to whom nothing remains to be granted again: when once he has given himself and all his possessions along with himself. To put it briefly: we either give nothing or we give everything. He who gives us a physical thing but not his soul does not offer a gift; instead, he either entrusts a deposit to us, or he buys us, or perhaps he is hunting us <note>original: "aucupatur"; a metaphor for seeking a favor or trapping someone with a gift</note>. But he truly grants all things suddenly who gives with a mind that possesses all things. Farewell.

## As it is shameful to love money, so it is honorable to love man; so also it is necessary and blessed to love God.

->Marsilio Ficino to Piero Guicciardini <note>Petrus Guicciardinus (1454–1513), a Florentine statesman and father of the historian Francesco Guicciardini.</note>, most distinguished in learning and character. He sends greetings.<-

As shameful as it is to love money, so honorable it is to love a man who is most worthy of love. No one doubts—provided they ever love anything—that the lover takes himself away from himself and gives himself over to the beloved. Money can indeed receive the man who loves it, but it can never return him. From this it happens that a lover of this kind possesses neither his money nor himself. But he who loves a person who loves him back, just as he gave himself to the other while loving, so he receives himself back while being loved in return. Indeed, to speak more accurately, he receives himself back twice over. For in this way, he who had given one soul receives two souls in return. Again, just as it seems honorable and useful to love a man worthy of goodwill, so it is necessary and blessed to love God: the first origin of love and beauty. Without His heat, no one can love anything; without His splendor, nothing can be loved. Farewell, be happy, and commend me to your most illustrious father, Jacopo. March 1st, 1476. Florence.

## As a person is in himself, such are the things he receives.

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Aurelio of Rimini and Giovanni Pietro Cortusio of Padua, with his fellow philosophers. He sends greetings.<-

It is not an evil to fall into those things which are commonly called "evils," unless you are worthy of evils. For no one suffers evil except the evil man. It is not a good thing to possess those things called "goods," unless you are a good man worthy of them. For no one enjoys good things except the good man. Internal things do not depend on external ones; rather, external things depend on the internal. As each person is within himself, so are the things he receives. We can complain less about our fate <note>original: "forte"; referring to chance or luck</note> than about our choices. We continually think evil thoughts; thus evils agitate us on every side. We follow evils daily; deservedly, then, evils follow us. We practice cruelty extensively; in turn, cruelty torments us. We flee from mercy <note>original: "clementiam"</note>; therefore, mercy also flees from us. The more we voluntarily flee from human justice, the more divine justice pursues us against our will. In the crime itself lies the punishment for the crime. The reward for the good man is found within the good itself. We only do good things "tomorrow"; thus we only receive good things "tomorrow." <note>Ficino critiques procrastination in virtue; if one delays being good, the rewards of goodness remain perpetually out of reach.</note>

# BOOK FOUR

CII

We do evil today; today we suffer evil. We are all out of harmony with ourselves. Everything in turn is out of harmony with us. If you have properly tempered the movements of your soul—as the Magi <note>Ancient Persian priests and philosophers whom Ficino and the Neoplatonists regarded as keepers of primordial wisdom.</note> of the Persians teach—you have already tempered everything for yourself: the humors of the body, the seasons of the soul, plants, all animals, and the heavens. You will temper them undoubtedly if you arrange your soul with as much diligence as architects arrange stones, painters arrange colors and lines, musicians arrange voices, or poets arrange words. And to speak briefly, nothing in you will seem disordered if you arrange the brain covered by your hair as carefully as anyone arranges their hair. Farewell; and lest you worship other things in vain: first of all, worship yourself <note>original: "cole teipsm"; Ficino uses the verb "colere," which means both to "cultivate" (like a garden) and to "worship" or "honor." He is likely referencing the Delphic maxim "Know Thyself."</note>.

---

All worldly things are composed of discord; souls themselves oppose discord both in themselves and in others.

->Marsilio Ficino wishes peace to his friend Pace, and fears war. He sends greetings. <note>original: "Paci suo pacem optat"; Ficino is playing on his friend’s name, Pietro Pace, and the Latin word for peace (*pax*).</note><-

<margin>5</margin>
You wrote to me recently, my Pace, in your usual elegant and friendly manner. But I was writing nothing to you because I thought peace existed nowhere, as I reflected that all things were utterly occupied by discord. But I have just now found my "Pace" <note>referring to his friend</note> where I have long since found my "peace" <note>the internal state</note>. Jupiter (as those who know celestial matters say) is the author of human peace. Rainaldus Ursinus <note>Rinaldo Orsini (d. 1503), Archbishop of Florence and a close associate of the Medici and Ficino.</note>, a foster-son of Jupiter, nourishes my friend Pace and my own peace. I will humbly commend you (as you request) to the foster-son of Phoebus <note>Apollo, the god of light and wisdom.</note>. You, in turn, please commend me to the foster-son of Jupiter.

But before I end this letter, I wish to philosophize a bit with you about war, starting from the name of peace, unless perhaps it seems ridiculous. Unfortunate demons are opposed to the happy angels; celestial signs to other signs. Planets to planets; even elements to elements. Plants to plants; animals to animals. Moreover, movements are opposed to rest, and privation to habit <note>term: habit (habitus) — in Aristotelian philosophy, the presence of a quality, while privation is its absence.</note>. Light to darkness; the bright and white to the black. Sound to silence; the sharp pitch to the heavy. The sweet-smelling to the foul. (As the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, known for their systematic classification of the physical world.</note> think) the false to the tasteless, the bitter and sharp to the sweet. Heat to cold, moisture to dryness, light to heavy, rare to dense, smooth to rough, and finally hard to soft.

Fortune and fate are opposed to the body. The humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to determine health and temperament.</note> of the body to other humors, and limbs to limbs. The body itself is opposed to the soul. Sense is opposed to reason; passion to passion; vice to virtue; vices to other vices; opinion to opinion; and finally, wish to wish. Virtues alone, if they are found anywhere, are truly in accord with one another, so that he who attains one follows and attains them all. But all other things are in accord in nothing else more than in discord itself. Therefore, why should it be a wonder that the human race is agitated by continual discord among themselves? All things are composed of discord. All things are opposed by discord both to themselves and to others. Everything harmonizes outwardly only where nothing clashes inwardly. But nothing clashes within where pure truth dominates. Either the splendor of such truth overflows, or the heat of such splendor glows. The first is indeed God. The second is the contemplation of God. The third is the love and worship of God. Nor for us, my Pace...

## Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to the human race.

<margin>q</margin>When I was asking myself today what the primary reason is that men continually lead such a laborious life on earth, there came to mind a certain game of this kind, in which some walk with their legs stretched high into the air while using their palms and the crown of their heads for feet. Furthermore, let us imagine they try to look around at all earthly things with one eye, but at celestial things with the other. Then, whatever meets them on the ground, they strive to grasp with their nostrils, lips, and fingers. Conversely, if anything looms from above, they try to touch and pluck it with their feet, and they look up at whatever they happen to reach so they might carry it. 

O most shameful sight! O wretched monster! These are not men; they are not even animals. They seem to me to be Stygian trees <note>Ficino refers to the River Styx in the underworld; he is likely referencing the "Wood of the Suicides" from Dante’s *Inferno*, where souls are trapped in gnarled, fruitless trees.</note>. Their leaves are indeed most bitter, and there is no fruit among the leaves. What more monstrous thing, what more laborious and burdensome thing can be imagined? 

We are almost all like this, my friends. Almost all of us—alas, wretched ones!—foolishly subject the head of the soul, which is Reason, to the senses, which are the feet of the soul. Therefore, with the mind thus pressed to the ground, we trust that we can know celestial and earthly things at the same time. With the lowest soles of the soul, we try in vain to touch the highest things of nature. And while we strive to seize everything for ourselves, we carry the burden of all things. Alas, meanwhile, we suffer from insane misery and miserable insanity. Why do we weep over our lot or fortune? Why do we rashly think to change fortune? Why do we think to bend fate? Change, I pray, this game of the soul. Turn this shape of yours around. For in this way, you will have changed your fortune and bent fate; and you will suddenly have turned the shape of the world itself into something better for you. Farewell.

->Do not seek pure things impurely. Nor, after you have found them, share them with the impure.<-

<margin>c</margin>When, on the first of last November <note>The Kalends of November.</note>, I had composed one letter about the "Rapture of Paul to the Third Heaven" to Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Ficino's closest friend and fellow academician.</note>, and another about the "Celestial and Super-celestial Threshold" to Phoebus Capella, I soon unhappily fell into that disease of the eyes which physicians call "images" <note>original: "imaginum"; likely referring to *scotomata* or visual floaters/hallucinations that Ficino feared were a precursor to blindness.</note> and which they claim portends imminent blindness. ...he seeks; for he who flees far away is accustomed to lose. Paul of Tarsus <note>St. Paul the Apostle.</note>, while he fled with a swift step and pursued the Sun and the light of the Sun itself with impious arms, is said to have been captured by that light. Marsilio, in turn, while he follows the Sun and pursues the light, has almost been captured by the light. Hence yesterday, while the Moon was joined to the Sun <note>original: "Luna Soli," referring to an eclipse or an astrological conjunction.</note>, a certain speech arose in me toward the divine Sun, perhaps somewhat obscure. But then at last (as I hope) it will emerge clearer once my **human Sun** <note>Ficino frequently refers to his patron, Lorenzo de’ Medici, as his "Sun."</note> has illustrated this Moon of mine—which is also his—at least once with the rays of his own eyes. Farewell.

-> O SUN, who purifies all the hearts of men with your flames: Why do you wish to be accessible to none among mortals when you are the one who is most open to all? O Sun of Justice, source and exemplar of bounty, how vehemently you inflame me to seek you; shine forth so clearly and healthfully to the seeker. Or perhaps I have suddenly dared to look upon the purest light with eyes that are too impure. I confess that in this matter I was, in a way, like **Phaeton** <note>In Greek myth, Phaeton tried to drive the chariot of the Sun and fell to his death.</note>. Yet I was and am your **Phoebus** <note>Phoebus is an epithet for Apollo, the sun god.</note>. Therefore, I pray, purge me with your heat and cherish me with your own. You, Phoebus, are able to heal all things with a healthful flame just as much as you can hurl your rays through all things. For I have not—like that **Julian** <note>Julian the Apostate, the Roman Emperor who attempted to revive paganism and wrote a "Hymn to King Helios."</note>, who was once a Platonist and a Christian but then an apostate—sung to the Sun itself without the Sun. Nor have I impiously sung of your dear sister **Proserpina** <note>Persphone, queen of the underworld.</note> being snatched to the underworld, as they say Claudian did. Rather, I have celebrated your son **Aesculapius** <note>The god of healing.</note>, a certain physician of souls from Tarsus <note>A reference to St. Paul as a spiritual healer.</note> who was snatched to the heavens, along with Luke, Hierotheus, and Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a figure Ficino synthesized with Platonic thought.</note>. Nor have I depicted the unhappy abduction of Helen—that is, of earthly beauty—as Stesichorus and Homer did; but as true Platonists are accustomed, I have painted the most blessed ascent of the celestial mind. I have not vulgarly published the **Eleusinian mysteries** <note>Secret religious rites of ancient Greece.</note> like a commoner, nor like **Pherecydes of Syros** <note>An early Greek thinker.</note> have I revealed the secrets of celestial souls to any earthly person. Nor like **Hipparchus the Pythagorean** did I make the Delphic mysteries of my holy teacher, which are rightfully shared with only a very few, common to everyone. Nor, in the manner of Dionysius of Syracuse <note>A tyrant of Sicily who failed to understand Plato's teachings.</note>, did I strive to unlock the Apolline meanings of Plato to the impure senses of the common people. I have not spoken openly of what is not permitted for man to speak; I have not given what is holy to be torn apart by dogs or pigs. But I have revealed the secrets of **Oedipus** <note>The famous riddle-solver.</note> only so much as I myself had seen; to the **Davuses** <note>A "Davus" was a stereotypical name for a simple-minded slave in Roman comedy. Ficino is saying he kept the truth veiled from the uneducated.</note>, however, I have given them entirely veiled.

What then after this? What do you most wish me to do, Phoebus? You will send me, I think, to **Ananias** in Damascus <note>Reference to the biblical account in Acts 9, where Ananias restores the sight of the blinded Saul/Paul.</note>, where you once sent the blind Saul, and where he immediately received his lost sight. I wish that my Ananias might be that foster-son of yours, Phoebus: **Lorenzo the Medici** <note>original: "Laurus Medices." Laurus (Laurel) is a pun on Lorenzo's name.</note>, who once rose under your rising rays. I set out for Damascus recently with a certain son of the **Platonic Sun** as my guide on the journey. There, to your foster-son—my truly own Ananias—I returned a certain small portion, as if a pledge of a grander whole-burnt offering <term>holocaust <gloss>a sacrificial offering consumed by fire</gloss></term>, which I shall return through the remainder of the day. Therefore, return to me now, Phoebus, if it pleases you, the light I have long desired; return it, I beseech you. April 14, 1477.

<meta>This page continues the correspondence of Marsilio Ficino within his collected letters. <header>BOOK</header>

One must act honorably because it is pleasing; it ought to please you so that you may please God.

->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Lottieri Neroni.<-

<margin>q</margin> However much all my written words pleased me at the beginning of my studies, Lottieri, nearly all of them now displease me more with each passing day. Nevertheless, I am driven to write something every day—I know not by what fate or spirit—even against my will. Therefore, this is always my primary goal in writing: to speak as briefly as possible so that I may offend myself <note>original: "Marsilium," referring to himself in the third person.</note> and others as little as possible. But while I strive through excessive brevity to avoid the boredom of wordiness, I sometimes somehow confuse even myself with a certain obscurity. Certainly, I often disturb others. This is what usually happens, by right, to those who have not learned to maintain a middle ground in things. 

Behold now how ridiculous it will seem, O friend; how absurd. I am forced to interpret a personal letter for my own close friend—who himself sometimes appears, by his virtue of interpreting, to be a second **Mercury** <note>The Roman messenger god, associated with translation and interpretation (hermeneutics).</note>. But indeed, I shall by no means be "forced," as I see it; for while you ask to be taught more clearly and easily by us, you actually teach us abundantly. You could not hide your cunning so well, O ironic friend, that I did not notice you requested a clearer interpretation of my letter out of a burning desire to speak with me longer, rather than a greed for clearer instruction. Therefore, **O crafty man** <note>original: "Callide vir."</note>, you now demand a certain lover-like wordiness, not just clarity. 

Otherwise, so that I may satisfy you with a longer speech—and satisfy anyone else who might truly require an interpretation—with plainer words, the summary of that old letter shall be as follows:

I strive with all my strength to always do that which both prudent counsel and diligent reason have persuaded me is good. Nor do I direct this action toward some external reward <note>original: "fructum," literally fruit or profit.</note> which would be both fleeting and short-lived, and placed in the judgment of men or fortune. But first, I direct it toward that true joy which is perceived in the very action of doing good. This good and this joy—even if it can be called "temporal" <note>Existing within time.</note> because it is not continuously practiced or felt in the same way—is nonetheless internal and situated within our own choice. Indeed, a good of this kind is pleasing both in the present and in **eternity**. 

I do not say this because I now fully enjoy eternity itself, but because I understand that it is so for no other reason than because it accords with the **Idea** <note>The Neoplatonic "Idea": the eternal, perfect pattern in the mind of God.</note>—that is, the eternal reason and art of Almighty God. It fits the mind and it pleases. Therefore, just as I referred that good to internal joy, so I refer joy to the Idea; so that in turn, the reason of the good may please me, and I myself may especially please God—the Good of all goods—without whom nothing can please me. 

"I do not possess happiness in the present," you say, "but I expect it in the future." Wait for happiness, Lottieri, as one who is about to be happy in the *present*—that is, in eternal happiness—rather than in the future. For if there is any future happiness in you, it is happiness only because it exists within that happiness which is touched by neither the past nor the future. Farewell. April 15, 1477.

Nothing is more wonderful or more lovable to anyone than **Learning joined to Integrity**.

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine sends greetings to Marc'Aurelio, the most illustrious Orator.<-

<margin>Q</margin>When your singular learning, Marcus Aurelius, is joined with a certain excellent integrity, so much splendor from that learning and ardor from that integrity immediately shines forth—as if from a conjunction of the **Sun** and **Jupiter**—that, with these rays and flames stretching from the East all the way to the West, the minds of even the most remote nations are incited, inflamed, and most enticingly allured and vehemently seized. By this same reasoning, therefore, did Marcus Aurelius once allure Marsilio Ficino as a youth, and now he seizes him as one more mature in age. Behold, now all this prey hastens to you, O Marcus: your Marsilio, both as a youth and as a man of maturity. He therefore offers to you six little declamations <note>Short, formal speeches intended for practice or public display.</note>, of which those first two regarding the praises of philosophy and medicine were born long ago in his tender youth; the four following, regarding the principal institutions of the human race, were truly born to him now. Thus, at last, they are born happily if they are continually nurtured by you.

### Marsilio Ficino’s Oration on the Praises of Philosophy.

<margin>C</margin>My mind is currently pulled in contrary directions, most distinguished men, just as is often accustomed to happen to those about to speak on these more serious matters. For both the ancient custom of this sacred **gymnasium** <note>original: "gymnasii," referring here to an academy or place of higher learning.</note> and the heavy authority of the Fathers—two things which rightly hold the greatest weight with me—compel me to speak today on the praises of philosophy. Yet, when I consider the power and nature of this faculty within myself, it seems so illustrious and excellent to me that I distrust whether it can be comprehended by the human mind or explained by the tongue. Nor is it only the sublimity of the subject on the one hand and the humility of my talent on the other, but even your revered presence now deters me from speaking. And so, I was wavering just now whether I should remain silent or rather speak. I shall speak, however, outstanding men, as best I can, judging it better that the matter itself about which I am to speak should seem less through Marsilio, than that Marsilio should in no way obey the precepts of his elders. Therefore, you will grant me pardon if I am unable to express its extraordinary praises in accordance with its dignity. And everything whatever that shall be said by me, you shall attribute entirely to the **Divine Light**, by whose light we observe, by whose rays we comprehend, and by whose splendor we explain all things.

It is an old opinion of theologians, outstanding men, confirmed by the reasonings of many philosophers, by which we are surely taught and instructed that individual things in the nature of reality seem more perfect and worthy the closer they approach the first principle of all things in perfection and dignity, and the more closely and expressly they embrace His image within themselves. Indeed, the ancient theology of the **Egyptians** and **Arabs** handed down that God is the principle of existing, of knowing, and of acting. From this, **Pythagoras**, **Heraclitus**, and **Plato**, transferring that theology into Greece, argued that from that same God comes the principle of nature, the truth of doctrine, and the happiness of life. This is testified by Plato’s *Republic*, the *Parmenides*, the *Timaeus*, and the theology of **Iamblichus** and **Proclus** <note>Iamblichus and Proclus were major figures in Late Antique Neoplatonism who heavily influenced Ficino.</note>. Following after those ancients was the Platonic **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A Christian theologian (Pseudo-Dionysius) whom Ficino and his contemporaries believed was a direct disciple of St. Paul and a link between Platonism and Christianity.</note>, first and then...

<summary>Ficino dedicates six short speeches to his friend Marcus Aurelius and begins a formal oration praising Philosophy as a divine pursuit rooted in the "Divine Light" and ancient theological traditions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s oration on philosophy. Having just introduced the topic to the "sacred gymnasium" (his academy of scholars), Ficino now moves to harmonize the teachings of ancient philosophers like Plato with Christian theology, specifically the nature of the Trinity and the divine origin of wisdom.</meta>

<header>BOOK FOUR</header>

...Christian. The same <note>Ficino likely refers to a Greek Father like Origen or a Neoplatonist mentioned on the preceding page.</note> discussed this very extensively in his books. This was long afterwards observed by Hilary and Aurelius Augustine, the leading theologians among the Latins. And so Augustine himself, in his books *On True Religion* and *On the City of God*, calls God himself the maker of all things, the enlightener of truth, and the giver of happiness. He confirms that this had been treated many centuries earlier by the Platonic philosophers, though in different words. Moreover, in these three titles for God, which were first introduced by the ancient philosophers, the Christian Trinity is also contained in a certain way.

Furthermore, the three types of philosophy discovered and divided by Plato correspond in all their parts to our Trinity. So that the capacity for philosophizing which speaks of the causes and progressions of things <note>Natural Philosophy or Physics.</note> accords with God as the Principle of things. The second part, where the origin and method of discussion are treated <note>Rational Philosophy or Logic.</note>, suits God as the Enlightener of truth. The final part of philosophy, by whose precepts and institutions we lead our lives, and direct ourselves, our families, and the republic toward attaining happiness <note>Moral Philosophy or Ethics.</note>, is in some way compared to God as the Giver of happiness. 

From this it can be sufficiently clear that philosophy agrees in every part, totally and perfectly (if I may say so), with the Divine; it contains—as much as is granted to us—a full and absolute image of the power, wisdom, and goodness of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit. Thus it happens that no other human capacity appears closer or more similar to the Divine; therefore, nothing among us seems more perfect or excellent than philosophy, except for God himself.

Therefore, Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius Aegiptiorū," the legendary Egyptian sage Mercury/Thoth, whom Ficino believed predicted Christianity.</note>, the wisest of the Egyptians, seems to have explained this divine matter when he said that men become gods by the light of philosophy. Pythagoras sang the same in his *Golden Verses*, and Plato, in his books *On the Republic*, established the ceremonies and mysteries of the gods for philosophers who have completed their lives. 

Empedocles of Agrigentum <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher.</note> said philosophy is a gift from the gods, which makes whoever receives it such that he contemplates all things that move with a high mind, is enlightened by divine rays in the innermost edge of the mind, and hopes for future happiness with a firm resolve. But what is more excellent than what was said by Aristotle? When other arts, terrified by the magnitude and difficulty of things, departed far from the inquiry of truth, philosophy alone fled from no laborious work, nor did she consider herself unworthy of the best things, but judged the knowledge of them to be fitting and kindred to her. And since it would be impossible to reach the celestial seats with a physical mass, the soul, having obtained understanding as its leader by the gift of philosophy, transcends the nature of all things through contemplation. Thus says Aristotle.

Finally, to speak briefly: since philosophy is a celestial gift, it puts to flight earthly vices. It most bravely subdues Fortune. It marvelously mitigates Fate, and uses mortal gifts with the greatest certainty. It bestows immortal rewards according to one's prayer. Oh, treasure most precious of all! Produced not at all from the bowels of the earth or of Pluto <note>The god of the underworld and wealth hidden in the earth.</note>, but descending from the highest peak of heaven and the head of Jove <note>Jupiter, the King of the Gods; a reference to Athena/Wisdom springing from his head.</note>, without whose...

<summary>Ficino argues that the three branches of Platonic philosophy (natural, rational, and moral) mirror the Christian Trinity and that philosophy is a divine gift that elevates the human soul to a god-like state of contemplation.</summary>

...possession, nor can we rightly use other treasures, nor can we possess anything happily. O most secure leader of human life! Which first, with the **club of Hercules**, utterly conquers the monsters of vice. Then, with the **shield and spear of Pallas** <note>Pallas refers to Athena/Minerva, the goddess of wisdom; Ficino uses her armaments as symbols of intellectual defense and active virtue.</note>, it avoids or overcomes the dangers of fortune. Finally, lifting up human souls on **Atlantic shoulders** <note>A reference to Atlas, who held up the heavens; here, philosophy performs a similar feat by supporting the human spirit.</note>, it both frees them from this earthly exile and restores them to their true and most happy heavenly homeland. Thus, it was not without merit that Plato once said that a golden age existed when wisdom reigned, and conversely, that a golden age would return if philosophy reigned again.

But what are we doing, O distinguished men? Why do we attempt to measure the eternity of time in a mere moment, so to speak, in vain? Not only days but many years would fail us if we attempted to pursue all the praises of sacred Philosophy. Therefore, nothing else remains to be said or done, except that with our whole mind and an ardent soul—leaving behind all changeable and empty things, in which nothing is found except certain shadows and phantoms—we should apply ourselves to the study of this divine gift. For those who are devoid of philosophy fall headlong, in a certain way, into the state of beasts, becoming inferior to the human race. But those who bestow even a moderate effort upon it will undoubtedly turn out to be such men that they can both teach the learned and rule over kings. Yet he who devotes himself entirely to this alone throughout his whole life, having as it were laid aside his body, will proceed free to the heavens and surpass the human species: *becoming a god of the nourishing ether.* <note>original: "factus deus ætheris almi." This is a poetic allusion to the soul's deification through wisdom.</note>

## Marsilio Ficino’s Oration on the Praises of Medicine.

The Pythagorean and Platonic philosophers, who flowed from the fountain of philosophy that is **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary figure who Renaissance scholars believed was a contemporary of Moses and the originator of all "ancient theology" (Prisca Theologia).</note>, judged that nothing can be sought or found by the human mind in any way without that Principle from which both the mind itself and those things that must be learned proceed. They wished that Light, for the inspection of all things, to be the same God from whom all things are perfected. For just as the spark of the eyes discerns the sparks of colors in the light of the sun itself—which is the author of both colors and eyes—so the truth-telling mind perceives the truth of any thing in the Supreme Truth, the creator of truth and of every mind. 

Therefore, since today—led by ancient custom and the command of our fathers—we are to treat the praises of **medicine**, which is said to have descended from **Apollo**, we humbly adore the rays of the true and supreme Apollo <note>Ficino, a priest and philosopher, frequently identifies the sun-god Apollo as a "type" or symbol for God or Christ.</note>, turning the sharp edge of the mind from darkness toward the Light. We pray that, purified by His salutary heat, we may pursue the perfection and praises of purification, either according to its own dignity or at least according to the strength of our own talent. 

There are three principal things among philosophers, O distinguished men: namely the end, the origin, and the matter, by which they are accustomed to judge the perfection of any teaching. The origin of Medicine, however—whether you follow the Hebrews and Arabs or the Greek and Egyptian theologians—flowed from Divinity itself. For the Hebrews and Arabs assert that **Adam**, the first parent of the human race, obtained this wisdom by divine light. The others have handed down that Apollo received that power from **Jove** [Jupiter], the parent of men, for the salvation of the human race; he then revealed it to **Aesculapius** <note>The Greek god of medicine and healing.</note>, from whom Podalirius and Machaon <note>Physicians mentioned in Homer’s Iliad as the sons of Aesculapius.</note> [descended]...

### BOOK FOUR

...excellent and outstanding physicians were born. Then, many centuries after, **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician of the 5th century BCE, often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> brought into the light those things which had been handed down by the ancients shrouded in obscure parables. And all these whom I have mentioned so far are said to have been admitted into the council of the gods by the universal religion of the gentiles. Why should I mention **Pythagoras**, **Empedocles**, **Democritus**, **Diocles of Carystus**, **Erasistratus**, **Praxagoras**, **Chrysippus**, **Herophilus**, **Serapion**, **Apollonius**, **Glaucias**, **Heraclides**, **Themison**, **Plistonicus**, and **Galen**? Or the eminent and most excellent Greek philosophers, **Plato** and **Aristotle**, all of whom we find to have been both the most acute philosophers and the authors of many books on the art of healing? What of the **Egyptians**, the oldest of all nations, whose priests were all outstanding physicians, as **Homer**, **Euripides**, and **Plato** testify? What of the Persian **Magi** <note>The term "Magi" refers to the hereditary priesthood of ancient Persia, renowned for their knowledge of astronomy and natural philosophy.</note>—that is, their priests—**Zoroaster**, **Ostanes**, **Abstrophic**, **Gobryas**, **Paxatas**, **Sinicariondas**, **Damnigeron**, **Hismosen**, **Johannes**, **Apollonius**, and **Dardanus**? Among them are found almost innumerable volumes in this art, which protect our health through the movements of the stars, words, herbs, small stones, and vapors. Did not also that **Mithridates**, King of Pontus <note>Mithridates VI was famous for his supposed immunity to poisons, achieved by taking small, non-lethal doses.</note>, who spoke twenty-two languages, devote long effort to the study of this discipline? **Shapur**, King of the Medes, and the divine **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose "Canon of Medicine" remained a standard medical text in Europe for centuries.</note>, as well as many Arabs, applied themselves with burning zeal to this wisdom: **Serapion** and his son **Johannes**, **Johannes Mesue**, **Abumero**, **Avenzoar**, **Rhazes**, **Averroes**, **Abugafis**, **Isaac**, **Haly**, and many other most excellent wise men of the Hebrews and the Arabs. I pass over the Latins, of whom **Cornelius Celsus**, **Apuleius**, **Quintus Serenus**, **Columella**, **Pliny**, and **Lactantius** were the first to compose books on the care of health, both in prose and in verse. Those who followed them are found to be almost innumerable and are so well known to us that they require no further narration. 

Now, can the origin of any other faculty be found that is more excellent than this birth of medicine, or even equal or similar to it? For it proceeds from heroes, kings, leaders, Magi, and philosophers—and indeed from those who were the most ancient and the wisest of all. Furthermore, the subject matter with which this art deals, and whose principles and properties man investigates, is **Man** himself, whom **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of esoteric writings (Hermetica); he was often synchronized with the Egyptian god Thoth.</note> esteemed so highly that he called him "almost the greatest of the gods after the first God." The **Stoics** and **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle, named for the covered walkways (peripatoi) of the Lyceum.</note> also held that all things which move beneath the sphere of the Moon move and exist for his sake. Moreover, Hebrew, Arab, and Christian theologians held that the world itself was established for the sake of man. From this, who cannot see that the human being—with whom our faculty deals—is almost the most excellent of all things flowing from God? And therefore, the doctrine of curing man must be judged the most perfect. Nor should anyone say that the physician’s art is concerned only with the human body. For indeed **Apollo**—as is read in the letters of **Hippocrates**—considered that the healing of the soul and the body should be joined as one. Hence, among the Egyptians and Persians, the priests and the physicians were the same people. **Plato** writes in the *Charmides* that those Magi were doctors of the soul and the body...

### BOOK FOUR

...of **Mithridates** <note>original: "Mithridatis". Mithridates VI of Pontus was famous for his study of poisons and antidotes.</note>; the followers of **Zoroaster** <note>The ancient Persian prophet and founder of Zoroastrianism, often associated with secret wisdom in the Renaissance.</note> think that all things of the body—both good and bad—flow from the soul into the body itself, just as the quality of the eye flows from the brain, and the quality of the brain from the whole body. And just as it is impossible for the eye to be cured unless the brain is cured, and the brain to be cured unless the whole body is cured; so too the whole body cannot be healthy unless the soul is well. Indeed, they say the health of the soul is cared for by certain incantations of **Apollo**—that is, by physical <term>ratios</term> <note>The text suggests that "incantations" are actually rational or natural principles.</note>. **Socrates** moreover related that it was common among the **Thracians** <note>A group of Paleo-Balkan tribes; Socrates mentions their holistic medicine in Plato's dialogue *Charmides*.</note> for those physicians to preserve some men as immortal by such a method; so great is the command of the soul over the body, and so great is its power. This magical opinion seems to agree with the sentiment of the **Hebrews and Christians**: that in **Adam** <note>original: "Ade"</note>, our first parent, all things were healthy as long as his soul was healthy. But afterward, when the soul became infirm, all things turned out infirm. **Cornelius Celsus** <note>A Roman medical writer of the 1st century CE known for his encyclopedia *De Medicina*.</note> also wished the art of medicine to be understood as whole and perfect only when one is able to protect a person's health through the knowledge of the movements of the soul and the body; within these two, natural and moral contemplation and practice are further contained. For **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians in history.</note> also judged that the quality of the body can affect the soul very greatly in either direction: and that the affections of the soul itself—its movements and images—have the greatest power over the body's health, whether for good or ill. Furthermore, who has not seen the goal of physicians? For by their care and diligence, life itself is preserved, and more than that, *living well*. What can be added that is better or more desirable than this? What is closer or more agreeable to nature than to protect and preserve what she herself has brought forth? None of you, most distinguished men, is ignorant of the fact that human prosperity consists not in the possession of things, but in a certain pleasant use of them. But truly, no one of sound mind is ignorant that without health, no use of things is pleasant to us. Thus did **Orpheus** <note>The legendary Greek musician and poet.</note> sing in his hymn to health:

->That is: without you, all things are<-
->useless to men.<-

Therefore, since medicine either protects or restores health, it seems to both preserve and return all good things at once. For this reason, the sacred letters of the **Hebrews** <note>A reference to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 38:1: "Honor the physician."</note> seem to have rightly commanded that the physician be honored; and **Homer** rightly says: "A man who is a physician is worth many others." <note>A famous line from the *Iliad*, book 11.</note> Wherefore I vehemently exhort all of you, friends, that you spare neither time, nor money, nor any labor in embracing with all your strength this most wholesome art, the preserver of human life. Do this so that you may protect your own life and prosperity, and those of your kin, and then of all others; and that you may assist the other liberal arts, which cannot be learned or practiced without health. And finally, may you happily hold sway over all nations and even the greatest kings, who all surrender themselves into your hands.

# BOOK

->In each matter, consult the expert.<-
->**Marsilio Ficino** to **Lorenzo Bonincontri**, Astronomer and Poet, Sends Greeting.<-

<margin>q</margin>When I was recently looking for one friend among many whom I might especially consult about whether I have argued the truth regarding **Paul's** rapture into the third heaven <note>original: "raptu in tertiū cœlū pauli". This refers to the vision described by the Apostle Paul in 2 Corinthians 12:2, which Ficino interpreted through a Neoplatonic lens of the soul's ascent.</note>, there occurred to me first of all **Lorenzo Bonincontri** <note>A famous 15th-century Italian astrologer and poet who wrote "Rerum Naturalium et Divinarum," blending science and verse.</note>, the astronomical poet and the poetic astronomer. Indeed, for a long time now his own **Atlas** <note>The Titan from Greek mythology who held up the heavens; here used as a metaphor for Bonincontri's mastery of astronomy.</note> has carried him into the heavens upon his high shoulders; to whom, in turn, father **Phoebus Apollo** <note>The god of both prophecy and poetry.</note> himself has sung of celestial things with an "elegant mouth" <note>original: "ore rotūdo", a classical idiom for polished, eloquent speech.</note>. Therefore, I shall only then believe that I have expressed a true image of divine things when my friend Lorenzo—who has seen their face intimately, with Atlas as his guide and Apollo as his teacher—has fully approved of it.

->It is better to bear ill health well than good health poorly.<-
->**Marsilio Ficino** to his Friends, Sends Greeting.<-

<margin>q</margin>Why do you ask so often, friends, how I am doing? Ask instead whether I have at last recovered. For others, indeed, seem to have been born for this: that they might be healthy. I, on the other hand, seem to have been born for this very purpose: that I might be continually unwell. For it was given to me from the beginning by a certain weakness of nature that I have never experienced a single whole day of firm bodily health. But by a most generous gift of God, I repay the damages of envious nature; for just as some people bear good health poorly, I bear ill health almost as well. Therefore, as much as some people owe to nature for the sake of a prosperous possession, so much do I owe to God for the sake of the use of it. Since God himself is our strength, we cannot be weak in all respects. For then the strength of the soul is perfected by the weakness of the body. For me, indeed, "it is good to cling to God" <note>A reference to Psalm 73:28.</note>. For, as **Augustine** says: "If I do not remain in Him, I will not be able to remain in myself" <note>Ficino paraphrases St. Augustine's *Confessions*, emphasizing that human stability depends entirely on the Divine.</note>. Stand firm, therefore, O friends; stand firm in God who is not moved, and you shall stand. Rest in Him who is not troubled, and you shall live in peace.

->He has given everything at once who has given himself.<-
->**Marsilio Ficino** the Florentine to **Bernardo Bembo** <note>A Venetian diplomat and father of the famous poet Pietro Bembo. He was a close friend and patron of Ficino.</note>, the Venetian, a most illustrious man, Sends Greeting.<-

<margin>v</margin>I had sent a letter to you by way of **Jacopo Lanfredini** <note>A Florentine diplomat and associate of the Medici family.</note>, in which I desired to be made more certain whether you had received all those things of mine—or rather, yours; when your letter was delivered to me, filled with gravity, wit, and affection. What truly shall I say of your wonderful gratitude? Others, when they have received the belongings of another for free, can scarcely bring themselves to give thanks at last. Our **Bembo**, however, gives thanks because he has received what was his by right—and most abundant thanks indeed. I, my sweetest Bernardo, have been able to give you nothing new for a long time; I gave you everything once and for all when I gave you **Marsilio** <note>The author is charmingly stating that because he gave himself to Bembo in friendship, everything he produces already belongs to his friend.</note>. And if such a possession is light—for I am not so great as to fulfill your merits—it is nevertheless not a light thing that you have seized all other men of letters by your character no less than you have seized me. For you are the desire of all these men. You are the delight of our people. April 25, 1477.

# FOURTH BOOK [PAGE] 107

## On the nature, training, and practice of the Platonic philosopher.

->**Marsilio Ficino** to the most distinguished **Count Giovanni Francesco Ippolito Gazolti**, Sends Greeting.<-

I wrote a rather long letter to the Venetian **Bernardo Bembo** <note>A Venetian diplomat and father of the famous Pietro Bembo; he was a close friend of Ficino.</note> some time ago regarding the praises of philosophy. Recently, I also wrote something on the same subject to the most distinguished orator **Marcus Aurelius**. It seems that what remains is for me to write something concerning the nature, training, and practice of the **Platonic philosopher**, so that it may be more clearly revealed by what path that most precious treasure of philosophy is chiefly found by us, and once found, by what method it may be lawfully possessed and put to use. 

Since philosophy—as the name itself, introduced by **Pythagoras**, indicates <note>original: "ut nomẽ ipm a pythagora inductum p̃hibet". Pythagoras is traditionally credited with coining the term "philosopher" (lover of wisdom) rather than "sophos" (wise man), out of humility before the divine.</note>—is defined by everyone as the "love of wisdom," and since wisdom is certainly the contemplation of divine things, then the end of philosophy is surely the knowledge of the divine. Our **Plato** testifies to this in the seventh book of the *Republic*, where he says that true philosophy is the ascent from those things which flow, arise, and perish, toward those things which truly are and always remain the same. 

Therefore, philosophy possesses as many parts and serving faculties as there are steps to be climbed from the lowest things to the highest. These steps require partly a natural disposition and partly human diligence. For—as **Plato** relates in the sixth book of the *Republic*—whoever is to be a philosopher must be so fashioned by nature herself that, first, he is easy and ready to learn all kinds of disciplines. Second, he must be truthful by nature and entirely foreign to every lie. In the third place, having despised all things subject to corruption, he must apply his mind to those things which always remain the same. It is also necessary that he be **magnanimous** <note>original: "magnanimus". In the Platonic and Aristotelian sense, this refers to "greatness of soul," a virtue of one who deems himself worthy of great things and is indeed worthy of them.</note> and brave, neither fearing death nor desiring empty glory. 

Furthermore, he must be born temperate in a certain way, receiving from nature those parts of the soul which are usually carried away by passions in a tamed state. For whoever, greedy for truth, turns his mind toward the contemplation of divine things, thinks little of the pleasures of the body. Besides this, the philosopher must possess a generous spirit; for the valuation of cheap or vile things is contrary and even hostile to a man who is to contemplate the truth of things. Moreover, his will shall love justice, since he is a great seeker of truth, temperance, and generosity. 

But of all things, it seems he has the greatest need for sharpness of intellect, a strong memory, and greatness of soul. And yet, while these three natural gifts—namely sharpness of intellect, memory, and magnanimity—create a man perfect in virtue when proper discipline and a decent education are applied, **Plato** says that if they are neglected, they can become the causes of the greatest crimes. 

Therefore, the greatest human diligence must be applied to this natural disposition, so that he who is so naturally inclined may learn letters and the elements of all the sciences from his very childhood. Furthermore, by the use of the **cithara** <note>original: "Cytharæ". The kithara or lute was used in Platonic education to harmonize the soul's inner proportions through musical ratios.</note>, his soul must be composed in harmony. His body must be exercised with gymnastic games so that, by its healthy condition, it may provide a fitting service to the studies of philosophy. Meanwhile, the institutions of the best laws must be instilled in his ears. With honorable exhortations...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s letter to Count Giovanni Francesco Ippolito Gazolti. On the previous page, Ficino began outlining the "Platonic" curriculum, starting from the basic definition of philosophy as the love of wisdom and the ascent of the soul. This page details the specific sequence of study—from ethics through the mathematical sciences and dialectic—leading toward the contemplation of the "First Good."</meta>

# BOOK

The soul of the youth must be formed in all its aspects so that it is rendered moderate and peaceful. This moral education is what they call **Ethics**. Truly, when the mind has been freed from the disturbance of appetite through those things we have mentioned, and has already begun to be released from the body, the knowledge of the **mathematical sciences** must soon be added to it. These deal with numbers, plane figures, solids, and their many motions. Since numbers, figures, and the principles of motions pertain to thought rather than to the external senses, by the study of these the soul is separated not only from the desires of the body but also from its senses, and betakes itself to inner contemplation. 

This is indeed **to practice death** <note>original: "mortẽ cōmentari"; this refers to the concept of *melete thanatou* found in Plato's *Phaedo*, where the philosopher trains the soul to detach from physical sensations to perceive higher truths.</note> (which **Plato** writes in the *Phaedo* is the duty of the philosopher), through which we are also made like unto God, as is learned from the *Phaedrus* and the *Theaetetus*. Among the Platonists, there is a specific order for perceiving these things: **Arithmetic** is followed by **Geometry**; **Geometry** by **Stereometry** <note>The study of three-dimensional or solid figures.</note>; this by **Astronomy**; and finally, **Astronomy** by **Music**. For numbers are prior to figures. Plane figures are prior to solid ones. Solid bodies exist before they are moved. And the order and principles of voices follow movement. 

Therefore, let **Arithmetic**, which deals with numbers, go first; let **Geometry**, which treats plane figures, follow. Let **Stereometry**, which considers solids, succeed this. **Astronomy** holds the fourth place, which looks upon the motions of solid bodies—that is, the spheres. Finally, let there be **Music**, which investigates the order of voices arising from motion. 

Once these have been grasped, **Plato** passes on **Dialectic**—that is, the science of demonstrating truth. He does not wish Dialectic to be merely that logic which teaches the first and smallest rules of reasoning, but also an art practiced by a clear mind to reach the very true and pure substance of every thing, first through **Physical** <note>Natural philosophy or the study of the physical world.</note> and then through **Metaphysical** <note>The study of things beyond the physical, such as being and divinity.</note> reasons. This is done so that a reason can be given for anything, and finally, above the nature of the senses and bodies, the light of the mind may be perceived and the incorporeal species of things, which we call **Ideas**, may be understood. 

From these Ideas, the **One** itself may be beheld—the source of all species, the origin and light of minds and souls, the beginning and end of all things (which **Plato** calls the **Good** itself). The beholding of this is **Wisdom**, the love of which is most rightly defined as **Philosophy**. After the philosopher’s soul has contemplated that first **Good**, judging from that vantage point which things in human affairs are good or evil, base or honorable, harmful or useful, he arranges human matters according to that exemplar. He is led away from evil and directed toward the good; and with this **Prudence** of governing, he administers his own affairs, his household, and the public state, and teaches the laws and methods of administration. From this source, laws had their beginning. 

For this reason, in the *Timaeus*, **Plato** asserts that philosophy is a gift of God, than which nothing more excellent has ever been granted to us by God. For the **Good** itself, which is God, could bestow nothing better on man than a complete likeness of His own divinity, as far as it is possible to achieve. For who would doubt that God is truth, free from the body, and providing for all? The philosopher, indeed, through moral instruction and that first education (which we mentioned), frees the soul from the appetite and sense of the body. Dialectic truly...

This contemplation provides the divine exemplar needed for ethical living and just political governance.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Marsilio Ficino’s letter to Count Giovanni Francesco Ippolito Gazolti concerning the definition and curriculum of philosophy.
