[...attains perfec]tion. He provides for men through civic teaching. Thus it happens that philosophy is both a gift from God and a likeness and most happy imitation of Him. If anyone is endowed with this, by his likeness to God, he will be the same on earth as God is in the heavens. Indeed, the philosopher is the mediator between God and men: a man toward God, and a god toward men. He is an intimate of God’s truth, a possessor of his own freedom, and a leader of the rest of men through civic prudence. Under such a governor, it is said that the **Golden Age** <note>A mythical era of peace and prosperity in Greek and Roman mythology.</note> once existed, and **Plato** prophesied it would one day return when power and wisdom coincide in the same soul. According to **Plato**, the souls of those who philosophize, having recovered their wings through wisdom and justice, fly back to their celestial homeland immediately after they have departed from the body. In the heavens, they perform the same duties as they did on earth. They rejoice with God in truth; they congratulate themselves in their freedom. They provide for men through piety, acting as if they were interpreters and prophets of God—which they had done here and continue to do there. They turn the souls of men toward God. They interpret the hidden mysteries of God for human minds. Therefore, the ancient theologians rightly honored the minds of those who philosophize—once released from the body—just like those **thirty thousand spirits** <note>original: "demonũ"; Ficino refers to Hesiod’s *Works and Days*, where 30,000 "daemons" or spirits act as guardians of mortal men.</note> of **Hesiod**, as semi-divine heroes and blessed spirits. 

Philosophy, therefore (to summarize in a few words), is the ascent of the soul from lower things to the heights, and from darkness to light. Its beginning is the instinct of the divine mind; the means are the faculties and disciplines we have described; the end is the possession of the **Supreme Good**; and finally, its fruit is the righteous governance of men. 

I have shared these things with our friend **Francesco Berlinghieri** <note>A Florentine diplomat and scholar, author of a famous rhymed geography based on Ptolemy.</note> as a philosophical companion. You also, **Giuliano del Borgo**, will share these same matters in the same spirit. Farewell.

### On the Life of Plato.

Marsilio Ficino to his friend Francesco Bandini, greetings.
I have attempted in recent days to paint the "Idea of the Philosopher" using Platonic colors. Truly, if I had brought **Plato** himself into our midst, I would have shown you not a mere picture of that Idea, but the **Idea itself** <note>Ficino plays on the Platonic theory of Forms (Ideas), suggesting Plato is the perfect embodiment of the concept of a philosopher.</note> of the true philosopher with my very fingers. Therefore, let us gaze intently upon **Plato**, so that we may see the philosopher, philosophy, and the Idea itself all at once.

### The Genealogy and Birth of Plato.

<margin>b</margin> **Plato** the Athenian, son of **Ariston** and **Perictione** (or Potone), traces his lineage from **Neptune** <note>The Roman name for the Greek god Poseidon.</note> on both sides. For **Solon** <note>The famous Athenian lawmaker and one of the Seven Sages.</note> descended from Nereus and Neptune. Solon’s brother, **Dropides**, fathered the elder **Critias**, from whom was born **Calaeschrus**, who had two sons: the younger **Critias** (who was one of the thirty governors of Athens) and **Glaucon**, the father of **Charmides** and **Perictione**. **Perictione**, having married **Ariston**, gave birth to **Plato**, **Adimantus**, and **Glaucon**, and also a daughter, **Potone**, who married **Eurymedon** and gave birth to **Speusippus**. On the other side, **Ariston**, Plato’s father, descended from **Codrus**, the son of **Melanthus**, who also (like Solon) trace their origin back to **Neptune**. It is famously reported in Athens that when **Ariston** was with **Perictione**...

### Education: Character: Training and Sobriety of Plato.

It is said that while he was an infant, bees poured honey onto his lips: a sign <note>original: "p̄sagiū"; a presage or omen.</note> of his future eloquence. They say **Socrates** saw in a dream a young swan <note>original: "oloris pullū"</note> grow feathers in his lap, which immediately sprouted wings and, with wings spread, flew high and gave forth the sweetest songs. The next day, when **Plato** was commended to him by his father, Socrates said this was the swan he had seen. He flourished in a poetic style in his youth; he composed elegies and two tragedies. These he himself gave to the fire <note>i.e., he burned his poems.</note> as soon as he first applied his mind to philosophy. He was taught his first letters by **Dionysius** his teacher. Then he studied under **Socrates** at the age of twenty. After Socrates' death, he devoted himself to **Cratylus** (a disciple of **Heraclitus**) and **Hermogenes** (who maintained the philosophy of **Parmenides**). At the age of twenty-eight, he went to **Megara** to join **Euclid** <note>Euclid of Megara, a Socratic philosopher, not the mathematician.</note> along with other students of Socrates. From there he set out for **Cyrene** and studied under **Theodorus** the mathematician; then he went to **Italy** to the **Pythagoreans**, specifically **Philolaus**, **Archytas of Tarentum**, and **Eurytus**. From these, he went to **Egypt** to the p... <note>original: "p."; likely "presbyteros" (priests) or "prophetas" (prophets).</note>

[...to the] prophets and priests. He had decided to proceed to the Indian Magi, but due to the wars in Asia, he abandoned this purpose. Returning finally to Athens, he lived his life in the **Academy**. He is said to have chosen this unhealthy spot in Attica—as even **Saint Basil** and **Jerome** confirm—so that the excessive vigor of the body might be pruned back, just as one prunes the over-luxuriance of a vine. Indeed, he possessed a most beautiful and robust physical build; thus, because of his broad shoulders, wide brow, and the excellent stature of his whole body—and also the richness of his speech—he was named **Plato** <note>The name Plato (Πλάτων) is derived from the Greek word *platýs*, meaning "broad" or "wide."</note>, though he had been named **Aristocles** at birth. There was nothing unseemly in him, except perhaps a somewhat thin voice and a certain protrusion under the neck that slightly disfigured him. Due to living in the Academy, he suffered from a quartan fever <note>A form of malaria where the fever recurs every four days.</note> for eighteen months, but through his sobriety and care, he recovered a strength even greater after the fever than before.

### The military service and the three voyages of Plato: The First Voyage.

He served as a soldier three times: first at **Tanagra**, second at **Corinth**, and third at **Delos**, where he even achieved victory. He sailed to **Sicily** three times. The first time was to see the island and the wonders of **Mount Etna** and its craters. He was then forty years old, at which time **Dionysius**, the son of **Hermocrates**, urged Plato to speak with him. When Plato there discussed tyranny, saying that it does not profit a man to have power useful only to himself unless he also excels in virtue, they say the offended and angry tyrant replied: "Your words are those of idle old men." To which Plato replied: "And yours savor of tyranny." Indignant at this, the tyrant first wished to kill him. Later, however, being pleaded with by **Dion** and **Aristomenes**, he did not do so. But he handed him over to **Pollis** the Lacedaemonian <note>A Spartan.</note>, who had come to him as an ambassador at that time, to be sold into slavery. Pollis brought him to **Aegina** and sold him, at which time **Charmander** also accused him as being liable for death. Indeed, according to a law promulgated among them, it was a capital crime if any Athenian set foot on that island. However, when it was argued by someone that he had come there for the sake of learning, and that the law spoke of [ordinary] men and not of the virtuous (who are above men), they released him, absolved. They decreed he should not be killed, but sold. By chance, **Anniceris** of Cyrene was present; he ransomed him for twenty minas <note>An ancient unit of currency.</note> and sent him back to Athens to his friends. The story goes that Pollis was later defeated by **Chabrias** and afterwards drowned at **Helice**, with a divine spirit <note>original: "demonio"; referring here to a supernatural sign or divine retribution.</note> announcing that he suffered such things because of his treatment of the philosopher. Nevertheless, **Dionysius** did not remain quiet; but when he learned what had happened to Plato, he wrote to him, begging him not to hurl insults at him. Plato wrote back that he did not have so much leisure time left over from philosophy that he could even remember Dionysius. To certain detractors who objected that Plato had been abandoned by Dionysius, he replied: "On the contrary, Dionysius was abandoned by Plato."

### The Second Voyage:

He set out a second time to **Dionysius the Younger**, having been summoned by him and by **Dion** for the sake of philosophizing. Led also by this hope, he believed that by his counsels he might bring it about that the tyranny there would become either a republic or a kingdom, and that he would see the form of government he had long and vehemently desired: namely, the highest philosophical rule, in which either philosophers govern or the governors philosophize. For he thought that cities could not otherwise avoid misery. All this was not done by force...

He released him and provided supplies. **Plato** returned to his homeland. Shortly after, **Dionysius** was driven from his tyranny by **Dion** and the citizens, paying the penalty for the crime committed against philosophy. **Plato** was received with wonderful honor in his homeland. There, although summoned to public affairs, he refused to join because the common people had accustomed themselves to evil ways.

### To whom Plato gave laws.

<margin>f</margin>
It is said that the **Arcadians** and **Thebans**, having founded a city of honorable size, asked him to establish a Republic for it; but when he understood that they were unwilling to follow equality, he decided it would be of no use. However, he gave laws to the **Syracusans** after the tyrant was expelled; and for the **Cretans**, in the newly founded city of **Magnesia**, he wrote laws arranged in twelve books. From among his close associates, he sent **Aristonymus** to the **Arcadians** to establish laws. To the people of **Elis** <note>Original: "ilios"</note> he sent **Phormio**. To the **Pyrrhaeans** <note>Original: "pyrteos"</note> he sent **Menedemus**.

### Continence, Gravity, and Courtesy of Plato.

<margin>v</margin>
He lived as a celibate and was extremely sober and (as **Aurelius Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo, who deeply admired Platonic philosophy.</note> affirms) chaste. Hence, even in old age, he is said to have performed the sacred rites of nature to absolve himself before the common people of the charge of sterility <note>Plato remained childless and unmarried; "rites of nature" likely refers to symbolic religious duties regarding family and lineage.</note>. As a youth, he was so composed by modesty that he was never caught laughing except moderately; moreover, no one ever saw him angry. For this reason, a boy educated by **Plato**, when he returned to his parents and saw his father shouting, said: "I never saw this in **Plato’s** house." But he was only secretly slightly angry at a boy who had committed a grave offense. He said to **Xenocrates**: "You beat this boy. For I am unable to do so because I am angry." He ate on any given day either only once or, if twice, very sparingly. He slept alone. He strongly criticized the opposite way of life. Toward loving youths, just like his master **Socrates**, he seemed somewhat more inclined. However, both were as continent in their reason as they were inclined in their senses toward what they loved as divine; how and in what way they spoke about love is sufficiently treated by us in our *Book on Love* <note>Ficino refers here to his own famous work, the *De Amore*, a commentary on Plato's *Symposium*.</note>. He wished to leave behind the memory of himself either in books or in friends. And although he was of a melancholic temperament <note>In Renaissance medicine, a "melancholic" temperament was often associated with genius and deep thought.</note> and of the most profound genius—as **Aristotle** writes—nevertheless he used many jokes and [urged] **Xenocrates**...

<margin>The principal disciples of Plato.</margin>
His disciples were: Speusippus the Athenian; Xenocrates the Chalcedonian; Aristotle the Stagirite; Philippus of Opus; Hestiaeus of Pontus <note>Original: "Esticus pintius"</note>; Dion of Syracuse; Amyclus; Heraclides; Erascus and Coriscus <note>Original: "Erascus & Doriscus"</note> of Scepsis; Timolaus of Cyzicus; Bebeon of Lampsacus; Pithon and Heraclides of Aenus; Hippothales and Callippus the Athenians; Demetrius of Amphipolis; Heraclides of Pontus and many others. They also say that Theophrastus was a listener of his, as well as the orator Hyperides, Chamaleon, Lycurgus, and Demosthenes; and also that Menesistratus was devoted to him. In the vestibule of the Academy was inscribed: "Let no one ignorant of geometry enter here." <note>This famous motto emphasized that mathematical study was the prerequisite for philosophical training.</note> Indeed, he wished this to be understood not only regarding the measure of lines, but also regarding the proper measure of the emotions.

<margin>The books of Plato.</margin>
He wrote a book on holiness: the *Euthyphro*. The *Apology of Socrates*. The *Crito*, concerning what he discussed with Socrates in prison. The *Phaedo*, on the immortality of the soul. The *Cratylus*, on the correct reasoning of names. The *Theaetetus*, on knowledge. The *Sophist*, on that which is. The *Statesman* <note>Original: "civilem"</note>, on kingship. The *Parmenides*, on the one principle of all things and the ideas. The *Philebus*, on the highest good. The *Symposium*, on love. The *Phaedrus*, on beauty. The *First Alcibiades*, on the nature of man. The *Second Alcibiades*, on prayer. The *Hipparchus*, on the desire for gain. The *Lovers*, on philosophy. The *Theages*, on wisdom. The *Charmides*, on temperance. The *Laches*, on courage. The *Lysis*, on friendship. The *Euthydemus*, the contentious one. The *Protagoras*, on morals. The *Gorgias*, on rhetoric. The *Meno*, on virtue. The *Greater Hippias*, on beauty; the *Lesser Hippias*, on lying. The *Menexenus*, on ancient Attic history. Ten books of the *Republic*. The *Timaeus*, on the nature of the world. The *Critias*, on ancient Attic history. The *Minos*, on law. Twelve books of the *Laws*. The *Epinomis*, or *The Philosopher*. Thirteen *Letters*. We ourselves have translated all these books of Plato from the Greek language into Latin. <note>The "we" refers to the 15th-century translator, likely Marsilio Ficino, whose Latin translations made Plato accessible to the Renaissance.</note> There are truly three types of Platonic dialogues: for he either refutes the sophists, exhorts the young, or teaches adults. Those things which Plato spoke with his own mouth in the *Letters*, the books of the *Laws*, or the *Epinomis*, he wishes to be held as most certain. However, those things disputed in the other books through the mouths of Socrates, Timaeus, Parmenides, or Zeno, he treats as probabilities.

<margin>The eloquence, wisdom, and authority of Plato.</margin>
The style of Plato (as Aristotle says) flows midway between prose and poetry; its sweetness and abundance are so great that Cicero said Plato was the most serious author and teacher of both understanding and speaking. He added: "If Jupiter had wished to speak in a human tongue, he would have spoken in no other than the tongue of Plato." Truly, there was such great learning in him that while before him all illustrious men among the Greeks traveled to foreign nations for the sake of wisdom, after Plato's time, all other nations flocked to Athens. And Aristotle, endowed with such miraculous talent...

...[Aristotle] was most eager for both established and new knowledge. <note>The OCR "ditus" is likely the end of "Aristoteles," as the text describes him as a student of Plato for twenty years.</note> When he came to Plato as a nearly grown man, he listened to him for twenty continuous years. Add to this that before he came to Plato, he was already advanced in letters. Afterward, he had Plato as his sole teacher. I pass over what is written by Cicero: "I would rather err with Plato than think correctly with the others." <note>Original Latin: "malo cum platone errare quam cum ceteris recte sentire." This is a famous quote from Cicero’s Tusculan Disputations expressing deep intellectual loyalty.</note> Furthermore, together with Panaetius, he calls him the "god of philosophers." I also pass over that remark of Quintilian: "Who could doubt that Plato is preeminent either in the sharpness of his arguments or in a certain divine and Homeric eloquence?" For his speech rises so far above prose—what the Greeks call "pedestrian" speech—that he seems to me to be inspired not by human genius, but by a certain Delphic oracle. Divine wisdom and integrity seem to have earned him a miraculous authority even in his own homeland, which is something that happens very rarely. 

When Plato returned from Sicily and arrived at that most magnificent celebration of the Olympics—which is like a gathering of the whole world—he was received with such joyful greetings by everyone that he seemed like a god sent down from heaven to mortals. You would have seen the games postponed and the spectacles of the athletes abandoned. You would see the boxers left alone; and what is more wonderful is that those who had come to the Olympics over such long stretches of land and sea for the sake of feeding their eyes, ears, and minds, forgot all pleasure and flocked to Plato. They gazed upon Plato. They rested in Plato as if in the most pleasant of inns. When someone was performing a tragedy and no one but Plato was present, some people objected that it was a disgrace for him to be there when no one else was; he replied: "This one man is more than the entire Athenian people."

<margin>The charity, magnanimity, and holiness of Plato.</margin>
For his great and constant mind, especially in the cause of his friends, is indicated by his letters, his contempt for the tyrant, and his defense of Dion. He boldly rebuked the tyrant Dionysius, even in the presence of witnesses, because he governed unjustly or because he deceived his friends; he was so far from flattering him. I pass over those smaller matters, such as this: Dionysius had ordered at a banquet that everyone should put on purple garments and dance. Aristippus danced immediately. Plato, however, refused, saying that womanly clothes do not suit a philosopher. 

Furthermore, when the wicked Crobilus had brought an accusation against the most brave general Chabrias and had threatened him with a capital trial, and when Chabrias had been abandoned by the rest of the citizens for fear of danger, Plato alone was always present to provide him aid. When the slanderer Crobilus, in order to deter him from his defense, said threateningly: "You come to provide a defense for others, ungrateful that the poison of Socrates also awaits you," Plato himself replied: "Long ago, Crobilus, when I was a soldier for my own dignity, I was not slow in the face of intolerable dangers; now, for my duty and the safety of a friend, though you may threaten swords, poison, and fire, I refuse no danger." 

When Socrates was most unjustly shut up in prison, Plato gathered money so that he might ransom the innocent man; and while the judgment was being carried out, ascending the platform, he began to speak thus: "Men of Athens, although I am younger than all those who have ascended the tribunal..." <note>This anecdote suggests Plato attempted to speak at Socrates' trial but was shouted down or prevented by the judges.</note> But the tyrant judges, fearing his authority...

and move the citizens with his eloquence. Suddenly they interrupted him, shouting: "Come down!" <note>Original Latin: "descende." This refers to the crowd demanding he stop speaking or step down from a podium.</note> Plato went home. For he was suffering as much from a physical illness at that time as the others were suffering from the seeds of their own disease. <note>The author contrasts Plato’s physical ailment with the moral or intellectual "sickness" of the crowd.</note> Truly, the persecutors of Socrates paid their penalties shortly thereafter. 

When a certain fellow student was driven by envy because Xenocrates was so dear and well-received by Plato, he attempted to stir up animosity against him by reporting many insults allegedly spoken by Xenocrates against Plato. In the middle of this speech, Plato rejected the accusation and refused to listen. The flatterer persisted, affirming the charge with severe solemnity. Finally, when the man swore by all the gods and goddesses, Plato, in order to free himself from the man's persistence, said: "So be it. But Xenocrates is so strong in his faith and gravity that he would never have said those things unless he judged it beneficial to do so." 

The life of Xenocrates, as recorded by Diogenes <note>Referring to Diogenes Laertius, a biographer of Greek philosophers.</note>, bears witness that Xenocrates, Plato's beloved disciple, imitated the gravity and magnanimity of his teacher; his life is indeed a model of courage and holiness. Plutarch is witness that Dion <note>Dion of Syracuse, a student of Plato and political leader.</note> also imitated him. Furthermore, Philiscus, in describing the life of the orator Lycurgus, says: "Lycurgus was a great man and many things were performed excellently by him, which no one could have done who had not been a student of Plato." 

When Demosthenes was fleeing from Antipater and Archias promised to save his life with flattering words, he replied: "Far be it from me that I should prefer to live basely rather than die honestly, after I have heard Xenocrates and Plato discussing the immortality of the soul." The same Demosthenes, writing to a certain fellow student named Heracleodorus, rebuked him because, after hearing Plato, he neglected the liberal arts and led a life that was hardly honorable. He said: "Are you not ashamed to neglect those things which you received from Plato?" 

Dionysius, writing to Speusippus <note>Speusippus was Plato's nephew and successor as head of the Academy.</note>, said: "Plato used to teach those who crossed his threshold for free, but you demand tribute and take it from those who come both willingly and unwillingly." Laertius also blames him because he did not imitate the chastity, courage, and gentleness of Plato as Xenocrates did. Truly, I cannot remain silent regarding the courage of Xenocrates: when Dionysius said to Plato, "Someone will take your head," Xenocrates, who was present, replied: "No one shall do so before they cut off this head of mine."

...then, regarding what the title of the book should be, he replied that it should not be contradicted. To this, Plato asked: "Why then do you do this very thing yourself? Why do you contradict those who contradict you? Why do you consult me, if you forbid yourself from being contradicted?" <note>This anecdote illustrates Plato's wit regarding the self-defeating nature of refusing intellectual opposition.</note> 

Leo, a powerful citizen, was being criticized in a gathering because he had delivered loud and immoderate outbursts in the senate. Plato said of this: "This is truly what it means to be a 'Leo.'" <note>A pun on the name Leo, which means "Lion" in Latin and Greek; Plato is suggesting the man acts with the ferocity or noise of a wild beast.</note> 

To Diogenes the Cynic, who said that he could indeed see these human things <note>Referring to physical objects like tables or cups.</note> but could not see "Ideas" <note>The Platonic "Ideas" or "Forms" are the perfect, abstract archetypes of things, which Plato argued were more real than physical objects.</note> at all, Plato replied: "That is no wonder. For you possess and use the eyes by which these physical things are seen, but you do not use the mind, by which alone those Ideas are discerned." 

When his disciples were marveling that Xenocrates—who was severe throughout his whole life—had said something that was received with laughter, Plato asked: "Why are you surprised that roses and lilies sometimes grow among thorns?" 

While he was living, he used to say frequently: "Place labor before leisure, unless perhaps you think that rust is preferable to splendor." He very often urged the youth toward a blessed life with this reasoning: "Observe the contrary natures of virtue and pleasure. For the momentary sweetness of the latter is followed by sudden repentance and perpetual pain. But the brief labors of the former lead to eternal pleasure." 

When he had seen a certain man playing at dice, he rebuked him. When the man said that Plato was reprehending him for a small matter, Plato replied: "But habit is no small thing." 

He was accustomed to advising the drunken and the angry to look at themselves diligently in a mirror; he believed they would immediately depart from such ugliness. He greatly detested drunkenness and excessive sleep. He said it was of the greatest importance in educating children that they be accustomed to finding joy only in honorable things. Otherwise, he said that pleasure was the "bait of evils." 

He added that health of the soul is true philosophy. He viewed other faculties not so much as philosophy, but as ornaments. He believed nothing was sweeter to the mind than to speak and hear the truth. For nothing is either better or more lasting than truth. 

When certain people asked what kinds of possessions should be especially prepared for one’s sons, he said: "Those which fear neither a hailstorm, nor the violence of men, nor even Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus, representing divine or natural catastrophe.</note> himself." 

Consulted on the manner of a son's education, he said: "The same care that must be used in planting and directing young trees must also be used in begetting and instructing sons. Here is the labor; there is the pleasure. But we must take care lest, falling asleep in this task, we seem to be anything but watchful." 

To a certain Philedonus, who criticized Plato because he was no less eager and diligent in learning than in teaching, and who asked how long he wished to be a student, Plato replied: "As long as I do not regret becoming better and more skillful." 

<margin>
What kind of princes and those governing the state should be.
</margin>

Asked what the difference was between the skillful and the unskillful, he responded: "The same as between a doctor and a sick man." 

He used to say that for princes, there is no more excellent kind of possession than the friendship of those men who do not know how to "play the middleman." <note>Original Latin: "cauponari," meaning to act like a shopkeeper or to haggle; here it refers to sycophants who trade flattery for favors.</note> Wisdom is no less necessary to a prince than the soul is to the body. He said that republics would be most happy if either philosophers should rule, or at least if those who govern should, by some divine lot, practice philosophy. For nothing is more pestilential than power and audacity when they are joined with ignorance. He also said that subjects tend to be of the same character as their princes. A magistrate must think not of his own good, but of the public good; he must care not for just one part of the city, but for the whole.

->FOURTH [BOOK] 112<-

## How much Plato disregarded human affairs and how much he loved the divine.

He sought daily to prove that only eternal things are truly real, while temporal things are merely "resemblances of the truth." <note>original: "verri similia"</note> He believed that for the soul to sleep in the body, and for it to desire or fear what the senses crave, was nothing other than a dream. Therefore, he taught that all these earthly things should be utterly despised; to avoid the evils with which the world is filled, one must flee toward the eternal. He argued that there was no other way to escape them. He also fulfilled in practice what he preached. For although he was destined to be a leader in the republic by both hereditary right and the favor of the citizens, he completely rejected all civil honors. Although he was very wealthy by inheritance, he bestowed everything upon his brothers except for a small suburban estate which they called the Academy. <note>The Academy was a gymnasium and grove near Athens where Plato established his famous school of philosophy.</note> Content with this alone, he lived his life; and if he stood out as a teacher and friend to princes, he nevertheless accepted no riches from them. King Dionysius used to say: "Aristippus always asks for money; Plato always asks for books." Add to this that he never took a wife, nor did he live in the city; free from all things, he served the truth alone. Regarding this, Saint Jerome <note>original: "diuus hieronymus"</note> said: "Plato traveled through Egypt, and to Archytas of Tarentum, and that coast of Italy which was once called Great Greece, <note>Magna Graecia: the Greek-speaking areas of Southern Italy.</note> with great labor. Thus, he who was a master and powerful in Athens—whose teachings echoed through the gymnasiums of the Academy—became a pilgrim and a disciple, preferring to learn the truths of others with modesty rather than to impudently thrust his own ideas upon them." Finally, while he was pursuing learning as if it were fleeing across the whole world, he was captured by pirates and sold; he even obeyed a most cruel tyrant as a captive, a conquered man, and a slave. Yet, because he was a philosopher, he remained greater than the one who bought him. These are the words of Jerome.
<margin>r</margin>

### The piety and gratitude of Plato.

He was grateful to God, from whom he said the beginning of thinking, speaking, and acting in all matters must arise; and he himself always acted on this principle. 
<margin>g</margin> Furthermore, he gave thanks to God daily that he had been born a human being and not a brute beast; that he was a Greek and not a barbarian; and that he lived in the times of Socrates. His dialogues serve as a testimony to how grateful he was to all his teachers and friends. In these works, he honors them all wonderfully, and he attributes his own books to Socrates. For not only does he introduce Socrates as the speaker in almost all his dialogues, but he also writes that all the things he composed were not his own, but belonged to Socrates.

### What Plato affirmed and those who confirmed him.

In those matters which are subject to the senses, he maintained the views of Heraclitus; <note>Heraclitus was a pre-Socratic philosopher known for his doctrine of change, or "flux."</note> 
<margin>i</margin> furthermore, in those matters which pertain to the intellect, he most closely agreed with Pythagoras. <note>Pythagoras emphasized mathematics and the immortality of the soul.</note> However, in civil matters, he embraced the views of his own Socrates. These are the things he asserted everywhere: That God provides for all things. That the souls of men are immortal. That there will be rewards for the good and punishments for the wicked. Augustine says in his book *Against the Academics*: "The authority of Christ is to be placed above all." However, if a matter must be dealt with through reason, he says he finds in the Platonists that which does not conflict with the sacred writings of the Christians. Dionysius the Areopagite indicated the same. Later, Eusebius and Cyril declared this more extensively. Hence, Augustine says in his book *On True Religion*: "With the change of a few details, the Platonists would become Christians."

And in his *Confessions*, [Saint Augustine] relates that he found almost the entire prologue of the Gospel of John the Evangelist among the Platonists. <note>Augustine famously argued that Platonic philosophy was the closest to Christian truth, though it lacked the concept of the Word becoming flesh.</note> Therefore, in the second book of *The City of God*, he says: Labeo, <note>Cornelius Labeo, a 3rd-century Roman theologian who wrote on the religion of the Etruscans and the nature of gods.</note> a theologian among the pagans, thought Plato should be counted among the demigods, like Hercules and Romulus. However, he places demigods above heroes. But he places both among the divinities. Nevertheless, I do not doubt that this man, whom he calls a demigod, should be preferred not only to heroes but even to the gods themselves. For this reason, [Augustine] says he chose the Platonists above others because they felt more correctly about divine and human matters than the other philosophers. Marcus Varro <note>A prolific Roman scholar and contemporary of Cicero.</note> had judged this before, and Apuleius <note>The author of *The Golden Ass*, who also wrote a treatise *On Plato and His Doctrine*.</note> made Plato not only superior to heroes but equal to the gods, clearly because he had penetrated the entrances to divine things. Plato was endowed with such modesty that, although he had acquired a marvelous authority above others, when asked by someone how far his teachings should be followed, he replied: "Until someone more sacred appears on earth who opens the fountain of truth to all, whom everyone should finally follow." He added that he discovered nothing by his own light, but only by divine light. As for what he felt regarding philosophy, <note>original: "pbia" (philosophia)</note> we have discussed it enough in our book *On Love* and in our *Theology*. <note>This identifies the author as Marsilio Ficino, the Renaissance Neoplatonist who wrote *The Platonic Theology* and a commentary on the *Symposium* called *De Amore*.</note>

<margin>n</margin> But he passed away on his own [birthday]; and he completed eighty-one years without any decline. Therefore, the Magi who were then in Athens sacrificed to Plato, thinking his lot was greater than a human's because he had completed the most perfect number, which nine multiplied nine times produces. <note>81 (9 x 9) was considered a mystical and perfect number in Pythagorean and Platonic thought.</note> And what is wonderful, even at that age and on that very day, he was writing. About this, Cicero says: "There is also the peaceful and light old age of a life led quietly, purely, and elegantly, such as we have heard of Plato's, who died while writing in his eighty-first year." Seneca also affirms that this happened to Plato by the benefit of his sobriety and diligence. Others say he returned to the heavens while writing; others while reclining at a wedding after the tables were removed; others while discussing. Aristotle consecrated an altar and a statue to Plato in a temple with this epigram:

<margin>that is, an altar. Aristotle</margin>
"He dedicated this to Plato, a man whom it is a sin for the wicked to praise." Aristotle added: "He who alone—by life, teaching, character, and speech—admonished all and gave monuments so that by virtue they might lead a happy life; no future ages will bring such a man." Other wise men also added many poems in praise of Plato. But there are three principal epigrams. The meaning of the first is this: "He excelled all in temperance and justice. Truly, he so surpassed in wisdom that he completely overcame all envy." The meaning of the second is this: "Plato has been translated into the number of the gods. Distant nations honor him because he himself knew the divine life and showed it to others." The meaning of the third is this: "Phoebus [Apollo] fathered Asclepius and Plato; so that the former might heal bodies, and the latter might heal souls." Furthermore, Mithridates, king of the Persians, [placed] a statue of Plato in the Academy...

This was clearly because the former was most human in his life and natural in his science, while the latter, in both his science and his life, applied himself most of all to divine matters.

### Defense of the Character of Plato.

I will now put an end to my words if I add a few things again. There are certain common versifiers who undeservedly usurp the name of poets. These men, provoked as much by the difference in their character as by the malice of envy, play most impudently against every excellent man. To these men, a certain extreme license is granted against the good rather than the bad, especially in our current age. But I would rather not remember our own times, which seem as inept at pursuing virtue as they are adept at persecuting it. 

Therefore, such petty poets of old did not hesitate to bite the divine Plato (whom the Greeks called the son of Apollo) and Socrates (judged by the oracle of Apollo to be the wisest of the Greeks). Diogenes Laertius <note>A 3rd-century biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note> greatly detested their impiety. And as he himself declares, the ridiculous insults of the comic poets were increased by Aristippus of Cyrene—a most wretched man and an adversary of every excellent person of his time. Just as he slandered many others who were most modest and learned with a certain fabricated history, he did the same to his teacher Socrates and his fellow students Xenophon and Plato. He even forged certain lustful poems about courtesans and boys in their names, clearly so that he might obtain for himself a freer license for sinning by the false example of great philosophers. 

But Aristotle, to whom "truth was a closer friend than Plato," <note>original: *veritas magis quam plato fuit amica*; a reference to the famous proverb "Plato is my friend, but truth is a greater friend."</note> could not tolerate such false slanders against this holy man. For in his elegies to Eudemus, he sang those things about Plato which we mentioned earlier, granting him this above all: that the profane should not only refrain from disparaging Plato in any way, but they should not even dare to name his famous name with a profane mouth under the pretext of praise. Nor was he content with the elegy; as Olympiodorus <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist who wrote a biography of Plato.</note> relates, he also composed a magnificent oration in praise of Plato. Therefore, let the hounds of hell fall silent among the living, and let them accompany Cerberus <note>The three-headed dog that guards the gates of the Underworld.</note> with their barking in the underworld. Let us, however, venerate the life and wisdom of Plato, which is most highly approved by the judgment of the wise. And together with Apuleius of Madaura, let us freely proclaim: "We of the Platonic family know nothing but what is festive, joyful, celestial, and supreme."

To inform you of our current studies: I am composing a book on the providence of God and the freedom of human choice <note>original: *libero arbitrio*; the classic theological debate on how God's foreknowledge coexists with human will</note>, in which I refute, to the best of my ability, those judgments of astrologers which detract from providence and freedom. Therefore, Bernardo, as often as you see him, bid him be well in the name of Marsilio. June 14, 1477.

->Marsilio Ficino to the most distinguished orator Marcus Aurelius. Greetings.<-

<margin>s</margin> If it were permitted for you to commend your own things to yourself, I would most highly commend to you my close friend Nicolaus, who is gifted in letters and character. ->Marsilio Ficino to the most distinguished lawyer and knight, Bernardo Bembo. Greetings.<-

<margin>a</margin> I received today, Bernardo, from our Marcus Aurelius, a certain letter that was entirely Mercurial <term>Mercurial: referring to Mercury, the god of messages and eloquence, associated with speed and intellect</term> in its very form and very much like its father, but born, as I think, with Saturn rising <note>In astrology, Saturn is associated with delays and slowness; Ficino is joking about how long the letter took to arrive.</note>. Indeed, walking with heavier steps, although it departed from the Venetian waters on the sixteenth day of May, it finally arrived at our shores on the nineteenth of June. I embraced it with the greatest joy and said in congratulation: "You have come at last. Your devotion has conquered the unfortunate journey." 

Even if this letter, as if born under Saturn, was somewhat slower in its motion, nevertheless, as if conceived by Mercury, it seems to have been most swift in its effect. For that which it asks of us today, it had already fulfilled while it was being born. Truly, on those same days in May when the "golden" <note>original: *aureus*; a pun on his friend's name, Marcus Aurelius</note> Aurelius wrote to me, I—driven by some hidden and almost divine instinct, whether from the letter or his Muse—dedicated a certain short work to Aurelius; which, unless it too has been Saturnian in its gait, I believe has already reached you. 

Observe for a moment, Bernardo, the wonderful power of our guiding spirits <term>geniorum: the "genius" or tutelary spirit believed to guide a person's character and fate</term>. While that Marcus was giving himself to me freely, I, by right, was giving the whole of myself to him in return. And as he embraced me, I was marvelously embracing him. And so, with a certain celestial spirit breathing together, we conspired into one almost without knowing it. I think indeed that either Mercury himself or Apollo <note>original: *Phoebus*</note> positioned in Gemini—so similarly did they tune the twin lyres of Aurelius and Marsilio—that when one sounds, the other resounds in turn. And from both, that sweet name "Bembo" will echo back <note>original: *bembireboet*; a playful invented verb combining "Bembo" and "re-echo"</note>; a name musical to the Graces and most pleasing to the Muses. Fare you well. But I see my Bernardo; for I know the nature of the man...

->When love is kindled by a breathing of the divine spirit, the one who is loved always loves in return; often, while one is thinking, the other thinks the very same thing.<-

# Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to the most distinguished orator Marco Aurelio. Greetings.

Your very elegant letter was delivered to us yesterday, most learned Marcus; a letter sweeter to me than honey and more precious than gold. But what am I doing? I am not permitted to proceed further in this praise now, lest I seem perhaps too vain if I should attempt to praise enough a letter that already praises me more than enough. 

Therefore, let us begin again from another point, if you please. When love is kindled in our minds by a certain breathing of the celestial spirit, the one who is loved always loves back. Often, while one is thinking, the other thinks the same thing in a similar way. For the celestial Author <note>God</note>, since He embraces both friends as the common cause of all things, creates a mutual affection in those who love. This affection of the lover—which hangs down from heaven through a human being—leaps back in turn upon the smooth face of humanity and into the hollows of heaven, creating an echo. 

Greetings, then, my celestial friend. Greetings always in God, the author of our benevolence. Neither the distance of lands, Marcus, nor any intervals of time seem to have been able to interrupt this celestial and perpetual love of ours while it was rising, nor delay it once it had grown; for as soon as one loved, the other soon loved by a certain divine fate. Also, while one was thinking and writing, the other at almost the same moment both thought and wrote the same thing. 

I think you have noticed, Aurelio—if you have just received that little work of mine <note>original: *opusculum*; likely a short philosophical treatise</note> recently sent to you—that at the very time you were writing to me, I was also writing to you in turn. Moreover, my letter would have signified and requested exactly the same things as yours. To me, indeed, nothing in human affairs is more fortunate than to have emerged as an equal through this affection to a man than whom, I hear, no one is superior in virtue. Nothing is more precious than to happily possess such and so great a "possessor" of myself. 

I have, therefore, everything I was seeking with my whole mind. But I grieve over this one thing: that I am by no means that "whole" which you yourself were seeking. My Aurelio: if you cannot have what you want, at least want to have what you can. Accept your Marsilio, Marcus—the whole of him, however small he may be. I pray you, do not look any further at that image <note>original: *simulacrum*; here meaning the idealized version of Ficino that Aurelio had imagined</note> which you had fashioned from the start. For Ficino is but a single member of that image. Look rather, friend, at what you actually possess than at what you imagine. In this way, you will recognize that you possess not a part of someone, but a whole something. For it is better to enjoy some "whole" pygmy than a mere limb of a vast giant.

->Nothing is weaker than human love; nothing is firmer than divine love.<-

# Marsilio Ficino to the most distinguished lawyer and knight, Bernardo Bembo. Greetings.

<margin>5</margin> You write an oratory letter to us, which is both poetic and amorous. But I do not know why you offer excuses in vain for something that no one at all finds fault with. Take care that where love is perfect <note>original: *perfectus est amor*</note>, you do not imagine that even the slightest bit of offense could ever occur. Perhaps you can offend charity in this one way alone: if you think she can ever be offended. 

Human love is indeed a thing full of anxious fear <note>original: *Res est solliciti plena timoris amor*; Ficino is quoting the Roman poet Ovid, *Heroides* 1.12</note>. Divine charity, however—if we listen to Paul—believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Nor does it ever fail <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13</note>. Or if we listen to John the Evangelist: Fear does not dwell in love, but perfect charity drives out all fear <note>A reference to 1 John 4:18</note>. 

Hence our Aurelius Augustine exclaims: He alone admits no dear one to his heart, to whom all are not dear in Him <note>God</note> who is not admitted <note>original: *Solus nullum charum admittit; cui omnes in illo chari sunt qui non admittitur*</note>. But I have somehow begun a certain "homily," as they say, right here. And I was delivering the duties of charity to that man whom the Florentine people admire, as a kind of image of charity and example of humanity.

*In these things which are by no means sufficient for themselves, we strive too much in vain for our own sufficiency.*

->Marsilio Ficino to the human race. Health and Greetings.<-

<margin>5</margin> You seek sufficiency <note>original: *sufficientia*; the state of having enough or being self-sufficient</note> everywhere with this purpose: that after you have found this one thing, you search for nothing further. But you always seek many things for this very reason: because you never attain this one thing. Do you want me to tell you the reason why you never attain sufficiency? Perhaps because you seek it outside yourself. 

If, therefore, mortal riches cannot suffice for an immortal soul, take care that at least the soul itself suffices for them. Note what I say. I do not say that the soul should satisfy itself. For how can he who is both made and perfected by another satisfy himself? Alas, wretched as we are, we strive too much in vain for our own sufficiency in these things which are by no means sufficient for themselves. 

Indeed, only that which is enough for itself satisfies everyone in every way. But nothing can be enough for itself except the infinite Good, which is from itself and toward itself. Here, then, only here, I say, let us seek what will satisfy us. And let us not be weary. No one ever follows the Good in vain who follows it well. For the Good itself, because it is infinite, flourishes and overflows everywhere and on all sides, and our desire to follow it well is undoubtedly something good. Only he who follows various individual goods for the sake of the supreme Goodness itself—through which each thing is good and is preserved—truly wills and follows the Good.

*A sudden transition from the least light to the greatest, and from the greatest to the least, hinders the vision.*

->Marsilio Ficino to Riccardo Angeleri of Anghiari, the distinguished theologian. Health and Greetings.<-

<margin>c</margin> Men of state <note>original: *ciuiles viri*; those involved in the "active life" of politics and civic duty</note> often rebuke philosophers because they seem, for the most part, inept at governing human affairs. Philosophers, on the other hand, frequently find fault with men of state because they are most inept at the contemplation of divine things. What then shall we say to these things? It is not our place between these...

### BOOK FOUR

...to settle such great disputes. But our Plato must be called here as arbiter: whom God himself appointed for both human and divine matters. He, therefore, judges that both citizens and philosophers were established from the beginning to carry out both duties—provided they do not jump suddenly from one extreme to the other, but move by the proper steps. It is better to translate Plato’s own Greek words from the seventh book of the *Republic* <note>original: *de rep. septimo*</note> here, word for word.

"After this, you may contemplate our nature, in respect to its enlightenment and its ignorance, through an image such as this. Imagine in your mind a kind of cave <note>original: *speluncā*; this begins the famous Allegory of the Cave</note> under the earth, whose entrance lies open to the light, extending through the whole length of the cavern. In it are men who have been nurtured there since childhood, with their necks and legs so bound that they are forced to remain motionless and look only at what is in front of them. Their heads are held fast by bonds so that they cannot turn them around. Behind them, however, from above and far off, the light of a fire is suspended. Between the fire and the bound men, a path runs above, along which a low wall has been built. It is like the screens <note>original: *cortinæ*</note> that illusionists <note>original: *præstigiatorib⁹*</note> who create wonders set up before the eyes of spectators, over which they show their marvels.

Think again of men behind the wall carrying vessels and various artifacts that project above the wall, as well as stone and wooden statues of men and other animals, crafted in various ways. And as is natural, some of those carrying these things are silent, while others speak. They are like us. For first of all, do you think such people see anything, either of themselves or of the men next to them, except the shadows <note>original: *umbras*</note> which fall from the fire onto the opposite part of the cave? And what of the things being carried past? Do they not see only the shadows? If, then, they were able to talk to one another, would they not think that the things they saw before them were the reality? And if an echo resonated from the opposite side of the prison, whenever one of the passers-by spoke, do you think they would believe anything was speaking except the passing shadow? Altogether, then, such people would judge nothing to be true except the shadows of manufactured things.

Now, on the other hand, consider what the release from their bonds and the cure for their ignorance would be like. If one of them were released and suddenly forced to stand up, turn his neck, walk, and look toward the light itself, he would feel immediate pain; because of the glare, he would be unable to look at the very things whose shadows he saw before. Then, if someone told him that what he had seen before were mere trifles <note>original: *nugas*</note>, but that now he was closer to true things and was looking more truly—and if the person pointed to each of the passers-by and asked what it was—do you not think he would be at a loss? Would he not judge that the things he saw before were more true than what was being shown to him now? And if he were forced to look at the light itself, do you not think his eyes would suffer? He would turn back to the things he could easily see before, believing them to be clearer than what was suddenly being offered. And if someone were to drag him by force up the rough and steep path, not letting go until he had been pulled into the light of the sun, do you not think he would be distressed while being dragged? And when he reached the light, his eyes filled with brilliance, he would be hesitant and able to see nothing of the things that are now considered true by men.

Therefore, there is a need for habituation <note>original: *consuetudine*</note> first, if he is to inspect the things above."

# BOOK [FOUR]

...at first he will more easily observe [shadows]. After these, he will see the images of men and other things in the water. Then, later, he will look at the things themselves; and after that, he will more easily contemplate the things in the heavens and the heaven itself at night, while he gazes at the light of the stars and the moon, rather than if he were to look at the sun itself and its brightness during the day. And so, at last, he will look up at the sun itself—no longer seeing its reflections in the water or in a place where it does not belong—but he will behold the sun itself, by itself, in its own domain, and he will be able to recognize what kind of thing it is. He will finally realize that it is the sun that governs the seasons and the years, that rules everything in the <term>visible world</term><note>original: *sub coelo*; literally "under the sky," referring to the physical world we perceive with our senses</note>, and is in some way the cause of all those things they used to see in the cave.

What then? If he recalls his former dwelling, the "wisdom" of the people there, and his former chains, do you not think he would consider himself happy for the change and pity the others? Moreover, if they used to grant honors and praises to one another, and give prizes to the person who could most sharply discern the passing shadows and best remember which usually came first, which followed, and which moved together—and from these observations could best predict the future—do you think he would desire those honors or envy those who are honored and powerful among the cave-dwellers? Would he not rather feel what **Homer** says—that he would choose "to be a servant to a landless man" <note>This is a reference to *Odyssey* 11.489, where the ghost of Achilles says he would rather be a poor servant on earth than king of the dead</note> and suffer anything else rather than be deceived by those old opinions and live in such misery?

Consider this also: if that man should descend again and take the same seat he had before, would he not be overwhelmed by darkness, having suddenly left the sunlight? And if he were required to judge those shadows again and compete with those who had been perpetually bound, at a time when his eyes were still swimming and before they had adjusted—which would take no short time—would he not provoke laughter? They would say of him that since he went up, he has returned with his eyes ruined, and that it is not even worth trying to ascend. And as for anyone who tried to release them and lead them upward, if they could catch him, they would surely kill him.

This entire image, my friend, must be applied to what was said before. This prison corresponds to the <term>visible world</term> <note>original: *mundi machinam*; the "machine of the world" or the physical universe</note> perceived by the eyes. The light of the fire in the cave corresponds to the power of the sun. Finally, if you interpret the ascent and the viewing of the upper world as the soul's journey into the <term>intelligible region</term> <note>The realm of abstract concepts and divine truths, accessible only through the mind rather than the senses</note>, you will not wander from my own hope, since you wish to hear my opinion. God knows whether it is true. 

But these things appear to me as follows: I believe that in the intelligible order, the **Idea of the Good** is the highest thing, and it is seen only with great effort. But once it is seen, one must conclude that it is the cause of all things right and beautiful. In the visible world, it created light and the lord of light [the sun]; in the intelligible world, it is the sovereign that produces truth and reason. It is necessary for anyone who wishes to act wisely, whether in private or in public, to know this Idea. 

Come now and consider this: do not be surprised that those who reach this height are unwilling to involve themselves in human affairs, for their minds are always drawn upward. This is quite likely, if we follow the logic of the image. But what about this...

**P 4**

Do you think it is a thing to wonder at, if someone—returning from divine spectacles to these human miseries—appears clumsy and is ridiculed? This is especially true if, before they grow accustomed to the current darkness, they are forced (while still stumbling) to contend in law courts or elsewhere regarding the shadows of justice, or the statues whose shadows these are. They are forced to debate the interpretations of those who have never seen **Justice** itself. 

But if anyone has an active mind, they will remember that the eyes are usually troubled in two ways and for two causes: both when we descend from light into shadow, and when we emerge from darkness into the light. One should believe the soul is affected in the same way whenever one sees it troubled or unable to see something clearly. Therefore, one will not break into laughter without thought, but will carefully inquire: is this soul descending from a brighter life and being overwhelmed by new darkness? Or is it rising from great ignorance toward a radiant vision, only to fail because it is overwhelmed by the excessive, flashing brilliance? Indeed, one would approve of the state of the former and judge their life happy, while feeling pity for the latter. But if one did choose to laugh, it would be less foolish to laugh at this one <note>The person rising into the light</note> than at the one who fell from the light above. These are the words of the divine **Plato**; nothing should be taken from them, nor can anything be added. Therefore, farewell.

### That the soul is immortal. And why, though it is divine, it often leads a life similar to a beast.

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Nesi, a man most distinguished in letters and character. Greetings.

<margin>Note</margin> Unless there were a divine vigor within us and a celestial origin for our minds, we could in no way recognize the inadequacy of mortal things. We would never imagine or desire anything at all beyond the order of physical things. No one would ever struggle to resist the body, even in the smallest matter. We would be satisfied at last by earthly riches. Either everyone, or certainly most people, would rest in this middle region of the world as if it were their natural birthplace and home. 

But now, since our circumstances are far different, I believe—and it is no empty faith—that our race is of divine origin. However, if we are divine, why do we so often lead lives like beasts? It is because the condition of this natural region is established such that we use our **senses** (like brute animals) far earlier than we use our **reason** (as humans). Furthermore, far more numerous and obvious incitements present themselves to our senses than to our mind. 

Lastly, there is only one "Man" within us, but there are many "Beasts." It is worthwhile to look at that image of ours which Plato paints in the ninth book of his *Republic*. Let us imagine a certain image of the soul, like those creatures of old—the <term>Chimera</term><note>A fire-breathing monster with a lion's head, a goat's body, and a serpent's tail</note>, <term>Scylla</term><note>A sea monster with many heads and barking dogs at her waist</note>, and <term>Cerberus</term><note>The three-headed hound of the underworld</note>—and many others in which various forms are said to have grown together into one. Imagine, then, a single shape of a very multifaceted beast that has many heads all around it—heads, I say, partly of domestic animals and partly of wild ones. A beast that can transform and produce all these things from itself.

# BOOK

Furthermore, add to these the form of a lion from above. To this, add one of a human; let the first <note>The "multi-headed beast" of desire mentioned in the preceding context</note> be the largest, while the second and third are narrower. Now, join these three together so they grow into one and cohere with each other. Surround them from the outside with the image of a single human being, so that to someone who cannot see the interior, but sees only the outer covering, the creature appears to be a single animal—a human. 

Therefore, let us say to the person who asserts that it is profitable for this man to act unjustly, and that living justly is of no benefit: he asserts nothing other than that it is profitable for him to feed that multi-headed beast and the lion, making the lion part even stronger, while allowing the human part to starve and weaken until, through feebleness, he is dragged wherever those other beasts snatch him. In this state, he neither tames them nor reconciles them to one another; instead, he allows the individual parts to tear each other with bites and to devour one another in their fighting. 

However, if someone says that just duties are profitable, they will advise doing and saying those things by which the "inner human" of such a creature may obtain the greatest power. Like a farmer <note>original: "colonus"</note>, he should take care of the creature, nurturing and watering the domestic heads while immediately pruning away the wild ones. He does this by taking the nature of the lion as an ally for this task, caring for all parts in common and reconciling them to one another through mutual goodwill. 

Thus, in every way, the one who praises just things speaks the truth, while the one who praises unjust things lies. Whether regarding pleasure, honor, or profit, the praiser of justice speaks truly; the critic, however, offers nothing of substance, nor does he even know what it is he disapproves of. 

Thus far **Plato**. That distribution of our soul’s figure agrees with what is read in **Plato’s** *Timaeus*. There, he divides the soul into three powers, or parts: namely, the natures of **Reasoning** <note>original: "raciocinandi"</note>, **Anger** <note>original: "iraſcendi," also known as the "spirited" part</note>, and **Desire** <note>original: "cōcupiſcēdi"</note>. 

He assigned the **Rational** power to the head, as if it were a supreme queen in a fortress, especially because the head seems to work harder than all else in contemplation, and the senses flourish there most abundantly. Furthermore, he placed the power of **Anger** in the heart <note>original: "præcordiis," literally the diaphragm or chest area</note>, because these parts are most agitated in moments of rage, boldness, and fear. Finally, he gave the nature of **Desire** to the liver, because within it resides the natural vigor for digesting food and increasing physical lust. 

Accordingly, in the *Phaedrus*, he calls **Reason** the **charioteer** <note>original: "aurigam"</note>, since by a certain natural order it is the leader of the remaining parts. He joins to this charioteer twin horses: one white and the other black. Regarding our purpose, these horses represent the powers of the heart and the liver, which ought to obey Reason as their charioteer. The "magnanimity" <note>Spiritedness or courage</note> assigned to the heart is called the **white horse**, for it is closer to Reason. However, the **desire** of the liver—being more remote from the excellence of Reason—is the **black horse**. 

Again, **Reason** within us is named **Hercules**. He kills **Antaeus** <note>In mythology, a giant who gained strength from touching the Earth</note>—represented here as certain manic phantoms of the imagination—specifically when he lifts him high off the earth. This occurs when Reason knows itself to be separate from the senses and bodily imagination. Here, too, he tames the lion...

that is, he restrains his anger. Here, Hercules beheads the Hydra sprouting many heads from every side—that is, he cuts away the power of concupiscence <note>The strong desire for worldly or carnal pleasures.</note>. This power does not lead to just a few things (and even those being greater things, as anger does), but is carried toward anything at all—indeed, toward innumerable things—by an insatiable whirlpool. Truly, while our Hercules cuts away the Hydra of the liver <note>In ancient and Renaissance medicine, the liver was considered the seat of the concupiscible soul or desires.</note> with a blade, the heads suddenly sprout back, because the very "tinder" <note>original: "fomes"; the internal spark or fuel that feeds passion</note> is left behind. However, when he consumes it with fire, he utterly extirpates the tinder, and nothing regrows from there. In Plato’s *Phaedo*, Socrates commands that you should not abstain from one bodily pleasure for the sake of another bodily pleasure. Otherwise, many others suddenly grow back in place of the one. Rather, he taught that we should strive to abstain from pleasures for the sake of reason. For he says that only in this way can vices be rooted out from the depths. 

I shall now bring an end to this letter, if I first offer this one warning: we should remember that if there are many "beasts" within us, it is no wonder that in Plato's writings, souls are said to migrate from a human into beasts. Certainly, we have from the beginning within us certain "tinders" and affections of beasts. When we have blindly nourished these for a long time, either reason is somehow lulled to sleep, or it remains awake only under the guise of anger and lust. Wherefore, under the very skin of a human, the human himself is seen to have passed into beasts. Hence Socrates says in the *Phaedrus*: "I am considering myself, Phaedrus, whether I am some beast more complex, fiery, and furious than Typhon <note>A monstrous giant of Greek mythology with a hundred dragon heads.</note>, or a calmer and simpler animal, a participant in some divine and gentle lot—that is, in tranquil intelligence."

July 1st, 1487.

->Only he possesses all things who is possessed by nothing except God.<-

### Marsilio Ficinus to Hieronymo Pasqualino, his dearest fellow-godfather, greetings.

<margin>s</margin>If you desire to possess as many things as possible, take care that nothing possesses you. For unless you have yourself—through whom you might possess other things—you will have nothing at all. Hence it happens that all men are always in need, and all are continually grieving. This is because each person has blindly and excessively lost and destroyed his very self and all his belongings long ago, since he was secretly snatched away while he was openly striving to seize things. 

Only he can belong to himself and another at the same time who has given himself to Him alone; who is "alone" among all things because He alone is all things. When one finds all things in Him, he also finds himself, and finds himself more perfect to the degree that He is more perfect than himself. Just as one who serves a slave is the most shameful and wretched of slaves, so the one who serves the Lord of all becomes, in a certain way, the lord of all. He alone is seen to serve freely who obeys infinite Liberty. In that place, servitude is free, where immense Liberty—that is, God—expels far away whatever servile or violent thing can be imagined.

<meta>This page concludes Ficino’s reflection on the philosopher’s will, transitions into a defense of his work on Divine Providence versus Astrology, and presents correspondence with the Venetian statesman Bernardo Bembo and the scholar Hermolaus Barbarus regarding the nature of friendship and service.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR

...philosopher. For this reason especially, I philosophize: so that, since things themselves do not follow my will in any other way, I at least might follow things with my will. For in this way, things obey a will that follows them. Third: how much I love you. If there is any measure for love, or any certain limit to a free will: measure your love for me, Francesco, and thus, perhaps, you will also measure mine for you. Fourth: what I am composing. I am composing a book on the providence of God and the freedom of human choice <note>original: "humani arbitrii libertate"</note>; in this work, I argue against the necessity of the stars and the claims of the astrologers. 

But perhaps someone might say it is the act of a fool to want to fight against invincible fate. Indeed, I respond: this can be refuted so easily that whenever someone wishes to refute it, they conquer it by that very act of willing. Surely the movement of the celestial spheres can never raise the mind higher than the spheres themselves. But now, he who disputes against them seems to have already transcended them, and to have reached God Himself and the free choice of the will. It is as if he were not compelled by celestial fate, but led by a "super-celestial" power, both by divine providence and the freedom of the mind. Furthermore, since any opposing and, so to speak, preemptive <note>original: "pemptoria," likely a contraction or error for "peremptoria," meaning decisive or final</note> action usually proceeds from one contrary to another, let no one dare suggest that the will itself—and the very argument that resists the forced violence of the stars—originates from that same violence of the stars. Rather, let us understand it to flow from providence and freedom itself, for the sake of which we have spoken against fate. October 28, 1477. Florence.

->He who serves many has many servants.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo of Venice, Greetings.

Phoebus Capella, Francesco of Esium, and Pamphilus the physician are asking us for the books of our Plato, all of which we have long since translated from the Greek language into Latin. If you happen to encounter these excellent men anywhere, command them in our name, and tell them the translations cannot be sent this month. You see, Bernardo, with what freedom I act toward you; for I seem, I know not how, to have issued a command. But you, my Bembo, are the cause. For you show yourself to be such a man to individuals that anyone who does not use the greatest freedom and confidence with you would undoubtedly seem the most servile and distrustful of all. Indeed, while you most willingly serve others, you meanwhile rule most greatly. But when others seem to rule you most, they then serve you most willingly. There is no easier, more outstanding, or more secure dominion than that of love. No service is more active, pleasant, or happy than voluntary service. August 1st, 1477.

# BOOK FOUR

...bare. <note>original: "bare", the concluding syllable of a word from the previous page, likely "scribere" (to write) or "libare" (to offer)</note> This is indeed the true bait of love; that is, it captures me with love itself and, having captured me, provokes me to love. And thus I must love you in such a way that what was intended for many, you alone now possess. Therefore, just as recently while writing to everyone I was led to write to one in particular, from now on, among all those I must love, I will love this one man above all.

### Marsilio Ficino to his fellow philosophers, and especially to Ermolao Barbaro, greetings.

<margin>a</margin>
All define friendship, by a certain common notion, as being some kind of union. Since a union cannot exist except toward a single point, it seems right to ask what that "one" thing is toward which two people, aspiring together, become and are called friends. Are they necessarily friends who hold the same opinion? Not at all. For we can hold the same opinion on many things, both human and natural, and yet hate one another. Or perhaps goodwill consists not in opinion, but in the will? Think then: should only those who want the same thing be called friends? Not even that. On the contrary, enmities arise for this very reason: because we want the same thing. Often those who seek the same treasure, the same rank of dignity, or the same honor in an art, envy one another, grow angry, and fight. 

Perhaps someone might say that discord of this kind arises among men because they desire certain finite goods, which one person possesses and the other does not, or possesses unequally. But if any are found who seek the same good which is also infinite—since that can never be hindered, but rather overflows everywhere into the immense—they are thought to have no enmities among themselves. And that friendship exists between those who want the same infinite good. But truly even this does not seem to me sufficient for goodwill; for all people, by a certain natural instinct, desire a good of this kind. Thus we all wish to be happy. Yet we do not all love one another. 

Where then shall we find goodwill itself, which is nothing other than wishing for the good, unless we find it centered upon that Good which is all Good—that is, God? Certainly nowhere else. Furthermore, the human will toward God can be affected in two main ways, as far as our purpose is concerned: it either desires to receive from Him, or to give to Him. The first is indeed a common and natural instinct for all. Indeed, we all desire and ask for as many things as possible. But we do not, for this reason alone, love God or men. The other instinct does not seem to belong to everyone equally. Indeed, very few are found who give themselves and all they have to God. Or rather, to speak more correctly, who *return* <note>original: "reddant"</note> them to God. For there is nothing we are, or possess, that we have not received from Him. 

Whoever returns himself to God—that is, converts every affection of thought and every effort and effect of action unto Him—he loves God for the sake of God alone, and loves all else for the sake of God. Clearly, a vain lover of bodily form loves a picture of a beautiful body for this very reason: because he loves the substance of the body itself. Thus the true and pious lover loves created things for no other reason than that they are either images or shadows of the Creator God whom he loves. And the more similar they are to what he seeks, the more he admires and praises them. Most similarly...

# BOOK FOUR

...truly belong to the divine mind: minds dedicated to God above all others. For this reason, minds of this sort are affected toward God and toward one another by an inestimable burning of love and sweetness. While they give themselves back to Him spontaneously as if to a father, they also give themselves most willingly to each other as if to brothers. Other things called friendships among men are nothing else than robberies. True charity—as Paul the Apostle <note>Ficino cites 1 Corinthians 13:5: "Charity... seeketh not her own."</note> says—seeks not its own, but what belongs to another. And if we daily boast magnificently of the noble titles of friendship, nevertheless each of us is usually such that he looks back at no one else but himself. For here, one does not truly give himself to another, but rather strives to receive from him either pleasure or some utility, whether it pertains to external things and the body or to the soul. 

Finally, to say it briefly, only that man is to be called a true and legitimate lover who understands that in all the good things offered to him and pleasing him everywhere, nothing else truly pleases him but the divine Good itself, from which and through which all things are good. Therefore, in all these things, he loves that Good, and in that Good, he loves all things. Thus, not even he himself is beloved by himself except in Him through whom he has this: that he is to be loved. He cares for all men according to his strength, as if they were created by the same father as himself. Some, however, he chooses above others as being more similar to that father, with whom he may lead both a heavenly life on earth and a super-heavenly life in the heavens. Among these alone is true friendship—that is, a true union from the one and in the one God. Indeed, a true and stable union among many cannot be achieved except through eternal unity itself. Moreover, true and eternal unity is God Himself, who alone is true simplicity and immense power. Therefore, these alone seem able to cry out freely with the Prophet: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity!" <note>original: "Ecce quàm bonum & quàm iocundum habitare fratres in vnum." This is the opening of Psalm 133 (132 in the Vulgate).</note>

->Fortune can neither do good for the wicked nor do harm to the good.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Ivani <note>Antonio Ivani (1430–1482) was a humanist scholar and chancellor from Sarzana (Serezanensi).</note> of Sarzana, sends greetings.<-

If you see someone suffering from an incurable disease of the body, and tortured by various pains in diverse limbs, you will not envy him his delicate feasts, his crowd of servants, his soft bedding, or his purple-draped, gilded bedroom. Surely, unless you too are as sick in soul as he is in body, you will not be able to envy him. Whoever serves pleasures, money, glory, or the desire for power, is oppressed by a certain incurable disease of the soul and manifold pain. Therefore, whoever envies these people sees nothing. 

For this reason, those people seem to me the most blind of all who consider Fortune to be blind for this reason: because she either benefits the wicked—for whom truly nothing is good—or harms the good—for whom, in the end, nothing is evil. For as each person is in himself, so are the things he receives. Among men, only those are deprived of the eyes of reason who do not see by what miraculous logic the individual parts of the world are arranged and moved. These people alone seem subject to what I might call "Fortune" and supreme injustice; where the most exact order of things indicates the infinite power, wisdom, and justice of the Author, they either think an irrational fortune commands, or they complain about divine governance as if it were less than just.
