<header>FOURTH 119</header>

### Praise of Matrimony.
->Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Pelotti, distinguished poet and friend, sends greetings.<-

<margin>q</margin> My dear Pelotti, I cannot but most highly approve of the fact that you have for a long time now applied your mind to marriage. By this means, man, as if he were something divine, preserves the human species through a perpetual succession. As if he were grateful, he returns to nature what he received on loan, and often with interest. As if he were a happy and true sculptor, he carves a living image of himself in his children. Furthermore, he achieves a dear partnership of life and a faithful guardianship of his affairs by this means, either primarily or even solely. He possesses, moreover, a domestic republic <note>original: "domesticam remp." Ficino views the household as a "mini-state" or microcosm of society</note> in the governing of which he may exercise the powers of prudence and all the virtues. He also prepares the greatest protection for old age, which he may lead more securely either in the bosom of a beloved wife, or in the arms of children and grandchildren, or in the dutiful service of his in-laws. Finally, a wife and family are either a sweet solace for our labors, or at least a certain supreme exercise for moral philosophy. For this reason, Socrates confessed that he had learned moral discipline much more from his wives <note>Socrates was famously married to Xanthippe; tradition suggests her difficult temperament served as a "moral exercise" for his patience</note> than he had learned natural philosophy from Anaxagoras or Archelaus. Who does not know that when man was once created, nothing was commanded and instituted by God earlier or more anciently than marriage? And that it is numbered among the sacred mysteries and celebrated most highly among all nations? Powerful men have always honored this, and wise men do not despise it. For they saw that it was conducive to conducting affairs; and as for letters <note>academic or literary pursuits</note>, it does not hinder them if you live temperately and spend your time sparingly. Our Plato, though he somewhat neglected marriage in his youth, was at last led by repentance in old age to perform the sacred rites of nature <note>original: "sacra de naturæ," likely referring to procreation or the social duties of a citizen</note>, so that he might absolve himself before the common people from the charge of both neglecting marriage and of sterility. He even established in his *Laws* that he who has not taken a wife should be removed far from all public duties and honors, and should be pressed more heavily by public burdens than other citizens. Hermes Trismegistus <note>a legendary Hellenistic figure regarded by Ficino as a primary source of ancient wisdom</note> says that such men are judged most unhappy by human law, and by divine law are judged like sterile and dry trees. However, only two kinds of men seem to be exempt from this law: either those who, because of a certain weakness of nature, are most unfit for this, or those who have uniquely devoted themselves to Minerva <note>the goddess of wisdom; here representing a life of pure intellect or celibacy</note> as if to a wife, having given her their word. Nature herself excuses the former; but chaste Minerva might perhaps accuse the latter if they were to follow Venus <note>the goddess of love and procreation</note>. Surely nature, who brought our Pelotti forth robust and handsome, would have disapproved if he had by chance neglected marriage. And if Minerva, whom he has long served, should perhaps refrain from blaming him because he mixes Venus with the Muses, Apollo and Mercury will immediately defend him. Certainly they will say that Pelotti dedicated more and better songs to the Muses after the sacred rites of Hymenaeus <note>the god of marriage</note> than he did before. Finally, they will command him to lift his face high to the stars, where Phoebus <note>Apollo</note>, the leader of the Muses, and Mercury, their companion, lead Venus in their midst—the mother of love and music; each of them walks, so to speak, in step with her, and they never depart far from her. But let us for the present leave the stars...

...let us return to men. I see you after this, Anthony, often declaiming among your friends in this manner regarding the matter of marriage. Man is either alone or most of all creatures a **social animal** <note>original: "animal... sociabile." A reference to Aristotle’s famous definition of man in his *Politics*</note>, as the philosophers say. To him alone has nature granted the faculty of speech and of establishing laws for this very purpose. Thus, whoever lives alone should understand that he is either perhaps something greater than man, or undoubtedly something less; for he who transcends human powers while living among men is rarer than the phoenix. He, therefore, shall fulfill the duty of humanity above all others who enters into a continuous, domestic, and indissoluble society. Through the dealings of this bond, he may strive to preserve the public society of the human race itself and learn how to govern it. 

Certainly, just as a city is made of houses, so is skill in the republic formed from the discipline of domestic affairs. He will not know how to rule a city who has not learned to govern a home. He will not love his country who thinks its successes or misfortunes pertain little to him. Perhaps he will not care to imbue himself with more serious character, since, being alone, he will not be providing an example of good character to a family. Through leisure and a certain license, whoever is not occupied in domestic business may become more negligent and worse every day. He will not know how to love anyone truly and steadily who does not experience the true and indissoluble love of a spouse and children. He will not learn to endure abroad and overcome by suffering, unless he has had a domestic teacher of patience. He will not learn to pity men who has never felt a spouse or a child weeping. For indeed, **a mind not unacquainted with misfortune learns to help the wretched** <note>original: "non ignara mali miseris succurrere discit." Ficino is quoting Virgil’s *Aeneid* (1.630), where Queen Dido speaks of her own hardships</note>. 

But what is worst of all is this: he who has neither to look out for his own family nor to call upon God often for their safety will, for the most part, neglect human laws, people themselves, and divine worship. Finally, it will be most difficult not to cast off our very humanity unless we put on the lawful cloak of marriage. Therefore, if you wish to be men, my friends, and if you wish to be legitimate children of God: increase the human race lawfully; and like gods—or rather, in the likeness of God—procreate, nourish, rule, and govern children similar to yourselves. Remember, moreover, that in governing domestic affairs most diligently, you cultivate yourselves. You learn the skill of the earthly republic and attain its honors, and you earn the rewards of the heavenly republic.

### Philosophy gives birth to wisdom. Wisdom brings forth happiness.
->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to his friend Bastiano Salvini of Amitinum.<-

<margin>v</margin> Where rich and powerful **Juno** <note>Juno here represents worldly wealth and civic power</note> does not hear us, we are not without fault; and we experience that divinity sparingly. Yet that power flourishes where it is present in abundance to all who wish to be present with it. It hears a man even before he calls. It listens to anyone who prays rightly. Therefore, Salvini, all our help must be sought from **Minerva** <note>Minerva, goddess of wisdom, represents the intellectual and philosophical life</note>. By her aid, we may one day raise ourselves from the ground and escape to the upper airs. For only that divinity can raise a man to the ethereal head of the world, which was born from the very head of **highest Jupiter** <note>In myth, Minerva was born from Jupiter's head; for Ficino, this signifies that Wisdom comes directly from the Divine Mind</note>. But since she does not listen to anyone except those praying rightly, let us strive, my friend, with all our strength, right from here...

# BOOK FOUR

...to seek help. For who rightly adores wisdom, except he who does so wisely? Moreover, he alone adores it wisely who asks for **wisdom from wisdom**. We cannot ask for anything wisely, whether from wisdom itself or from another, except through wisdom. This was taught to us by **Socrates**, the man judged wisest of all by the oracle of Apollo. Indeed, as Plato recounts in the *Phaedrus* <note>original: "in phaedro." A reference to Plato's dialogue where Socrates prays for inner beauty and wisdom.</note>, in his daily prayers he desired nothing from God except wisdom. For that man knew—as we say to the foolish—that those things which the common people usually see as "good" are actually "evil." To the wise man, however, even those things called "evil" eventually turn out to be "good." Happy is he for whom all things go well. But things go well only for him who uses all things well. He alone uses individual things well who has learned the strengths of himself and of others from wisdom. 

Happy, therefore, are the **priests of wisdom** alone. They are blessed even amidst human miseries (if I may call them that). Others, however, are so unhappy that they are miserable even amidst human happiness itself. From this, it is apparent how great the dignity and divinity of legitimate **philosophy** is. For in this especially consists the perfect priesthood of wisdom. Nevertheless, it is treated so unworthily and impiously by the common crowd that those who alone are truly wise—and from whom all others receive whatever little wisdom they have—are judged to be the most foolish of all. Furthermore, they are wrongly thought to hold ill opinions of God by those very people who learned how to worship God from the philosophers; for it was through the reasonings of philosophers that they understood that the God they worship truly exists. 

Oh, most false judgment of the crowd! They thought the philosopher **Democritus** <note>Democritus was known as the "laughing philosopher" because he mocked the vanities of mankind.</note> was insane at the very moment when, having become most wise, he began to mock the foolishness of mortals; he was eventually judged the most prudent of all by **Hippocrates**, the wisest of physicians. Then they condemned the divine **Socrates** as if he thought ill of the gods, even though he was called the wisest of all by their own god <note>The Oracle of Apollo at Delphi.</note>, because he thought more rightly about God than all others. But let the insane crowd laugh as they please; let them laugh at philosophers as if they were insane and impious. Meanwhile, let philosophers both mourn the tearful laughter of the crowd along with **Heraclitus** <note>Heraclitus was known as the "weeping philosopher" for his grief over human folly.</note>, and laugh at their ridiculous weeping along with Democritus.

# BOOK FOUR

...you have strived to deserve through elegance of character. In this, you are judged all the more worthy the further you seem to be from the crime of ambition. Therefore, I congratulate your virtue and my own good fortune—provided, however, that you conduct yourself rightly in the role which you have properly earned. Otherwise, I do not doubt that you will be subjected to dangers and I to the tongues of detractors. For Rome does not tolerate the laziness of its rulers, and public talk usually blames the faults of students on their teachers. Thus **Seneca** <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC – AD 65), a Roman Stoic philosopher and tutor to the Emperor Nero. He was often criticized for failing to restrain Nero's tyranny.</note> is torn by the tongues of detractors for the faults of his Nero. The rashness of his youths is blamed on **Quintilian** <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus (c. 35 – c. 100 AD), a famous Roman rhetorician and teacher.</note>. And **Socrates** is blamed for having been too "mad" regarding his pupil <note>Likely referring to Alcibiades, the brilliant but erratic Athenian general whose scandals were sometimes blamed on Socrates' teaching.</note>. You, indeed, will conduct whatever you wish most rightly if you do not withdraw from yourself. If you first compose yourself, and if you direct all things toward virtue, then everything will go well for you. I have described for you the strengths of political constitution and morals. If you obey these, you have **Plutarch** <note>Plutarch (c. 46 – 120 AD), a Greek philosopher and biographer whose works on morality and the education of princes were highly influential in the Renaissance.</note> as your authority for living. Otherwise, I invoke this present letter as a witness that you do not pursue the destruction of the empire with Plutarch as your author. Farewell.

### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine’s disputation against the judgment of astrologers

### Marsilio Ficino to the most distinguished man, Count Francesco Ippolito Gazolti, sends greetings.

I have written a book against the empty judgments of astrologers. I am sending the preface <note>original: "phemium," from the Greek "prooimion," meaning introduction.</note> to you; I will send the rest as soon as our scribe has finished copying it. Those who affirm that every single thing happens by necessity because of the stars are themselves entangled—and entangle the common people—in three especially deadly errors. For, as far as they are capable, they take away from the highest and almighty God His own providence over things and His absolute rule over the whole world. From the **angels**—who in the astrologers' view move the heavens in such a way that all the crimes of men, all evils for the good, and all good things for the evil proceed from there—they take away justice. Finally, from **men**—who seem to them to be driven here and there no less than beasts—they take away freedom and deprive them of all peace of mind. For if they promise good things (which they are accustomed to do only rarely, with difficulty, and quite obscurely), they usually entangle those promises in the greatest difficulties, so that they benefit us very little. And if sometimes—and indeed very rarely—they predict things will come without great labor, we are thereby rendered vain, proud, and negligent. Furthermore, if by some chance it happens as they promised, the long-awaited pleasure arrives less gratified because it was expected for so long. 

If, however, they threaten evils (which happens much more often), we either anticipate for a long time evils that will occur late, or, wretched as we are, we imagine things that will never happen and suffer through the imagining. Finally, if fates cannot be avoided, they are foreseen and predicted in vain. If they can be avoided by some means, then the "necessity of fate" is falsely defended by astrologers. Perhaps they will say, as I suppose: that it is also "in the fates" that something out of many things is occasionally foreknown and guarded against. If so, there will be a controversy among the **Fates** <note>original: "parcas," referring to the Parcae or Moirai, the three goddesses who spin, measure, and cut the thread of human life.</note>, such that one might decide to wound a man while another decides to protect him. But let us grant them this for the time being, if you please, so that we do not perhaps seem too stubborn to anyone. However, we will never concede this: that it also stands in the decrees of the Fates that many people do not believe in them, and many more even contradict them. For how could the fates...

# BOOK FOUR 121
Q

...at one moment, he now impels Marsilio to struggle against fate with all the strength of his mind. He certainly does not attack fate with his own power, but rather by the virtue of some contrary or at least superior force. For **necessity** <term>Necessity: In philosophy, the idea that things must happen in a specific way and cannot be otherwise</term> itself cannot be entirely at odds with itself, such that it might deny its own existence by its own instinct or destroy itself with its own stings. What does that most common saying mean? "We are driven by the fates: trust in the fates." <note>original: *Fatis agimur: credite fatis*. This is a famous line from the Roman astronomical poet Manilius.</note> But if we consider the matter more carefully, we are driven not so much by the fates themselves as by the **fools** who assert those fates. <note>Ficino here makes a biting pun in Latin between *fatis* (fates) and *fatuis* (fools/idiots).</note> Do not trust me—trust the fates, if you will not trust the fools. Like the **Sibyl** <note>The Sibyls were ancient prophetesses famous for giving true but cryptic oracles.</note>, they cloak things in darkness—not true things, but false ones. They do not predict specific things for individual men, but only what is common to everyone. 

These most talkative men bring so many things into the open that it is no wonder if, among many lies, they occasionally stumble upon some truth by chance. They wish to seem wise to others when they are least wise to themselves. It is worth considering how destitute they are, how filthy, and how unfortunate in their own affairs. They are imprudent and inept in conducting business. If they happened to practice trade, they would foresee the outcome of commerce far less than other merchants; if they practiced medicine, they would foresee the course and end of a disease less than other doctors. They care for bodies worst of all, and though they profess to tell the future, they themselves seem to live and fall by chance everywhere. 

Rise up, therefore, I pray, you philosophers! Rise up, all you who are most precious lovers of **liberty** and tranquility. Come, act now! Gird yourselves with the shield and spear of **Pallas** <note>Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare.</note>. A war now looms over us against those wicked "little giants" who try to equal the vastness of God through their foreknowledge of the future, and who try to take away free dominion from the super-celestial God (who is supreme liberty) through the density of celestial fate. But those who so proudly strive to climb to the heavens will be miserably cast down to the underworld. Reach out your hand to us from on high, almighty God! Supply strength to your soldiers. It is your empire we now move to defend. Help us, you divine powers who rotate the ethereal spheres! Help us as we justify your justice against impious enemies who accuse us of a kind of extreme injustice. You too, O human race, look upon us without envy. Surely we are defending your most precious liberty and peace. Thus, after we have triumphed over these "diviners"—who are not divine but truly profane, and who have enslaved us with their delusions for so long—we may finally be able to cry out freely: "Impiety, cast beneath our feet, is crushed in its turn; victory makes us equal to heaven." <note>original: *Impietas ergo pedibus subiecta vicissim obteritur nos exequat victoria cœlo*. This is a paraphrased triumph from Lucretius’s *De Rerum Natura*, celebrating the victory of reason over superstition.</note>

### Preface of Marsilio Ficino for his little work on the Life of Plato, addressed to Francesco Bandino.

A certain **Plato** <note>Ficino refers to his newly finished translation or biography of the philosopher Plato as if it were a child born to him.</note> was recently born to me, **Bandino** <note>Francesco Bandino (1440–1489), a member of the Platonic Academy in Florence and a close friend of Ficino.</note>, on the very birthday of almighty Christ. Although he is far inferior to that ancient father of his, our Plato, yet he seems somehow similar in character. Turning to him, I said: "O Plato, will you seek again your father’s house and the ancient seats of **Athens**?" But he suddenly exclaimed: "O unjust fate! To my great sorrow, no paternal home remains for me anywhere. O iron age, in which that most cruel **Mars** <note>Referring to the god of war, symbolizing the Turkish conquest of Greece or general European warfare that destroyed classical sites.</note> destroyed the Attic dwellings..."

...to the pale citadels. ->Mountains do not separate souls that are higher than mountains.<-

### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to the Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Miklós Báthory, Bishop of Vác in Pannonia, sends greetings.

<margin>c</margin>When I received your letters and those of Bandini, in which you strongly urge me to set out for Pannonia—where I would be most welcome to Matthias, the most serene King of Pannonia—I had already completed **five keys** <term>Keys: Ficino often referred to his summaries or introductions to Plato’s dialogues as "keys" (claues) to unlocking wisdom.</term> to Platonic wisdom, one of which, shorter than the others, comes to you. 

However, for me to come in person is difficult. To live afterward under that sky <note>Ficino frequently complained that the cold climate of Hungary would be fatal to his delicate "melancholic" constitution.</note> is perhaps even more difficult. But to speak more accurately: if I am to come to you, I must first depart from those with whom, through the mediation of the **Muses** <term>Muses: The Greek goddesses of inspiration in the arts and sciences.</term>, my soul has long since become one. 

I pray, continue to love your Marsilio, who loves you ardently for your outstanding virtues. Likewise, love our Francesco Bandini, a man of magnificent talent and excellence; commend them both, if it is appropriate, to the most fortunate King Matthias. He will commend us, since something from our workshop will soon come forth to him in a short time. Farewell, happy souls, and live with me. Despite the mountains that seem to separate us, live with me, happy souls, for you are much higher than even the highest mountains. What I am to you, each one is to himself; what you are to me, is what two eyes are <note>A metaphor for the unity of friends: though separate, they work together to provide a single vision.</note>. 

May 25, 1479. Florence.

### Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo, the most illustrious Venetian knight, sends greetings.

<margin>l</margin>The fifth book of our letters, beginning with the letter on **Divine Law**, seems by that same law to demand the name of that famous **Bembo** <note>Bernardo Bembo (1433–1519), a Venetian diplomat and father of the famous Pietro Bembo.</note> as its head. For Divine and celestial law has joined him with us, as we demonstrate elsewhere. Therefore, let it be deservedly and happily dedicated to you above all others. Read happily.

# The Fifth Book of Letters by Marsilio Ficino the Florentine.
## Divine laws and faith are confirmed by knowledge.

**Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to his most reverend associates: Greetings.**

<margin>1</margin>
Human laws are either accepted from the start or spread after being accepted for no other reason than this: either through the customary and common persuasions of human and natural reasoning, or by some imperial authority and the force of arms, or by the ease and convenience of living and the lures of pleasure. Furthermore, the disposition of the stars can introduce such laws among men using no other instruments than these. Therefore, if we understand a certain law to have both arisen at some point among men of sound mind and to have been spread most widely, even while those many probable arguments were opposing it; while the weapons of the powerful were raging against it everywhere; and while the use and hope of human pleasure were openly and utterly taken away by it—then we shall necessarily conclude that a law of this kind is neither human, nor does it depend on celestial fate <note>Ficino often argues against "hard" astrology, asserting that while stars influence the body, they do not dictate divine law or the soul's will.</note>, but it is entirely divine and proceeds from a certain super-celestial power. Moreover, what is concluded by necessary proof is, without doubt, grasped by certain knowledge <term>scientia: in the Renaissance, this refers to systematic, certain knowledge based on logical demonstration, rather than just "science" in the modern experimental sense</term>. Therefore, whoever has once believed in such a law by such a reason will possess both knowledge as the mother of faith, and a faith confirmed by knowledge. He who does not consider such things cannot consider himself. He who does consider them in a certain way but does not believe, believes nothing. What others may choose, I do not know. I certainly prefer to believe in divine things rather than to know human things. Indeed, if divine faith is far more certain than the wisdom of men, that belief <note>original: *credulitas*. The OCR suggests *crudelitas* (cruelty), but contextually and in other editions, this refers to the act of believing or faith.</note> is always confirmed by true knowledge. This knowledge sometimes wavers in mere credulity. Therefore, so that we may be able to believe in anything true anywhere, let us now believe in Truth itself; since it admits nothing of ignorance or the false, it certainly ignores or deceives no one. Furthermore, so that we may be able to hope for something of the good, let us hope in the Good itself; since it does nothing of evil and suffers nothing of injustice, it never frustrates those who hope, nor does it abandon those who love. It has both illuminated them so that they might hope, and likewise inflamed them so that they might love. For the movement toward the Good itself can depend on nothing other than the Good itself, nor can it flow back there by any other path than that by which it flowed out.

->Nothing can be personal property where a soul is held in common.<-
**Marsilio Ficino to Naldus the poet, sends many greetings.**

<margin>r</margin>
I recently entered into the small room <note>original: *cellanum*, likely a variation of *cellulam*, referring to a small study or monk-like cell</note> of my Naldus—or rather, ours. For nothing can be personal property where a soul is held in common. On the second day of my stay in the country, I composed a very brief summary for our book on religion. And when I was addressing it to my friends, Naldus came to my mind first: the first of all to be loved by us. Indeed, the rest owe this very fact—that they are steadily loved by me—entirely to him. Since, in loving him first, I learned how to love the others.

Therefore, I am sending the summary. I have written much concerning what I have been doing. You, too, write what you are doing and how you are faring. But why, I ask, have I written? And why have I asked you to write? Let those who love only moderately be content with letters alone; but indeed, I know that neither Naldus <note>Naldo Naldi (1436–1513), a Florentine humanist and poet close to Ficino.</note>, as I speak, nor Marsilio will be content with a mere exchange of letters.

### One should speak briefly, but one should not briefly either think or love.

->Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Ivani. <note>original: "Anthonio byuano"</note> Sends Greetings.<-

You see, Antonio, that I consider you a man of sharp wit. Whenever you ask for books, I send the summaries of the whole works. First, you asked for the book *On the Sovereign Good*; I sent the summary. Then you requested our *Platonic Theology*. I gave the summary, which I received shortly before. But so that I might make you, who are already sharp, the sharpest of all: receive this third summary for our book *On Religion* which you have read. You were desiring the *Banquet* <note>Ficino's *De Amore*, a commentary on Plato's *Symposium*.</note> concerning love. Here alone, Ivani has received not just a summary in our name, but the entire work. For it is as if not some small portion of Marsilian benevolence is imparted to him, but the whole of it is poured thoroughly into the man himself. I have learned to discourse briefly; I have not learned to love briefly. As narrow as our speech is, so vast is our affection. Often the flame that is less spread about burns more intensely.

### Priests and philosophers should speak and think piously.

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend. Sends Greetings.<-

You will demand from us, my Giovanni (as I suppose), the first fruits of this country retreat of ours. Since all "firsts" are owed by the best right to the "first" <note>Ficino often refers to Cavalcanti as his "unique" or "first" friend, implying a primary soul-bond.</note>, I wrote a certain short exhortation to piety today for my associates—or rather, primarily for myself. I never seek to persuade others of anything through study that I have not first persuaded myself of. It is the duty of a priest to speak nothing unless it is seen to lead toward piety. It is also the profession of a philosopher to act no differently than he speaks, and to speak no differently than he thinks. Yet, it is one thing to feel with the mind, and another with the senses. Finally, lest I have attempted to write such an exhortation in vain: read this diligently, my Giovanni, I implore you. For I would neither wish to have written to my friends, nor am I able to write to myself, unless you read it.

### In evils there is no refuge except in the highest good.

->Marsilio Ficino to his associates. Sends Greetings.<-

Tragedies most truly weep over the wretched fate of mortals. The lot of mortals also performs a most true tragedy. Tragedy is a kind of imaginary life of men; the life of men seems to be a most true tragedy. I set aside now those declamations of the orators, poets, and philosophers in which they recount the individual evils and inconveniences of the human race; for the present, I shall express in few words how great the misery of our race is: namely, that for the most part, those men are the most miserable of all who are commonly seen to be the most blessed of all. Three kinds of life are numbered among the philosophers: the first is attributed to contemplation, the second to action, and the third to pleasure. Whoever in any of these lives is held to be at the height of happiness, they are for the most part, in reality, at the height of misery. Indeed, those who are commonly seen to excel in the contemplation of truth, they are often the most...

Following the previous page's discussion on the "summary" of his works, Ficino here pivots into a deeply Neo-Platonic and Christian critique of worldly wisdom, arguing that true peace is found not in the restless pursuit of multiple "curious" facts, but in the stable unity of the Highest Good, which is God.</meta>

<page-num>CXXIII</page-num>
<header>FIVE</header>

...they are held by an insoluble ambiguity of doubts. For while they studied to learn individual things too curiously <note>In this context, "curiosity" (curiositas) implies a prying or vain interest in trivial details rather than a healthy desire for truth.</note> and dared too boldly to profess everything in each instance, they deservedly learned to doubt everything in each instance. And since they believe they have no superior or equal, they now have no one left to believe, nor anyone to console them. O tasteless wisdom! O knowledge more confused than any ignorance! Solomon—the wisest of all by divine judgment—says that this brings labor and sorrow. The Apostle Paul asserts that this is considered foolishness before God. The prophet Isaiah exclaims that its thoughts are held as vain before God. It seems this happens to them not without cause: they trust to see true things in something else rather than in the light of Truth itself, just as if someone whose mental light was failing believed they could see the colors of things not in the sun's own splendor, but in a ray from their own eye. <note>Ficino refers to the ancient "extramission" theory of vision, where the eye was thought to emit rays to perceive objects.</note> Therefore, those who think they hold the first rank in *action* actually hold the first rank in *passion*; <note>term: passion (passio). In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to being "acted upon" or suffering external influences, the opposite of "action" or self-directed agency.</note> and when they are said to rule most, then they serve most. Finally, those who more readily obey pleasures fall more often into sorrows; and when they seem most to gorge themselves, they thirst and hunger most vehemently. O wretched lot of mortals! A lot more wretched than misery itself!

Since therefore, poor wretches, we shall flee, so that we might escape our misery: where shall we go? To that philosophy of the sophists, which is most inquisitive? Or to power? Or to pleasure? Alas, too many times we have already fled to these in vain. For that prouder philosophy entangles us in the most troublesome questions. Power oppresses us with a certain extreme and most dangerous servitude. Pleasure, finally, short and false, infects us with true and long-lasting sorrows. Perhaps it will be worthwhile, if we wish to reach what we are pursuing, to flee only to those things which never flee from us. Indeed, that alone cannot flee which is never moved, since it fills the universe. But what need is there for us to move toward that which is never moved, which is present everywhere to everyone? Let us not be moved, then, nor distracted by many things; but let us remain as much as possible in unity. For we attain eternal unity and one eternity not by movement or by a multitude of things, but by stillness and union.

But what is this, friends? Come, say what is this? Is this not the Good itself? Which fills the universe. For nothing can be found which is not good by the presence of the Good itself. This is it—do you not see? This is what all things desire, since all things come from it. And therefore, individual things are perfected through it, in so far as they strive to cling to it. But to the Good—as it seems to me—we can cling by no other means than by the love of the Good. Since this is the very nature of the Good: that it be desired; and the nature of the Desirable: that it be the Good. And to that which is best for us, as soon as we love it, we cling. Indeed, since love is some kind of good very close to the Highest Good, because it is the flame of the Good. Wherever the flame of the Good burns more ardently, there the light of the Good shines forth more clearly. Why say more? If God is the Good itself, the very light of the Good, the very love of the shining Good: let us love, O friends, let us love, I beseech you, before all else the luminous Good and the kindly Light. For in this way we shall love not only our God, but...

...we shall also enjoy Him by loving; for if God is love itself, then love itself is God. Therefore, let us burn above all with Him, without whose heat nothing is warm. Let us shine with His kind light according to our prayer, for without His splendor nothing shines. Come, friends, let us remain in Him who never departs, and we shall remain forever. Let us serve only the Lord of all, who serves no one, so that we may serve no one else but instead rule over all things. Let us enjoy Him if we are able; and we are able if we will it. For by willing we enjoy, and by enjoying we will. Let us enjoy Him, then, who alone overflows beyond all measure; and thus alone shall we be truly filled. Thus alone shall we rejoice truly and fully. For where the Good flourishes without failing, there pleasure is felt without pain, and there joy is everywhere complete.

### God did not create humans for small things, but for great ones.
->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend. Greetings.<-

<margin>f</margin>
The <term>dialecticians</term> <note>Philosophers who specialize in logic and the art of investigation through dialogue.</note> are accustomed to saying that it is a condition of contradiction that if someone is already leaning toward one side of it, they cannot at the same moment lean toward the other. Truly, my own mind has been so distracted this autumn that I neither wish to speak nor to remain silent; again, I can neither act nor refrain from acting. Perhaps this is because I am somehow double, even though I seem to be simple. But let me be both double, as <term>Plato</term> wishes in the *Phaedrus*, and even triple, as the same man disputes in the *Timaeus*; <note>Ficino refers to Plato’s division of the soul into different parts: the rational, the spirited, and the appetitive.</note> provided that the part in me which draws toward honorable business always overcomes that which pulls me back toward idle leisure and lethargy. Behold, that which invites me to act and speak is now prevailing; and so I speak as best I can, and I act. 

Yet another question immediately arises within us, I know not how. For I wish to joke for a little while as I often do, and at least write something witty to my friend Cavalcanti. Although I took up my pen with this primary purpose, I find myself writing more rigid things; and while I attempt something lyrical or comic, I meanwhile complete something elegant or tragic. Shall I tell you why, my friend? It is because <term>Saturn</term> <note>In Ficino’s astrological philosophy, Saturn represents the "melancholy" temperament of scholars and priests, often associated with gravity, deep thought, and hardship.</note> has chosen me as his own in these times, that he may test all the strengths of his rigidity upon me. But you do not wish for that, as I see, my Giovanni, nor do I. What then shall we say, my friend? That God wishes His priests to be the most serious of all men, and that sacred matters should not be treated lightly, but with gravity. It was perhaps for this reason that <term>Pythagoras</term> <note>The ancient Greek philosopher and mathematician whose "symbols" or maxims were often interpreted allegorically by Renaissance thinkers.</note> commanded his disciples in his symbols "not to cut their nails during a sacrifice." God did not create humans for certain small things, but for great ones—those who are not filled by small things and have known great ones. Indeed, He created them only for the infinite, for they alone on earth have discovered an infinite nature; to them, nothing finite—no matter how large—is entirely satisfying.

### No incontinent person can be wise.
->Marsilio Ficino to the philosophers and sophists. Greetings.<-

<margin>i</margin>
Among all the powers of the soul that are engaged in knowing, the highest are the <term>intellect</term> and <term>reason</term>. The lowest, however, are taste and touch. These latter indeed descend by their nature toward the most corporal things. The former, however, ascend toward an incorporeal and divine substance. Whoever, therefore, [serves] these...

--- Page 251 ---
<meta>This page continues the letter from Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti. Having established that the human mind is restless until it finds the infinite, Ficino now argues that one cannot serve both the physical senses and the divine intellect simultaneously. He cites the authority of Aristotle, Socrates, Pythagoras, and Plato to demonstrate that purification of the soul is the necessary prerequisite for true wisdom.</meta>

<page-num>CXXIIII</page-num>
<header>BOOK FIVE CXXIIII</header>

...if one strives to serve everyone <note>original: "omnibus," referring here to both the worldly/bodily demands and the divine.</note> at the same time, he will surely strive in vain. For neither will the ray of the highest things be illuminated for whoever has entirely immersed himself in the darkness of the lowest things; nor will he listen to the ridiculous allurements of the lowest things, he who has tasted the true goods and joys of the highest. The mind will not reach the truest <term>essences</term> <note>original: "rationes rerum," the underlying principles or Platonic ideas of things.</note> of things which are separate from bodies, unless it has first separated itself from the body, both through the purification of morals and by the focused intent of contemplation. He will consider of no value those things which are subject to time on earth, he who already possesses heaven itself and, if I may put it this way, measures eternity itself. 

I pass over the fact that, just as eyes suffering from <term>ophthalmia</term> <note>A generic historical term for various inflammatory eye diseases that distort vision.</note> or a bitter tongue perceive nothing but redness or bitterness, so the mind—which, because of long-standing love and obedience toward bodily things, has now become almost like a body itself—will either think that divine things do not exist at all, or will at least judge them to be merely physical. I pass over the fact that free and long-lasting <term>leisure</term> <note>original: "ocio" (otium), meaning time set aside from business and political duties for study and reflection.</note> is necessary to investigate the most hidden principles of things. Nothing more slavish, nothing more busy and anxious can be imagined than the troubled life of one who serves the senses as if they were his masters—masters who are both numerous and insane. And while he is enslaved to these foolish tyrants, he nonetheless professes his obedience to Wisdom. 

Therefore, whenever you find someone foolishly serving the body, you must deny that they are wise. But those whom you know to be wise, you will judge not to be servants of their own body, but its masters. Certainly, those who serve only the pleasures of the body live in anxiety. But those who try in vain to join the lowest pleasures with the highest are much more anxious. For since they labor too much on both sides, they enjoy the pleasures of neither the mind nor the body. 

There are none whom God rejects more than those who expect to drink <term>nectar and ambrosia</term> <note>In Greek mythology, the drink and food of the gods that grant immortality; here used metaphorically for divine wisdom.</note> from the filthy vessels of vice. There are none he approves of and loves more—as *Aristotle* <note>The great Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE). Ficino refers here to Aristotle's "Nicomachean Ethics," where the contemplative life is deemed the highest happiness.</note> argues—than those who cultivate above all a mind most similar to God, and separate it far from the dissimilar stain of the body, and who strive to perceive the divine light not through the clouds of vice, but with the pure serenity of the mind. 

This reasoning is what led *Socrates*, as we believe, to present moral discipline to men above all else, and *Pythagoras* to drive the profane far from his sacred schools. For just as a foul-smelling vessel makes whatever liquid you pour into it—even the sweetest—stink by its own contagion, so a corrupted mind, having received knowledge, produces malice rather than wisdom. 

Furthermore, as the air is to the light of the sun, so the mind is to the light of truth and wisdom. Therefore, neither the air nor the intellect, while it is cloudy, can grasp those rays. Yet both grasp them suddenly as soon as they have become pure and serene. This is the point of that famous saying of *Plato* in his letter to the people of Syracuse <note>A reference to Plato’s Seventh Letter, a crucial text for Neoplatonists regarding the sudden "spark" of divine illumination.</note>: "That which is divine," he says, "cannot be expressed in words like the other things we learn. But from long-standing habit concerning divine things and a similarity of life, suddenly, as if from a sparking fire, a light shines forth in the soul, and henceforth sustains itself." 

Why then do you devote yourselves to so many late-night studies, O philosophers? Why is there need for such long-winded disputes, O <term>Sophists</term> <note>Teachers in Ancient Greece often criticized by Plato and Ficino for prioritizing rhetorical trickery over the pursuit of actual truth.</note>? To the one...

...do you not see? The only way for us to reach the light itself is through serenity <note>original: "serenitas," implying both peace of mind and the clarity of a cloudless sky.</note> itself. Alas, you often trust in vain to touch the pure with what is pure—a notion which Socrates condemns. Come now, learn from the Platonic Galen <note>Ficino refers to the famous physician Galen as "Platonic" because Galen acknowledged how the physical state of the body affects the soul's functions.</note> that it is impossible for a soul suffocated by blood and fat to contemplate anything celestial. Learn again from Pythagoras and Plato: that the wisdom of the mind is nothing other than the light of the highest Good itself, diffused everywhere through souls that are truly good, like the clearest mirrors. Therefore, as soon as you have emerged inwardly good, you will shine back with the brilliance of the highest Good itself, which is wisdom. The celestial sun, which generates the eyes of animals and the colors of things, reveals those colors to eyes that are fit and pure. The **supracelestial Sun** <term>supracelestial Sun</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, the physical sun is a visible metaphor for the "Intellectual Sun," which is God or the Truth that illuminates the mind.</note>—that is, Truth itself—creates both real things and minds. This same Sun reveals real things to minds that are pure and turned toward it. Purge the eyes of reason from all the filth of this harmful body. Turn the gaze of the mind away from the shadow of the lowest matter. Turn the sight of your inner intelligence toward the light of the heavenly form itself. From that source, matter (once sufficiently prepared) is suddenly formed by bodily shapes; from that same source, the mind (once sufficiently prepared) is immediately affected within those bodily forms. And as it is illustrated by the bright rays of truth, so it is abundantly bathed in true joy.

**Philosophers, while they learn to dispute too curiously, often meanwhile unlearn how to take counsel.**

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, sends greetings.

<margin>q</margin> What is this you say, O man who is most delicate in our affairs? Do you complain that you have been overwhelmed by us in these days by a mountain of letters? Ha! What are you doing, my Giovanni? Bear these lighter things, I pray, with a calm mind if you can, since we ourselves bear much heavier things. Why do I disturb you with such a number of letters? Because, clearly, I myself am confounded by an excessive crowd of thoughts. This is what usually happens to those who are made very busy by too much leisure. However, it is better to be busy while leisure oppresses than to be idle when business presses. Consult with that fellow-philosopher of ours as to what he should best do in his own case. Forgive your friends who are philosophers; for often philosophers, while they learn to dispute too curiously, often meanwhile unlearn how to take counsel.

**Solitude for philosophers is usually, and ought to be, not a relaxation of the mind, but its intensification.**

### Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Bernardo Bembo of Venice, sends greetings.

<margin>s</margin> I departed on the <term>Nones of September</term> <note>September 5th.</note> for our Mount Celano <note>Ficino's country retreat near Careggi.</note> for the sake of relaxing—or rather, intensifying—my mind. Truly, whatever is said to Bembo, we consider said also to **Phoebus Capella** and to **Marcus Aurelius** <note>Giovanni Francesco "Phoebus" Capella and Marco Aurelio, Venetian friends of Ficino and Bembo.</note>. ->Wisdom is not granted to the profane.<-

Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Lorenzo Bonincontri, astronomer and poet.
<margin>salutations</margin> You are often accustomed to saying, Lorenzo, that impious men can never turn out to be true astrologers. This indeed seems to me to be most true. For if the heaven is the temple of God Himself, it is fitting that profane men be driven far away from the heaven and from celestial secrets. Moreover, not only astronomy, but indeed all wisdom, descended from the "barbarians" <note>original: "barbaris"; in the Renaissance, this referred to non-Greek ancient civilizations like the Egyptians, Persians, and Chaldeans, whom Ficino believed held the original divine revelations.</note>. Our Plato and the rest of the Greek sages undoubtedly confess this. Indeed, we have found that among those barbarians, only the priests handled the sciences of physics, mathematics, and metaphysics. This was because they knew that wisdom, the principal gift of God, neither ought to be nor could be granted except to minds that are most sacred and divine. For this reason especially (as I think), Christ, the master of life, said that the sacred mysteries are given to the common people in a veiled manner, but are fully revealed to the chosen disciples. But why do I progress further in this matter now? Read, if you please, what we wrote regarding the same opinion in previous days to the philosophers and the sophists. Introduce these to a reader, my friend, if you find anyone who has joined learning with integrity above all others. Tell me, I pray, Lorenzo: whom do you think most of all to invite to read these things now? Is it Angelo Manetti? <note>A Florentine diplomat and scholar.</note> I see you are thinking of this very man; and I myself had just now thought of him before all others.

->He has won every point who has mixed the useful with the agreeable.<- <note>A famous line from Horace's *Ars Poetica*.</note>

<margin>note</margin> There is no one among all my associates with whom I speak more deeply or more sweetly, my sweetest Foresi, than with you. Among the dwellers of heaven, Bastiano, Apollo <note>original: "phoebus".</note> indeed plays the lute but does not make it. Mercury, however, makes it, but does not play it. Therefore, let no one on earth trust that he can exercise both skills equally—both making and playing the lute. If anyone should object to us that they are too "delirious" <note>original: "delirare," literally meaning to go "out of the furrow" (lira) of a plowed field.</note> who are too much occupied with the lyre, you will respond in turn, I know: that we "lyre" <note>original: "lyrare"; Ficino is punning on "lyre" (the instrument) and "lira" (the furrow), suggesting that playing music keeps them from "de-lyre-ing" or going crazy.</note> for this very reason, so to speak, so that we do not go "out of the furrow." Those who always handle heavy matters are surely weighed down by the very weight of that gravity. Those who are continuously occupied with light things are deservedly driven here and there by every light breeze. We must be pitied just as...

->No remedy for evils is more convenient than patience.<-

### Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to his kinsman Bastiano Salvino.

<margin>❦</margin>There is a common proverb, Bastiano, that says nothing is more difficult than patience. We, however, feel the opposite: that nothing is particularly difficult which is not also very laborious. Nothing is laborious which is not full of toil. And nothing seems to involve toil where no labor <note>Ficino is playing on the Latin words "opus" (work/need) and "opera" (effort/service).</note> is required. But in what way is labor required where one does not have to act, but rather to endure? Patience does not command you to act, but to suffer. To the extent that it is more difficult to act than to endure, it is likewise more difficult to act well than to endure well. All other virtues are concerned with acting well, but patience alone consists in enduring well. What else is "enduring well" but not increasing that suffering which comes from evils? What shall we say this is, except a willingness to suffer that which you are destined to suffer even if you were unwilling? For unless you suffer willingly, you will certainly suffer against your will; and unless you allow yourself to be led, you will be dragged and snatched away with greater violence.

O, the wonderful power of patience! Other virtues, in a certain way, fight against fate. But patience alone, or most of all, conquers fate. For fate has decreed that things shall be immutable and necessary. Patience, by consenting to the will of divine providence, changes things in such a way that it turns necessities into voluntary acts. Just as he who acts badly turns good things into evil for himself, so he who endures well turns evil things into good for himself. Truly, in the bearing of evils, he himself becomes good. Just as gold is tested by fire, so is he proven and made bright by adversity. Like a veteran soldier, he becomes both skillful and fearless through the frequent exercise of dangers. Like one who has already tasted the bitter, he thereafter perceives the sweet more sharply. He uses these things more wisely and enjoys them more sweetly. A man does not rightly estimate how great a good is if he has not experienced evil. He will never know how to enjoy good things who has never learned how to use evil ones. No man’s prosperity is more fragile than his to whom all things seem to have happened prosperously. It is the mark of a prudent man to expect rain even in clear weather, and to expect clear weather even in the rain. Indeed, in this dark life, one should think nothing is clear, unless—

# BOOK V 126

...if it exists under a serene mind. A continuous storm strikes us from without. Tranquility must be sought by us only from within. From where the heat comes, from there comes serenity. From where the heat comes, from there comes light. Light, however, proceeds not from the shadow of matter, but from the light of the mind. My friend, he errs in speech who says that many **passions** <note>original: "passiones"; in the Renaissance, this refers to "sufferings" or "being acted upon" rather than just strong emotions.</note> occur in the lives of men from many evils. It would be more correctly said that life itself is a certain passion, pressing upon the wretched without any intermission. Remedies for continuous diseases are not those which act for a time, but those which help continually. To consult, to fight, to resist: we are not always able. However, we can always endure well those things which we always suffer, and we are taught to suffer by suffering. We are surely always able to do that, the power of which consists in the will itself. As soon as we wish to endure well, we do endure well; for indeed, to endure well is nothing other than to wish to endure. If we act badly, we will undoubtedly suffer both evil things and suffer them badly. If we endure well, we act well. 

If we fight persistently, my friend, we will be exhausted, and at last by that very exhaustion we will be completely defeated by ourselves. If we yield at the right time, we will undoubtedly prevail. The most fluid air <note>original: "liquidissimus aer"</note> yields to the blows of hard bodies; the air suddenly returns into itself, just as it was before. But hard bodies are crushed and broken entirely. The softest and most flexible things endure unbroken and bind the hardest. The hardest, because they do not know how to yield, are forced to be yielded, broken, and bound. Therefore, my Salvino, conquer fortune by enduring; and so that you may conquer other things (as you have begun), **conquer yourself**. Remember also that in this malignant region of the world, nothing escapes untouched by evils. But under a just judge—or rather, under Justice itself as judge—no good can lack a just reward, and no evil can lack its due punishment. 

Indeed, **patience** is a good so perfect that without it, the other goods of men cannot be perfected. For those things which are begun by other virtues are finished by patience. Farewell, most beloved brother; and so that others may bear with you, bear with others. I certainly, as often as I see things in a man that offend me, remember that I myself am a man. Therefore, I possess something that may offend others. By this reasoning, I bear with many daily, so that many may bear with me. Also, bear patiently with the stiffness and length of this letter of ours. Let it not be that I have disputed about patience in vain, or that you seem to have heard to no purpose those things which you already began to speak and observe through your own wisdom long ago.

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his Unique Friend, sends greetings.<-

<margin>a</margin> That friend of ours has already complained to me in two letters about his fortune or fate. # BOOK V 126

->True friendship does not stand in need of external services.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, sends greetings. <note>The Latin abbreviation "S.D." stands for "Salutem Dicit," a formal greeting meaning "sends health" or "sends greetings."</note>

<margin>r</margin> Answer me, I pray, Giovanni—if indeed I ask what is just—why you do not respond to so many of my letters. You do not know how the flavors of your words bring the sweetest seasoning to our people. What is sweet to me among bitter things? Giovanni. What again is bitter among sweet things? Giovanni. Or perhaps you think that as soon as you read our letters, you have already responded? Especially since you always respond to my words with your affection and your deeds. And often, before I even speak, you have already accomplished everything yourself. It is surely so. But I know you have proceeded even further. For you first thought to respond, and even what you would most especially respond. Then you saw—as you had also seen before—that your tongue and hand are closer to Marsilio’s thoughts than to your own. And therefore, the ministry of the tongue and hand cannot come between your soul and mine. You divine this quite rightly, and I divine it rightly as well. For you, in your thinking, have written, Giovanni; and I, in my meditating, have read while you were writing. But so that others also may be able to read these things which you have answered to me, I will now transcribe them myself.

**Giovanni to Marsilio sends greetings.** Our old custom, Ficino, has now ensured that you can bring nothing new to me. I have known your genius, Marsilio, for a long time now. I possess your every feeling, and I hold your words. I have erred just now. For it was not so much the long duration of our custom that brought this about, but the very beginning itself. Indeed, from the very beginning of this divine love, my Marsilio, you did not impart to me a part of your soul gradually and then another part soon after; rather, you poured the whole, at once and entirely, into me as one. And only as much of this gift is poured out upon others who are loved by you as I myself pour back into them. What then do you try to give to us further? You have nothing at all that he who has you does not already have. Therefore, the frequent duty of writing and writing back—which among others is a sign of more perfect benevolence—would be, between us, an indication of the imperfection of benevolence if it were referred properly to us. Much more, perhaps, would you fail our friendship by speaking than I by remaining silent. For you would seem to suspect some sort of number <note>In Platonic thought, "number" implies division or multiplicity, whereas "unity" represents perfect friendship or the Divine.</note> and absence still remaining between us. But I truly confirm a simple unity and a continuous presence, just as it is, and as you most greatly desire it to be confirmed. What then? Shall letters never be exchanged between us? Far be it that nothing should ever flow out from the most affluent abundance of the inward fountain; far be it that nothing should overflow outside. Far be it that what burns within should never shine forth without. But for this reason, we have written and will write frequently back and forth: so that what our minds—or rather our single mind—think in turn, and what the mind says to itself in thinking, others also may sometimes understand by the use of letters. But you wish me to be well; which certainly, above all things, you wish well. Farewell.

### 127

...which is then stored in the capacious hives of memory and, through a certain meditation, is digested; it then becomes the honey-sweet flow of learning and eloquence. But if anyone should deny such a comparison—though it is confirmed by the best authors—he would seem to me worthy of bringing back gall <note>A bitter substance, often used to symbolize spite or misery</note> rather than honey from the very fountain of the Muses. Therefore, I shall not take anything away from this comparison, but rather add to it. You have heard, I think, my friend, that when bees sip from many wormwood <note>original: "absinthii"; a proverbially bitter herb</note> flowers, they very often produce honey which, when tasted with the tip of the lips, seems somewhat sweet; yet, once it is swallowed into the throat, it is not sweet at all, but almost as bitter as gall. We find almost the same thing in certain literary enticements and the "sucking" of books, which often have neither limit nor selection. Indeed, the more greedily they seem to drink the sweetest waters of the Muses, the more they meanwhile desire something bitter in their hearts. This the Latins perhaps call bile, and the Greeks call melancholy <note>original: "melancholiam"</note>; a disease which Aristotle proves is peculiar to diligent men of letters. For this reason, Solon calls the study of letters a most burdensome occupation, and he added sadness as a companion to knowledge itself. What, then, shall we say to that Aristotelian saying: "The tree of science," he says, "has bitter roots, but the sweetest fruit"? We shall certainly grant this to Aristotle, but we will add this: such fruits are perhaps like peaches, where a certain bitter pit <note>original: "nucleus"</note> lies beneath the sweetness. What then? Shall we detest the Muses? Far be it from us to think that the fountain of celestial nectar and ambrosia pours out Stygian <note>Referencing the River Styx in the underworld; i.e., hellish or gloomy</note> and bitter streams. As much as we praise the use of the Muses, so much do we condemn their abuse. For who abuses the Muses most? None but he who either follows their tracks recklessly and at the wrong time, or imprudently mixes them with vulgar Venus <note>Ficino distinguishes between "Heavenly Venus" (divine love) and "Vulgar Venus" (base physical desire or vanity)</note>, or separates them from their leader, Apollo <note>The god of light, reason, and harmony</note>. Even ignorant little men do not grasp it, for they take hold of wisdom itself without "flavor" <note>A play on the Latin "sapere," which means both "to taste" and "to be wise"</note>. The Muses <note>original: "camenæ"</note> do not sing rightly—rather they are silent or shriek—wherever the petulant son of Venus <note>Cupid; representing unruly passion</note> interrupts. The choir of the Pierides <note>Another name for the Muses</note> does not dance fittingly, but rather limps and wavers, when Apollo, the leader of the choir, is far away. Accordingly, he who trusts he can perceive the light of the sun without the help of the sun deservedly wanders in darkness and does not rise into the light. Because he seeks this truth or that truth apart from the Supreme Truth, he undoubtedly falls not into the true, but into the false. He who seeks heavenly nectar in a Stygian swamp will, under the shadowy appearance of honey, deservedly drink the true gall of opinion.

->Perfect friendship does not need words or letters.<-

## Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Francesco, the Cardinal of Siena.

<margin>q</margin> Whenever, Reverend Father, I take up my pen—which I certainly try to do every day—in order to write something to my patron, it is through your efforts (or rather, through your business) that I have obtained the leisure <note>original: "otium"; a state of productive peace or scholarly withdrawal</note> to write so much daily. Every time, my patron himself interrupts me with these quite welcome cries: "I am here, the one you seek. Put down your pen, Ficino! What need is there for any letters when one is permitted to hear and return true voices continually?" Those who see each other in person may perhaps be made present even when absent; but these, on the contrary, who are present to each other everywhere, might perhaps show themselves to be absent if they relied on letters. Do not, therefore, separate yourself from this person with a pen, when you are always joined to him in your heart. What shall I do here? I do not know, my patron. While you yourself do things that are contrary to me, I meanwhile suffer two contrary things in turn. You urge me with spurs to run more frequently, yet at the same time, you restrain me with a bridle so that I may rest. Indeed, if I do not move, I seem lazy and ungrateful. If I am moved, I seem insolent and inept. But while you distract my mind in this way, and I am mutually distracted, this internal letter somehow breaks out from my hands—not with the intention of speaking to you, with whom I speak at will without a letter, but rather for the people, so that everyone may perceive how much a patron and his humble client <note>original: "clientulus"</note> agree in all things. I see that a letter would have commended our Cavalcanti <note>Giovanni Cavalcanti, Ficino's closest friend</note> to you as if he were absent, had it not seen your dear Giovanni standing there before you the moment it first greeted you.

->Rightly does he who voluntarily lacks God—who is all good—unwillingly lack every good.<-

## Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Leone Michele, the Venetian Peripatetic.

<margin>s</margin> If any of us loved the Good itself—which is the sum of all good—with as much passion as we daily love these "goods" and those things which are not good without the Good itself, we would certainly feel at least as much constant good and joy as we now all feel constant evil and pain. Indeed, the joy of that Good would be as much more powerful than this true pain of ours, and sweeter than false pleasure, as the substance of the Good itself is both mightier than evil and truer than the image of goodness. Furthermore, a pure mind is more perceptive than an impure one. Now, however, what wonder is it if all evils follow us, while we ourselves, having abandoned the First Good (that is, God), wrongly pursue individual things as if they were goods, when all things without the First are evil? Justly do we fall unwillingly into every evil as often as we voluntarily fall away from Him who is the All-Good. Why then do we wander, so insane and unhappy, for so long hither and thither? Certainly, while we pursue only individual things, we meanwhile flee the One Himself who is all things. But he who follows only the One, soon attains all things in Him. Doubtless, the mind can attain all things, for it depends solely on Him who is above all. From this, certainly, man alone among the animals has received the power that whatever he wills...

# BOOK FIVE CXXVIII
### FIFTH [BOOK] 128

...may be able to attain exactly what he wishes; and moreover, may he wish to do whatever he is able. Therefore, I approve of you, great-hearted Leo, in that you are no longer troubled about many things. But just as Carlo Valgulio <note>original: "Carolus Valgulius"; a humanist and secretary known for translating Greek musical and philosophical texts.</note>, a most reliable witness among us, testifies: you have long since chosen that best part <note>A reference to the "better part" chosen by Mary in Luke 10:42, often used by Ficino to signify the contemplative life over the active life.</note> which, since it not only flows from its own source but also flows back into the same, therefore completely quenches the thirst of those who taste it; and from that mind which has tasted it, it will never be taken away.

Since God is love itself, whoever strives to love anything without God, tries to love without love.

### Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Lottieri Neroni.
<note>original: "Locterio Heronio"; Lottieri Neroni was a member of a prominent Florentine family and a close friend of Ficino.</note>

I wrote a certain letter last summer, my excellent Lottieri, to my friends concerning true friendship. Perhaps it would have been written in vain to true friends unless it were read by those who are our friends in Him—He without whose heat no one can love anything, without whose splendor nothing can be loved, and without whose love whatever we seem to love (since we attempt to love outside of Love itself), we are forced to hate rather than cherish. Without His friendship, anything is more an enemy to us the more it seems to be a friend. Oh, what a wonderful union of Goodness itself, Beauty, and Love! For where the goodness of good things shines, there the beauty of beautiful things gleams; and there the very love of loves burns. Indeed, beauty follows the light of the Good itself like a splendor. Then the ardent heat of the lover follows the rays of beauty like a reflection of those rays.

->He alone rules happily who rules those who are willing.<-

### Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to Francesco, Cardinal of Siena.
<note>Francesco Todeschini Piccolomini (1439–1503), the nephew of Pope Pius II, who would briefly serve as Pope Pius III in 1503.</note>

Tell me, I pray, with what words especially I should address you now, my most kind patron. The great dignity in which you have been placed seems to require that I begin with "Reverend Father in Christ." But your far greater mercy and immense <term>humanitas</term> <note>The Latin "humanitas" refers to more than just "humanity"; it encompasses kindness, refinement, and the shared cultural values of the Renaissance humanists.</note> entice me to address you almost more familiarly: "Greetings, my sweetest friend." And lest the name "patron" itself—so sweet to the mouth of a client—be omitted: "Greetings again, my Francesco, sweeter than sweetness itself." For I do not struggle with ambiguity as to what I should do: certainly, where the rank of dignity surpasses the affection of humanity, we are accustomed to open with certain worthy and lofty titles. But where singular humanity exceeds the power of dignity, we ought to begin with human and familiar names. Especially since, in your presence, we are not strangers and foreigners, but rather, through your kindness, members of your household. 

Clients, my sweetest friend, are usually most pained when it seems their patrons will give them nothing; I, on the contrary, rejoice most greatly in this very fact: that my patron is to give me nothing further. Indeed, he has left nothing of himself for himself, but has long since given himself and all his possessions to us. Live happily, my most lovable patron. Your friends cannot help but live happily while you live happily, you who live entirely for your friends. For this reason, all your servants serve you most closely, because they serve most freely. No service is either closer or more pleasant than that which is voluntary. No rule is safer or easier than that which is based on love.

# BOOK FIVE

->God approves the outstanding flock which the crowd disapproves: with Him there is gratitude and liberty.<-

## Marsilio Ficino to his unique friend Giovanni Cavalcanti, sends greetings.

<margin>a</margin>
Receive, Giovanni, copies of two letters which I composed this dawn in the cause of our friend, and which I gave today to those priests whom you know. I do not know by what fortune [they were sent]; indeed, that is not my concern. Would that I at least knew by which Muse <note>In the Renaissance, the Muses represented different modes of divine inspiration; Ficino is wondering which spiritual "flavor" inspired his writing.</note> they were inspired. I am no mercenary. I know that the reward of a mercenary is to receive well; but the end of a liberal art <term>liberal art: from the Latin "ars liberalis," meaning the skills befitting a free person (liber), practiced for their own sake rather than for profit.</term> is to have done well. 

Whatever the case, I will at least bring our friend back to memory; perhaps you will say it is better to seek oblivion than memory, and to lie hidden well than to be exposed poorly. But let the others forget him, if oblivion delights them; He <note>Ficino likely refers to God here, the ultimate witness.</note> cannot forget His own. We have found it to be true that no great man was ever recognized by his own people. Is this any wonder? Indeed, the outstanding do not fit with the flock. <note>original: "egregii græci"; likely a scribal error for "egregii gregi" (the outstanding [do not fit] with the flock), playing on the word "egregius" which literally means "out of the flock."</note> Opposites do not love opposites. Envy occupies the place of veneration. Weak eyes are blinded by too much splendor. Those who are filled with small things cannot grasp great ones. 

But perhaps you will grieve this one thing with me, my Giovanni: that perhaps he is unknown to his fatherland not because he is greatest, but because he is judged as least. Let us not grieve, friend, as long as both he and we please Him who discerns the smallest things as well as the greatest, and grasps the greatest as easily as the smallest. No one will be considered the least who is approved by Him, to whom—on account of His own magnitude—the greatest things are infinitely less than the smallest things. He will never be obscure who shines in Him, who shines in all things, and in whom all things shine. 

Nothing, however, is easier than to please Him; for to please Him is nothing other than to *will* to please. Therefore you see something wonderful: that various small goods are much more expensive than the Infinite Good. For the former are obtained only with great labor and cost; but the latter, if it is bought, is bought by the will. But why is this so, friend? Perhaps because He overflows immensely and because His price is within Himself. We buy other things; but He, in truth, buys us of His own accord. He buys us, I say, both by the goodness of His will and by our will for His goodness. Therefore, since this is done by goodness, and goodness itself is God, God is the price on both sides. 

We are never entirely free until we have freely sold ourselves to Infinite Liberty. As soon as we belong to Him—who alone belongs to Himself—only then do we also belong to ourselves. Sons are nowhere more free than in their father’s house and under his commands. Parents obey no one more willingly than their children. But lest I seem to wander too far from where I began, I will make an end in Him, to wander toward whom is nothing other than to return.

### That philosophy does not teach—nay, rather forbids—one to live or associate with princes.
## Marsilio Ficino to his unique friend Giovanni Cavalcanti, sends greetings.

<margin>i</margin>
In that book which I composed this year for Bernardo Bembo <note>original: "Bernardum Bembum"; a Venetian statesman and diplomat, father of the famous poet Pietro Bembo.</note>, the Venetian ambassador, concerning the praises of philosophy, I attempted to assert through many reasons that philosophy teaches all things. I ought to have excepted this one thing: that it does not teach us to lead a life with princes. For if it forbids it entirely, as it certainly does, it in no way teaches it. Indeed, it seems to me to forbid it utterly...
