<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s letter to Giovanni Cavalcanti regarding the incompatibility of true philosophy with the corrupting influence of royal courts. It follows a discussion on how the "outstanding" do not fit in with the "flock" of the common people or the elite.</meta>

# BOOK FIVE CXXIX

Since indeed [court life] commands the opposite. For by finding a love of the truth, the soul desires tranquility of mind and the liberty of life. But among princes, truth does not dwell; rather, lies and pretenses reside there. Dissimulations and slanders; flatteries. Not tranquility of mind, but care and anxiety; envy and, finally, every kind of disturbance. Not liberty, which is dearer than all gold, but rather a slavery so wretched that it never spares the subjects nor the princes; and its end is either servitude or ruin. 

And let no one throw in my face the example of Aristippus of Cyrene, who was no philosopher, but a <term>lover of money and a lover of the body</term> <note>original: "phidolosum & phylosomatum." Ficino is punning on the word "philosopher" (lover of wisdom) by creating Greek-sounding terms for "lover of thrift/money" and "lover of bodies."</note>, who once lived so pleasantly with Dionysius, the tyrant of the Syracusans. For he stripped off philosophy—if indeed he had ever put it on before under Socrates—at the very moment he "clothed" himself in Dionysius. Yet he eventually regretted wearing that garment. For he discovered that while a sword hung over the head of Dionysius, that same sword and Dionysius himself were hanging over the neck of Aristippus. 

In this matter, those who were much more prudent, or certainly more fortunate, were Democritus, Heraclitus, Socrates, Antisthenes, Diogenes, Crates, Xenocrates, Apollonius of Tyana, Plotinus, and many others who preferred a free and most wealthy poverty to the servile and most impoverished riches of kings, and the sweetest sobriety to the most bitter delights of tyrants. 

It is worthwhile to consider those great philosophers whose memory we venerate, who would have lived much more happily than other men with princes and kings, if only philosophy could teach men how to do so. I pass over how the young Octavian <note>The future Emperor Augustus.</note>, ungrateful for past favors and led by a trivial cause, handed over his own Cicero—a philosopher of no mean status—to a wicked enemy to be killed. Nero, without cause, condemned his holy teacher, the philosopher Seneca, to death. Alexander, King of the Macedonians, is said to have thrown his master, the philosopher Callisthenes, to be torn apart by lions for no other reason than that he was being bested by him in debate. 

But who would not wonder greatly at those "divine" philosophers, our Plato and Aristotle—men of the highest gravity who knew all things that are, that were, and that are yet to come—that they dealt so unhappily (I might even say imprudently) with tyrants? For the smallest reasons, they were frequently brought into extreme peril of their lives. This was because when they "clothed" themselves in the prince, they did not "strip off" the philosopher. Perhaps Xenophon, the student of Socrates, was forced to strip it off before Cyrus, King of the Persians. 

O, truly miserable is the lot of philosophers among the powerful. The divine Plato was twice sold into slavery—oh, the grief! Three times he underwent the danger of death under Dionysius the Elder and the Younger, because of a certain theological book written by Dionysius as if from the mind of Plato, which Plato had somewhat revised; but mostly because, while he instructed them as a teacher, he daily exhorted them toward a more just governance. Alexander the Macedonian ignominiously expelled that man of great wisdom, Aristotle, his master and tutor; afterward, he even cruelly persecuted him, whether for the sake of Aristotle’s relative Callisthenes, or because Aristotle published the "secrets of nature" to the common people after having first entrusted them to Alexander. For the slightest cause, the celestial Pythagoras, when he involved himself as a teacher with the aristocrats in the republic—or rather the tyranny—of Croton...

# BOOK FIVE

...worthwhile. Zeno of Elea, that singular metaphysician, was destroyed for a trivial reason under Hiero <note>original: "sub hieron." Ficino likely refers to the tyrant Hiero of Syracuse, though historical accounts of Zeno's death often involve the tyrant Nearchus or Diomedon.</note>; similarly Anaxarchus was destroyed under Nicocreon. And lest I move away from these philosophers to the poets at this time, I shall pass over the unjust exile of Ovid. I shall pass over how, because of a musical contest, Nero hated his own Lucan for a long time and finally brought his life to an end. I shall pass over how Domitian, driven by some petty ambition or other, killed his close friend Statius in that "school of the Muses" of his. But to conclude my discourse regarding philosophers: let no one be so ignorant of human nature as to trust that he can philosophize properly and freely and, at the same time, live his life securely and safely among princes.

->**One is never deceived in loving and praising if God is the law of their**<-
->**loving and praising.**<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Georgius Cyprius, a lawful physician. Greetings.

<margin>q</margin>Who indeed serves most shamefully? He who serves his own slave. Who serves most miserably? He for whom the reward of servitude is punishment. Therefore, he is most shameful and miserable who serves the body. Again, what is he like who serves the rumors of the common people? Vain, restless, and unfortunate. But what is he like who binds himself to those who appear "outstanding" to the common crowd? He is not very prudent. For humans are to be loved, not adored. Rather, they should be judged by a long-lasting, or at least a fifteen-year <note>original: "trilustri." A 'lustrum' was a Roman purification ritual performed every five years; here it refers to a duration of time.</note> examination, and loved most diligently only after you have truly chosen to love. Otherwise, love deceives the judgment and the outcome frustrates the love. Moreover, very few are to be praised, and these only once they have matured and have long been perfected—and even then, only with great moderation. Otherwise, by praising, we are ourselves blamed, and we often regret having given praise. Only he is never deceived for whom God is the law of loving and praising: so that he worships God alone for His own sake, loves men in God, and praises God in men. To what end is this? Truly, so that I might discuss the principal instructions of character with a man established in moral precepts. Farewell.

->**Faith gives birth to sight. Hope brings forth charity. The ardor of charity**<-
->**brings clarity to the intelligence.**<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo, Venetian patrician, legal consultant, and most illustrious knight. Greetings.

<margin>p</margin>Paul the Apostle, that chosen vessel of divine wisdom, when he was caught up into the third heaven—from where celestial love is kindled in the minds of earthly beings—suddenly saw that invisible Sun; no one can look up at its splendor unless they are first kindled by its flames with a certain divine love. Only he, however, is first kindled by such flames who always maintains true faith in its rays that illuminate all things, and who most firmly places all hope in the heat of that same Sun which most kindly nourishes all. When I did not sufficiently understand how much light had recently shone upon me from that Sun, most illustrious Bernardo, I called upon Giovanni Cavalcanti to act as judge in this matter. But since he, like me, seems to be in the dark, we have both decided by common agreement to appoint our friend Bernardo Bembo—endowed as he is with lynx-like eyes <note>A common Renaissance metaphor for exceptionally sharp or penetrating sight.</note>—as the judge in this affair.

# BOOK FIVE
R 2

<margin>q</margin>How different is the nature of love from almost all other things, my most beloved of the beloved! <note>original: "mi amatissimi mi amati." Ficino often uses superlative wordplay in his greetings to emphasize deep Neoplatonic friendship.</note> For in other matters, the greater they are, the more stable they are judged to be. But with love and favor, it is the opposite: the more immense it appears, the more fragile it seems. Indeed, a great love is often offended by more frequent and trivial causes than a moderate one. Either the heat of the emotion itself stirs up a "fiery bile," <note>original: "igneam bilem." In Renaissance medicine, an excess of yellow bile was associated with a hot, irritable temperament.</note> which by some small breath often fluctuates with a great tide of anger; or, a fixed obsession produces "black bile," <note>original: "bilem... atram." This refers to Melancholy, which Ficino believed made the mind fearful and prone to dark imaginings.</note> fearing even where all is safe. Or certainly, it is the greed of one who thinks he has given his whole self to another, and therefore demands the whole in return from the beloved; he never possesses entirely what he sought with his whole mind. 

But these adversities are rightly suffered by the emotion of a childish mind, which is either utterly soft or mercenary. Since it feeds only on the earthly wind, when it seems most to grow, it then becomes fearful rather than increasing. Therefore, the greater it strives to be, the weaker it truly is. As the human saying goes: *Love is a thing full of anxious fear.* <note>original: "Res est solliciti plena timoris amor." A famous quote from Ovid’s *Heroides*.</note> But divine charity, set ablaze by the flames of virtue and celestial rays, seeks again all the sublime heights of heaven, where no dread of earthly evils ever causes anxiety. Such is our mutual love, my beloved. Therefore, just as you are certain of your love toward me, be first just as certain of my love toward you. Far be it from us that a human heart should not respond to a human heart that calls it often, since even strings of a lyre, tempered alike, are seen to respond to one another; and one echoing lute resounds when another is struck; and even a solid wall sometimes echoes back to those who call out.

->Nemo vere fuit nisi qui fuit volens: nemo dominatur vere nisi qui volentibus dominatur.<-
->**No one has truly existed except he who existed willingly; no one truly rules except he who rules over the willing.**<-

### Marsilio Ficino commends himself to Raffaele Riario, Cardinal of St. George.

<margin>p</margin>After we parted from one another yesterday, I could not restrain myself from vehemently envying your household for your company—which is, if I may say so, sweeter than ambrosia and nectar. Therefore, lest I perish from envy, I return quickly today to those who are granted (if it is lawful to say) to feast at the table of the gods. And lest I be forced to depart from there any further and be tortured by spite again, I return to you now with a guide who never departs far from you, and from whom I myself never depart; one who commands me and obeys you. Who is this, you ask? It is Great Love. Who this may be, you shall hear in a moment (if you wish). 

Yesterday, the guide of my journey was the most beautiful Venus in Taurus, <note>In astrology, Venus is "at home" in the sign of Taurus, representing a highly favorable and harmonious influence.</note> with the Moon accompanying her, holding the middle region of the sky. This, I believe, Pierleone <note>original: "petrus leo." Pierleone Leoni of Spoleto was a famous physician and astrologer to the Medici family.</note> the physician and excellent mathematician, will confirm for you. But the guide of today's journey will be that most pleasing celestial Love, the son of Venus. Therefore, receive your lover Marsilio with a certain (if you please) amorous affection. Since indeed, by a certain wonderful kindness of nature, you love (as I hear) even those who do not love you. 

See, venerable father, with what freedom—or rather license—I deal with you. I have just called myself your "lover." Perhaps I ought to have said "servant" instead. Alas, I have erred! But you yourself are the cause, my lord. For you present yourself such to everyone everywhere that he who does not use the greatest freedom and confidence with you would undoubtedly seem the most servile and distrustful of all. But perhaps I did not err. For I have confessed well enough that I am your servant by professing myself your lover. No one truly serves except he who serves willingly. No one truly rules except he who rules over those who are willing. Oh, how wonderful!

# BOOK FIVE

...unstable is the empire of Venus and love. Indeed, as the poets tell: neither the most ferocious Mars nor almighty Jupiter himself can tame Cupid. But among the poets, all the gods are either burned by the flames of love itself, or at least they shine with its rays and reflect its splendor. Farewell.

## Truth on the Instruction of a Prince, to Cardinal Raffaele Riario.

I pray, O happy Prelate <note>original: "Antistes." A term used for a high-ranking priest or bishop; Ficino uses it here to address the Cardinal with religious gravity.</note>, that you are not overcome by wonder that you read no man's name as author of this letter. What is so strange? For it is not a human emotion, but Truth herself speaking with you in this moment. Truth now approaches you not only unarmed, but even naked, as you see. She is not fortified by the sharp points of clever arguments. She is not dressed in the ornaments of elegant words. For she knows she is the most powerful of all and the most beautiful. She knows how whatever light is added from the outside does not illuminate the light, but obscures it. Thus Truth itself is weakened—so to speak—and deformed by outside additions. She would plead at this moment with many words that you might listen to her for a short while with a kind mind as she speaks on your behalf, were it not that she knows you always listen to her gladly; for whatever else is heard is heard poorly and unhappily.

## TRUTH says many greetings to her most beloved son, Cardinal Riario.

And she promises the truest greetings. The Sceptic philosophers <term>Sceptici: a school of ancient philosophy, such as the followers of Pyrrho, who argued that certain knowledge is impossible to attain.</term> and many others falsely slander me, claiming that I am never accessible, as if I were the most obscure of all things. The matter is far otherwise. For what is brighter than my light, through which the sun itself and the world shine? Again, what can lie open more easily or clearly than truth? Through her alone is revealed whatever is revealed anywhere. Whatever they say is revealed outside of her is nothing other than darkness, in which all things lie hidden. Therefore, I am not greedy in any way, nor envious. I meet everyone everywhere of my own accord and most gladly. But many approach me with a cloudy mind—I who can only be grasped by a serene mind. Most people think I dwell in the high palaces of princes. On the contrary, I am more often forced to seek out huts and live in humble cottages. Truly, roofs full of holes do not hinder me here. Walls full of cracks on every side do not hinder me. Here the doors are open to me. An empty house receives me. On the other hand, I am repelled by the solid roofs and walls of the richest estates; and if ever these doors are open to me, a crowd of innumerable lies suddenly meets me. I do not think I should remain among enemies. Therefore, taking flight from there at once, I leave that house full of gold and falsehood, but destitute and empty of truth. But I come to you today, happy Prelate, to live with you gladly forever, if only you wish it. I have hurried, indeed, at the very beginning of your dignity, before my enemies—that is, the pestilential lies of flatterers and detractors—besiege your hearth.

FIRST, do not attribute such a high level of dignity to your own merits. Which, in so few years of a younger age, are so many (as... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence, continuing the argument that the Cardinal's rise is a gift of providence or grace rather than mere personal achievement.</note>

# QUINTUS

...to confess) they could not be. Nor, on the other hand, should you ascribe it to fortune or luck. For the sacred mysteries and divine orders do not proceed from the rashness of fortune, but from the eternal wisdom of God. Therefore, divine providence has decreed to nurture a certain perfect shepherd of the Christian flock for our ages, constantly in its own bosom from the very nest (as they say), and to raise him only on sacred nourishment. And before he might be ensnared by childish games, or apply his mind to things either wicked or trivial, to imbue him with manly character and to instruct him in the greatest and best duties.

God, therefore (as you have heard), God himself has recently given birth to you as a new man. And you, in turn, having left the earth behind, must embrace your heavenly Father—who encompasses all things—with heavenly conduct. Believe me, you will stand for as long as you cling to Him who is not moved. Do not trust in any way in the strength of human height or greatness. All the highest things are shaken most often by winds and lightning. Massive structures collapse with a heavier fall and rise again with greater difficulty. Rise up, then, into Him who cannot fall, and you yourself shall never fall. For then men unhappily desert themselves when they most foolishly and ungratefully desert Him without whom they cannot exist in any way. Alas, whoever tries to leave a guardian of this kind does not leave Him entirely. For at the same time, he falls back into that same punisher <note>original: "sedultore" – This likely refers to God in His capacity as an avenger or judge, or perhaps a typo for "ultore" (avenger).</note>. Whoever impiously neglects the Father who shines with kindness will, in the meantime, experience Him as a burning judge.

**THEREFORE.** You know that legitimate Cardinals <term>Cardinals: Ficino is playing on the Latin word *cardo*, meaning "hinge." He suggests that Cardinals are the hinges upon which the door of the Church turns.</term> are nothing other than certain hinges of the Christian Church and vicars of the Apostles. And for that reason, they ought to consult not their own advantage—nor that of themselves or another—but the common good of the Church. Furthermore, they should do, think, or speak nothing that is not worthy of apostolic holiness. Those who do the opposite are not Cardinals but rather sacrilegious men; they are not vicars of the Apostles, but enemies. Shall I say it? And shall I say this one thing further with the pardon of many? I shall certainly say it, even without pardon. For who will ever be allowed to tell the truth if Truth itself is not permitted? Know also that almost nothing should be more foreign to apostolic men than pride, pomp, and luxury.

**AS MUCH AS** you rejoice in ruling over external servants, give just as much effort to serving divine laws and ruling over your internal servants—that is, your senses. Remember that your servants are human beings, equal to you in origin; and that the human race, free by nature, ought to be or can be bound not by some fear, but by love. As much as almost all powerful men take delight in individual things arranged and adorned in a certain order at home, you shall take just as much delight in a composed mind and in graceful words and character. Your music shall be the tempering of the soul's emotions and of all actions, lest while all things harmonize on the outside, the soul alone sounds a discord. Your game, too, shall be the frequent reading of the most choice writers, lest perhaps in the midst of the greatest wealth, your soul alone might appear destitute. Let your hunters and fowlers <note>Ficino uses these metaphors for the Cardinal’s advisors or courtiers—those who go out and "catch" the favor of the people.</note> be certain men near you of the highest proof and learning, who, through their prudence and marvelous humanity <term>humanitas: This term encompasses kindness, refinement, and the shared bond of human nature.</term>, may acquire the grace and benevolence of all for you. Humanity alone is the bait by which men are caught.

The text uses musical and hunting metaphors to describe the cultivation of a virtuous soul and the winning of public favor through kindness.</summary>

# BOOK

Only through the favor of men are human affairs conducted successfully. Nothing is more dangerous for a prince <note>The term "prince" here refers generally to a high-ranking leader or ruler, including a Prince of the Church like a Cardinal.</note> than if many people should despise him, or hate him so much that they envy him excessively. Contempt is avoided through knowledge, gravity of character, and integrity. Hatred, however, is softened by innocence and humanity. Finally, envy is calmed by generosity, liberality, and magnificence. Since all men are equal in their appearance and free in their will, they bear servitude with a very resentful spirit—unless, perhaps, those who rule are as equal to them in humility as they exceed them in height. They should appear to excel far more in wisdom than in fortune. Nature gave to the limbs—which are lower than the head—only the power of touch. But the head alone she adorned with the rights of all the senses. By this, Nature seems to have warned men that those who strive to lead others as the head must surpass the rest in wisdom as much as the head itself surpasses all the limbs in sensory perception.

No great man at all should trust that his habits can remain hidden. For the greatest things are always the most visible; they are what everyone envies, what they forgive the least, and what they disparage the most. Let the prince see to it—since he himself can hardly hide from others—that nothing at home or abroad remains hidden from him. First, let him be an Argus <note>In Greek mythology, Argus Panoptes was a giant with a hundred eyes, making him an all-seeing guardian.</note> himself. Then, let him nourish a "lynx" <note>Referencing the lynx's legendary reputation for sharp eyesight that could see through solid objects.</note> near him. And if it is possible, let him not lack an Oedipus <note>Oedipus was famous for his intellect in solving the unsolvable riddle of the Sphinx; here it means a solver of mysteries or difficult problems.</note> as well. It is very dangerous in great matters to despise small ones. A small spark, once neglected, often excites a massive fire. It is neither decent nor safe for a man to surrender himself entirely to sleep when he must remain awake for the sake of many, or when many are watching him in turn. Nor is it fit for the "head" of many men to be enslaved to a beast—that is, to serve the belly and its lusts. The best and safest thing is never to be angry. For what else is seething with anger but becoming drunk and insane? When one has shaken off the reins of self-control, then, until the anger cools down, the tongue must be held back with a bridle. And as is usually done with the insane, the hands and feet should be bound, lest anything be said or done in that very fury. The disciples of Pythagoras <note>A Greek philosopher who emphasized self-discipline and harmony.</note> could never detect any sign of anger in him. Socrates's <note>The Athenian philosopher known for his composure.</note> friends had no other proof that he was angry than his silence. Plato, the father of philosophers, once became somewhat angry at a misbehaving boy and said to Xenocrates: "You beat this boy yourself. For I cannot do it while I am angry." 

LET your mind be equally humble and exalted. Let gravity be mixed with courtesy, and your life be sober. Let your tongue be truthful, but very sparing. Let your hand be most generous. Let your promises not be rash. Let your faith be firm and your observance full. Let your counsel be long-lasting, diligently examined by the opinion of the wise. Do not let many people deceive you easily every day, nor should you yourself believe many, nor believe them easily. Let no soft persuasion or any light conjecture move you, but only certain reason. Do not undertake a beginning unless you have looked ahead to an end that is as good as it is certain. Avoid bad and infamous ministers, lest you yourself be considered a bad master. # BOOK V
### CXXXII

R 4

...we passed through with blinking eyes. Poets paint Love <note>original: "Amorem"</note> as blind for this reason: because a lover is very often deceived when he judges either himself or the thing he loves dearly. Since men love no one more vehemently than themselves, they are certainly deceived by no one more than by themselves. Therefore, do not believe anything regarding yourself. Do not, moreover, commit yourself entirely to a single advisor. Instead, have many; and let them be quite elderly, those whom long experience <note>original: "experientia"</note> of affairs has taught, whose character a most constant reputation commends to you as the best, and whom reality itself most clearly proves. Whenever you deliberate on a serious matter together with your elders, take care that they do not perceive your will, lest they perhaps follow your desire rather than usefulness and dignity in their counsel.

BY ALL MEANS, tell your household daily that the gift of truth (from wherever it is offered) will be as pleasing to you as the most precious gifts usually happen to be to greedy tyrants. Open your ears, I pray, to those who warn you, lest you be forced to open your heart itself to the arrows of fortune. Block your ears entirely to flatterers <note>original: "adulatores"</note>, as if to the wicked songs of the Sirens. Remember that you are a man. Therefore, you always have things in you that could be rebuked; for this reason, whichever of your servants praise you without exception: they are either blind, or they are the sort who want you to be blind. If the laws punish most severely those sorcerers who bewitch the eyes with their gaze, or capture the ears or infect the body with certain spells, what then do we think should be done to those who, by fawning and flattering, blind the eyes of the mind and seize the ears? Therefore, if you wish to see, if you wish to hear, if you wish to live: remove all flatterers and ministers of pleasure far away like enemies.

Regarding those who occasionally accuse others before you: what shall we say? These perhaps should sometimes be heard for a moment, but never fully listened to <note>The Latin distinguishes between "audiendi" (hearing the sound) and "exaudire" (listening with the intent to grant or believe fully).</note>. If ever they are heard by you, let them make you cautious rather than an avenger. Do not be content with a single kind of vengeance even if you show you are able to take revenge. But as for detractors <note>original: "Detractores"</note>, the malicious, and the envious: drive them far from your threshold no differently than dogs driven by madness.

FINALLY, let your HOME <note>original: "DOMVS"</note> be: a temple of God, the eye of Prudence, the scale of Justice, the seat of Fortitude, the rule of Temperance, the model of Integrity <note>original: "Honeſtatis"</note>, the splendor of Charity. A fountain of graces, a choir of Muses <note>In Greek mythology, the Muses were the goddesses of inspiration in the arts and sciences.</note>, a gymnasium <note>Here used in the classical sense of a place for training and exercise of the mind.</note> for orators and poets, a sanctuary for philosophers and theologians. A senate of the wise, a nourishment for talents. A reward for the learned, a table for the poor, the hope of the good, the refuge of the innocent, the protection of the miserable. If you observe these and other things of this kind to the best of your ability, you will finally hear that most happy voice: *Upon this rock I will build my church.* <note>A famous biblical quotation from Matthew 16:18, here used to suggest that a leader’s moral household is the foundation of his ecclesiastical authority.</note>

### I commend to you Marsilio Ficino the Florentine: through whose mouth I have spoken the previous things to you.

We ought to congratulate a man who has obtained high office <note>original: "dignitatem"</note> only when he appears worthy of that honor.

## Marsilio Ficino humbly commends himself to Cardinal Riario.

<margin>n</margin>Unless Truth herself had commanded you in days past to block your ears to flatterers, you would now follow your letters with wonderful praises. Which indeed—O Almighty God—how much! But look, who would not rebuke me if I began a song of praise (so to speak)? Truth, however (as I hear), the most modest Riarius, interrupts. You do not wish to be praised to your face, venerable Father. Let it be so, then. But at least permit me to praise, at my own discretion, this very fact that you forbid being praised in such a way. Or do you perhaps forbid this as well? Lest a sharper sting of glory <note>original: "acrior gloriæ stimulus"</note>, which did not prick you from the front, should strike you from behind. I shall indeed obey my lord. But meanwhile, you will grant me this little bit: that if I congratulate you less, I may at least congratulate the dignity of your office itself, because it has finally decided to adorn that man by whom the office itself now seems almost equally adorned in turn. Then I shall rejoice in my own fortune: that, since I am a lover of truth, I have recently found a patron whose own patroness is Truth herself. I shall also congratulate the happiness of Truth herself, who, since she has come forth unarmed and naked, has found not enemies but friends. Yet, venerable Father, Truth has often corrected me in these days: not because I sent her unarmed, but unadorned. Who could deny that she left our threshold unrefined? For Religion herself, who contains all the cultivation of Truth, did not accompany her at all. Therefore, lest Truth complain further about me, or with me, or in your presence, I am also sending you Religion, her handmaiden. But I send her likewise unarmed and naked. Yet I do not think that either Truth or her companion Religion will be in any way unrefined in the presence of our Cardinal, who is a diligent cultivator of both.

### Truth makes a man worthy of high office.

## Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Soderino, most skilled in civil law, sends greetings.

<margin>v</margin>Dearest Soderino, Truth herself, entreated by our prayers, greeted our Cardinal Riario in recent days. Yet she does not seem to have satisfied my wishes according to my vow unless she also greets Soderino, a most true friend. But anyone who thinks that this Truth has come to you later is mistaken. For surely, the same Truth who approaches Riario after he has obtained office, sets out to you before your attainment of office with this purpose: so that she may either make you, or at least declare you, already worthy of that office <note>Soderino would eventually become a Cardinal himself in 1503.</note>.

### Marsilio Ficino gives greetings to Giovanni Pietro Apollinari, a singular Peripatetic. <note>A "Peripatetic" refers to a follower of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note>

Whether the same cause is able to produce contrary effects regarding the same subject is a great controversy among philosophers. Our friend Amantius recently settled this dispute for us, showing that it could be done—not with words, as the practitioners of logic <term>dialecticians; those who use logical argumentation to find truth</term> are accustomed to do, but by the thing itself. Indeed, he led us into contrary emotions at the same time. He wonderfully praises Giovanni Pietro here as a singular philosopher and loves him ardently. However, while I hear him praising you so, I am utterly impelled to write something; yet while I see him loving you so ardently, I recognize the beloved philosopher is present to us within the lover. Therefore, I am called back from writing, thinking that friends who are present do not need letters. What then shall I do? Shall I write? I shall certainly write, so that I too might distract you in a way with diverse emotions: namely, so that you do not respond and yet you do respond at the same time. I, excellent man, who write so tepidly—believe me—love just as ardently. Therefore, respond to me as I write ineptly, but with nothing from your pen. Instead, I pray, respond with love to one who loves you fittingly. And if you love us, take the greatest care of your health. For philosophy cannot be in good health in these times unless you yourself are well.

->Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.<- <note>A quote from the Gospel of John 15:13.</note>

### Marsilio Ficino to the Magnanimous Man, Lorenzo de' Medici, sends greetings.

Greetings, our magnanimous Medici, best of doctors. <note>Ficino frequently makes a pun on Lorenzo's last name, "Medici," which means "doctors" in Latin.</note> Truly, you alone perform the office of a heavenly doctor. For He sent His eternal son down from heaven to the earth as a doctor for human diseases. You also yesterday, of your own accord, sent your dearest son <note>Likely referring to Piero de' Medici, Lorenzo’s eldest son.</note> to us, who might heal our very weary minds. He did not spare His son for the safety of the human race; you yourself did not spare your son for our consolation. For the common suspicion of this epidemic <note>Referring to the plague, which often broke out in Florence and drove the elite to their country villas.</note> did not restrain you from consoling your deserving friends with the presence of your noble son, so that you might perfectly fulfill that divine precept: **Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.** Lorenzo, while you look out for our safety from every side, you draw all our things toward yourself, so that we now live in you rather than in ourselves. Thus it happens that we are unable to repay you in kind. We would certainly lay down our lives for you, if we had them; you, doctor, possess them yourself. Therefore, wherever it pleases you, lay them down yourself. Farewell happily, my one and only patron until now; now, my one and only father.

## Happy is he who has all that he wants; moreover, he has all that he wants who wants all that he has.

### Marsilio Ficino wishes happiness to Francesco Sassetti. <note>Francesco Sassetti (1421–1490) was a prominent Florentine banker for the Medici family and a significant patron of the arts.</note>

<margin>5</margin>Wise men, Sassetti, consider only that man happy for whom all things happen according to his will. But all things happen according to the will only of him who has everything he wants; and he has everything he wants who wants everything he has. He wants each individual thing he has—that is, whatever happens by nature or by chance—who first understands that he ought to wish for no good other than what exists. Then he judges that He who made all things good from the beginning daily disposes each thing well everywhere. Finally, so that he may never be at odds with himself, he himself agrees with the Author of all things. I consider only that man happy who, with the highest piety, has committed himself to God the governor; whatever happens, he either approves of it as though done by God, or at least praises it as something to be brought back into the order of good things by God. Perhaps you ask by what reasoning I might best demonstrate this. Only by this one for now, for a letter rejoices in brevity: if even the light of the sun were infinite, or the heat of fire immense, no place would ever lie open to darkness, nor would any cold be felt anywhere. We know that that one ruler of the one world—who rules and moves so great a mass so well through time and is never weary—is an entirely immense good. If He is immense, without doubt He propagates Himself into infinite space (if I may say so) and surpasses all things by an infinite degree of power. Where then does evil dwell, if it cannot exist with the good, and the good itself occupies the universe? Therefore, evil has no true seat anywhere, but only an imaginary one. It is by no means in nature itself, but rather in that mind which lies to itself so much about divine goodness that it thinks things could be disposed otherwise than well under an immense good. On the contrary, nothing happens to that man that is not good, who thinks that nothing is not good. But so that we might think of things in this way, and thus live happily, religion alone provides for us. And this will be provided for you, my Francesco, more than twice as much as for others, if you surpass others in religion as much as these most magnificent houses of yours surpass others. Your home, Sassetti, is twice as religious as others. Others certainly have scarcely one chapel. Yours truly contains a pair, and those most beautiful. Live twice as religious as others, my Francesco; farewell, twice as happy.

### We use prosperity more childishly <note>original: "puerfius"; likely a typographical error for "puerilius," meaning more childishly or foolishly.</note> than adversity.

### Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to Raffaele Riario and Francesco Salviato, Archbishop of Pisa. <note>Raffaele Riario was a powerful Cardinal; Francesco Salviato was the Archbishop of Pisa. <margin>5</margin>Aristotle writes in his book on ethics <term>De moribus; referring to the Nicomachean Ethics</term> that it is more difficult to endure pains than to abstain from pleasures. This indeed seems probable perhaps for this reason: because pain is more powerful in destroying nature than pleasure is in preserving or repairing it. Furthermore, a man of sound mind (if the choice were given) would choose to abstain from pleasures rather than suffer or bear pains; yet, I know not by what foolish or rather wretched lot of mortals...

<meta>This page continues the text from page 133, where Ficino was discussing the nature of the good and how a person should relate their will to God’s providence. Here, he concludes that discussion by contrasting how humans handle prosperity versus adversity, before beginning a new, more personal letter to his friend Bernardo Bembo.</meta>

<header>FIFTH BOOK 134</header>
<sig>t</sig>

...may happen. Would that many did not use prosperity more perversely than they use adversity; and would that those who did not yield to the threats of pain did not nonetheless surrender to the allurements of pleasures. I pass over now Achilles, Hannibal, Mark Antony, and many others, who stood firm while the North Wind <note>original: "borea"; the Boreas was the Greek personification of the cold north wind</note> was raging, yet fell when a flattering breeze blew. When they had emerged from the deep gall <note>original: "felle"; gall or bile was a common metaphor for bitterness or intense suffering</note> of life, they were immediately submerged by a little bit of honey.

And if I were permitted to compare heroes to flies in the Homeric style, I would add that flies are very often choked by sweet, unmixed wine rather than by sour wine. Truly, who would not wonder greatly if they considered how wisely Solomon, the wisest of the Hebrews, endured in labor, yet how foolishly he succumbed to lust? Furthermore, consider how bravely Hercules, the strongest of the pagans, overcame the greatest dangers, yet how softly he submitted his neck to the yoke of pleasure.

If by chance you ask for what reason prosperous things soften and break spirits more than adverse ones do, Philosophy will answer briefly: Prosperity inflates the soul with a richer breath. An abundance of things makes men immoderate and negligent. License renders them worse—that is, more prone to all crimes. Indeed, every natural appetite chooses and follows the good, while it flees and puts to flight the evil. Pleasure seems to present an image of the good, while pain, by contrast, presents an image of the evil. Therefore, when pleasure meets us, not only do we not resist, but we voluntarily follow it as a friend and yield to it and obey it. And so, by this—as it is said in Plato <note>Ficino refers to the *Timaeus* or *Laws*, where Plato describes pleasure as the "bait" or "hook" of evil</note>—we are captured as if by a hook by our enemies (that is, by evils). Then, because they are hidden under pleasure, we are secretly killed.

But when the grim face of pain shows itself, the whole force of our nature is immediately armed within us as if against an enemy. For this reason, we often fight strenuously; and we conquer this open enemy more easily than we do a traitor. Therefore, so that we may use prosperity well, let us remember that the nature of evil—acting like a female hunter—offers itself to us daily under the pretext of good (that is, pleasure) in order to deceive and destroy the wretched. Otherwise, evil itself—especially the beginning of a spiritual evil—if it met us naked, would be more foul than foulness itself and would be fled from instantly. But because it is covered by pleasure, which is the image of the good, it is very easily received by anyone as a guest, as if it were a good. Yet a little later, it deservedly overcomes its unwary host in secret with a blade. Let us therefore flee pleasure, so that we may escape pain in the distance. Pleasure bought with pain is harmful. <note>original: "Nocet empta dolore voluptas"; a famous line from Horace's *Epistles* (1.2.55)</note>

->Material for writing is never lacking for those who love.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo, Venetian Jurisconsult and most distinguished knight. Greetings. <note>Bernardo Bembo (1433–1519) was a Venetian diplomat and the father of the famous humanist Pietro Bembo. He was a close friend and correspondent of Ficino.</note>

<margin>t</margin>For a long time now, I have been searching for a legitimate excuse to give you for this daily silence of ours. And for that reason, I remain silent all the more in the meantime, because I cannot find a sufficiently great cause to bring forward for my silence. I am writing to you now, however, for this very reason, best Bembo: since I cannot find what I should preferably write, I am writing this very thing—namely, that I have nothing to write. What indeed are we doing, my sweetest Bernardo? Do you see what harm expectation does to us? Truly, while I was expecting yours any day now...

### Marsilio Ficino to Pierleone da Spoleto <note>Pierleone (d. 1492) was a physician and a very close friend of Ficino; he served as a doctor to Lorenzo de' Medici.</note>, his fellow philosopher. Greetings.

<margin>Y</margin>our letter, our fellow philosopher, seeks Platonic mysteries from us, and at the same time, it treats them. You seek so beautifully that I do not know how to refuse the seeker. You treat them so well that I am unable to send anything in return. Indeed, I have nothing at all that I might send to one who already possesses everything. Therefore, what shall I do? Shall I be stingy toward one who asks so graciously? Or rather, shall I be a superfluous giver to one who possesses all? Yet I prefer to sometimes give what is extra rather than risk denying what is due.

### Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Marco Aurelio <note>Marco Aurelio was a prominent Venetian orator and diplomat.</note>, the most illustrious Orator. Greetings.

<margin>J</margin>ust as all things seem to mourn when the sun sets and to rejoice when it rises, so this entire people clearly grieved when Bernardo Bembo <note>Bernardo Bembo (1433–1519) was a Venetian diplomat and the father of the famous Pietro Bembo; he was a key figure in the cultural exchange between Venice and Florence.</note> once departed from here, and now they rejoice as he returns. At this point, it is pleasing to address the Venetian Senate for a moment. If ever, O divine Senate, you should wish to stop rivers or move stones, you will not call upon an Orpheus or an Amphion <note>In Greek mythology, Orpheus and Amphion were musicians whose songs could move inanimate objects and charm wild beasts.</note>; rather, you will call upon Bernardo. For he persuades no less here through his silence, by a certain marvelous grace, than those men did by their singing. If it should be necessary to subdue distant or rebellious nations, you will not send Caesars or Pompeys <note>A reference to the great Roman generals Julius Caesar and Pompey the Great.</note>; rather, you will send Bernardo. For he captures more people, and more easily, through kindness and love than those commanders did through arms. Why do I say these things to you, excellent Marco? So that you yourself may understand—and signify to your close friends—how much this choice of yours is approved by everyone; and so that you may ask Bernardo himself, especially in the name of our men of letters, to take up his journey both swiftly and eagerly. And may he, upon his arrival, happily restore me to myself, whom he so easily carried away when he departed.

<margin>a</margin> You would never have thought, Venerable Father, that such a long silence could have fallen between us. But you will cease to wonder at this one thing (as I believe), if only you perhaps consider diligently the common state of all things in these times. Do you not see how ominous it is? The year acts with too much of a prodigious nature <note>The "prodigious year" likely refers to the tumultuous period following the Pazzi Conspiracy (1478) and the subsequent wars involving Florence, the Papacy, and Naples.</note>. Every day so many new and unheard-of things happen, that one must daily repeat the phrase: "I would not have thought it." 

But to leave public matters and come to private ones: I had indeed long desired to find some prince who would please me entirely, and whom I myself might please in turn. At last, I have found him. I was summoned a thousand times. I did not follow. I would never have thought this could happen; ah, how often I cursed that very impossibility (so to speak). You indeed, my Raphael <note>original: "Raphael"; likely Raphael Maffei or Cardinal Raffaele Riario.</note>, were at first commanding impossible things when you begged me to follow in your footsteps. For it was not only private causes that I brought forward, but also certain very powerful public ones which I could not declare, that held me back. 

However, a few days after your departure, affected by weariness of myself and inflamed by longing for you, I similarly began to wish for impossible things: namely, that I had not only come to you, but had even arrived before you. Yet again I was held back by those same wretched causes. But what the cruelty of Mars and Saturn <note>In astrology, Mars represents war and conflict, while Saturn represents hardship and delay. Ficino uses these as metaphors for the political strife in Italy.</note> had attempted either to tear apart or unravel, the kindness of Venus and Jupiter <note>Venus represents love and harmony, while Jupiter represents justice and growth; here they signify a turn toward peace and favor.</note>, striving to mend things on every side, has meanwhile suddenly brought back our Archbishop of Amalfi <note>Raphaele Riario, who held the title of Archbishop of Amalfi.</note> to Florence. He is indeed most familiar to me, and most devoted to you above all others. 

Since I could speak of my Raphael as often as my burning affection urged me to do so, I found in him a mutual admirer of yours above all men. He stood forth as the chief healer of my affliction. He restored my Raphael to me; for indeed, wherever two are gathered in your name, you yourself are present there. You remember how often and how much I praised the judgment and integrity of the Archbishop to you. If ever you come to know the man from Amalfi by his actual presence, you will affirm that I praised him truly indeed, but most sparingly. His brother, Pietro Micholino, an excellent man, will commend his cause. Your Marsilio would commend him to you above all his own merits, if he had ever deserved anything well from you. But since there are no merits—which I grieve over greatly—he commends the Archbishop's business to you again and again, if only on account of your kindness and his own virtue.

->Patience cannot be maintained without religion.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Coccio <note>Antonio Coccio (also known as Sabellico) was a humanist scholar and legal expert.</note>, the distinguished legal expert, sends greetings.<-

<margin>t</margin> There are three things especially, as it seems to me, that patience commands. First, that you should be willing to suffer gladly those evils which nature itself commands you not to want to suffer. Second, that you make voluntary for yourself those things which fate has decreed to be necessary. Third, that you turn any evils whatever into goods—which is the duty of God alone. In the first, patience commands one to resist nature. In the second, to conquer fate. In the third, finally, it commands one to make oneself equal to God. Long ago, it was far easier for Hercules to obey the commands of Eurystheus <note>In Greek mythology, King Eurystheus set the twelve impossible labors for Hercules.</note> and to tame those wild monsters than it is to do these things.

This page concludes a philosophical meditation on the nature of patience and its relationship to the Divine Will. It then transitions into a formal letter of greeting to the Venetian diplomat Bernardo Bembo. The text is characteristic of Marsilio Ficino’s Neo-Platonic philosophy, which seeks to reconcile Christian faith with Platonic thought.

than for us to obey the precepts of patience itself. And indeed, with how much difficulty we struggle in this; it shows us this most of all: that in other things, whatever we handle most frequently, we eventually tend to perform best and most easily. But truly, in the duties of patience, I do not easily see how much the common people progress. Indeed, the whole life of men in this region of the world—which is malignant and contrary to heavenly minds—seems to be nothing other than a certain disease and perpetual pain. However, although we endure evils constantly, we almost continually endure them badly. And to the rest of the evils, which are innumerable, impatience itself is added to us as the greatest of evils. It is so evil that without it nothing would be an evil to us, and with it nothing is good. For impatience alone causes adversities—which might only pertain to external things and the body—to pass over into the soul as well. It causes, moreover, that we enjoy the goods provided by nature or fortune very little. 

Patience, however, by bearing evils well, transforms them into good; and by using goods well, it enjoys them most happily. Surely, just as badly—that is, with difficulty and unhappily—as we bear evils when we are separated from the <term>Highest Good</term><note>original: "summo bono"; the Neo-Platonic concept of the ultimate source of all goodness, identified here with God.</note>, so well—that is, easily and happily—do we endure them when we are joined to the Highest Good. For where every good is, there alone is found the medicine for all evils. But we are joined to it when we most willingly harmonize with the very will of God, the governor of all things. Finally, we harmonize if we love. Nay, if in loving individual goods we recognize that we truly love nothing other than the Highest and Divine Good itself—from which individual things have the quality of being good and lovable, and we ourselves have the quality of both needing to be loved and being able to love. 

Let us recognize, therefore—O friend, I pray let us finally recognize—since nothing pleases us anywhere except for the image of God itself, and nothing in those things that please us pleases us other than God himself (from whom individual things have this very quality of pleasing): so indeed in all things to be loved, let us notice that God himself is loved by us. Thus we shall willingly harmonize with His will; thus, joined to God, we shall happily overcome fortune, nature, and fate. 

Surely we shall understand that just as individual things that are either hot or bright are necessarily traced back to the highest heat and light, so whatever things have some part of the good—that is, all things well and wisely arranged in the single order of the world—are clearly led back to one supreme goodness and wisdom. Since nothing of the good is lacking in it, eternal life is utterly present there. It is the highest understanding of all things, the highest kindness, complete beneficence, and perfect happiness. And since all things are arranged from there as well as possible, we shall always accept whatever happens for the better. In this one thing the entire force of patience consists: that we endure well, as if it were a good, whatever happens under the governance of infinite goodness.

<margin>How often</margin>As often as I take up my pen in these times—which I do frequently—it comes to mind that I should write something about patience. These iron ages <note>original: "ferrea secula"; a reference to the classical concept of the "Ages of Man," where the Iron Age is the final, most degenerate and cruel era.</note> bring us nothing but evil. The Muses bring us nothing but patience: the virtue of enduring evils. Now, I have need of that alchemical metamorphosis which turns iron into gold. Thus, these most wretched times—which come to us as "iron" because of the suffering itself—may at least be made "golden" through the gift of patience.

Receive, therefore, most patient man, these copies of three letters that briefly discuss patience.

->Nothing is more either necessary or voluntary than love.<-

### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Antonio Vinciguerra, most learned scribe of the Venetians. Greetings.

<margin>Read</margin>Read happily, along with Bembo, our book on religion. And live always mindful of your Marsilio—or rather (to speak more correctly) of Bernardo Bembo. Into him, that <term>magical god</term><note>Ficino refers to Love (Eros) as a "magician" because it has the power to transform the lover into the beloved, a central theme in his Neoplatonic philosophy.</note> (who alone among the divinities holds power over free wills) has long since transformed me. Heavenly love, most beloved Antonio, alone often makes the will "necessary," for I love in such a way that I cannot *not* love. And in turn, it sometimes renders "necessity" itself voluntary, when I love in such a way that I neither wish to stop loving, nor wish that I were even *able* to stop. Therefore, whether you choose to call me Marsilio Bembo or Bernardo Ficino, you will name me correctly in either case. Do you not notice that you, too, are bound to us by the same reasoning? A <term>threefold cord</term><note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 4:12: "A threefold cord is not quickly broken," symbolizing the strength of their three-way friendship.</note>, Antonio, is difficult to unravel; but in all things we must look to our friend Bembo. Yet perhaps in this one part, he is sometimes to be avoided. Shall I say it? I shall certainly say it: for where love overflows, there forgiveness also abounds. 

In a certain way, Bernardo seems to be an <term>Averroist</term><note>Followers of the philosopher Averroes, some of whom argued for a single "collective" intellect shared by all humans. Ficino usually opposed this as a heresy against individual immortality, but here he uses it as a poetic compliment for their shared friendship.</note> rather than a Platonist; for by his silence, he persuades one of that Averroistic heresy much more than all the Averroists do by their disputations. Indeed, while by a certain marvelous grace and melting love he makes one single will out of many people, he also seems to signify—as it is in Averroes—a single intellect among many. But lest we prophesy anything impious while we are discussing piety itself, let our Bembo be "Davidic" and not "Averroistic": <note>original: "o quam bonum, o quam iocundum habitare fratres in unum"; a quote from Psalm 133:1.</note> *O how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity.*

->An excuse for when we respond too late.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Lotterio Neroni. Greetings.

<margin>Do not</margin>Do not wonder, my excellent Lotterio, if you receive our letters, in which we respond to yours, somewhat late. For your letters reach us late as well, being sent down from (as I might put it) heaven itself. And our letters, in turn, seek heavenly things from the earth too slowly. However, I have recently discovered, I know not how, the best way I might lift myself from the ground and climb a little way up the heights of heaven. I shall catch, however I can, the rays stretched out from the sun itself all the way to the earth. By these rays, as if by certain ropes, I shall climb with all my might to the ethereal regions. And there, Lotterio...

### Marsilio Ficino to Girolamo Rossi of Pistoia. Health and Greetings.

<margin>Read</margin>Read happily our volume on pious faith, <note>Likely referring to Ficino's "On the Christian Religion."</note> our pious friend, who is more faithful than faith itself. If you find anything in it worthy of praise, praise God, without whose gift nothing is truly to be praised. If something should happen to please you less, take care lest religion itself please you less on that account. Do not wish to measure the height of divine things by the humility of human intellect. For divine things do not depend on human ones, but human things on the divine. Live happily, mindful of us, most beloved brother.

->It is not the husk that nourishes, but the marrow.<-

### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to the Reverend Father in Christ and his Lord, Giovanni Nicolini, Archbishop of Amalfi. Health and Greetings.

<margin>Not</margin>We should not read the writings of the holy Theologians with the same eye as we read those of poets or orators. Elsewhere, even if something delights us on the outside, almost nothing is found that truly nourishes. Here, however, it is not the "husk" that nourishes some, but the "marrow." <note>Ficino uses the "husk vs. marrow" (cortex vs. medulla) metaphor to distinguish between the superficial literal meaning of a text and its deep spiritual truth.</note> It is one thing to smell flowers; it is another to pluck the fruit and drink the juices. Therefore, the fruits of wisdom must be diligently shelled so that they may nourish. Not he who has merely seen wine judges correctly how much strength is in it, but he who drinks it. Not he who only touches pepper with his hands, but he who tastes it with his tongue, recognizes first how much heat it contains. We do not gaze upon the immense splendor of the sun from this side of the clouds, but from beyond them—or rather, after the clouds have been scattered. "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it." <note>A quote from the Gospel of John 1:5.</note> Therefore, you will often warn your household to remember that among the ancients, Minerva <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom.</note> was veiled in a robe. And let them not run past the wonderful works of Minerva herself with half-closed eyes, as they usually do with other things; but rather, let them dwell upon them more vigilantly, with "lynx-like eyes," <note>original: "lynceis"; referring to the mythological Lynceus, famed for his piercing sight.</note> so to speak. But enough of these things for now. I hear, Giovanni, that you enjoy the most sweet and familiar company of the Archbishop of Florence. You have made me blessed, my dear Nicolini; you have certainly made me too blessed. You have prophesied, I think, since I have long and vehemently desired to lead a "Jovial" life near someone. <note>original: "Iouiale"; referring to the planet Jupiter, associated with joy, justice, and authority.</note> By this, some bitterness—Saturnine, <note>original: "Saturnii"; referring to the planet Saturn, associated with melancholy, deep study, and hardship.</note> so to speak—which my birth either implanted in me or philosophy added to me, might sometimes be sweetened by the Jovial...

### Marsilio Ficino to Lorenzo de’ Medici the Younger, Greetings.

<margin>1</margin> My great love for you, excellent Lorenzo, <note>Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici (1463–1503), the younger cousin of Lorenzo the Magnificent.</note> has long commanded me to give you great gifts. A contemplator of the heavens considers nothing among all the things he sees with his eyes to be great, except the heaven itself. Therefore, if I give the heaven itself to you today, Lorenzo, behold, what will its value be? But I would not wish to mention a price just now. For love, born of grace, gives and receives everything for free; nor can anything under the heavens be paid back in equal measure for the heaven itself. Astrologers claim that he is born most fortunate of all whose fate has so tempered the celestial signs that the Moon first looks not unfavorably upon Mars and Saturn. <note>In traditional astrology, Mars and Saturn are "malefic" planets. Ficino is describing a birth chart where their negative influences are neutralized.</note> Then, that it looks favorably upon the Sun and Jupiter, and upon Mercury and Venus. Just as much as astrologers make a man fortunate for whom fate has well-disposed the celestial bodies, so much do theologians make that man blessed who has himself likewise attempted the same things. But you will say that this is far too great a task. Great, certainly. Nevertheless, approach it with good hope, noble Lorenzo. He who made you is much greater than the heaven. You yourself will be greater than the heaven as soon as you resolve to approach the task. For these things are not to be sought by us anywhere outside ourselves. Indeed, the whole heaven is within us, in whom there is a fiery vigor and a celestial origin. To begin, what else does the Moon signify in us except that continuous motion of our mind and body? Mars signifies speed. Saturn, however, signifies slowness. Furthermore, the Sun signifies God; Jupiter, the Law; Mercury, reason; and Venus, humanity. <note>original: "humanitatem"; for Ficino, this signifies the virtue of being "human," involving both kindness and the cultural refinement of the liberal arts.</note> Come now, prepare yourself, noble youth, and in this manner temper the heaven for yourself along with me. Let your Moon—that is, the continuous motion of mind and body—avoid the excessive speed of Mars or the slowness of Saturn; that is, let it handle each thing maturely and at the right time. Let it not hurry faster than is right, nor delay longer than is fitting. Moreover, let this Moon within you look continually toward your Sun—that is, God himself—from whom souls always receive their rays, so that you may worship Him everywhere above all others, from whom you have your being, and so that you yourself may be worthy of honor. Let it also look upon Jupiter, that is, divine and human laws, which it should never transgress. For indeed, to depart from the laws by which all things stand is nothing other than to perish. Let it direct its gaze again toward Mercury, that is, toward counsel, reason, and knowledge. Nor...

...and let whatever he attempts be by the counsel of the wise; nor let anything be said or done for which he cannot provide a probable reason. Again, let him consider a man who is unskilled in knowledge and letters to be, in a sense, like you, but mute. Finally, let him fix his gaze upon Venus herself: that is, upon **Humanity**. <note>Ficino famously reinterprets the goddess Venus not as lust, but as *Humanitas*—the sum of human virtues including kindness, culture, and social grace.</note> By this, he is clearly warned to remember that nothing great can be possessed by us on earth unless we possess the men themselves for whose sake all earthly things were created. Moreover, men are captured by no other bait than by humanity. Take care never to despise her, perhaps thinking that humanity was born from the ground <note>A play on words: *humanitas* (humanity) and *humus* (ground/earth).</note>. For Humanity itself is a nymph of outstanding body, born of celestial origin, and beloved by the ethereal God above all others. Indeed, her soul and spirit are love and charity; her eyes are gravity and magnanimity; her hands are liberality and magnificence; her feet, moreover, are courtesy and modesty. Finally, her whole being is temperance and honesty, honor and splendor. O, what an outstanding form! O, what a beautiful sight! My dear Lorenzo: a nymph so noble has been placed entirely at your disposal. If you join her to yourself in marriage and dedicate her as your own, she will bring you all sweet years and make you a parent of beautiful offspring. Finally (to speak briefly), if in this way you prudently temper within yourself both the celestial signs and the gifts, you will flee far from all the threats of the fates; and by divine auspices, you will undoubtedly lead a blessed life.

I am writing a letter to Lorenzo the Younger <note>Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici, the cousin of Lorenzo the Magnificent.</note> concerning "fated prosperity"—which we often obtain by lot from the stars that are outside of us—and also concerning "free happiness," which we acquire by our own will from the stars that are within us. ### On the salvation of philosophers before the coming of Christ.
### Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Biuano of Sarzana. Greetings.

<margin>p</margin>
The Mosaic precepts are distinguished into two kinds among theologians. Some belong to natural and moral law. Others belong to ceremonies and judgments. Those first ones were given by God to Moses and to the people. The second, Moses himself established, being divinely inspired. Again, the first are commanded to be observed forever by every kind of human being; the second bind the Jews alone: namely, until the coming of the Messiah himself. The first which we mentioned are so common that they could have been known even to someone less liberally educated by the power of natural judgment alone. For what else is contained in them besides the worship of the one God and a moral life? Pythagoras, Socrates, and Plato, and other similar worshippers of the one God, were established in the best of morals. By this kind of discipline—whether Mosaic or natural—they avoided the underworld. <note>original: "inferos," referring here to hell or spiritual descent.</note> Truly, if the heavenly things...

### Exhortation to Respond.

-> Marsilio Ficino to Phoebus Capella, the most distinguished Venetian orator. Sendeth greetings. <-

Phoebus, unless you give me a response eventually, though I have called you many times, perhaps we shall deny that you are **Phoebus** <note>Phoebus is an epithet for Apollo, the god of prophecy and oracles; Ficino is joking that if he doesn't give an "oracle" (a reply), he doesn't deserve the name.</note>: whose principal duty they say was to give responses. Perhaps you will say: "You are not so great, Marsilio, that Phoebus himself should respond to you." But come now, my Phoebus: respond anyway. For suddenly I shall be great. Oh, if only I could say, "Phoebus himself once responded to me." Oh, how great I would be!

Happy is he who truly rejoices. He alone truly rejoices who rejoices in truth alone.

-> Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Bernardo Capponi, son of Niccolò. Sendeth greetings. <-

I have composed a certain short declamation <term>declamatiuncula</term> <note>A brief rhetorical exercise or informal speech.</note> addressed to the human race, briefly disputing the conduct of life. I shall think I have handled such a great matter well only when I seem to have correctly instructed the human race according to your own most upright instruction. I have transcribed a copy of it for you; read it happily. But I shall have said too little unless I add this one thing further: and live happily. For what else is happiness but true joy? For the sake of which everyone does everything. Therefore, that you may live happily, truly rejoice. And so that you may truly rejoice, rejoice in the truth alone.

### A Picture of a Beautiful Body and a Beautiful Mind.

-> Marsilio Ficino of Florence to his close friends: again to Lorenzo de' Medici. Also to Bernardo Bembo. Sendeth greetings. <-

Philosophers dispute much, orators declaim, and poets sing of things by which men may be exhorted to the true love of virtue. I indeed praise and admire these things. Otherwise (unless I praised good things) I myself would not be good. But I think that virtue itself (if ever it were brought into the midst) would exhort all to lay hold of her much more easily and better than the words of men. In vain do you praise a girl to the ears of a youth and describe her with words to strike him with the stings of love, when you could instead offer the very form of the beautiful girl to the youth's eyes. Point out the beautiful one with your finger (if you can); here you have no further need for words. For it cannot be said how much more easily and vehemently beauty itself provokes one to love than words...

<summary>Ficino concludes a theological point on how ancient souls in Limbo were saved by Christ before moving into a series of letters emphasizing that true happiness comes from the truth and that the visual presence of virtue is more persuasive than mere words.</summary>

--- Page 280 ---
<meta>This page concludes the philosophical argument regarding the visual beauty of virtue, continuing from the theme of "Humanity" and moral excellence as a reflection of divine order. It likely concludes a letter or an oration within Book Five.</meta>

<header>BOOK</header>

...to be loved. Therefore, if we bring before the sight of men the wonderful appearance of virtue itself, there will be no further need for our persuasions. It will persuade more quickly than can be imagined. 

Imagine a man endowed with the most vigorous and sharpest senses: with a robust body, prosperous health, a becoming form, a suitable size of limbs, and a decent height. Imagine this man moving himself promptly and speaking skillfully and ornately; singing sweetly and laughing graciously. You will love no one, you will admire no one, if you do not love and admire such a man the moment you see him. 

Come then, so that you may more easily conceive of the divine appearance of the soul from the congruent likeness of a beautiful body, assign each trait to its counterpart. For the body is the shadow of the soul itself. Indeed, the form of the body, as much as it can, reflects the form of the soul. Therefore, that vivacity and sharpness of sense in the body reflects, in a certain way, the wisdom and prudence of the soul. The strength of the body signifies the fortitude of the soul; the health of the body—which consists in the tempering of the humors <note>In Renaissance medicine, health was defined by the balance of the four "humors": blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile.</note>—signifies the temperance of the soul. 

Beauty, which the order of the limbs and a becoming color constitute, shows us the order and splendor of justice. Greatness of size <note>original: *amplitudo*</note> signifies liberality and magnificence. Stature, indeed, signifies magnanimity. That dexterity represents urbanity and courtesy; ornate speech represents oratory. Sweet song represents the poetic faculty. Finally, that most pleasing laughter represents the perfect joy with which virtue itself imbues us, as well as the secure happiness of life. 

Now, gather together the individual members and gifts of virtue we have described into one, and you will clearly see a sight to be venerated and suddenly admired. Oh, how lovable, oh, how wonderful is this form of the soul! The form of the body—so commonly loved and so wonderful—is merely its shadow. Indeed, just as virtue itself, if it could be seen by the eyes, would immediately entice everyone to itself with its most pleasing appearance, so too without doubt would vice (if clearly seen) immediately terrify and put them to flight with its deformity. 

Come then, oh friends: let us always have before our eyes this divine idea and form of virtue. It will immediately entice us by the grace of its splendor; it will continually delight us with the sweetness of its order and harmony; it will fill us completely with an abundance of good things.

->•THE END<-

<term>virtus</term>: Excellence or virtue. For Ficino, this is not just moral behavior but a dynamic power or "virility" of the soul.
<term>magnificentia</term>: Magnificence. In the Aristotelian sense, the virtue of spending large sums of money appropriately on great works.
<term>proceritas</term>: Stature or height. Neoplatonists often associated physical height with "high-mindedness" or magnanimity.

## Sixth Book of Letters.

->A prayer of the Christian flock to their shepherd, Sixtus, urging him to say to his sheep, "Peace be with you." The Christian Flock humbly commends itself to its most blessed shepherd, Sixtus.<-

<margin>b</margin> I do not easily find now, O best of shepherds, where it is most fitting to begin. For on one hand, I am moved to praise by the wondrous virtues of your holiness; on the other, I am pulled back to complaints by the mournful evils of my own misery. What, therefore, shall I do in this present moment? Shall I recount your praises? Or shall I rather number our hardships? Yet (as it seems) we gain nothing by praising you. For singular excellence does not grow through common praise. It is better, therefore, to uncover our wounds to our physician—who is most likely to heal us for this reason—than to fruitlessly count his most famous and innumerable praises. And if, compelled by a certain miserable necessity, we beseech him somewhat importunately, we nevertheless hope—trusting in his mercy rather than in our own prayers—that he will utterly drive out every plague from his sheepfold. If I were entirely made of tongue <note>original: "si totus essem lingua"; a common rhetorical figure meaning "if I were nothing but speech itself."</note>, most blessed father, I could not explain with how great a calamity I am now pressed, or by how much grief I am consumed. It cannot be told with what immense joy I was once filled when God himself set you over me as my shepherd. I had indeed heard that you were the "phoenix of philosophy," possessing the sublime citadel of Minerva <note>Minerva was the Roman goddess of wisdom; the "citadel" refers to the highest peak of intellectual achievement.</note> beyond all others. This is indeed so manifest to everyone that it cannot be denied. Truly, I hoped that when the highest power was joined to the highest wisdom, that Golden Age would return, which Plato once prophesied would come when power and wisdom coincided in the same person. In short, just as I had long ago heard true things about your wisdom, I hoped for things nearly as false concerning my own happiness. I fear lest someone, becoming too reproachful or less patient, might eventually dare to cry out: "Alas, how much my own opinion has deceived me in this hope! My joy has been turned into mourning." Not the Golden Age (which I hoped for), but an Iron Age <note>In classical mythology, the Golden Age was a time of peace, while the Iron Age was the final, most corrupt and violent era of humanity.</note> has returned under the most wise Pontiff. Who would have believed it? The Iron Ages have returned. I see nothing anywhere except weapons forged for my destruction. I hear nothing but the clatter of arms, the trampling of horses, and the thunder of bombards <note>term: "bombardarum" (bombards); an early type of cannon or heavy artillery used in the 15th century.</note>. I feel nothing anywhere but weeping, robbery, fire, and slaughter. Add to this that I am tormented by hunger and epidemic; day by day I am more and more consumed. And as if internal troubles were not enough to exhaust me without end, there constantly hangs over my head a most voracious wolf, a roaring lion, a vast elephant, and a pestilential dragon—Teucer <note>original: "Teucer"; a name for the Trojans, used here as a humanist code for the Ottoman Turks, who were at war with Christendom.</note>, the monstrous enemy of the Church. Even now, unless you are quickly present, he is about to devour this poor little flock of yours, and you most of all. Upon you alone, as the head, the entire Christian state depends; upon you alone redounds either the highest glory or the deepest infamy. Either the greatest reward or the greatest punishment awaits you above all men. Therefore, lest any such thing happen or any chance lead to a complaint in suffering, look to yourself first, most holy father, and look out for us. We pray that you preserve yourself first for us; and in turn, preserve us for yourself.
