<meta>This page continues the personified "Christian Flock’s" appeal to Pope Sixtus IV. Having established the Pope’s reputation for wisdom, the text now transitions into a direct plea for mercy and peace, contrasting the duties of a true shepherd with the violence of war.</meta>

<header>BOOK</header>

Most blessed father. Forgive, we pray, your children, O most indulgent father and fountain of indulgence: if, driven partly by pressing evils and partly by love—using our own and relying on yours—we attempt to advise your holiness, just as the **"pig advises Minerva"** <note>original: "sus minervam"; a Latin proverb for an ignorant person trying to teach an expert. The speaker is being humble by suggesting they are the ignorant pig and the Pope is the goddess of wisdom.</note>. Charity believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails; likewise, the highest kindness cannot receive anything unkindly.

**REMEMBER** that you are the vicar of the most gentle and merciful Christ: forget (as you used to) injuries, the memory of which is nothing other for a man than the forgetting of himself. Put aside any hatred you have toward your own people, so that you may receive your usual innate kindness—unless you have lost your very self, you cannot lose it. Therefore, you will retain your former charity (we know what we speak), lest you be forced to lose that pious spirit of yours. You will not allow anyone to rage further against your flock with your weapons, lest you yourself, through another's fault, either become or at least be considered a wolf instead of a shepherd. Whoever takes up arms against your people undoubtedly wounds you before all others. For there is no shepherd without a flock. And he who either denies or loses any part of the flock ceases to be a shepherd for everyone. If you belong to no one, you will belong to all; if you belong to someone, you will belong to no one. Christ granted you, above all, a divine empire—not primarily of arms, but of souls. Furthermore, he gave you keys, not a helmet or a sword. Keys with which you might close the gates of Janus and Pluto <note>Janus was the Roman god of beginnings; the doors to his temple were closed during times of peace. Pluto was the god of the underworld. Closing these gates symbolizes ending war and death.</note>, but open the doors of the heavenly kingdom. Three times he declared to you: "Do you love me?" Then he added: "If you love me, feed my sheep." If any should wander, forgive them seventy-seven times. Leave for a time the ninety-nine who are obedient, so that you may redeem the hundredth who is less obedient. When you have redeemed it, rejoice in this one more than in all the others. He did not say: "Pursue it with any curses," but rather "Follow it kindly with prayers." He did not give you any rod with which to strike the straying sheep, but rather gentle words with which to kindly call them back to the stables, and keys with which to guard them most safely. A <term>hireling</term> <note>original: "mercennarius"; a worker who acts only for pay rather than out of love for the sheep.</note> sometimes strikes someone else's straying sheep harshly. A shepherd, however, always forgives and looks after his own. The Lord did not appoint you as a hireling, but as a shepherd.

**BUT** I see what you will charge. You will say it is one thing for a sheep to wander from the path, and another for a ram to strike the shepherd with its horn. And so perhaps you complain of some "ram" <note>This likely refers to a political rival or a defiant leader within the Church, such as the Medici or a rebellious prince.</note> among us. We have looked all around, good shepherd. We have found no such ram among us. There is no such violence in our minds, nor such pride in sheep bound by a celestial and unbreakable fold. But you, because you are angry at I-know-not-what ram, you are in a way losing or destroying almost your entire sheepfold. Your flock is hidden (I know not how) from your eyes, O shepherd—scattered among forests and cliffs. O, would that you might look upon it for a little while! For you could not look upon such a great slaughter of your people with dry eyes. Alas, your entire flock is vexed on every side by all diseases and evils. Everywhere the shepherd is accused...

is criticized everywhere; meanwhile, distress presses upon miserable me from every side. On one hand, I grieve for your ill-repute <note>original: "infamiam"; referring to the public scandal or bad reputation the Pope was garnering through his wars.</note>. On the other, I mourn my own misery. If only the ears of Fame herself could be brought to you for even an hour—so that you might hear both the reports of your disgrace and the sound of my weeping—you would surely bewail your own lot no less than I bewail mine. O my shepherd, unfortunate in this matter (if I may say so); O flock, utterly unhappy—oh, the wickedness of it! 

Do you not hear what is said against you? Against you, Supreme Pontiff <note>original: "summe pontifex"</note>, biting satires are beloved everywhere. Upon me, indeed, more mournful tragedies weigh down. Nowhere will a more bitter satire be read, even if it were false; no tragedy will ever be more true or more sorrowful. If you remove the material for tragedy, you remove the material for satire as well. Erase your name from the book of infamy—a name already written long ago by God in the book of life. Arise, our guardian, arise at last as our lawful guardian. Say, along with your Lord: say, I pray, "Peace be with you." He spoke, and it was done. There will be peace and glory for both you and your people. A golden age will be led by us together with you. Under the military service of Constantine <note>original: "constantini militia"; a reference to the tradition of the Emperor Constantine as the defender of the Church, suggesting the Pope should use his power against external enemies rather than fellow Christians.</note>, the iron shall be turned from your sheepfold against the barbarian wolves. 

Without a doubt, a shepherd will be praised only when the wolves are slaughtered or tamed—just as he is now criticized everywhere while the lambs are cast down. A thousand shall fall at your side, even if you are unarmed, and ten thousand at your right hand <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 91:7, implying divine protection for a peaceful leader.</note>; Almighty God himself will fight for you.

### BUT LOOK
You accuse the ram again. Accuse him once more (if he truly seems to deserve your accusation). But let your accusation be Christian rather than hostile. Let it not lead to some destruction, but rather to salvation. Your Lord did not come to destroy anyone, but to save. He willed you to be a physician <note>original: "medicum"</note>, not an executioner <note>original: "carnificem"; literally a butcher or public executioner.</note>. Yet I would not wish to have uttered that harsh word "executioner" in the presence of your most holy majesty; indeed, let no executioner even dare to suspect such a vice in your piety. 

Almighty God gave weapons to you (as the Apostle Paul says), not carnal weapons, but rather spiritual and divine ones. He commanded you to provide for and spare the sheep subject to you, but to war down the proud wolves—that is, the barbarian enemies of the faith—by the hands of Constantine. This should be done not for the sake of war, but for the sake of peace. Thus, once the wild beasts are tamed and the livestock saved under one shepherd, there may finally be one sheepfold. 

But spare your own people first, O kind shepherd. Spare your own, lest while we fight amongst ourselves over wool and grass <note>A metaphor for fighting over petty material wealth or territory.</note>, the wolves meanwhile more easily and fiercely attack the very life of the sheep and the shepherd. It will not be considered a disgrace to you if you spare one of your people who errs even seven times, since it was commanded to you by the Lord that you ought to forgive them even seventy times seven. 

It is your duty (as you well know) to investigate every detail so that you may forgive; to cleanse the sick so that you may restore health. Your victory consists not so much in war as in peace. Indeed, if you conquer Christian men in war, you are meanwhile conquered (may it be far from you!) by demons and public infamy. If you kindly correct and show indulgence, you conquer everyone, and you preserve for yourself an uncorrupted empire <note>original: "imperium"; here meaning authority or rule.</note> over each and every one of your people.

# BOOK

Your greatness shines through endurance, not through inflicting suffering. All your loftiness is humility. You tame all people most effectively when you yourself are the gentlest of all. You will easily move all people wherever you please, if you yourself are never moved. Do you wish to gain a sudden and at the same time most fortunate victory? Do not conquer your own people in war; rather, conquer war itself. Rule over the movements of the heavens with a providence more than celestial. By your kindness, tame the malignant and savage Mars, and rigid Saturn <note>The author uses astrological metaphors here, suggesting the Pope should use his spiritual influence to calm the "warlike" and "harsh" planetary forces driving men to conflict.</note>. It is no great victory to overcome the smallest things. For what is truly great on earth, when the whole earth itself is a tiny thing? Therefore, heavenly High Priest <note>original: "Antistes"</note>, having left the earth behind, conquer heaven. You will conquer earthly things sufficiently if you have conquered the celestial ones. Where your kingdom is, there is your victory. For your kingdom (as Jesus says) is not so much of this lower world as it is of the higher and divine. See which you would prefer, most holy Father; both options depend upon your choice. On earth, do you wish to be regarded as a soldier or a high priest <note>original: "pontifex"</note>? In heaven, do you wish to be rejected by Christ—who was himself unarmed—because you are weighed down with weapons and thus unlike him? Or would you rather be received by him as like him, having laid your weapons aside?

Perhaps you will say that it is not permitted for the flock to advise the shepherd. Let it be so; we admit that our Father, supreme in providence, needs no admonitions. But let us at least be allowed to pray at the opportune time—indeed, even importunely, when necessity compels—to beseech you. Let it be permitted for us to fear for him whom we both fear as our only leader and love uniquely, worshipping him like a divinity. Look up at the heavens for a moment, we beseech you, just as you used to do before you focused your mind on these earthly battles. You will see that first high priest, Peter, clearly seeing these wounds of mine (which perhaps you do not see). You will see the merciful Peter grieving heavily over my suffering. Perhaps it is necessary for him to be angry with you (unless you take care) while he pities us so much. But far be it from us, far indeed, that even Peter should be angry. Or that Sixtus should be angry with this, his sheepfold, unworthily. It is a sin even to omen anything bad for a good shepherd, or to expect anything from him at last except good. For our most prudent high priest has not forgotten himself. He did not lose his singular wisdom when he began to be wise for all people; he did not strip off that natural kindness when he put on the cloak <note>original: "pallium"; the liturgical vestment symbolizing papal authority and the succession of St. Peter.</note> of the most kind Peter.

What then shall we say? Perhaps it pleased the skillful pilot to threaten his own people for a time, so that his perpetual and unheard-of mercy would not be thought of as laziness. And so that his incomparable sweetness might be tasted more sweetly after a certain austerity. Perhaps he has even permitted his flock, unaccustomed to battles, to fight among themselves for a certain time so that, by this exercise, they might become better prepared to join the battle against the barbarian wolves <note>A common Renaissance reference to the Ottoman Turks, who were actively expanding into Europe during Sixtus IV's papacy.</note>. O our Sixtus, stop the battle now. We have been practiced enough, and now we are utterly exhausted. Kind Sixtus, have mercy on your own. Come, speak at last, most blessed Father. Say now with your good will to your sheep: "Peace be with you" <note>original: "Pax vobis"</note>. So that your sheep in turn may cry out together with you: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will" <note>original: "Gloria in excelsis deo, & in terra pax hoibus [hominibus] bone voluntatis"</note>.

# SIXTH

### Exhortation to live in the country.

### Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo and Antonio Vinciguerra, most distinguished men, sends greetings.

<margin>S</margin>alutations forever, my Castor, Bernardo; salutations again, my Pollux, Antonio. <note>Ficino compares his two friends to the Dioscuri, the mythical twin "saviors" of sailors, signifying their inseparable bond and his devotion to them.</note> Either flee and (if it can be done) preserve us from this plague—that pestilence upon which everyone calls down a curse—or at least flee yourselves. Alas, flee these lethal lands as soon as possible! Flee the bitter shore! I pray that you retreat into the very suburbs (if it is permitted), leaving the city behind. There I shall see those eyes of mine <note>original: "oculos meos" — a common humanist metaphor for dear friends who are as precious as one's own sight.</note> again with my own eyes; you who are always stored in the depths of my mind. What I am to you, each of you is to himself. You are to me what two eyes are to a person. Farewell, happy ones. But why have we just now passed over our Cristoforo Landino, the phoenix of the muses? <note>Landino was a leading Florentine humanist and close friend of Ficino.</note> Because when I said "Ficino" in the very greeting, I thought I had said "Landino." <note>Ficino is emphasizing how closely his identity is bound to his friends; to name one is to imply the others.</note>

->One who loves ardently grasps nothing except the beloved.<-

### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine humbly commends himself to Raffaele Riario, Cardinal of St. George.

<margin>B</margin>y that hour of the night in which the highest creator of nature—without whom nothing is born—God, was born a man for men, so that men might be reborn as divine beings for God: this letter to Raphael is also born to me. <note>This letter was clearly written on Christmas Eve or Christmas Day.</note> Truly, as I was wondering with what nourishment I might best foster and nurture this newborn letter, I know not what spirit among those who sang the divine Word to the shepherds on that same night said: "Why do you seek what to write, Marsilio? Penetrate now the individual inner chambers of your soul. You will find your mind entirely empty of all other things, but full of Raffaele Riario alone. Therefore, you will not be able to write anything to Raphael except Raphael himself. He rendered you so empty of all others when he made you full of his own presence. He is so dear to you that you cannot grasp anything else while you grasp him. If you wish to express whatever you have, whatever you think, and whatever you speak most appropriately to Raphael: come, use that same art of painting with which you have long since painted him in your soul, and then paint this tablet." This is what that spirit said to me, my Raphael. But I am unable to paint it with my hands. Fashion it yourself in your mind. But where, indeed, where is our man of Amalfi? <note>Referring to Giovanni Niccolini, the Archbishop of Amalfi.</note> For a long time now I have been searching here and there to greet him (as I was commanded). But I sought him outside of you in vain, for I could not find him except within you.

->It is neither safe to accuse princes, nor right to accuse fortune.<-

...nor would I wish to write anything bad, nor could I write anything good. For nothing of good offers itself to us among these innumerable evils. Therefore, what shall I do? ### Marsilio Ficino humbly commends himself to the Reverend Father in Christ and his Lord, Raffaele Riario, Cardinal of Saint George.

<margin>n</margin>
Behold, you write to your little client <note>original: "clientulo" — a diminutive used by Ficino to show humble status in relation to his patron</note>, yet you do not write back anything, my one and only patron. And indeed, he endures this with as calm a mind as that with which he endures... <note>Ficino likely refers to his own physical infirmity or the distance between them</note> He indeed denied his feet to you when you were departing from here. Truly, in this common misery of the human race (which the mind shudders to recount), in which none of us is not miserable, he alone is less miserable concerning whom most merciful God has commanded his angel to guard him in all his ways. <note>This is a reference to Psalm 91:11: "For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways."</note> It seems to me that God himself wished to provide in this matter. But you cannot commend me as a whole if in that very commendation you pass over the Archbishop of Amalfi. <note>original: "Amalphitanum archiepiſcopum" — likely Rinaldo Orsini, a close associate.</note> What God has joined, let no man put asunder. His brother, Angelo Niccolini, a distinguished legal expert and prominent citizen, wishes to be yours as much as his own.

# SIXTUS 142

If the friendship with the most distinguished patrician, Francesco Michiale—contracted with me long ago—should need any guardians, I would implore you by the very divinity of love to preserve me in his goodwill with all your zeal. Indeed, I could not explain how much I value being loved by men worthy of love. For unless I am pleasing to myself, nothing else can please me. But then I am truly most pleased with myself when I feel I am approved by the most esteemed men. No one is more unfortunate than he who neither sees himself nor sees the one who sees him.

Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Cocchi, the distinguished legal scholar; likewise to Francesco Berlinghieri, Pietro Arenense, Master George the Cypriot, and Lorenzo de' Medici the Younger.

I wrote some time ago a certain letter resembling a prophecy to the Pope; but I wish it were truly "papal" <note>original: "pontificiam" — Ficino likely means a message worthy of the Pope's authority or one that the Pope would truly take to heart</note>. If it is as divine among others as it is among us, it will surely drive far away the internal and external ruin already threatening the necks of the Christian flock. I call God to witness, my friend, that I have fulfilled my duty in this matter to the best of my strength. Let others see to the rest—those to whom eyes were given so that they might see first of all, and ears so that they might at least hear. Otherwise, even if they are eventually forced to cry out: "Alas, I did not see," it will never be permitted to say: "I had not heard." 
January 13, 1478.

Know other things so that you may know yourself. Know yourself so that you may know God.

Marsilio Ficino of Florence: To the Reverend Father in Christ and his Lord, Lord Giovanni, son of the Most Serene King <note>Giovanni of Aragon was the son of King Ferrante of Naples</note>, Cardinal of Aragon, he humbly commends himself.

I have written in the past three days three declamations, venerable Father, which are Platonic rather than Ciceronian <note>original: "tullianas" — referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero, the model for Latin prose</note>. In these, I intended to deter my companions from vices and exhort them to virtue as much as I am able. The first describes a certain wretched shadow of an immoral life. The second reflects a happy image of an upright life. The third, finally, expresses the divine model of goodness itself. I decided to send these three to you as if they were mirrors, because I knew that all those who are most beautiful are greatly delighted by mirrors. Gaze a little, venerable Father, into these. In the first, you will immediately recognize what you never were. In the second, what you have long since become. In the third, you will recognize what you are right now. You will rejoice in your good qualities in no small measure. But so that you may rejoice happily in your blessings, give thanks in all things to God, the giver of all good things. Why indeed did God command "Know thyself" except so that in knowing yourself, you might recognize that whatever good you have, you have from him first.

If I now commend Marsilio to you, understand that the Archbishop of Amalfi <note>Rinaldo Orsini, a close associate of Ficino</note> is likewise commended. Whom God has joined, let no man put asunder.

->The Spirit blows where it wills.<- <note>A quote from the Gospel of John 3:8</note>

<meta>This page continues the prophetic and astrological discourse Marsilio Ficino addressed to Pope Sixtus IV, as mentioned in the closing of the previous page dated January 13, 1478. Ficino is interpreting recent miraculous finds and celestial alignments as omens for the Church.</meta>

# BOOK

...to whom all things are subject: to obey whom willingly is nothing other than to reign. God himself commands us both to cry out in your presence and you to listen. Furthermore, if you listen to us patiently, not only will you not repent of it, but—as we hope—it will be a help to have heard. 

Last year, Most Blessed Father, on the very birthday of the almighty Christ <note>Christmas, 1477</note>, certain relics of the apostle Peter were found in the city of Volterra; they showed twelve great miracles in a single month, manifest to all the people. Stirred by these new signs, we, four fellow philosophers, gathered together, being equally students of both Prophecy and Astrology. First, by the examination of prophetic mysteries, we agreed that it was portended by those miracles of the relics of Peter that Sixtus, the successor of Peter, would one day perform miracles most well-known to all peoples and nations. 

Then, turning ourselves to astrological matters, we diligently considered that past and future conjunction of **Saturn** and **Mars** in **Virgo**. Likewise, the next approach of the **Sun** to **Aries** <note>the spring equinox</note>. Also, the beginnings of the four quarters of the entire year. Furthermore, the future eclipses of the **Moon** in **Aquarius** and of the **Sun** in **Leo**. And again, other eclipses of the following year; finally, the discordant mixing of **Mars** with **Jupiter**, and many other things besides. From this, we concluded that the next two years would be so miserable that it will be commonly thought that the very destruction of the world is imminent. 

Specifically, we foresee a common and extreme calamity of the human race, pressing upon us through war, plague, and famine; the death of very many princes of every kind; and then a new heresy arising under a false prophet. This mind shudders to narrate what follows: soon—may it be averted—Peter’s little boat <note>original: "Petri nauiculā" — a traditional metaphor for the Catholic Church</note> will swim in the waters of the Tiber. Finally, barbarians will devastate Italy. Indeed, because **Mars**, the leader of war, overcame **Saturn**—the author of plague, famine, betrayal, and heresy—in all those dispositions of the heavens which we have described, we agreed that all the other remaining evils would arise out of war itself. 

Here, therefore, wondering among ourselves, we said: "Where then are those healing miracles of Sixtus? Those which were portended to us from the miracles of Peter, if—as both we judge and the other astrologers of the whole world believe—such dire slaughter during his Pontificate will everywhere vex both private citizens and princes, and the Church itself?"

At last, a long discussion led us by certain reason to this opinion which we now relate: namely, that the virtue of physicians and pilots is demonstrated by diseases or storms. Therefore, divine providence permitted—while Sixtus is caring for and governing—that many stars and elements should for a time conspire together, both for the common destruction of the human race and especially for the tossing of the Christian ship by very cruel waves. This is so that Sixtus, rising like **Neptune** in the midst of the storm, might temper the angry **Aeolus** <note>the ruler of the winds in mythology</note> and the raging winds with the very trident of his power, wisdom, and kindness. May it please him to calm the swollen sea. May he command the celestial movements with a virtue more than celestial. May he, by his wonderful kindness, tame cruel Mars and rigid Saturn. And indeed, not only the oracles of the prophets but also certain celestial signs clearly demonstrate that Sixtus will do this in a short time.

<summary>Ficino describes a dire astrological forecast of war, plague, and heresy for the years 1478-1480, but frames these calamities as a divine opportunity for Pope Sixtus IV to prove his greatness by calming the metaphorical storm like a "Christian Neptune."</summary>

# SIXTVS

Here, then, all the Christian peoples will proclaim: "Who is this man? Who is he, that the elements obey him so easily, and the stars follow him?" This is surely that legitimate and most merciful vicar of Christ. Having received the keys from Christ at the times ordained by Him, he closes the gates <note>original: *hostia*, likely a variant of *ostia* (doors/gates)</note> of Janus and Pluto <note>Janus was the Roman god of beginnings whose temple doors were closed during peace; Pluto is the god of the underworld.</note>. He opens the temple of nourishing peace to his children. For since he understands that it is no great victory to overcome the smallest things—and that nothing on earth is great since the whole earth itself is tiny—he has decided, having left the earth behind, to overcome celestial things. He seeks to conquer his own people not so much through war, but rather to conquer war itself.

SIXTUS, the phoenix of sublime Theology <note>A reference to Pope Sixtus IV’s reputation as a brilliant Franciscan scholar and theologian</note>, possessing the high citadels of Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom</note> before all others, consults the divine oracle there in every matter. He does not rely on human counsel in administering divine affairs, but rather on divine counsel. Furthermore, he looks up from there to almighty God, who does all things through goodness and subjects all things to Himself through beneficence. Therefore, at the times ordained by God, he likewise now rejoices in a beneficent victory; for he conquers all well when he binds the hearts of all to himself through kindness. Truly he understands that the one to whom command over beasts is entrusted obtains an anxious service rather than a true empire. Indeed, the bodies of men—which alone are captured by violence among us—are almost nothing other than beasts. Certainly, souls, being free by nature, cannot be conquered otherwise than by a certain noble beneficence. The magnanimous Sixtus now rejoices not in an anxious service over beasts, but in a command over men themselves—that is, over their souls. Our Sixtus, a father distinguished by piety, in the manner of pious parents, kisses his children more gently after fatherly threats and reproaches. He cherishes them in a favorable bosom and embraces them in nourishing arms. And as much as a short while ago a certain ill-will seemed to falsely pursue his children, so much now does beneficence truly follow them. Hear now, all of you, hear the very voice of our shepherd. Look more closely: do you not see the joyful face of the shepherd, which makes all things serene in blessing? He opens his mouth, about to cry out thus to his sheep with his Lord:

->**PEACE BE WITH YOU**<-
<note>original: *Pax Vobis*</note>

"PEACE BE WITH YOU, O children, in a truly new spring <note>original: *vere nouo*. Ficino often plays on the Latin words for 'truly' and 'spring' (ver), suggesting both a literal season and a spiritual renewal</note>. Do not be afraid; I am not a wolf, but a guardian. I am not a hireling, but a shepherd. A shepherd sent into the world by Him through whom the world was made; who was both in the world and was sent into the world, not to lose His sheep, but to save them, and to lay down His life for His sheep. The Savior of the world sent me to you, so that I might save you for Him, without whom nothing is saved. He willed that I should come to you, and not depart from Him. Indeed, to depart from Him through whom we exist is nothing other than to perish. In the name of Him who is always with us until the end of the age, I give my peace to you again, O children, in a truly new spring, though the world be unwilling—a peace sent to Sixtus by Him who moves and brings the world to a standstill. God is dear light, in which there is no darkness at all. God is shining charity, in which there is no hatred at all. He who remains in dear light and shining charity remains in God, and God in him. Therefore, children, love one another just as I have loved you. My children, let us love one another in Him, without whom no one ever has the quality of being lovable. No part of the world can stand without concord, since the world itself consists only of concord."

The Pope is depicted delivering a message of universal peace and love, functioning as a stabilizing force in a world threatened by celestial discord.</summary>

# SIXTH BOOK CXLIIII

...he began: indeed, almost as many as the year nourishes and the Pisan sea <note>original: *aequorque pisanum*; likely referring to the coastal waters near Pisa, part of Florentine territory</note> supports. Sixtus, certainly the legitimate vicar of Christ, remembers that when his Lord Christ was about to choose His disciples, He chose the first, the most eminent, and the majority from the rank of fishermen; and that He would likewise make them "fishers of men." To these He then gave three baits especially and three nets, with which they might fish successfully in this deep sea of the human race. The first bait was truly a singular piety toward God and religion. The second was sobriety of life and integrity of character. The third, toward men, was both the good example of deeds and the true teaching of words. 

He also added three nets. The first net was a burning charity <note>original: *charitas*; the Greek-derived term for divine, selfless love</note> by which they would always love everyone in God no differently than they love themselves. The second was a supreme understanding, through which they would as willingly forgive everyone (as if they were children) if they were thought to have erred, just as they themselves easily hope their own errors will be forgiven by our Father who is in heaven, as if they were His children. The third net was a beneficence so abundant that it would do good not only to those who do good, but even to those who do evil. And those whom he considered either less virtuous or even enemies, he would overcome with a certain goodness and benevolence; he would thus imitate the heavenly Father, who abundantly bestows the nurturing Sun and timely rains upon all equally, even if they seem less friendly. 

Therefore, Christ Himself once commanded His disciples to entice everyone with this triple bait and to ensnare them with these three nets; and the vicar of Christ, Sixtus, likewise decreed the same for himself, so that his Lord might one day meet him with joyful and congratulatory voices: "I shall come, Sixtus; Come, I say, blessed son of my Father. Enter into the joy of the Lord." 

December 1st, 1478. Florence.

### Marsilio Ficino to the Reverend Father in Christ and his Lord, Giovanni Niccolini, Archbishop of Amalfi, sends greetings.

I write many things to you in few words for the Pope. But you, in turn, speak a few things about me to the Pope with many supplications. You cannot recount many "good things" <note>likely referring to material assets or worldly successes</note> about me. Nevertheless, in my misfortune, perhaps you ought to—and certainly you can—pray with many words. Oh, how many things my soul urges me to speak about myself here! But the letter cannot hold them. You, therefore, grasp them in your mind. I would be foolish if I tried to commend your own things to you; it does not seem right that in this time of adversity, the "Florentine name" should be a disadvantage to me among those at the papal court, if indeed it can be a disadvantage, since it never profited me at other times in prosperity. 

Others more fortunate—I will not say more happy—rejoice in our things. "We are but a number, born to consume the fruits of the earth" <note>A quote from Horace, *Epistles* 1.2.27, used here to suggest a sense of insignificance or being reduced to mere survival</note>. I said "fruits": let it be that the fruits do not go missing. Farewell. 

But before you go, it pleases me to speak briefly here to our Cardinal Riario <note>Raffaele Riario, a powerful cardinal and nephew of Pope Sixtus IV</note>. You, indeed, my lord: remember now your servant, if he seems at all worthy of memory. You have come into your kingdom; alas, that I am now forced to seek it against my will, compelled by the malignancy of the times—things which I never otherwise thought should be sought by those practicing philosophy. Shall I say it? What is perhaps less fitting for a philosopher, but truly befits a needy man. May I perish, Herdes <note>A reference to a contemporary or literary figure</note>, unless I say it: Those who would snatch our dinner from us rise daily from the mud.

->Nothing is more hidden than the human will.<-

# BOOK

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Nicolini, Archbishop of Amalfi, sends greetings.

I am sending a certain Prophecy <note>original: *Vaticinium*; a prediction or prophetic message</note> to the Pope. The spirit blows where it wills <note>original: *Spiritus vbi vult spirat*; a reference to the Gospel of John 3:8</note>. I have not been moved by the will of any man, nor by human agitation, but compelled by I know not what spirit, yet I know by what love <note>original: *charitate*; divine or brotherly love</note>. If it were read with the same spirit in which it is written, it would offend absolutely no one; for indeed, divine truth joined with love ought to offend no one. Many philosophers claim that the truth of things is the most obscure of all. I, however, think that the human will is far more obscure. The truth of things is sometimes tracked by its own footprints and can be discerned by certain signs, because it depends on a determined cause and always remains the same. But the human will, since it has no determined cause due to its freedom and is changed at any moment, can be tracked neither by footprints nor by certain signs. Especially since, because of simulation and dissimulation <note>the act of pretending to be what one is not, or hiding what one truly is</note>, it often presents signs that are contrary to itself. 

Therefore, before you publish this, consult both yourself and especially those who are most dear to the Pope. Let it finally be read to the Pope and the others only if it is judged that it can be read with the same good favor from everyone as the good will with which it was composed by us. If not, keep it to yourself. Indeed, where nothing can benefit me, I wish for nothing to harm me. God gave me a humble fortune. Fortune once gave me a slender means, and now the slenderest. I obey God; I yield to fortune. I agree with my means. I am content with a small lot, provided it is safe. Fortunate is he to whom a moderate fortune has fallen. Happy is he who is content with his own fortune. I certainly am content with a few things for that reason: even if I am often content with many, these "many" are few in number and many are of contemptible price. Blessed are the poor in spirit. Blessed are the peacemakers <note>original: *Beati pauperes spiritu. Beati pacifici*; references to the Beatitudes from the Sermon on the Mount</note>. A monstrous year has been acted out thus far; a more monstrous year looms. Daily you will say, daily you will hear: "I would not have thought it."

### Marsilio Ficino humbly commends himself to the Most Reverend Father in Christ and his Lord, Lord John, Cardinal of Aragon, son of the most serene King Ferdinand.

<margin>a</margin> Alfonso, the most happy King and your grandfather, O venerable father, recently poured out an oracle from on high in the angelic tongue <note>The OCR reads *anglica* (English), but the context of "angelic" later in the sentence suggests a common Renaissance typo for *angelica*</note> to your father Ferdinand, the most happy King. Marsilio Ficino (carried away by I know not what spirit) was present. He heard it, preserved it, and today he himself has translated that oracle—then pronounced by Alfonso in the angelic tongue—into human language for you. He does this with the plan that you first (if it pleases you) may read it yourself. Then, send it to your most Serene father, so that what he perceived in recent days from Alfonso with only the eyes and ears of the mind, he may now also receive with the very ears and eyes of the body through our work. 

But let no one wonder that an oracle of this kind, though it is about to appear in the exalted sight of the Royal Cardinal and the Serene King himself, nevertheless proceeds without any human ornaments. For that which is clothed in the splendor of the divine sun—that is, of heavenly truth—to attempt to dress it in human garments is, I think, nothing other than to [obscure] the pure light of the sun itself with a certain thick darkness...

# BOOK SIX
### 145

...to pour around. I would recommend to you and to your father our Archbishop of Amalfi <note>Giovanni Nicolini, a close associate of the Medici and Ficino</note>, who is by far the most worthy of all recommendation, were I not aware that he is rightfully of such great authority among us that he himself is likely to recommend his Marsilio and many others to you. February 28, 1478. Florence.

## The Oracle of King Alfonso to King Ferdinand, first delivered between them in the Angelic tongue <note>original: *anglica lingua*; while the OCR reads 'English,' in this context it is almost certainly a scribal error for *angelica* (Angelic), as Ficino frequently claimed to translate divine or celestial messages into 'human' language</note>, and then translated into human language by Marsilio Ficino.

<margin>a</margin> King Alfonso <note>Alfonso V of Aragon, known as 'the Magnanimous' (1396–1458)</note>, most blessed, to the most blessed King Ferdinand his son <note>Ferdinand I of Naples, also known as Ferrante</note>: congratulating the former preserver and now the author of peace upon the established peace. He prophesies true health, certain victory, complete glory, and full joy.

### The Descent of Souls

<margin>q</margin> Why are you so amazed, O son? Why do you tremble? I fly down here as easily and as favorably whenever I please as the rays of the stars and the sun continually descend to us. Neither do the rays of the stars desert their own stars while they are sent down to you, nor do the supernal <note>heavenly or higher-level</note> minds leave the heights while they inspire you. Observe, I pray, my sweetest son, how much the inhabitants of heaven rejoice in peace as if it were celestial nourishment. Indeed, as soon as you began to think of reconciling that peace—which for some time now has been disturbed by an envious fate—I immediately arrived here, enticed by this thought of yours as if by the sweetest bait for the gods. Therefore, with all amazement and horror driven far away, stand with attentive ears and preserve what you hear from heaven, like an oracle stored in the depths of your mind.

### How Pleasing Peace is to the Higher Powers

<margin>p</margin> In the beginning, most beloved son, perhaps you have heard nothing of my fate until now, nor have you ever clearly understood your own. But today, having become not only a preserver of peace (as you were before) but now its greatest author, you are judged worthy by the heavenly inhabitants to have the house of almighty Olympus <note>a classical reference to the dwelling of the divine</note> opened to you; and from there, the most beautiful order of Providence itself and the harmonious series of the fates shall be related to you.

### The Divine Soul

<margin>a</margin> Come now, Ferdinand: leaving the senses behind, I turn your mind back upon itself in a certain circular observation of its own being. You will immediately see that when your mind is turned into itself and the body is dismissed, it is a certain incorporeal <note>without a physical body</note> sphere. Its circumference—that is, its intelligence and will—revolves through incorporeal things. Its center, however—that is, its life and substance—does not rest upon any physical axis.

### God. Angels. Souls.

<margin>a</margin> Come again: in that clearer circle of your mind, as if in a mirror, look closely, and by looking, reach out into the world everywhere and...

# BOOK SIX

...and beyond the spherical world, an intellect and an intelligible sphere <note>An "intelligible sphere" refers to a realm of pure thought or divine reality, rather than a physical object.</note>, whose center is everywhere as it infinitely penetrates the universe, but whose circumference is nowhere, as it infinitely stands above the universe. Behold, contemplate the divine form, the fountain of all forms, the uniform shape of all shapes. This form meets all minds everywhere, especially those that are pure, as if meeting mirrors. Here, that God of gods flashes for you, besides whom there is no true God. Here overflows the eternal goodness of good things, entirely devoid of evil. Here shines the immense light of lights and the sun of all other minds. Into this Sun, angels—much like stars—and souls—much like the moon—revolve from every direction.

### The Immortality of Souls

<margin>e</margin> Certain eternal rays of this sun are the minds of men, surrounded by the dark cloud of the body. But by reflecting themselves back into their own sun through thought and affection by their own choice, they leap back just as they originally leaped forth from their beginning. Therefore, since they are able at some point—once every obstacle is removed—to flow back into their sun as much by rightly contemplating as by rightly loving, they undoubtedly flowed out from there without an intermediary. That is to say, they come from eternity itself and are, without doubt, nearly eternal. They reveal their own immortality most clearly when they think little of mortal things as if they were trifles, especially for the sake of eternal things. Furthermore, they grasp immortal things insofar as they themselves are immortal. They perceive immortality itself—that is, God—through a certain firm reasoning under the very principle of immortality.

### Divine Providence

<margin>b</margin> Moreover, God, who sees all things, provides for those who see Him before all else. Truly, if God is (as He certainly is) the cause of all things above all things, He is undoubtedly all things. If He is most simple <note>In theology, "simplicity" means God is not made of parts, but is a single, unified essence.</note>, as His supreme power demonstrates, then certainly in Him, to see is nothing other than to be. Therefore, because He is all things, He most easily discerns all things within Himself. If He is the most good, which no one doubts, then rightfully, to see in Him is nothing other than to provide. For this reason, by seeing all things, He perfectly provides for the whole universe—but especially for minds, which see Him in individual things and worship Him above all.

### Fate and Free Will

<margin>c</margin> Furthermore, to return at last to our own lot, that God of gods, besides whom there is no true God, alone granted me a mind—a mind that turns itself toward God by its own will. But the constellation of Capricorn <note>Alfonso V’s personal emblem and a significant sign in his horoscope</note> joined the body to this bright mind by God’s command. Saturn, the lord of Capricorn, infused the spirit <note>term: spirit (*spiritus*), the subtle "knot" or vapor that Ficino believed connected the immaterial soul to the physical body</note> which is the bond between mind and body. The genius <note>a guardian spirit or guiding intelligence</note> who accompanies the "Thrones" <note>The third highest order of angels, associated with divine justice and the planet Saturn</note> ruled and led me as far as God foresaw. I once lived among mortals in the past, between labor, hope, and glory. Burning desire for command brought about labor (as usually happens), but singular magnificence and incomparable greatness of soul brought about glory. Finally, through wonderful piety toward God and mercy toward men, as if on two wings and with my genius as a guide, I flew back to the heavenly fatherland. There, happily restored to the Father of myself and of all, I lead a blessed life somewhat similar to the Thrones, who primarily adorn the sphere of Saturn.

<meta>This page continues the discourse of the spirit of King Alfonso to his son, Ferdinand. Having previously discussed the nature of the soul and its divine origin, Alfonso now elevates the vision to the celestial and super-celestial realms, describing the bliss of the afterlife and the astrological influences on Ferdinand’s birth.</meta>

# BOOK SIX
CXLVI

->The Celestial Paradise.<-

Here among us, amidst the innumerable spirits who feed on ambrosia and nectar <note>In classical mythology, these are the food and drink of the gods, granting immortality.</note>, it is granted to recline at the feasts of the divine. Here, even if a certain star seems more familiar to each spirit, the whole universe is nonetheless as accessible and transparent to each one at will as if through certain rays of light. You blind ones on earth think you see the sky itself and the stars through your thick air, just as fish might think the same from beneath the vast, churning depths. O, how much this ridiculous opinion of yours deceives you! Truly, fish see not the sky itself but the water; they see not the pure lights of the heavenly bodies, but only certain small images of them in water that is always muddy and dark. 

The same happens to you, O wretched ones, living under the thick air; and yet you greatly admire these heavenly things, though they have become earthly to your sight. As much as daylight surpasses the darkness of night, and as much as the circumference exceeds the center, so much more luminous and greater are these ethereal things to us than they are to you. What shall I say to you of the unknown abundance of those innumerable stars? What of the wondrous diversity and order of their movements, which remain unknown to you? What of the inestimable sweetness of that harmony <note>original: "harmonie". This refers to the 'Music of the Spheres,' a Pythagorean and Platonic concept where the movement of celestial bodies creates a perfect musical scale.</note> which the varied motion of the spheres and globes returns in a completely consonant proportion?

->The Super-celestial Paradise.<-

But why do I praise the heavenly things to you at such length? For these are almost as much the shadows of the "super-celestial" things as earthly things are shadows of the celestial. O, the true light above the ether! A light so true that it cannot be truly expressed in words. O, truth shining wondrously above the heavens, so wonderfully translucent that no one can ever wonder at it enough according to its dignity; for it wonderfully exceeds all admiration itself. Here, O son, here, I say, one lives most truly, most clearly, most excellently, and most joyfully; where all life is nothing other than truth, clarity, goodness, and the fullest joy. 

Here, in the immense light of lights itself, we behold the lights and the Ideas <note>original: "ydeas". In Platonic philosophy, these are the perfect, eternal patterns of all things that exist in the physical world.</note> of all things, and in those lights, we clearly perceive individual truths. It is just as if someone standing within the sun were to look upon all the rays emanating from it, and within those rays, see the individual colors created from them. Although I wish to show you many more things here—infinitely greater and more beautiful than the physical heavens—your human weakness of eyes prevents me. Therefore, lest you be forced to go blind from too much splendor, I will not show the wondrous light of the divine kingdom and the infinite sun any further. Let it be enough to have indicated how blessed your Alfonso is, and how blessed you yourself shall be, if only you wish it. Therefore, rejoice now in this present happiness, sweetest son. Rejoice greatly in this happiness; rejoice in your own; now joyfully hear your fate, unheard of until now.

->Fate and Liberty.<-

The same Father created a mind for you as He did for me and others; for only He procreates the mind who alone restores the mind, who is grasped by the mind alone, and who alone feeds and fills the mind. However, Aries, the head of the stars <note>Aries is the first sign of the Zodiac, often called the "head" as it marks the beginning of the astrological year.</note>, once wove that body for you; and Mars, the lord of Aries, kindled your fervent spirit. A guardian genius <note>original: "genius". In the ancient world, a 'genius' was a protective spirit or 'daimon' assigned to a person at birth to guide their destiny.</note> has been assigned to you as the protector of your life, a genius from the number of those who lead the choirs of angelic virtues...

<column-break/>

<meta>This page continues the discourse of the ghost of King Alfonso of Aragon to his son, Ferdinand I of Naples. Having previously described the celestial spheres, Alfonso now provides specific astrological guidance based on Ferdinand's temperament and the influences of the planets Saturn, Mars, and Mercury.</meta>

# BOOK SIX

...accompanying you before. You too live, my son, continuously between labor and glory. Rigid Saturn himself threatens you with labor and indeed danger, while that prudent Mercury, the attendant of the Sun <note>original: "solis pedisequus". In classical astronomy, Mercury is never far from the sun.</note>, promises glory. From the former, a certain harshness can sometimes be an obstacle to you. From the latter, on the contrary, a wondrous prudence is of benefit.

### The nature of Saturn and Mars.

Among the planets, those which most persistently devise dangers for men are Mars and Saturn. Yet each of them—as experience teaches you—usually spares his own. Saturn, I say, spares those of Saturn; likewise, Mars for the most part does not know how to harm those of Mars. Therefore, as I was once a companion of Saturn, as often as I spared my own—that is, the Saturnians—so often did Saturn favor me. Against them, however, he never showed favor. Therefore, my Ferdinand, as a companion of burning Mars (if you desire to reign happily), spare your own. Those who are especially yours among all people are shown to you by that fiery quality of <term>Aries</term> <note>The first sign of the Zodiac, associated with fire and ruled by Mars.</note>; with whom <term>Leo</term> and <term>Sagittarius</term> agree. Therefore, hold all the "sons" of Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius as if they were your brothers. Furthermore, forgive, indulge, and be compliant (if it please you) toward my people as well. You ask who are mine especially? Those, namely, who are ruled by <term>Capricorn</term> or <term>Aquarius</term>, the seats of Saturn.

### A moral admonition.

Above all, however, be content within your own borders. Believe me, Fortune will give you more and greater gifts of her own accord than when she is provoked. For as many as you pursue with violence, surely just as many will flee from you and—heaven forbid—if they are able, perhaps they will put you to flight. However, as many as you pursue with benevolence, just as many will follow you willingly and obey. You will conquer well as often as you conquer by a kindness <note>original: "beneficio vinces"</note>. You shall rule most securely for as long as you rule those who are willing. You will easily move all people (to whatever you please) if you yourself are never moved. As you know, it is the highest prudence either never to enter into a contest with most deceitful Fortune, or certainly only when compelled. Where Mars rages most, there Fortune dominates the most, and most easily deceives.

### Divination.

Thus far, let it suffice to have advised a dear son with paternal charity, however most prudent he may be. Now it pleases me to prophesy a little for my happy son in few words. I see you will quickly do what I have advised. For I had foreseen through your prudence that you would act thus, long before I predicted it. A distinguished victory awaits you in peace itself, full of safe triumphs. In victory, there shall be tranquility. In tranquility, there shall be piety and the cult of <term>Minerva</term> <note>The goddess of wisdom, weaving, and strategic war.</note>. Listen, I pray, now listen more attentively with your whole mind, Ferdinand, to what follows. If you adorn your crown with three gems especially—that is, divine Faith, Hope, and Charity—then surely from that third heaven where the angelic Principalities adorn the gracious globe of Venus, the three <term>Graces</term> <note>Aglaia, Euphrosyne, and Thalia; goddesses of charm and beauty.</note> breathing happily upon you shall put to flight the three Furies from your threshold and appease the three Fates. And when you have completed two courses of Saturn <note>A "course of Saturn" is approximately 29.5 years; two courses would signify Ferdinand reaching roughly 60 years of age.</note>, then especially, son Ferdi...

<summary>King Alfonso advises Ferdinand to rule with benevolence rather than force, using the astrological "triplicities" of Mars and Saturn to identify allies, and concludes with a prophecy of a peaceful and pious reign.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the speech of the ghost of King Alfonso of Aragon to his son, Ferdinand I of Naples, providing a final astrological blessing and a vision of the afterlife. It then transitions into a personal letter from Marsilio Ficino to a Venetian official.</meta>

# BOOK SIX

...Ferdinand, by your happy aspect <note>A term in astrology referring to the angular distance between planets that influences their effect.</note> of the Sun to Jupiter, and also by the conjunction of the Moon with Jupiter—indeed, by the greatest gift of Almighty God—they shall shine before you in the splendor of your exalted power. But truly, after you have fulfilled your father's years, and have furthermore added many cycles of Mars <note>The "cycles of Mars" refer to periods of roughly two years; Alfonso is wishing his son a long life through many such planetary revolutions.</note> known only to us—that is, to the celestial beings—at last, by those same wings with which your father Alfonso here ascended (namely, through both piety toward God and clemency toward men), you shall return to the heavenly homeland under the guidance of your divine genius. There, just as the angelic Virtues <note>original: "virtutes angelice". The Virtues are the seventh rank of angels in the traditional hierarchy, often associated with the movement of the celestial bodies.</note> (who especially illuminate the sphere of Mars) do, you will enjoy a blessed eternity, and in that enjoyment, you will rejoice.

->How wondrous is the joy in the homeland.<-

A truly wondrous and incomparable joy, where we rejoice infinitely in all good things within that infinite Good of goods itself. O, we enjoy a complete joy there, where each of us (however great he may be) is entirely joy, and joy is everything. Indeed, my son, I would most gladly sing to you now with the angelic voice of the Thrones <note>The "Thrones" are the third rank of angels, representing divine justice and steadfastness.</note> of the marvelous sweetness with which we are always filled in the homeland; were I not afraid that perhaps, after experiencing the comparison of such sweetness, your whole life on earth would seem to you not only most bitter, but even bitterness itself. Therefore, I shall restrain myself out of a certain mercy, lest I compel my son to grieve more vehemently than the rest of the mournful lot of mortals. But so that you may one day happily enjoy eternity, never seek to enjoy fleeting things, but rather to use them; and so that you may always truly rejoice, rejoice always in the truth alone.

<margin>The ascent of souls.</margin>
Farewell now in gladness, and live happily, my sweetest son. Behold now—do you not hear the voices? By the voices, I say, of the Archangels who especially adorn the sphere of Mercury, I am called back to the heavens. But before you say farewell, I pray you, embrace this spirit of mine with your own spirit, since I have long embraced yours. Live with me always and willingly, O son; for indeed I live with you even beyond the consummation of the age. But look now, my Ferdinand—or rather, look upward—to see how wonderfully I now return to the sublime seats of the Thrones in a moment of time, supported by Seraphic wings. And in the meantime, I do not truly leave your household, remaining there in a certain way like a ray of light. Farewell again from on high.

He is as foolish who gives thanks to a friend who has already departed, as he is grateful who holds no thanks in his heart. <note>This proverb suggests that true gratitude is a state of being between friends, rather than a formal transaction of words.</note>

### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine writes to the distinguished Rainaldo Gauardio, scribe of the Venetian Senate. Heartfelt greetings.

You sent your son Domenico to us in recent days for the sake of greeting your Marsilio; he is a young man graced by character, morals, and literature. Furthermore, you gave him such a letter addressed to me that you seem to have fathered sons not only in body but in mind. Then, while I was thinking of a letter in which I might respond to you and give you thanks, behold, you yourself arrive to us as the "faithful Achates" <note>A reference to the loyal companion of Aeneas in Virgil’s Aeneid; here meaning a most trusted friend.</note> of our Bernardo Bembi <note>A Venetian diplomat and humanist who was a close friend of Ficino.</note>. By this kindness, you have bound me to you to such an extent that you have now truly made one soul out of our two. Because, therefore, I shall no longer give you any further thanks for this or any other kindness...

Indeed, distinguished Rainaldo, you are the reason. For you yourself did not want us to be two any longer, but one. I consider him as foolish and insane who gives thanks to himself as the one who is ungrateful because he does not give thanks to another.

### Marsilio Ficino to Lorenzo Lippo, Rhetorician and Poet, sends greetings. <note>S.D. stands for "Salutem Dicit," a standard Latin epistolary greeting meaning "sends health/greetings."</note>

<margin>f</margin>
Greetings, most sharp-sighted Lippo. If you return to me the Alcinous <note>Referring to the "Handbook of Platonism" by Alcinous, which Ficino translated into Latin.</note> translated by us as easily and gladly as I gave it to you to read long ago, you will have done me a most pleasing favor. Virtue commends more than friendship; integrity persuades more easily than eloquence.
<margin>tas</margin>

### Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Francesco Bandini, sends greetings.

<margin>g</margin>
Giorgio Antonio Vespucci <note>A prominent Florentine humanist and uncle/tutor of the explorer Amerigo Vespucci.</note> will inform you more clearly through his own letters in what matter he needs your assistance. But this matter is as close to my heart, Bandini, as it is to his own. For a cause cannot fail to be shared where the soul is shared. But our Vespucci—you know the nature of the man—is more modest in making requests than is right. Truly, the distinguished integrity and learning of the man, even while he remains silent, ought to both forcefully demand and most easily obtain everything from fair judges. Therefore, I commend this man to you (who is, as you know, a most dear friend) not so much for the sake of friendship as for his own virtue. For he is our friend because of virtue itself.

->A Vow. An Oracle. A Miracle.<-

### Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Bernardo Bembo, Doctor and Knight, Most Illustrious Ambassador of the Venetians, sends greetings.

<margin>f</margin>
Greetings, friend of a heavenly and divine spirit. Chance brought some other friends to me; my own choice gave others; but heaven joined Bernardo Bembo <note>A Venetian statesman and father of the famous poet Pietro Bembo. He served as ambassador to Florence.</note> with me from the beginning. Then, divine providence
<margin>tia</margin>
confirmed it wondrously. I say "heaven" because we were born in the same year and on the same day under the same star. Furthermore, I assert that divine providence bound us to one another especially because in that year when you first came to Florence as an ambassador—nearly four months before your arrival—when I was gravely ill, immediately after a certain vow was piously made for my health to God and the Blessed Mary, you (though previously entirely unknown) appeared to us in a dream, certainly then first known to us, promising a speedy and prosperous recovery. Having woken up, I was almost healthy and soon recovered entirely. In the fifth month afterward, on the day I fully satisfied the vow, at that same hour, you came to our academy <note>original: "gymnasium". Here referring to the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note> of your own accord for the first time with a large entourage. And in that form which I had previously seen by divine intervention in my dreams, you greeted me. And many things were then said and done between us in exactly the same way I had seen while dreaming. In that same year, as if restored to life by religious vows, I composed a book on the Christian religion <note>original: "de xpīana religione". This refers to Ficino's work "De Christiana Religione," which attempted to harmonize Platonic philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note>. Now, therefore, read it happily, heavenly and divine friend. Surely heaven itself bound you to us from the beginning; then religion, higher than heaven, rebound <note>original: "religavit". Ficino is playing on the etymology of "religion" as a "binding" or "rebinding" (religare).</note> us. Your Marsilio wrote this with his own hand. On the Ides of July <note>July 15th</note>, 1479, in the countryside of Careggi <note>The location of the Medici villa where the Platonic Academy often met.</note>.

# A true friend foresees what a friend is about to desire and anticipates the requester.
->Marsilio Ficino of Florence to the distinguished physician, Georgius Cyprius, <note>Georgius Cyprius (George of Cyprus) was a scholar and physician in Ficino's circle.</note> sends greetings.<-

<margin>f</margin>If love is a god—as both the poets sing and the theologians confess—then love is surely divine. If it is divine, it is more than divine since it is God; therefore, love divines <note>Ficino is making a wordplay on "divinus" (divine) and "divinat" (to prophesy or foresee), suggesting that love has a prophetic quality.</note>. Thus, a true friend foresees what a friend is about to desire and anticipates the one who would ask. Such a friend to us is certainly our George of Cyprus, born in the place where Venus herself was worshipped, the mother of the twin Loves <note>Cyprus was the legendary birthplace of Aphrodite/Venus. The "twin loves" refers to the Platonic concept of Heavenly Love and Earthly Love.</note>. Indeed, if I did not fear that I might offend our friendship with words that are perhaps more than familiar, I would give great thanks for your promises. But he who treats familiarity itself with less than familiarity is no longer to be considered a familiar friend. We are most grateful toward a very gracious friend when we receive as gracefully as he himself either generously gives or promises.

Do not commend them to him. <note>original: "Neq[ue] illi comendabis." Ficino likely means the letters should speak for themselves without forced praise.</note> Farewell happily.

# Who are the blessed: those closest to the blessed, those further away, and those furthest away.
->Marsilio Ficino to his fellow philosopher, Locterius Neronius, <note>Lottieri Neroni, a member of the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note> sends greetings.<-

<margin>b</margin>Blessed are the celestial beings, who never perceive anything other than the good. Closest to them are those who, although they are placed in a most wretched region <note>Meaning the earthly, material world.</note> and necessarily perceive evils on every side, nevertheless, because they never disagree with the Highest Good, they do not consent to the evils anywhere. Those hold the third place who, after a fall, eventually rise back up to the Highest Good, so that they recognize that it was indeed an evil to have yielded to evils. Let them recognize that they yield to evils only when they themselves will that greater goods should yield to lesser ones within themselves. Let them recognize that where the Good of all goods is found, there alone is found the medicine for all evils. Finally, those must be considered the lowest and most miserable who have closed their eyes to the rays of the Highest Good which shine everywhere, so that they never see—even in that very light outside of which nothing is seen—how great an evil it is to always be without Him, without whom whatever is perceived is evil. These people, to be sure, do not look up at how great the misery is outside of divine happiness while in the divine splendor, lest by looking up they become blessed; rather, they look up and perceive it in their own darkness through certain small rays of that light, as if hallucinating, so that by looking up and perceiving in this way, they remain miserable. The world (as Christ, the master of life, says) is set in wickedness <note>original: "in maligno positus est," quoting 1 John 5:19.</note> chiefly for this reason: because we have been placed—or rather, we are smoke <note>Ficino makes a pun here: "positi sumus imo fumus" (we are placed, or rather, we are smoke/filth).</note>—in a wicked world. To those who are unhealthy and restless, nothing seems healthy and nothing seems quiet. Why do we so often unjustly blame the "Iron Age"? Since man first became "iron" by preferring iron to gold, the age which before was golden by nature deservedly turned into an iron one for him first. What wonder is that?

<meta>This page continues the correspondence of Marsilio Ficino. If all evils follow us from every side while we ourselves, having left behind the first good—that is, God—wickedly pursue individual things as if they were goods (which are all evil without the first good), it is not without justice that we fall into every evil against our will just as often as we willfully fall away from Him who is every good. Therefore, it is not permitted for us to complain about the ages; rather, it is permitted for the ages themselves to complain most vehemently about us. Let us, therefore, buy for ourselves—let us buy with all zeal—that **glowing gold** which the **heavenly eagle** <note>original: "aquila cælestis". This likely refers to Saint John the Evangelist, often symbolized by an eagle, who "soared" to the heights of divine revelation in his Gospel.</note> reveals: that is, the pure light of truth, burning with the very love of goodness. But we shall not easily buy the splendor before the heat; rather, let us buy the splendor through the heat. For indeed, gold itself does not glow when it is struck by the rays of a fire from a distance; but when it is occupied by the heat of the fire at close range, it shines forth. Nor does it shine properly because it glows, but because it seethes with the fire, it becomes thoroughly ignited. In this way alone, if we first burn with the love of the good alone—that is, of God—we shall suddenly shine with His splendor; and we shall be divine. **God is light. God is love.** To whom God is dear above all things, to him God shines above all things. To whom that sun shines through which all things shine, to him all things easily shine back everywhere. To him, moreover, all things become wonderfully sweet, for he tastes nothing except in that very sweetness, without whose flavor nothing can be made or felt to be sweet.

To what end is this? Namely, so that I might respond to your theological letters with whatever joy I can. For you yourself recently stirred me to look up to these things with your most splendid letters. Accept these things, therefore, gladly. For these things are yours; whatever they are, I return them to you. 

August 1st, 1488. At the Careggi estate. <note>Careggi was the location of the Medici villa where Ficino's Platonic Academy met.</note>

->He is not harmoniously composed who is not delighted by harmony.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to his dearest fellow-countryman Bastiano Foresio, <note>Bastiano Foresio (1435–1491) was a Florentine poet and a member of Ficino's inner circle.</note> sends greetings.<-

<margin>f</margin> Our Aurelius Augustine writes in his books *On Music*: that he is not **harmoniously composed** who is not **delighted by harmony**. Nor indeed is this an injustice. For since pleasure is usually produced by a certain likeness, it is necessary that he who is not delighted by concords is, in some way, devoid of concord himself. This man (if it is right to say so) I would say is not composed by God, who composes all things in **number, weight, and measure**. <note>A reference to Wisdom 11:20, a foundational text for the Medieval and Renaissance belief in a mathematical universe.</note> I would say, furthermore, that he is no friend to God, who rejoices in consonance to such an extent that He seems to have created the world for this very reason: so that the individual members of the world might harmonize both with each other and with the universe, and that the universe itself might harmonize with the intelligence and goodness of its author according to its strength. Add to this that He disposed the spheres and tempered their movements in turn so that (as is pleasing to **Pythagoras** and the **Platonists**) they produce an inestimable harmony and melody. We have discussed many things regarding this opinion elsewhere. One thing further it will be helpful to have recorded: that I have observed quite diligently that many talented people are found daily who are scarcely moved by nature toward these or those pleasures and pursuits of the other senses. But we have never found anyone endowed with genius who was not enraptured by musical modes. Also, we have known none of those who are *not* so enraptured to excel in sharpness of mind or judgment. The cause of this matter is chiefly twofold: one part **physical**, the other **mathematical**.

### A slanderer cannot harm you in any other way than if he makes you a slanderer in return.

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cocchi, greetings.

<margin>1</margin> Your enemy disparages you for no other reason than to make you appear publicly as one to be blamed, and so that you might be disturbed in your soul. If you are moved and you yourself break out into insults in turn, he has gained against you exactly what he sought with his whole mind. For he has already rendered you evil, slanderous, and infamous. Wisely, our Plato not only said nothing against his slanderers and enemies, but did not even think about them, teaching us to imitate nature, which drives its opposite far away from itself. For so we shall do, if we drive enemies out of our mouths and our minds. Add to this that if everyone else conducted themselves toward our enemies by this same reasoning, those enemies would be utterly erased from all human memory. But much more divinely, Christ, the master of life, instructed us: commanding that we should most willingly return blessings for curses, and good deeds for evil deeds. For in this way, we ourselves most easily remain unconquered and we tame our enemies. We also imitate nature itself in this way, which cures opposites, tempers opposites, and overcomes evil with good. Furthermore, we follow God, who does good freely to all, even to His enemies—that is, the impious and the unjust—commanding His sun to rise and His rains to fall upon the evil just as upon the good. Whenever I have wandered from this path, I have been filled with regret; but whenever I have followed it entirely, then all things have turned out happily for me. I believe you will follow these same precepts, and I congratulate you as if you were already following them.

->Since truth itself is immobile and eternal happiness, only those live<-
->truly and immovably blessed lives who spend their life in the study of truth.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Bastiano Salvini, his cousin <note>original: "amitino" - a cousin on the father's side.</note>, greetings.

<meta>This page continues the correspondence of Marsilio Ficino within Book Six. The previous page discussed the physiological and astrological underpinnings of musical talent, specifically the influence of Mercury on the brain's ability to perceive harmony. This page shifts to a philosophical meditation on the nature of truth and the soul’s middle position between the temporal and the eternal.</meta>

# BOOK

<margin>a</margin> I received your letter arguing **immutably** about the **mutability** of things. I say "immutably," that is, truly; for indeed, I consider immutability itself to be nothing other than truth. Truly, truth itself is so immobile <note>original: "immobilis." In this context, it refers to that which is fixed, certain, and unchanging.</note> that even the truth of motion is immobile. For what else is the truth of motion except its very **reason** <term>ratio: the underlying logical principle or definition</term> which encompasses its true definition? This reason maintains itself in such a way that it cannot be otherwise. Therefore, truth is always present. It neither passes from the past into the present, nor does it cross from the present into the future. Truth is so present that even the future and the past exist as a present truth. Indeed, by the same truth, it is true in the present that this or that either is, was, or will be, just as it will be true from eternity that this or that will at some time be, and it will be true forever that this or that once was. Truth is so eternal that even if it were said to have begun at some point, it would certainly have been true before that from eternity; and it would not have been true except through that same truth: that truth itself would one day exist. And even if truth were thought to ever cease, it would thereafter be true forever; and it would not be true except through truth itself: that truth once existed. If truth is immobile in motion, if it is present in the past and the future, if it is without beginning in the beginning, and likewise without end in the end, it is certainly nothing other than immobility itself and eternity. Therefore, the **Mind** <note>original: "Mens." For Ficino, this refers to the highest, most rational part of the human soul.</note>, being by nature capable of truth, is a participant in immobility and eternity. The **Will** also, being by nature hungry for truth, can make the fields of its own desire immutable and eternal. A life dedicated to the choice of truth, its study, and its worship, alone lives immutably and eternally most happy. Indeed, whichever things impiously and ungratefully depart from truth—the fountain of true blessedness—fall meanwhile wretchedly away from blessed eternity. But those who approach truth—the origin of true happiness—according to their strength, rise again blessed into a blessed eternity. Therefore (just as you have begun), live happily in the study and worship of truth. For only those live truly and happily who live in truth itself, the fountain of true blessedness. Furthermore, only those can eventually live in truth itself who always, as much as possible, live for the truth.

---

->Where the Good of goods flourishes, there alone is found the medicine for all evils<-

### Marsilio Ficino & Giovanni Cavalcanti send greetings to Leonardo Colesi, legitimate Professor of Civil Law.

<margin>a</margin> Our soul (as it is held among the **Platonists** <note>Ficino refers to the Neoplatonic tradition which places the soul as the "horizon" or middle point of the universe.</note>) occupies a certain middle region between eternal and temporal things. And as a participant in both, it turns toward either at its own will. When it plunges itself into temporal things, it seems at first to feel a certain brief and false sweetness; soon, however, it is utterly overwhelmed by a long and true bitterness. But when it raises itself to eternal things, the opposite occurs. For indeed, after a certain brief and false bitterness, it is drenched in a true and lasting sweetness. This is because truth—not the temporal, but the eternal—is the nourishment of eternal intelligence. Other human pursuits for the most part separate themselves from divine things; they are mortal...
