### As the beauty of the body fades, the soul’s beauty grows

->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Angelo Poliziano, <note>Poliziano (1454–1494) was a brilliant poet, classical scholar, and a close protégé of Lorenzo de' Medici and Ficino.</note> his fellow philosopher.<-

<margin>f</margin> Now then, Poliziano, if I say that I admire the sharp wit and eloquence of your letters in no small measure, someone might think I am a man too prone to wonder—since novelty alone usually gives rise to admiration in others. Indeed, it might seem that I am admiring things in Poliziano that have been very well known to me for a long time. But in truth, I am not marvelling at an old thing now, but a new one. For my Poliziano has matured so successfully in a very short time that, with his form changed, he appears to me now as someone else and someone new. Therefore, he who pleased me not a little as a boy, and much as a youth, pleases me the most as an adult. Justly, as his form grew day by day, so too did his grace. And that has pleased me for this reason as well: because I often prophesied that it would be so. Proceed, therefore. I beseech you, make yourself divine (as you have begun), so that you may simultaneously make me a true diviner. 

As for the fact that you extol "Marsilian" things <note>Refers to Ficino’s own works or ideas.</note> everywhere with such great praise, I am not surprised. For who would not be forceful, who would not be set on fire, when singing their own praises? Who lacks taste to such an extent that his own things do not please him most of all? Francus <note>likely Francesco da Castiglione, a priest and scholar.</note> reported to us what you have been doing with all the learned men, especially with Ermolao Barbaro, <note>Ermolao Barbaro (1454–1493) was a prominent Venetian humanist and diplomat.</note> regarding us, and what you ask me to do. I will certainly act gladly—and I hope, beautifully. Certainly, I act beautifully and well in whatever I do with my Bernardo Bembo. <note>Bernardo Bembo was the Venetian ambassador to Florence and a close friend of the Platonic Academy; he was the father of the famous Pietro Bembo.</note> Landino <note>Cristoforo Landino, a major Florentine humanist and commentator on Dante.</note> and Cavalcanti <note>Giovanni Cavalcanti, Ficino’s closest friend and "beloved" soulmate.</note> overwhelm you in turn with countless greetings.

->Flee far from seditious cities.<-

->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to his most beloved Girolamo Rossi.<-

<margin>n</margin> Naldo, <note>Naldo Naldi, a Florentine neo-Latin poet.</note> our poet, requested from me in your name the *Rapture of Paul*. <note>Refers to Ficino’s work *De raptu Pauli* (The Rapture of Paul), a commentary on St. Paul’s mystical ascent to the third heaven.</note> I am sending the original manuscript <term>archetype: the author's original draft or master copy</term> of this little work. But since it is the original, please return it safely as soon as you have transcribed it. Naldo and Angelo Poliziano, our other poet, have sung many things to me about Ermolao Barbaro. Moreover, they have sung much to me about Ermolao himself. Therefore, when it is convenient for you, go to meet this most Latin-literate "Barbarous" friend of ours. <note>Ficino is punning on Ermolao's surname "Barbaro" (meaning Barbarian) by calling him "most Latin."</note> Tell him that I have decided never to write anything to him that is not exceptionally good—yet at the moment, nothing good occurs to us. ### An Orphic comparison of the sun to God, and a declaration of the Ideas.

### Marsilio Ficino and Giovanni Cavalcanti send greetings to their fellow philosopher Lotterio Neroni.

The entire sphere of the sun (as the Orphics <note>Followers of the legendary poet Orpheus, whose mystical hymns were central to Ficino's Neoplatonism.</note> pass down) possesses a soul far more excellent than all other spheres. This soul exercises life and motion throughout the entire body of the sphere and diffuses it from there through all things. Through the actual globe of the planet Sun, it exercises primarily intellect and sight.

It exercises intellect through a certain intelligible light <note>Light perceived by the mind rather than the eyes; the "light of truth."</note> reigning in the very center of the sun as if in a head. It exercises sight through visible light shining throughout the whole circumference of the sun, as if through an eye. There, indeed, from intelligible light comes visible light; and in the intellect, sight also comes to be. For there, intellect is nothing other than that same intelligible light. Sight is nothing other than the visible light itself. Its being is nothing other than to shine. Its shining is nothing other than to see. Its illuminating is nothing other than to create all its things and to preserve what has been created.

Just as easily as it shines inwardly by its own nature by its very being, so easily does it illuminate outwardly by shining; and just as easily by illuminating, it makes and preserves all its things. But let us set aside for the moment the other duties of the sun. Let us consider only its innermost and visible light—that is, its sight itself. There, sight is as supreme as the thing seen is supreme. It is the sight through which all other sights see. It is the visible thing through which all visible things are seen. To what place, above all, does that sight direct itself so that it might see something, if not into itself?

Into which [the sun] all other things gaze, however they are able, so that they may see. But what does it see especially when it sees itself? Surely it sees visible light, the fountain and origin of all visible colors. If there the sight is supreme and the visible thing is supreme, certainly there is supreme and perfect vision. And those things which we count as three in number because of their differences <note>Ficino refers to the Trinity of the Seer, the Seen, and the Act of Seeing.</note>, in reality exist as one and the same. For if sight of this kind and the visible thing are one (as we said), it follows that vision—which is thought of as a kind of middle action between both—is the same as both.

Accordingly, if that light sees itself perfectly, it certainly looks deep within to see how much it can do in itself and how many things it can create from itself. But to omit other things, which are innumerable, it certainly creates and preserves all colors. For as it diffuses itself in various ways here and there through various subjects <note>The physical objects that receive light.</note>, it brings forth various colors everywhere. Therefore, it sees all colors in itself while it sees itself. 

But if that light is most simple and (as I might put it) of a single color, in what way will it be so manifold and all-colored? Surely because of this very fact—that it is most simple—it is the first in its kind and the most common of all. If this is so, it rightly embraces all the degrees of its kind within itself. For only that form in any genus which is entirely "uniform" <note>unified or consistent</note> within itself is "all-form-like" <note>original: "omniformis." A technical term meaning containing the potential or pattern for all possible forms.</note> in every way. And the multitude of forms, which leads to composition and diversity in subjects formed from elsewhere, signifies an outstanding abundance in the forming cause itself. It signifies a power that is both most unified (so to speak) and most strong. For the rest, lest we wander too far: however many species of colors there are in composite things, so

<meta>catchword: so-</meta>

<summary>Ficino uses the sun as a Neoplatonic metaphor for God, arguing that just as sunlight contains all colors within its simple light, the Divine Mind contains all "Ideas" or archetypes of the world within its unified essence.</summary>

### SIXTH BOOK CLI ###

->**SIXTH [BOOK] 151**<-

...Likewise, that light <note>The "intelligible light" of the divine or the sun's soul discussed on the previous page.</note> beholds the ideas of colors within itself. For according as it sees itself communicable only in the first degree, it is the idea of the color **black**. According as it is in the **second degree**, it is the idea of the **dusky**; in the **third**, of the **tawny**; in the **fourth**, of the **azure** and the **green**; in the **fifth**, of the **sky-blue** and the **sea-gray**; in the **sixth**, of a **fuller red**; in the **seventh**, of a **brighter red**; in the **eighth**, of **saffron**; in the **ninth**, of **white**; in the **tenth**, of the **clear** or the **shining**; in the **eleventh**, of the **brilliant**. Finally, in the **twelfth degree**, it is the idea of **Splendor** itself. 

Degrees of this kind, which are many when found in various physical subjects formed from external sources, are but a single and supreme degree within the one Cause that forms them all. It is no different than how innumerable numbers are but unity in their own origin, and how innumerable lines are one and indivisible within a single, indivisible center point. Nevertheless, while that light gazes upon its own supreme degree, it likewise perceives how that same supreme degree can be diffused through all the following degrees, and how many species of colors it can procreate from there. It is the triple cause of colors: the **efficient**, the **exemplary**, and the **final** <note>Ficino uses Aristotelian categories here: the 'efficient' cause brings the color into being, the 'exemplary' is the perfect mental pattern or Idea it follows, and the 'final' is the purpose or end toward which it moves.</note>. It is the efficient cause insofar as it produces them from itself and its own power; the exemplary cause insofar as it expresses them according to its own likeness; and the final cause insofar as it raises and leads them back to itself. 

And the colors themselves, by a certain natural instinct implanted from that source, strive to reach the likeness of the light itself as much as their species allows. Colors in physical subjects are indeed divided by quality, location, and time; but in their Cause, they are entirely united in these three ways. Furthermore, in physical subjects they are confused and mixed together through opposition; but in the Cause and the productive power—through the clarity of a sense discerning each one and a will choosing many—they are distinct without any confusion. Finally, in physical subjects they are imperfect because they are everywhere diminished; but in the Cause they exist as entirely perfect, because they are most pure and most full. 

Therefore, just as they are more divided among themselves in physical subjects, so they are more truly present in the Cause itself, because there they suffer no deprivation of their essence or nature. You will perhaps ask in what way they are distinguished within the Cause. I respond by following that mystery (still an Orphic one <note>original: "orphicum". Ficino frequently cites Orpheus as a "theologian" who prefigured Plato.</note>) for the sake of example: colors are considered in that light in three ways. First, according to the **absolute essence** and nature of the light. Second, according to its **vision**. Third, according to its **affection and will**. 

By absolute essence they are not divided at all, for there all colors are one pure light. They are distinguished from one another through vision and will, because the light both sees and wills for its one light to be diffused in many ways through many subjects. Does that light therefore become composite and multiple because it sees many things within itself that can be made from it, and wills them to be made? Not at all. Indeed, it does not see many things by means of many forms, but through one: namely, through the one Light that is the origin and exemplar of the various colors. Nor does it use many visions or many choices to perceive and select many things; rather, it discerns many through a single vision and likewise chooses many through a single will. 

Therefore, they seem to be discerned only by **reason**—that is, by the clarity that discerns many things and the will that deliberates upon many. I do not mean by the reason of our eyes, which look from here at one thing and then another; but by the reason of its own eye, which there beholds and deliberates upon those things within itself. For this reason, those respects by which the ideas of colors are discerned from one another are not from...

<summary>Ficino explains how the twelve degrees of color exist as a single, perfect unity within the divine light (the Cause) but appear divided and imperfect in physical objects. He uses the concepts of Essence, Vision, and Will to explain how God perceives diversity without losing His own absolute simplicity.</summary>

...create with these eyes. Indeed, [these things are created] by that very light, which is as most piercing as it is highly visible; by that light, I say, relating itself to the various species of colors. For there are so many viewpoints thus perceived and chosen. Such a multitude, however, does not stand in the way of the simplicity of its own nature in the one who perceives and chooses. But enough, now enough, my Lotterio, have we fixed our gaze upon the celestial Sun, according to our strength, like the eagle <note>In medieval and Renaissance bestiaries, the eagle was the only creature believed to be capable of looking directly into the sun without being blinded, symbolizing the soul’s contemplation of God.</note>. Therefore, lest we be forced to grow unhappily dim-sighted, let us now turn our vision back to our own things: to our own, I say, that is, to our Idea—the Sun of that super-celestial one, who does not permit his ardent lovers and contemplators to grow blindly dim. But as much as he flashes in their eyes, so much does he both confirm and strengthen their vision. Therefore, if we do not wish to admit that Orphic mystery <note>Marsilio Ficino translated the *Orphic Hymns* and often used "Orphic" to refer to ancient, mystical theological truths that prefigured Christianity.</note> to be true, let us at least for a little while pretend it is true: that we might so look up and see the celestial Sun, and in it that super-celestial one, as if in a mirror, "Who has set his tabernacle in the sun" <note>original: "Qui in sole posuit tabernaculum suum." This is a quote from Psalm 19:4, frequently used by Ficino to link the physical sun with the dwelling of God.</note>. December 19, 1479. Florence.

->It is better to be an exile than to look upon an eternal fatherland.<- <note>This likely contains a pun or a scribal error; in the context of the letter below, it usually implies it is better to be in exile than to watch one's "eternal" home or fatherland perish.</note>

### Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Bernardo Bembo, Venetian Ambassador, greetings.

<margin>r</margin>You ask, most refined Bembo, for what reason our friend from Naples <note>Likely referring to Giovanni Cavalcanti or another member of their circle who had withdrawn from public life.</note> wishes to be a rustic for so long. Clearly, it is because he cannot be "Urban" <note>original: "Urbanus." A wordplay on being a city-dwerller (urbanus) versus a country-dweller (rusticus), and perhaps the name Urban.</note> in these times. If he were able, Bernardo, he would either openly express the immense grief with which the condition of that city—once happy, now nearly wretched <note>A reference to the political instability in the Kingdom of Naples or the fallout of the Pazzi Conspiracy.</note>—presses upon him, or at least he would know how to remain cautiously silent. He would never flee from the sight of that city which loves its Bembo. But in such great evils of the fatherland, he cannot help but grieve deeply. It is not granted to him to help—nay, I should say, it is not permitted. He does not wish to feign; he prefers to be absent. But perhaps you will say: "This is a labor for those upright men; that care disturbs the quiet." Indeed, if given the choice, he would rather, with Democritus, laugh at the mad Abderites from a high mountain peak far from the city, than with Heraclitus, mourn the Ephesians from a tower's watch <note>Democritus and Heraclitus were the "laughing" and "weeping" philosophers of antiquity, respectively.</note>. Yet he is one who strives to imitate Jesus in this one thing at least by nature: Jesus weeping on the mountain over the wretched fate of the city of Jerusalem. Again, let him follow Pythagoras, Plato, and Aristotle, who once fled far from the deformed face of Athens. Finally, so that he might not be a Socrates <note>Socrates chose to stay in Athens and die; Aristotle chose to leave.</note>, he strives to be (if I may say so) an Aristotle. You know, I believe, for what reason Aristotle, after the death of Socrates, left Athens and went to Chalcis <note>Aristotle famously left Athens saying he would not let the city "sin twice against philosophy."</note>. June 1, 1480.

->Happy is he who truly rejoices; he truly rejoices who rejoices in the truth alone.<-

Read it happily. And live happily; but so that you may live truly happy, rejoice; and so that you may truly rejoice, rejoice in the truth alone.

->Public affairs cannot be governed rightly or successfully without divine help:<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Berlinghieri. Sends Greetings.

As much as most people are accustomed to congratulate friends who have <margin>q</margin> attained <note>The marginal 'q' likely corrects or notes the Latin word *adeptis* (attained).</note> magistracies and dignities: so much do I, in this matter, usually make a vow to God and pray for divine grace for my friends. One learns, indeed, from Plato <note>Marsilio Ficino was the central figure of the Platonic Academy in Florence; he viewed Plato's philosophy as a precursor to Christian truth.</note> that those arts which deal with private goods can sometimes be sufficiently governed by human prudence. But in that faculty which cares for the public good, one must confess that God himself must be the governor; for to Him belongs the providence of all things, but especially of common and public matters. Human prudence in such a faculty is not the governor; rather, it is the handmaid and servant of divine governance.

This is the meaning of that Platonic mystery in the *Protagoras*: that Prometheus—that is, human foresight—found all the arts except for civic skill. For this, he says, is supplied to us daily from Jove through Mercury—that is, from divine providence through angelic inspirations. This is also the point of that Platonic comparison: just as beasts cannot be led rightly and fortunately by a beast without a human, so men cannot be led by a man without God. What else does that prophetic saying mean: "The heart of the king is in the hand of God, and He turns it wherever He wills" <note>original: "cor regis i manu dei: et quocūq; vult vertit illđ." A reference to Proverbs 21:1.</note>? And also this from the Gospels and the Apostles: "You would not have this power unless it had been given to you from above" <note>original: "Non haberes hanc poteſtatem niſi tibi data eē̅t deſup." A reference to John 19:11.</note>. Again, "there is no power except from God. And those that exist are ordained by God" <note>original: "nō eſt vlla poteſtas niſi a deo. Que vero ſunt: a deo ordinata ſunt." A reference to Romans 13:1.</note>.

For this reason, Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A mystical theologian highly esteemed by Ficino, believed at the time to be the convert of St. Paul mentioned in the Book of Acts.</note> placed archangels as leaders and masters over human leaders. Hence David, in the Psalms, moderated his governance of the kingdom with certain reins. For he knew: "Unless the Lord watches over the city, the one who watches it keeps vigil in vain" <note>original: "Niſi dominus custodierit ciuitatem. fruſtra vigilaturum. qui custodit eam." A reference to Psalm 127:1.</note>. From this, Solomon introduces Divine Wisdom crying out: "By me kings reign, and the makers of laws decree what is just; by me princes rule, and the powerful decree justice" <note>original: "Per me reges regnant: & legum conditores iuſta decernūt Per me prīcipes iperant: & potētes decernūt iusticiā." A reference to Proverbs 8:15-16.</note>. Here also the religion of the Romans commanded that nothing public be attempted, whether in peace or in war, without vows and auspices. Whence Scipio <note>Scipio Africanus, the Roman general, was famous for his habit of praying at the Temple of Jupiter on the Capitoline before starting public business.</note> never approached public business before he had applied himself to divine vows. Skillfully, the Orators and Poets [call] those who preside over public duties...

...offices: [they say] that they are like pilots of ships. And as those who are always tossed among reefs, waves, and storms, they continually stand in need of the protection of the divine powers. Therefore, just as I am accustomed to act toward other friends who have obtained magistracies, so am I now disposed toward you, my dearest friend. Truly, first of all, I make a vow to God for your happiness. Then, I do not so much congratulate you as I offer a wish—I wish, I say, for divine help: so that you may conduct and complete this and all other magistracies piously, prudently, justly, mercifully, and finally, happily. This indeed I hope for you; for I know that by your nature (through divine grace) you will achieve it. Farewell.

### Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo, most illustrious jurist and knight, Ambassador of the Venetians. Sends Greetings.

<margin>n</margin>
I have written nothing to you for a long time, my Bembo. Because the malice of the times suggested nothing to me, while I was hearing or thinking, except for evil. But although I cannot unlearn how to write poorly <note>Ficino plays on the words *male scribere* (to write with poor style) and *mala scribere* (to write about bad things).</note>, I have not yet learned how to write of evil things. Yet I recently heard this one thing, which I would approve of if only it were true: namely, that the Supreme Pastor <note>The Pope.</note> (relying on heavenly counsel) did not wish to separate the Venetians from his flock. On the contrary, what could have been heard or thought more profanely than that this Republic—which is judged by the Vicar of God himself to be the most divine of all that are or have been on earth—should be either attacked or abandoned? Therefore, I will finally approve of all things when everyone else feels the same about the Venetians, and when the Pope himself feels almost the same about all others—that is, about all Christians—as he does about the Venetians. Namely, let him consider and show that he has been judged by the divine oracle to be the common father of all Christians. For in truth, he is not a father who does not have sons; nor does he truly have sons, who does not hold his sons as sons. I truly wish for this, not only out of my charity toward all, but I also hope that the Pope himself will do this out of his own piety.

->Only that grace does not grow old which arises from things that do not grow old.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Domenico Galletto. Sends Greetings.

<margin>c</margin>
I was just now thinking quite diligently to myself by what reasoning I might best beseech and entreat you to help our relative, my cousin Bastiano Salvini <note>Sebastianus Salvinus, a relative of Ficino and a fellow scholar who assisted in translating and editing texts.</note>, in his legal case (if you are able by any means). First, indeed, friendship offered itself to me. And when I had already decided to write thus: "I ask you through our friendship, my Galletto," and so forth—Virtue herself suddenly interrupted me, saying: "Do not, Marsilio, ask through friendship, which follows me (that is, Virtue), but entreat through Virtue herself, who leads and sustains friendship." Therefore, Galletto, having changed my plan, I have decided—both in this matter and in all others—to ask you not so much through our love as through that very Virtue which is the conciliator of our love. Certainly, gratitude <note>The Latin word *gratia* carries multiple meanings: grace, favor, and gratitude.</note> owes much to virtue, since it is because of virtue that it becomes immortal. You have heard (as I believe) that proverb: "Nothing grows old more quickly than gratitude," namely that which arises from things that eventually grow old. But that which [arises] from ever-green virtue...

# SIXTH BOOK
## 153

...is born; it never withers. What else does that poetic line mean: "To Apollo and Bacchus alone belongs eternal youth"? <note>original: "Solis æternæ est Phœbo Bacchoq; iuuētus." Ficino uses these gods to represent the intellect and the soul's joy.</note> Truly, grace itself is nothing other than splendor and joy. Splendor indeed among the poets received the name of Apollo, while joy took the name of Bacchus. Virtue, however, brings both splendor to the mind and joy to the will: ever living and ever flourishing. Farewell happily, my Gallectus; and just as you always shine through virtue alone, so may you always rejoice in virtue alone. Furthermore, whomever you encounter who rejoice in virtue alone, bid them greetings in the name of Marsilio, as if they were already known and intimate friends to me. Let others go. For I do not wish those to be well who do not wish themselves to be well. Indeed, those do not wish themselves well who do not wish for virtue, without which they cannot be well. The beginning and end of human virtue is to remember that human virtue does not exist without the grace and love of divine virtue. Farewell again.

### Recommendation of a friend.

-> Marsilio Ficino the Florentine humbly commends himself to the Reverend Father in Christ <-
-> and his Lord, Raphael Riario, Cardinal of Saint George. <-

<margin>Grace</margin> A steady opinion has now spread through Florence: that Marsilio Ficino is vehemently loved by Raphael Riario. And this opinion was born long ago from our intimacy, and has been confirmed by my letters, which are circulated everywhere as witnesses of my reverence toward you. Therefore, many ask me daily to commend their causes to you. I, however, lest I be more troublesome to you, have undertaken to commend the cause of only one person during all this time: namely, that of Francesco Petrucci, the priest. You know (I am sure) the son of Cesare. Whom I could not fail to commend to you, both because of the kinship I have with his family and because of his own virtues. But although you predicted at your departure that unless I went there with you, you would never respond to me either by letter or by messenger, you did not however threaten that you would fail to respond at some time with affection and deeds. Therefore, lest you be a perjurer—if you indeed confirmed by oath that you would not respond by letter or messenger—do not respond at all. But lest you seem to have departed from your natural character, you will respond at last with pious affection and deeds. Thus magnanimous men are accustomed to act, who abound in deeds as much as others abound in words. Whose affection we recognize in the outcome rather than in the words. Indeed, if I had been able to obey your commands formerly as much as I wished, you would certainly write nothing to this man of yours as if he were present, just as you now write nothing to him while he is absent. Thus by a certain fate (so to speak), it seems to have been ordained that I should by no means receive any letters from you, and you would give your Marsilio no words, but give him your services. Would that all others also gave services, not words.

Antonio Benivieni <note>Antonio Benivieni (1443–1502) was a pioneering Florentine physician and a friend of Ficino.</note> and several others: they all intended to test every art of Apollo <note>In this context, the "arts of Apollo" refers to the practice of medicine, as Apollo was the god of healing.</note> upon me to see if I could be sustained by any means. Live happily, and may you be armed happily. July 24, 1480. Florence.

->There are four kinds of divine madness: love is the most excellent of all.<-

### Marsilio Ficino and Giovanni Cavalcanti to Naldo Naldi the Poet. Greetings.

Your most elegant letters were delivered to us at the very hour when the Moon was joined to Mars in a straight line. Who would have thought—so far as one could conjecture from the heavens themselves—that those letters would wander with a certain lunar instability and be full of Martian fury and hatred? On the contrary, however, they are entirely different. Indeed, they do not wander with the lowliest motion of the Moon, but are wonderfully tempered by the sublime harmonies of Urania and Calliope. <note>Urania is the Muse of Astronomy; Calliope is the Muse of Eloquence and Epic Poetry.</note> They do not burn with the fire of Mars, but with the fire of Venus. They do not seethe with hatred, but with charity. In this matter, we clearly see the truth of that poetic and astronomical saying: that Mars is conquered and tamed by Venus. <note>Ficino refers to the astrological idea that the influence of the aggressive planet Mars can be mitigated by the harmonious influence of Venus.</note> That theological truth is also evident: namely, that divine madness <term>furor</term> <note>Ficino uses the term "furor" to describe a state of divine inspiration or "madness" where the soul is elevated above its ordinary state.</note>, being superior to celestial motions, does not obey the stars at all but commands them. Since, indeed, the kinds of divine madness (as your Plato pleases) are four—Love, Prophecy, Mystery, and Poetry—and since Love is attributed to Venus, Prophecy to Apollo, Mystery to Dionysus, and Poetry to the Muses; this divine Love itself, by which you were seized when you wrote to us, is judged the most excellent of all for two reasons. One reason is that the other madnesses are never obtained nor preserved without the instinct of love toward the very thing about which the mind is stirred in madness. The other reason is that since love transforms the lover into the beloved, whenever it is directed toward higher things, it joins the mind more closely with God than the other madnesses do. If we were to attempt to praise this amatory madness of yours according to its dignity, we would have need of poetic madness ourselves. But since the Muses do not breathe upon us at present, what we cannot praise with poetry, we certainly approve with mutual love, and shall always approve.

...to Francesco Soderini, Bishop of Volterra. <note>Francesco Soderini (1453–1524) was a member of a powerful Florentine family and a student of Ficino.</note> Heartfelt Greetings.

### The Philosophical Education of a Prince.

<margin>p</margin>
Philosophy, the mother, to Cardinal Giovanni of Aragon, her most beloved son. She promises and provides true health <note>The Latin *salutem* carries the double meaning of "health" and "salvation" or "well-being."</note> through the true knowledge of oneself. Almost all mortals, most beloved son, seem so blind to me that they occasionally appear like owls. <note>Philosophy suggests that people are like owls because they see "dark" worldly things clearly but are blinded by the "light" of spiritual truth.</note> I will set aside for now many other signs of human blindness. But since I am addressing a man established in the highest dignity, I will only reveal how much blindness involves mortals in matters of this kind. First, by a false definition, they judge dignity to be nothing other than **obtaining** things worthy of honor. But I define true dignity as nothing other than **meriting** things worthy of honor. Next, they hope they will be masters and peaceful only when they are occupied with ruling many things and people. But I—as the outcome itself proves—think they are then the servants of all and oppressed by every disturbance, when they have rashly subjected their shoulders to sustaining the weight of all. I also judge that to be the true lordship which serves no slave. Which, if it ever serves, then serves only Him who alone is the slave of no one. <note>This refers to God, the only being who is truly sovereign and serves no master.</note> Again, I judge true tranquility to be that which is so established that either no disturbances occur, or if they do occur, they serve the mind as much as they dominate others. Furthermore, mortals are so insane that when, either by chance or by some vice, they have obtained certain great things, they suddenly believe they have become great themselves. Just as if someone out of their mind, when they put on a longer garment or enter a spacious house, were to boast that they had become taller or larger because of it. But I, on the contrary, affirm that only those are truly great men who perform great things with similarly great virtue, and are not overcome by great things, but either overcome or equal them. Finally, those raised to the highest peaks of status are accustomed to regard others as inferior and much smaller—indeed, as nothing. As if someone were so delusional that after climbing a very tall tower, he thought he had become as tall and lofty as the tower is high. And he might think whatever he looks down upon from the tower is truly as tiny as it appears to one looking down from a height. But I judge those to be truly the highest who, because of the very height of the soul...

<header>BOOK SIX</header>

...the disturbances of the clouds do not reach those settled on the summit of Olympus. <note>In Greek mythology, Mount Olympus was the home of the gods, often used by Ficino to represent a state of philosophical detachment and higher consciousness.</note> I am accustomed to look down upon all others as if they were the lowest. Finally, I judge those to see all things most sharply and judge most correctly who decide that individual things are not as they appear outwardly to one looking from the outside, but as they truly are within. I am also accustomed to hold in high regard those men of great spirit and judgment who do not value things according to how they happen to appear from elsewhere, but rather by the value that things give to themselves through their own virtue.

I (my sweetest Giovanni) <note>Giovanni Cavalcanti (1444–1509), to whom Ficino dedicated many of his works.</note> father such sons for myself, as you hear, though the common crowd is uninvited. I also nourish my students in this way. By this reasoning, I separate them from the blindness of the masses and their pitiable misery. By this path especially, I lead my followers—far removed from the darkness of Lethe <note>The river of forgetfulness in the underworld.</note> and the Stygian storm <note>The River Styx, associated with the underworld and gloom.</note>—happily toward the ethereal light of Phoebus <note>The sun god Apollo, representing reason and divine light.</note>, to Elysian tranquility, and to the immortal food of ambrosia and nectar-like sweetness. 

Nor have I ever demanded, or will I ever demand, any other payment from my followers for such a happy gift than two "coins." The first is that they be as willing to receive gifts from me as I am to give them. The second is that they should give thanks not so much to me—the lover of truth—as to Philosophy, or rather to Wisdom itself: that is, to the supreme and divine Truth which I love. For that Truth fills me with eternal light, just as the sun fills the moon. You, however, my sons and students, perceive those things which I show you everywhere most sharply whenever you correctly discern them as they are shown to you by me—like a moon—only by the rays of the sun itself, that is, of Truth, even if those rays are slanted. Surely, sons affected in this way will one day gaze upon those things in the divine Sun itself during the day, which they now see during the night as if in the moon. 

To what purpose is all this? So that you may remember, my sweetest Giovanni, that I have for a long time now gladly embraced you as a son. Remember that I have educated you from the beginning just as I am accustomed to educate my own. I will never demand present money from you for that education, other than those two "coins" I mentioned a moment ago. Farewell, and live happily in the blessed arms of this your mother, Philosophy. 

20 August 1480, Florence.

### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to his fellow philosopher Francesco Berlinghieri, son of Niccolò. Greetings.

<margin>s</margin>If by chance you were about to hand over a house to be guarded, or a deposit to be kept, or sheep to be fed, or a field to be tilled, would you choose just any man, even the richest or most powerful? Or rather will you choose him above others who is endowed with that very ability which your business requires? If you are wise, you will commit the house to be guarded and the deposit to be kept only to one who is prudent, brave, just, and faithful. Similarly, you will entrust the sheep to be fed to a most blameless shepherd; and if you are wise, you will commend the field to be tilled to some excellent farmer.

Furthermore, if you desire to adopt someone as a son, would you ever consider his external fortune rather than his character and virtue? When about to buy a slave, would you value the slave's clothing more than the strength of his body and the faith and diligence of his mind? When about to buy a horse, will you inspect the painted trappings or the beautiful bridle, or much more carefully the limbs and dexterity of the horse? When about to build a house, would you lay the foundations in sands, however golden, or rather in stone? 

You have a daughter (as I hear) of marriageable age; a daughter is far dearer and more precious to you than all these things I have recounted above. I beg you, pay careful attention to what you do. For there we err most gravesly, where mistakes can always be more openly blamed than corrected. There we fall most dangerously, where once a person has fallen, all ability to rise again seems to be lacking. There we grieve most bitterly, where we grieve by our own fault and always believe we will have to grieve. What is it, then, to give a daughter in marriage, if not to commit her to a husband to be guarded, preserved, fed, and cherished? The husband's fortune will indeed promise all these things, but only virtue itself will provide them. No one is more blind than he who [follows] <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note> blind fortune as if it were a [leader]...

### Marsilio Ficino commends himself to the Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Francesco Soderini, Bishop of Volterra <note>Francesco Soderini (1453–1524) was a high-ranking Florentine diplomat and clergyman.</note>.

I write frequent letters (as happens daily) to many; but hear, venerable father, what has been happening to me for a long time in this matter, and it is indeed undoubtedly strange. My genius <note>In the Platonic sense, a "genius" is a guiding spirit or personal daemon.</note> never prompts me to copy out what I write to the many for my own Soderini—a man certainly of the very few. But whenever I compose something for princes and great prelates, for Cardinals, for the Pope, or for kings, so often does that same genius suddenly command and urge me to send the same gift to Soderini, as if it has long augured and desired something great for my Soderini. Perhaps it also warns me in this way: lest I think I will ever truly satisfy the great, unless I satisfy, according to my strength, this one man who is truly worthy of great gifts. Read therefore this letter of ours which I am sending to Matthias, King of Hungary <note>original: "Mathiam Pannonie Regem." Matthias Corvinus (r. 1458–1490) was a famous patron of the arts and humanism.</note>; would that it were kingly. Take diligent care of your health and keep yourself for favorable times. November 30, 1480.

### Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo <note>Bernardo Bembo (1433–1519) was a Venetian diplomat and the father of the famous humanist Pietro Bembo.</note> of Venice sends greetings.

When I wished in recent days to exhort my friends to a truly burning love of virtue with words as brief as I could manage, I attempted to paint an image of a beautiful mind from a certain congruent likeness of a handsome body, using certain Platonic colors (as I often do). But while I attempted to express a very similar image of a beautiful soul and body, during the painting—because of my lack of skill and laziness in painting—it was not so much the image itself (which I desired) that was expressed as a shadow that resulted. Indeed, it is so certain that every shadow is always forced to follow the thing itself of which it is a shadow, that if anyone were ignorant of this, he alone would seem not to be a man in truth, but the shadow of a man. Therefore, when such a shadow first arises among us, having left Florence, it go...

## An uncommon commendation: The training of a citizen is not made common.

->Marsilio Ficino commends himself to the Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Gentile,<-
->Bishop of Arezzo.<-

<margin>q</margin> Whoever understands, venerable father, how ancient and how strong our friendship has always been, might think that Marsilio has long since recommended to his friend Gentile <note>Gentile de' Becchi (1430–1497) was a tutor to the Medici family and became the Bishop of Arezzo.</note> various causes of more than a thousand friends and relatives. However, until now, he has recommended none. For, by some instinct or prophetic spirit, I foresaw that I would one day recommend the cause of Giovanni Maria, my maternal uncle and the most beloved of all my kin. I was already setting aside for this uncle whatever weight might have been found in ten thousand recommendations. If, therefore, you grant this one favor, consider that in this one act you have favored me ten thousand times. Yet I do not ask this now of my bishop—and a most just one at that—so that, because of our friendship which began and remains in justice itself, he should ever do anything that might seem less than just to anyone. Far be it, venerable father; far be it from us that, to please a man, we should meanwhile displease God—without whose splendor or grace neither can other things please us, nor we please others, nor can we please ourselves, nor, finally, can we in any way please God. But enough on these matters.

It cannot be said how much I approve of Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" (1449–1492), the de facto ruler of Florence.</note> having dedicated his first-born son, Piero <note>Piero de' Medici (1472–1503), known as "Piero the Unfortunate," succeeded his father as ruler of Florence but was later exiled.</note>, to the instruction of his former teacher, Gentile. For I hope that by such an education, this boy will shortly—even in his very childhood—emerge as a wise elder. Our Plato considers nothing more fundamental, nothing more necessary for those who are to successfully take up the rudders of the republic. And indeed, not without reason. For if any art, even the smallest, must be learned by us from childhood and practiced with all our strength, then surely public governance, the mistress of all arts and the most difficult, must be learned from "tender fingernails" <note>original: "a teneris unguiculis" - a Latin idiom meaning from earliest childhood.</note> as much as age allows. Thus, so that a very short life may suffice for an exceedingly long art and discipline, a capacity of this kind must be begun together with the spirit itself and with life itself (so to speak). One must strive above all that those who are to be the head of others, as if of limbs, should surpass the rest in wisdom and prudence at least as much as the head itself surpasses the members subject to it in the abundance and sharpness of the senses—not to mention that reason itself reigns only in the head. They should remember that we never think with our feet or hands, but only with the head. Therefore, those who strive to be the head must necessarily be able to think and deliberate for themselves and for all others...

### Marsilio Ficino to Angelo Poliziano, the Homeric Poet. Greetings.

<margin>a</margin>
Our friend Alamanno Donati <note>Alamanno Donati was a Florentine nobleman and a member of the Platonic Academy.</note> has for some time now, with that "round mouth" <note>original: "ore rotundo" — a phrase from the Roman poet Horace meaning eloquent or polished speech.</note> of his (you know the man, Poliziano), been sounding loudly in our ears in this manner: "Commend me, I pray, by your humanity, Marsilio; commend me, I beseech you, by that sacred love of yours for me—than which no plea is more sacred; commend your Alamanno to Poliziano as soon as possible." When I diligently seek the reasons for such an ardent and persistent petition—or rather, demand—from him, he simply repeats the same thing again: "Just commend me, Ficino. Commend me at once." Yet he still explains no reason for this so-desired recommendation.

I therefore recommend his cause to you—the cause of one who brings no cause for his petition—similarly without cause. But take care, Poliziano, that you do not think this present recommendation is the lightest of all just because it seems to lack a cause. On the contrary, for that very reason, I want it to seem most weighty to you. For indeed, among philosophers, the highest thing in any category is that which has no cause outside of itself, as if it depends on nothing else but its own nature. <note>Ficino is using Neoplatonic logic here: the "First Cause" or God has no cause above it, therefore things without external causes are closer to the divine or absolute.</note>

Therefore, let this present recommendation, for which no cause is brought to you except the recommendation itself, be judged by you as the highest of all. And if Alamanno himself (as those who are moved by some excitement usually do) only shouts and repeats that same shout into our ears, yet cannot clearly explain any reasons for his shouting—his tongue hesitating under the most rapid emotion of his heart—I, however, led by certain signs, believe that he is now entirely burning with a healthy love for some beautiful Muse. I believe he vehemently desires, through the favor of Poliziano, the priest of the Muses, to enter into a friendship. With such a mediator, he might more easily possess his beloved Muse.

"That she may spend all her years with him in such studies, and make him a parent with beautiful offspring." <note>original: "Omnes vt secum studiis per talibus annos Exigat: & pulchra faciat se prole parentem" — This is a clever adaptation of Virgil’s *Aeneid* (1.74-75), where the goddess Juno promises a nymph to the wind-god Aeolus. Ficino replaces "merits" with "studies" (studiis).</note> Farewell. But before I seal the letter (with Angelo as witness), I declare you to this Alamanno: if ever he should seem less dutiful or grateful for this great service of mine—God forbid—I shall reproach him thus: "Ha! You are too ungrateful!" I will say. "Did you not think I had done enough for you if I had at least introduced you to the priest of the Muses? But when I introduced you to my Poliziano, I seem to have commended you not so much to the priest of the Muses as to the Muses themselves (which is a much greater thing)."

BOOK SIX

### A Portrait of the Bad and Good Mind. Likewise, of the Ignorant and the Learned.
->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Lorenzo de’ Medici the Younger, a Magnanimous Man.<-

<margin>a</margin> I have heard for a long time, Lorenzo, that men imbued with bad habits are greatly displeasing to you. I have also heard recently that for this very reason you are pleasing to good men: because the bad ones are displeasing to you. In the former, I certainly approve of you; but in the latter, I congratulate you greatly. For there is no shorter path to the good, and none more convenient, than to hate the evil. There is no surer judgment of a healthy taste than to reject those flavors which are harmful to health. There is no life more secure, nor glory more firm, than to be loved by good and prudent men. For those whom honest and prudent men love, even the wicked are eventually compelled to honor. 

But so that bad men might be for you not only an object of hatred, but even of horror, I desire (if it please you) to pay attention for a moment and point out to you with my finger (as they say) the most foul and miserable life of the shameful. Lorenzo, a soul infected with perverse habits is like a forest rough with thorns in every direction, bristling with savage beasts, and infested with venomous serpents. Again, it is like a swelling sea, tossed by contrary winds or by cruel storms and waves. Furthermore, it is like a human body that is as utterly deformed on the outside as it is tortured on the inside by the immense pains of various limbs. 

On the other hand, a mind adorned with the best habits is almost like a cultivated and fertile field. Like a tranquil and peaceful sea. Like a human body that is as beautiful as it is strong. We have seen, my friend, first a certain shadow of the bad mind, and then the contrasting image of the good mind. When we first perceive the former clearly, we cannot help but shudder violently. But we cannot help but love and venerate the latter with wonder. What else is it to turn out to be a good man, than both to follow this latter image with all our might and at the same time to shrink back from that former one deep within? 

But tell me, I pray, best Lorenzo: do you wish that just as we considered the bad or good soul a moment ago, we might next look more clearly together at an ignorant mind, and again at another that is learned? Indeed, you desire it vehemently (as I judge), and I likewise desire to show it to you briefly. Certainly, a mind ignorant of the truth is like the moon when it suffers an eclipse <note>original: "æclípſím patítur"</note> because the earth has been placed between it and the sun—that is, it is deprived of the sun’s brightness. Again, it is like the cloudy, cold air of the night. Finally, it is like a human body with blind eyes, deaf ears, and a mute tongue. 

By contrast, we think that a mind both endowed with the knowledge of things and powerful in the abundance of words is no different than either the moon full of the sun’s light, or the daytime air, serene, abundantly bright, and moderately warm. Or finally, a body with sharp senses and a ready tongue. Whoever does not immediately flee the ignorant mind when he first sees its most foul image or shadow will flee nothing. But whoever does not ardently pursue the learned mind wherever it appears, I see nothing at all that he might pursue. Proceed then, my Lorenzo. Proceed, I beg you...

<summary>In this letter to Lorenzo de' Medici the Younger, Ficino uses vivid allegorical imagery—comparing the state of the soul to landscapes, weather, and physical health—to illustrate the beauty of virtue and knowledge versus the horror of vice and ignorance.</summary>
<keywords>Lorenzo de' Medici the Younger, virtue, vice, ignorance, wisdom, soul, allegory, health, light and shadow</keywords>

BOOK SIX

Flee (as you have already begun) long ago. Alas, flee far from that land and the wretched image of a wicked and ignorant mind. Come! Pursue with all your strength (as you are doing) more and more every day: the bright and blessed appearance of a good and wise soul. So that, just as nature initially and then fortune afterwards enriched you, so you at least might enrich yourself through your own industry. Lest perhaps, when nature and fortune have supplied everything else to your wish, you might some day appear to someone to have failed only yourself. And while all your surroundings—fields, houses, furnishings, clothes, and finally every single limb of your body—shine almost like stars, you too may shine with the rays of your mind, both of character and of letters <note>original: *literarum*, referring to scholarship and learning</note>, appearing among all these things no differently than the sun itself shining among the stars.

### A recommendation of learned men that is not common.
## Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Giacomo Lanfredini, a lawful citizen.

<margin>s</margin> If I were to write to my Giacomo in the common tongue <note>The "vulgar" or Italian/Tuscan language</note>, I would undoubtedly err twice. For if I sent common things to a man and a friend who is not common, I would fail. Therefore, I will write in Latin as best I can; provided I am not a barbarian, I prefer to be Latin rather than Florentine <note>Ficino values the prestige of Latin over the local vernacular for serious correspondence</note>. But what should I write most of all? If I recommend my own affairs at present, perhaps I will seem less trustful in friendship; certainly I will appear more confident in domestic matters. But I prefer to trust too much in domestic matters than to distrust a friend in any way. Therefore, this letter will not petition, but will congratulate. Not, however, my Lanfredini, on whose shoulders—however robust—the senate has recently placed a huge weight; rather, it congratulates the learned. For on the same shoulders with which Atlas supports the heavens fitted with burning stars, our Giacomo will certainly support men dedicated to the contemplation of heavenly things. Indeed, since he himself was first nourished by the Muses, and then devoted his son Antonio to be nourished by the kind Muses from a tender age—and they have fortunately nourished him for his father—surely, as one pleasing to the Muses, he will everywhere gladly recognize all their pupils as brothers and protect them with all zeal and resources.

### One must respond to love not with words, but with faith.
## Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Antonio Lanfredini.

<margin>a</margin> I received letters from your father Giacomo and from you at the same time, most full of elegance and love. Since I often hear Jesus crying out: "I and the Father are one" <note>John 10:30</note>, for that reason I will respond with only one letter to both father and son together. All love of the best friend (as the proverb says) demands faith <note>original: *fidem*, implying loyalty and trust</note>. Therefore, I have decided to respond to the greatest love toward me with a certain greatest faith according to my strength. But if perfect faith needs witnesses for them, certainly this letter of mine will bring as the chief testimony of my faith toward you the very volume composed by us concerning true faith <note>Ficino refers here to his work *De Christiana Religione* (On the Christian Religion)</note>.

...I would have thought: several friends have objected that I have discussed so much about black humor <note>original: *bochumore*, likely a typo for *melancholia* or *atrabili*, referring to "black bile," the humor associated with melancholy</note> in vain for two reasons. Therefore, my dear Bernardo <note>Bernardo Rucellai, a Florentine diplomat and scholar</note>, I could not help but grieve heavily that this diligence of mine, or rather my curiosity, would be utterly in vain. 

But yesterday our friend Piero Guicciardini <note>Petrus Guicciardinus, father of the historian Francesco Guicciardini</note>, the son of that most distinguished citizen Giacomo, easily refuted those objections and freed me from the distress I had conceived from them. Indeed, he read through our book in one breath (as they say); he grasped every single point so suddenly and retains them so memorably that he has shown those things can indeed be understood. He further demonstrated that the most happy genius we wished for already exists, most especially in him, a man who understands and remembers so clearly. And although he alone is a most sufficient and wealthy witness for me—showing that I have not composed vanities—nevertheless, because a judge usually requires at least two witnesses in a case: I pray you too, my excellent Bernardo, read our book. If you do this, I hope a second witness for my cause will soon not be lacking. Farewell.

### That this World is Unclean, how False, and how Deceptive.

->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to his fellow philosopher Lottieri Neroni.<-

<margin>f</margin> For a long time now, our own true and truthful guardian spirit <note>original: *genius*</note> has been commanding Marsilio to write something to Lottieri Neroni—a most refined man and a most true friend of all—something that is the most "true" among human affairs. As I sought something of this kind that could be proven as most true, and not finding it easily enough, that same guardian spirit showed me: among these lower things, since they are in truth false, nothing truer can ever be found than this one thing: namely, to consider all these things (just as they are) as undoubtedly false. 

For in what way can anything "worldly" (so to speak) be true in the world <note>Ficino plays on the Latin word *Mundus*, which means both "world" and "clean/ordered"</note>, when the world itself is false? For it is indeed "unclean" <note>original: *immundus*, a pun on *in-mundus* (not-clean/not-world)</note>. Perhaps when God had created a globe of this kind—like a sort of round fruit, such as that which we commonly call an "evil apple" <note>original: *pomum malum*. In Latin, *malum* means both "apple" and "evil," allowing for a pun on the Forbidden Fruit and the nature of the physical world</note>—and saw that it was too unclean, as if it had been drawn out from the filthiest chaos (as one of the poets might say), He immediately began to clean and Georgic-ally prune <note>original: *mundare purgareque*</note> the very surface of the world as if it were a bad apple. 

But the peelings <note>original: *putamina*</note> fell by their own weight into the middle center toward us wretched people. If, therefore, there are any things in the universe that are "clean" <note>original: *munda*</note>, they were granted to the heavenly beings. To us, however, as is fitting, there fell not clean things, but (so to speak) certain dregs and peelings. Hence that Christian saying: "Woe to the earth and the sea, for the devil has fallen to his own, raging with ire" <note>original: *Ve terræ ac mari...* Reference to Revelation 12:12</note>. Or again: "Woe to the world because of scandals. For it is necessary that scandals come" <note>original: *mundo a scandalis...* Reference to Matthew 18:7</note>. 

From this comes that Platonic saying: "It is necessary that there be evils contrary to goods." Since evils cannot exist among the higher beings, they necessarily circle this lower region. No other remedy is given to us than to flee from here to that place as quickly as possible, by a certain most pure imitation of the divine life. For (as it is said in Hesiod): "The earth is full of evils, and the stretches of the sea are full" <note>original: *Plena malis tellus plena & sunt æquora ponti.* Reference to Hesiod’s Works and Days</note>.

But the Platonists do not think that even the celestial bodies are the purest of things, if they are compared to those things which exist above the heavens. For those things which are above the heavens surpass the celestial bodies in purity much more than those celestial bodies surpass the things placed beneath them. Therefore, even if it is not permitted to agree entirely with the <term>Manichaeans</term> <note>Followers of Manichaeism, a dualistic religion that viewed the material world as inherently evil and created by a dark power; Ficino clarifies he is not a heretic, even if he speaks harshly of the world.</note> regarding the world, let us at least be allowed to cry out against it along with them in this way:

> O most filthy world! You who stain and defile most of all those who try to embrace you more greedily and tightly. O most false, most deceitful, and most ungrateful world: which, as a whole—as Jesus says—is "set in malice," <note>original: "poſitus in maligno"; a reference to the First Epistle of John 5:19, "the whole world lieth in wickedness."</note> lies to them; it often deceives them, and it harms most greatly those who, above all others, place their faith, hope, love, and service in it. Like a certain eel, or rather a slippery snake, it glides through the palms of those clutching it too tightly more quickly than it can be squeezed; at the same time, flying into their faces, it bites immediately and flees; and though absent, a little later it destroys the one it left behind with its poisonous bite.

But lest certain speakers seem perhaps too bold or rather foolish, let us set aside these oratorical flourishes for the present. Let us bring into the open, with the brevity required for a letter, the reasons and the authorities we rely upon to hold these views concerning the filthy <term>mechanism of this lower world</term> <note>original: "immunda mundi huius inferioris machina"; a common Renaissance metaphor for the structure of the physical universe.</note>.

## The soul in the body sleeps: it dreams, it raves, it is sick.

<margin>e</margin>
We experience within ourselves, not only daily but almost every hour, that whenever some small vapor—somewhat thicker and more humid—exhaling from the lower parts of the body seeks the head and fills the passages of the brain, we are immediately weighed down by sleep and soon deluded in our dreams by images. We also experience sometimes that if a certain vapor of <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "bilis atre"; one of the four humors of ancient medicine, associated with the Greek term "melancholia."</note> (which the Greeks call melancholy) besieges and captures the citadel of the body, our queen—that is, <term>Reason</term> <note>original: "ratio"</note>—is immediately (so to speak) cast down headlong, and men are seized by manifest insanity. If a tiny smoke has such power within us—if such a slight motion changes us so much—how much more must we think that the celestial and immortal soul is changed from its state when, from the beginning, it falls in a moment from that purity in which it was created? That is, when it is shut in the dark prison of a terrestrial and dying body. Then (as the Platonists say) it is changed from its true state, for it is then weighed down not just by the single and customary smoke of some humor, but by all the new vapors of all the humors equally, and moreover by the unaccustomed mass of the humors and limbs themselves. Furthermore, it is submerged in that formless matter—which is the very opposite of the most beautiful form of the Mind—as if in the <term>River Lethe</term> <note>In Greek mythology, the river of forgetfulness in the underworld; here used as a metaphor for the soul forgetting its divine origins upon birth.</note>. Therefore, the Pythagoreans and Platonists believe that all that time which the sublime soul spends in the lowest body, our mind is tossed here and there, up and down, like a sick person with a certain perpetual restlessness. Nor do they think anything else: but that the soul is always drowsy and raving, and that the individual motions, actions, and passions of mortals are nothing other than the <term>vertigo</term> <note>original: "vertigines"; the dizziness or reeling sensation experienced by the sick.</note> of the ailing.

He synthesizes classical Greek thought (Euripides, Homer, Plato) with Biblical wisdom to argue that our physical existence is a mere shadow of the true, eternal reality.</meta>

# SIXTH

...the dreams of sleepers: the delusions of madmen: so that not without reason **Euripides** <note>A famous Greek playwright known for his tragedies; Ficino frequently cites him to bridge classical and Christian thought.</note> called this life the "shadow of a dream." Therefore, although everyone is deceived, those are usually less deceived who, meanwhile, sometimes—as happens occasionally in sleep—suspect and say to themselves: "Perhaps these things appearing to us now are not true. Perhaps at present we are dreaming." Whoever is so affected among dreamers is certainly to others as **Tiresias** <note>A blind prophet of Apollo in Thebes, famous for spending seven years as a woman and for his wisdom even in the afterlife.</note> is said by **Homer** to be among those in the underworld. He says, "He alone is wise. All the others flit about like shadows; indeed, they are shadows." Here the divine **David**, in an ecstasy of mind, exclaims: "Every man is a liar." <note>original: "Omnis homo mendax"; Psalm 116:11, suggesting that human perception without God is inherently false.</note> Here the most wise **Solomon**, having awakened and come to his senses a little before the others, cries out: "Vanity of vanities," says Ecclesiastes. 

> Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. <note>original: "Vanitas vanitatum & omnia vanitas"; Ecclesiastes 1:2.</note>

Here **Jeremiah** thus warns the foolish wise men. God saw that the thoughts of men, even of the wise, are vain. Here **Christ**, the master of life, says: "My kingdom is not of this world." <note>original: "non est in hoc mundo regnum meum"; John 18:36.</note> Christ himself, though he was the eternal king of all things—since all things were made through him and for him, and therefore he was appointed heir of all things from eternity—nevertheless, whatever things flow and fluctuate without any stability under the most rapid whirling of the heavens, and are confounded and utterly infected by a certain hostile mixture of opposites, such things, I say, Christ denied were his: as if such things do not truly exist, but falsely appear to us—namely to the sick, the sleeping, and the delirious—since these temporary things are by no means the things themselves, but rather merely shadows of things: namely, of eternal things. Whoever accepts images instead of the things themselves is, without a doubt, mocked by shadows and dreams, like those who are drunk, frantic, or sleeping. These people surely: 

> Wander obscurely through the shadows under the lonely night, 
> And through the empty halls of Dis and the vacant kingdoms. <note>A quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book VI, describing the journey through the Underworld; Ficino applies this to people living in the physical world.</note>

**Orpheus** says that **Plato** rules among the "people of dreams" in the underworld. The <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras; in this context, they believed the soul was "buried" in the body and that our world is a lower, darker realm.</note> however, specifically call the entire region below the moon "the underworld." Our Christ did not wish (as I judge) to be called similarly the king of dreams and delusions. Therefore, by the best right, rejecting the empty kingdoms of this world, he seems to resound in our ears thus: 

> O too-demented minds of mortals! 
> O blind hearts: where are you rushing? 
> Why do you tremble here so fearfully, frantic minds? 
> Why do you anxiously follow after things there? 
> Alas, miserable ones, do you not see? 
> An insane fury agitates you everywhere. 
> From this side, false shadows of evils terrify you. 
> From that side, vain shadows of goods snatch you away. 
> You are tossed about everywhere among playful spectacles and terrors. 
> Nor does the vain desire for good things solicit and fatigue your minds—inflamed by furies—any less than the fear of false things.

Indeed, there is but one medicine for so many and such great diseases: trust the divine doctor so that you may awaken thoroughly and always stay awake, or at least consider those who sleep to be sleeping. Therefore, rise now from such a deep sleep, you miserable ones. Rise, I say, happily from your unhappy sleep. Breathe at last, my children. Watch with me, my children; come to your senses now and be wise with me. So that you yourselves may also, according to your strength, eventually enjoy that same most happy light and truth which I also enjoy.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s philosophical argument that our sensory life is a dream-like state. After citing biblical and poetic authorities on the "vanity" of life, he now turns to his primary inspiration, Plato, specifically the famous Allegory of the Cave, to provide a structural explanation for why human beings mistake shadows for reality.</meta>

Or at least meanwhile, until you wake up: say to yourselves now and then while sleeping: "Perhaps these things that occur to us are not true. Perhaps we are dreaming." For in this way, your dreams—whether they seem good—will less deceive, inflame, and tire you; or if they appear bad, they will certainly frighten you less.

Things truly exist in the <term>invisible world</term> <note>In Platonic thought, the "invisible world" (mundus invisibilis) refers to the realm of eternal Forms or Ideas, which are more real than the physical objects we see.</note>; but in the visible world, there are only the shadows of things.

> <margin>o</margin> I think it would be worthwhile to now confirm the mysteries we related above using the very words of **Plato** himself, translated from the seventh book of the *Republic*. <note>original: "ex septimo de rep. libro"; this refers to one of the most famous passages in Western philosophy, the Allegory of the Cave.</note> Imagine, he says, a certain cave underground. In it are men raised from childhood, their necks and hands tied behind their backs and their feet bound to certain columns, so that none can move or see anything except what appears in their sight on the opposite side of the cave. Behind their backs, higher up, let a lamp be lit. And between the lamp and those who are bound, let many others walk and speak to one another, carrying in their hands various <term>simulacra</term> <note>Likenesses or models, such as puppets or statues.</note> of trees and animals. Those who are thus bound will therefore never see the reality of themselves or any of those other things we mentioned. Instead, they see only their own shadows or the shadows of others which, because of the fire lit behind them, are projected before their eyes onto the opposite wall of the cave. For this reason, they will think that they themselves are nothing other than their shadows, or that other things are nothing other than their shadows; nor will they judge the light itself to be anything other than that small reflected glimmer that appears there. But if one of those who are bound should happen to be released and suddenly forced to turn around and look at the lamp and the other things behind him, his vision will be blurred; he will immediately suffer pain. And because of the brightness, he will be unable to look at those things whose shadows he was seeing just moments before. And much more will this distress happen to him if he is suddenly dragged up out of the cave toward the celestial and divine light. Therefore, he must be led, not suddenly but gradually by suitable steps, from the shadows of things to the things themselves. Likewise, he must be led from the image of light to the light itself, so that he may see those things that are in the cave first in their reflections in the water before he looks at them directly. Again, for those things which are outside the cave with us, let him first look at night by the light of the Moon at their reflections in water likewise; then let him look at these earthly things themselves, and similarly at the celestial bodies in the heavens at night. Afterward, by day, let him look at the sun itself and the things seen under the sun—first in the water, then at the things themselves, and finally let him look up at the sun in the heavens. By this method above all, he clearly and easily discerns individual things and will come to think that he had been blind, deceived, and miserable when he was occupied with the small shadows of things while bound under that appearance. Therefore, as that cave is compared to this world which we call "visible," so is this world almost exactly compared to that which we call "invisible and divine." For here, souls are miserably enclosed in the darkness and blind prison of the dying body; they never see themselves or any other things in reality, nor the true sun, but rather only the shadows of themselves and others, and a certain faint image of the true sun...

they behold. For true minds, true things of any kind, and the true sun exist only in the **invisible world**; if I were to attempt to behold these things suddenly, without the suitable steps of education and discipline, we immediately grow dim-sighted and suffer pain. But once we have been led through the appropriate stages of morals, doctrines, and time, we discern clearly and judge those people to be blind and wretched who are deceived, occupied, and weighed down by the false shadows and images of this world.

Nevertheless, when the soul descends from the immense light of the invisible world into the dark body—which it must rule and move—it is overwhelmed by a new darkness contrary to its own nature and is compelled to go blind, to hallucinate, and to stumble for a long time. Add to this that, because of this sudden and massive change for the worse, it is forced to be "sick" for a long duration. It is affected almost like those who, due to madness, sleep, or drunkenness, are mocked and vexed by false images. Or certainly, its condition is like someone who is suddenly plunged from the light of the sun into that cave we described. He will be so overwhelmed by the new darkness that he will be able to discern those shadows we mentioned under the cave’s tiny light only with difficulty, or not at all. Furthermore, because of that sudden change for the worse, he will fall into various diseases of both the senses and the body. Thus far **Plato**.

Therefore, let mortals rejoice—let them rejoice far too blindly and without envy—when on the stage they take on the roles of the rich, even if they themselves are poor, or when they represent the majesty of kings though they are but slaves. Let them also grieve in vain, but let them not grieve too much without a certain mercy, when in a tragedy they are commanded to perform the gestures of the wretched and the wailing, and to mimic the movements of the sick, even though they are perhaps not otherwise miserable. 

We, however, if we considered those people truly wretched and deceived who are so moved by a play that they exult or lament as if they were in the midst of true goods or evils, then we must judge all mortals to be much more vain and wretched. For mortals, lulled by the deepest sleep, accept shadowy <term>simulacra</term> <note>Likenesses or phantom images.</note> of goods or evils as if they were real. This is especially true since, even if they briefly and falsely rejoice in fleeting "goods," they truly grieve and are tormented for a very long time by "evils" that are false and shifting—which is a truly miserable thing. And they deserve this, since they allow themselves to be so foolish as to think this anxious dwelling-place of the celestial and immortal soul, located in the earthly region of death, is "true life." Yet they see clearly that this life begins immediately with weeping and crying, and is finished thereafter with perpetual complaint and extreme misery. 

On the contrary, when the immortal soul is released from the mortal body and wakes up, people think it is undergoing "death"—a belief that is far too false. For only then, once "frequent death" has itself died, does the true and eternal life rise again. For this reason, and not without cause, among the **Gymnosophists** <note>original: "gymnosophistas"; literally "naked wise men," referring to ancient Indian philosophers known for their asceticism and wisdom.</note> (the philosophers of the Indians) and even among the Getae (the peoples of Thrace), they used to mourn at births; for...

<meta>This page concludes Ficino’s commentary on the soul’s journey and the errors of earthly life, transitioning into a celebratory piece where he personifies the city of Florence. Having previously discussed the soul's adjustment to the light of truth, he now addresses the "homecoming" of Dante Alighieri through Cristoforo Landini’s 1481 commentary.</meta>
