<f>

...they were lamented; indeed, funerals were festive and celebrated with play and song as if they were sacred rites. This is indeed seen to be confirmed by the philosophers Hegesias <note>original: Hegesia; a Cyrenaic philosopher nicknamed "The Death-Persuader" because he argued that life's pains outweigh its pleasures</note> and Plotinus, who believe it is best for minds not to enter a dying body in the first place, or next best, to exit it immediately after having entered.

But of these matters, more elsewhere. Meanwhile, another error approaches, and then another. For mortals either too foolishly believe this anxious and laborious pilgrimage to be their true homeland, or at the very least—even if they have learned they are pilgrims—they hope that they might occasionally find some rest during the journey itself. Yet they could and should be sufficiently warned by the most rapacious rotation of the heavens that they cannot rest for even a single moment under that swiftest celestial course, since the machine of the world itself, by its nature, never possesses a single moment of rest. 

Therefore, let miserable mortals now recognize how much they wander from the truth and let them cease their error. For in doing so, they will undoubtedly cease their labor. Let them begin at some point—indeed, as soon as possible—to live wisely; for only then will they truly begin to live happily. Farewell. December 3, 1480.

### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine imagines Florence congratulating Dante through the pious work of Cristoforo Landini: now revived, restored to his homeland, and crowned.

Florence, long mournful but at last joyful, congratulates her Dante Alighieri, who after nearly two centuries is now revived, restored to his fatherland, and finally crowned. You once prophesied, my Dante, while settled in exile, that perhaps a time would come when piety, overcoming impiety, would happily return you to your homeland and crown you with the wreaths of Apollo in the exalted temple of John the Baptist <note>original: Baptiste Ioannis aede; referring to the Florence Baptistery where Dante hoped to be crowned poet laureate</note>. That omen was not in vain, for the parents of wisdom have taught it so. 

Indeed, recently your father Apollo, pitying my long weeping and your lengthy exile, commanded Mercury to glide entirely into the mind of the divine seer Cristoforo Landini <note>original: Xpofori Landini; the humanist scholar whose commentary on Dante was a major intellectual event in 1481</note>. Assuming the features of Landini, Mercury first woke you from sleep with his life-giving wand; then, lifting you on the rowing of his wings, he brought you into the Florentine limbs; and finally, he bound your temples with the laurel of Phoebus Apollo. Today, at last, the command of Phoebus, the pious work of Mercury and Landini, the prophecy of Dante, and the prayer of Florence have been divinely fulfilled. 

You have come at last, with Minerva <note>Goddess of wisdom</note> showing the way and Mercury as the guide of the journey, accompanied by a most brilliant throng of all the poets. Finally, as you entered, the Graces received you happily. The Muses <note>original: Pierides</note> and the nymphs gave you embraces and kisses. You have come at last, in the manner expected by a parent. Piety has conquered the hard journey <note>A reference to Virgil’s *Aeneid*: "Vicit iter durum pietas"</note>; I am permitted to look upon your face, my son, and to hear and return your familiar voice. So indeed I gathered in my mind and thought it would be, counting the times; nor did my care deceive me. 

O, how much more beautiful and blessed do I receive you now, sweet son, than when I lost you! That earlier mortal face of yours has been transformed into one immortal and divine. The night of your Florence has been turned into day. All the sorrow of your Florentines has been turned into joy. Rejoice, all of you, and exult, most happy citizens, for whom a twin Sun <note>The literal sun and the "sun" of Dante’s genius</note> now marvelously rises instead of one—not with scorching flames, but with doubled rays. Today, for our happiness, heaven itself...

### THE END OF THE SIXTH BOOK.
### Preface to the Seventh Book.
### Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Berlinghieri, son of Niccolo, most distinguished in letters and character, sends greetings.

<margin>1</margin> The seventh book of our letters has as its opening chapter a letter discussing the care of the health of scholars. Since it begins its journey from that letter—as if from the best and greatest of all—it follows most willingly wherever that letter leads. In the present moment, it leads to that man for whom the <term>Academy</term> <note>the Platonic Academy of Florence, the circle of scholars led by Ficino</note> especially desires prosperous health. Greetings then, my excellent Francesco. Greetings as many times as not only here, but as all the books of my letters command friends to be well. But receive this greeting in such a way that you believe you have received it not from Marsilio alone, but from the entire Academy, which is most fond of you. All things among us are held in common, after the manner of the <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>followers of Pythagoras, known for their communal lifestyle and belief that "friends hold all things in common"</note>. What the Academy itself wants, everyone wants. What individuals desire, the Academy also greatly desires. Nor should this seem a wonder. For we are all one in Him who is, in truth, the only One. We all stand in Him who alone remains through His own power; we all love one another in Him who alone is to be loved for His own sake—He for whose sake alone individuals are lovable, and for whose grace alone they are to be loved. Only those who love each other in this One seem to be able to cry out together with the Prophet: *Oh, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity!* <note>Psalm 133:1</note>

### Marsilio Ficino to the reader, sends greetings.

<margin>p</margin> I was just now assigning to this seventh book a lead letter intended to discuss the health of scholars. This piece, however, grew so much thereafter that it no longer wished to be the head of such a small body, but desired to be an entire body of its own, separate from the rest. Therefore, by a better plan, it has now withdrawn. It has happily grown into the book *On Life* <note>original: "In librum de vita"; referring to Ficino's famous three-part treatise on health, longevity, and astral influences on scholars</note>.

-> Wisdom comes from God alone. <-

# BOOK

**Friend, return like for like at least**, for since I have written hardly anything, you should hardly read it. Yet whatever these writings are, read them anyway, however you read them. Indeed, in these days I have often taken up the pen with the intention of thinking many things to a man, but writing few. But it suddenly occurred to me that I would be writing in vain to a man who would not read. Finally, I preferred to speak in vain than to say nothing at all. Listen, then. There are many kinds of fictions among the poets. But why do I interrupt a pious man with these trifles of mine, while he is commenting on the *Soliloquies* of Augustine <note>A work by St. Augustine written as an inner dialogue between himself and Reason</note> and speaking with God alone? Letting go of the poetic mask, then, I only advise this for the present: remember that when we form speech, it is not so much the tongue (which is moved from elsewhere) that is accustomed to speak, as the mind itself, which both moves the tongue and distinguishes the voices. And it forms words according to its judgment as a model of itself. Now, what the tongue is to the mind, the religious mind is almost that to God. Therefore, it is not so much your mind speaking to God now, as God speaking to you through your mind. Wherefore, my John, when you think you are speaking to God, in truth you are then hearing God. Remember, therefore, that you frequently hear the divine majesty. And by a life most wisely established, declare to us and (as you have begun) confirm that you, as a disciple, have heard Divine Wisdom itself. I wanted here (as you see) at this third hour of the day <note>About 9:00 AM in the medieval system of counting hours from sunrise</note> to put an end to the letter, so that I might not disturb that divine *Soliloquy* of yours any longer. But as soon as I had set down the pen, it came back to my mind that it is not becoming to spit out a completely fasting letter from a completely fasting stomach <note>original: "stomachus"; Ficino frequently makes puns regarding his physical health and his "disposition" or "stomach"</note>. But rather let my heart pour forth a good word <note>original: "eructet cor meum verbum bonum"; a reference to Psalm 45:1</note>. A good one indeed (as I think), if I briefly confirm that earlier opinion about the "highest good." All sacred writings among both the Jews and the Christians cry out that wisdom cannot be learned unless God is the teacher. Therefore, it must be sought from Him alone by faith, asked for by hope, and knocked for by charity. When our Plato <note>Ficino famously sought to reconcile Platonic philosophy with Christian theology</note> noticed this, not trusting in his own studies, he often asked for wisdom from God alone in his daily prayers. In this matter, Orpheus <note>The legendary Greek poet whom the Neoplatonists viewed as a theological authority</note> told a most beautiful myth when he sang that wisdom was born from the head of supreme Jupiter alone. He sang also that the Muses have their beginning from Jupiter; "all things are full of Jupiter" <note>original: "Iovis omnia plena"; a famous line from Virgil’s Eclogues, originally from the Greek poet Aratus</note>. But if you were able to obtain this wisdom from everyone, perhaps you would also—if not perfectly, then at least conveniently—obtain it from that friend of yours <note>Ficino refers to himself</note>. But by what means will you obtain wisdom from one whose mind is always unhealthy because his body is never healthy? And lately, when he labored not a little from the weakness first of the soul, then of the stomach, and finally of all his limbs, he changed his sky (though not his mind) <note>A play on a famous line by the Roman poet Horace: "They change their sky, not their soul, who run across the sea." Ficino suggests he moved to find better air for his health but remains the same person</note>. And since he seeks strength from the air—the weakest of the elements and of all things—he has deservedly sought it in vain so far. But you, meanwhile, cry out along with your Aurelius <note>Saint Augustine, whose full name was Aurelius Augustinus</note>:

> O almighty God, when our strength is You Yourself, then alone is it truly strength; but when it is our own, it is weakness.

I, too, shall finally do the same.

<summary>Marsilio Ficino writes to his friend John regarding the nature of prayer and divine wisdom, arguing that wisdom is a gift from God rather than a human achievement. He blends Christian thought (Augustine) with classical mythology (Orpheus and Plato) while reflecting on his own poor physical health.</summary>

->Where wisdom is greater, speech is shorter.<-

Marsilio Ficino to Lord <note>Latin: "D." for Dominus, a title of respect</note> Bernardo Bembo of Venice, health.

<margin>f</margin>Those who have been silent for a long time are usually accustomed, when they finally break their long-lasting silence, to burst forth more abundantly; and, as if they have been in labor for a long time, they finally give birth to some larger offspring of thought. But your Marsilio, on the contrary, does not conceive longer things due to a long time of silence. For the longer he thinks to himself in silence, the more sharply he discerns that it is better for us to be silent than to speak—and that there are very few things that we either know how to express worthily, or ought to express honestly, or are able to express safely. Therefore, I will respond to your [letters] very briefly for the present. First, indeed, I rejoice in your prosperity—or rather ours. I wish you happiness. Next, I give great thanks for the little vessel of <term>Theriac</term> <note>original: "Tyriace"; a famous ancient medical concoction used as a universal antidote and tonic</note> you sent; certainly, I shall give even greater thanks when you send a large jar instead of a little vessel. Although I confess that I have received something great even in this healthy little vessel, not only from <term>Apollo</term> <note>The god of healing and medicine</note> himself but from you as well. Finally, regarding the <term>Alcinous</term> <note>Refers to a manuscript of the *Epitome of Platonism* by Alcinous, a standard textbook of the era</note> you seek: know that he is currently staying in the country at the home of our friend Cavalcanti. As soon as he returns to us, he will return to you (as is right).

->Even if one is absent from friends in letters at times, never is one absent in spirit.<-

Marsilio Ficino and Giorgio Antonio Vespucci <note>A scholar and uncle of the explorer Amerigo Vespucci</note> to Giovanni Battista Boninsegni, health.

<margin>p</margin>Plato, the divine conciliator of our friendship—or rather of our close bond—has long commanded that we should never wish to be absent from our friend Boninsegni. Since he has always wanted us to be with you, we have often prepared ourselves to write so that we might satisfy both Plato and our bond to the best of our strength. But as often as we took up the pen, that conciliator of ours restrained us, clearly suggesting that we should not interrupt Boninsegni with our letters while he is continually speaking with him [Plato]. What then shall we do while our Plato both commands and forbids us at the same time? Certainly, so that we may fulfill whatever he commands, we shall always speak to your soul with our own soul. And at the same time, so that we may avoid whatever he forbids, we shall remain silent with our mouth and pen. But let us be allowed now, at least for a little while, to interrupt—with Plato’s permission, of course—while we come from Athens to you, as you reside in his very <term>Academy</term> <note>Likely referring to the Medici villa at Careggi where the Platonic Academy met</note> in the countryside, and we greet you in the name of all Platonists. Furthermore, we commend ourselves to your father Roberto, the distinguished presiding official there.

...a friend doesn't care at all. On the contrary, what is even more wonderful and even more wretched is that, like a second Pamphilus <note>A character name from Roman comedy, often used to represent a typical young lover</note>, out of a love for others, he hates himself like a Timon <note>A reference to Timon of Athens, the legendary misanthrope who withdrew from human society</note>. Therefore, while toward others he is sweeter than Venus herself, toward himself he is fiercer than Mars and harsher than Saturn. 

I have been reproaching him for a long time, though in vain: "Where are you fleeing, wretched Narcissus? You flee yourself. To follow a madman, you flee yourself more swiftly as you follow someone else who flees you. You will never be able to catch up when you have once lost yourself. Alas, whom are you losing, insane Narcissus? You are losing yourself entirely to pursue a shadow—certainly a fleeting shadow which you, wretch, cannot embrace. But since love usually transfers the lover into the beloved: you, Narcissus, the lover of a shadow, will soon be turned into a shadow." Thus I often speak to him. You too, my Bernardo, should similarly advise him either with words or letters.

### On the best way of living.
#### Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Antonio Ivani of Sarzana, sends greetings.

<margin>r</margin>Your letter was delivered to me, dearest Ivani, in which you collect many things in few words regarding the best way of living. Indeed, I think you judge that way of living to be best which is far removed from the "dead life" by which the mortal lives and, in a way, the immortal dies—specifically as long as the heavenly soul is not only joined by nature to the earthly body from the beginning, but is also enslaved to it daily by affection. From this it follows that only he truly lives who lives at the furthest possible distance from the false affection of this life. How false and deceptive this life is, this Platonic letter will discuss with you, which I wrote to Loterio Neroni in previous months and have now also gladly transcribed for you. Farewell.

### An excuse for when a friend is not greeted.
#### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his one and only friend, sends greetings.

<margin>r</margin>To live in the country, Giovanni: this autumn I know indeed with what affection you do so, but I do not know well enough for what reason I wished to. I was afraid, however, that for the first time I might want what you do not. Therefore, leaving for the countryside, as if already a rustic, I did not say "Friend, farewell" <note>Latin: *vale*, which means both "be well" and "goodbye"</note>. Lest you, contrary to everything, should respond with something less good—perhaps that you might not "fare well" <note>original: "ne valeas"; Ficino is playing on the dual meaning of the word as a greeting and a wish for health/strength</note>. For you know that I am sometimes (as they say commonly) superstitious about omens. I would hardly have hoped that I could ever fare well once the heroes <note>Refers to the *daemones* or protective spirits in Platonic thought</note> prohibited "faring well" even once. Be well. And permit me to stay in the country for a few more days for the sake of stronger health.

### The studies of agriculture and literature are happily joined together.
#### Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, sends greetings.

<margin>c</margin>When today at sunrise I sought the highest peaks of the ancient mountain—the mountain, I say, of Vecchio, which <term>Cosimo</term> <note>Cosimo de' Medici "the Elder" (1389–1464), Lorenzo's grandfather and Ficino's patron</note> himself entrusted to his Marsilio to be cultivated—and while wandering here and there in this forest, I was contemplating the <term>Careggi palaces</term> <note>The Medici villa at Careggi, where Ficino's Platonic Academy met</note>, it suddenly came to mind that the feast day of <term>Cosmas and Damian</term> <note>The patron saints of the Medici family, traditionally celebrated on September 27th</note> has already dawned, which has been celebrated every year by Cosimo himself and his sons and grandsons. Here, indeed, I could not help but grieve...

...as I looked out and saw no citizens flocking to the Cosmic <note>A pun on the name of Cosimo de' Medici and the Greek word 'kosmos' (order/world). Ficino is likely referring to the feast day of Saint Cosmas, the patron saint of the Medici family</note> solemnities, as is usually done. When suddenly that Jovian Cosimo <note>Cosimo de' Medici 'the Elder' (1389–1464), Ficino’s late patron, described here with the majesty of Jupiter</note>—to whom Jupiter, having now reconciled Juno, gave civil power without end—breathing favorably upon us from a high oak tree, consoled us, who were grieving, with such oracles as these:

"My Marsilio," he said, "pious Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo 'the Magnificent' de' Medici, Cosimo's grandson</note> is now restoring my sacred urban rites. But you, if you obey me, will soon restore these same rites for us here in the woods in a rustic fashion. And do not be ashamed to receive as guests those elder and Saturnian <note>Associated with the god Saturn, representing both agriculture and deep, melancholic contemplation</note> farmers of mine under the peak of this mountain in the little Academy <note>original: *achademiola*; Ficino's preferred name for his villa at Careggi</note> sacred to Phoebus <note>Apollo, the god of light and wisdom</note>. Since today (as astronomy teaches you)—look up now, do you not see?—today Saturn and Phoebus are joined in the heavens. This, Marsilio, is our will: just as it happens in heaven today, so let it be on earth, so that Apollonian things may now be joined with Saturnian things in both places. O most happy human race, if the rustic pipe of Saturn were to harmonize with the urban lyre <note>original: *cythare*</note> of Phoebus, and the gifts of both gods were always joined among us! These things are mixed in heaven (as you see) among the gods today. You too shall always mix them among men on earth. Farewell."

These things are almost exactly as I tell them, magnanimous Lorenzo. Thus I first mourned with myself as I remembered. Thus afterward Cosimo seemed both to console and to advise me. Thus at last I prepared an Apollonian—that is, philosophical—banquet for the Saturnian men—that is, your elder farmers. And indeed, I did not do this without the Delphic lyre <note>The lyre of Apollo, which Ficino famously played during his philosophical sessions</note>. And whatever Cosmic solemnities we could manage according to the time, place, and means, we celebrated joyfully and happily in the little Academy of the Saturnian mountain. 

Why all this? So that, warned by the Cosmic oracles, we might remember (if we wish to live happily) to put aside or pause other matters as much as possible, and worship both Phoebus and Saturnian Pan <note>The god of the wild and shepherds</note> together. Namely, all rustic things must be dedicated daily to the Muses, and the Muses in turn must very often be moved from urban business to the fields of Ceres <note>Goddess of the harvest</note> and the hills of Bacchus <note>God of wine</note>. Farewell happily.

### An Invitation to Country Life.
#### Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend.

<margin>a</margin> I would think you lighter than any breeze if you yourself thought that I had withdrawn from the city to the hills of Careggi <note>The site of the Medici villa where Ficino lived and worked</note> moved by some light breeze, whether in the past summer or this present autumn. But far be it from me to think him light in any way, who is heavier <note>In the sense of being serious, grave, or stubborn</note> even than rocks. Truly, since I judged not without reason that it would be much better for you to ascend the mountain here to me than for me to descend from the mountain to you in these times, I have often beseeched Apollo <note>original: *appollineum*</note> that he might now dictate to our lyre those songs of Orpheus and Amphion <note>Mythical musicians whose music was so powerful it could move trees and stones</note> with which they once moved oaks and stones, so that I might draw you—who are, in my judgment, like a tree or a stone—to me. 

Phoebus replied: "Marsilio, you are greatly mistaken. For Giovanni is not made of wood or stone as you suppose. Otherwise (believe me), your lyre <note>original: *Cythara*</note> would have carried him away long ago. Giovanni, I say, is not made of stone; rather, he is made of iron!"

->Friendship is between equals and is free.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Alberto Liseo of Verona <note>Alberto Liseo was a Veronese humanist and close correspondent of Ficino</note>, sends greetings.

You remember how, in days past, near the church of Saint John <note>Likely the Baptistery of San Giovanni in Florence</note>, while I was speaking about you and a certain Jacob in the presence of Riccardo the Theologian, I compared you both to myself and to each other with these words: "My Riccardo," I said, "I am placed in the middle as Air, between Alberto as Fire and Jacob as Earth." And if then, Alberto, I seemed to utter those words in a joking manner after the Socratic custom <note>The Socratic method often used irony and playful analogies to reveal deeper truths</note>, they nonetheless contain no less power than fire, and no less weight than earth. As for the other things comprised within this enigma, you will interpret them well enough by your own judgment. One thing, however, I wish to interpret myself at present: namely, that just as much as fire surpasses earth, by so much in dignity have I placed the fiery man before the earthly one. Again, as much as air agrees more with fire than with earth, so much was it signified that a fiery man is loved more ardently by me than an earthly man. You, therefore, as a logician, will now clearly conclude: if honor and love produce trust, to which of you two I would rather wish to keep my faith. 

Add also another argument besides: In what way is it likely that I, a follower of Platonic philosophy, ever thought to violate my trust toward you—to whose trust, meanwhile (as you yourself will not deny), I was committing all my affairs, and into the future (as you clearly perceived) I had decided to commit them? Since these things are so, what then was the cause that in the Chapel of Novoli <note>The *Sacello Nouolano* refers to a church or chapel in Novoli, a district of Florence</note>, now one and then another minister of the sacred rites could be under me rather than my own Alberto? At first, I thought some earthly demon <note>term: *demon* (original: *demon*). In the Platonic tradition, a *daemon* is a spirit or intermediary power, not necessarily "demonic" in the modern sense, but here a disruptive one</note>, envying our celestial friendship, had thrown into disorder that ministry established between us. For which reason, fleeing suddenly to the deities of the learned, I implored Minerva and Apollo that she might pierce that Pythonic demon <note>A reference to the monstrous serpent Python slain by Apollo; here used to describe a divisive or deceptive spirit</note> with her spear, and he with his arrows. 

But then, that common guardian spirit <note>term: *genius*. A personal protective spirit assigned to a person at birth</note> of mine and yours corrected me in my error. "No demon, Marsilio," he said, "has tried to separate you from Alberto. On the contrary, you yourselves, through some ignorance, were in a way severing what I declare to be a single work of heaven. Know that Saturn, the ruler of Aquarius, has infused almost a single spirit into both of you, since you were both born with Aquarius rising <note>An astrological reference indicating they share the same 'Ascendant,' making them kindred spirits</note>, and from this he has given you a celestial friendship without end." Indeed...

...what Saturn <note>The Roman god identified with the Greek Cronus; in astrology, Saturn is the planet of depth, stability, time, and melancholy. Ficino often viewed his own temperament as Saturnian</note>, the highest and most stable of all the planets, constructs, no one (as the astronomers say) either dares to destroy or even can. Therefore, since heaven willed you to be friends, it also established that you should always be equal among yourselves. But you, as if ignorant of this heavenly mystery, were establishing a certain commerce between you in which one of you would seem to be under the other, as if you were to be unequal in the future. But let disparity be far away from heavenly friendship (at heaven's command). Let domination and servitude be far off. Rather, let friends always be equals among themselves and be free; let them love each other mutually, equally, and freely. This the Genius <note>A personal guiding spirit or "daimon" believed in antiquity to oversee an individual's destiny</note> says. You indeed, my most beloved Alberto, farewell happily. Remember that the service which did not please the higher powers was rightly not permitted to us: and the mystery, in turn, which pleases them, ought also to please us entirely. October 20, 1481. 
From the estate at Careggi <note>The Villa di Careggi was the Medici family's country estate near Florence where Ficino’s Platonic Academy met</note>.

### On the Three Graces and the Genius.

->Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous Lorenzo de’ Medici the younger <note original="Laurentio medici iuniori">This likely refers to Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici, a cousin of Lorenzo the Magnificent, for whom Ficino often acted as a tutor and mentor</note>, sends greetings.<-

<margin>q</margin>As often as I take up my pen in these times, magnanimous Lorenzo—which I do indeed daily to write to you—so often I suddenly seem to myself to have become quite productive and I bring forth much. But truly, as soon as I have written only these two words ("Marsilio to Lorenzo"), I, the same man who just now as if most fertile was laboring with many thoughts, soon, as if having become entirely sterile, give birth to nothing. Hence, I often stand amazed and, being out of my mind, I accuse the higher powers of being envious and greedy toward me. For I see that both by nature and by art, shortly before I was about to write to you, I was abundantly supplied; but shortly after, when actually writing, I see that this could not be inhibited by anything else than by the higher powers. Wherefore, I frequently (as I said) accuse them: sometimes as if they were envious, clearly because they perhaps envy heavenly friendship and pleasure here on earth; and sometimes as if they were greedy, because where both nature and art are so prodigal, there the divine power seems in a way (if it is right to say) stingy.

**Minerva.** Finally, Minerva <note>The goddess of wisdom and strategic war; for Ficino, she represents the divine intellect that guides the philosopher</note>, the leader of philosophers, so that I would not be sterile to you any longer nor sin so gravely against the deities, said: "Do not impiously accuse the heavenly beings, who meanwhile, in turn, accuse and condemn you for your unjust rashness. You do not know, impious one. You do not know that nothing is ever either commanded or prohibited by the higher powers without the highest reason. Learn, therefore, by what reason they now often forbid you (by my brief teaching) to write to Medici in these words (namely: Marsilio to Lorenzo)."

### The Three Graces and the Three Planets.

<margin>p</margin>In the beginning, those whom the poets among us paint as the three Graces <note>The Charities: Aglaia (Splendor), Euphrosyne (Mirth), and Thalia (Abundance). Ficino interprets them here as planetary harmonies</note>, like three girls embracing one another; there are three planets especially among the higher beings: Mercury, Jupiter (that is, a certain beneficial disposition of Jupiter), and Phoebus [the Sun] and Venus, companions mutually and favorably to each other in the heavenly circuit...

The names of the Graces—namely Greenness, Light, and Joy—suit those same stars <note>Ficino is linking the mythological Three Graces (Aglaia, Euphrosyne, and Thalia) to specific planetary influences</note> most aptly. These stars, when thus disposed among the heavenly bodies, especially favor human genius. Therefore, they are called the Graces not of just any animals, but of humans alone; nor are they truly the handmaidens of Venus <note>The goddess of love and beauty</note>, but of Minerva <note>The goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare; Ficino suggests the Graces serve the intellect rather than just physical beauty</note>. If you should ever hear that Jupiter is the first of the Graces, do not understand it as Jupiter himself so much as "Jovian Mercury"—that is, Mercury aided by some aspect or other gift of Jupiter. For Jovian Mercury, by his vital and prompt mobility, urges you to investigate things themselves constantly. But the Sun, through discovery, reveals everything to you who seek by his light. Finally, Venus always adorns whatever has been discovered with her most pleasing beauty.

->The Genius—that is, the guiding spirit of the mind—proceeds from the three Graces.<-

Therefore, these planets, by a certain common consent among themselves, immediately 
<margin>the</margin> distribute various genii <note>plural of genius; a personal guiding spirit</note>—that is, leaders of the mind, or spirits—to various people at their very birth, 
<margin>region</margin> accordingly as they look upon those being born daily from one region of the sky or another. It is placed within your own free will (for the most part) to follow these spirits as leaders more or less closely. But if the planets look upon any persons from the exact same region of the heavens and in a similar way, they bestow upon them the same or certainly a very similar Genius. Where indeed the same or a similar Genius presides, the same or a similar inclination follows that Genius. Here there is a similar mind and a single will; and even if two living beings are seen, nevertheless inside there is only one man. Therefore, Marsilio <note>Ficino refers to himself in the third person here, recounting a vision or inner dialogue with Minerva</note>, cease now to sin against the gods, or rather against yourself. Recognize at last your own birth and that of the Medici. You will recognize immediately that Jovian Mercury, Apollo, and Venus looked upon both of you as you were born from the exact same part of heaven—namely the Ninth House, 
<margin>B</margin> which astronomers call the house of faith, religion, genius, and wisdom, and the "Joy of Phoebus" <note>In traditional astrology, the 9th house is the place where the Sun (Phoebus/Apollo) is said to find its "Joy" or greatest strength</note>. From this it follows that not only a similar, but even one and the same Genius was granted to both from that place: namely, an Apollonian spirit. Since Apollo rejoices in the ninth dwelling of the heavens, he sends down Apollonian genii to men from there. From the number of these spirits, Apollo himself placed one in charge of you, with Venus and Mercury consenting. Hence a single mind followed in you both. To this also a single will betook itself on both sides. If all these individual things are one, the man is also one in spirit; lest by chance you should further separate with words those whom heaven and reason have joined in reality, remember that as often as you write to your Medici, it is necessary to address it thus: (*Marsilio to his own Marsilio, greetings* <note>original: "Marsilius Marsilio.S." — The OCR "Narfilio" is a typo for "Marsilio". Ficino is arguing that since he and Lorenzo are one soul, he is essentially writing to himself</note>). And thus at last, with the powers above breathing upon you, the vein of discovery will flow most abundantly for you. Thus far spoke Minerva.

Thus indeed, my friend and "other self" <note>original: "alter ego"</note>, it has often happened to me in these times (as I was saying). Thus I consulted Minerva, that leader of philosophers. And I myself will always ensure hereafter that I act as she advised, so that discovery does not dry up for us. Fare you well. But why did I just now say "Farewell," as if one were departing from another? Nay, let them fare well—or rather, let them fare ill—all those who seek discord between us...

->A Fable.<-

->The divine race is nourished only by divine food<-

### Marsilio Ficino on the Fable: What it is, from whence it is born, and where it leads.

<margin>v</margin> Once, while Venus was gathering various flowers and fruits in the Pythian gardens of Apollo, Mercury, wounded by love, pursued her. At last, with Apollo acting as both his witness and guide, he successfully caught her beneath a certain Laurel tree and knew her, to the greatest pleasure of them both. From their union was born a boy, exceptionally clever and handsome. In him, anyone could easily recognize the piercing perception of his father Mercury, the pleasing charm of his mother Venus, and the splendor of Apollo. Therefore, his patron Apollo named him "Apologue" <note>A fable or allegorical story. Ficino provides a mythical "etymology" for the literary genre.</note> after the surname of his father Mercury, whom they call "the long-speaker." <note>original: "superflongum." This is a play on Mercury as the god of speech (Logos) and the length of narratives.</note> Apollo ordered him, as he ran about everywhere, to be as useful to the human race through a certain healthy delight as his brother Cupid was harmful through the hook of noxious pleasure. 

And so, being ignorant of the surroundings, while the Apologue was wandering outside the Pythian gardens in the nearby woods, he happened upon some shepherds. They, being wonderfully delighted by the boy’s divine form and character, kept him with them for a long time. They fed the refined Apologue with rustic foods—that is, with acorns and chestnuts and other things of that sort. For this reason, his form eventually changed, and he would have turned from a refined city-dweller into a coarse rustic, had his patron Apollo not recently stretched out a propitious hand and successfully led him back from the woods to the Pythian gardens (which the Florentines today call the Pinti). <note>A reference to the Borgo Pinti area in Florence, where scholarly gardens were located.</note> The Fable teaches this: the divine race grows only on divine nourishment.

### A philosopher ought to avoid three things above all: Lust, Avarice, and Ambition.

->A Fable.<-

<margin>m</margin> Minerva, whom the ancient sages call Wisdom, <note>original: "Sophia"</note> when she realized she had been born from the head of Jupiter alone, considered this a divine work. Thinking that she, being born from the head alone, should also give birth, she prayed to her father—and finally won him over—that she too, as a rival to her parent, might give birth from her head at least once. She gave birth to a daughter who was very similar to her grandfather Jupiter and her mother Minerva. Indeed, as soon as she was born, she displayed a certain grandfatherly equity in her mind, and dignity in her face and her whole body. Furthermore, she reflected both the mother's strength and her modesty in her mind and gestures. Her grandfather Jupiter wished her to be named "Philosophy" after her mother, Wisdom. 

He decreed to Philosophy that just as she had her origin from Wisdom (who is the daughter of the highest head of all things), so she should always seek the highest heads <note>or "sources"</note> of things, setting aside the low plants of the world. He commanded that she should never have any commerce with the "inferior Venus" <note>Physical lust or earthly desire, as opposed to "Celestial Venus," which is the love of divine beauty</note> or her poisonous son, Desire. Otherwise, eternal Philosophy would immediately turn into a temporary "love of baubles," <note>original: "philocalia," literally a love of [physical] beauty, used here disparagingly to mean superficiality.</note> both in reality and in name. He added that she should all the more...

### Apologue. The impure never attain the Muses or the Graces, but rather magpies and furies.

<margin>o</margin> Orpheus, having once entered the Delphic groves to consult the oracle, immediately encountered Apollo, as if he had already been purified. Indeed, when he saw at the right hand of Apollo the divinity of the Muses and the three Graces accompanying him closely, but on the left, some distance away, magpies <note>original: "picas." In classical lore, the Pierides were sisters who challenged the Muses, lost, and were turned into magpies—symbols of mindless chatter and false art.</note> and furies following him, he exclaimed in great wonder: "O, how different and how adverse are the armies that follow this leader!" "But do not wonder, O poet," said Phoebus <note>Another name for Apollo, the god of light and prophecy.</note>. "Truly, many sacrifice to me every day so that they may obtain from me the gifts of the Muses and the Graces. Therefore, whoever performs the sacred rites with pure hands receives the Muses and the Graces from us freely. But whoever dares to touch the sacred things with polluted hands brings back, against their will, only magpies and furies."

### Apologue. Power without wisdom does not reign.

<margin>p</margin> When Prometheus <note>The Titan who stole fire from the gods; in this context, he represents the human intellect seeking divine secrets.</note> had ascended into heaven and there had learned many mysteries from Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus, the king of the gods.</note> himself, the author of all things, he humbly asked about this one thing with great curiosity: for what reason had Jove, from the very beginning of things, established the Sun and Mercury to be such close and constant companions to one another in their heavenly circuit, above all other planets? Jupiter responded: "So that whoever sees the Sun, the lord of the stars, without the wise Mercury, may clearly understand that he walks nowhere in heaven; and that on earth, power <term>potentia</term> <note>Represented by the Sun.</note> ought never to be granted without wisdom <term>sapientia</term> <note>Represented by Mercury.</note>, nor, if granted, can it reign for long."

### Apologue. On the translation of the book on love sent by Alamanno Donato to Lorenzo de' Medici.

<margin>c</margin> When Alamanno <note>Alamanno Donato, a Florentine scholar and diplomat who translated Ficino's *De Amore* from Latin into Italian.</note> was recently walking among the laurels (as is his habit), he frequently encountered Cupid flying about the laurels, and at last he caught him. Then the pious youth, gently handling the tender boy with light hands, soothed him; he adorned the god, now clearly recognized, with wreaths and flowers. And so, while adorning him, he asked: "What new breeze, handsome Cupid, has directed your wings here? Paphos and Idalium are yours, as is high Cythera." <note>Places sacred to Venus, Cupid's mother.</note> Then, sighing, the boy said: "Alas, for a long time now I have been anxiously seeking my mother everywhere. Neither Paphos nor Idalium returns my mother to me, nor does high Cythera. However, Apollo alone, having at last pitied my long wanderings, twice reminded me with these words: 'O Cupid, your mother used to delight only in light songs and dances; but having later become more ambitious, she began to envy Homer for his Achilles and Virgil for his Aeneas. She desired for herself a similar poet, who might sound forth her arts and praises with a grander lyre <term>cythara</term>. Finally, after many centuries, she found such a poet named Laurentius <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (1449–1492). His name "Laurentius" is a pun on "Laurus" (Laurel).</note> singing among the Laurels...'"

### Apologue.

->How Lucilia <note>The name Lucilia is derived from the Latin *lux* (light), signifying the soul as a spark of divine light.</note> (that is, the soul) fares badly when she departs from Phoebus (that is, from God).<-

Phoebus, the light of life and author of vital medicine, gave to his daughter Lucilia this one precept especially from among many: namely, that she should never depart from her father's side. Otherwise, it would happen that she would fall into various and most serious diseases. In the beginning, Lucilia, as if compelled by the harshness of the approaching winter, obeyed her father’s commands. But then, relying on the prosperity of the now-smiling springtime, the girl began to wander further from her father's hearth. She began to roam more freely everywhere through the beautiful gardens of charming Venus and the painted meadows. 

And there, enticed partly by the soft pleasantness of the herbs, and partly by the beauty of the flowers and their sweet scent, she wove not only wreaths and crowns for herself, but even entire garments from ivy, myrtle, lilies, roses, violets, and other plants. Soon, plucking sweet fruits and mellow apples from all sides, she did not merely taste them, but even gorged herself with a full throat. And now, behaving wantonly in her unusual new finery and completely forgetting her parent, the increasingly vain girl—having escaped—approached the neighboring cities full of pride. 

But meanwhile, in passing, snakes hiding in the grass bit the dancing girl's feet, and bees nested in her flowers and wreaths stung her neck, cheeks, and hands. And her belly, swelling from the excessive and harmful food, became most painfully distended. For this reason, the ungrateful Lucilia—who before, charmed by the enticements of pleasure, had neglected her father the Physician—was driven by a certain extreme torment to return home, to acknowledge her father, and to implore his paternal help with these very words: "Alas, help your daughter! Help Lucilia now, Father Phoebus! Hurry, I beseech you, most merciful father, bring aid to your little daughter, who is even now perishing without your help!" 

But Phoebus said: "Why do you, empty Flora <note>Flora was the Roman goddess of flowers and spring. By calling her 'Flora' instead of 'Lucilia,' Apollo suggests the soul has lost its identity of 'Light' and become merely a creature of material, fleeting beauty.</note>, call me your father? Cease now, wicked one, cease! I never fathered you, most vain Flora. Go hence to your Venus, O profane Flora; go far away as quickly as possible!" But when Lucilia had persisted longer as a suppliant and had beseeched Phoebus with many prayers that he—who alone had given her life—should alone redeem her from death...

->Divine law cannot be created by the heavens, but perhaps it can be signified by them.<-

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine sends greetings and wishes for happiness to Federico, Duke of Urbino, always unconquered.<-

<margin>s</margin> The star which today happily led the Magi—the greatest astronomers of the East—to Christ, has also led me into this very contemplation: how to easily and briefly reconcile legitimate astronomers <note>Ficino uses "astronomer" and "astrologer" almost interchangeably, as was common in the Renaissance, but he is careful to distinguish "legitimate" study from "superstitious" belief.</note> with Christians. Today the Magi, opening their treasures, humbly offered to Christ myrrh as to a God, incense as to a Priest, and gold as to a King. Marsilio, however, offers to the always unconquered, exceptionally wise, and merciful Duke Federico a small gift from the treasures of philosophy itself—a gift at once theological, astronomical, and physical. I shall give more at another time when God grants it.

### Universal religion does not originate from the stars.

<margin>g</margin> Regarding the very nature of religion—than which nothing in human affairs is more universal or firm—no astrologer has ever believed it to be created by the movement or arrangement of the heavens. For they know that whatever things are created by movement must necessarily be changeable, and what is created by a certain arrangement of the stars is eventually dissolved when the stars reach a contrary position. Yet the very nature of religion, by which God is recognized and worshiped by the human race as the governor of the world, remains the most firm of all human pursuits and works, everywhere and always.

### The Christian religion does not originate from the stars.

<margin>v</margin> But if any astrologer should say that the Christian law arose following some conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter <note>Great Conjunctions of these two planets occur every 20 years and were historically believed by "astrometeorologists" to signal the birth of new religions or empires.</note>—in which conjunctions certain astronomers place the greatest power for establishing laws—we will respond briefly here, as much as this letter requires. For we have argued about these matters more extensively and subtly elsewhere. First of all, Saturn and Jupiter are joined every twentieth year, and in every conjunction, they are thought to extend the force of that conjunction into the years immediately following. From this it follows that whenever a divine law is given to us by God, it is equally permitted for astrologers to invent some celestial power as either the author or at least the indicator of such a law. I pass over the fact that the types of religions are rarely changed, even though those planets meet often. Moreover, since they perpetually return to those same conjunctions every nine hundred and sixty years, and in that same interval they are joined four times in any given sign, it is a wonder that the divine law—that is, the Mosaic <note>The Law of Moses/Judaism.</note> and Christian law—either did not exist before in so many ages of the world, or at least has not been destroyed after such a long time. Especially...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s letter to Federico da Montefeltro, Duke of Urbino. Having transitioned from a mythological allegory to a philosophical defense of Christianity, Ficino now argues against "judicial astrology"—the belief that the stars determine the fate of religions or the human soul.</meta>

<header>SEVENTH BOOK 167</header>

since many contrary conjunctions have already occurred long ago.
Accordingly, those astrologers who lived closest to the time of Christ
could have judged much better concerning the fate of the Christian law <note>original: "xpiance legis" (christiane legis). In the Renaissance, "law" often referred to a religious system or dispensation.</note> (if it were indeed subject to fate) than those who came later. Yet those men wandered so far from the truth that they too rashly claimed it would undoubtedly fall as soon as it had completed three hundred and sixty-five years. In this matter, even the oracle of Apollo <note>Ficino refers to a famous anti-Christian prophecy attributed to an oracle of Apollo, which claimed Peter used magic to make Christianity last exactly 365 years.</note> is proven to have lied. Indeed, iniquity has lied to itself; yet the divine truth has not lied—that truth which inspired many Prophets and Sibyls, who were unskilled in astronomy <note>original: "expertes Astronomiae." Ficino emphasizes that their foresight came from God, not from calculating the stars.</note> from the very beginning of things, to foresee and predict the Christian law through divine inspiration. Then, after Christ, He brought forth countless martyrs as witnesses to the Christian truth; among these were many who were learned not only in all the liberal arts but especially in astronomy, and who most willingly endured all evils and finally death for the glory of Christ. But let us now return to the astrologers. Certainly, it seems much more difficult to judge matters that pertain to the counsel of the mind and God than those that pertain to the affections, actions, passions, and works of the body. But in truth, they judge matters of this kind with extreme difficulty and very often falsely. This is evident not only from experience itself but is also confirmed by those reasons which I shall briefly touch upon here. (We discuss these more extensively elsewhere.) Plotinus, following the opinion of Plato and Avicenna, argues most subtly that both the whole and every individual thing are contained under divine power and providence. This is arranged in such an order that incorporeal causes—namely God, the angels, and the souls of the celestial bodies—are the "craftsmen" of natural things. Corporeal causes, however, are the instruments of those higher craftsmen. They then show that whatever earthly things happen on earth proceed from a certain common concurrence of all the superior and inferior causes together. Since no one can ever comprehend all of these, it is no wonder that no one can have a certain opinion about any such earthly matter. Astrologers, however, having cast aside both divine and inferior causes and dispositions, look only at the heavens as best they can. Nor do they even look at all of those, but only a very few; and they touch upon the power of those very few through a certain experience—which is remote, rare, and deceptive—rather than through any certain reasons. Furthermore, they can only with great difficulty grasp the certain moment of our birth. But they predict the moment of conception with even more difficulty; and finally, they cannot predict the infusion of the soul <note>The "infusion of the soul" refers to the theological moment when the soul enters the body, which Ficino argues is a divine act outside the stars' reach.</note> at all. Nor do they understand the complexions <note>A "complexion" in the medical sense refers to the balance of humors inherited from parents.</note> of the parents and ancestors of the child being born. Neither do they seek to account for nutrition, education, habitation, habit, discipline, or counsel—or even if they studied these most diligently, they could never fully grasp them. Yet Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most famous astronomer/geographer of antiquity.</note> ordered all these things to be diligently considered for this reason: because he knew that the power of superior causes is received by us only through subsequent causes, and also through the matter by which we are disposed. Whence he says...

<summary>Ficino argues that Christianity is not subject to astrological fate, noting that past predictions of its downfall failed. He asserts that astrologers cannot predict human affairs accurately because they ignore divine providence, upbringing, and the specific moment the soul enters the body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s letter to Federico da Montefeltro. Ficino is refining his critique of "judicial astrology," moving from the physical limitations of star-signs to the philosophical argument that spiritual matters—like religion—belong to a higher realm than the celestial bodies.</meta>

<header>BOOK</header>

The effects of the stars are often changed and hindered here among us by the diverse disposition of movable matter. Indeed, one sees things born daily at the same moment that are different from one another: in genus, in species, in number, in form, in fortune, and in their outcomes. Thus, we can in no way sufficiently judge anything solely from the moment of an earthly birth or a celestial conjunction. This is especially true since, beyond the individual lot of each person, common fortunes <note>Ficino refers to "universal" events like plagues, wars, or famines that override an individual's personal horoscope.</note> must also be considered and more diligently compared with one another. For these two factors are mutually either a hindrance or a help to each other. Truly, no one can grasp all these variables together. For this reason, Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential ancient astronomer and author of the *Tetrabiblos*.</note> undoubtedly confesses that the judgments of astrologers are confused rather than distinct regarding common matters, and that they concern what is possible rather than what is necessary. So, let us eventually return to where we digressed. If astrologers see visible things so obscurely (if I may say so), how much more obscurely will they see invisible things?

### Religion can perhaps be signified by the heavens.

But lest we seem too obstinate, let us grant that they see something. <margin>f</margin> Yet they see it more often through certain signs than through causes—and those signs are indeed ambiguous and most difficult to know. They are able to discern something only when they understand what follows, whether harmonious or dissonant, from the various strings of the world’s lyre <note>original: "mundane cithare." A Pythagorean and Platonic metaphor for the cosmic order as a musical instrument where the planets and elements are the strings.</note>; or rather (to speak more truly), they are merely prophesying. Plotinus the Platonist <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD), the founder of Neoplatonism, whose works Ficino translated into Latin and viewed as essential to reconciling philosophy with Christianity.</note> teaches that almost all effects below the Moon are signified by the heavens, yet not all depend on the celestial body. For only bodily things can be produced either by a celestial body or, rather, through a celestial body acting as an instrument for the movers of the heavens themselves.

If any things among us entirely exceed the bodily kind and approach the mind and divinity, they proceed only from the divine mind and the minds that follow it. Indeed, the counsels and wills of these higher minds can often be indicated by celestial figures and motions, as if by their own eyes and minds. But to clearly perceive those signs is the work of an exceptionally wise and divine man. So says Plotinus. For this reason, the Mosaic <note>Referring to the religious law of Moses (Judaism).</note> and Christian religion, being entirely spiritual and divine, could in no way be produced by the heavens nor through celestial bodies. This is especially true since those celestial motions are accustomed to perform their works on earth only through earthly aids. But the divine law <note>original: "Diuina vero lex." In this context, "law" refers to the entire revealed religious system.</note> not only lacked earthly help everywhere, but was also troubled and afflicted for many centuries by every kind of hindrance.

Perhaps, however, it seems it could have been signified in some way by the stars; namely, that God himself moved and tempered the spheres in such a way as to designate that time, just as He foresaw and decreed that His law would exist at such a specific time. This is indeed confirmed in the *Metaphysics*. Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath. Ficino cites him to show that even Islamic philosophy supports the idea of divine providence acting through, but not being caused by, the stars.</note> affirms that moral and divine laws are established in certain ages through the souls of the Prophets, sent and inspired by the providence of God alone. Meanwhile, the whole order of the universe is so directed under the divine Mover and His ministers that it disposes the body of the prophetic soul somewhere on earth, and in the heavens...

<summary>Ficino argues that while stars may act as signs of future events, they do not cause spiritual phenomena like religion. He uses the authority of Ptolemy, Plotinus, and Avicenna to claim that divine laws (Judaism and Christianity) originate directly from God's providence, not from celestial mechanics.</summary>
<keywords>astrology, providence, Christianity, Plotinus, Ptolemy, Avicenna, divine law, prophecy, celestial signs, Moses</keywords>

...signifies His arrival to the lands as well. Perhaps David truly intended this with these words: *The heavens declare the glory of God: and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands.* <note>Psalm 19:1. Ficino interprets this famous verse not just as general praise, but as a specific claim that the stars "speak" or "signify" divine truths.</note> Perhaps it also points in some way to what Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a Persian astrologer whose works were widely read in the Latin West. He famously claimed that the sign of Virgo represented a virgin nursing a child.</note> says: that the Egyptians and Indians considered a certain beautiful Virgin sitting in the region of the sign of Virgo, nursing a boy whose name, according to some nations, Albumasar believes to be Jesus. Indeed, that image which is thought of in that sign—or rather, is imagined rather than seen—if it were the actual cause of Jesus himself, surely it would have produced either Jesus himself or someone very much like him many other times both before and after the time of Christ. Therefore, if such an image exists there, it is a certain sign of the Christian law, not its cause.

->Many things are signified through the heavens which are not caused by the heavens.<-

<margin>q</margin> Furthermore, it is established that many things are indeed signified by the heaven, yet are not caused by it, because evil and the experience of disorder cannot proceed from those most excellent and perfectly ordered things. Nevertheless, they are often predicted through celestial things as if through signs, not as if through causes—not unlike how many things are thought to be portended through birds in auguries and auspices <note>Ancient Roman practices of interpreting the will of the gods by observing the flight or behavior of birds.</note>, which are nevertheless not caused by the birds at all. For this reason, Plato in the *Timaeus* did not say that the stars *make* the future, but that they *announce* it—though not to everyone, but only to those who can follow these things through reason. Moreover, in anyone's birth-horoscope <note>original: *genesi*</note>, astrologers are accustomed to judge many things that must be considered regarding their homeland, parents, ancestors, brothers, spouses, servants, friends, and enemies; the fate of these people in no way proceeds from another person's birth-horoscope, but is rather indicated by it. This is also clearly seen in those inquiries <note>Horary astrology, where a chart is cast for the moment a question is asked rather than a birth.</note> regarding past events which are performed and handled by them. Indeed, just as we daily foresee through someone's eyes, gestures, and words that they are about to do something—though they do not perform what they chose because of those indicators, but because of their own will—so too, many things are portended through the "nods" of the celestial spheres. These things are neither caused by those celestial bodies, nor through them, but by the divine minds <note>Ficino refers to the Intelligences or Angels believed to move the planetary spheres.</note> which rule and move those globes. Through celestial things, as if through their own facial expressions, they signify these events; but through their own counsel, these events are either most orderly arranged or brought back into order. At the very least, events destined to come from human causes are both foreseen from above by the divine and demonstrated to us through certain celestial signs. In this matter, Ptolemy and Albumasar, as well as Zael <note>Sahl ibn Bishr (c. 786–845), a Jewish astrologer and mathematician who wrote in Arabic.</note> and Manilius <note>Marcus Manilius (1st century AD), author of the *Astronomica*, a Roman poem on astrology.</note> and the other principal authors of astronomy, seem to agree with us. This is evident when he affirms that celestial bodies are endowed with divine souls and minds, and like certain divine living beings <note>original: *animalia*</note>, they obey God himself, the ruler of all. And this is not without reason. Indeed, since Ptolemy himself confesses that human wisdom so dominates the work of another (that is, the stars) that it can often, through its own industry, resist their threats and favor their promises, who would wonder if he conceded that Divine Wisdom completely dominates its own work? Hence that saying of Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian philosopher and physician.</note>: "The heaven is a living being obedient to God." Since, truly, all these understand...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument that celestial phenomena act as signs rather than causes of divine events. ...are performed and governed by divine providence. Therefore, when they speak of the power of celestial bodies, they very rarely say that the heavens *do* this or that. Most frequently, however, they assert that they *signify* something of this or that nature. And just as they believe false or merely human laws are portended by the stars, so too are true and divine ones often foretold.

### Signs and testimonies concerning the divinity of Christ.

Perhaps for this very reason, the Magi—the wisest of all in the study of astronomy—set out from the East to Jerusalem at the time Jesus was born. They asserted that they had been alerted by a certain star <note>original: "sidere"</note> that a boy had been born at that time and in that region who was to be the King of Israel and was worthy of adoration. The fact that such great men came from so far a journey to worship a helpless infant clearly demonstrates that the Magi believed there was a divinity in the boy proceeding from a principle higher than the heavens, especially since they were led by a miraculous star rather than a natural one. 

Calcidius the Platonist <note>A 4th-century philosopher known for his commentary on Plato's *Timaeus*. He is one of the few pagan authors to mention the Star of Bethlehem.</note> adduces various histories concerning stars which, when they rarely appear in great size, portend calamities. He then adds: "There is also another holier and more venerable history which relates that by the rising of a certain star, not diseases and deaths were announced, but the venerable descent of God for the sake of human salvation and mortal affairs." He testifies that this was observed by the Chaldeans, who worshipped the newly born God with gifts. These are the words of Calcidius. 

Nor should it seem surprising that the Magi noticed this. For in that same eastern region—and, as some say, in the very same city as the Magi—the prophet Balaam flourished long before them. He predicted that the Messiah would then arise like a rod out of Israel with a new star of Jacob, namely in these words: *A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a rod shall arise out of Israel.* <note>Numbers 24:17. Ficino connects this Old Testament prophecy to the Magi’s astronomical knowledge.</note> 

The fact that the Magi came to Jerusalem to worship Christ is evidenced for us by that cruel slaughter of the infants under Herod. Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman writer. This famous anecdote puns on the fact that Herod, as a practicing Jew, would not eat pork, yet he killed his own family members.</note> asserts that Augustus was informed of this, writing thus: "When Augustus heard that among the boys in Syria under the age of two whom Herod, the King of the Jews, ordered to be killed, his own son was also slain, he said: 'It is better to be Herod's pig than his son.'" <note>original: "praestat herodis porcum esse quam filium"</note> 

Suetonius <note>Roman historian (c. 69–122 AD). He and Tacitus recorded a widespread belief that a world-ruler would come from Judea.</note> also writes that there was an ancient and constant opinion throughout the whole East that it was in the Fates that around the time of Nero, those departing from Judea would take command of the empire. Josephus writes that this same oracle was found in the sacred scriptures <note>original: "sacris litteris"</note> before the siege of Jerusalem. Indeed, it seems this can be applied to none more fittingly than the Apostles; for in these oracles, the Jews are designated as the ones who, like the Apostles, departed from Judea to give laws everywhere to all nations. 

Even the Cumaean Sibyl <note>A priestess of Apollo. Her "prophecy" is famously quoted in Virgil's Fourth Eclogue, which many Renaissance Christians viewed as a pagan prophecy of Christ’s birth.</note> seems to have described the same time, when a "great order of ages would be born anew," and a Virgin would flourish, and a "new lineage would be sent down from high heaven" through the nations. For this reason, the sentiment was both ancient and constant throughout the East, both in the regions of the astrologers and in the sacred scriptures—namely in the prophets and the Sibyls—and was most consistent regarding the divinity and the timing of Christ.

He emphasizes that the Magi recognized Christ’s divinity as something originating from a power higher than the physical heavens.</summary>

## The Christian religion depends on God alone.

<margin>1</margin>But concerning the divine oracles of the sibyls and prophets, we discuss this more extensively in our book *On Religion*. In this letter, however, we shall briefly conclude regarding the divine law as it pertains to the question at hand. If anyone should object to us that Christ performed miracles by some fate of his "genesis" <note>original: "genesis," referring here to a natal horoscope or birth-chart</note> or by some conjunction of stars favoring that birth, we shall ask them: how is it that countless holy men among the Christians, arising at different times and places long after Christ, have performed many miracles and continue to do so daily? Furthermore, that eclipse of the Sun at the death of Christ, occurring contrary to the order of nature, most clearly declared that Christ was born from an order higher than the celestial one. That it was indeed an eclipse is proven to us by this: it would not have been permissible for Christ’s disciples, preaching such a portent everywhere, to lie about a matter so manifest. What is more, Eusebius <note>A 4th-century bishop and historian known as the "Father of Church History."</note> asserts that he read the same in the histories of the pagans themselves; Lucian of Antioch and Tertullian say the same before Eusebius. Phlegon, too, a writer of the *Olympiads* <note>A 2nd-century Greek historian whose lost works are often cited by early Christians to verify the darkness at the Crucifixion.</note>, confirms that a prodigious failure of the sun occurred at the same time we record. That it was indeed miraculous, Dionysius the Areopagite and the philosopher Apollophanes—who were walking together near Heliopolis—saw clearly with their own eyes and proved through subtle disputations. We read of this in the letter of Dionysius to the wise Polycarp. We also conclude the same from this: there is no doubt that the Jews, according to the law, always celebrated the Passover only at the full moon, and at that very time Christ was fixed to the cross. From this, by most certain reasoning, it is understood both that the sun failed and that it failed against every order of nature <note>A natural solar eclipse can only occur during a new moon, when the moon is between the earth and the sun; at Passover/Full Moon, the moon is on the opposite side of the earth.</note>. Thus, just as the heavens bore witness to the dying Christ with strange darkness, so too they bore witness to Him at His birth with a new light.

### Conclusion concerning the Divinity of the Christian Law.

<margin>v</margin>But to return to our purpose: why should it be a wonder if the Creator of the world so tempered the individual parts of the world that, amidst a marvelous arrangement of the stars and the highest peace of the entire globe, He visited men in human form? For long before, He commanded His own celestial prophets to retreat against nature. Dionysius relates that the Babylonians and Persians recorded these portents in their annals as divine works. We read of similar things in Plato’s book *The Statesman* <note>original: "in libro de regno." Ficino refers to the myth of the reversed cosmos in Plato's dialogue *Politicus*.</note>. The poets (as they usually do) transformed this history into the fables of Phaethon <note>In Greek myth, the son of Helios who lost control of the sun chariot, used here by Ficino as a distorted memory of a real divine miracle.</note> and other similar tales. Finally, the divine law and holy religion proceed neither from the lower nor from the higher bodies of the world. Since the grace of the incorporeal and good God despises all bodily things, it transcends them all through life, affection, and thought. Nor does it depend in any way on fate, for religion always denies and condemns fate. Nor is it born from human nature or human prudence, which religion ignores; rather, by a certain immense space, it is elevated above human nature toward the infinite God. But without doubt, it proceeds from the infinite Principle alone...

<summary>Ficino argues that the miraculous eclipse during Christ's crucifixion, occurring at a full moon, proves Christianity's divine origin above the laws of astrology. He asserts that true religion transcends both celestial influence (fate) and human reason, originating solely from God.</summary>

...only seeks the infinite; but it helps to seal our letter with a seal from Plato. Our Plato, in the *Protagoras* and the *Statesman* <note>original: "politico," referring to Plato's dialogue *Politicus*</note>, posits two principles of religions. By one of these, religion was born immediately at the very beginning of things; by the other, it was confirmed after many centuries. But it was confirmed by the divine law which God alone, through his singular mercy, eventually sent to men through a messenger chosen by Him. Farewell. January 6, 1481. Florence.

### Philosophy and Religion are Kindred.

->Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Antonio Ziliolo and Sophronio the Venetian. Greetings.<-

If anyone should have a massive and wondrous piece of workmanship <note>original: "opificium," referring here to the created universe as the product of a master craftsman</note> always before his eyes—constructed and set in motion with such marvelous reason and manifest art, and moreover perfectly suited to the use and wishes of those who behold it—yet he never noticed that such a work was made and is moved by a supreme power, reason, and goodness, would we not consider him blind in the eyes of reason? Or if perhaps someone does notice it at times, yet never fears, reveres, or honors the architect of such a beautiful and useful work, must he not be considered worthy of extreme hatred, both by other observers and by the architect himself? 

But out of all human arts and faculties, pious philosophy alone always provides with every effort that we do not fall into such miserable blindness, nor undergo such heavy hatred. For there is no other duty for the one who truly philosophizes than to always investigate and teach the individual reasons and causes of both the parts and the universe. Then, in assigning the reasons and causes of things themselves, to finally ascend to the supreme reason and cause of all things. Furthermore, to lead others with him to the higher realms as far as his strength allows. And while he shows by how much wisdom the world is ruled, he demonstrates at the same time with certain proofs of providence <term>providence: the protective care of God or of nature as a spiritual power</term> for how great a benefit to the human race he leads it. 

Therefore, that we may recognize and love God, the whole world cries out from every side, and the true philosopher—the interpreter of the world and of God—diligently demonstrates and exhorts. Thus, unless we are completely deprived of every sense, we ought now most aptly to know that in such a great order of the universe, nothing at all is accidental—unless perhaps those people alone are "accidental" who believe such a skillful piece of workmanship is the result of chance. 

Accordingly, when the wise philosopher raises us to the contemplation of God and when he inflames us with the love of divine goodness, he must be called pious and religious. For this reason, the whole philosophy of the ancients is nothing other than a "learned religion." I shall pass over other matters for the present. For they are innumerable. Plato, imbued with the divine mysteries of Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, regarded by Ficino as the original source of an ancient, "pious" philosophy that prefigures Christianity.</note>, disputes in the *Republic* and elsewhere often that unless one has seen and recognized the goodness of God himself by a certain light, he can neither see anything else that is true nor ever act well, whether in public or in pri-

<summary>Ficino defines religion as both an innate instinct and a divine revelation, then begins a new letter arguing that true philosophy is essentially a "learned religion" that leads the mind to God through the study of his workmanship in the universe.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument that philosophy and religion are essentially the same pursuit. Having established that the universe is a product of divine craftsmanship, Ficino now draws on a lineage of "ancient theologians" (the *prisca theologia*)—including Plato, Pythagoras, Hermes Trismegistus, and Zoroaster—to show that true wisdom has always been rooted in piety and the purification of the soul.</meta>

...privately. But as for the Divine Sun: it is perceived only by its own light. Finally, that light is usually infused only into a mind that is serene. For this reason, Plato himself used to purge his own mind in the Socratic fashion, and he taught others everywhere to purge theirs. Furthermore, he commanded that one should begin from God in every single thing—not only in speaking but also in thinking—and he himself always began from God. 

For the sake of a similar purification, Pythagoras—imitating Orpheus—beyond a singular sobriety of life, sang sacred hymns every day at sunrise to those above <note>original: "superis," referring to the celestial or divine beings</note>, accompanied by the lyre. He persuaded Empedocles and his other followers to do the same, so that they might imitate the celestial spheres singing to God. Moreover, when he discovered that the long side of a triangle <note>the hypotenuse</note> had as much power as the other two sides joined together, he humbly sacrificed a hecatomb <term>hecatomb: a massive ancient Greek sacrifice, traditionally consisting of 100 oxen</term> to God. For he understood that nothing can ever be truly seen except by the light of the Supreme Truth. 

If he sacrificed such a grand victim for the knowledge of so small a matter, do you not think he dedicated himself to God for the knowledge of his own self? Again, for the contemplation of the universe, he must have consecrated the universe as a suppliant to the Creator of the whole. What shall I say of Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurio Trismegisto"</note>? All of his discussions begin with vows and end with sacrifices. What of Zoroaster? His philosophy (as Plato testifies) is nothing other than wise piety and divine worship. 

Finally (to speak briefly), that Saturnian <note>referring to the mythical Golden Age ruled by Saturn</note> and golden discipline of the ancients should be called *Philothea* <term>Philothea: "Love of God," a term Ficino uses to elevate philosophy into a religious act</term> rather than Philosophy. Their speech is entirely an oracle rather than a mere oration. Why do I mention this union of wisdom and piety? Clearly, so that we may first remember how much we owe to those golden ages of sacred philosophy. Then (so that you yourself may understand) by what reasoning Marsilio, a follower of antiquity, always joins religious matters with philosophical ones according to his talent—not only in that one book on religion which you requested, but also in all his writings. Finally, may you recognize yourself and Antonio Chronicum together as his fellow philosophers in that philosophy which embraces wisdom and piety simultaneously. Farewell.
