## That the Platonic teaching is pious

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Niccolini, Archbishop of Amalfi, sends greetings.<-

Numenius the Pythagorean—whom Origen <note>a highly influential, though sometimes controversial, early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD)</note> prefers to all other Pythagoreans—having read the books of Moses and Plato, judged that Plato was simply "another Moses speaking in the Attic tongue" <note>original: "moysen attica lingua loquẽtẽ." Attic refers to the dialect of ancient Athens.</note>. Furthermore, Aurelius Augustine writes that we are led toward the truth by a double path: namely, by authority and by reason. He states that he prefers the authority of Christ above all others; however, as for the reasons that best harmonize with this authority, he finds them only among the Platonists. He notes that among them, almost the entire prologue of the Gospel of John can be found. Finally, he affirms that with the change of only a few words, the Platonists would unquestionably be Christians. He chose them from the entire number of philosophers for this reason: that because they feel more correctly about divine matters than all other philosophers, they are rightly seen as superior to the rest.

Therefore, I—led first by the authority of the divine Augustine and then confirmed by the testimony of many holy men among the Christians—judged that if I were to practice philosophy, it would be worthwhile to do so primarily in the Academy <note>The "Academy" refers to the school founded by Plato, which Ficino revived in Florence under the patronage of the Medici</note>. Indeed, so that the Platonic doctrine—which stands in relation to the Divine Law (that is, the Mosaic and Christian law) as the moon does to the sun—might shine more widely, I have translated all the books of Plato from the Greek language into Latin. Furthermore, lest anyone’s eyes be dazed by the sight of this new light, I have composed a volume as a commentary, divided into eighteen books. In these, the Platonic mysteries are explained to the best of my ability, so that we may follow his mind rather than merely his words; having removed the poetic veils, we may grasp the Platonic sentiment which harmonizes everywhere with the Divine Law. 

I truly believe (and this is no vain faith) that it was decreed by Divine Providence that those sharpest of minds, who do not easily yield to the authority of the Divine Law alone, might at last yield to Platonic reasons which strongly support religion. Why do I say this, Reverend Father? So that you may read this to your associates, so they might cease to wonder why Marsilio (since he is a priest of philosophy) devotes himself to this so frequently. Farewell.

### A Fable.
### Marsilio Ficino on Plato's book *The Kingdom* <note>Referring to Plato's *Republic*</note> to Federico, Duke of Urbino

<margin>1</margin>When Jupiter, the Best and Greatest, desired to look down upon such a kingdom on earth as he always beholds beside himself in heaven—according to the very Idea <term>Idea: In Platonic thought, the perfect, eternal blueprint of a thing in the divine mind</term> of the Divine King—he sent a certain royal and divine soul down to earth. Having called together the heavenly inhabitants, he commanded that they all support this future king. The gods above already named him the "Orbinate Leader" <note>original: "Urbinatem ducem," a play on the word "Urbs" (city/Urbino) and "Orbis" (world/circle)</note> from both his royal faith and the circle of the world; but humans, by changing the letters, would call him Federico, Duke of Urbino. All the deities assented to Jupiter except Juno. For Juno alone—the ambitious queen of the thicker air <note>In Renaissance allegory, Juno often represents worldly wealth and the "lower" atmosphere of ambition</note>—envied a celestial kingdom on earth until now. However, Pallas <note>Athena, goddess of wisdom</note> and Mercury <note>the messenger god of eloquence and interpretation</note>, with others favoring him (and with Truth as a witness), have long since granted the crown and royal scepter to this same man...

<summary>Ficino defends his translation of Plato by arguing that Platonic philosophy is a "moon" reflecting the "sun" of Christian truth, specifically citing Saint Augustine's approval. He concludes with a mythological tribute to Federico da Montefeltro, Duke of Urbino, framing him as a divinely appointed ruler.</summary>

to whom Jupiter also most willingly granted gifts. Since the Academy everywhere worships and follows Pallas <note>Athena, goddess of wisdom</note> and Mercury <note>the messenger god, associated with eloquence and interpretation</note>, it most fortunately bestows the kingdom and monarchy of the entire world—such as the divine Plato describes—upon Federico, Duke of Urbino <note>Federico da Montefeltro (1422–1482), a celebrated condottiero (mercenary general) and one of the greatest patrons of the Italian Renaissance</note>, both by the judgment of Jupiter and by the testimony of his excellent merit toward the truth.

### Marsilio Ficino’s Apologue to Federico, Duke of Urbino, regarding the book of *Cosmography* by Francesco Berlinghieri, son of Niccolò, dedicated to the same.

<margin>q</margin>He whom almighty Jupiter, Lord of the entire world, created for the rule of the earthly sphere, and whom Pallas and Mercury, the children of Jupiter, have long deemed worthy of such great power: to him, the Academy, the least of its cultivators, justly dedicates the Platonic form of the earthly kingdom. To him also our fellow Academician Berlinghieri <note>Francesco Berlinghieri (1440–1501), a Florentine humanist who wrote a famous verse geography based on Ptolemy</note> presents the entire shape of the terrestrial globe. This comes at a time when republics, leaders, and kings again and again grant to his fortunate auspices both the spear of Pallas and the club of Hercules, as he is the powerful master of the Italian war. And while many powerful men wish Italy to obey Duke Federico, always undefeated in war, meanwhile both the Academy and the Academicians subject the whole world to him in both peace and war.

->Let the sacrilegious not touch sacred things.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Carlo Ristori, sends many greetings.

<margin>q</margin>Our Plato was being transcribed during these days by a certain impious German, who recently shed sacred blood before the altars with sacrilegious hands <note>This likely refers to the violence of the Pazzi Conspiracy (1478) or a similar event where the sanctity of a church was violated</note>. Suddenly, that man—that "priest-killer" soldier, if I may call him so—took flight after the priest was slain. By his very flight, he committed a second sacrilege: namely, leaving the sophisticated Plato to wander among the unrefined. He is, moreover, about to commit a third sacrilege if, upon returning, he should ever dare to touch the sacred Plato with his bloodstained hands. Therefore, I beg you, best of men, to see to it that Plato does not wander too long in the woods or perhaps—which would be even more cruel—be polluted at some point by the contaminated hands of that profane man.

->In God alone is salvation.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Bandini, sends many greetings.

<margin>f</margin>Greetings, my most dear and equally loving Bandini. Greetings, I say, a thousand times, or rather always, in God, the eternal author of salvation. I would have added "and in Plato," if only salvation were to be sought in a man after God. We are doing well, which I know you desire to hear above all. We recently heard the same regarding you, and we hope to hear similar news from day to day. I have dedicated two books of our letters to Matthias, the undefeated King of Pannonia <note>Matthias Corvinus (reigned 1458–1490), King of Hungary and a massive patron of humanism; Pannonia is the Roman name for the region</note>, which are now being transcribed by the work of Francesco Iunio. Our other books, which you desire, are already in the hands of the printers; when they have been expressed <note>printed</note>, they will come to you as messengers fortunately expressing our mind to you. Meanwhile, this letter commends to you three friends especially dear to us among the Muses, who are to be greeted again and again: the Bishop of Kalocsa, the Bishop of Vác, and Peter Garasda. Farewell, and be happy. May 8, 1482.

We can only approve of ourselves as much as we are approved by those who are proven.

BOOK EIGHT

<margin>A</margin>Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Pietro Molino of Venice, many greetings.

Our Antonio <note>likely the famous Florentine artist Antonio del Pollaiuolo (c. 1432–1498), known for both painting and sculpture</note>, a distinguished painter and sculptor, when he greeted me and my close companions in your name yesterday evening, he so vividly painted your features upon our faces and so deeply carved your character upon our emotions that it seemed not as if your greetings were being related to us by him, but as if you were clearly present before us in person. Therefore, we all stood up suddenly and no longer recognized the Florentine Antonio, but rather acknowledged Pietro Molino himself as present; and with heads bared (as is proper), we honored you. Greetings to you also, most learned spirit, Pietro; return to us frequently through this presence of yours, just as you have begun to do. We shall truly consider ourselves worthy of honor for as long as you yourself honor us. Our city will please us only so much as we know it pleases you. Would that our affairs might please you more every day, so that we ourselves may take greater pleasure in our own lives daily. Farewell.

->An honest excuse for a long silence.<-

Marsilio Ficino to his unique friend, Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Giovanni Cavalcanti (1444–1509) was Ficino’s most intimate friend and the person to whom he dedicated many of his works, often calling him his "unique friend"</note>, many greetings.

<margin>C</margin>When at dawn today I was entirely occupied with finishing the work on sacred theology <note>original: "sacro theologiæ opi"; this refers to Ficino's masterpiece, *Platonic Theology*, which sought to prove the immortality of the soul</note> that I have been laboring on for a long time, and while no one, even among my closest friends, dared to interrupt me then, I was nevertheless interrupted quite boldly by you alone with these reproaches: "Marsilio, you are usually the first to greet your Giovanni with letters during your days in the country; but now you have long abstained from your usual greetings. Do you not see how much your silence detracts from a friendship that is more sacred than sacrilegious?" To this, Plato seemed to respond in this manner for our common cause: "See how great a power is in your words, Giovanni. Indeed, for others, saying one thing is different from doing it; but you, by speaking, actually act. For with the very words you call Marsilio sacrilegious, you yourself make him sacrilegious, if indeed he is to be considered sacrilegious for interrupting a sacred and public work for the sake of a private, however singular, friendship." A controversy of this kind, as I was saying, fell upon us this dawn. But you have won at last (as you usually do), and so, with the Platonic mysteries briefly interrupted, you now receive the usual greetings from us. Do you wish to win again? Do you wish to overcome Plato again? Answer my friend, I pray; answer not as you usually do (or rather, as you usually do not). But if you do not wish to answer me, at least answer Plato. But look, while I am speaking to you (as it happens), I suddenly see a double face there—a marvelous sight to see—where just now I saw only one. And if I recognize the faces of my friends correctly, I seem to see the pleasing face of Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" de' Medici (1449–1492), the de facto ruler of Florence and a great patron of the arts and philosophy</note> reflected in your mirror, as it were; and I am scolded by him almost as much as by you. Therefore, since your faces are now doubled for me, let those greetings in turn be doubled for me; and what I said a moment ago to two as if to one, let it now be said to one as if to two.

<margin>A</margin>lthough I do not have those instruments here with me now by which celestial matters are usually weighed and examined with precision, nevertheless, to act for the present with my rougher wit <note>original: "pingui minerva," a Latin idiom for a plain, common-sense approach rather than technical expertise</note>, that figure of the heavens does not please me much in which Mars holds the mid-heaven <note>the highest point of the zodiac at a given time</note>, Saturn occupies the sixth house, Jupiter is combust <note>an astrological term for a planet being too close to the Sun, thus having its influence "burned up" or weakened</note>, and the Sun looks upon the Moon from a square aspect <note>a 90-degree angle, typically considered a stressful or challenging alignment in astrology</note>. But it is neither helpful to omen bad things, nor does it suit one much to believe in them. For since judgment is often fallible in nearby and daily matters, it is surely most fallible in things most remote—especially since our affairs depend on many other causes besides the stars: on ancestry, nutrition, location, education, counsel, and chance. This is clearly evident from the fact that even those things which are carried and born at the same moment nevertheless differ most widely among themselves in kind, species, number, quality, fortune, and outcome. Farewell.

->Divine things are not admitted while they are being sent.<-

## Marsilio Ficino to Lotterio Neroni, his fellow philosopher, many greetings.

<margin>G</margin>iovanni Cocchi, our fellow Academician, met with me yesterday evening and, in his usual theatrical manner <note>original: "terentiano... more," referring to the witty style of the Roman playwright Terence</note>, he said: "I bid you greetings, our Marsilio, in the name of our Lotterio. Do you wish to return any message to Lotterio? For I am flying back to him (as you see)." But I, while I greatly wished you to be greeted in turn, said: "You shall return those same greetings to Lotterio." Giovanni replied: "But if you return the same greetings to your friend, you will seem perhaps to be rejecting what he had sent." To this I said: "If my left hand returns to my right what it received from the right, I have certainly not lost it, but rather preserved it by a certain exchange. Surely Lotterio and Marsilio are the right and left hands of the same man."

Perhaps a certain Dialectician <note>a scholar of formal logic; humanists like Ficino often mocked them for being overly literal or narrow-minded</note> was present and objected: "Even if the same man possesses whatever either hand possesses, nevertheless, that which he has already returned to the other is no longer in the first." Then I responded thus: "If a mutual exchange of pity were made between us, what you object, O Dialectician, would surely follow. But if it were a ray of light, it follows not at all. For a ray is accustomed to leap from a bright body into a mirror and to leap back. This ray does not abandon the body from which it shines while it is being emitted, nor is it lost when it leaps back by reflection; furthermore, whatever the ray warms by its strike is not broken, but through mutual percussion, it rather appears to be doubled. You do not know, O Dialectician—you do not know that Marsilio is greeted by Lotterio through rays sent in divine light, and he is greeted in turn by the other through rays sent back. Furthermore, nothing here is offended but rather cherished; nothing is broken but rather doubled. Therefore, O Dialectician, farewell, you wretched man, with those shadows of yours! You shall only be happy when you gratefully look back upon the light that always looks upon you freely."

But you, Giovanni, carry between me and Lotterio these indivisible rays of divine greeting without any fear of division, and report back happily.

->An artful petition and recommendation.<-

<margin>M</margin> I have recently brought forth certain things for Matthias, the invincible King of Pannonia <note>Matthias Corvinus, King of Hungary (r. 1458–1490), was a great patron of the arts and Ficino’s work</note> from this workshop of ours. What then? I have found a way, Ficino; rejoice in the discovery: a way that may return you to so great a friend." But I asked, "By what way will you accomplish this, Salvini?" He replied, "If I, as a second Ficino, travel there, you will have traveled at least in me to the place you desired." Indeed, I have decided to set out for Pannonia under happy auspices—that is, on the safe feet of our friend Bandini, who has himself departed happily. Truly, my dear Francesco, I would both praise this man to you and commend him to you most highly, if it were either fitting to praise myself anywhere or necessary to commend myself to me. Farewell happily; live happily. Love me as you do; write back what is sufficient. Our friends send greetings. Greet our friends. I commend you to the royal family; commend us to the King. From the countryside at Careggi <note>the site of the Medici villa where Ficino’s Platonic Academy met</note>, September 20, 1482.

### In what respect Platonic discipline especially surpasses the Peripatetic.

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, his fellow Platonist, sends greetings.<-

<margin>M</margin> Your elegant letters have indeed affected me with great pleasure, for they clearly prove you to be outstanding in eloquence by our judgment. They bring even greater pleasure because they signify that you have also emerged as a Peripatetic <note>a follower of Aristotle's philosophy</note>. Finally, they bring the greatest pleasure because they undoubtedly promise a Platonist—in which you seem to have most excellently cultivated your singular and happy genius. For after your studies of human eloquence, you have tracked down the reasons of natural things among the Peripatetics. And now you betake yourself to the divine mysteries of our Plato. For the Peripatetics indeed most diligently dispute with what great reason natural things are arranged everywhere. But the Platonists, besides these things, show moreover how much we owe to Him who arranged these things by number, weight, and measure <note>a reference to the biblical Wisdom of Solomon 11:20, a favorite concept for reconciling Christian and Platonic thought</note>. For this reason, the former easily make us learned; the latter, moreover, make us wise and blessed. Therefore, my excellent Giovanni, proceed happily as you have begun. I promise that I shall not be wanting in this honorable purpose of yours, if only (as you say) you should need our labor. Farewell.

### An honest and at the same time vigorous demand for entrusted books.
### Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to his friend Dolce, the famous jurist.

Greetings, my sweetest friend. Sweeten <note>original: "Dulces," a pun on his correspondent's name, Dolce</note> my bitterness with your sweetness (if you can, and would that you could) during these times. I (as you know) have never fathered any children <note>original: "liberos"</note> except for books <note>original: "libros"</note>. No one is ignorant of how dear children are to their parents. Yet, insofar as children of the mind are more intimate and excellent than those of the body, they are held so much dearer. To what end is this? Truly, that unconquered leader of yours <note>Federico da Montefeltro, Duke of Urbino (1422–1482)</note> asked me most vehemently, both by letter and by voice, that I should entrust my books to be sent to him at Urbino. I entrusted them indeed as willingly as he desired them. Vespasiano <note>Vespasiano da Bisticci (1421–1498), the celebrated Florentine bookseller and manuscript producer who helped build the great library of Urbino</note> therefore handed them over to hired couriers to be delivered. But when those men received them, having not received their pay, they have held them captive from me for a long time now. Meanwhile, I burn with the most ardent longing for them, and I fear a thousand dangers for them every day. I beseech you by the Muses, my Dolce, and I beseech your Graces, the lords: do not allow me—while I strive to obey the Duke's will and think to honor them besides—to suffer so heavy a loss. Farewell.

### A busy man should not be interrupted rashly.
### Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to Bernardo Rucellai, Orator of the Florentine Senate.

It is the opinion of the wise that a man occupied with weighty business should not be interrupted without a weighty cause. For me, will not "Platonic weight" <note>original: "platonica grauitas," a play on the word "grauitas" meaning both "weight/seriousness" and "pregnancy"</note> now be a sufficiently weighty cause to interrupt you? Certainly it is enough that you yourself (as I believe) will easily admit: this academy or library of ours is daily laboring to give birth to a Latin Plato, long ago conceived from Greek seed. Truly, he cannot easily give birth without the hand of a midwife. Therefore, my Bernardo, apply the "midwife hands" of the printers, so that they may draw out the now-mature offspring and shape it once it is brought forth. Farewell.

### They are not friends unless one depends upon the other.
### Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to Francesco Bandini.

Your letters, my Bandini, signify to me your very prosperous health, and indeed they confirm my own. I reply in turn for this reason: that while I indicate mine to you, I may also confirm yours. Not without reason does one of two friends depend upon the other, if indeed one exists within the other. Regarding our Bishop of Vác <note>Miklós Báthory (c. 1435–1506), Bishop of Vác in Hungary, a patron and student of Ficino's philosophy</note>, what shall I say? Truly, I have said enough just now when I spoke of us. Thus, if I wish to explain my love for him, I shall be most lengthy to others, but to myself, most brief. Therefore, lest others be weary of my prolixity or I regret my brevity, I shall be content with affection alone, since I cannot express it in speech.

->Solitude is necessary for the learned<-

### Marsilio Ficino to the most upright man, Piero Nero. Many greetings.

<margin>a</margin>You yourself complain, along with our other friends, that I have now been away from the city for too long (as I suppose). But cease your complaining. For truly, I am never less absent from the Academy than when I am absent from the city. Indeed, urban affairs often distract me from you all, but rural affairs restore me: here I am entirely yours and unencumbered. For whether I walk abroad, I flourish everywhere for you and for myself; or whether I sleep, our dreams always bring you back to me. Farewell, and give my greetings to everyone—but to whom? To which ones? To no one in particular, so that I might address all the members of the Academy <note>original: "academicos," referring to the Platonic Academy in Florence</note> by a single name. Again, fare well. April 1, 1483.

->They do not truly love one another who do not constantly think of one another.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Filippo Valori. Many greetings.

<margin>v</margin>You see, Filippo, when I was about to write to Valori, I truly wrote that I had written to Carduccio. <note>original: "carducio," likely a wordplay on the name of a mutual friend or a reference to a specific family connection</note> Why is this a wonder? Certainly, each of them is as one to the other, and each is as one to me. From which it also happens that whether I strike the lyre or sing poems, the one strikes along and the other sings in harmony. But hey, Valori, had we not decided to "rusticate" <note>to spend time in the countryside; Ficino views this as a spiritual retreat</note> together during these sacred days, not for the sake of cultivating the field, but for the sake of cultivating the soul? And by now we would have exchanged words, were it not that those who live together always cannot help but rusticate together. But here is the difference: with you as my guide, I was going to seek the field of Maiano <note>Maiano was the location of the Valori family villa</note>. Now, however, with me as your guide, you have sought Careggi <note>the site of the Medici villa where Ficino’s Academy met</note> instead. Since there is a change in all things, soon I shall seek Maiano with you as my guide. But so that nothing remains hidden from you: where you read "I" <note>original: "ego"</note>, understand it as if I were speaking as a placeholder for a "greater I"—namely, Berlinghieri <note>Francesco Berlinghieri (1440–1501), a diplomat and geographer who was a close associate of Ficino</note>. I desire to return you all here laden with many greetings. These you may then pour out everywhere upon our fellow Academicians: upon our godfather Boninsegni, upon our godfather Guicciardini, and finally upon all the brothers. Farewell.

->Praise of the Platonic philosopher.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to his distinguished fellow-Platonist, Piero Leoni. Many greetings.

<margin>s</margin>If the word "sophist" <note>In the Renaissance, a "sophist" was often used as a pejorative for a philosopher who uses clever but fallacious arguments, as opposed to a true seeker of wisdom</note> is derived from "sophos" <note>Greek for "wise man"</note> by a certain diminution, it is more just for the sophist to follow the wise man than the reverse. Therefore, my wise friend, do not seek the sophist any further, for he will soon (as is right) follow you. Farewell.

->All pains are born from the soul’s love toward the body.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved Amerigo Corsini. Many greetings.

<margin>a</margin>They say that Apollo, the source of Medicine, fathered two sons in particular: Aesculapius and Plato. Aesculapius was to heal bodies, while Plato was to heal souls. The physicians who are followers of Aesculapius are accustomed to apply certain poultices and ointments to the pains of the body, which they call "anodynes" <note>original: "anodina," from the Greek "anōdynos," meaning "painless" or "pain-relieving"</note>—that is, things that soothe pain. So too the Academy, devoted to the study of Platonic Medicine, is accustomed to apply a servant of this kind, like an anodyne poultice, to grieving souls. I myself use this in the first place...

HEADER: SEVENTH AND EIGHTH BOOKS

I share this thought with my dearest friends as well. To my dearest friends, and therefore to Amerigo, who is most dear of all. Where there is pain, there is love <note>original: "Vbi dolor Vbi amor"</note>. Cast off love, and you shall cast off pain. I do not say to cast off the love of the Good itself—far be it from me to command something either evil or impossible. For it is both an evil thing not to love the Good itself, and it is impossible not to love that which you love by the very necessity of nature. Therefore, I command you to cast off not the love of the Good itself—which is the first, highest, and universal Good—but rather the love of those individual things which are judged as "goods" among men. Indeed, since turning toward these things in love is nothing other than turning away from the Good itself. To the extent that we turn away from Him—through whom alone these things have their goodness—and turn toward these things which are evil without Him, to that same extent we are cast headlong into evils.

Again: where there is pain, there is love. Namely, the love of these "goods" which can be both delayed and snatched away. If the possession of what we desire is delayed, pain burns and torments us. If we possess what we know can meanwhile be taken away, pain distracts us; if that which we sought and possessed through love is taken away, pain overwhelms us. Therefore, lest we be forced to grieve, let us love only the Good itself for its own sake, which alone is good through itself. Because of its infinite nature and power, this Good is never absent and thus cannot be delayed; it never fails and thus cannot be snatched away. It never deserts us unless we are the ones deserting; it never leaves us unless we are the ones leaving. The quest for the Infinite Good is not a very laborious task, for it is sought and found by the will alone. Nor is its possession a cause for anxious suspicion, for it is retained by that same will by which it was sought and acquired. In loving and possessing this One, we embrace all things as being good; once this One is abandoned—by whom alone the rest become good—all things everywhere turn into evils for us. 

Let us therefore cast off, let us cast off the affection that twists wretched men toward lower things. Let us put on the affection that raises us to the sublime. This will free our minds from evils; this will rescue us from sorrows and fill us with every good; it will affect us with every joy—a joy, I say, that shall never be taken from us. These things, dearest Amerigo, are applied briefly by us to the languors of the soul; the same are treated more broadly and elegantly by Plato, and more powerfully and divinely by the Sacred Scriptures. Farewell.

...they designate by the name of **Saturn**. But they name the Mind occupied in actions **Jupiter**: then they judge the soul made harder by anger to be **Mars**, or made softer by pleasure to be **Venus**. Furthermore, they consider that under the first leader <note>Saturn, representing the contemplative life</note>, life is led both publicly and privately as **Golden**—that is, precious, shining, and eternal. Under the second leader <note>Jupiter, representing the active/political life</note>, they consider it **Silver**; for just as silver follows gold in value, so also action ought to follow and observe contemplation, as a handmaiden follows her mistress. Next, under the third <note>Mars</note>, they think life is led as **Iron**, due to the harshest cruelty of arms. Finally, under the fourth <note>Venus</note>, it is **Lead**. For lust and pleasure are like lead: both softer and, by a certain weight, more prone to sink toward lower things. 

However, as much as those most vain men whom they commonly call **Alchemists** are deceived by both opinion and fortune as often as they attempt to melt base metals into gold, so much do those who subject lust, anger, and action to contemplation—according to their strength—succeed daily in their desire. This is so much the case that, compared to other "metals," they carry back **Gold**—that is, the most precious things in place of the worthless, and eternal things in place of the perishable. Go on then, happy James <note>Jacopo Antiquari</note>, as you have begun: as a cultivator of golden antiquity and Platonic contemplation, favor the ancients (as you already do); favor golden things, and thus you shall be **golden** to us instead of an **antiquarian** <note>Ficino is punning on the recipient's name, Antiquari, suggesting his love for the "Golden Age" makes him more than just a scholar of the past.</note>. Farewell happily, man of the Academy, dearer than gold.

->The cycle of all things exists.<-

->**Marsilio Ficino to Matteo of Forlì, Commissary of the Pontiff, sends greetings.**<-

The poets relate that **Jupiter** once snatched the empire from his father **Saturn**. But I believe that in these times, **Mars**, acting as the avenger of Saturn, has usurped the kingdom of Jupiter for himself. Indeed (as the astronomers say), religious men are signified and ruled by Jupiter. For daily, the goods of religious people are transferred to "Martial" men <note>Men of war or soldiers</note>. But I wish that, in turn, the celestial empire would follow: so that just as Jupiter once yielded to Mars, so Mars may eventually be compelled to yield to Jupiter. Surely only then, when Jupiter alone reigns, do we hope that pious men will (so to speak) reign. And perhaps within two years (unless astronomical calculation deceives us), a **Great Conjunction** of Planets <note>Referring to the 1484 conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter, which contemporaries believed would herald a major religious or political shift</note> will either achieve this or (to speak more correctly) signify it. Meanwhile, you commissaries, to whom the care of the pious flock is committed, hold that flock commended to you—commended not in a small way by God. We desire this from others, but from you, a man of distinguished piety, we now truly hope for it. Farewell. June 15, 1484.

# SEVENTH BOOK

CLXXV

->SEVENTH<-

But truly, if it is even permitted for a lover to swear falsely <note>original: "peierare"; a common classical trope that "Jove laughs at lovers' perjuries"</note>, let it also be permitted for you to discourse while speaking of love. Therefore, the first cause of this matter is **human**; the second, **natural**; the third, **celestial**; the fourth, **divine**.

The **human** cause, I say, is because love itself is the true foundation of friendship. Indeed, the power of friendship is so great that by this alone, even without any laws, the human race could live tranquilly and blessedly. But if friendship were removed, neither laws nor any other human pursuits could produce happiness. I will set aside the fact that love makes men sharp in invention, powerful in speaking, manageable, pleasant, sophisticated, and faithful to reason and custom.

The **natural** reason, moreover, is of this sort: certainly, a certain similarity is everywhere the cause of love. This is clearly perceived in the stars, the elements, plants, and animals. Whoever, therefore, is most inclined to love humans is undoubtedly judged to be most similar of all to the very <term>Idea</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, the "Idea" is the perfect, eternal blueprint of a thing existing in the divine mind</note> of the human race, according to which the divine craftsman created humanity. Conversely, whoever is most alienated from love is both most dissimilar to the divine Idea and most remote from the human species.

We receive the third and **celestial** cause from the astronomers in this way: those in whose <term>nativity</term> <note>original: "genesi"; a birth chart or astrological horoscope</note> **Venus** and **Mercury** are so disposed that, due to their mutual aspect, conjunction, reception, or <term>term</term> <note>An astrological subdivision of a zodiac sign</note>, they take up the helm of the character with a concordant will, are usually more prone to love. Then, indeed, Mercury—the master of wit and eloquence—transfers both to Venus; and Venus herself, the mother of grace, beauty, and faith, seasons the wit and eloquence with charm. She adorns them with elegance and forms them with truth-telling faith. For this reason, none are truly sharper or more elegant than lovers. However, we wish it to be hidden from no one: lust is one thing, which seeks touch; but love is another, which the Platonists judge to be content with sight, hearing, and contemplation.

Finally, the fourth reason is **divine**, which the divine **Plato** proves extensively in the *Phaedrus* and the *Symposium*. Since the exemplary <term>Forms</term> <note>The perfect "originals" of all things</note> of all things are in the divine mind, and certain shadows of them appear among us, the beauty of the Creator himself reflects more expressively in these shadows than in created beauty. Nor does Plato think we can investigate divine wisdom and the other virtues of God through human wisdom or any other virtue of ours as easily as we can find divine beauty through human beauty—and, once found, love it. For while the similarity of the other virtues that are in God belongs to and is perceived only by minds, the image of divine beauty pours itself through all things. It is clearly perceived not only by the mind but even by the eyes, which are the most piercing of all the senses.

Hence, he considers that love proceeds from the human to the divine. Accordingly, he defines love as nothing other than the **desire for beauty**. Beauty, moreover, is nothing other than **grace**—grace, I say, implanted chiefly in three things from the three Graces, and coming similarly from three divinities. For **Apollo**, through the harmony of music, attracts the listeners; **Venus**, through the grace of color and shape, ravishes those who look; **Mercury**...

<summary>Ficino outlines four foundations of love—human, natural, celestial, and divine—arguing that true Platonic love is a desire for beauty that serves as a bridge to the divine, distinct from mere physical lust.</summary>

...finally, through a wonderful grace of intelligence and eloquence, he turns contemplatives primarily toward himself, and he inflames them with the love of divine contemplation and beauty. But because it is not so much intelligence that usually transfers us into the thing we understand, but rather love that transfers us into the thing we love; therefore, our **Plato** believes that by this very desire for divine beauty, rather than by the pursuit of knowledge or any other virtue, the mind flies back to its <term>homeland</term> <note>In Platonic thought, the "homeland" or *patria* is the celestial realm of forms from which the soul originated.</note> once it has recovered its wings. ### An entreaty that the books of Plato, translated by us into Latin, be redeemed from the hands of the one who had hidden them.

### Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to Girolamo Canciano, envoy of the Duke of Urbino.

<margin>d</margin>
When your **Plato** was sold in Aegina, **Anniceris of Cyrene** redeemed him from servitude; and when he was placed in the greatest danger of his life in Sicily, **Archytas of Tarentum** liberated him from destruction. However, when the children of **Plato** <note>Ficino uses the Latin *liberi* (children) as a metaphor for Plato's books or dialogues.</note>, having left behind a Greece occupied by barbarians, betook themselves to Italy, they were by chance cast into prison; and for two whole years (oh, the shame!) they have been held in chains. But behold, now **Girolamo Canciano**, a man distinguished by piety, shall loosen them from their shackles and restore them to the light. Therefore, as much as Greece once owed to the man of Cyrene and the man of Tarentum for **Plato** himself, so much will Italy owe to **Canciano** for **Plato’s** children.

### Charity, rather than science, transports us into God.

### Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Filippo Carduccio, a man most distinguished in letters and character.

<margin>d</margin>
I decided that our little declamation, in which I was exhorting friends to piety and charity in days past, should be dedicated to my **Filippo Carduccio**, a man most full of piety and charity. But when I call him **Philip** by name and "pious," I wish for a double Philip to be understood: **Carduccio** and **Valori** <note>Filippo Valori was a wealthy patron who funded the printing of Ficino's works.</note>; therefore, may you both read this happily.

<margin>s</margin>
If God, strictly speaking, made all things by a certain bare intelligence, perhaps all things would both understand and would least of all stray from right intelligence. For through whatever property effects proceed from a cause, through that same property—as if by an image impressed upon them by the cause—they represent their own cause continually and stably. However, since not all created things have knowledge, and those which do have it often stray in their knowing, yet they all possess a natural <term>inclination</term> <note>original: "affectum"; referring to the natural drive or "appetite" of a thing toward its own good.</note> and do not err in that inclination itself, it follows that all things were created by the Creator not so much through intelligence as through **will**. This is indeed confirmed by the fact that just as they proceeded from the cause, so also are they turned back toward it. Therefore, since all things are turned back toward the Good through inclination, and not through knowledge...

# SEVENTH 176

...it follows that all things have proceeded from the Good through affection. And just as they proceeded by His affection, so everywhere they are turned back by the same. For what we call "appetite" <term>appetitionem</term> <note>In this context, *appetitio* refers to the natural inclination or "gravity" that pulls all created things toward their source.</note> in things signifies nothing other than a passion—that is, a being-seized <note>original: "raptum"</note> infused into all things by that First Principle Himself. But those who see these things moving, yet do not see Him drawing them, are deceived; they are like those who might think iron seeks the magnet of its own accord when they do not see the magnet anywhere. From this, it is clear that the divine will is the gate through which minds go out when they are created, and again the gate through which they return when they are restored.

Therefore, to the melodious psalter of David, the sacred poet, that true and almighty Apollo <note>Ficino often identifies the Greek sun-god Apollo (Phoebus) with the Christian God or Christ, as both represent the source of light and harmony.</note> from on high thunders to our minds: **"Lift up your gates, O you princes; and be lifted up, you eternal gates, and the King of Glory shall enter."** <note>original: "Attollite portas principes vestras: & eleuamini porte eternales & introibit rex glorie." A quote from Psalm 24:7.</note> O princes—O minds, princes of bodies! O princes of living things, whom "I have made a little lower than the angels, whom I have crowned with honor and glory, and whom I have rightfully set over the works of my hands." <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 8:5-6.</note> Lift up your gates: raise your wills upward! O eternal gates—O eternal wills, created from eternity and capable of eternal things—do not open yourselves to receive lower things whose entry might stain you; open yourselves to receive higher things which, by their entry, will restore you.

Then indeed I shall enter through you as the King of Glory—the King, I say, of both light and joy. "I will seal the light of my countenance upon your intellects; and I will give you my joy." <note>Reference to Psalm 4:6-7.</note> I am the gate; "whoever does not enter through it is a thief and a robber." <note>Reference to John 10:1.</note> My will is the gate through which you all went out; your will is the gate through which you shall all return to me. I am a "consuming fire" <note>Hebrews 12:29.</note> and a perfecting fire. Consuming indeed the matter, but perfecting the form. Consuming material deformity, but perfecting spiritual beauty.

Observe what fire does everywhere: fire illuminates and heats. Yet, that which is illuminated by fire does not become fire simply because it receives the light of the fire, but because it receives its heat. Similarly, like a fire, I illuminate intellects and kindle <note>The Latin "accedendo" likely stands for "accendendo" (kindling), matching the fire metaphor.</note> wills. You, however, cannot become divine simply because you seek my light by the power of understanding alone, but because you seek my heat through the burning passion of willing. Acknowledge, therefore, how great a thing love is. For I created you by my love; and you, in turn, by your love—by your love for me, I say—shall restore yourselves in me. By love I made you minds; and you, by the love of God, shall one day restore yourselves as gods. Then I shall say: "You too are gods, and all of you are children of the Most High." <note>Reference to Psalm 82:6.</note>

BOOK VIII

## Marsilio Ficino’s Preface to the Eighth Book of Letters to Filippo Valore, a Magnificent Man.

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to the most noble Filippo Valore, heir to the virtue of Valore.<-

Since I had often tried, most beloved Valore, to place a "head" <note>Ficino plays on the word *caput*, meaning both the "head" or title of a book and a person who acts as a leader or "head."</note> upon the eighth book of letters, yet was unable to do so by any means, I at last beseeched the divine power as a suppliant that it might supply me with at least as much *valor* <note>original: "valoris." A pun on his friend’s name, Filippo Valori, and the Latin word for strength, worth, or value.</note> as would suffice for applying this head. It was certainly a most happy prayer. For while I wished for *valor* in order to add the head, Valore himself has meanwhile become the head for me. Greetings, therefore, sweetest head of my book—or rather, of my child—by whom my book is led and by whom it lives; or rather, by whom many of my children <note>Ficino frequently referred to his books and students as his "children."</note> now live. Most opportunely, the Medici house <note>original: "domus medica." A pun on the name of the Medici family and the Latin word for "medical."</note> has long breathed life into them, and the Valori house breathes it as well. For since these families desire exactly the same things everywhere, and *valor* [strength] himself soon follows the *medical* [Medici] aid of prosperous health. May Almighty God always breathe upon the happiness of both families and preserve this ancient harmony. Read happily and live happily together with your most elegant brother Niccolò; and for this reading, invite Antonio Lanfredini, an excellent academic, not only as a reader but as a judge.

## Beginning of the Eighth Book.

### Giving thanks for the books of Plato redeemed by Girolamo from an occupier.

->Marsilio Ficino to Girolamo, envoy of the Duke of Urbino, sends greetings.<-

I was just thinking, Girolamo, of giving thanks to you through a letter because you freed the divine Plato from a certain daily prison and harsh shackles. But the spirit <term>genius</term> <note>original: "genius." In Neoplatonism, a guardian spirit or the higher essence of a person.</note> of Plato himself rebuked me with almost these words: "Do you so greatly magnify your eloquence, Marsilio, and so little value my freedom, that you trust you will give Girolamo thanks worthy of my liberation? I myself shall greet my Girolamo. I myself shall give thanks and I shall return them; for I shall number him among my academics, and I shall name him as my third liberator after Anniceris and Archytas." <note>According to tradition, the philosophers Anniceris and Archytas were responsible for ransoming Plato after he was sold into slavery in Syracuse.</note> Thus the spirit of Plato spoke to me just now, Girolamo; but you, listen soon to the spirit of Plato himself resonating in this very volume as if in his own body.

## Love does not endure absence.

->Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved Piero Compagni, sends greetings.<-

I first began to suspect you were absent from here when I read your letter, in which you asked when I would set out to join you. Truly, I would have arrived there long ago if I had sensed you were absent from here. Now I set out toward others because I love them less; I do not set out toward an academic because I love him too much, and I so embrace him that I do not allow him to depart. Farewell.

# BOOK EIGHT

### Marsilio Ficino to George of Cyprus, his dearest fellow-godparent and most excellent physician, sends many greetings.

<margin>c</margin>
When several learned men were speaking at your house during dinner about the most elegant *Apologues* <note>original: "Apologis." These are short fables or allegorical stories, specifically those written by the humanist Bartolomeo Scala.</note> of our writer Scala, they demanded a judgment on them from me, especially since I had read them recently. I said, "Every apologue of our Scala seems to me both elegant and masculine." But they smiled and mocked me at the same time: they smiled at "elegant," as if it were elegantly expressed, but they mocked "masculine" as if the word were used improperly. Therefore, I affirm (with you as judge) that I called Scala's apologues masculine not only properly but most truly. For who could rightly deny they are masculine when they, with a single breath, made me—who was previously sterile in such things—so fertile that I gave birth to many "apologue sons" in nearly the same labor? Indeed, this is confirmed by the fact that after those works left my household, no further apologues were born to us. Those, however, who were then born to us—perhaps somewhat weaker because of my prior sterility—I commend to you, both as a fellow-godparent <note>original: "compatri." A term of close intimacy, often implying a shared spiritual bond or actual godparenting relationship.</note> to be nurtured and as a physician to be cherished and strengthened. Farewell, my dearest fellow-godparent and best physician, and may you read with joy.

->An amatory excuse for silence when we do not respond to our friends' letters.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Filippo Valori, sends many greetings.

<margin>2</margin>
We received your letter long ago, my Valori—a letter common not only to me but also to Pietro Nero, Filippo Carducci, and finally to all the members of the Academy. Thus, it is no wonder that none of us has yet replied to the letter, since each of us thought the others would respond daily. Added to this is that a certain dialectician <note>A student or teacher of logic and formal argument.</note> from the Academy, when he heard we were being blamed because we seemed to think little of our Valori’s letter—which is in a way full of *valor* <note>A pun on the recipient's name, Filippo Valori, and the Latin word "valor," meaning worth, strength, or value.</note>—began to argue in roughly this manner: "It can easily be shown, friends, that not so much we, but Filippo himself has been the cause of this long-lasting silence. Therefore, he rather than any of us should be blamed. Truly, if Filippo Valori is our friend, he is surely our *valor* [worth]. Again, if he himself is our *valor*, then he is certainly our [own] strength. But if he is our strength, it follows that while he is absent, we ourselves are worth nothing at all <note>original: "nihil penitus valeamus." A continuation of the pun: "we have no strength/health/value."</note>. Therefore, let Valori return, and our voice will suddenly return. He gives us our wit; he takes it away." When that dialectician had concluded these things, all the others immediately agreed with most joyful applause. Only one man, a bit more curious in his arguing, set out not to disapprove of the love we all feel for you, but to reject the very form of the logical argument. But all the others, turning to him and imposing silence, concluded that "amatory conclusions," no matter how or from where they are derived, must not be dissolved, but confirmed with all one's might. Therefore, fare well...

### How individuals have guardian angels.

### Marsilio Ficino to Filippo Callimaco.

It is the opinion of the Platonists—and quite Platonic, my dear Callimaco—that there are as many legions of demons <term>demons: from the Greek *daimones*, these are not "evil spirits" in this context, but intermediary guiding spirits or "genii" that bridge the gap between gods/stars and humans</term> around the earth as there are gods (that is, stars) in the heavens. They claim that within each legion, there are as many individual demons as there are stars in the sky. There are twelve princes of these demons, just as there are twelve signs in the zodiac. Furthermore, some are of the nature of Saturn, others of Jove, others of Mars, and others of the Sun. They categorize and name these various demons according to both the name and the power of the different stars.

They add, moreover, that there are as many orders of human souls as there are stars and legions of demons counted. Souls are said to receive their nature, duty, and name from these various demons and constellations. These spirits they call "genii," the noble leaders assigned to individual souls by the "law of fate"—that is, by the very arrangement and influence of all the celestial spheres at the moment souls descend into bodies. Our minds are daily guided by them through a certain easy and hidden persuasion—so long as we do not obey certain inferior demons and the physical senses—just as ships are steered by a rudder in the hand of a pilot.

But enough about these matters for now. For this letter, whose tone of humanity and humility scarcely admits such sublime contemplations, objects to further discussion. You admit these ideas in words (as I hear, at least), my Callimaco, as a follower of our Plato. But as I see it, you do not confirm all these things in actual practice. For although you say each person has a single "good demon," you yourself most aptly possess many good ones. At one moment, your poetry brings forth an Apolline spirit; at another, your oratory shows a Mercurial one; your philosophy shows a Saturnian spirit, and your gravity a Jovian one. Magnanimity always displays a Martial spirit, while your humanity and sophistication show a Venerean one. Thus, we might rightly name our Callimaco "Polydemon" <note>original: "polidemon." From Greek, meaning "of many spirits" or "having many geniuses."</note>.

Greetings, then; greetings again, Callimaco "Polydemon." Or rather, greetings as many times as you obey your good spirits, while meanwhile ruling over the evil ones; and as many times as you, fighting nobly—which is what the name "Callimachus" <note>original: "callimachus." A Greek name meaning "beautiful fighter" (*kallos* + *mache*).</note> sounds like—conquer nobly. Is it any wonder that you bring back victory from every contest? For if Ulysses escaped safely from many dangers through a single spirit (specifically a Mercurial one), Achilles through a Martial one, and Aeneas through a Venerean one, you surely will walk most safely everywhere under the faithful guardianship of so many.

### Marsilio Ficino highly commends himself to Sebastiano Badoer and Bernardo Bembo, most distinguished Venetian ambassadors to the Supreme Pontiff.

So that you may approach the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope.</note> under more certain auspices, being about to establish that public harmony throughout all Italy which he desires: carry with you the harmony of the most excellent pagan philosophers with the divine law, and humbly commend your Marsilio, a most devoted servant to the High Pontiff.

# The Concord of Moses and Plato:

->Marsilio Ficino to Braccio Martelli, a man most highly distinguished in letters and character: Sends Greetings.<-

<margin>n</margin> Numenius the Pythagorean—whom Origen <note>A prominent early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine</note> prefers not only to the Pythagoreans but to nearly all natural philosophers—having read the books of both Moses and the Platonists, said that he recognized Moses in Plato. He famously remarked that Plato is nothing other than "a Moses speaking in the Attic tongue" <note>Attic refers to the dialect of Greek spoken in Athens; this famous quote suggests that Plato’s philosophy is simply the Hebrew truths of Moses translated into Greek philosophy</note>. Therefore, those who call you to the Academy, my best Braccio, are calling you not so much to the Platonic discipline as to the Mosaic law. For as soon as you enter the Academy, you will encounter Parmenides, who will demonstrate that there is one God, the King of all, who contains or produces the "Ideas"—that is, the most eminent models and reasons for all things. You will meet Melissus and Zeno, who demonstrate that only God truly exists, while all other things merely appear to be. You will come across Timaeus, showing that the world was created by God for the sake of His own goodness, and that God created the heaven and the earth in the beginning; then, He poured an airy spirit <note>original: "aereum spiritum," a reference to the "Spirit of God" hovering over the waters in Genesis</note> over the waters, and ordained that all these things should last according to measure as long as the divine will shall please. He will show that God made man so much in His own likeness that He established him as the unique worshiper of God on earth and the master of earthly things.

There, Protagoras, Menexenus, Critias, and the *Statesman* <note>Plato’s dialogue *Politicus*</note> will present themselves to you, discussing how men were created from the earth at the beginning of things by the power of God, and how they were placed under the perpetual custody of divine spirits. They will explain how they received the law from a certain messenger of God alone, and finally, how they shall rise again from the earth at the end of the world’s course by God’s command. There Philebus, Theaetetus, Phaedo, and Phaedrus—and Socrates himself—teach that our happiness lies in the likeness and enjoyment of God alone.

You will also hear a certain "Old Athenian" <note>A character in Plato’s *Laws*, often thought to represent Plato himself</note> asserting that the world was arranged by the Word of God <note>original: "verbum dei"</note> and that God the King is the measure of all things. This is especially true if God becomes man, striking down the proud as rebels against God, but approving the humble as most dear to Him. Finally, he proclaims to all that whether they descend into Hell or ascend into Heaven, they will find the divine judge everywhere. You will hear there Hermias, Erastus, and Coriscus being taught that God is the leader and cause of all things, both Father and Son, and that the highest good is established in the singular love of Him. Furthermore, you will hear Dionysius <note>Ficino refers to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, whom he believed was a contemporary of Paul but who used Platonic language</note> being taught that the King of all things exists, and that all things are for His sake, and that He is the cause of all good things. He will explain that the blessed spirits are distinguished in this order: some reflect the power of God as the "efficient cause," others His wisdom or "exemplar," and others His goodness as the "end" or goal of all things. Finally, you will hear from the Syracusans <note>Refers to Plato’s Seventh Letter, written to the associates of Dion in Syracuse</note> that divine mysteries cannot be grasped by reason, but by purity of mind, until finally one becomes like God; then, just as if from a flickering fire, a light suddenly shines in the soul and henceforth nourishes itself.

Next, you will look upon Er the Pamphylian <note>A character from the end of Plato's *Republic* who returns from the dead</note> rising from the dead by divine command to report the secrets of souls to the living. He will lead you through the Elysian Fields, which our people signify by the name of "Paradise." He will point his finger toward the underworld, the cavern of Purgatory, and Limbo. Socrates tells you these same things in many...

Everywhere he will confirm with reasons and teach that we must have a care for eternity much more than for time. He will teach that transitory things should be despised so that we may obtain eternal ones, and that it is better to suffer even the gravest injuries than to inflict them. Nothing else should be cared for or striven for than that we might offer a most pure soul to the Judge who sees all things. Therefore, he will prove that confession and voluntary repentance for sins are, above all, necessary for the salvation of men. But he will command that one must hasten to it especially, lest the old disease of the soul become utterly incurable. Finally, he will warn us that we are carried through the sea of this life on the ship of most exact reason until we are finally carried forward more safely and happily by the divine word. There, Laches <note>The title character of the dialogue *Laches*, which discusses courage</note> will also exhort us to frequent confession and repentance of faults. But why had I passed over the noble Charmides? For here he will shortly reveal to you that all the inconveniences of both the body and fortune proceed from a certain ancient intemperance of our souls. And again, he will add that if that original purity of souls is restored, immortality also must be restored. Finally, the *Critias* <note>A Platonic dialogue that Ficino here interprets as an allegory for the Book of Genesis</note> in the very inner sanctum of the Academy will proclaim like a Mosaic oracle: That God, when He had created the world, finally made man (as Protagoras also said) on earth most like Himself, and filled him with a certain nourishing grace, by which, so long as it remained, he would perpetually enjoy all the goods of the soul, the body, and fortune. He also placed him in His gardens under a perpetual spring, where he would prolong his happy life by a meager tasting of healthy fruits. He moreover fenced the gardens so that nothing foreign might enter. But when man turned aside little by little from divine things to transitory ones and obeyed the laws of his Father less and less day by day, that divine grace vanished. And for this reason, he fell into a shameful state of mind, diseases of the body, the anxiety of life, and labors; and finally, he was moved from those gardens to regions very different indeed. That this indeed happened unhappily through a certain evil demon lying in wait under the bait of more insolent pleasure. Timaeus, Phaedrus, and Diotima <note>original: "Diotinia," a likely typo for Diotima, the priestess in Plato's *Symposium*</note> in the Academy will bear witness to this. Nor indeed should that golden sentence of Plato, the leader of the Academy, be passed over, when he says that one must acquiesce to his precepts only until someone more sacred than a man appears on earth who might open the fountain of truth to everyone, whom finally all might follow. ### The Confirmation of Christians through the Socratic Way.

### Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Paolo Ferobanti, a distinguished theologian.

If I did not fear, excellent Paolo, that there would be some who—either through the depravity of their nature or the smallness of their judgment—might seize upon my words in a sense other than I intend, I would demonstrate that Socrates (though not in the same form as Job or John the Baptist) perhaps prefigured Christ, the author of our salvation, in a certain foreshadowing. I would do this chiefly for this reason: to confound that detractor Lucian, <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125–180 AD), a satirist known for mocking both traditional religion and the early Christians</note> who, after he had slandered all good men, finally did not spare the Christians, daring to mock the martyrs of our faith because they, as if they were too simple, willingly gave up all things held to be good among men, and as if they were unfortunate, voluntarily exposed themselves to tortures and slaughter. 

Against Lucian, who mocks the simple, one must hold up Socrates, judged the wisest of all by the testimony of great philosophers and the oracle of Apollo. This man, not out of some crude simplicity, but rather through a singular excellence of mind and (as Plato and Xenophon testify) a certain innate divinity and prophetic gift, preferred eternal goods to fleeting ones throughout his whole life. He voluntarily sustained the hardships of the body—especially hunger and nakedness—and all the misfortunes of fate, terrified only by the evil and everlasting damage to the soul. He was intent solely on the duty of piety and charity. Indeed, neglecting his own advantages and held back by no danger, he applied himself everywhere to purging the minds of men as if he were a physician of souls, even beyond the borders of his own country. While he detested pride above all else, he approved of gentleness, charity, and religion more than all other things. He professed only the study of true love and charity, and excluded the ambitious profession of the sciences. 

He leaned everywhere upon divine testimonies and clung to them with firm faith; he was content with pious and just character. And—what is marvelous—he hoped for no human reward for such a laborious duty, but rather subjected himself to certain danger and death for its sake. Truly, he asserted that he was sent by God for this one purpose, and he said he preferred to obey God rather than men. But let us hear Socrates himself for a moment, crying out thus before his unjust judges: "But that I am such a person as to have been given to the city by God, you may observe from this: It certainly does not seem human that I have entirely neglected all my own affairs, and in this matter..."

...[Socrates said:] I have persevered for so many years in this familiar negligence and poverty, always focused on your good, while I meet each of you like a father or an older brother, so that God may have his own care for virtue. If I were to receive some human reward for my duty, that would have a certain logic. These are his words. And so, while he corrects sinners, and being struck by a heel, he greets the striker; and having been struck on one cheek, he offers the other. <note>Ficino is drawing a direct parallel between Socrates’ behavior in Plato's dialogues and Jesus’s command in the Sermon on the Mount to "turn the other cheek."</note> Finally, he brought back such hatred from the truth that he was accused of impiety by the very people to whom he had openly preached the duty of piety. What indeed shall I say of the fact that, although he could easily have defended himself in court, he did not? Nor did he excuse himself, but rather accused the judges. And when he could have left the prison, he refused, and most willingly endured an unjust death, about to give examples of the highest constancy and patience to posterity. 

I pass over for now the thirty pieces of money—the price set upon Socrates—and Socrates' own prophecies, as well as the vengeance that followed suddenly from God after his death. <note>Ficino likens the "thirty pieces of silver" paid for Judas's betrayal to the legal fees or bribes associated with Socrates' trial, and the later plague or misfortunes in Athens to the divine "vengeance" for his death.</note> I pass over the washing instituted by Socrates in the evening shortly before his death and his exhortation to piety at the time of the meal. What about the fact that in that same hour mention is made of a cup and a blessing, and at his very death, a rooster? <note>Socrates drank a cup of poison (hemlock); his last words were to Crito, asking him to sacrifice a rooster to Asclepius, the god of healing—an act Ficino interprets here as a symbolic religious ritual or "blessing" at the hour of death.</note> I pass over, moreover, many deeds and words of Socrates, written not indeed by himself but by four of his disciples especially, by which a Christian is greatly confirmed against Lucian. <note>Lucian of Samosata was a 2nd-century skeptic who mocked both Christians and philosophers. Ficino notes that Socrates had four main biographers (likely Plato, Xenophon, Antisthenes, and Aeschines), just as Christ had four Evangelists.</note> For there are many things, and those indeed the greatest, which they pass down concerning the divine spirit <note>original: "numine," referring to the *daemon* or inner divine voice of Socrates</note> infused into him, the abstraction of the mind from the body, and a certain kind of transfiguration. Truly, a letter could not easily contain these things, nor would some perhaps receive them kindly, thinking perhaps that Socrates is now being compared as a rival, whereas I am preparing him as a defender.

### In What the Praise of a Prince Consists.

->Marsilio Ficino sends warmest greetings to Galeotto, Prince of Faenza.<-

<margin>a</margin> My friend Lamanus just now asks me to set out for Faenza, where I am also about to go of my own accord. Indeed, even long ago (at Plato’s command), since he has for a long time prophesied to me from on high that what once happened to him not at all on his third journey to Sicily, I would immediately achieve and find in this present first journey: namely, a man who is a prince of himself before he is a prince of the people, and not so much a lord as a father of his country. One who honors not only the citadels of Mars <note>The god of war; i.e., military strength</note> but also of Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom; i.e., intellectual pursuits</note>; who represents Mars among the soldiers and plays the role of Apollo among the Muses. O happy city, O truly Faventia <note>The Latin name for Faenza, *Faventia*, is related to the word *faventia* (favor/goodwill). Ficino is making a pun on the city's name and the Prince's favor.</note>, which God has favored so wonderfully and propitiously, and which He has made happy through the favor of a most happy prince.

### He who commends everyone is to be commended by everyone.

### Marsilio Ficino to Bandino. <note>Probably Francesco Bandini, a member of the Platonic Academy and a diplomat.</note>

<margin>f</margin>If anyone is to be honored by all, it is undoubtedly the one who himself honors everyone. Therefore, everyone owes honor to the poet Verrino <note>Michele Verino (1469–1487), a brilliant young poet in the Medicean circle who died young.</note>. For he is so grateful and so full of grace that he honors everyone: both those to whom he owes it, most gratefully, and those to whom he does not owe it, freely. He favors the good; he exalts geniuses; he adorns the learned; he illuminates princes; he cherishes the holy; in short, he venerates the divine in all things. Why say more? Listen to the man himself. For he who praises everyone will himself be praised in everyone. Unless, indeed, that man to whom all honest men are commended is commended to you, I do not know whom you could ever have as a recommendation.

### Praise of Charity.

### Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to Hermolao Barbaro of Venice. <note>Ermolao Barbaro (1454–1493) was a famous Venetian scholar and diplomat known for his elegant translations of Aristotle.</note>

<margin>c</margin>Charity seeks not her own interests, but those of others. Charity believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity thinks no evil. Charity never fails. Finally, in charity there is no fear; but perfect charity casts all fear far away. <note>Ficino is quoting and paraphrasing the famous passage on Love/Charity from St. Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, chapter 13.</note> The prelates of divine religion cry these things out with simple words but with a certain immense mystery. You, most kind Barbaro, observe all these things toward me—perhaps by some fate—as if toward one who is unrefined <note>original: "inhumanum." Ficino is playing on the contrast between Barbaro's kindness ("humanitas") and his own perceived lack of it, or perhaps playing on Barbaro's name, which literally means "Barbarian."</note>, so that I do not doubt that this very charity, which the fathers of Christian piety desire above all, burns greatly within you. Truly, my most beloved Hermolao, I call God to witness—who is Charity itself—that you have so expressed that very <term>Idea of Charity</term> <note>Ficino blends the Platonic concept of an "Idea" (the perfect, divine form of a thing) with the Christian virtue of Charity.</note> and placed it before my eyes that I, who until now loved you as much as I could and as a free man, am now compelled to love you beyond my strength and of necessity. Until now, therefore, I was able not to love and to bear your absence; but now, for the future, I cannot help but love you, and I cannot bear your absence with a calm mind as I used to. I hope, however, that God, who has miraculously joined our souls, will one day similarly join our eyes. Nor would we wish anyone to think that Hermolao and Marsilio are perhaps for that reason less "one" or should be considered less joined: just because one seems to favor Aristotle and the other Plato. For we are one in the same cultivation of truth and virtue, in which Plato and Aristotle could not fail to be one. Continue, therefore, most broadly and in the <term>Attic style</term> <note>original: "attice." Referring to the pure, elegant Greek of Athens, as opposed to the "barbarous" translations of the Middle Ages.</note>, Barbaro, and (as you have begun) vigorously rescue the Attic Aristotle from long-standing barbarism...

->More should not be demanded of a friend than he possesses.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Aurelio of Rimini sends many greetings.<-

<margin>e</margin> You will think, most just Aurelio, that I have done enough for you if I am yours as often as I am my own. Indeed, I think it is enough. For I know your fairness and modesty will demand nothing more of me than I myself have of myself. Until now, I have not been under "Marsilian" law, but rather under Platonic law. Having been entirely devoted to the interpretation of this man for a long time, I finally—with God's help—finished the Platonic work yesterday. Now for the first time I am restored to myself, and likewise restored to my friends. You sent many poems to us during this past summer, composed partly by you and partly by friends, in which I praise the human art, marvel at the Apolline fury <note>original: "apollineum furorem"; referring to the Platonic concept of divine poetic inspiration.</note>, and greatly approve of your piety toward deceased friends. I give you immense thanks for this immense gift.

->Commendation of Platonic books.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Bandini sends many greetings.<-

<margin>a</margin> Plato finally comes to you through the pious work of Filippo Valori <note>Filippo Valori was a wealthy patron who funded the printing of Ficino's Latin translation of Plato in 1484.</note>; certainly, without his singular "valor," Plato would never have been able to travel across such vast distances. Therefore, act now, my fellow-Platonist Bandini: as much as I love you and you love me, honor Plato as you usually do. And if Plato, a traveler once again, has need of hospitality, be his host. Again, if he has need of a herald because he is little known there, be his herald. If, finally, <margin>b</margin> a defense becomes necessary for him as he trembles among adversaries, be his patron.

->Excuse when answering friends briefly.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Calderino sends many greetings.<-

<margin>n</margin> No one looks upon the letters of friends more happily or responds more eagerly than Marsilio, for whom nothing is pleasing without friends. However, as to why I have scarcely returned one reply to your two letters, that great Platonist Plotinus <note>Plotinus was the 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism; Ficino began translating his "Enneads" immediately after finishing Plato.</note> is the cause. Since he recently learned (with me as his guide, or rather his translator) that his beloved Plato has moved into another land, he urges me diligently day and night not to allow Plato to wander among the Italians any longer without his "faithful Achates" <note>Achates was the loyal companion of Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid; here, Ficino means Plotinus's writings are the necessary companion to understand Plato.</note>. I am, therefore, so vehemently intent upon this huge work that I sometimes hardly remember myself. As soon as Plotinus restores me to myself, he will restore me to my friends.

...indeed, you demonstrate that you are most occupied with divine matters. On this subject, I would most willingly discuss more things with you, were it not that our Plotinus <note>Plotinus was a 3rd-century philosopher and the primary developer of Neoplatonism; Ficino spent years translating his difficult Greek into Latin.</note> recalls me at every moment to the work of interpretation. ## That one must proceed where God leads by His guidance.
### Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Bandini, many greetings.

<margin>p</margin> Bandini, I believe the Plato you seek has already reached you before these letters. Read him happily in the meantime, while I devote my efforts so that you may eventually read [the rest]. After reading Plato, read Plotinus. Plotinus, easily the chief of our Platonists along with his master Plato, composed fifty-four divine books. At this very hour (God breathing upon me), I have placed the final hand on his thirtieth book. So indeed almighty God commands; divine providence leads us this way; therefore, let us follow.

## A Question: Whether philosophical works are governed by fate or by providence.
### Janus Pannonius to Marsilio Ficino the Platonist, many greetings.

<margin>l</margin> I read in Buda <note>The capital of the Kingdom of Hungary, where Janus Pannonius served as a bishop and diplomat.</note> in the letter to Bandini, as well as in your preface to Plato and in the preface to your *Theology* <note>Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*, his major work reconciling Platonic philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note>, how much you attribute to providence. Yet someone might suspect it to be a matter of fate. First, I do not clearly see to what end the renewal of the ancients serves providence. Furthermore, that ancient theology of the ancients is not Christian. Besides, I remember when I once traveled to Italy to be educated in Latin and Greek literature in Florence, I heard from two of your astrologers that, based on a certain position of the stars, you would renew the ancient opinions of the philosophers. Although I heard that stellar position, I do not recall it well enough; but I think you remember it, or rather discovered it yourself. Those astrologers also brought to confirm their judgment the fact that at a certain fated time, you had restored to light the ancient sound of the lyre, and the Orphic songs and poems <note>original: "carmina orphica"; Ficino was famous for singing these "Hymns of Orpheus" while playing a lira da braccio.</note> previously consigned to oblivion. Soon you also translated the very ancient Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "mercurium trismegistum"; a legendary Egyptian sage thought to be a contemporary of Moses.</note> and many Pythagorean works. Likewise, you explained the poems of Zoroaster, and before I returned here from Florence, you had laid your hand on translating Plato—under the same (as I indeed suspect) astronomical auspices. Moreover, that these things happen not so much by providence as by a certain fate is also evidenced by the fact that before all these things, you slightly promoted a certain ancient philosopher or poet when you were still a youth. Whom you then, relying on better counsel, suppressed <note>original: "supraexisti"; this likely refers to Ficino's youthful interest in Lucretius and Epicureanism, which he later renounced and reportedly burned his commentaries on.</note> and (as I hear) pulled out with all your strength. Nor had that been a gift of divine providence, which you yourself, having become more prudent with age, rightly judged worthy of condemnation. Indeed, I warn you as a friend to beware lest perhaps a certain curiosity—if this renewal of the ancients is that, rather than religion...
