### That divine providence has decreed the renewal of ancient things.
->Marsilio Ficino to Janus Pannonius, many greetings.<-

<margin>s</margin> If you had understood our writings, which you say you have read, you would not now doubt for what reason this renewal of ancient things of ours serves divine providence. To begin with, we ought not to demand the highest Christian standards from those who lived before the coming of Christ, nor should we consider that the sharp and, in a sense, philosophical wits of men could be enticed and led bit by bit toward perfect religion by any bait other than a philosophical one. For sharp wits entrust themselves to reason alone, but when they receive religion from a certain religious philosopher, they immediately and willingly embrace the common faith. Once imbued with this, they are more easily led toward the better form of religion contained within that genus. And so, it has happened not without the will of divine providence—which wishes to recall all people to itself wonderfully according to their individual talents—that a certain pious philosophy was once born among the Persians under Zoroaster <note>Zoroaster was the legendary ancient Persian prophet to whom many mystical texts were attributed in the Renaissance.</note> and among the Egyptians under Hermes <note>original: "Mercurio". Ficino refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of Egyptian wisdom.</note>; in both places, it was consistent with itself. It was then nourished among the Thracians under Orpheus and Aglaophemus. It grew up soon after under Pythagoras among the Greeks and Italians, and finally, it was brought to completion in Athens by the divine Plato. However, it was the old custom of theologians to cover divine mysteries with both mathematical numbers and figures, and with poetic fictions. Plotinus <note>A 3rd-century philosopher who revived and expanded Plato's teachings; Ficino considered him the most important interpreter of the Platonic tradition.</note> finally stripped these veils from theology, and he was the first and only one—as Porphyry and Proclus testify—to penetrate the divine secrets of the ancients. But on account of his incredible brevity of words, his abundance of thoughts, and his depth of meaning, he requires not only a translation of the language but also commentaries. We, therefore, have labored thus far in translating and explaining the earlier theologians. Now, however, we labor daily in the books of Plotinus in the same way, having been destined by divine power for this work just as they were for theirs. Our hope is that when this Theology comes into the light, poets may cease to count the deeds and mysteries of piety among their impious fables, and all the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle. In Ficino's time, "Peripatetic" was often synonymous with "university philosopher."</note>—that is, all the philosophers—may be warned that one should not think of religion, based as it is on reason, as if it were an old wives' tale. For the whole world is occupied by Peripatetics and is divided largely into two sects: the Alexandrian and the Averroistic. <note>The Alexandrians followed Alexander of Aphrodisias and believed the soul dies with the body; the Averroists followed the Islamic philosopher Averroes and believed there was only one "intellect" for the whole human race, effectively denying individual immortality.</note> The former think our intellect is mortal, while the latter contend there is only one. Both groups utterly undermine all religion. If anyone thinks that such widespread impiety, protected as it is by sharp wits, can be erased among men by a certain simple preaching of faith alone, he will soon be proven by the facts to be wandering far from the truth. There is need here of a much greater power: either by divine miracles appearing everywhere, or at least by a certain philosophical religion which may one day persuade the philosophers, who will listen to it more willingly. It pleases divine providence in these centuries to confirm the nature of its own religion by philosophical authority and reason, until at a certain appointed time, it may manifest the lowest form <note>Ficino uses "infimam speciem" likely to mean the most accessible or fundamental version of religion.</note> of the true religion (as it once did long ago) through clear...

<summary>Ficino defends his revival of ancient Neoplatonism as a tool of divine providence designed to convert skeptical Aristotelian intellectuals to Christianity through reason. He outlines a lineage of "pious philosophy" stretching from Zoroaster to Plato and Plotinus.</summary>

<header>EIGHTH BOOK 182</header>

...and confirms all nations with miracles. Now, regarding the fact that you, wishing to attribute the cause of this work of ours to Fate, have touched upon our birth chart: I do not indeed deny the nature of this very figure. That Saturn was ascending in Aquarius, and the Sun and Mercury were in the ninth house of the heavens <note>In Renaissance astrology, the ninth house is the "House of God," governing religion, philosophy, and long journeys.</note>, and the other planets were in aspect to that same ninth house: these signify a man who is a renewer of ancient things, but I deny that they *cause* it. 

You too, if you read our letter on the star of the Magi <note>original: "de magorum stella"</note> and a similar discussion in our *Platonic Theology*, as well as the books of Plotinus <note>Ficino translated the works of Plotinus, a 3rd-century Neoplatonist, into Latin.</note> dealing with this very matter—which we have also translated—you will clearly understand that services to the public good pertaining to souls depend chiefly on the supreme minds who are the ministers of the highest God, as if from common and primary causes. They also proceed, in a way, from human counsels as if from their own and ultimate causes, whenever they accommodate themselves to those heavenly things. You will learn, moreover, that things are signified by the heavenly figures and motions as if by the instruments of divine minds, and that Fate—that is, the series of celestial causes—serves divine providence. Indeed, our souls are judged to be most free when they most fully agree with the divine will. 

Since I know you to be a great student of the poets, I shall conclude the whole matter with Virgil <note>original: "marone". Publius Vergilius Maro is the Roman poet Virgil.</note>. Aeneas—that is, the heroic soul—is about to descend to the underworld and ascend again; that is, he is about to penetrate the secrets of divine mysteries and bring obscure things into the light. He is led to this very thing by divine providence, as one who is (as Virgil says) "born of the gods" and whom "impartial Jupiter loved" <note>original: "divinitus genitus... aequus amabat Iuppiter". A reference to Aeneid VI.129-131.</note>; and divine oracles urged him toward the same. Again, he proceeds toward this by a certain free will, where "burning virtue carries him to the heavens," and where he consults what is best to be done and consults the oracles of his own accord, and always most willingly agrees with the divine judgment. Fate also contributes to the same, serving the providence designated by the oracle. For the poet says: *Seize it with your hand; for it will follow of its own accord and easily if the fates call you; otherwise, you will not be able to conquer it by any strength, nor tear it away with hard iron.* <note>original: "Carpe manus nanq[ue] ipse volens facilisq[ue] sequetur. Si te fata vocant: aliter non viribus vllis Vincere: Neq[ue] duro poteris conuellere ferro". This describes Aeneas plucking the Golden Bough in Aeneid VI.</note> 

Truly, Fate, like a herald of providence, calls you to that and signifies to you what providence has ordained and commanded. You, however, are able to bring the arduous work to its conclusion only insofar as these two things breathe upon you. You also act freely only insofar as you willingly obey providence. And then, in truth, you are a master in the kingdom of Fate when you are seen to be a servant in the kingdom of providence. Fare well.

Ficino is apologizing for the many typographical errors in the first edition.</note> than they should have been, you should think happened to us partly through the negligence of the printers—or rather, the oppressors—and partly (if it is right to say so) through the malice of fortune. You grieve, however, because of your devotion, that this old man of ours [Plato] has come to you in such a squalid state. Stop grieving, I pray, my dear Bandino. For thus...

### A defense for silence.

->Marsilio Ficino to Amerigo Corsini. Many greetings.<-

I indeed said to your brother Filippo—a man of integrity and learning—that in these times it is not permitted for me either to write to friends away from the city or even to greet those who are present. For Plotinus the Platonist <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism. Ficino spent years translating his difficult Greek works into Latin.</note> claims me entirely for himself. Because of this, you immediately accuse Plotinus of jealousy with a forceful speech and a very sharp poem. You claim that he, who belongs to no one himself, contends that I—who usually belong to almost everyone—should belong to no one. But I now, Amerigo, am striving in turn so that Plotinus shall belong to everyone; and while I diligently indulge this one man who will soon belong to all, I seem in the meantime to indulge everyone. Farewell.

### Prophets and the interpreters of prophets.

->Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to his fellow Platonist,<-
->Domenico Benivieni.<-

You were asking in recent days (and very subtly, as is your custom) by what power everything remains alive after such a long reading of Plato, since your first reading of our Plato seized your soul and suddenly transferred you entirely into Plato himself. Unless our Plato were alive, my Domenico—and indeed, unless he lived far better than we do—we would surely slip into death during the process of being transferred into Plato. But since he once lived a life of eternal character among men, he now rightly lives an eternal life and does not turn his readers toward death, but more happily converts them toward life. For the moment, I set aside the arguments for such a great gift. Let us discuss what is urgent now. Tell me, who would now heal our wounds—which the Hebrew physicians <note>The term "physician" here refers to scholars or "doctors" of philosophy and scripture.</note> inflict on us daily—unless it be our Plato, the physician of souls? You too were present at the disputes which were often handled, and are still handled, in the home of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <note>Pico was a brilliant young philosopher who attempted to harmonize all branches of knowledge.</note>—a man to be admired above all others. There, Elia and Abraham, Hebrew physicians and Peripatetics <note>original: "peripatetici." These were followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy. Elia del Medigo and Abraham Farissol were Jewish scholars who debated with Pico.</note>, argue against Guglielmo the Sicilian <note>Guglielmo Raimondo de Moncada, a Jewish convert to Christianity and teacher of Pico.</note>. They contend that the oracles of the prophets do not pertain to Jesus at all, but were spoken in some other sense. They turn everything elsewhere and wrench the texts from our hands with all their strength; they seem unable to be easily convinced unless the divine Plato comes forward into judgment as an undefeated supporter of holy religion. Therefore, let us hear him and consider carefully what he said on this matter in the <term>Timaeus</term> <note>The *Timaeus* is Plato's famous dialogue on the creation of the world; Ficino uses it here to explain the nature of prophecy.</note>, and let him now bring it forward for us. "Some," he says, "are seers, others are interpreters of seers. For those who prophesy often do not know what they prophesy, while those who interpret quickly..."

<meta>This page continues the letter from Marsilio Ficino to his friend Domenico Benivieni regarding the nature of prophecy. ### EIGHTH BOOK 183

...is more likely to err in foreseeing. The reason for this is that hunting-like shrewdness <note>original: "solertia venatoria." Ficino uses this metaphor to describe an active, searching intellect that "hunts" for answers, contrasting it with the passive reception of divine prophecy.</note> requires a swift and versatile wit, whereas a presaging faculty <note>original: "praesaga facultas." The ability to sense the future before it happens.</note> requires a mind that is peaceful and quiet. These qualities, being somewhat contrary to one another, do not easily occur in the same person.

Therefore, from this opinion of our Plato, we can gather that certain foreknowledge of future things exists in God alone. We can conclude that the divine mind speaks of future things through the prophet as if through a tongue, and while the mind understands, the tongue meanwhile is ignorant. Nor is it without merit that they are called "Prophets"—that is, "fore-tellers"—and "fate-speakers" <note>original: "fatidici." From the Latin 'fatum' (fate) and 'dicere' (to speak).</note>—that is, "fore-tellers of the fates." Yet they are not called "fore-knowers" or "the fore-knowing," as if it were their duty to understand; rather, their duty is solely to announce the things foreknown by the divine mind.

If they are called "presaging"—that is, "pre-sensing"—this very presage seems to pertain not to the mind and reason, but to the senses and the imagination. Therefore, let the prediction of the future reside in the tongue of prophecy, and let some imagination of the future reside in the prophet's senses. But the certain reason and the final outcome of that future thing reside in the divine mind.

Yet the prophet does not speak entirely at random. For while he thinks he is imagining something of his own and hopes he is saying that very thing, he may meanwhile announce something else; though it is similar, it is nonetheless different. He who blows the prophetic trumpet <note>Ficino uses the "trumpet" as a metaphor for the prophet being a vessel for God's voice.</note> to its sound foreknows this distinction clearly. Finally, after the event has occurred, it is discovered by an interpreter that it happened exactly as the prophet had uttered—almost beyond his own expectation—and as God Himself had foreknown.

It did not escape the Evangelist <note>The "Evangelist" refers to the author of the Gospel of John (John 11:49–52).</note> that the predictions of those prophesying are of such a kind when he says that Caiaphas the high priest prophesied, saying: *It is better that one man should die for the people than that the whole nation should perish.* The Evangelist indeed accepts these words as certain prophecies concerning the death of Christ for the sake of the people; however, he knows that they were announced by Caiaphas with a entirely different meaning <note>Caiaphas meant it as a political necessity to kill Jesus to satisfy the Romans; God meant it as a spiritual sacrifice for humanity.</note>.

It did not escape the Apostle Paul that the prophets by no means understood what they were saying when he said that the entire Old Testament existed "under a cloud and a veil," and that all things happened to them "in a certain figure" <note>original: "sub figura." This refers to typology, the idea that Old Testament events were "types" or shadows of New Testament truths.</note>. He wishes, therefore, that almost everything—not only the words but the deeds—signified future things. Yet he would not admit that the ancients, whatever they spoke or whatever they did, knew that these actions of theirs portended our own times.

It did not escape the prophet David that the prophets, like "infants and sucklings," do not sufficiently understand what they predict. I pass over what others say about Balaam’s ass <note>A biblical story (Numbers 22) where an animal is granted the power of speech by God to deliver a message, illustrating that the speaker need not be a rational human to be a vessel for prophecy.</note> fore-signifying future things, and what the Gentiles write so extensively about auguries and auspices. For the birds know that they signify and announce certain future things, yet they are entirely ignorant of what those things actually portend.

Therefore, let the mockers of the Jews be silent now. Let it be, if you like, that Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, and others announced some things in the sense in which the Hebrews everywhere interpret them. But meanwhile, as they were announcing them, it was hidden from them what God Himself intended, or what event—similar to the prophets' words yet nonetheless different—He had predestined to occur.

By this very opinion and exposition of Plato, my dear Domenico, the commentaries of the Jewish interpreters may proceed in their usual course, yet Jewish "cunning" is broken and Christian truth is preserved. Farewell. But after I said farewell, I remembered: Christian doctors count wisdom together with prophecy. And the same...

# BOOK

...that Iamblichus the Platonist <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Neoplatonist who emphasized the role of divine inspiration over human logic.</note> and Paul <note>St. Paul the Apostle.</note> affirm and say: he who predicts or presages something without wisdom is not to be approved <note>original: "probabilem." In this context, it means one whose words are backed by their own understanding or merit.</note>, but is perhaps prophetic. Therefore, by this distinction, we can more safely accept those things which have been brought from Plato into the sacred scriptures.

### Marsilio Ficino commends himself to the Reverend father and lord in Christ, Lord Marco of Venice, Cardinal of Saint Mark:

Our Plato, having set out for Rome, has been wandering for a long time, seeking everywhere a lodging most suited to his genius and character. This divine guest desires a pure and sacred host: a wise man for the learned, an elegant man for the eloquent. At last, after long wanderings, he rests most willingly in the narrow halls of Marco of Venice, the Cardinal, as if in a port. He considers that he has attained a second Academy <note>The "Academy" refers to the Platonic Academy in Florence, which Ficino led under Medici patronage.</note> there; and he hopes—which he desired above all—that the singular wisdom of his host will not lack supreme power. Plato, therefore, having entered your household by this choice and these two auspices, lives with you especially in that spirit. Meanwhile, Plato himself will prophesy to you with what mind I am toward you, and with what love and observance I am affected, until our friend Antonio Calderino <note>A scholar and secretary who served as a go-between for Ficino and his Roman patrons.</note> reveals my mind to you—a most rich witness of your doctrine and probity, a herald of your virtues among us, and a messenger of our singular observance toward you. Farewell.

### A man's enemies are those of his own household: <note>original: "Inimici hominis domestici eius." A quote from Matthew 10:36.</note>

### Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to Pierleone, the singular Platonist and Peripatetic.

Greetings for a long time now, my fellow Platonist; and greetings for a long time now with Plato being safe; greetings also recently, my fellow Platonist, with Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism. Ficino had just finished translating his massive "Enneads" from Greek to Latin.</note> now safe. Receive some books of Plotinus which you were expecting here; yesterday I put an end to the task of translating them all. What remains is to revise the words and to make the often obscure sense clearer with certain arguments. You indeed were wishing that, with these things finally settled, I would make many books of Hippocrates Latin. But I, once Plotinus is soon finished, am compelled not to translate the physician but to act as one. Yet you will say it is not becoming for a priest. Why a priest? It is better for a priest to serve as a physician than to need a physician. I have lived until now, and I still live, as most becomes a philosopher, content with slender means. But the nephews and orphaned nieces, now of marriageable age, living at home do not live with that same contentment—a man's enemies are those of his own household. I have indeed always lived in the manner of the plants <note>original: "phantis," likely a corruption of "plantis" (plants/lilies), referring to the lilies of the field from the Sermon on the Mount.</note>, never thinking of tomorrow; but today the domestic crowd compels me against my will (which God forbids) to think of tomorrow. I have tried to open my fortune more often this year to our Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, the ruler of Florence and Ficino's primary patron.</note>, hoping that I would only need a sign for him rather than prayers; but a somewhat rustic shame has often restrained me. Perhaps a letter or a friend will blush less. Farewell. Florence, the 17th day of January, 1485.

# EIGHTH [BOOK] 184

<margin>m</margin> They say that Mercury (as is not hidden from you, Reverend Father <note>Likely Marco Barbo, Cardinal of St. Mark, mentioned on the previous page.</note>) is accustomed not only to announcing words but also to interpreting the mind of the sender. They also attribute to Mercury the timely gift of remembrance, and not without reason; for just as they attribute the movement of the body to the Moon, they attribute the movement of the soul to <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurio." The Roman messenger god, identified with the Greek Hermes, associated with communication, intellect, and the movement of the spirit.</note>. Therefore, while he moves sense in the soul, he seems to announce; while he moves reason, he seems to interpret. But when he excites the memory, he is seen to awaken remembrance. To what end is this? Truly, our friend Calderino <note>Antonio Calderino (1448–1503), a scholar and diplomat who served as a bridge between the Florentine Academy and the papal court in Rome.</note> seems to perform the complete office of Mercury among us. For he not only delivers your letters to me as a messenger and reports your words, but he also interprets your mind toward me. Finally, he does not "teach" me of your love, but rather recalls it to my memory. For I have known for a long time that I am vehemently loved by you, announced not by any other means but by the consciousness of my own soul. Other human things, Reverend Father, we learn from external conjectures: how learned someone might be, how handsome, how powerful and wealthy. But that someone loves us is not taught by external things—for these very often deceive—but the soul, affected by love toward that person, teaches it most certainly. For by that same similarity of either <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "ingenii."</note> or even <term>guiding spirit</term> <note>original: "genii." In Neoplatonism, the "genius" is a personal protective spirit that defines one's character.</note> by which I have long loved you, I am loved in return. Since there is a mutual similarity, I do not doubt that I am loved by you. Therefore, let our Mercury, who recently performed his duty among us in your name, perform it in turn among you in our name. Yet even so, he could not express how much I value your judgment and how wonderfully I honor your singular virtues. But what even Mercury himself (so to speak) cannot explain, let Apollo at least bring forth by prophecy, and finally, let Jupiter happily fulfill the duty.

->Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Calderino, sends many greetings.<-

<margin>f</margin> Greetings, our Calderino. May our letter also be well. Since you departed from us during a solar eclipse, who would wonder that our letter then suffered an "eclipse" as well? Truly, two closing remarks were somehow missing at its end; perhaps because two quarters of the sun’s light failed. Phoebus <note>Apollo, the sun god.</note> suddenly resumed his light, and soon our letter resumed its ending.

->Marsilio Ficino to Braccio Martelli, a most distinguished citizen of excellent character, sends many greetings.<-

<margin>c</margin> When in recent days I was staying with Filippo and Niccolò Valori at their estate in Maiano <note>A hillside area near Fiesole, home to the villas of many Florentine humanists.</note>, and was investigating the nature of <term>demons</term> <note>original: "demonum." In the Platonic sense, *daemones* are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil.</note> in a certain retreat there, Plotinus <note>The founder of Neoplatonism (c. 204–270 AD).</note> was suddenly present and poured out a divine oracle concerning demons for us, cloaked in words both very brief and very obscure. It therefore seemed worth our effort to summon Porphyry <note>A student of Plotinus who edited his works; known for his interest in the hierarchy of spirits.</note>, who was both a disciple of Plotinus and most devoted to scrutinizing demons, so that he might easily unfold for us the "demonic" covering of his teacher. Porphyry arrived, therefore, called by his own Plotinus and by his own demons, and opened to us what the teacher had felt. He confirmed what Origen <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) who attempted to synthesize Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note> had argued concerning demons. Porphyry indeed spoke with us in Greek words. I shall interpret the sum of these for you in English <note>original: "Latinis" (Latin).</note> words; if you read this summary with the letter which...

# BOOK EIGHT

...which I have dedicated to you concerning the agreement of Moses and Plato. Once you have examined it, you will clearly recognize how much not only Plato but also the Platonists agree with our religion. Farewell.

->The Platonists sacrifice nothing to God and to the soul of the world except contemplation. However, to the souls that move the stars, they sacrifice flowers as well as the fruits of the earth and trees.<-

The First God, since He is incorporeal, immovable, and indivisible, is contained in no place—not even within Himself. He requires nothing external. Nor does the <term>Soul of the World</term> <note>original: "anima mundi." In Neoplatonism, this is the unifying spirit that connects the divine intellect to the physical universe.</note> require external things; for it possesses and contains that which is extended in three dimensions. It possesses a faculty that moves naturally, and by its own nature it has decreed that the body of the world be moved and move in a well-ordered and beautiful manner according to the highest principles. It received the physical body into itself and embraced it, even though the Soul is incorporeal and free from all suffering. But to the remaining gods—both the world itself and the "wandering" [planets] and "non-wandering" [fixed] stars, which consist of soul and body and are visible to the eyes—one must sacrifice only with inanimate sacrifices.

The powers beneath the Moon which are not seen, the ancient peoples called <term>demons</term> <note>original: "demones." Derived from the Greek "daimon," these are intermediary spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note>. They thought that each demon sometimes benefits us and sometimes harms us.

There remains a multitude of invisible beings, whom Plato called "demons" without further distinction. Some of these, named by men, have obtained honors equal to gods and other forms of worship among various peoples. Others for the most part are not named, but are allotted a name and secret worship by certain people in specific villages or cities. The remaining crowd is commonly called by the general name of "demons." A firm belief held by all is of this kind: that they will certainly harm the human race if they are angered because they are neglected or do not receive their lawful worship; and conversely, that they will do good to men who have won them over through vows, supplications, sacrifices, and other associated rites. Since this opinion about demons is very confused and carries much slander against them, it is necessary to distinguish their nature by reason; for perhaps it is necessary, they say, to declare where the error concerning them fell upon men. One must therefore distinguish them in this manner:

**ALL** demons are certain souls proceeding from the Total Soul—that is, from the very <term>Idea of Souls</term> <note>The archetypal source or "Blueprint" of all individual souls in the Platonic hierarchy.</note>. They also possess a spirit—that is, a thin, subtle body. But those demons who most greatly rule over their own subtle body are good and beneficial. Those who rule their body the least are evil and harmful.

Therefore, whatever souls sprouting from the Total Soul govern large regions beneath the moon—leaning upon or adhering to their spirit, but surpassing it according to reason—these are surely to be judged as good demons. They manage all things for the benefit of what occurs, whether they preside over certain animals, or specific fruits, or other things ordained for their sake, such as rains and temperate [weather]...

# BOOK EIGHT CLXXXV
<a>a</a>

...to the winds and the clear air, the tempering of the seasons, and the remaining things that contribute to all these. Among us, in turn, they contribute to the arts, the discipline of music, medicine, gymnastics, and similar pursuits. However, this does not happen primarily so that those who look out for the utility and convenience of things should, in turn, cause harm. Among these are to be numbered the <term>demons</term> <note>original: "demones." In this context, these are not "demons" in the modern sense of pure evil, but "daemons"—intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between the divine and the human.</note>, whom Plato says translate and report human things to the gods and divine things to humans. While they carry our prayers to the gods as if to judges, they bring back their commands and warnings to us along with prophecy. 

Those souls that do not rule over their joined spirit but mostly yield to it are surely led and carried by it when the anger and lusts of the spirit grow strong. These souls are also demons, but they are rightly named <term>evildoers</term> <note>original: "malefici."</note>. All these, as well as those we mentioned who differ from them, are invisible and not readily manifest to human senses. For they are not clothed in a solid body; furthermore, they do not all have one form, but are marked by many figures. These forms, which seal their spirit, sometimes appear, but at other times not at all. Sometimes they even change their forms—namely, those who are of the worse sort. Their spirit, insofar as it is something corporeal, is subject to <term>suffering</term> <note>original: "passioni." This refers to being affected by external forces or emotions.</note> and is dissoluble; but because it is so bound by the souls, its form can persist for a long time, though it is not eternal. For it is natural that something always flows out from it and is nourished. 

The body of good demons consists in harmony, just as the bodies of those things manifest to us; but the bodies of the malevolent demons are discordant and inhabit a place near the earth. There is therefore no evil they do not dare to commit, for they have an entirely violent and unhealthy character, being deserted by the guardianship of better demons. From there, they plot and rush into violent and sudden ambushes; and while they carry out their incursions, they partly try to hide and partly inflict violence.

For this reason, the <term>afflictions</term> <note>original: "passiones."</note> brought by them are sharp and swift. However, the healings and corrections from the better demons seem to be slower. For every good thing is easy and balanced in its governance, proceeding in order and never overstepping what is appropriate. If you think of demons in this way, you will never fall into that most absurd opinion by which you might think either that evil comes from the good or that good happens from the evil. Not only is such a claim absurd, but many, having conceived the worst opinions of the gods from this, spread them among many men. 

For this is one of the greatest harms inflicted by the malevolent demons: although they themselves are the authors of the unfortunate <term>calamities</term> <note>original: "passionū."</note> occurring on the earth—such as plague, famine, earthquakes, heat, fire, and the like—they meanwhile persuade us that they are the makers of good, while those who are actually the authors of fertility and prosperity are instead the authors of the opposite. Thus they try to absolve themselves from being the cause of the calamities. Plotting this very thing, they first strive to hide their injustice from us. Then they turn us toward prayers and sacrifices suitable for seeking favors from the gods, as if the gods were angry with us. These and similar things they do, striving to turn us away from the right knowledge of the gods...

# BOOK
### EIGHT

...beings lead us away and bring themselves in. For they take great delight in all things done in such an unjust and discordant manner. And as if assuming the masks <note>original: "facies," literally "faces" or "appearances."</note> of other gods, they take into their company the crowds of our own counsel within our prudence. Because of such <term>lusts</term> <note>original: "concupiscentias."</note>, they set the minds of men on fire with loves and desires for riches, power, and pleasures. Again, they wrap us in new opinions from which seditions and wars are born, and other things of the same kind. 

But what is most serious of all: they persuade us that similar things are carried out by the higher beings, so much so that they even subject the greatest God to such accusations. They claim that He throws everything into turmoil, turning things upside down and downside up. This happens not only to unrefined people but also to many who are dedicated to <term>philosophy</term> <note>original: "phiæ," an abbreviation for "philosophiae."</note>. Indeed, the cause of this error proceeds and is confirmed mutually; for those practicing philosophy who never withdrew from the common filth have fallen into the same errors as the common people. On the other hand, the crowds, hearing from praised writers things similar to their own opinions, are even more confirmed in this view concerning these spirits. 

For poetic artifice has even more sharply excited such suspicions in men, because it uses an eloquence violently adapted for amazement and a kind of magic attraction, easily able to soothe and entice the soul. Therefore, it brings us to believe in things that are utterly impossible. But surely it must be firmly believed that a good thing never harms, nor does an evil thing ever benefit. For it is not the nature of heat—as **Plato** says—to make things cold, but of its opposite; likewise, it is not the nature of the just to harm. Moreover, the most just of all things by nature is divinity itself. 

Otherwise, nothing would be lasting. Must not this power, then, be separated from the lot of the beneficent <term>demons</term> <note>original: "demonum." In this context, the author is distinguishing between "agathodaemons" (good spirits) and "kakodaemons" (evil spirits).</note>? For that which is naturally prone to harming is the opposite of the beneficent. Opposites regarding the same thing never occur naturally. Therefore, since such demons harm mortal nature in many ways—and sometimes in great matters—the certain good demons meanwhile never desert their duties. Instead, they signal imminent dangers from the evil ones everywhere according to their ability, sometimes showing them in dreams, sometimes through divinely inspired minds, and through many other means. 

But if anyone were able to discern the signs, they would detect and avoid all the machinations of the wicked. For these good spirits signal to all, but not everyone recognizes the signs; just as not everyone is able to read writings, but only those who have first learned their letters. 

Through the contrary demons, however, all <term>sorcery</term> <note>original: "veneficium." While this word can mean "poisoning," in this philosophical context it refers to harmful magic or witchcraft.</note> is accomplished. For those who inflict evils through sorcery are accustomed to honor these demons and their leader above all; these demons truly abound in all kinds of shapes and images, and they vigorously deceive with a machinery of portents. By their work, unhappy people devise <term>love potions</term> <note>original: "philtra."</note> and amatory spells. For all intemperance and the hope for riches and glory grows strong through them, but especially deception. 

For lying is the property of such demons. They wish to be seen as gods, and the very power presiding over them wants to be held as the greatest god. These are surely the only ones who delight in libations and the savory smell of meat; for their <term>spiritual body</term> <note>original: "spiritale corpus." In Neoplatonic thought, this refers to the "astral vehicle" or "pneumatic body" of the spirit, which was believed to be semi-material.</note> is accustomed to grow fat on these. For this body lives on vapors and fumigations, and in various ways—as is fitting—takes in strength through the various smells of blood and meat.

It contrasts them with benevolent demons who send warnings through dreams, and explains that these lower, evil entities physically sustain themselves on the vapors of animal sacrifices.</summary>

# BOOK EIGHT
### PAGE 186

Those who sacrifice animals secretly attract evil <term>daemons</term> <note>original: "demones." In this context, daemons are not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits that can be either helpful or harmful.</note> to themselves; but to good daemons—that is, the angels—we ought to consecrate only inanimate things with a purity of mind.

Therefore, a wise and temperate man will take care to avoid using the kind of sacrifices that attract such spirits to himself. Instead, he will strive to perfectly purify his soul. Such spirits never approach a soul that is not pure, because of the total lack of similarity between them. Furthermore, if it should happen to be necessary for cities to reconcile these spirits to themselves, such a practice has nothing to do with us. For in the city, riches and external or bodily comforts are held as "good" among citizens, and their opposites as "evil." They have almost no concern for the perfection and purity of the soul. 

We, however, will not require the comforts that these spirits provide, at least as much as is possible. Instead, through the soul and through external matters, we will contend with all our zeal to become like God Himself and those beings near to Him. This is surely achieved through tranquility of the soul, a clear understanding of the truth of things, and a life intensely focused on these matters. We must become entirely unlike wicked men and daemons in every way that delights in what is mortal and material. 

For this reason, according to the teachings of **Theophrastus** <note>a Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle</note>, we shall also perform sacrifices of the kind that the <term>theologians</term> <note>original: "theologi," referring here to ancient authorities on sacred mysteries like Orpheus or Pythagoras</note> have agreed upon. They recognized that to the extent we neglect to purify the soul from disturbances, to that same extent we are joined to a wicked power. Whence we are rightly compelled to soothe this power further; for as the theologians teach: those who depend on external things and do not yet rule over their own passions are forced by that very condition to repel the assault of such a power from themselves. Otherwise, they will never be able to find rest from their labors.

->Purity and abstinence from evil spirits protect us; those who contemplate divine things ought to sacrifice nothing to them.<-

Wherefore, if the theologians ever permit the slaughtering of animals to wicked spirits for the sake of avoiding the evils they might inflict, they simultaneously forbid anyone from *tasting* such sacrifices. Moreover, they command that before you sacrifice in this way, you must purify the soul with fasting and especially with <term>abstinence</term> <note>original: "abstinentia," specifically referring here to avoiding meat</note> from animals. 

For they consider the holy purity of the soul to be like a symbol or a divine seal <note>original: "caractere," a mark or character</note> by which you are guarded, so much so that you suffer nothing from those spirits to whom you are near while reconciling them through sacrifice. For when you are of an opposite nature to those for whom you perform the rites—if you are purer and therefore more divine—you will remain unharmed in both body and soul, held fast in pure holiness as if in a fortress. 

Therefore, such caution seemed necessary even to sorcerers and enchanters, who believe it makes them safer from danger, yet they can never be entirely safe. For they are accustomed to calling upon wicked spirits for the sake of their own lusts. Wherefore, purity and holiness are not the proper traits of sorcerers or enchanters, but certainly of divine men and those contemplating divine things. Now indeed, everywhere chastity and abstinence protect their observers against evil spirits...

# BOOK EIGHT

...demonstrates that divine familiarity protects the soul. Therefore, if sorcerers <note>original: "fascinatores"</note> had established this practice for themselves first, they would certainly never dare to cast spells; for through this discipline, they would have been called back from those lusts for whose sake they pollute themselves with impiety. Thus, full of disturbances and barely—or only slightly—abstaining from impure foods, they themselves are utterly impure and pay the penalties for their wicked transgression against the universe. They suffer partly under the power of the <term>daemons</term> <note>original: "demones." In Ficino's Platonic theology, these are intermediary spirits that inhabit the air and are attracted to material vapors.</note> whom they themselves provoke, and partly under the divine judgment that inspects all the works and plans of mortals.

A wise man will abstain both from the food and the sacrifice of animals; for through these things, evil spirits are summoned to us.

A divine man will fortify his soul with divine wisdom and with abstinence from those foods that incite passions in men. He will strive for a likeness to God Himself and will consider his soul to be an uncontaminated temple of God, situated within this universe—which is itself the temple of God the Father. Finally, since every physical body gives off certain "outflowings" <note>original: "defluxus." The idea that material objects emit subtle particles or energies that attract similar spirits.</note> of material spirits to us, it is certain that together with the impurity of nourishment drawn from flesh and blood, a demonic power is present with us. This power is friendly to such matter and is easily enticed because of the similarity and very familiar nature of the substance. For this reason, all the great theologians have rightly focused on abstinence above all else. Remember, therefore, that while evil spirits are delighted by animal victims, God has no need for such sacrifices. He looks instead upon the character of those who worship Him, considering the greatest sacrifice to be a correct understanding of divinity. For in the sight of God, the best offering is a pure mind and a soul free from disturbances. Hence, Plato says it is fitting for a good man to perform sacrifices and be present at divine rites, but for an evil man, to linger among sacred things is in vain.

### A defense regarding silence, to a friend.
->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Bandini. Sending many greetings.<-

You say, my dear Bandini—indeed, you have been saying it for a long time—that you see Marsilio writing rarely and too little to his friends, which is the opposite of what a frequent and long-lasting love requires, often demanding much. I, however, always seem to myself to be writing much to my friends, since I am constantly composing many things to be read by my friends and everyone else. For a long time now, Plotinus <note>Plotinus was the founder of Neoplatonism; Ficino’s translation of his works into Latin was a monumental intellectual feat of the 15th century.</note> has been speaking in the Latin tongue, as I promised, in fifty-four books; but besides these, he demands commentaries from us. We have already finished eight, and trusting in God, we proceed eagerly to the rest. Commend us to Matthias, the unconquered King of Hungary <note>original: "Pannoniæ regi." Refers to Matthias Corvinus, a great patron of learning.</note>; but tell him that he cannot truly have Marsilio commended to him unless he first holds our "delights," Jacobus and Zarolus, as commended.

### An apology for the brevity of writing to a friend.

## Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Bandini, sends many greetings.

<margin>I</margin> gave letters to you some time ago through Giacomo Azarolo, a true friend and elegant man, whom you—along with me—should remember to often commend in my name to Matthias, the unconquered King of Hungary <note>original: "pannonie Regi." Matthias Corvinus was a major patron of the arts and a supporter of Ficino’s work.</note>. I had written that I had already finished the commentaries on the eighth book of Plotinus. Now I am contemplating commentaries on the twelfth, and because of this constant care, it happens that friends receive only very rare and brief letters from me. And truly, since you receive such, others perhaps receive none. Indeed, I find wonderful mysteries in Plotinus; and (what is more wonderful) they are very frequent. I hope I might at least explain them in words just as I seem to perceive them in my mind. But farewell now, my sweetest Bandini; Plotinus meanwhile summons me.

### Commendation of a friend.

## Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Bandini, sends many greetings.

<margin>I</margin> have asked you elsewhere and I pray again that you commend the long-standing case of Vincent the priest, our close associate, to the great King. The whole life of the poor wretch depends on this. It will certainly be a matter of royal clemency to bring help to a needy priest seeking what is just. Farewell.

-> What happiness is. <-

## Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Seraphico, his fellow philosopher, sends many greetings.

<margin>Y</margin>our letter was as pleasing to me, Seraphico, as your freedom was pleasing. For it indicated that you have finally liberated yourself from business into leisure <term>leisure</term> <note>original: "ocium" (otium). In the Renaissance, this was not "laziness" but the productive, contemplative time required for philosophy and study.</note> and liberty. If happiness—for the sake of which we all do everything—is the end; if the end is rest; if rest is leisure, then nothing is more opposed to happiness than business <term>business</term> <note>original: "negocium" (negotium), literally "not-leisure." This refers to worldly affairs, commerce, or political duties.</note>. Should I therefore do nothing so that I might be happy? Far from it! For if life is an internal and perennial act of nature, and he who does not live cannot live happily, then we certainly would not be happy by doing nothing. What then? Surely we will avoid the action that consists in motion, if indeed happiness is rest—which would otherwise be multifaceted since the highest end is one, or it would refer to something else. For the ultimate end does not refer back to a goal. Therefore, we will flee external actions which are involved in motion, which are distracted, and which serve a foreign reward. Meanwhile, we will be content with the internal act of the mind. This action does not depend on anything else but dwells within itself. It does not wait for a reward. For its own pleasure is its reward. Finally, whoever acts in this way, alone among all people, does not act so that he may *eventually* be happy, but acts because he is *already* happy.

### Praise of intellect.

## Marsilio Ficino to the illustrious Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, his fellow philosopher, sends many greetings.

<margin>O</margin> wonderful things! O incredible matter to those who do not remember "remembrance" <term>remembrance</term> <note>original: "reminiscentia." This refers to the Platonic doctrine of anamnesis, where learning is actually the soul recalling knowledge it possessed before birth.</note>! We have read the nine hundred problems <note>A reference to Pico's famous "900 Conclusions," a massive list of philosophical and theological propositions he intended to defend in a public debate in Rome in 1486.</note> you sent, each of which (what is more wonderful) is singular. Therefore, let me be permitted to publicly propose one single thing to be defended beyond these: namely, that the cognition which is called "science" is remembrance. This I shall assert not only with twice nine hundred arguments, but I shall prove it by your entire genius. So—

## Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo, most distinguished Venetian Knight, sends many greetings.

<margin>d</margin> You desired, as I hear, some testimony of our incredible goodwill toward you from the works of Plato. Our love, my Bembo, is witnessed by the sixth book of my *Platonic Theology*. The daily speech of Marsilio is a book of so many letters; yet Plato did not come forward as a witness there, lest perhaps he might appear at an inopportune time. You know that a witness brings no credit unless he comes at the right moment. But Plato has entrusted his testimony on this matter to Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism, whom Ficino spent years translating and interpreting</note>. He is a witness so faithful to Plato that in Plotinus alone Plato himself is faithful. He, therefore, will fulfill more easily what Plato perhaps would have performed with more difficulty; he composed fifty-four books of divine philosophy in all. I have long since made all of these Latin <note>meaning he translated them from the original Greek into Latin</note>. I have composed commentaries on eighteen of them; the rest I am diligently pursuing, hoping for a happy end to so great a work, God willing. Farewell happily, and be forever mindful of your Marsilio, who is always mindful of you.

->Commendation of a friend in the name of a philosopher.<-

<margin>f</margin> Greetings, my dearest Bandini. I am writing to you now for the third time on behalf of our close associate, the priest Vincenzo. I pray that, if you are able, you commend him opportunely to King Matthias <note>Matthias Corvinus, King of Hungary, a major patron of Ficino</note>, and do so in my name: if indeed a philosopher's name can be of any weight with kings. For such is usually the humility of the philosopher's lot: that among mimes <note>comic actors or entertainers</note> it can do something, but among the greatest men it can do very little. And we ourselves are content with this lot, provided we are philosophers; that is, that we at least have great power within ourselves. Nor do I deny that I have sometimes been able to do something with Matthias, nor do I doubt I shall have power again, since he shines not only in power but also in wisdom. Farewell.

### Oration of Marsilio Ficino on Charity, delivered to the people in the College of the Florentine Canons; he divides the proposed oration into three chapters.

<margin>a</margin> "Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of Glory shall enter" <note>Quoting Psalm 24:7</note>. Lift up your ears, raise up your minds; the living and effective word of God shall enter into you, and along with the word of God, charity, which is salvific above all things. Together with charity, the King of Glory, God, immediately enters. For "God is charity," and "he who remains in charity remains in God, and God in him" <note>Quoting 1 John 4:16</note>.

### ->Chapter one: That God is charity.<-

That God is the highest charity, venerable fathers and most beloved brothers, not only does the apostolic trumpet sound, but all of nature proclaims it. For the whole nature of things was created and is preserved because from the beginning God the creator himself willed and wills it. And "will" in God is without doubt nothing other than charity and God himself. I say that "will" in God is not a craving or a wanting at all, but joy; a joy perpetually rejoicing in its own goodness. For since we can consider two things in the will—craving and joy—and since in the First Good there can be no stimulus of craving <note>Since God is perfect, He cannot "want" or lack anything</note>, certainly there the will and charity differ in no way from joy. For just as light and heat, which are two things in fire, are one...

BOOK EIGHT PAGE 188

...finally they are in the Sun: thus appetite and joy are two things in us outside our fatherland <note>original: "patria." In Neoplatonic thought, the "fatherland" refers to the celestial realm or the soul's true home with God</note> regarding a finite good. But in the presence of the infinite good, all will is pleasure itself. Now indeed, in the elements subject to heaven, the movement of the elements to a place is one thing, and their rest in that place is another; but in heaven, the movement and the rest of the celestial bodies are absolutely the same in their perpetual revolution. Similarly, above heaven, heat itself is both charity and joy.

### Chapter Two. He who remains in charity remains in God

Divine charity, while it rejoices in its own good, loves and cares for the common good of all. Human charity, in turn, insofar as it rejoices in the common good of all, brings back a private good for itself from that source. Therefore, he who remains in charity remains in God, and remains always in joy. This is both because God is charity itself, and also because while the mind—ardently moved by the flames of charity—loves the high God in himself and loves men in God, in the meantime it is moved by God himself (who is charity) and is wonderfully made divine. 

Indeed, just as any matter does not usually become fire simply because it receives light from fire, but rather because it receives heat; so also the mind sometimes becomes divine: not so much because God shines upon our intelligence, but because our will glows with the burning of divine love. Amidst these things, the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 13</note> seems to cry out to us in this manner: "Prophecy will finally cease for you in the fatherland where the past and future end. Knowledge will also cease for you where argumentation ends and the manner of seeing changes. But charity alone will never cease." <note>original: "Charitas vero sola cessabit nunquam." A translation of 1 Corinthians 13:8: "Love never fails."</note> Indeed, the condition of loving, under the nature of rejoicing, will always remain the same.

### Chapter Three. And God in him.

By this reasoning, therefore, charity alone remains, and he who remains in charity remains in God. But in what way does God remain in him? In the finite mind, I say, the immense God himself remains; our mind remains contained within God, but God remains containing the mind. Certainly, the almighty God remains even where charity is not, but there he acts as a sharp judge and a demander of punishments. Conversely, the most merciful God remains where charity flourishes as a saving Eucharist <note>term: "eucharistia" (thanksgiving). Ficino uses it here both as a general term for grace and a specific reference to the Sacrament</note> and an abundant giver of all graces.

### Epilogue and exhortation.

O almighty charity, which is God, which makes, preserves, and perfects all things! O most wise charity, which, divinely kindling the mind, wonderfully transforms it from a soul into God! O charity, undoubtedly most kind, which communicates the immense grace of the Creator with the finite creature through the communion of the holy Eucharist! 

In this, Christ himself, the merciful Savior of the world—while he is in heaven—is nonetheless everywhere with us until the end of the age, converting the fragile substance of our food into his body as celestial nourishment: preserving the dimensions of the bread, while not admitting its own <note>Ficino is describing the doctrine of Transubstantiation, where the "accidents" (appearance/size) of bread remain while the "substance" changes</note>; moreover, dividing the dimension of the bread while remaining undivided himself. By this food, entirely new and greater—lest perhaps he lose us as if we were profane, but so that he may healthily cherish and nourish us as his own—let us close, most beloved brothers, let us close...

## Fortune is most opposed to virtue.
### Marsilio Ficino to Rainaldo Gauardo of Venice. Heartfelt greetings. <note>original: "S. P. D.," an abbreviation for "Salutem Plurimam Dicit," the standard formal greeting in Latin letters meaning "sends many greetings."</note>

<margin>f</margin> **F**ortune is thought by many to be blind, because she never sees whom she supports or whom she opposes; instead, she takes up the patronage of any client at all without selection. And perhaps someone could imagine Fortune not as blind indeed, but rather as envious and entirely ambitious. This is because she is unwilling to favor men who excel in talent and prudence, whose brilliant deeds are ascribed not to luck but rather to virtue. Truly, she is accustomed to favor most where whatever greatness emerges can be attributed to Fortune alone. On the other hand, she follows good men with all her strength and tries to suppress virtue to such an extent that the common people think nothing brilliant can be done or acquired by virtue itself. Whence we all finally make Fortune a goddess and place her in heaven. You have no reason, therefore, my Rainaldo, to grieve that you are counted among those whom Fortune is accustomed to pursue.

## Response to all things.
### Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Micheloctio.

<margin>n</margin> **N**ever did I think that any curses, even those hurled at an enemy, could ever please me—so much do I fear omens. Or perhaps that Muse of yours, Micheloctio, is so vigorous and plays so beautifully, that even with many curses heaped upon us from every side, she has in the meantime wonderfully delighted me. What if I should hear her in turn pleading against these things and praying for happy outcomes? Sing, therefore, I beseech you, a recantation <note>original: "palinodiā," a Greek-derived term for a poem or song that retracts a previous statement.</note>. Farewell.

I value my recommendation to you so highly that I do not recommend myself to you daily so much through light letters as through the serious hearts and conversations of our friends. ### Marsilio Ficino to his Antonio Calderini. Heartfelt greetings. <note>original: "S.P.D.," an abbreviation for "Salutem Plurimam Dicit," a standard Latin greeting meaning "sends many greetings."</note>

<margin>a</margin> I have long since emerged from the commentaries on Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism. ### Marsilio Ficino to Miniati. Heartfelt greetings.

<margin>q</margin> That you love me, Miniati, you do justly and likewise as a friend: justly since you love one who loves you; as a friend because you honor me by loving me. Moreover, in that you follow the Platonic discipline with public praise everywhere, you fulfill the duty of divine piety. For divine providence established that for the common salvation of talents, especially those of philosophers. This is indeed what I have been working toward for a long time; this I labor at industriously, although in the manner of water-carriers <note>original: "aquarianorum." A metaphor for someone who gathers water from a source to distribute it; Ficino sees himself as a conduit for ancient wisdom.</note> I gather daily what I may scatter and pour out to the grateful and ungrateful alike—even to those who would gladly obscure me if they could in any way. But I know for certain that as Plato comes forth into the light, a legitimate friend of Plato cannot be obscured. Finally, as for your complaint that you have recently received bad things in exchange for good ones from a certain Hugo, this is a complaint common to you, to me, and to many others. Therefore, you shall (if it is permitted) console yourself for your own loss by the fact that it is shared. Especially because God, the avenger, sees all things.

### Marsilio Ficino to the Most Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Marco of Venice, Cardinal of Saint Mark. Heartfelt greetings.

<margin>s</margin> Parents are sometimes accustomed to imprint their image so effectively upon a son that whoever sees the child has also seen the parent. *Many things which the stars signify, the demons persuade us to do, and we perform.*

### Marsilio Ficino to Nicolaus Bathory, Bishop of Vác. Heartfelt greetings. <note>original: "S.P.D.," for "Salutem Plurimam Dicit." Nicolaus Bathory (1435–1506) was a Hungarian bishop and a key figure in the Renaissance in Hungary.</note>

**Y**ou write that Matthias, the unconquered King of Hungary <note>original: "Pannoniae Regé." But it would be a wonder for me to change my ancestral home: whether Saturn in Aquarius, rising at my birth, prohibits the change (as an astrologer might judge), or some genius <note>original: "genius"; a guiding spirit or personal divinity in Greco-Roman belief.</note> of that kind forbids it (as a magus might perhaps think), or whether this poor body, unfit for labors, hinders the journey, or my mind, always intent on contemplation, commands me to remain at rest. I have indeed assigned ambiguous causes for this matter. For the Platonists think that human events are sometimes signified by the stars, but are frequently incited by the demons who act as the stars' attendants, and are finally carried out by men according to the condition of the things nearest to us. Farewell.

->Consolation on the death of a son.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Ugolino Verino, the poet. Heartfelt greetings.

**T**he opinion of the ancient sages is most strongly confirmed by Plotinus in his book on Providence: that humans—that is, souls—descend into this life from God himself as if into a comedy or tragedy. In this play, all the things that are commonly thought to be either prosperous or adverse are fables: riches and poverty are fictional, kings and servants are fictional, and births and deaths are fictional. Perhaps that Platonic saying tends toward this: "the human race on earth is God's plaything." <note>Ficino refers to a famous concept in Plato's "Laws" where humans are described as puppets or playthings of the gods.</note> God himself is the author of this play and these fables, and he is the father of the souls; therefore, he sends them down from on high into this play like actors. Nature herself provides the masks for them by the union of male and female serving this very purpose. Certainly, one departs from the play more happily who returns more acceptable to the Author, God; and one is more acceptable the more obediently they performed the acts assigned to them. He is the happiest of all to whom more honorable and shorter acts were given than to the rest. For a longer tragic play usually inserts comic bits more frequently. Why then, Verino, will you weep for that noble youth? Why complain that your son has departed with a tender mouth? <note>Referring to his youth.</note> Was he your son? No, he was not yours, for you did not create him, but God did; you merely equipped him with a certain mask when he was sent by God to play for a short time, and once he was equipped, you instructed him for this play to the best of your ability. He has not returned from life, but from a certain play of life into the substance of life itself. Since he performed a learned, honorable, and pious [part] in this play...

### The pursuit of riches and honors harms the study of literature most of all.

->Marsilio Ficino to Piero Soderini, the Academic. Heartfelt Greetings.<- <note>original: "S.P.D.," for "Salutem Plurimam Dicit." Piero Soderini (1450–1522) was a Florentine statesman who would later become the Gonfaloniere of Justice.</note>

**T**he ancient astronomers found two dwellings for Jupiter among the heavenly bodies: Pisces and Sagittarius; and two also for Mercury: Virgo and Gemini. But since Pisces is placed opposite to Virgo, and Sagittarius is opposed to Gemini, we rightly consider ourselves to be warned by the heavens that nothing is more opposed to the natural talent and the study of literature—which they attribute to Mercury—than the immense pursuit of riches and the unholy pursuit of power, which are attributed to Jupiter above all others. Furthermore, since Leo, the house of the Sun, is most distant from Aquarius, the house of Saturn; and again, since Aries, the exaltation of the Sun, is most remote from Libra, the exaltation of Saturn—and since the Sun signifies kings, while Saturn signifies philosophers and contemplatives—who, understanding these things, would ever hope that either philosophers might become kings or kings might be philosophers? Certainly, this cannot be achieved otherwise than by divine means; and our Plato <note>Ficino refers to Plato as "ours" because he translated the complete works of Plato into Latin for the first time in the West.</note> used to desire it vehemently as a divine gift. Indeed, I know this to be your own opinion, my dear Piero. For I know the excellence of your talent and the superiority of your mind. Therefore, I decided to discuss these things with you alone, so that I might confirm you in this opinion of yours by celestial reasons. Farewell.

### He who seeks wisdom throughout the whole world is to be commended above all.

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, his fellow philosopher. Greetings.<- <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) was a brilliant young philosopher and a close associate of Ficino. He had recently faced charges of heresy in Rome for his "900 Theses."</note>

**G**reetings. Roberto Salviati, a faithful and energetic friend, read your letter to me yesterday evening, in which you refute the slanders of your adversaries there with certain arguments. We agreed, therefore, that I should recount these things to the magnanimous Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, "The Magnificent," the de facto ruler of Florence and patron to both Ficino and Pico.</note>, so that if he had previously received anything false from the city of Rome dictated by your adversaries, he might be convinced of the falsehood. I recounted it, therefore, gladly, and he listened gladly. From this we gather that no hatred toward you lies hidden in his mind, but only love. In particular, it had to be pointed out that those men <note>Pico's accusers.</note> were cast into prison not for your sake, but for their own; for the opposite had been rumored from there even to here. That they were seized due to their own fault, you sufficiently declare in your letter, and Pierleone <note>original: "Petrus Leo." Pierleone Leoni was a famous physician and scholar.</note> was a witness to me, for he had heard that they had spoken out too rashly and arrogantly against the Pope. Meanwhile, however, this magnanimous "lion" of ours <note>A play on the name "Leo" (Pierleone) or perhaps a reference to an envoy.</note> departed from here eagerly to travel the world, seized by the love of truth. And even if he seems to us to have already attained as much as is permitted to a man, he nevertheless pursues it more intensely. Furthermore, he is likely to bring back a divine fruit instead of a human one, if God breathes upon him. It is our duty, therefore, to provide divine protection for such a great friend through religious prayers and vows amidst the various dangers of an uncertain journey. May that happy man be well; and you also, fare you well happily.

Therefore, I congratulate you most highly, and I congratulate our friend; finally, I rejoice for myself, because I recognize that I have such great influence with so great a king. I indeed give thanks to God for your most happy victory, and after God, to you, for the freedom of my friend—not in a small way, but greatly—for the sake of my influence with you. I also wish for you far greater victories hereafter, and for my friend, gradually smaller favors; so that you, who have bestowed the greatest of benefits—freedom—upon him, may not disdain to bestow lighter ones if the situation requires.

<margin>Knowledge of the divinity of the soul is necessary above all else.</margin>
**W**hat does it profit a man if he gains the entire world, but suffers the loss of his own soul? <note>original: "Vidnam prodeſt homini ſi vniuerſum mundū luaretur: animæve ro ſuæ detrimentum patiatur"; a reference to Matthew 16:26.</note> You labor in vain, O Philosopher, while you strive to comprehend all things, unless you first comprehend the soul, through which you are to comprehend the rest. What does it profit you, O Theologian, to assert eternity to God, unless you also assert that same eternity for yourself, so that through your own eternity you might be able to enjoy the divine eternity? Therefore, philosophers and theologians alike, come together, I pray you all. Hear the prophet wondering at how great the things are that God has done for our soul. Why do you cry out, O prophet, when you say "Come"? Why do you wonder again when you say "how great"? What, finally, do you portend where you add "God"? Indeed, I cry out, I wonder, I portend that God himself has given divine things to our soul. If you believe the prophets less, O brothers, then seek, ask, and knock <note>A reference to Matthew 7:7: "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened."</note> as much as is permitted for the God who is present within us. Therefore, you, good Jesus, who hang there for the sake of the soul, did you wish to suffer for a corporeal soul? To die for a mortal soul? Look, O brothers; listen, I pray; do you not see that He opens His mouth and answers? "Far be it from me that I should have traded the most precious thing for the most worthless; rather, for the sake of man's divine soul, God became man; for the sake of the immortal soul, I have died." Let our enemies, therefore, be ashamed; let them be troubled; let them be confounded very quickly, since our God has done great and wonderful things for us. Our enemies are not those who steal our money—for money is not ours, but belongs to fortune. Our enemies are not those who kill the body—for the body is not so much ours as it is the property of fortune, nature, and fate. Our enemies are those who oppress the mind <note>original: "animum," which Ficino uses interchangeably with the soul ("anima") to denote the seat of reason.</note>; for this alone is ours, and this is our very self. They kill the mind who declare it to be corporeal and mortal. Therefore, let the Aristippics <note>Followers of Aristippus, who believed pleasure was the highest good.</note> be ashamed; let the Epicureans be troubled; let the Lucretians be confounded. Let them be ashamed if they are philosophers, for they rely on no reason. Let them be troubled if they are eminent men, for they are deceived by common, vulgar habit. Let them, finally, be confounded by the Platonic arguments that will follow.

# BOOK EIGHT

...possesses both light and heat at once. Grasp the light in your hand if you can: you will bring back not light, but shadows. Seize the heat in your fists: you will be burned immediately. God is a consuming fire <note>original: "Deus ignis consumens est"; a reference to Hebrews 12:29</note>, not to be grasped by fists—that is, not by the imagination, nor by the reach of mortal emotions. Even if you have lingered in contemplation, you will perceive the light of divine truth with no fist of the imagination. You will immediately slip back into the shadows of falsehood. Therefore, there is a need for dialectic <note>the art of logical discussion or reasoning used to clear away mental confusion</note> to dissolve all the clouds of the imagination. Again, even if you are a master of dialectic, if you are weighed down by mortal emotions, you cannot healthily enjoy the vital heat of God yourself; for that heat dissolves whatever material residue creeps in. But whatever presents itself free from matter, that heat assists and reconciles to itself. Therefore, cast off earthly emotions, and you will immediately and healthily enjoy the divine fervor.

### Why we must start from the love of God to understand God.

God is love <note>original: "Deus charitas est"; from 1 John 4:8. Ficino uses "charitas" (charity) to denote the highest, most selfless form of divine love</note>, and he who remains in love remains in God, and God in him. But if love is a craving of desire, a sting, or a state of need, and yet God is in need of nothing, how then is God himself love? In love, there is fervor, there is light, and there is joy. Thus, God is love; but the fervor of this love is indeed ignited in the soul, while the light flourishes in God, and the joy exists in both. It is just as a ray of the sun within a concave mirror is light in itself, but becomes heat in the wood it touches, and from that heat, light is produced in that same place. Therefore, he who remains in the fervor of love immediately remains in the light of God himself. Immediately, divine joy remains in him. 

Indeed, a celestial body <note>meaning a heavenly or divine entity</note> communicates light to transparent bodies—which are very similar to it—before it communicates heat. To earthly things, however, which are quite dissimilar, it imparts heat before light; thus, once these earthly things are purified by heat and made most similar to heaven, they immediately carry light from it. Therefore, the soul, enclosed in an earthly body, must begin from the love of God so that, purified by love, it may then obtain divine light, and in that light, joy.

### An introduction to friendship.

-> Marsilio Ficino to Francisco Scali, Secretary to the King of Naples. Sends many greetings. <-

While I was dining with my friend Filippo Valori, I received a letter from my friend Nicolaus Valori <note>The Valori family were prominent Florentine nobles and dedicated patrons of Ficino</note>, in which he indicates how ardently you love me and with what great praises you follow my work. He adds, moreover, that you are a man whom I ought to have loved intensely of my own accord, even if you did not love me first. Therefore, I—knowing for certain that the testimony of my friend Valori is most powerful—not only love you in return, you who have loved me for a long time, but I wish that I had even surpassed you in love. I honor you in a marvelous way and give you immense thanks that you have judged me worthy of your benevolence and your praise. For in this way, I believe I have been made worthy of the love and praise of excellent men. 

What, therefore, shall I pay back to you for such a great gift? Even if it is not as much as I owe, at least let it be as much as I am able. Perhaps I shall be able to do quite a bit, insofar as I shall have much "value" <note>original: "valoria"; Ficino is making a pun on the surname "Valori" and the Latin word "valor" or "valere," meaning to be strong or of worth</note> in the house of Valori. This family flourishes greatly in the city of Florence through its nobility, authority, and justice...
