### An Exhortation to Defend a Just Cause

Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Giovanni Vittorio of Siena, the distinguished legal expert.

<margin>s</margin>Sebastian Salvinus <note>Sebastianus Saluinus was a theologian and Ficino’s cousin; he often assisted Ficino in editing his works</note>, a doctor of theology and our learned cousin, requires your patronage in his legal case—and a most just one at that. Indeed, while Justice is robust in her celestial homeland, she becomes weak once outside her country here on earth, so that she continually requires a support. However, only a just man—as they say you are, and which I easily believe—is both able and willing to sustain his mother, Justice. I hope, therefore, and I vehemently desire, that you will easily take up this most just cause of our close friend, and that you may resolve it quickly and successfully. Farewell.

### Commending a Friend to the King

Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Matthias, the ever-invincible King of Pannonia <note>Matthias Corvinus (r. 1458–1490), the King of Hungary, who was a great patron of Neoplatonism and a regular correspondent of Ficino</note>.

<margin>o</margin>Most Serene King, I desire to send you letters almost worthy of your majesty. But the pressure to write quickly is great: both because the priest Vincentius himself, my close associate, now urgently asks for a recommendation, and because the messenger is about to depart at this very hour. You will receive, therefore, letters not of the kind that leisure and freedom usually produce, but such as a more pressing necessity creates. Accordingly, if I perhaps seem a bit more forward in my request, it is because your habitual clemency toward me has granted me such great freedom. Therefore, I more freely beseech you: just as you once, by your own will and for my sake, released a man from prison, so now, at my request, you might grant this additional favor: that he may (if it is possible) eventually recover his money that was lost there. Truly, I give you thanks that I already have so much influence with you, and for my part, I rejoice. Finally, I pray to God that He may always breathe favorably upon you.

### Why Great Dangers Threaten Great Men <note>original: "iuris"; likely a transcription error for "viris" (men), given the context of the letter regarding Moses and Lorenzo de' Medici</note>

Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, his companion <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous philosopher and polymath; "compatri" implies a deep bond of spiritual kinship</note>.

<margin>s</margin>In recent days, I was consoling Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent," the de facto ruler of Florence and Ficino's primary patron</note> using friendly words (as is customary) regarding the too-recent death of his daughter. Although he is a high-minded man who needs no consolations, I was nonetheless strengthening my consolation—even if it was superfluous—with necessary reasons and examples from the Old Testament. During the conversation, we soon happened upon Moses, whose life and deeds from the beginning we recounted at Lorenzo's command. When he had heard these things, he said: "Do you see, Ficino, how many, how diverse, and how great were the dangers that stood in the way of Moses' future greatness? Not only from infancy through his whole life, but even at his very birth and before his birth? Surely we have found that immense dangers often loom everywhere for men of great undertakings and those destined for future greatness. This may be so that hardships and difficulties might soften the high-spirited, or so that the strongest and wisest men might be produced by having been tested and having overcome adverse fortune more often. Or it may be because common envy and the ambition of the many always oppose the excellent. Or perhaps Divine Providence has so tempered the life of men with comforts and discomforts for the sake of our salvation. Or there may lie hidden, besides these, a certain cause lower than God but superior to man, which so mixes human affairs—the investigation of which belongs to those with leisure and perhaps sometimes to the curious." But wherever it comes from, it certainly comes to pass; and lest I now turn back to past examples (which are innumerable), you see... [continues]

### BOOK VIII

...said. For we were many who [saw] how certain the proofs of singular greatness are in Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a brilliant philosopher and close friend of Ficino</note>: not only signs of a future greatness, but almost experiments of a present one; besides which, the youth is driven here by grave dangers. Finally, both he wonderfully approved of you and the others approved. A little later, turning to me, he said: "But you idlers, have you found any more hidden cause for these things?" To this I replied: "A figure or the harmonies of the heavens portending a secure ease of life is so different from that which promises excellence of virtue and glory that they can very rarely coincide, or perhaps they cannot. Added to this is that there are <term>demons</term><note>In Neoplatonism, *daemons* are intermediary spirits or guardian geniuses, not necessarily evil beings</note> in the air like secondary stars in this heaven closest to us. Among them, like stars, there are higher demons and lower ones; both are shepherds of men. The higher ones guide the distinguished; the lower ones the common folk. The lower demons, being like certain men, are moved by human emotions, especially touched by pride and envy; therefore they grieve that men commended to the higher demons are publicly esteemed as more excellent than their own [charges]. And for that reason, they do not want them to rule, to prosper, or to live. They therefore stir up many from their own flocks everywhere against them. They also oppose beasts and even elements. These things were said there."

But did not that heavenly Saturn, the lord in the birth chart of both from the beginning, decree that the union of two Platonists would be something great? Being the Lord also in the chart of Plato, the Saturnian demons especially rule the union of these men. But meanwhile, the Martial demons <note>Demons associated with the planet Mars, characterized by conflict and aggression</note> everywhere plot to dissolve this. Indeed, Mars himself came into your charts (as I said) as an enemy. Finally, this union destined by powerful origins will overcome the powerful adversaries it has sustained so far, just as Saturn is superior to Mars—Saturn, who once, when I was being born, touched his own Aquarius with his head, and thirty years later, when you were coming into the light, returned to the same place. This is the point (as I think) why Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (the Magnificent), the ruler of Florence and patron of the Platonic Academy</note>, the most outstanding among the Saturnians, both protects me and calls Pico back to the city of Florence. And if every land is a homeland to the brave, yet the Saturnian powers especially command their brave Pico to take hold of this one, and they commanded it long ago when he first arrived to live here under a great conjunction. Be happy; be a Florentine. May 30, 1488. Florence.

### Marsilio Ficino to Probus, Commissioner of the Pope, sends greetings.

<margin>q</margin> Since we read in the Gospel regarding the feast: "the last shall be first," sit down, most proven Probus <note>Ficino plays on the name *Probus*, which means "upright" or "virtuous"</note>. Today you are the last at this table, but in my mind, you are the first. However, I do not dare to demand that I be first in your mind; I will consider it sufficient when I obtain the second rank with you. For from that, I shall herald a second <note>or "favorable"</note> fortune for myself. Furthermore, he who is second to Probus will eventually need to be "proved." Indeed, many of us men of letters have approved of the Pope's choice, because he committed us to be judged by a man who is exceptionally learned. For when men of letters fall in with an unlearned man, they fall; but having found a learned one, they rise again. Finally, having found one who is equally learned and upright, they rise, never to fall again. Farewell.

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Marsilio Ficino, Platonic philosopher, sends greetings.

<margin>f</margin> Greetings, father of the Platonic family. It is now beyond all controversy that the star of Saturn is both harmful and ill-omened, and that you, my Ficino—though perhaps for your own good—were certainly born under Saturn to my misfortune. For just as that planet is frequently <term>retrograde</term><note>Appearing to move backward in the sky; in astrology, this often signifies delays, obstacles, or internal withdrawal</note>, so you too are endowed with a similar nature: coming to me twice now, you have become retrograde; twice you have turned your step back. And what is more, you did so at sunset, lest you say you were revereing the radiance of Phoebus <note>The Sun, or the light of reason</note>. But, I ask, what was the cause of this repeated retreating? Was it your Saturn, or rather we the Saturnians? But whatever it was that took you from me—that is, took me from myself—I beg you, see to it in the future that he who once joined us does not separate us. Nor should you ever believe that you will come to me as one who is "about to speak," you whom I always hunger and thirst for as the solace of my life, the delight of my mind, the teacher of my morals, and the master of my learning. Farewell, and come; so that your Saturn—that is, your "fullness" <note>A pun on *Saturnus* and the Latin *satur*, meaning full or satisfied</note>—might also render me full. Farewell again; or rather, since you are now arriving, greetings.

I have stepped back. If there is any fault among the gods, let Jupiter be at fault. For yesterday Jupiter began to be retrograde <note>In astrology, a planet is "regradarius" or retrograde when it appears to move backward in the sky; this was often interpreted as a time of delay or reversal</note>, as he was coming into a trine aspect with the Sun. For he [Jupiter], from the sign of Pisces, was looking at the Sun sitting in Cancer. Since it is the custom and nature of the superior planets that when they first appear in opposition to the Sun, they then move backward or forward—with both Saturn and Jupiter as witnesses—you shall be my Phoebus <note>Apollo, the Sun god, associated with clarity and truth</note>. Therefore, however much faith there is in Jupiter, and however much firmness in Saturn, with such firm faith you shall be my Phoebus to me. Farewell. July 3, 1488.

->Persistent labor conquers all.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, his fellow philosopher, sends greetings.

Hail, the only salvation <note>original: *salus*</note> of the Muses. But for this very reason—that you may be safe—nothing in human affairs seems more expedient than that our Salviati <note>Roberto Salviati was a close friend to both Ficino and Pico</note> wishes you to be safe. Therefore, as much as I always desire you to be safe, I desire that Salviati always desires your safety as he does now. Truly, besides him, I have known no one who immediately attains whatever he wishes. For whether men attain their desires through the very virtue of a prayer, this man alone, with his whole mind and spirit, assiduously affects whatever he chooses; or whether begun tasks are instead perfected by diligent work and care, this man alone pursues whatever he follows ardently right to the end. Thus, what is said—"only he who perseveres to the end shall be saved" <note>Matthew 24:13</note>—seems to portend that this man alone shall be "Salviated" <note>Ficino puns on the name Salviati and the Latin *salvatus*, meaning saved or made safe</note>. Perhaps our friend even possesses that grain of mustard seed by which mountains are moved. For yesterday he moved a giraffe <note>original: *cameleopardalum*. A famous giraffe was gifted to Lorenzo de' Medici in 1487, becoming a sensation in Florence</note> through the eye of a needle, leading an animal through pathless ways that were entirely unsuitable for travel. Why then do we need those hundred reasons of Nicolaus <note>Possibly Nicolaus Leonicenus, a scholar who challenged traditional authority</note> which we are now reading to refute the astrologers? Let this one case be enough for us instead of a hundred. Indeed, since our friend quickly carries out even the hardest tasks with a certain burning zeal—despite Saturn being retrograde and denying him the service of a speedy expedition—we have sufficiently explored from this that our affairs are carried out by our own zeal rather than by celestial instinct. The soul will be recognized to possess a truly wonderful power, if only it uses its whole power for the work. Farewell. July 6, 1488, in Florence.

### On the three Graces and Concord.
### Marsilio Ficino to Roberto Salviati and Girolamo Benivieni, sends greetings.

Many writers are accustomed to address Pico as the "Count of Concord." <note>Pico was the Count of Concordia, but Ficino treats the title as a description of his character</note> Up to this point, he has been called the Count of Concord quite rightly, as he himself sought concord and gladly followed men of concord. After this, however, he should be called not a "count" (companion), but the undisputed "duke" (leader) of Concord. For now Concord herself follows him as her leader. Indeed, just as mists are scattered by the approach of the sun, so at the arrival of Pico all discords flee far away. Suddenly, Concord follows this leader everywhere, so much so that he alone is able to do what some once attempted, and he does it assiduously: to reconcile Jews to Christians, <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> to Platonists, and Greeks to Latins. And rightly so...

EIGHTH [BOOK] CXCIII

...those three Graces <note>In mythology, the Graces (Aglaia, Euphrosyne, and Thalia) represent charm, beauty, and creativity</note> who once accompanied their Venus. Immediately upon the birth of Pico <note>original: *pico*; a pun on Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s name, which also means "woodpecker" in Latin</note>, the woodpecker was left behind; leaving Venus, they now accompany him by the command of Jove, Phoebus, and Mercury. The first Grace, indeed, formed his mind from the beginning; the second confirmed the state of his mind and body; the third, finally, commands fortune to obey his counsel. And because he cultivates the soul, he applied three Graces to his mind: Wisdom, Eloquence, and Probity. For so Phoebus, Mercury, and Jove decreed. Therefore, just as the Furies give birth to discord, so the Graces procreate concord. Rightly then, concord follows Pico—whom the Graces accompany—everywhere as its leader.

->How friends may speak even while silent.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Pierleano <note>Pierleone Leoni of Spoleto, a famous physician and close friend of Ficino</note>, his fellow Platonist, sends greetings.<-

<margin>n</margin>
**I** do not know by what counsel—or rather by what fate or perhaps chance—it happened that yesterday, when you departed from Florence, you did not say even through a messenger (as you usually do), "Farewell, Ficino." This I know for certain: you ought to have done it, if not by other necessity, at least by the law of friendship, if only you were able. Nor would it have been done in vain. For I indeed desired, as I even indicated, to converse with you at greater length. But while I was forced to postpone my conversation for three days, this unexpected departure of yours frustrates my discourse. Thus, this long-invented story leaves me while the great-souled lion <note>A pun on Pierleone’s name, *Leoni*, meaning "lions"</note> leaves here. For me, it is no mere story; I just erred. For what has been discovered cannot vanish, so long as the story has not yet been announced. What then? If my genius <note>In the Platonic sense, a *genius* is a personal guiding spirit or higher consciousness</note> and yours judged volatile voices unworthy to have the eternal meaning of this story committed to them? And so, if it disdained voices that are in a way "living," for what reason will it deign to accept letters that are "not living"? Therefore, that which I did not commend to voices, I shall not commend to letters either. This intimate conversation, then, my genius—who is never and nowhere absent—now begins, departing from yours to speak with you, destined to continue for eternity. While they converse thus within, no envious or dark demons meeting from the outside shall insert themselves further. A thousand shall fall at my side, and ten thousand at your right hand <note>A reference to Psalm 91:7, suggesting divine protection over their friendship</note>. Farewell happily. Philosophize more happily still. You shall one day return most happily to the city of Florence, which is so friendly to you. August 2, 1488. Florence.

->All things are to be resolved into fire according to Orpheus.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Callimachus <note>Filippo Buonaccorsi, known as Callimachus Experiens, a humanist poet</note>, the wise poet, sends greetings.<-

<margin>o</margin>
**T**hey say that Orpheus and some others sang that since all things are composed of four mutually contrary materials <note>The four elements: earth, air, fire, and water</note>, and fire is the most ample and powerful of all, and by its perpetual motion wears down the rest little by little, all other things must finally be resolved entirely into fire. What then? If the divine Intellect, the moderator of all, has granted such a great resolution to the world, so that just as it is compacted into a most beautiful form as long as it remains consistent with itself, so when it is finally dissolved, it may be reduced to the most beautiful matter. This great death of the universe, then (if we believe it), we bear with an equal mind. We shall bear it, my great-souled Callimachus, with the most equal [mind]...

### One must consider in what style one writes to whom.

### Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings <note>original: *S. D.*, abbreviation for *Salutem Dicit*</note> to Hermolao Barbaro of Venice.

<margin>a</margin> I hear that the case of Mattia Cini is being handled before you; he is a citizen and a very dear friend of mine who manages business there. Unless he had asked me, I would not commend his rights to you. For I think it is superfluous to commend justice to a man who is both prudent and just. This cause, Hermolao, has compelled me to write something to you after a long silence. I would certainly write more often if I could write more elegantly. For I hear that nothing except the most exquisite things please your most refined ears. You are blessed, my friend, to have attained the first degree of eloquence. Yet I am not wretched, for I am content with the tenth. Farewell, and love me very much, as I love you. Our friend Giovanni Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, the famous polymath</note>, who is now philosophizing excellently in Florence, commends himself to you. September 13, 1488. Florence.

### On the flight of Fame. And that one’s own things are most dear.

### Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to Paolo of Florence, the Theologian <note>Paolo Orlandini, a Camaldolese monk and theologian</note>.

<margin>g</margin> Your letter was most welcome to me. By it, I understood both that you are well and that I am "flying." For since (as you write) I have already subjected all of Europe to a "service of love" <note>A reference to the wide distribution and popularity of Ficino's translations of Plato and his own work, *De Amore*</note>, I could not achieve this by physical travel; therefore, I did it by flight. But you, with the spirit of your praises—or rather your proclamations—have added wings to this flight. You, therefore, be my Daedalus <note>The mythical master craftsman who built wings for himself and his son</note>—provided that I am not an Icarus <note>original: *bycarus*; a pun on Icarus, who flew too close to the sun, and *bis-carus*, meaning "doubly dear"</note> to you—though I am indeed very dear [*carus*]. And rightly am I especially dear to you, since your own things ought to be most dear to you. Your affairs are also so dear to me; and let that noble youth recommended to you before all others be most welcome to me as well, especially because, as you say, he is already "old" in learning and judgment. Truly, nature often repays the turns of things in this way: for there are also many old men who are children in their character. Finally, as much as I am my own, I am yours, my Paolo; and I am also that young man's own. Farewell.

### Nothing hinders learning more than civic ambition. Proved by Astrology.

### Marsilio Ficino of Florence sends many greetings to the most illustrious Hermolao Barbaro, orator of the Venetian Senate.

<margin>a</margin> I have heard from many this year—and recently from Pietro Alamanni, who served as ambassador there and greeted me yesterday in your name—that in your embassy <margin>is</margin> you have been no less devoted to letters (and what is more wonderful) you even philosophize <margin>more sharply</margin> than you are accustomed to. Men are usually inclined, my Barbaro, to interrupt the study of letters when they conduct public business, or even as soon as they touch it. This is partly because a life of business takes away the leisure that is the primary requirement for the work of a free mind. It is also because we then approach closer to Jove, the planet of governance and power...

...is perished. The further we move away from Mercury, the prince of letters <note>In astrology, Mercury governs communication, writing, and the intellect</note>, the more we are lost. For even the Moon and the other celestial bodies are nowhere more separated from the houses of Mercury than when they enter the seats of Jupiter. Since the Maker of the world himself opposed Pisces to Virgo and Sagittarius to Gemini <note>Virgo and Gemini are ruled by Mercury; Pisces and Sagittarius are ruled by Jupiter. In astrology, these signs sit opposite each other, creating a natural tension</note>. Besides, do they not think the Sun signifies princes and honors, while Saturn signifies philosophers? In the heavens, their kingdoms are opposed to kingdoms, and their houses to houses. Rejoice therefore in such power. Your friends congratulate you on the same. Farewell. October 11, 1489.

->Few join public business with the study of letters.<-

Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings <note>original: *S. D.*, for *Salutem Dicit*</note> to Francesco Gaddo, Orator of the Florentine Senate.

<margin>S</margin> I am writing to Hermolao Barbaro, praising him because, amid civil and turbulent business, he seeks the accustomed leisure for the study of letters and (what is even more wonderful) he even philosophizes most ardently. And the more Jupiter <note>Representing the active life of politics and governance</note> presses his head with public cares, the more he himself should press Minerva, who was born from the head of Jupiter <note>Minerva/Athena represents wisdom; the myth describes her springing fully formed from Jupiter's skull</note>. Few are those whom "just Jupiter" has loved—not the planet, but the Creator of the planets. Few join together these two things so far apart from one another. Only those born of the gods could either pursue both at once, which Hermolao does, or, while following the one, complete the study of philosophizing in a moment, which others could scarcely do in a long time. Our friend Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</note> achieves this latter feat; in him truly there is a "fiery vigor and celestial origin." Water scarcely transforms wood into water in a thousand years; fire converts it into fire in almost a moment. Theologians have called Saturn the "most voracious" <note>Referring to the myth of Saturn/Cronus devouring his children</note>. Pico, born under Saturn, is the same: just as that Saturn devoured his children, so he daily devours great, entire books. These he does not reduce to ash like our fire, but like celestial fire, he turns them into light. Therefore, our most beloved Francesco, imitating Hermolao Barbaro, you shall not cease to philosophize in the meantime during your embassy. You will greet him, when your business allows, in the name of Marsilio and Pico, and you will signify that just as we are both ours, we are both his. When I name both, I wish Poliziano <note>The humanist poet Angelo Poliziano</note> to be understood as well, the indissoluble bond of both. Farewell. October 11, 1489.

->One only truly lives where one lives by the intellect.<-

Marsilio Ficino humbly commends himself to the Reverend Father in Christ and Lord, Marco of Venice, Cardinal of San Marco.

<margin>V</margin> Do you see how clever our friend Calderino is? He has long ago devised a most easy and safe travel-provision <note>original: *viaticum*</note> by which he might always safely seek Florence and return to Rome. For he always supports and arms himself with your greetings, by which he may go safely through weapons and through fires, and return a safe friend, and report back safely to you. Your greetings are such, whether they go from you or return to you. Indeed, him whom I just now called "clever," I call "prudent." For others...

...the same men sleep very much at the doors of the foolish; but our friend meanwhile watches there at the doors of the wise, so that he may drink salvation from the Lord. Which he also imparts to his friends. Indeed, so that they may find life: for he hopes that he will live only there where he lives most especially through the intellect. ->Preface to the ninth book, on the 19th day of October 1488.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Martinus Uranius of Constance <note>Martin Prenninger, a German humanist and jurist who was a devoted student of Ficino's work</note>, his unique friend, sends greetings.<-

<margin>1</margin>
The Ninth Book of our letters—by which one can perceive movement in every direction—has for a long time demanded a "head" <note>Ficino plays on the word *caput*, meaning both the start of a book and the anatomical head</note> that is the citadel of the vital power <term>vital power: *virtutis animalis*, the faculty of the soul that governs sensation and movement through the brain</term> and the origin of sense and motion. While I was deliberating on choosing a head for this book, our very guardian Angel presented himself to the book, commanding that this ninth number be consecrated to him. Indeed, nine orders of angels were accepted not only among Christians, but also among the Hebrews and the Platonists. Therefore, under such a great head and leader, we ask: whenever the book or the man whom the angel guards wanders here and there, does the angel similarly wander? By no means. For the Angel, whom they call a good demon <term>demon: *daemon*, in the Platonic sense, a guiding spirit or intermediary between the divine and human realms, rather than an evil spirit</term> or genius, is either always everywhere—which Plotinus, Porphyry, and Iamblichus <note>Key philosophers in the Neoplatonic tradition who wrote extensively on the soul and spiritual hierarchies</note> believe—or is present wherever he wishes as easily and swiftly as a ray of the sun. It reaches here in a moment and is reflected from here to there and everywhere in the same moment; indeed, it is much more rapid and easy, since a ray is the action of a luminous body, but an Angel exists by his own right. Or, just as each person’s star governs by an influence diffused everywhere without descending. Why we have begun the book with an angel, I seem to have said enough. But why do we dedicate it specifically to Martinus Uranius? Because my book has now, by its own right, become the property of his "genial" <note>A pun on *genius*, suggesting their guardian spirits are linked</note> affection, since he shares the same genius with me. Receive it then gladly, and read it fortunately, Uranius, my celestial friend—letters that are equally Martinian and Marsilian. Farewell happily, my other self. July 4, 1490. Florence.

The ninth book of letters follows, to be dedicated to Martinus Uranius Prenninger.
->Description of a healthy villa.<-
->Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Filippo Valori <note>A Florentine nobleman and patron of the arts who supported Ficino’s work</note>.<-

When in recent days I and our Pico della Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, the famous polymath and philosopher</note>—a man to be wondered at for his virtue—were wandering through the Fiesolan hills, or rather the sub-Fiesolan hills, we were looking out over the whole field of the city of Florence spread before our eyes. We were imagining, therefore, a house on the hill at the roots of Mount Fiesole, so that we might avoid the fog from the one side and the North Wind from the other. Yet not wishing to be in a hollow...

...so that it might more abundantly receive the breeze under the summer heat. We desired, moreover, it to be situated equally among cultivated lands and groves, and abounding everywhere with springs, looking toward the south and the east. Aristotle altogether prescribed this in his writings on household management <note>original: *de re familiari*, referring to the *Oeconomica*</note>. Later, our fellow citizen Pandolfini—named Pier Filippo—certainly with the same prudence as those others, happily chose it as his home." "O happy man," said Pico, "to whom it happened that upon withdrawing from public business, he inhabits a sacred house. I said 'sacred house' because it is placed near this sacred grove, and twenty shrines of the gods surround it. This place is therefore sacred above all others and especially fit for oracles; hence Pandolfini seems to be rightly named. For if we interpret this name from the Greek, 'Delphic' <note>Referring to the Oracle of Apollo at Delphi; Pico is playing on the name Pandolfini containing 'delphi'</note> is entirely signified by it." These things, my Valori <note>Francesco Valori, a diplomat and student of Ficino</note>, were said and approved between us then. You should necessarily report these same things to your most distinguished fellow citizen, so that he may hereafter inhabit and frequent more willingly these healthy seats dedicated to him by divine providence. Farewell. October 29, 1488.

->Lamentation and consolation regarding the death of friends.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Amerigo Corsini, his fellow philosopher, greetings.

<margin>c</margin>Our friend Corsini was complaining yesterday, together with Giovanni Canaccio and the Ricasoli brothers—our companions in Plato—about the all too cruel death of Alamanno Donati, the "Mars of the Academy." I call him the "Mars of the Academy" for this reason: because that high-minded and eloquent youth most fiercely defended every one of us against envious detractors. Yesterday, therefore, Mars—traversing through the sign of Leo with a cruel Moon joined to him—struck this Mars of ours by a most cruel chance, throwing him from his mule against a rock and immediately removing him from our midst. I blame Mars here above the others (if it is permitted for us to blame any of the heavenly beings), because he himself was occupying Leo along with the Moon, which was once ascending at Alamanno's birth, but was now, at the moment he was struck, holding the Eighth House in the heavens <term>Eighth House: the section of an astrological chart traditionally associated with death</term>. But at the same hour in which he fell and, alas, perished, Saturn was rising from the east in Capricorn. Pitying the heavy lot of the philosopher—for Saturn himself loves philosophers—he received his soul through Capricorn, the Gate of the Gods <term>Gate of the Gods: a Neoplatonic belief that souls enter the heavens through the sign of Capricorn</term>, and numbered him there among the angelic Thrones. And although that ought to be enough to console our sorrow, I was nevertheless weeping (as I said) for the untimely death of the noble youth.

To these words, our friends replied: "Alas, our Marsilio, the Academy has suffered more than just this one loss. It has also recently lost Lottieri <note>original: *lotteriũ*, referring to Lottieri della Tosa, a member of Ficino's circle</note>, a man of great learning and piety. ### The Position and Aspect of the Planets Contributing to Genius
### Marsilio Ficino to Ermolao Barbaro <note>A famous Venetian humanist and diplomat</note>, greetings.

Friends are often in the habit of writing to one another that the souls of friends are not separated by mountains. In saying this, they surely lie, or at least they are frequently mistaken. For souls are indeed far apart when one is entirely ignorant of the other's genius <note>original: *ingenium*, referring to one's natural character, intellect, and spiritual inclination</note>. You, therefore, are a true man; and so that you may be as truthful in this as in all other things, should you happen to write the same to us as you do to others, you recently sent us a certain pattern of your genius—a truly beautiful one <note>Ficino is referring to Barbaro's birth chart or a description of his planetary alignments</note>. It is beautiful indeed if Mercury, the giver of genius, inhabiting his airy home of Gemini, provides a broad and ample intellect. And perhaps it is even more charming and elegant than if he were in Virgo; looking out from there in a sextile aspect <note>An angle of 60 degrees, considered a favorable and stimulating influence</note> to Jupiter rising in Aries, he adds integrity and humanity to beauty. And while from that position he also looks upon Saturn reigning in a trine aspect in Libra—holding, as I believe, the western angle of the chart, just as Jupiter holds the eastern—he decrees for your genius a certain gravity, a devotion to ancient wisdom, and a character that is firm and perpetual. 

Thus, your soul, Ermolao, has come to us. But so far it is without its body; it dwells with us naked, until we receive from you the rest of your heavenly figure <note>the complete horoscope</note>, by which the form of the body may be more distinctly and fully expressed. You are so humane, my Barbaro, that you could not bear to leave the soul of your friend in the prison of its own mind any longer. Will you now be so "inhumane" <note>A play on words between 'humanus' (kind/learned) and 'inhumanus' (unkind/lacking a human form)</note> toward your own soul that you allow it to long for its body any longer? Far be it from you to allow that. For if you perform what we so vehemently desire, you will be entirely with yourself, Ermolao, and you will be entirely with us as well. To this is added the fact that once your birth chart <note>original: *genitura*</note> is finally inspected, we shall write to you something that may be of use to your health. We hope that while we look after your life, we are looking after the life of our own century. 

Farewell happily, and so that you may fare even more happily: be entirely yourself, everywhere. 

November 12, 1488.

### On the Efficacy of Speaking and the Method of Joking

# BOOK NINE
# PAGE 197

<margin>P</margin>Do not deny that you are at least now a poet <note>The word "poet" comes from the Greek *poietes*, meaning "maker" or "creator." Ficino is making a pun on this etymology.</note>. For by speaking, you have just become a "maker." Your letter certainly proves this twice over, right in the opening words: "I am," you say, "so difficult in writing," and so forth. What else are you trying to do with these words, if not to describe the difficulty of writing? Yet, in the meantime, you create that very difficulty by saying it. I mean a difficulty not only of writing but, moreover, of reading. These words of yours are so full of blotches, both large and dark. Thus, you are so truthful and effective that you actually bring about the very thing you are talking about. But why do I joke now with such a grave philosopher? Truly, I do not joke so much as one philosopher with another, but as a friend with a friend. However I may joke, what of it? Does not Mercury <note>The Roman god of communication and wit, also associated with the planet Mercury</note> himself now joke in the heavens and play within us? He is accustomed to speak seriously when with Saturn or Jupiter, but to joke when with Venus. Therefore, at this hour, being joined with Venus and the Moon—and now ascending on this day <note>original: *feria*, referring to the day of the week or a festival day</note>—he rejects serious things and delights in the ridiculous. 

But setting these jokes aside for a moment (if we can), as for the fact that you are spreading our Platonic works far and wide: I am as truly grateful as I am delighted by the light. For while our "Solar man" <note>original: *Solaris nanq̃ viro*, likely referring to a patron or a person of high intellect, possibly Apollo/Phœbus metaphorically</note> sings—just as when Phœbus <note>The sun god Apollo, patron of truth and light</note> shines—we cannot remain in the dark. You are waiting for Proclus <note>A late antique Neoplatonist philosopher whose works Ficino was translating</note> from us. Wait for Proclus, and at the same time for the divine Iamblichus—that divine Iamblichus who responds wonderfully to the many and most weighty questions of Porphyry <note>Porphyry was a student of Plotinus; Iamblichus later critiqued and expanded upon his work</note>, and who meanwhile reveals the divine mysteries of the Egyptians and Assyrians. We shall soon make up for the slowness of our promises with a great abundance of gifts (if GOD helps us). In the meantime, fare you well and happily.

But after I said "farewell," our friend Pico della Mirandola <note>A famous young philosopher and protégé of Ficino; Ficino puns here on his name *Mirandulanus* and the word *mirandus*, meaning "wonderful" or "to be admired"</note>—a man certainly to be admired—reached for this letter and read it. And he read it so beautifully and judged it so sharply that I would not say it was so much mine as his own. What then? What if, by his touch and his gaze, he has so influenced it that he made it his own on the spot? Nevertheless, in the meantime, it does not cease to be mine. Therefore, where I said "farewell," I should have said: Ficino and Pico wish you prosperous health. January 3, 1489, immediately at sunrise.

->He writes enough to a single friend who writes to all his friends at once.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Bandino <note>A Florentine humanist and diplomat living in the Hungarian court</note>, greetings.<-

<margin>N</margin>I have written nothing to you for a long time, my dearest Bandino, because in the meantime I am writing many things for both you and everyone. I wish they were as good as they are numerous. You have known for a long time that I have finished turning all the books of Plotinus into Latin <note>This was Ficino's massive project of translating the *Enneads* of Plotinus</note>, and that I soon began to write commentaries on them. I have already brought those halfway to completion. And perhaps I would have finished them, had I not been forced during the course of commenting to translate additionally into Latin the work of the Platonist Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, an 11th-century Byzantine scholar</note> *On Demons*, and Synesius *On Dreams*, and part of Porphyry *On Abstinence*, and also the divine Iamblichus *On the Theology of the Egyptians and Assyrians*. And finally, the work of Priscian the Lydian <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist</note> on the mind of Theophrastus, diligently interpreting the Mind. In the midst of these things, Filippo Valori <note>A wealthy patron and friend of Ficino who funded the printing of his works</note>—full of value <note>Ficino puns on the name *Valor* and the word for value/courage</note> and grace—dedicated to your King [Matthias Corvinus]...

# BOOK NINE

...the most noble text of Plotinus and the commentaries are being transcribed for the King in a royal volume; thirty-three large gatherings <note>original: "quinterniones," referring to quires or booklets of five folded sheets</note> are now finished. Farewell. January 6, 1489. Florence.

->A friend within a friend. Likewise, an excuse for a journey not undertaken.<-

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine Platonist humbly commends himself to the most serene <margin>of Hungary</margin> King Matthias, ever-invincible.<-

<margin>F</margin> **I**f the remarkable power of friendship can achieve what the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed in the mystical unity and "shared soul" of true friends</note> promise—that the soul of a friend resides within the friend—then certainly my soul is now within Filippo Valori, who recently departed for Pannonia <note>The Roman name for the region comprising modern-day Hungary</note> to greet your Majesty before all else. Thus, when you hear him speaking his humble greetings, you may consider that you have heard Marsilio himself. I have indeed desired for a long time to visit your Majesty, being wished for there by many; however, I feared that my strength would not suffice for such a long journey. I finally decided to "come within Valori," hoping that in this way Valori would not be lacking in my strength for making the journey—especially since I have brought "provisions" <term>viaticum: literally food or money for a journey; here used metaphorically for books</term> with me: books full of the healthy nourishment of the mind. These shall serve as both nutrition on the road and a carriage for me. 

You will therefore happily read Priscianus Lydus <note>A 6th-century philosopher who fled to Persia after the closing of the Academy in Athens</note>, the philosopher who carefully interprets the mind, imagination, and intellect according to the thought of Theophrastus and Aristotle. I have not only translated this from the Greek but also explained it with brief notes. In reading this, you will clearly recognize what Themistius <note>An influential 4th-century commentator</note> also asserts: that the opinion of Plato, Aristotle, and Theophrastus regarding the mind is the same. They hold that there is one divine mind common to all men, which illuminates human minds everywhere—which the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's school</note> call the "Agent Intellect." Yet, there are as many individual minds as there are souls, and these are likewise immortal. These they were accustomed to call "Possible Intellects"—that is, those capable of being formed by the divine mind. Through these things, you will understand that Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias</note> and Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher; Ficino refutes his idea that humanity shares only one single soul</note> have been refuted, and you will fully recognize the divinity of our soul. 

Furthermore, you will not disdain to read the book by Michael Psellus on demons, briefly translated by me, which reconciles the Platonists with the Christians regarding the nature of demons. After this, you will see the laborious work of Plotinus, now brought in part to Pannonia (so that the whole may be shown to you in part). It remains for me to most strongly commend my Filippo Valori—and myself within Valori—to your most happy Majesty. February 6, 1489.

->Preface to Theophrastus on the Soul.<-
->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Filippo Valori.<-

<margin>P</margin> **W**hen the god commands, "Know Thyself" <note>The famous Delphic maxim</note>, he seems to be admonishing us to know the soul. Since the soul is in the middle of all things, it is surely everything; therefore, once the soul is known, we will easily come to know all things. I, therefore (so that I might first grasp the soul, through which everything else is to be obtained), have for a long time turned to the philosophers—not those common ones, but the most excellent...

# BOOK NINE CXCVIII

...I applied myself studiously. However, while I was anxiously questioning the Platonists on one side and the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, so named because they walked about while teaching</note> on the other, and saw their responses seem to differ from one another, I initially despaired of ever achieving my wish. But not long after, Themistius <note>A 4th-century philosopher who sought to reconcile the different schools of Greek thought</note> gave me the best hope, affirming that such great philosophers do not differ in their fundamental meaning, but only in words; and finally, that the opinion of Plato, Aristotle, and Theophrastus <note>Aristotle's successor as head of the Peripatetic school</note> regarding the soul is the same under diverse expressions. Finally, by a certain divine fate, I came upon a book by Theophrastus *On the Soul*, briefly but nonetheless diligently explained by a certain Priscian the Lydian; primarily following the method by which Plutarch and Iamblichus—illustrious Platonists and Peripatetics alike—had explained the Aristotelian opinion on the soul. 

When I noticed that the Platonists and Peripatetics were in agreement in these readings, I had almost everything my mind sought. And so that others might also have it as soon as possible, we have translated this book from the Greek language into Latin. We have also added certain brief explanations devised by us while reading and translating. Nevertheless, I did not think I should labor too excessively on this matter for the present, or refine it more broadly. For our friend Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <note>A brilliant young philosopher known for his attempt to harmonize all human knowledge</note>—certainly a man to be admired—is already working on this to the highest degree; he most diligently discusses the thoughts of all philosophers on any given subject, and wonderfully shows that Plato and Aristotle are in agreement regarding the soul. 

I decided that this book should be dedicated especially to you, my dear Valori <note>Filippo Valori, a close friend and financial patron of Ficino's work</note>. For you, along with me, have long and vehemently desired the concord of philosophers. Indeed, our Medici patrons, to whom we are accustomed to give all things—or rather, to return them—will undoubtedly agree that this one little gift out of many should be dedicated to my dear Valori: a most loyal friend of the Medici house and the ever-most prompt assistant of Platonic works. Although we found only a single Greek manuscript, and a faulty and fragmented one at that, read it securely nonetheless, and provide it to others to be read. For I have studied most diligently to correct and unlock this, and our friend Angelo Poliziano <note>A leading humanist scholar and poet in the Medici circle</note>, a man of the sharpest judgment and great learning, has approved this diligence of ours. Farewell. March 25, 1489.

There, by a certain divine fate, I first encountered Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher from the 3rd/4th century whose works on theurgy and the soul were central to Ficino’s philosophy</note>, known among Academics as the "divine and great priest." To him I said, "Greetings, Iamblichus, great priest. There is a man in Florence sent from God, whose name is John [Giovanni]; born of the heroic Medici stock, he comes into..."

He granted these prayers; and with this sentiment, John, the great priest, comes to you. Receive him joyfully, then, as a mere greeter; and after the first greeting, and after the letter has been read, listen more attentively (if you please) to what that divine man says. For he promised that he would say things worthy of both his person and yours alike: that he would express to you in brief what the Egyptian and Assyrian priests thought concerning religion and divine matters.

### Summary of the Book

<margin>p</margin>Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus</note>, who is called "the Philosopher" among the Platonists because of his excellence, sent a long letter to Egypt to Anebo the priest, full of various and serious questions looking toward all parts of philosophy—especially regarding God and angels, demons and souls, providence, fate, prophecies, magic, miracles, sacrifices, and vows. Iamblichus <note>A 4th-century Neoplatonist who emphasized ritual and theurgy</note>, his student, responded to Porphyry’s questions. However, he introduces an Egyptian priest, Abamon, as the respondent on behalf of his pupil Anebo, to whom Porphyry had sent the letter. Of this entire (surely divine) question and response, I have translated nearly every sense rather than every word, as if I were still too occupied with Plotinus. Thus, it should not be considered a wonder if the speech appears disjointed in places, especially among the very beginnings of the dispute where the loss of words is less significant; for hereafter, the context of the words will appear more continuous. I was forced, however, now and then to interpose some word of my own for the sake of continuity or understanding. Pierleone <note>Pierleone Leoni, a renowned physician and scholar who was a close friend of Ficino</note> was also a cause of a faster publication—a man most desirous of all secrets; but what I wonder at most of all is that he seems to strive for that which he already possesses. For by a certain divinity of genius, he attains the secrets of the philosophers, both Greek and barbarian, even those not yet read.

NINTH BOOK CXCIX

in whom all nations will be blessed: it is Giovanni <note>Giovanni de’ Medici (1475–1521), later Pope Leo X</note>, born of Lorenzo; to whom, while still a young youth, divine providence miraculously conferred the dignity of the Cardinalate <note>original: "Cardineam dignitatem," a play on the word "cardinal" and "cardo," meaning a hinge</note>—an omen of the future Pontiff, in whom all nations are indeed blessed in the place of Christ. To this family, chosen by God long ago as the best, every excellent man of letters ought to consecrate (so to speak) all his works, and indeed his most select ones. For Marsilio <note>Ficino refers to himself in the third person</note>, an old foster-son of the Medici house, it was not permitted by reason of his age to dedicate anything to Giovanni di Bicci <note>The great-grandfather of Lorenzo the Magnificent</note>. It was permitted, however, to first dedicate several things to Cosimo; then to Piero; and thirdly, to Lorenzo. Now, by the grace of God, it is permitted to offer to a fourth, Giovanni—the sacred flower of the Florentine Medici house—flowers gathered from the meadows of the Platonic philosophers. These I offer indeed with happy omens, so that my books—or rather, my children—when at last the nations are blessed in you, may themselves also become partakers of that blessing. You recently received, venerable patron, those flowers which I had gathered from the meadows of Iamblichus. Now, receive with favor those I have plucked from the fields of Porphyry and Proclus. Having sipped from them in the manner of a bee, may you fashion honey in the gardens of the Academy.

### Preface to Synesius and Psellus

Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to the Magnanimous Piero de’ Medici <note>Piero "the Unfortunate" (1472–1503), the eldest son of Lorenzo the Magnificent</note>, greetings.
<margin>q</margin> Although you read many things daily that are better than mine, I nevertheless believe that almost none please you more than ours—if indeed it is true that one's own things usually please a person most. And those things are most truly one’s own which have been possessed for the longest time; certainly, "Marsilian" things have been possessed by you for the longest time. I hope, therefore, that these will be especially dear to you; so that even if I send dreams, these too might be held as true by you first, and through you, they might be held as true by others. Therefore, since I desired that the book of Synesius the Platonist <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414), a philosopher-bishop</note> *On Dreams*, which we recently translated from the Greek, should have authority and trust especially with its first reader, and through him with others, I have sent it primarily to you. You are now the fourth generation after the great Cosimo to read our works, and by your excellent learning and authority, you shall immediately prove these works to everyone through your approval. I have joined to the book on dreams the book of Michael Psellus the Platonist <note>Byzantine philosopher and historian (c. 1017–1078)</note> *On Demons*, and not without reason, since the ancients believe that dreams are sent by demons. Farewell. April 15, 1489.

### Commendation of Style

Marsilio Ficino to his excellent godfather, Andrea Cambini <note>A Florentine historian and associate of the Medici circle</note>, greetings.
<margin>m</margin> I have long owed you much for many reasons, my dearest godfather. But for this reason especially I owe you the most today: you have lightened our mind, which was weighed down by some unknown weariness, of a most troublesome burden. For you gave us three speeches by your kinsman, Francesco Pucci <note>A Florentine politician and diplomat</note>, to read. The reading of them delighted me so much that I can hardly express this pleasure in even as many or as great speeches of my own. For those things usually provide the most delight which sufficiently satisfy a desire. In speeches, I desire these things above all others: witty insights, yet not obscure; an abundance that is not at all superfluous; and a concise...

## Response to one seeking Platonic instruction and a list of books.

## Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Martinus Uranius <note>Martin Prenninger (1450–1501), a German jurist and humanist</note>. Heartiest greetings.

<margin>d</margin>
The divine Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who emphasized ritual and theurgy</note> describes two paths to happiness according to the mind of the Egyptians: one philosophical, the other priestly. The former is indeed clearer for finding happiness, while the latter is shorter for achieving it. The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school</note> and similar philosophers chose the former above all. The religious populace walks chiefly in the latter. Our Plato wonderfully joined both paths into one; he is everywhere equally religious and philosophical: a subtle disputant, a pious priest, and an eloquent orator. Therefore, if you follow the footsteps of the divine Plato for a longer time (as you have begun), you will both find happiness (with God as the indicator) and achieve the same (with God as the guide). This is especially so because our Plato, along with Pythagorean and Socratic reasoning, follows the Mosaic law and portends the Christian one. As for what you ask regarding Platonic understanding, you will be led by our arguments in his books and by our own books which you already possess—principally those titled *On the Immortality of Souls* <note>Ficino refers to his masterpiece, the *Theologia Platonica*</note>, which nevertheless encompass the whole of Platonic thought. Likewise, Alcinous <note>Author of a 2nd-century handbook on Platonism</note> has been sent to you today, and furthermore, much more the divine Iamblichus, recently translated by us, to be sent to you at another time.

<margin>a</margin>
But most of all, the fifty-four books of Plotinus <note>The *Enneads*, the foundational text of Neoplatonism</note> will introduce you into the inner sanctums of all wisdom; these we have translated and have now interpreted for the most part with commentaries.

You may perhaps receive these shortly. You ask, however, what books I have either translated or composed besides these.

<margin>Translated</margin>
I have indeed translated Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurium," referring to the *Corpus Hermeticum*</note> *On the Divine Mind* and *On the Crafting of the World*; Synesius *On Dreams*; Psellus *On Demons*; some works of Porphyry on the soul and intellect; certain works of Proclus on the *Alcibiades*; and the Platonic commentaries of Priscianus on the books of Theophrastus *On the Soul*.

<margin>Composed</margin>
I have composed *On Pleasure* and *On Caring for the Health of Men of Letters* <note>Part of his famous medical/astrological work *De Vita Libri Tres*</note>, which you will receive now; eight volumes of our letters; a commentary on the *Philebus*, not yet finished; *On Love*; and *On the Christian Religion*. I have also attempted and indeed composed certain other things: a book against the plague in the Tuscan tongue <note>Written in Italian rather than Latin to reach a wider audience during an outbreak</note>. You ask which Platonic books are found again among the Latins. The works of Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian whose works were deeply influenced by Proclus</note>—all are Platonic. Many of Augustine's. Boethius's *Consolation*. Apuleius *On Demons*. Calcidius's commentary on the *Timaeus*. Macrobius's exposition on the *Dream of Scipio*. Avicebron <note>Solomon ibn Gabirol, a Jewish philosopher</note> *On the Fountain of Life*. Al-Farabi *On Causes*, and the works of Henry of Ghent. Many things of Avicenna and Scotus <note>Duns Scotus</note> reflect Plato... <note>The text cuts off here mid-sentence</note>

He frames Plato as a figure who unites philosophy with religion, harmonizing the "Mosaic law" with Greek wisdom.</summary>

[...they] grieve. They read also, in whatever way they were translated, the *Elements of Theology* by Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was the last great head of the Platonic Academy in Athens; his "Elements" presented Neoplatonism in a geometric, axiomatic style</note>, as well as his *Theology* itself, and the book *On Providence and Fate* together. Similarly, we have translated, as best we could, Hermias <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> on the *Phaedrus*, and Iamblichus on the Pythagorean sect. There exists, furthermore, the defense of Plato made by Cardinal Bessarion of Nicaea <note>Basilios Bessarion (1403–1472), a Greek scholar and Cardinal whose work "In Calumniatorem Platonis" defended Plato against Aristotelian critics</note>. There are also certain speculations by Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa <note>A German philosopher and mystic (1401–1464) known for the concept of the "coincidence of opposites"</note>. I believe I have now answered sufficiently the things you have sought so far. But as for your love for Marsilio, my Martin—which I know for certain is unique—I do not believe I could ever respond to it even with innumerable letters. But so that I am not entirely ungrateful, to your unique love I first respond with a similarly unique love (believe me), and I embrace your soul, which burns toward me, with a similar ardor of mind. These things you shall receive first from us as the preliminary rewards for your love. But would that I could give some gift to Uranius <note>A play on Prenninger’s humanist name "Uranius," derived from the Greek "Ouranos" (Heaven)</note>—that is, a heavenly gift—or at least that I could suspect a heavenly one. Indeed, I wish, my Uranius, and I also hope that before you return to the heavenly fatherland, you will be a participant in happiness and blessed in heaven. Florence, June 12, 1489.

### Marsilio Ficino to Pierleone <note>Pierleone Leoni of Spoleto (d. 1492), a famous physician and personal doctor to Lorenzo de' Medici</note>, his fellow philosopher. Heartiest greetings.

<margin>q</margin>As much as you yourself were desiring to see Proclus, so much was I desiring to send him to you. For those who share the same will, there is surely an equal and similar desire. Why, then, not sooner? His hour had not yet come; his hour comes now, although it is a bit late for departing from here. Would that he does not arrive late to you; he will certainly come as a good companion, whenever he arrives. Practice philosophy happily, friend most wished for by all. And if you desire anything from us, ask—but with such trust that you may receive it more quickly hereafter. Our Pico della Mirandola <note>The famous young philosopher and polymath</note> philosophizes excellently and loves you excellently. Farewell. August 2, 1489.

### A light recommendation.
### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Nesi <note>A devoted student of Ficino and a Florentine humanist</note>. Heartiest greetings.

<margin>s</margin>Greetings. The priest Bernard asked me to recommend him to you regarding the upcoming vacancy of a certain small church. Therefore, I recommend him to you; however, there is no need to bring forward reasons for the recommendation, for he is better known to you than to me. It will therefore be the part of your kindness to help a friend, since he well deserves it. Farewell. August 8, 1489.

### Study on the long life.
### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, fellow philosopher. Heartiest greetings.

<margin>q</margin>On the day you left here, I completed the little book *On Obtaining Life from the Heavens* <note>original: "de vita coelitus comparanda," the third book of Ficino's influential "Three Books on Life," dealing with astral influences on health</note>. But the day before, I had opportunely come across a certain book by Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous medieval physician and alchemist</note> on retarding old age, long desired by us, but difficult to read and very difficult to understand due to the fault of the scribes. Meanwhile, the owner of the manuscript presses for its reading quite urgently. Therefore, the difficult and rather hurried reading on the retarding of old age retards the arrival...

BOOK NINE

[...your love] toward me. But this (as I judge) we will endure with an even mind. Only may this diligence of yours sometimes retard old age for you. For me, truly, I must think not so much about retarding old age, but rather about retaining it <note>Ficino plays on the idea of not just slowing down aging, but holding onto the vitality of youth</note>. Meanwhile, while we seem separated and to handle separate things, we do the same; we emulate Prometheus. We fashion a human being: You the soul, I the body. You lead her from the divine; I receive this from the heavens. Since this was wonderfully demonstrated by you in the sevenfold mirror <note>A reference to the seven planetary spheres</note> after the creation of the world, we immediately, by common labor, compose the human being, the spectator of the world. Farewell. 9 August 1489.

### On the poetic style in the aphorisms of Hippocrates.

->Marsilio Ficino to Antonio of Faenza <note>Antonio Faventino (d. 1509), a noble physician and professor of medicine</note>, the noble physician, sends greetings.<-

<margin>1</margin> Perhaps you gave your letter to us on the day or hour of Saturn, or with Saturn himself ascending, or at least with the Moon entering a fixed house. For they reached Florence from Ferrara in scarcely four months. Nevertheless, that Saturn of yours has brought forth a Jupiter <note>Saturn was associated with delays and melancholy, while Jupiter represents joy, speed, and benevolence; Ficino is saying the long delay was worth the beautiful result</note>: a letter full of humanity and elegance. If the speech of the gods and the style of oracles is song <note>original: "carmen"</note>, and since Hippocrates <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine"</note> was once held to be a God, and his aphorisms were rightly considered oracles, you have translated them into poems quite appropriately. But indeed, lest perhaps what you have done well should seem badly placed, you seek a Maecenas <note>A historical Roman patron of the arts; the term became a general word for a wealthy protector of scholars</note> for your poem. Now, my Antonio, there is no choice among patrons; there is scarcely one whom you name. Let him, therefore, be the protector of your songs. It will be very pleasing to me to read your verses. It is already most pleasing to be loved by you. For what is more lovable than to be loved by one who loves with judgment and is himself worthy of veneration? Our commentaries on Plotinus <note>A 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism; Ficino's translation and commentary on him was a massive undertaking</note> have been interrupted by Theophrastus, Iamblichus, Proclus, and certain others. They too are eager to travel through us from Greece into Italy at some point. But I have recently returned to Plotinus, intending to follow through on the commentaries on him assiduously. Farewell, be happy, you who are most desired to return to us eventually. 15 August 1489.

### Astronomical auspices for the book "On a Long Life".

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, his fellow philosopher, sends greetings.<-

<margin>q</margin> Just as our Plato—provoked indeed by Lysias but invited by Timaeus, Zeno, and Parmenides, who had themselves written—wrote also himself; so now I have been led by the philosopher Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician whose works Ficino drew upon for his medical writings</note> to compose a little book on delaying old age. Since I knew I was attempting a task beyond earthly powers, I began the little work under celestial auspices: starting from Mercury, indeed, correctly proceeding under his Virgin <note>the zodiac sign Virgo</note> happily; then from the Moon again, entering Taurus, and joining there with Jupiter, and from there looking up at Phoebus <note>the Sun</note> through a trine aspect <note>A "trine" is a favorable astrological alignment where planets are 120 degrees apart</note>, and similarly Venus and Mercury. Thus our composition, born under vital planets with Mercury ruling, might benefit those philosophizing for the sake of life. Especially for you, most beloved Pico, the most worthy of life among all philosophers. To ensure our diligence would be of greatest benefit to you, I even observed today the Moon <note>original: "phoæbem"</note> playing with Taurus, just as you yourself happily obtained at your birth; finally, with the wanderer <note>original: "peregri," likely referring to a planet in a "peregrine" or traveling state</note> coming to a trine aspect with Saturn...

[...Diana: so she will] care for Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous "Phoenix" of the Renaissance and close associate of Ficino</note>, the son of sublime Saturn, above all others. Especially since Saturn, meanwhile, sits victoriously in Capricorn: and holds the great Head of the Dragon <note>The North Node of the Moon, considered a point of increase and good fortune in astrology</note> in his right hand. Proudly, he gazes upon Apollo <note>The Sun</note> with a triple-rayed glance: by this very aspect, he is destined to confirm the promises of the heavenly beings to his own followers through an entirely stable covenant: if only (as is to be hoped) that supreme Jupiter should nod with the Head from which he gave birth to Minerva <note>Athena/Minerva was born from the head of Zeus/Jupiter; Ficino refers here to divine wisdom</note> toward the cultists of Minerva. 23 August 1489.

->Response to one desiring his birthday and other matters.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Martin Uranius Prenninger of Constance <note>Martin Prenninger (1450–1501), a German jurist and humanist who used the name Uranius</note>, sends many greetings.<-

<margin>m</margin> I am sending you the works of Iamblichus, which you first requested, and Proclus in addition, as well as Synesius. For you now demand our works by such great right that more must always be sent to you than you ask. Eight books of our letters, which you also desired, we will grant to the scribes very soon to be transcribed. We shall send the first book first; thereafter, I have indeed decided this very dawn to dedicate a nearly finished new work chiefly to your name. For our affection and your virtue demand this and more from us. Furthermore, you ask for my birthday. Although our Plotinus <note>The 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism; his biographer Porphyry noted that Plotinus refused to celebrate his birthday or have his portrait made, as he was "ashamed to be in a body"</note> never granted this to friends who frequently begged for it, I am nonetheless moved by a certain immense love of yours toward me, such that I will never deny you anything, unless it is perhaps denied to my own ability.

Therefore, the nineteenth day of October was my birthday: specifically in the year of our salvation 1433. The hour of the day, however, was not recorded by my father, Ficino the Physician <note>Diotifeci d'Agnolo, the personal physician to Cosimo de' Medici</note>; yet from his and my mother’s words, we have conjectured it was the twenty-first hour <note>In the "Italian hours" system of the time, hours were counted from sunset; the 21st hour would be mid-afternoon</note>. I believe Aquarius was then ascending nearly at the middle, together with Pisces. Saturn then held the angle of the East <note>The Ascendant</note> in Aquarius. Mars was in the same sign, holding the "prison" of the twelfth house. The Sun was in Scorpio, and Mercury was in the ninth house, with the Moon in Capricorn. Jupiter was in Leo in the seventh house. In that same place, in Virgo, was Venus; in Aries, was the Lot of Fortune. You have the birthday, such as it was. You have the man born, as great as he happened to be.

And even if fortune was never ample, and a certain perpetual weakness of the body always hindered our books—either in their writing or their publication—we nonetheless never ceased from the duty perhaps decreed for us. Now indeed, in this eighth septenary <note>A seven-year cycle of life; at 56, Ficino was entering his eighth cycle</note> of our age, you have provided the cause for a new edition, and even a new composition. For when you asked us this year for the book on *Caring for the Health of Scholars*—composed in our seventh septenary, during which we published the books of Plato—your genius truly excited my own genius to compose a book on *Prolonging the Life of the Gifted*. I did this so that they might not only be well as long as they live, but also that they might live well for a long time. Therefore, we have now finished this book on prolonging the life of students (God favoring), and to this we have then added a little work on *Obtaining Life from the Heavens*, so that by remedies and medicines—not composed haphazardly, but crafted by the observation of the stars—we might provide prosperous health and a long life to the gifted.

### Artful Recommendation of a learned man.

->Marsilio Ficino of Florence humbly commends himself to the Most Serene King of Pannonia <note>Pannonia: An ancient Roman province, used here by humanists to refer to the Kingdom of Hungary</note>, Matthias <note>Matthias Corvinus (1443–1490), King of Hungary and a major patron of Renaissance scholars</note>, always unconquered.<-

<margin>b</margin> Until now I did not think that the same man could exist in two places at once: especially those separated far from each other. But now I not only think this can happen: I actually know it. I hear it, I see it: for I know that our Nicolaus <note>Nicolaus de Mirabilibus (d. 1495), a Dominican theologian and protégé of Ficino</note>, a singular theologian, recently betook himself from Italy to Pannonia. Yet I hear that same man speaking in Florence (as he was accustomed) in the public gymnasia <note>Latin: "gymnasiis," referring to schools or universities</note>: in the forum: in the churches. I hear him reading frequently and diligently debating. We see him daily crowned in the very circles <note>original: "coronis," referring to the circular crowds of students or listeners surrounding a master</note> of those practicing philosophy. Your Nicolaus, therefore, now lives among you; meanwhile, our Nicolaus also breathes among us. He still shouts in the schools, and the echo resounds from the very walls themselves. In this way, therefore, that man has deceived our expectation, but has sufficiently satisfied our desire. For we so longed for the presence of such a great man that he would never be missed by us as if he were absent. 

He will perhaps deceive you also in another way, unless I warn you. Actors on stage are accustomed to hide their own persons beneath a borrowed mask <note>The Latin "persona" means both a person and the mask worn by an actor</note>. Nicolaus, however, in turn hides a borrowed person beneath his own. When, therefore, you listen to his disputations, know that you indeed look upon Nicolaus, but you do not hear him. For you will instead hear that blessed Thomas Aquinas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent medieval theologian</note> arguing, now living within Nicolaus’s own breast and shouting from his mouth. For either Thomas was reborn in this man at his birth—as some Platonist might believe—or at least the sublime Thomas breathes favorably from heaven upon him as he speaks. Therefore, revere that Thomas of Aquino in Nicolaus as if in a certain living statue. 6 September 1489. In the countryside of Careggi <note>The site of the Medici villa where Ficino lived and worked</note>.

### A Playful Expression of Thanks.

->Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to Roberto Salviati <note>A member of a powerful Florentine banking family and a close friend of the Medici and Ficino</note>.<-

<margin>a</margin> The poets sing of Atlas, the prince of astronomy: that he attained the heavens not only by a certain perpetual observation of the stars, but also by a marvelous height of body. You too, by a perhaps similar reasoning, seem to me to have recently reached the stars. For at that moment when Jupiter from on high "libated kisses to his daughter" <note>A poetic allusion to Virgil’s Aeneid (1.256), describing a moment of divine favor</note>—at which coupling he is indeed accustomed to deny nothing to the one asking—you yourself gave letters to me. On which account, I do not wish to deny anything to you, my Roberto, although I cannot return what you have given. Now, if I truly owe more to each person the more I have received, I certainly owe nothing more to anyone than to you, through whom I am most magnificent, my Roberto. Do you laugh at this word "most magnificent"? Perhaps this very grand word has not come unseasonably into our mouths: for that which you gave, and that which I owe, is immense. Since indeed you have given me the whole world at once, when you sent that world to us...

<meta>This page concludes Ficino’s playful letter to Robert Salviati (begun on the previous page) regarding a gift from Pico della Mirandola, likely his "Heptaplus". It then introduces a preface to Ficino’s work "On Long Life," dedicated to Filippo Valori and referencing the patronage of Lorenzo de' Medici.</meta>

...divinely described by John <note>A reference to the Book of Revelation, traditionally attributed to John the Apostle</note>. I was reading your timely letters just as I was gazing at the gift with my own eyes in that chapel of ours, the Chapel of Saint Christopher, which we have long possessed and cherished. I was then surveying that globe with my eyes—the one that, like Atlas, the Saint carries on his shoulders—to see if perhaps anything in the whole world might occur to us that was equal or similar to your gift. Meanwhile, that Saint seemed to say to me: "Why, mad Ficino, do you seek beneath the heavens something equal to the heavens? Have you not recently received the whole world from a friend? And meanwhile, that friend of yours has made you more than a prophet." A prophet once saw a new Heaven and a new Earth. You, through the works of your friend, have not only seen these things, but have even held them in your hands. In the beginning, God created Heaven and Earth in the abyss of darkness, having previously begotten them in the abyss of light. He recreated them once in the wisdom of Moses. And he has recreated them recently in the spirit of Pico: in the words of Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a brilliant philosopher and close associate of Ficino</note>. Robert gave this to you as a gift along with his letters. Only you can now match such a gift. I, though so tall and large, will scarcely match it. Farewell for a long time, Marsilio; and may your friend also fare well. These things, my dear Robert, that Saint seemed to say to me. Therefore, may you also fare well and happily with this very long-lasting health, provided you frequently greet our fellow Platonist, Pico, in my name. 

But hey, tell me, I pray. Should I have called him "Democritus" <note>Democritus was an ancient Greek philosopher known for the atomic theory and the idea of infinite worlds</note> these days rather than "Platonist"? The Maker of the world rested on the Sabbath from all his works. But Pico, having now completed the "Fabric of the World" <note>This refers to Pico’s *Heptaplus*, a sevenfold narration of the six days of Genesis</note>, is striving for something great (I know not what). Is he then constructing new worlds along with Democritus? But while writing, it comes most opportunely to my mind what our friend is primarily striving for. He is not following the wandering madness of Democritus, counting innumerable atoms; but rather surely him whom we hear crying out daily: "My Father works even until now, and I work" <note>Quoting John 5:17</note>. The Son of God works: that is, he procreates new souls every day like worlds. Therefore, through these worlds—since one is now finished—our Pico, the contemplator of the soul, follows Christ, not Democritus.

->**Preface to the book on a long life.**<-

->**Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Filippo Valori, an excellent and most noble citizen.**<-

Although our Plato lives by his own genius, and will live (as I believe) as long as the world itself lives, my own genius always impels me toward this: that after divine worship, I should look to the life of Plato before all things. The House of Medici <note>original: "Medica domus." Ficino often makes puns on the name "Medici" and "medicus" (physician)</note> has long aspired to this very thing above others; and you, my Valori, a most dear friend to physicians and most studious of Platonic glory and discipline, conspire with them toward the same goal. Therefore, the same life that I always desire for Plato, I desire for physicians and for someone like Valori. For this reason, I urge and beseech you, my Valori, that with the same effort you always favor Platonic glory, you might one day read and keep these precepts of ours concerning the prolongation of life with equal diligence. Living long by these means, you may be able to patronize the recently reborn discipline of Plato for a longer time, together with the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici. Farewell.
