# BOOK

### Irony regarding his book against a grammarian detractor.

->Marsilio Ficino to Tideo, Royal Procurator, sends greetings.<-

<margin>d</margin>The day before yesterday, I gave the bookseller Antonio, at your request, the Platonic philosopher Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced Ficino’s views on theurgy and ritual</note> to be transcribed. If by chance, while reading, you do not encounter a continuous order in the book, know that I have not expressed this book word-for-word, but according to the sense. This was not so much because I was entirely occupied with the commentaries on Plotinus <note>Plotinus was the founder of Neoplatonism; Ficino spent years translating and commenting on his "Enneads"</note>, but because the only copy we have is full of errors and—what is worse—fragments. However, Tideo, if my style there does not satisfy your judgment, send it back since it does not please you. At least accept the meaning. Sometimes silver lies hidden beneath bronze. Just as, conversely, bronze is often covered by silver. But lest some "grammarian" <note>In the Renaissance, a "grammarian" was a philologist who focused on linguistic correctness, often clashing with philosophers like Ficino who prioritized metaphysical meaning over polished prose</note>, that severe judge of philosophers, accuse me of arrogance—because here I seem, in a way, to claim the "silver" for myself—I most willingly concede that "gold" to him, if by any means I might appease so rigid a judge against me with such a great gift. And so that I might gratify him even more generously, I shall indeed call that source a fountain, and myself a cistern. Farewell, and be happy. I commend myself to you. Commend me also to the Great King.

### A playful letter against a long silence.

->Marsilio Ficino to Pierleone, his fellow philosopher, sends greetings.<-

<margin>c</margin>Others are accustomed to clear the crime of a long silence with some apology, and often a long one at that. You, however—a new kind of orator, if indeed he is an orator who keeps silent—wash away the accusation of silence with silence itself. You are certainly a "new physician" <note>Pierleone Leoni was a famous physician as well as a philosopher</note>, acting contrary to what others are accustomed to, who cure likes with likes; for a long time now, all your friends have been condemning you because you write nothing to any of your people, neither of your own accord nor even when provoked. But Preculus <note>likely Ariculo or a similar diminutive for a mutual friend</note>, who recently set out from you to us in Florence, did so with your verbal instructions but without your letters; he has put an end to our accusations of silence against you by commanding us to bear the longing for your letters, so long delayed, with an even mind. Surely, since such a great man and so great a friend to you was unable to obtain a short letter from you upon his departure, he said it ought not seem strange to us, nor was it done by you thoughtlessly, that we have not obtained for a long time the letter which even he did not receive. Thus, you do not only always speak of wonderful things, but you do them, my friend: you defend silence with silence; you cure likes with likes; you even persuade by being quiet. But I pray, do not let that book of yours—or should I say your "child" <note>original: "liber." Ficino plays on the Latin word "liber," which means both "book" and "child/son"</note>—which went some time ago to Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" de' Medici (1449–1492), the de facto ruler of Florence and Ficino's patron</note>, keep the same silence with us as you do. To Lorenzo he speaks scarcely at all; to me, however, he says nothing at any time, perhaps forbidden by his father. Grant at last, I beseech you, that your "child" might at least speak with your Marsilio, with his father's permission and indulgence. October 12, 1489. Florence.

### Regarding the book *On Life*, following the books *On Dreams* and *Demons*.
### Marsilio Ficino to Piero de' Medici <note>Piero "the Unfortunate" (1472–1503), son of Lorenzo the Magnificent and successor to the leadership of Florence</note>, sends many greetings.

<margin>e</margin>Some time ago, I and my personal courage sent to you the "Dreams" of Synesius the Platonist <note>Synesius of Cyrene, a 4th-century philosopher whose work "On Dreams" Ficino translated</note> and the "Demons" of Psellus the fellow Platonist <note>Michael Psellus, an 11th-century Byzantine scholar; Ficino translated his "On the Operation of Demons"</note>. But at the very threshold of your gates—by some unknown fate—the dreams immediately vanished, and all the demons suddenly disappeared. Therefore, let at least this "Life" of ours (which we send now) appear before you. Perhaps the loss of dreams and demons is a light matter; but the loss of life is no light thing. Go now, therefore, O "Life" <note>Ficino personifies his book, "De Vita" (On Life)</note> more dear than the others; enjoy a better fate. Approach now with alacrity Piero de' Medici, our pride; in his care, you will live more happily. December 15, 1489.

---

### Preface by Marsilio Ficino of Florence to the tenth and eleventh books of his letters, addressed to Niccolò Valori, a man most distinguished in letters and character.

### Marsilio Ficino to Niccolò Valori, his Twin Friend, sends many greetings.

<margin>c</margin>When I had already completed twelve books of my letters and began to review them, I discovered that the tenth and eleventh books still lacked a specific inscription <note>In this context, "inscription" refers to a formal dedication at the start of a volume</note>. Therefore, as I considered to whom I might best dedicate this twin work, you, my Valori, came first to mind—a friend who is himself a "twin." For until now, your excellent brother Filippo and you were the twin guardians of my works, like Castor and Pollux <note>In Greek mythology, the Dioscuri or "Gemini" twins; Ficino uses them as a metaphor for the brothers' joint patronage</note>. But now, since Filippo has recently passed away, you alone remain as my "twin," offering yourself to me as such—which you indeed do daily through your great kindness toward me. You also represent Filippo, who was loved by us beyond compare. And as much as the heavy loss of our Filippo distresses us, so too does the sufficient compensation found in you console us. Marsilio is also consoled by the firmest hope that his books will hereafter be no less commended to Niccolò than they once were to Filippo. Read happily, and live long and happily; as a diligent observer of Platonic wisdom, continue to be the long-term guardian of my studies.

---

### Book Ten. For the book *On Life* sent to a friend.
### Marsilio Ficino to Giacomo Martini, Jurist, sends greetings.

<margin>f</margin>In vain would I have composed the book *On Life* <note>original: "De Vita"</note> to be of use to my friends if it did not benefit, above all, my Giacomo, the dearest of all my friends. Therefore, lest I have written in vain, receive gladly this "Life" of ours which I send. Read it diligently. Hold it in your memory. Guard it zealously. Live long according to your wish, and live happily. December 16.

We desire our book *On Life* <note>original: "Librum de vita nostrũ"</note> to be of benefit to all our friends, both the learned and the good. Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Michelozzi <note>The private secretary to Lorenzo de' Medici</note>: and if perhaps to his Rival, yet nonetheless his most Dear friend. Many greetings.

Last summer, I dedicated to our Piero de' Medici a book by Synesius the Platonist *On Dreams* and a short book by his fellow Platonist Psellus *On Demons*. Once he received the book, Piero immediately read the preface; having read it, he set it down. Shortly thereafter, the book itself was carried off by I know not whom. After this, although sought for a long time, it has not yet appeared. It truly seems that as soon as they touched the inner chambers of that House (hardly different from a sacred temple), the demons disappeared and the dreams utterly evaporated. I pray you, my Bernardo, search most accurately to see if those dreams and those demons have flown off to your place. If you find it so, I warn you: purify yourselves and drive them back to us. Finally, I suspect that perhaps the Cardinal <note>Giovanni de' Medici, Lorenzo's son, recently made a cardinal at age 13</note> or Gregorio have taken this book to read. If by chance they have it, let them send it to us once read. At the very least, let me know if they do not have it, so that we may search more diligently elsewhere. Commend me to the venerable Pandolfo della Luna <note>A Florentine official; Ficino puns on his name "Luna" (Moon) in the next sentence</note>; but why indeed should I have passed over the Sun? Commend me, then, first of all to our Sun, the Cardinal; then to Pandolfo of the Moon—and fully indeed—so that having begun here, we may follow the catalog of the heavenly bodies. You will also commend me to Giovanni Battista, who is like Jupiter on account of the laws; and even to our Gregorio, who is as Mercury. But tell me, I ask you: where shall we place Venus? Let Matteo, then, be Venus. But since he is a Venus unarmed and without desire, you yourself shall act the part of Cupid. Otherwise, my Bernardo, you will scarcely be loved today. As for Saturn and Mars, let joy and humanity expel them far from your festive company. Farewell, and may you all fare well. December 21, 1489.

### Preface to the books first sent to the sons of Lorenzo and to Valor: Then to Lorenzo de' Medici.

Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, savior of the fatherland. Many greetings.

Synesius, Psellus, Iamblichus, Porphyry, and Proclus <note>A list of major Neoplatonic philosophers whom Ficino translated</note>—all Platonists—having long ago entered your most ample home, greeted your noble sons. Up to this point, they seem to have acted quite rightly. However, because they left you ungreeted, they neither acted prudently nor did they turn out happily. Recognizing at last their own imprudence, so that they might finally be more fortunate, they now revisit your threshold to come to know the father, and in turn to recognize the sons together with the father; thus they shall immediately live more happily. For they have recently discovered that not even our own books *On Life* <note>original: "libros... de vita nros"</note> wished to live without your patronage. Furthermore, these philosophers are accompanied by Priscianus Lydus and Theophrastus. These men, since they have long since greeted my friend Valor...

->A gathering of certain elegant citizens, desiring tranquility under the name Mammola.<- <note>The "Mammola" (Little Bloom) was an informal social and intellectual club in Florence that Ficino frequented.</note>

### Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved brother, Bernardo Rucellai <note>Bernardo Rucellai (1448–1514) was a prominent Florentine diplomat, scholar, and the son-in-law of Piero de' Medici.</note>, in the liberty of Life and a certain carefree negligence. Sends many greetings.

<margin>c</margin>Since there is to be a certain cycle <note>original: "vicissitudo," referring to the natural turning or revolution of things</note> of all affairs, it is certainly my lot (by what fate I know not) to return that cycle in many things. Others, indeed, are accustomed to a long servitude and finally take up for themselves a brief dominion and a prefecture held with the highest diligence. I, in turn, through liberty rather, and a certain negligence, have obtained a prefecture or censorship of "yesterday" <note>original: "beri," likely a typo for "heri" (yesterday), though it may play on a local term</note>. And in this dignity, too, the cycle is clear: for other censors correct imprudence, but I, thereafter, am (I know not how) about to correct prudence. Now truly the cycle rises here as well: for the "prudence" of the Mammola club is "imprudence" to the common folk; and conversely, the prudence of the common folk is a certain manifest imprudence to the Mammola. Finally, the cycle of things in which the duty of this fellowship is engaged is supreme. If it has any duty, it is surely this: that while others zealously seek security with all care, we, through a certain supreme lack of care, do not seek it at all, but already possess it. For to seek is certainly the mark of the anxious; to possess is the mark of the secure—nor is it so much to possess what you have desired, as to desire whatever you happen to possess. And to want that very thing which you have. January 4, 1489.

### A bit concerning charity, along with a recommendation of his own affairs. Marsilio Ficino to Alessandro Filicaja. Sends many greetings.

<margin>s</margin>If all charity begins with itself (as is commonly said), yesterday indeed I did not follow the duty of charity among you: for I recommended others to your magistracy, but meanwhile I overlooked myself. But if the opinion of the Apostle Paul is truer, when he says: "Charity does not seek its own things, but those of another" <note>1 Corinthians 13:5</note>, I have had great charity, and therefore I am worthy of charity. Therefore, I need as much diligence from friends in my affairs as I am negligent in my own affairs and diligent in those of others. Since you are a friend to us, I commend myself to you, so that you may have Careggi <note>The site of the Medici villa and Ficino's home</note> recommended to you in my person, as "Little Careggi" <note>original: "Caregiolum"</note>. January 22, 1491.

However, the books *On Life*...

<meta>This page continues the correspondence of Marsilio Ficino. The previous page ended with a letter to Bernardo Rucellai regarding his "censorship" of the Mammola club. ...A most noble as well as excellent man recently took care that our writings be printed perhaps more fortunately; he is a man as most devoted to renewing antiquity as you are, my dearest antiquarian. In him, certainly, we see that Platonic principle realized: that noble offspring proceed from a generous stock, especially if diligent education is added to an excellent nature. Therefore, the book *On Life* <note>original: "librum devita," referring to Ficino's famous work *De Vita Libri Tres*, which dealt with health, longevity, and astral influences</note> which this man of ours gave to me today as a gift, I am giving to his brother Nicolaus to bring to you. Nicolaus is an elegant and serious young man, the nephew of the Florentine Ambassador <note>original: "Oratoris," a term for a diplomat or public speaker</note>; I send it so that if this diligence of ours is to be of any use to the life of scholars, it might be of use to you especially, who are certainly most worthy of life. 

But since mention has been made of our Ambassador: Francesco Valori <note>A prominent Florentine politician and diplomat, later a supporter of Savonarola</note>, who comes there as an envoy, is the uncle of Filippo and Nicolaus; to me, he is a brother in age, but a father in the reverence I owe him. He is truly a man of the highest wisdom, integrity, and authority. Whenever we look at him and hear him (which we do daily), we seem to see and hear that great Cosimo de' Medici <note>The patriarch of the Medici family and Ficino’s first great patron</note>, whom he resembles in both face and speech. Why tell you all this, best of antiquarians? So that while I send the book to you through the envoy, I might signify to you who he is and how great he is. I also signify to you that our friends Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <note>The famous "Phoenix" of the Renaissance, known for his *900 Theses*</note> and Angelo Poliziano <note>The leading humanist poet and scholar of the age</note> love you no small amount.

### Commendation of a cause to a Legal Expert.

->Marsilio Ficino to Leonardo the legal expert. Sends greetings.<-

<margin>c</margin>We judge it superfluous to recommend our cause with many words to a very dear friend. It is also unnecessary to recommend the just cause of a client to a just patron. What then? Let us use a notification rather than a recommendation with you. The Hebrews name Jupiter *Sedecbi* <note>original: "Sedecbi," a transliteration of the Hebrew *Tzedek*, meaning "Justice"</note>; that is, Justice. For when he reigns in a birth chart, he signifies a just man who will fight strenuously for justice; and in the handling of legal cases, if he looks upon them powerfully from the heavens <note>A reference to a favorable astrological "aspect"</note>, he portends that the sentence will be just. Since, therefore, you are not only excellently learned and eloquent, but also "Jovial" <note>Influenced by the planet Jupiter, associated with justice and good cheer</note>, and are to fight for our cause tomorrow while the Sun is fortunately looking upon Jupiter, we hope (provided you exert the nerves of your genius) that you will defeat the wicked quibbles of our adversaries. Farewell.

### On love and friendship, and the recommendation of a friend.

->Marsilio Ficino to Girolamo Donato, most distinguished Ambassador of the Venetian Senate. Sends greetings.<-

<margin>a</margin>Antonio Pelotti <note>A member of Ficino's Platonic Academy</note>, the Apollonian charm of our Academy—a man otherwise incapable of deceiving—deceives me daily, and I am a willing victim. Always, indeed, I thought yesterday that I owed so much to Pelotti that I would deny I could ever owe more in the future. Yet always thereafter, by some even greater service toward me, he binds me more closely to himself. Whence I am immediately convinced that I was deceived by my previous opinion. Today, finally, he has affected me with the greatest benefit of all, since he has made us friends instead of merely people who love one another. For truly, each of us, my dearest Girolamo, has for a long time loved the other ardently. Ha...

...[hitherto] nevertheless, neither was (as it seems) a friend: namely, not knowing himself to be loved in return. But our poet Antonio, now having performed the duty of a poet—that is, a mover of affections and a transformer—has forged a friendship between us and transformed lovers into friends, while he rendered each of us certain that he is not only loved in return by the beloved, but was indeed loved first and for a longer time. The friendship of men who philosophize certainly seems to be of no less importance among mortals than the gathering of happy planets is among the inhabitants of heaven. 

Peloctos <note>Likely Francesco "Pelotto" da Castiglione, a mutual friend and priest</note> moreover indicated to me how much you yourself desire to see me. I certainly, my Girolamo, have long desired to see you. But you will see me, however great I am, in my very Worth <note>original: "Valore," a pun on the surname of the man he is about to mention</note> proceeding all the way to you; you will see me, I say, in Francesco Valori, the Ambassador <note>original: "Oratore," meaning a diplomatic envoy</note> of the Florentine Senate. Him I love and admire above all others. For he brings back that great Cosimo <note>Cosimo de' Medici, Ficino's late patron</note>—whom he, as a youth, so revered as an old man—in his heart, his face, and his speech. Therefore, as soon as you look upon him, you immediately behold Marsilio living gladly within his own Cosimo. But you will not see me exactly as I am (as I was just saying) in my "worth" [Valori]; rather, as if looking through a glass, you will see me made greater in him. Finally, however small I am in myself, or however great I am in him, I am entirely yours, my best Girolamo. 

Furthermore, the love that joins us would urge me to write more, were it not that Nicolaus Valori, the nephew of the Legate <note>Francesco Valori</note>—a young man indeed elegant and quite mature despite his youth—is coming to you, intending to speak much with you in my name. Farewell.

### On friendship and the immortality of the soul.
### Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo of Venice, S.D. <note>original: "S.D." for *Salutem Dicit*, "sends greetings"</note>

Since the singular love between us, my Bernardo, was created not from a mortal cause, but rather from one immortal and heavenly, I have decided that it is right—beyond the monuments of letters—to commend its memory not to just any book, but especially to my books on immortality; thus commending an immortal thing to immortality. 

Witness to such great love has long been the sixth book of my *Platonic Theology* <note>Ficino's magnum opus, *Theologia Platonica de immortalitate animorum*</note> on immortality. Witness also is the recent divine book of Plotinus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher whom Ficino translated and commented upon</note> on immortality, in the argument of which we wrote today what follows: 

"You desire, great-souled Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, 'The Magnificent'</note>, a brief summary at last of a long disputation—a disputation, I say, on immortality, which has already been drawn out at length both in my theology and in my present works. Our same Bernard [Bembo] also desired this, when he, as the ambassador here for the Venetian Senate, heard us disputing most extensively on this matter—Bernard Bembo, I say, a man especially learned and a patron of the learned, and my brother in star and spirit <note>original: "in sidere genioque," suggesting an astrological or spiritual affinity</note>. To you, therefore, and to him equally, this shall be the summary, distinguished by four chapters: 

First: that the soul can rule over fleeting things and resist the incitements of the body. 
Second: that it frequently contemplates many things separated from bodies..."

...whether it touches things themselves as they are separated, or whether the soul separates them itself. Third: because the soul naturally desires eternal things and, through its trust in the eternal, frequently neglects temporal things. Fourth: because the soul worships the eternal God for the sake of everlasting life. Finally, the whole of natural religion in man is the firmest foundation of immortality.

## Demons are the unique concern of the Physician: Also, a recommendation of the book *On Life*.
## Marsilio Ficino to Pierleone the Physician, greetings. <note>original: "S. D." stands for "Salutem Dicit," a formal Latin greeting wishing health.</note>

Greetings, my most beloved Pierleone; greetings again, great lion <note>Ficino is punning on the physician's name, Pierleone Leoni.</note>. But lest you perhaps think yourself judged inferior to a man by the name of "lion," I mean a celestial lion, not an earthly one—unless perhaps I call "earthly" one who has descended from heaven to earth. For we read in the poems of Zoroaster <note>The legendary ancient Persian prophet, whom Renaissance scholars believed was a source of ancient wisdom</note> that twelve governors preside over the twelve signs of the Zodiac. There, he names the one who presides over Leo as *Laonduchus*. He adds that if this spirit is duly called, he will appear on earth in an immense form, occupying the whole world. To this spirit, therefore, the Chaldeans gave the name "lions" to the demons <note>term: "demones" (spirits) — In Ficino’s Neoplatonism, these are not necessarily evil but are intermediary spirits or "daemons" that bridge the gap between gods and humans.</note> subject to him. These spirits also occasionally present themselves to our eyes in various human figures at their pleasure, often intending to practice the arts of Apollo <note>The god of healing and prophecy</note>. They heal equally with herbs and words. If I now name you alone as a "lion" from among these, truth will not be indignant, and you therefore will not disdain it. 

But enough of these things. Our magnanimous patron, Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" de' Medici</note>, brings both his life and mine to you. Since he entrusts his life to you, he also recommends mine. Here, I pray you act with both medications: cure his indeed with herbs, but with words, cure and adorn mine equally. You will understand what I wish more clearly if you ever hear our Bernardo <note>Likely Bernardo Bembo, a Venetian diplomat and close friend of Ficino</note>—a youth of excellent natural talent and a man of outstanding virtue—reading our works.

> Those are called "Sons of the Sun" upon whose birth the sun breathes. The sun is in Leo in the ninth region of heaven. <note>The "ninth house" in astrology is the house of philosophy, religion, and long journeys.</note>

## Marsilio Ficino to Lorenzo de' Medici the Younger, greetings.

You have rightly requested the account of Julian the Platonist <note>The Emperor Julian "the Apostate," who wrote a famous Neoplatonic hymn to the Sun</note> addressed to the sun, in which he himself recognizes the sun as his father by certain arguments. For you too—unless perhaps you are ignorant of your own horoscope—derive your lineage from Phoebus <note>Apollo, the sun god</note>. For he, at your birth, immediately looked upon you from his royal throne and with his joy. You imitate that parent in the splendor of your virtue and in your poems.

## Recommendation of a man of letters to a man of letters.
## Marsilio Ficino to the venerable Father Joachim, General of the Preachers, greetings. <note>Joachim Turrianus, the head of the Dominican Order (Order of Preachers) from 1487 to 1500.</note>

Since I am about to recommend a youth of letters, endowed with a natural talent for virtue, to a most learned man—a friend of outstanding virtue to my very dear friend—I shall be brief for the present. For I will easily persuade you. Domenico the Florentine, born of Giovanni, who is taking his profession as a Dominican preacher under you as Father, requests your patronage; and I ask it for his sake. Farewell.

<margin>1</margin>
Our book *On Life* <note>original: "Liber de vita"; this refers to Ficino's famous 1489 treatise on health, longevity, and astral influences.</note> has been printed. I received one from the printers in recent days to send to you. And you shall receive this one not for sale (like the others) but for free; or rather, as if it were already bought by you, and at a great price: for since you have given your soul to us in love, you have claimed our life for yourself beyond all controversy. I recently received in your name a case of cutlery <note>original: "thecam Cultellariam"</note> adorned with handles of gems and gold, a gift not only philosophical but even royal. It is certainly worthy of your royal mind. To me, it was moreover most pleasing, especially because through this gift I clearly perceived that the same guardian spirit <note>term: "Genium" — In Neoplatonic thought, a 'genius' is a personal guiding spirit or tutelary deity assigned to an individual at birth.</note> guides both me and you. For since I held it as certain that Chalcedony <note>A type of quartz gem believed in the Renaissance to have cooling properties and to dispel melancholy.</note> is under the influence of Aquarius—especially the middle of the sign—while Jasper belongs to Saturn in the dominion of Aquarius, and Saturn rose for me in that same degree, I was ardently wishing for both stones. Therefore, my wish, known to my guardian spirit, is suddenly declared known to you: that we are governed by the same spirit. Indeed, why is it that in this past autumn I began to desire such things? You, meanwhile (as I guess), were deliberating at that same time on sending them to us as a gift. If anyone, therefore, is never to give thanks to himself, certainly Marsilio now gives great thanks to Martin. Indeed, he can give thanks to himself, provided he is a twin. Each of us is a twin, my sweetest Martin. By that same logic, the constellation of the Twins <note>The zodiac sign Gemini.</note> in heaven will be one—as I hope—a shared lodging for our souls. Farewell happily. The books of letters are being copied for you daily. We will soon put the finishing touches on Plotinus <note>Ficino spent years translating the works of the Neoplatonist philosopher Plotinus from Greek into Latin.</note>. And you will have this soon, as soon as it has been printed. You certainly always have me. April 10, 1490. In the countryside of Careggi <note>The site of the Medici villa where the "Platonic Academy" met.</note>.

## The approval of the book from the endorsement of doctors.

**Marsilio Ficino to Matteo Aretino, his indispensable physician. Greetings.**

<margin>1</margin>
I composed the medical book *On Life* last spring and summer among the flowers in the countryside of Careggi: would that it were flourishing! I was only going to approve of it myself once I learned it had been endorsed by physicians. I received your letters in recent days, so full of spirit <note>original: "spū" (spiritu); here implying both intellectual vigor and the 'vital spirit' that connects soul and body.</note> that by their breath my life—which having been published long ago had (so to speak) expired—immediately breathed again for me; and by your approval, it was approved in my eyes. See then, my Matteo, how much you please me, in whom I also please myself. Continue, I pray: and as you love us now, love us always, and recommend us to the physicians. You ask further if I have published anything lately. I recently gave seven books of the Platonists to the great Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent," the de facto ruler of Florence and Ficino's patron.</note> to be copied at his discretion. When they have been copied, you may have them. Not long after, you shall have the books of Plotinus and our commentaries upon them. Farewell happily. April 29, 1490. In the countryside of Careggi.

### On worshiping God in the Confessions of Augustine.
### Marsilio Ficino to the Great-Souled Lorenzo de' Medici. Greetings.

<margin>t</margin> He who has God present with him is safe alone and everywhere. "The Lord is near," says David, "to all who call upon him: to those who call upon him in truth." <note>Psalm 145:18</note> He who is first in truth, alone calls upon God: a man who is simultaneously wise and holy. We do not doubt that Saint Augustine was such a man. Therefore, my Lorenzo—who are both my teacher and my patron—let us humbly adore God together with Augustine. In this way, God himself will undoubtedly be present for those who pray. For he is mercifully present even to those about to pray, and he brings it about that we may pray in truth. Indeed, the prophet himself teaches by what means we, worshiping in truth, shall obtain our requests. For after he says, "The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth," he adds: "He will fulfill the desire of those who fear him, and he will hear their prayer." <note>Psalm 145:19</note> Furthermore: "The Lord preserves all those who love him." Finally: "My mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord." <note>Psalm 145:20-21</note> In these words, he warns us to always fear, love, and praise God, if we desire to be heard when we ask. Now indeed, he similarly reveals in these same words what should be sought above all in prayer. Since these three—fear, love, and praise—bring it about that we obtain our requests, it rightly seems that these same three must be asked for by us while we worship. Namely, may God grant us that we may fear him rightly, love him ardently, and praise him properly. In short, David teaches how to worship and obtain when he says: "Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the petitions of your heart." <note>Psalm 37:4</note> But now let us listen to Aurelius <note>Aurelius Augustine (Saint Augustine).</note> praying. For in this way, you shall build a divine temple for the same King to whom you recently established a royal temple. 12 May 1489. In the Careggi countryside.

### Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Calderini, his most dutiful friend. Greetings.

<margin>l</margin> You shall give the books *On Life* <note>original: "Libros de vita" — Ficino's famous three-part treatise on health, longevity, and astral influences, often criticized by the Church for its focus on magic</note> to Hermolao Barbaro in the name of Valori and Marsilio. ### Marsilio Ficino commends himself to the Most Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Francesco Soderini, Bishop of Volterra.

<margin>a</margin> I received your most kind letters recently. Therefore, I thank you greatly for so willingly patronizing our friends. But I give much greater thanks because you have offered your most reverend patron, the Cardinal of Aleria <note>Ardicino della Porta the Younger (1434–1493), who held the bishopric of Aleria and was a protector of Ficino at the papal court</note>, as a patron to me as well. For I learned through the letters of our Antonio Calderini that this man, formerly your master and recently mine, has strenuously protected us against a certain slanderer <note>Ficino was frequently attacked by critics who accused him of practicing illicit magic in his medical writings</note>. I attribute this not to any merits of my own toward him, but to your recommendations and his own piety and mercy. It will be your duty or at least your love hereafter, best Soderini, to preserve that relationship by the same means you won such a great patron for me. And as for the thanks I can scarcely express, you must express and return them even more abundantly. Finally, let me know if there is anything in which I can gratify this father and lord of distinguished piety.

...not so that a familiar demon would approach him (at his calling) for immediate inspection. Plotinus easily complied. The invocation of the demon took place in the Temple of Isis <note>original: "Isio" — a temple dedicated to the Egyptian goddess Isis in Rome</note>. These are the words of Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus who wrote his biography</note>; but how opportunely we have now come across this story! For just as a god is said to have appeared instead of a demon to the Egyptian priest once summoning a demon, so to me, recently calling upon Hercules and Apollo <note>Ficino uses these names to represent his scholarly and heroic defenders</note> in my defense, their very Jupiter himself seems to have appeared. For the Venetian pillar of the Church, sent from heaven by Saint Mark <note>Ficino refers to Cardinal Marco Barbo of Venice</note>, stood by me as a most safe patron. That he was sent to earth from the order of Jupiter itself is testified to us by his fortune, which is indeed great. But his virtue is even greater. For astronomers have named Jupiter the "First Fortune." And the Jews call the same *Sedech* <note>original: "sedech" — from the Hebrew *Tzedek*, meaning righteousness or justice, the name for the planet Jupiter</note>, that is, justice in the common tongue. Greetings and fare well happily, O Jupiter who is our salvation on earth, signified indeed by the heavenly Jupiter, but created by the higher one. I, however, shall be forced to be Mercury <note>The messenger of the gods; Ficino views himself as the communicator of these celestial truths</note>, if I am to give thanks worthy of your service. June 26, 1490. Florence.

->A thanksgiving for the patronage shown to us by the Prince,<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Rainaldo Orsini, Archbishop of Florence. Greetings.<-

<margin>s</margin> Hail for a long time, hail always, good shepherd; the salvation of the sheep. A good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep, so that he may both feed them and protect them from wolves. Thus you recently snatched your lamb Ficino quite piously from the devouring jaws of wolves; and while Saturn <note>In astrology, Saturn is often associated with melancholy, restriction, and misfortune; here it represents Ficino's legal or social troubles</note> was already heavily attacking us, you were set against him like a protective Jupiter. Indeed, I seem to have prophesied that "Jovial" <note>Those born under the influence of Jupiter, characterized by magnanimity and benevolence</note> prelates—that is, magnanimous and truth-telling men—would patronize me in my danger, when, discussing the planets and stars, I so often placed Jupiter above the others.

Indeed, I have called you "Jovial" for a long time, even before I examined your birth chart; and when I did examine it, I asserted the very same thing: namely, because Cancer <note>The zodiac sign where Jupiter is traditionally "exalted" or at its most powerful</note>, the kingdom of Jupiter, was rising, and Jupiter himself was happily positioned in the eleventh house <note>The house of friends, hopes, and patrons, where Jupiter is said to "rejoice" in traditional astrology</note>, in his own joy, and from there was beholding his Cancer in a hexagonal figure <note>A "sextile" aspect, an angle of 60 degrees, considered a very harmonious and beneficial alignment</note>. But finally, we believe that good things proceed from the highest heavenly Jupiter, the Creator of Jupiter. Since we are his vicar, your work as high priest has begun to breathe life into us. I wish for him not only to breathe upon us, but also to breathe himself for a long time. Therefore, if I understood his birth chart and the habit of his body, and from what disease the doctors most fear a collapse, I would carefully devise some medicine or treatment that would benefit a long life and prosperous health. This favor, at least, I desire to return to you. But truly, not even Venus herself, the leader of the three Graces, would be able to return a comparable amount of thanks. June 26, 1490. Florence.

## Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Calderino: once a certain man, but now 'Caliderino' <note>original: "Anthonio Calderino quodā: ſed iã Caliderino"—Ficino is playing on the name Calderino, shifting it toward the Latin word 'calidus' meaning warm or hot</note>.

With as much warmth of heart as you love us, with just as much cleverness do you manage our affairs. You recently sent letters full of warmth and elegance; indeed, you have long performed your duty. Look, what shall be your reward? Among these Jupiters, Apollos, Hercules, and Amphions <note>Ficino uses these mythological names to refer to his various high-ranking patrons at the Papal court</note>, you shall henceforth be my Mercury <note>The messenger of the gods, representing Calderino's role as a diplomat or intermediary</note>. And indeed, you have stood as such for us for a long time now. This was clearly shown by your letters to our Cardinal. You report the news, you interpret, you persuade, you reconcile, you expedite. Therefore, our eloquent Mercury: those thanks which I, a stutterer, cannot express, you yourself must give to our heroic patrons. Persuade them, furthermore, not to desert the cause; if they persevere to the end, I shall be safe.

### A declaration of unique love.

## Marsilio Ficino to Martin Uranius of Constance. Greetings.

<margin>5</margin>Greetings, my "other Marsilio," <note>original: "Marſili alter"—a sign of deep friendship, suggesting they are two halves of one soul</note> my sweetest Martin, my friend Uranius—given to me, in truth, from the heavens. In you, I am especially pleased with myself; and for you, I especially wish for health and prosperity. I received the letters you sent on the 23rd of May. I had also received those you gave on the 12th of March. These were not just the small tokens you wrote of sending, but gifts worthy of a king. However, I have not yet received the letter sent by you with three Rhenish gold coins on the 26th of April. I sent letters to you some time ago by the man who had delivered the gifts to me in your name. Today I am giving George seven <term>quinterniones</term> <note>original: "quinterniones"—sections of a manuscript consisting of five folded sheets of paper; here, sections of his letters or works-in-progress</note> of letters. I will send the rest, which are many, at another time—perhaps soon, if I happen upon a courier. The end of my work on *Plotinus* <note>Ficino’s massive project of translating and commenting on the Neoplatonist philosopher Plotinus</note> is now imminent. I do not want gold or silver from you, Martin; I want only you. You alone are enough for me.

### An apology for the delay in responding.

## Hermolao Barbaro of Venice to Marsilio Ficino the Platonist. Greetings.

<margin>f</margin>I would be a barbarian indeed—not just in name <note>A pun on his surname "Barbarus"</note>—had I responded neither to your gift nor your letters, were it not that I know your character: you love your friends most when they act freely with you and are not anxious that they might seem to have been less than dutiful toward you. Indeed, I have regarded your painstaking work not merely as a gift, but as a true benefit. Nothing could have happened more pleasingly to me under this infamous sky <note>Referring to unhealthy weather or perhaps the political climate in Rome</note> than your *Book of Health* <note>original: "liber ſanitatis"—referring to Book I of Ficino's "De Vita" (On Life), which focuses on the health of scholars</note> containing precepts for studies. As for your request that, just as you recommend me to God, I should recommend you to his Vicar <note>The Pope, as the Vicar of Christ</note>: know that I have not only done this, but have done so diligently and frequently from the heart. And so you may understand this to be most true: the most gentle Pope <note>Pope Innocent VIII</note>, having spoken many things about you in the most honorable way, replied that it was because of Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici</note> that he had not summoned you here sooner; he remains firm in his intention of seeing you in his presence. If this is to happen at some point, I hope it falls within the time of my embassy; I know that would be pleasing to you, and it would certainly be convenient for me. This is enough for now; farewell to you and to me. I would like greetings to be said in my name to those there...

### A Petition for Help with Public Burdens.

**Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Dovizi <note>Bernardo Dovizi da Bibbiena (1470–1520), a high-ranking secretary to the Medici and later a Cardinal and famous playwright</note>, Secretary to Lorenzo de' Medici. Sending Greetings.**

<margin>t</margin>I have such reverence for the magnanimous Lorenzo that even a letter—which is usually not prone to blushing—now feels ashamed. Therefore, this letter, about to approach Lorenzo, is meanwhile held back by its own redness and flees instead to you, my most beloved Bernardo. But it comes to you too slowly, for it is not festive—as perhaps you might wish—but comes as a complainer. Furthermore, it is a letter that does not even know how to complain, coming as it does from a philosopher who is least accustomed to complaints. What then? It will at least tell its story. Public stipends are usually given to men of letters everywhere. I will not say they are "owed" in one’s own fatherland, but very ample ones are certainly given in Florence to both foreigners and citizens. Yet I, a lettered old man, ask for nothing in the way of a literary stipend. No, I do not claim so much for myself. It would be enough for me if I simply did not have to *give* money. I recently withdrew to the retreat of Montevecchio so that the frequent greetings of friends might not interrupt this work on Dionysius <note>Ficino was translating the "Divine Names" and other works of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist</note> upon which I am now entirely focused. But truly, what is far more annoying is that my friends do not interrupt me (whom I now miss), but instead, wicked tax collectors disturb and—to speak more truly—extortionists harass me daily. After those tithes, they soon came in the name of the Studio of Pisa <note>The University of Pisa, which was funded by taxes levied on Florentine citizens</note> to separate a Florentine man—who is certainly most studious—from his divine study of Dionysius. Fortune is an enemy to good studies, and she prevents me from bringing this divine work to completion; she agitates me with such injuries and, in the meantime, affects me with frequent physical weakness. But it is better to cut short this growing complaint. I hope at last (God willing) for prosperous health, and for relief from these cares with Lorenzo’s immediate help. Farewell happily, my best Bernardo, and give what aid you can yourself.

### An Excuse regarding Infrequent Greetings.

**Marsilio Ficino to Pandolfo of Pesaro <note>Pandolfo Collenuccio (1444–1504), a humanist and diplomat who was then serving as a magistrate (Praetor) in Florence</note>, Florentine Praetor. Sending Greetings.**

<margin>s</margin>Indeed, I intended to greet you frequently, my most beloved friend, but that great Plotinus <note>Ficino was editing and commenting on his massive translation of Plotinus's *Enneads* at this time</note> intercepted the earlier greetings. Now, the greatest Dionysius the Areopagite intercepts the ones that follow. We shall bear such great "interceptors" with a calm mind. For even if they prevent our formal greetings, they cannot and will not take away the mutual health of our souls, which are always speaking to each other. Wherever I am occupied among my books, I am certainly never far from my most lettered Pandolfo. Farewell.

### On fate, fortune, and each person's own daemon.
->Marsilio Ficino to Gregory of Alexandria, the distinguished physician.<-

<margin>q</margin> What Plato proves in the *Timaeus*, *Phaedrus*, and *Symposium*: that love is the beginning of all perturbations. What he proves again in the *Phaedo*: that pain always succeeds pleasure, and often vice versa. Indeed, I find this to be more and more confirmed every day. I certainly experienced it recently in your departure, my most beloved Gregory. I had finally found (as they say) a man after my own heart. Therefore, as much as I loved your presence, I was driven by an equal measure of pain by your absence. And just as your departure from here affected me with pain, so your letter yesterday delighted me. For it restored you to my presence; never again (as I believe) to depart. You will therefore be a unique friend to me, at least in Florence, where (as you yourself say) the fates do not wish you to be otherwise, with fortune also sufficiently consenting. Fortune indeed consents with fate—that is, with the series of celestial causes—according to the Platonists. For the leader of our fortune is the <term>daemon</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, a 'daemon' is not an evil spirit, but a personal guardian spirit or tutelary divinity assigned to a person at birth</note> of each individual, destined for everyone at birth according to the celestial harmony (to speak in the Platonic way). This daemon, most sagaciously and powerfully gathering the causes that are scattered among us, leads them toward a single outcome, often beyond our own counsel, and for that reason, it is called "fortuitous." The Platonists refer those effects for which there are no manifest causes among us primarily to this kind of fortune and to this Daemon. Indeed, they refer to it even those things for which evident causes seem to struggle against. If your daemon, Gregory, were itself a desire for Florence, you would certainly lead your life where you most desired to be, and where I, your other self, most desired you to live. But it has decreed (as I guess) that you lead your life in Siena, where Venus reigns on account of the ascending Taurus. Yet, as I see, it is not Cupid, born of Venus, who leads you, but Mercury. For against the usual barbarism of physicians, you retain a Mercurial eloquence, by the benefit, of course, of a Mercurial daemon. Otherwise, it would immediately flee from a physician. By the service of that same spirit—that is, by constant meditations and frequent letters—we shall always be present to each other (with fate and the daemon never opposing). October 27, 1490. In the countryside at Careggi.

### Marsilio Ficino to the Most Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Francesco Soderini, Bishop of Volterra, sends greetings. <note>original: "S. D." for Salutem Dicit, a formal greeting</note>

I have written thus far, my most secure patron, what you will primarily do in the case of your little client <term>clientuli: a humble reference to Ficino himself as a protégé of the Soderini family</term> according to your humanity and beneficence. By this omen we were hoping to rest from labors hereafter. 

But the opposite happened to me, just as it did to the omnipotent craftsman of heaven. For He is said to have rested on this day from all His works. I, however, am like the heaven that never rests, which has found its rest in motion, and which establishes the beginning of an imminent revolution at the very end of a revolution. With such a great work just finished, I am already beginning a new work, and perhaps not entirely new. Just as the heaven perhaps performs no new circuit, but always repeats the accustomed one. For it soon returned to my mind that there remained to be finished by me the commentaries on Plato's *Philebus* <note>A Platonic dialogue concerning the nature of pleasure and the "Highest Good"</note> concerning the highest good, once brought forward as far as the halfway point.

->On Adoration<-

Marsilio Ficino to Bindaccio Ricasoli <note>A nobleman and scholar from the prominent Ricasoli family of Florence, known for his interest in the "New Learning" of the Renaissance</note>, a man noble and learned, joined to him with singular affection, sends greetings.

**I** have promised for a long time, my dearest Bindaccio, to write something about the power of divine prayer. But I cannot fulfill these promises without the beneficial power of Him who is to be adored. Therefore, so that we may fortunately begin this sacred discussion on divine adoration, I pray, O nourishing God, breathe upon us. Having thus begun fittingly, we lay the divine foundation for this sacred building with that saying of Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus</note>: "Inquiry into divine things purges the soul; but imitation makes one a god." <note>original: "Inquisitio quidem diuinorum purgat animam. Imitatio vero facit deum."</note> We believe, therefore, that people certainly seek God when, first of all loving God who is known in some way, they diligently investigate all His works and testimonies as if they were footprints, so that they may more truly venerate Him once found. And that kind of scrutiny is considered to first purge the soul of all disturbances, and then of its clouds.

But imitation, which is thought to "make the soul a god"—that is, as much as is possible, divine—is of such a kind that you yourself, being set apart, may provide for others, intending to please God, who provides for all while being set apart. Indeed, we cannot emulate divine power or wisdom; we are always weak, always wavering, and frequently uncertain whether we have attained the truth. But it is possible, rather, to imitate divine providence <term>Providence: the concept of God's caring and governing influence over the universe</term>. For if anything about God is known to us—both by reason and by testimony—it is specifically this: that God is a certain power and wisdom, ruling all things in such a way that He is not mixed with the conditions and passions of the things He governs, but is entirely separate. Where indeed nothing prevents Him from being both sublime and separate, while also being present to and providing for individuals; rather, it is thought to contribute to this very purpose. Where, again, the most diligent stewardship of all things does not disturb His sublime status. Therefore, so that you may imitate Him to the best of your strength—He who dwells on high and looks down upon the humble in heaven and on earth—you will strive above all to be set apart from earthly disturbances and vices, and with as much charity as possible, you will benefit and provide for men everywhere as if they were brothers. By imitating this "separated providence," you will most especially please God, who Himself provides for all while being separate from all. This, then, is the imitation of God which is thought to make the soul, as it were, a god. Once, Socrates attempted this to the best of his ability. And after him, Apollonius of Tyana <note>A Neopythagorean philosopher and reputed miracle-worker of the 1st century AD</note>. Christ, the Master of Life, fulfilled this. All those have followed this who are reported to have finally performed, through the duties of such a life, certain miraculous works, as if they were already divine. Of these, only the prayers...

### BOOK

...petitions <note>original: "tiones"; likely continuing "orationes" (prayers) from the previous page</note> as if they were divine smoke, God hears them. For their will concurs as one with the divine will: and God frequently uses minds affected in this way as instruments or subjects to perform miracles. Finally, since by divine decree any matter is most ready under certain causes—suddenly receiving a certain influx of causes as if they were joined—it is right that minds, having already become divine through the imitation of God and through love, and approaching closer to God through their vows, soon capture a certain divine effect themselves. They are thought to transfer this effect into their own body, their affairs, and neighboring men, especially those who are similarly affected.

**Avicenna** and **Algazel** <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) and Algazel (Al-Ghazali) were influential Islamic philosophers whose works on the soul and metaphysics were widely studied by Renaissance thinkers like Ficino</note> seem to confirm these things where they say: souls of this kind often move not only their own bodies by their prayers, but even the elements of the world miraculously. Furthermore, Damis and Philostratus <note>Philostratus (c. 170–250 AD) wrote the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*, which the disciple Damis supposedly narrated</note>, with **Apollonius** confirming it, relate that certain wise and holy men among the Indians—who are called the **Oxydracae** <note>original: "Oxidracbi"; a legendary tribe in India mentioned in classical histories as resisting Alexander the Great</note>—defend their cities from enemies not with hands, but with prayer. For they say that God, humbly entreated by them, puts the enemies to flight with thunder and lightning.

That God hears the prayers of holy souls, our **Thomas Aquinas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Catholic theologian, whom Ficino calls "ours" to signify their shared Christian tradition despite Ficino's Platonism</note> proves from this: since every "mover" moves something in a way similar to itself, and therefore the movement of those praying is directed toward the good and depends on the Good itself (which surely does not move in vain), it naturally leads those whom it moves to pray toward their desired end. With the same faculty once imprinted, God helps them to pursue it and brings it about that they finally achieve it. For even in the movements of nature, He established a similar rule and power of inclination and attainment; furthermore, those things that are closer to their mover are moved more effectively by it. Now, the <term>Prime Motor</term> <note>The source of all movement in the universe, identified by Ficino and the Scholastics as God</note> moves all things. Rational natures are closer to Him than physical ones.

Since, therefore, physical natures are moved from there through a natural appetite toward their own ends and achieve them, much more so do rational substances—which are moved toward the good by the First Good in their prayers—sometimes achieve the desired good, insofar as they are moved from that source. They are driven from there insofar as they proceed toward the true good with desire and prayers; to that extent, therefore, their prayers are heard, and the desired outcome occurs.

These things are confirmed by a certain opinion of the divine **Iamblichus** <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher who specialized in theurgy (ritual prayer to connect with the divine)</note>: just as the sun has impressed a property on solar things, and the moon on lunar things, and the hollow of the moon on light things, by which they are moved toward the sun, the moon, or the hollow, so God Himself infused into souls an instinct to turn toward God by praying. This instinct is by no means in vain, since nature itself gives nothing and moves nothing in vain, being guided by the divine.

Finally, if it belongs to a friend to comply with the honorable desires of a friend, surely the Divine Mind—to which the very similarity, partly natural and partly acquired, makes our minds friends—satisfies the legitimate desires of minds. To His immense goodness, it belongs to bestow goods most widely, everywhere, upon minds, especially those turned toward the divine...

<summary>Ficino argues that prayer is a natural and effective power because holy souls align their wills with God, acting as His instruments. He supports this by citing Islamic philosophers, ancient accounts of Indian sages, Thomas Aquinas, and Iamblichus.</summary>

# Preface to the books composed in my youth: But finally collected and sent to Lorenzo.

->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici<-

<margin>v</margin> All the books have already come to you, my dearest patron. My children <note>original: "liberi"; Ficino uses a common Latin pun where *libri* (books) and *liberi* (children) are nearly identical</note>, I say, whom I brought forth in my youth or a slightly more mature age. And there come to you daily those whom I give birth to even in old age itself. But those who were born to me when I was once a youth, having become wanderers, still roam about with that same fortune—I should not say recklessness. But I have recently recalled these wanderers home, and I ordered them to flee immediately to you. Thus all my "sons" might recognize you as their patron, and in this way at last live more happily. And I, likewise, being with him whom I have always loved entirely through every stage of his life, might be with you entirely as a youth, a man, and an old man. Accept your own gladly, best Lorenzo. Read happily; live happily, the sure happiness of our fatherland. Love Marsilio Ficino, who is entirely yours, entirely. October 27, 1490, in the fields of Careggi <note>The site of the Medici villa where Ficino’s "Platonic Academy" met</note>.

# Preface of Marsilio Ficino to the book entitled *Man*, addressed to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici.

<margin>b</margin> The **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for walking while they taught</note> compose man from soul and body; **Christians** teach that the soul of man is created as soon as the body is born. Behold, our "Man" <note>Referring to the title of his treatise</note> comes to you, most humane Lorenzo, constituted of soul and body. First you will look upon the body, where we discuss the care of the body as if we were physicians. Then you will look within at the soul, where as if theologians we turn the soul from care of the body toward contemplating God. There indeed, through five little books, we ascend as if by steps to divine contemplation (the <term>Platonic Scale</term> <note>A philosophical concept where the mind ascends from material things to the ultimate Truth or God</note>). The sixth book then leads the man who has already been made "divine"—that is, toward **Christ**—along with the Magi, with a star as the judge. In the seventh at last, the Apostle Paul, having been caught up to the third heaven, catches up the mind along with him, to rest in God on the seventh day. October 30, 1490, Florence.

# Through which regions of the sky souls descend and ascend.

->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Lorenzo de' Medici<-

<margin>n</margin> The day before yesterday, you diligently investigated (as you usually do, like a **Platonist**) the causes for which souls slip into bodies. But by which region of heaven they mostly descend, you omitted (as I think) due to shortness of time. If therefore you desire this as well, accept it in a few words. Through **Cancer**, the home of the Moon, the ancient theologians said souls pass to the lower realms. For since they come into the region subject to generation <note>The physical world of birth and decay</note> through an affection for generation, they rightly thought souls made their way through the region of the Moon, which favors generation. For this reason, the ancients called Cancer the "Gate of Mortals." But they named **Capricorn**, which is opposite to this, the "Gate of the Gods." For they believe that through this gate, souls that have finally been purified fly back to their heavenly fatherland. For just as...

...from the world <note>original: "mulo", likely a typo for "mundo"</note> for the sake of generating they descend; likewise, they ascend in turn through the zeal for contemplation. Indeed, all astrologers, along with the Platonists, have agreed that Saturn, the lord of Capricorn, is the author—or at least the signifier—of divine contemplation. Therefore, this "Gate of the Gods" <note>Porta Deorum: In Neoplatonic thought, Capricorn was the gate through which souls ascended to heaven, while Cancer was the gate through which they descended into bodies</note> lies open to you, Lorenzo—a man distinguished by piety and a sublime contemplator. To you, I say, born under happy auspices, it is opened by divine will. Astronomers therefore consider Capricorn the head of the tropic circle, because the circle itself touches this sign, and the Sun, the lord of the heavens, reaching Capricorn, immediately seeks its ascent. But we seem to have happened upon the mention of this circle quite opportunely during our discussion. For it intersects that most beautiful path in Capricorn which astronomers have named the "Celestial Way"—called *Galaxia* in Greek, and the "Milky Way" in Latin. Little stars, but very many and frequent, create as it were small dwellings for souls (as they say) dedicated to the blessed. However, they assert that Capricorn is the head of this happy path and of the humble but celestial houses. You, Lorenzo, are now constructing a similar golden way under an age that is now nearly Saturnian <note>A reference to the "Golden Age" of Saturn, implying Lorenzo’s rule is bringing back a time of peace, wisdom, and justice</note>. Certainly, it is a way consecrated by the houses of piety and the dwellings of charity. May it finally lead you—who were happily born from the rising of Capricorn—to Capricorn, the head of the celestial way and the Gate of the Gods.

->The carefree care of love.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to the elegant Paulantonio Soderini, sends many greetings.

<margin>c</margin>When last night we heard Lorenzo de' Medici—like Apollo in the tranquility of Mammola <note>A Medici villa near Florence</note>, singing divine mysteries of love as if to a choir of Muses—I and a certain other companion from that same circle discussed late into the night whether Mammola admits loves and lovers, or not. He indeed denied it for this reason: because a gathering of this kind, desiring peace <note>original: "securitatem"; literally "freedom from care"</note> above all, drives all cares far away. But Love is a certain care, surely the heaviest of all, and the miserable lover is continuously vexed in this way. But I, not easily yielding to this reasoning, soon objected in this manner: Just as a great light completely extinguishes smaller lights, so Love, the most burning care of all, drives far away all others. Since, therefore, other mortals are oppressed by innumerable cares, all of which a lover (at Love's command) has set aside, no one lives more securely than a lover. Therefore, no one comes more acceptably into the pleasant company of Mammola. Then he said: "On the contrary, he comes full of cares, since he burns with the care of love, the sharpest of all cares." But I said: "Mammola does not reject a lover for this reason. For if the lover has long since been transferred into the beloved person, and has carried his cares where he transferred himself, the lover now enters Mammola secure." Finally, if by chance you are convinced that he (because he loves for a long time) cannot be secure—so be it; let the lover care for something, and indeed as much as possible (if you wish). But he no longer cares for human things (as I believe), but for divine ones. Now, Mammola does not prohibit caring for divine things, but for human ones. For as much as the pursuit of mortals is disturbed, so in turn the worship of divine things is everywhere tranquil. Because the soul wounded by love does not [care for] anything human...

# BOOK TEN CCXII

...desires <note>The text likely completes a word like "cupiditatem" (desire) from the previous page</note>. On the contrary, our Platonists are accustomed to infer something divine from this: because the fire of love is not settled at all by any sense or use of a beautiful body. It is as if the soul secretly desires something else beyond the bodily form—something shining from above upon such a form, hidden from us in some way. ### Marsilio Ficino to Pietro Filippo Pandolfini, most distinguished Orator of the Florentine Senate. Greetings.

<margin>d</margin> I have described for you the individual days of the coming year one after another, which I observed twice as the great nocturnal studies of my birth. I foretell happy days for you; I abhor the unhappy ones. I pray for the former, but I deprecate the latter. Jupiter, that helping father and signifier of high priests, stepped back into your sign of Gemini on the seventeenth day of last September; and having regressed as far as Taurus, he will finally direct his step on the tenth day of this January. From then on, walking in a straight path, he will happily return to your Gemini at the end of February. And on the twentieth day of October, he will proceed so happily toward Cancer. In this time, therefore, when Jupiter moves forward in a straight path—and especially through Gemini—"the fates will find a way, and Apollo will be present when called upon." 

Then, therefore, "pluck with your hand that golden branch of the tall tree; for it will follow willingly and easily if the fates call you." <note>Quoting Virgil's Aeneid VI.146-147 regarding the Golden Bough, which Aeneas needed to enter the underworld</note> Previously, it was not permitted to overcome it by any strength, nor to pluck it with hard iron. But do you see that Maro <note>Virgil's family name</note> joined our own judgment of action together with fate when he said: "Pluck with your hand"? And also that religion dominates fate when he says: "Apollo will be present when called upon"? Ptolemy himself confirms the same, saying: "The wise man will assist the work of the stars," just as the farmer assists the nature of the earth. Farewell; fortunate indeed in the heavens, but blessed in the Ruler of the heavens. December 26, 1490. Florence.

### Marsilio Ficino to Braccio Martelli. Greetings.

<margin>a</margin> Astronomers tell us that Jupiter, about to breathe the vital force into the fetus, shapes the spirit for human life through Mercury above all. The poets also sing that Jupiter, intending to bring souls back from the underworld, commands Mercury to touch the souls to be awakened with his caduceus <note>The staff carried by Mercury/Hermes</note>. Therefore, if Lorenzo de' Medici is like Jupiter to us in the awakening of Plato—He who shakes the world with a nod—it would be enough for him to have signaled with his eyes, with which he often clears our personal and public affairs. To you, my vigorous Braccio <note>Ficino puns on the recipient's name: "Braccio" is Italian for "arm"</note>, your arm shall be the caduceus, with which you, as if another Mercury, may touch where our Jupiter has nodded, so that Plato finally might not...

...might have risen half-alive. But now, my dear Braccio, our Plato has risen fully alive, loving the beautiful Eurydice as much as Orpheus did. In this Eurydice lies the greatness of judgment. Orpheus indeed descended to the underworld to see Eurydice again, but Plato (as we hope) will soon ascend to the heavens to see her. He will live more happily in Florence than in Athens. For that Eurydice he once wished to see there, he will now see for the first time in Florence. He will possess all that his mind sought. Surely you know that greatness of judgment exists only where contemplation joins with public governance—where the ruler himself philosophizes. It belongs to a narrow mind to follow one without the other; it is unfortunate to achieve one without the other. But most blessed is he who embraces both equally. Live then, happy with us under the great shadow of the Laurel <note>original: "Lauri" - a frequent pun on the name of Lorenzo de' Medici</note> alongside Plato. January 20, 1490.

### Harmony of Jupiter and the Sun: Harmony of Colleagues
### Marsilio Ficino to Angelo Nicolini and Filippo Valori, distinguished citizens in the Florentine Republic.

<margin>a</margin>Ptolemy, the prince of astronomers, says that in celestial harmony, Jupiter resonates most of all with the Sun. This harmony sounds most happily for men whenever those heavenly bodies behold each other in a trine aspect <term>trine aspect: an astrological position where planets are 120 degrees apart, considered a highly harmonious and beneficial alignment</term>. Yesterday, they finally joined in this alignment. In their union, they immediately decorated you with a distinguished magistracy. They declared that one of you is Jovial (like Jupiter) and the other is Solar. And just as the Sun and Jupiter are in accord in the heavens, so too will both of you be in accord in this office. I congratulate you, not so much because you have been adorned with such an office, but because you have been happily placed in dignity under a most fortunate star and the luckiest omens. This happened at almost the same time that the lucky star once led the Magi to Christ. January 20, 1490. In the fields of Careggi <note>The site of the Medici villa where Ficino translated many of his works</note>.

### Thanksgiving for an Immense Benefit.
### Marsilio Ficino to the Magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici. Greetings.

<margin>d</margin>While just recently you performed almost divine miracles in my friend and restored him to life, you also returned this mute man to us. For as soon as he revived by your inspiration, he conceived such a great thanksgiving in his mind for this immense benefit that he cannot give birth to it through his mouth. Therefore, let praise (as David said) be silence. January 20, 1490, Florence.

### An Allegory of how Mercury, the smallest of the heavenly bodies, signifies Wisdom, the greatest of virtues: Marsilio Ficino to the Noble and Learned Bindaccio Ricasoli. Many greetings.

<margin>q</margin>You ask quite subtly, noble Bindaccio (as is your custom in other matters), why God willed that through Mercury—the smallest of the heavenly bodies—Wisdom, the greatest of virtues, should be signified. So that I may answer your brief question with brevity: God has warned us in this matter that we should remember...

...we see that wisdom in men is very small. Indeed, it is granted to us by the smallest of the stars <note>Mercury, often associated in the Renaissance with the intellect and wisdom.</note>. Furthermore, it has taught us that wisdom is not established by the size of the body, nor does it proceed from the mass of matter itself. Sometimes men who are very small in body, daring, or fortune are the greatest in wisdom. Finally, while the Sun represents God himself, Mercury represents the wise man. Therefore, Mercury never departing from the Sun signifies that only that soul will be wise which never departs from God. Moreover, since the Sun is thought to signify princes, and since the Sun has no star closer in its path than Mercury, it warns that princes should have no one more closely joined in familiarity than wise men. Since the same Mercury promises wisdom, eloquence, and a love of letters, he commands us to join the study of eloquence with the study of wisdom. **"He has won every point who has mixed the useful with the pleasant."** <note>original: "Omne tulit punctum: qui miscuit vtile dulci." A famous quote from Horace’s *Ars Poetica* regarding the ideal balance in art and life.</note> February 14, 1490.

->Pallas, Juno, and Venus: The Contemplative, Active, and Voluptuous Lives.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to the Magnanimous man, Lorenzo de' Medici, greetings.<-

No one living by reason doubts that there are three types of life: the Contemplative, the Active, and the Voluptuous. This is because men have chosen three paths to happiness: Wisdom, Power, and Pleasure. By the name of "wisdom," we mean any study of the liberal arts, religion, and scholarly leisure. Under the title of "power," we include authority in both civil and military governance, an abundance of wealth, the splendor of glory, and the virtue of business. Finally, under the name of "pleasure," we do not doubt that the delights of the five senses and the avoidance of labor and cares are contained. Therefore, the poets named the first Minerva <note>Also known as Pallas Athena.</note>, the second Juno, and the third Venus.

Once, these three goddesses competed before Paris for the Golden Apple—that is, for the prize of victory. Paris consulted with himself as to which of the three paths to happiness he should choose as the most powerful. In the end, he chose pleasure. But because he despised wisdom and power, he foolishly hoped for happiness and instead fell into misery. 

It is said that only two goddesses appeared to Hercules: namely, Venus and Juno. Hercules, neglecting Venus, followed the spirited virtue under Juno. Yet, he was not perpetually happy among mortals because he was tormented by the continuous labor of his struggles; but at last, victory made him equal to the heavens. To him, finally, the conquered earth gave the stars. 

Two goddesses also met a certain Philebus <note>The namesake of one of Plato's dialogues concerning the nature of pleasure.</note>: Pleasure and Wisdom. They contended for victory, and in his judgment, Venus seemed to have overcome Pallas; but a little later, as Socrates judged more correctly, Minerva carried off the victory. However, because Venus and Juno were despised, they eventually hounded Socrates under false judges and condemned him to death.

Finally, our own Lorenzo <note>original: "Laureus," a play on the name Lorenzo and the laurel tree associated with Apollo and poetry.</note>, taught by the oracle of Apollo, has neglected none of the higher beings. For he has seen all three, and he has adored all three according to their merits. On account of this, he has received wisdom from Pallas, power from Juno, and from Venus, both the favors of wealth and the gift of music. February 15, 1490.

<summary>Ficino explains the mythological "Choice of Paris" as a metaphor for three lifestyles, arguing that Lorenzo de' Medici is unique because he successfully balances wisdom, power, and pleasure.</summary>

### Congratulations on a new dignity: with astronomical auspices
### Marsilio Ficino to the Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Ermolao Barbaro, Patriarch of Aquileia, sends many greetings.

<margin>i</margin>Poets often say that Mercury is accustomed to sending an eagle. But at your birth, Jupiter himself sent both. For Jupiter, sitting at the eastern region in the citadel of the Zodiac <note>original: "arce Zodiaci." This likely refers to the Midheaven or the Tenth House, the highest point in an astrological chart, associated with career and public honors.</note>, commanded the constellation of the Eagle <note>original: "aquilã quidẽ sydeream." A play on the name of Ermolao’s new see, Aquileia, and the constellation Aquila.</note> to fly through the summit of the sky under Capricorn. Meanwhile, he commanded Mercury to enter the Twins <note>original: "Dioscuros." Castor and Pollux, the sign of Gemini.</note> in a hexagonal aspect <note>A "sextile" aspect in astrology (60 degrees), usually considered harmonious and beneficial.</note>. Furthermore, he commanded his own Chiron <note>The centaur associated with the sign of Sagittarius.</note> to inhabit the ninth region of the sky, which is consecrated to sacred rites and wisdom. Therefore Jupiter—the author, or at least the signifier, of both our common religion and your own—when he first revisited his Twins (from where he once sent Mercury down from on high), declared you a sacred Prelate. He placed you in charge of the Eagle—namely, the Church of Aquileia—commending it just now to your care and providence. But setting aside for the moment the stars and the portents of the heavens, I truly wish, my dear Barbaro, that this dignity will be a happy one for you; and for this I pray to God, the creator of the heavenly bodies. I also congratulate this high office itself, which will certainly be honored as much by you as most men are usually honored by their offices. Finally, I rejoice for myself and for our age: for we have long seen learning joined with integrity of life, and perhaps we shall also see power conspiring with wisdom <note>A reference to Plato’s ideal of the "Philosopher King," where political power and philosophical wisdom are united.</note> (which our Plato desired above all else). We consider such a great good, even if signified by the sky, to have been made by the Ruler of the sky himself. Farewell, and be happy; keep your Marsilio in your good graces. March 12, 1491. Florence.
