### The life of heroic men is indeed full of labor, but it is glorious.
### Marsilio Ficino to Pierleo the Platonist <note>Pierleo da Spoleto was a famous physician and a member of Ficino's inner circle.</note>, sends many greetings.

<margin>b</margin>One may perhaps conjecture from this that among the poets, the hero Hercules was once considered primarily "solar": for the very name of Hercules signifies the "splendor of glory" <note>A common Renaissance etymology: *Hera* (glory/Juno) and *kleos* (fame/splendor).</note>, which pertains most of all to the Sun. Moreover, Hercules himself overcame twelve monsters, just as the Sun, overcoming the twelve animals of the Zodiac, completes his perpetual course. Therefore, hard labors celebrate the solar hero; to him, at last, the trampled earth grants the stars. Our "Lion" of Apollo <note>original: "Phœbeũ quoq̃ leonẽ nr̃m." A play on Pierleo’s name (*leo* means lion) and his association with Apollo, the god of healing and the sun.</note>, the Apollonian People, are about to celebrate you openly. They have decided to test you not in a single combat—that is, a duel—but to lead you everywhere into the crowd of enemies, so that from this, your high virtue may at last carry back a more ample victory. Under these auspices, therefore, magnanimous Pierleo, you have successfully competed everywhere in the public schools <note>original: "gynmasiis." Referring to the university halls where public disputations and lectures took place.</note>. Thus, finally, "the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered" <note>A biblical reference to Revelation 5:5, applied here to Pierleo’s success in intellectual or professional "battles."</note>. Now, therefore, was the first time we had to write to each other, since there was so much to congratulate. Until now, however, your frequent occupations provided the cause for a long silence, not only for you but for me as well. As for what you ask—what I am working on at present—I am re-reading the writings of Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century Christian theologian whose works were heavily influenced by Neoplatonism. At the time, he was believed to be the Dionysius converted by St. Paul in Athens.</note>. I began this last summer, as soon as I had put an end to my commentaries on Plotinus. Dionysius alone remained for me to be clarified, undoubtedly the highest of the Platonists. Him, therefore, in the same order as Plato and Plotinus, we are attempting both to translate and to interpret in summary—namely, according to the Platonists' way. His book...

### Preface to the fables on pleasure.

Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to Martin Uranius, his friend given by heaven.

<margin>n</margin>The ninth book of our letters took its beginning from Martin. The tenth, however, now receives its end in Martin. For the Martinian spirit and the Marsilian spirit are utterly the same <note>Ficino often plays on the "identity" of souls between close friends. Here, he suggests their "Genius"—a protective spirit or essential nature—is identical.</note>. He claims the number nine for himself. But the singular perfection of our love demands the number ten, which is the perfection of numbers <note>In Pythagorean numerology, ten (the Decad) represents the completion of a cycle and total perfection.</note>. Since love desires nothing other than pleasure, this tenth book rightly makes its end—consecrated to love—in pleasure. In pleasure, I say, that is "Uranian," which means heavenly <note>original: "vrania .i. cœlesti." A play on his friend’s name, Uranius, and the "Celestial Aphrodite" (Venus Urania) who represents intellectual and divine love rather than base physical desire.</note>. Since this "Uranian" work is indeed dedicated to you. You, my other self, will therefore read here at the heel of the tenth book several fables about pleasure dedicated to you today, though thought up by us long ago while we were commenting on Plato’s *Philebus* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the nature of pleasure and its relation to the Good.</note>. That commentary was intended for Lorenzo de' Medici. But it is to be transcribed for you as soon as the occasion offers itself. For now, our scribes are occupied in copying out letters to you.

->Fable.<-

->The evil demon draws one toward the false through a likeness of truth via pleasure.<-
<margin>toward evil.</margin>->God, however, draws us through these same things toward the true and the good.<-

<margin>d</margin>God is truth and goodness; therefore he composed all things out of truth and goodness. For any thing, insofar as it remains in its integral purity as it was made by God, is called "true." Insofar as it leads to something for others, it is called "good" for others. Likewise, insofar as it leads to something within itself, it is called "good" for itself. God impressed upon the reality of things a "likeness of truth" <note>original: "verisimili." A "verisimilitude" or something that resembles the truth.</note> as a sort of mark; he poured "pleasure" over goodness as a sort of bait <note>original: "esca." This metaphor of pleasure as a lure or bait is central to Ficino's ethics.</note>; so that the hidden truth of each thing might be tracked through a likely image, and finally, through all truth, one might find the truth of God. Again, his purpose was that through the bait of pleasure, individual things might be lured toward the good—which is hidden in itself—and through all good things toward the good of God.

But when the envious demon saw that God was drawing all things to Himself—partly by the mark of the "truth-like" and partly by the bait of the "good-like"—he plotted, as a rival of divinity, by what method he himself might similarly draw all things to himself. Thus, he applied a "likely" mark and a "good-seeming" bait in an imitation of that divine pattern, but he attached the former to the *false* and the latter to the *evil*. By this, it happens that through the former he draws minds toward the false, and through the latter he draws affections toward the evil, and finally to himself. For since he is a rebel and a stranger to divine truth and goodness, he is himself a certain kind of falsehood and malice. Hence Plato, in the *Timaeus*, calls pleasure the "bait of evils" <note>original: "maloꝝ escā in Timeo." Refers to *Timaeus* 69d: "pleasure, the greatest incitement to evil."</note>.

->Fable concerning good and evil things.<-

<margin>e</margin>Once there were two certain things alone: namely, Good and Evil. As long as the Good was generating, the Evil was not at all provoked to generate, because of its pride, thinking that it alone could resist the Good. Nevertheless, the Good began to generate good things. Then Evil, fearing for itself from the Good and the good things, desired to generate evil things against them. But when, on account of its sterility, it was unable to do so, it by chance invoked its Fortune with weeping; and with her favoring, it began to generate evil things and...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s tenth book of letters to Martin Uranius. The previous page ended mid-sentence, discussing fables about pleasure that Ficino had composed years earlier.</meta>

...in the opposite way that the good <note>original: "bonū"</note> relates to good things. For you see that good things relate to the Good itself, and confer the possession of virtue. They preserve that in which they exist; they harmonize with one another in their own safety; and they have pleasure following at their back. Against these, he [the philosopher] has set the opposites: namely, degeneration, hindrance, a numerous and turbulent crowd, and the impatience of that which sustains the good. Likewise, he noted an unfitness for various similar goods. Finally, he placed pleasure in the front of evil, rebuking the good itself along with the evil, because it had hidden the bait of the good. By placing pleasure behind the good, he perhaps proposed it more correctly. But indeed, so that the good itself might not have its kingdom dissolved by evil, he first established that it is the nature of evil things to suffer. He set up two contraries: namely, one evil and one good, since one good cannot be contrary to another good. Then, he established that evil does not only destroy another evil, but even itself. For whether it happens through defect or through excess, it eventually destroys the foundation by which it is sustained, and from which it cannot stand apart. From this it follows that evil cannot be infinite in its power, whereas the good can be. Finally, he established that even if evil things offer the bait of pleasure for a short time, they nevertheless fall into long-lasting pain. Pythagoras signified this when he said:
> Abstain from any animal having a black tail; that is, from vices. <note>original: "Ab aiali caudā bñte nigram abstine.i.a viciis." This is one of the famous "Pythagorean Symbols," brief enigmatic precepts used by the ancient school to teach moral lessons through metaphor.</note>

# A Fable.
### Concerning Pleasure, who defeated the ambitious, but was defeated by Pallas.

Once upon a time, when the Pleasures <note>original: "Uoluptates." Ficino personifies the Pleasures as a group of characters.</note> heard that they were being reviled everywhere by ambitious preachers, they conspired together for their own defense and chose "Impudence" to be their representative, speaking these words: "See what shameless ingratitude everyone shows toward us! Indeed, since their entire happiness is situated within us, they nevertheless dare to publicly disapprove of us." 

Then Impudence replied: "I marvel at your cowardice. For although you possess them and their very houses, you do not even dare to occasionally show your faces to the people from their windows and gates, so that everyone might understand that you are held in high delight among them, and that you are only reviled by them so that no one might steal you away from them."

After this, the Pleasures, relying on the counsel and even the help of Impudence, opened their faces through the windows. Because of this, it happened that those ambitious detractors lost all their credit and authority among the people; and those who had reviled Pleasure were, in turn, reviled by her everywhere. 

But after they had conquered these vain and false enemies, it remained for them to defend themselves against their true and legitimate enemies: the philosophers. Because the philosophers prefer Minerva <note>Roman goddess of wisdom and strategic war; the Greek Pallas Athena.</note> to Pleasure, a judgment was recently transferred to Jupiter <note>The king of the gods, representing supreme reason.</note>, with "Temerity" <note>original: "temeritate." Personification of reckless boldness or thoughtlessness.</note> acting as the advocate for the Pleasures. 

When they had come before Jupiter, Temerity, as the orator for the cause of the Pleasures, said it was only right that Minerva be summoned to judgment, whom her followers prefer—more than is divinely permitted—over Pleasure, the mistress of all things. Pallas, having been summoned, appeared. 

Suddenly Temerity added: "Neither is your Pallas, O Jupiter, born from the mouth of philosophers, who, while holding Pleasures as nothing, boasts that she is your daughter. But I respond that Pleasure herself was born from you under the name of Venus; and that Minerva is actually the daughter of Pleasure, under the name of Wisdom, whom all the followers of a certain pleasure of the mind pursue. Why say more? Venus was born from you. Even if Pallas boasts that she came forth from your head, I would assert that she too was fathered by you along with Pleasure."

To this Pallas replied: "But I affirm, O Pleasure, that you originated from me: first within Jupiter, who as Wisdom rejoices in himself by his own benefit; then among men, where you also originate from me, the inventor of various things..."

# BOOK TEN CCXV

...of delights. Rather indeed, they are delighted by an image of me within their fantasies <note>original: "phātes" / "phantasias"</note>. For these are delighted and seized by a certain image of my splendor. Then Rashness <note>original: "temeritas"</note> said: "Let us set aside these dialectical subtleties. Pleasure, being simple and innocent, does not arm herself with such thorns. Look around, Jupiter, at how vast the empire of Pleasure is: behold Venus, behold Cupid, her attendants—her handmaidens and even the god of gardens himself <note>The "god of gardens" is Priapus, associated with fertility and the physical aspects of pleasure.</note>, her minister. In her tavern is Ceres <note>Goddess of grain/bread.</note>, and Bacchus <note>God of wine.</note> in her pantry. All the heavenly beings feed upon her ambrosia and nectar. Why should I mention Mars, the most ferocious of the gods? Or you yourself, Jupiter? Or the others everywhere entangled in the snares of Venus? And what others hardly achieve or retain through violence, she alone happily fulfills with a single nod: dragging no one, leading all who are willing, and holding those who are glad to stay. She leads not only those who live on earth, but those who are in heaven and those who lead the heavens. Pleasure seizes not only living things, but even non-living things to their respective ends. Furthermore, lest Pallas, Diana, or Vesta <note>Athena (Pallas), Diana, and Vesta were the three virgin goddesses of Olympus, traditionally immune to the power of Aphrodite/Pleasure.</note> boast of their sterility and escape the empire of Pleasure: Pleasure herself, O Jupiter, commands Pallas to take delight in bows, Diana in the hunt, and Vesta in the hearths."

At this, Pallas was indignant and said: "O Jupiter, you will soon see how strong Pleasure really is—she who so insolently boasts of her empire over everyone. Summon Fear <note>original: "pauorem"</note> here, the most abject not only of gods, but of all things." Jupiter cried out: "Hey, Fear! Come here, Fear!" Immediately at the name of Fear being called, all pleasures, trembling together with Rashness, took flight. Then all the heaven-dwellers laughed and condemned such a cowardly flight with a mocking judgment. Finally, Pallas sealed the verdict of the gods thus: "What is more vile than fear? For nothing is created from that which does not exist, except when an image of an absent evil is formed. This Fear, in turn, kills from that which does not exist, when it is destroyed by the image of an absent good. But Pleasure is even viler than so vile a Fear. For she is put to flight not only by Fear itself, but by its shadow: when she not only fears, but even *thinks* of fear, she suddenly flees. Nay (to speak more truly), she perishes; and so that she may perish with greater ignominy, she is not transformed into anything similar or friendly, but into an enemy—and that quite suddenly—as she is unwillingly converted into pain."

->A Fable. Concerning Pleasure: that she should not be engaged with, nor hoped for on earth.<-

<margin>c</margin> When Jupiter realized that souls were not returning to heaven because they were held back on earth by Pleasure, he sent Mars and Vulcan, as the strongest and most armed, to destroy Pleasure. But at their first encounter, being young men enticed by the charms of Pleasure, they laid down their arms. He sent Pallas again, armed and wise, thinking that the others had succumbed because of their rashness. To her, Pleasure said: "Are you not ashamed, O Pallas, a goddess clothed and armed, to struggle with me, who am human, unarmed, and naked?" She replied: "It pleases me to struggle with you in this way so that I may overcome you." To this, she [Pleasure] replied that there was no reason of either glory or utility in the struggle: "For you will achieve neither if you defeat me; it is clear that you yourself while..."

<meta>This page continues the allegorical struggle between the gods and the personification of Pleasure. Pallas (Minerva/Athena), representing human wisdom and discipline, attempts to subdue Pleasure through force and logic, but fails. The narrative then shifts to a higher strategy proposed by Saturn (representing contemplation), suggesting that Pleasure cannot be destroyed but must be relocated to the divine realm through the allure of the arts.</meta>

# BOOK [TEN]

...only conquered by the pleasure of victory, to struggle without any regard for glory or utility. Then Pallas, overcome by words <note>original: "verbis cōuicta"</note>, broke out into violence and directed a weapon against her [Pleasure] many times. But she, whose nature is yielding and subtle, and being most fleeting, evaded the blows beforehand. Therefore, Pallas held out a wide shield <note>This refers to the Aegis, the traditional shield of Athena/Minerva.</note> over her head; but Pleasure penetrated the shield. Indeed, she is so powerful at penetrating that she pierces both body and soul.

After this, Pallas summoned Pain <note>original: "dolorem"</note>, so that she might destroy Pleasure through an opposite enemy. But because opposites do not receive one another, Pain did not rush into the face of Pleasure, but instead stretched out alongside her. Then Pallas, together with her companion Vulcan, having taken up bellows, tried to thin out and dissolve Pleasure. But she could neither thin her out, since she is already most thin, nor dissolve her into anything further, since she is an ultimate end <note>original: "cum sit ultimum." In Aristotelian philosophy, an "ultimate end" is something sought for its own sake, not for the sake of something else.</note>. For when it is asked why someone does this, and the answer is "because of that," and it is asked again "why that," and the answer is "because it is pleasing," if it is asked again "why is it pleasing," they will not answer otherwise than "because it pleases." 

They say that Pallas, pale with grief <note>original: "Palladē ergo pallidā" — a Latin pun on the goddess's name and the word for "pale."</note> because she had not overcome Pleasure, returned to Jove. Then Rhea, being more ready because of her own flowing nature <note>original: "a fluxu proprio." Rhea's name was etymologically linked by Renaissance thinkers to the Greek word "rheo," meaning "to flow."</note>, approached Jove and said: "O son, now you will recognize that you have need of the counsel of old Saturn, from whom you hitherto took the kingdom and whom you shut up in the inner chambers of the palace." This signifies that the active life distracts men greatly from the contemplative life. Therefore, the doors having been unlocked, Saturn is summoned for consultation. 

Then he said: "There are two principles of motion: Pleasure for seeking, and Pain for fleeing. Indolence <note>original: "indolentia," meaning a state of feeling nothing.</note>, however, does neither. Therefore Pleasure is not to be killed. Otherwise, souls would not seek heaven if Pleasure were extinguished even here. Instead, Pleasure should be drawn here [to heaven], and Pain left among men, so that from the earth, everyone may flee toward us." 

The old man's counsel pleased them. Spirits <note>original: "demones." In this context, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits or personified forces.</note> who are satellites of Mars and Vulcan were sent to seize Pleasure. For it was feared that the gods might indulge in her beauty and be defeated. It was certain that these spirits would have no regard for beauty. But the spirits could never hold Pleasure with their hands, as she wonderfully surpasses eels in her slippery softness. For her softness is confirmed by the constant use and habitation of soft and sweet things. Finally, Pleasure overcame both gods and spirits, so that no one dares to contend with her. 

For she is rather to be fled than attacked. But lest we offend longer against divine names: let us admit that Minerva on earth and other gods on earth—that is, human wisdom and power—are greatly conquered by pleasure. But she is overcome by divine wisdom. For Saturn, together with Minerva, deliberated again: they should try to seize Pleasure not through violence opposed to her, but rather through grace, her friend. 

Therefore they sent Mercury, Apollo, the Muses, and the Graces to entice Pleasure upward. Mercury first gave a speech to her, persuading Pleasure that it was wasteful to linger on earth among her enemies: fear, pain, anger, hatred, envy, labor, poverty, and disease. Phoebus [Apollo] also charmed her with the lyre; the Muses with songs and melodies; the Graces with dances and choirs. Enticed by these things, Pleasure joined herself to the singing Muses and, with hands outstretched, entwined herself with the Graces as they played charmingly. And so, with these deities singing...

<summary>Pallas fails to defeat Pleasure through force or logic, prompting Saturn to advise that Pleasure be lured to heaven through the arts (Apollo and the Muses) rather than suppressed, as she is a necessary "ultimate end" for the soul.</summary>

...and playing, accompanied by those returning to heaven, Pleasure was carried into the sky. Earth was deserted by Pleasure; therefore, one must depart from here to there. Yet in such a way that, in departing, you do not turn back: lest (in the manner of Orpheus) you lose the prize. <note>Orpheus famously lost his wife Eurydice by looking back at her as he led her out of the Underworld, breaking his pact with Hades.</note> But at what time did Pleasure flee into heaven? At the same time as the original Astraea—that is, Justice—when Adam sinned. <note>Astraea was the last of the immortals to leave Earth at the end of the Golden Age in Greek mythology. Ficino here merges Greek myth with the Biblical Fall of Man.</note> But lest mortals, deprived of pleasure, should afflict and destroy themselves amidst so many adversities, Jupiter, pitying our misery, while he took away pleasure, multiplied hope for us. 

But the hope of attaining pleasure here—that is, obtaining it from mortal things—is deceptive. For she has been translated to Minerva <note>Roman goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare.</note>, with Mercury, Apollo, the Muses, and the Graces leading the way. Wherefore we can only attain full pleasure in the possession of divine wisdom, and even a certain delight from the liberal arts. After this, Pluto, king of the earth, seeing that his bait for detaining souls in the underworld had been taken away, thought to at least fashion a bait similar in appearance to Pleasure. Therefore, having taken the clothes and dyes left behind by Pleasure, which she used to wear on earth—for she went into heaven pure—he decided to equip and substitute another in place of Pleasure. Yet he did not equip Demons, for they are necessary ministers, nor did he use souls, for they have already been judged; rather, he chose a certain Fury. Not Anger, nor Envy, Hatred, Fear, or Pain. For the clothes and shoes of Pleasure did not fit these, being too different; but he equipped Loss <note>original: "iacturam". In Latin, this implies both a financial loss and a "throwing away" of one's life or resources.</note>, whom he knew was always most familiar to earthly pleasure. Hence we must be warned to flee pleasure far away; otherwise, under the pretext of pleasure, we will immediately fall into hidden loss.

### Response for the gift of a silver cup.

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine sends many greetings to Georg Herwart the German.<-

<margin>c</margin> Since my tender years, my Georg, a certain natural goodwill toward Germans <note>original: "germanis"</note> has been instilled in me, brought about by hidden causes. Thus, the Miniatensian associates of the Florentines, a German race, are our guests above all others; and the family of the Pico and Cavalcanti, tracing their origin from Germany, is most dear to us. For which reason, if Germans (generally all) are brothers <note>original: "germani". Ficino is playing on the Latin word "germanus," which means both a person from Germany and a "true" or "full" brother.</note> to me, what shall I say of the excellent men and friends among you? Of Martin Uranius <note>Martin Prenninger, a German humanist and jurist who took the name Uranius.</note>, a heavenly friend; and of you, above all, my best Georg? Truly, whoever is more than a brother to me is, without doubt, another self. So it is no wonder if your things, which are most dear to you, please me as if they were my own. I wish that I were as great in virtue among myself as I am held to be among you friends! Certainly, my goodwill toward you is such as the very cup you recently gave me as a gift. Silver on the outside, indeed, but gold within. I believe your own talent, under the appearance of silver, possesses that gold which Socrates humbly requested from God in the *Phaedrus* <note>In Plato's dialogue *Phaedrus*, Socrates prays that he may be beautiful within and that his external possessions be in harmony with his internal self.</note> and recognizes in heroic natures in the *Republic*. Finally, how pleasing your letter and the received gift were to us, the eleventh book of our letters shall be a witness. Taking its beginning from your letter, inscribed first, and this my response. Farewell, be happy: and if you love Marsilio, love Martin, surnamed Prenninger. If you desire to embrace me with a certain heavenly love, embrace my love, Uranius, with your whole mind. April 29, 1490.

### How someone, while thinking, might encounter themselves under another's persona.

->Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to his fellow Platonist Pierleoni.<-

<margin>a</margin> I have received your letter, Pierleoni, full of love and grace and (to praise it in one word) truly Platonic. In it, you write that as soon as anything Platonic occurs to you, Marsilio immediately comes to your aid. But beware lest perhaps the external image deceives you. I suspect, indeed, that Pierleoni himself is hiding there under the persona of Marsilio. For since human signs and appearances offer themselves to you as you contemplate Platonic matters, it is probable that a most Platonic appearance offers itself above all others. Now, what in human affairs is more Platonic than the Great Leo <note>original: "leo magnus". A pun on his correspondent's name, Pierleoni (Petrus Leo).</note>, the dwelling of the Platonic sun? Perhaps, therefore (just like Narcissus), while gazing at yourself, you imagine you are gazing at another. Especially Marsilio, whose image you burn for.

love clothes you. But since we have happened upon the subject of the image: you surely know that reason is the mediator between the imagination and the intellect. It is into reason that the images of natural things flow from the side of the imagination, while from the other side, the forms <note>original: "species"</note> of divine things flow down from the intellect. For this reason, it often happens that a certain divine form takes on a natural image within human reason. Thus, that which is divine within often appears as something natural to the eyes of reason. What if, by a similar logic, Pierleoni <note>Pierleoni of Spoleto, a physician and friend of Ficino</note> often encounters himself under the figure of Marsilio? But enough of these matters for now.

Regarding Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century Christian theologian whom Ficino believed was the original 1st-century convert of St. Paul. This "Pseudo-Dionysius" was the bridge between Christian doctrine and Neoplatonism.</note>, you seem to me to hold a very correct view. Certainly, for me, no form of knowledge is more pleasing than the Platonic, and this form is nowhere more to be venerated than in Dionysius. Indeed, I love Plato in Iamblichus; I admire him in Plotinus; but in Dionysius, I venerate him. I often suspect that the Platonists older than Plotinus—such as Ammonius and Numenius, or perhaps those even earlier—read the books of Dionysius twice over before they were hidden away by some calamity of the Church. From there, the truly Platonic sparks of Dionysius were transferred into Plotinus and Iamblichus, from which so great a fire was kindled. Regarding Dionysius, this is enough; Galen’s work *On the Teachings of Hippocrates and Plato* will be quite pleasing to me. 

We often speak of you with Lorenzo de' Medici <note>original: "Laurentium medicē"</note>. He truly loves you wonderfully (as is his custom) and, as is right, he respects you greatly. 

May 12, 1491. In the countryside of Careggi <note>The site of the Medici villa where the Platonic Academy met.</note>.

### It belongs to the great to bestow benefits even upon those who do not deserve them.

->Marsilio Ficino humbly commends himself to the Reverend Father in Christ and Lord Raphael Riario, Cardinal of San Giorgio.<-

Even if perhaps there are no merits by which I ought to obtain anything from you, I will nevertheless dare to ask for a favor—relying not on any merits of my own, but trusting in my respect for you and your clemency toward all. To provide a benefit to those who deserve it is just, but it is a human act; however, to grant freely even to those who do not deserve it is most clement and divine. Great and divine things are especially becoming of a great and holy Prelate.

->A defense regarding letters not delivered.<-

Marsilio Ficino humbly commends himself to the Most Reverend Father and Lord in Christ, Lord Raphael Riario <note>Raphael Riario (1461–1521) was a powerful Cardinal and patron of the arts in Rome, known for his involvement in the Pazzi Conspiracy and later his patronage of Michelangelo.</note>, Cardinal of St. George.

<margin>c</margin>Christopher Marsuppini <note>A member of a prominent Florentine humanist family</note>, our close friend, recently returned to Florence from Rome. Immediately after his first words of greeting, he told me how much your Clemenency loves me. Indeed, I could hear nothing more pleasing than this. But in the meantime, this was distressing to me: that he immediately began to accuse me of negligence, as if I had sent no letters to you after your departure from here. But I immediately opened the register <note>original: "Archetipum," referring to Ficino's personal copy-book of his outgoing correspondence</note> of my letters to him and read at least four letters sent to you during this time. Certainly they were far too unfortunate on their Roman journey, for they do not yet seem to have reached you. Yet elsewhere, relying on a happier fortune, they have flown long ago not only through all of Italy, but even into Spain, France, Germany, and Hungary <note>original: "Pannoniam"</note>, witnessing everywhere—except in Rome—my observance and reverence toward you. Therefore, I was rightly to be blamed, not because I sent none, but because I sent so few letters to you. But I wish that those which seem to have been born once under an unlucky star might at least be reborn today more fortunately, so that using better fates they might eventually reach their happy patron and commend your little client to you. June 4, 1491.

->On behalf of the youths sent from Swabia to the Florentine Academy.<-

Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Louis Nauclerus <note>Ludwig Nauclerus (c. 1430–1508), a German humanist, legal scholar, and historian</note> and Johannes of Pforzheim <note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous German humanist and the first great German scholar of Hebrew, often called "Phorcensis" after his birthplace</note>, German legal experts.

<margin>s</margin>You write to us that the princes of Germany are sending, in your name, youths to Florence to be educated, as if to an Academy. But you write with such elegance in the meantime that you seem to be sending sons not *to* an Academy, but rather *from* an Academy. You seek among foreign nations a discipline that is already domestic to you. What a reversal of things this is! To the same degree that most men, in the insolent manner of the sophists, rashly profess things that belong to others, you most modest men, in the Socratic manner <note>Socrates famously claimed to know nothing, a stance of intellectual humility</note>, deny even your own excellence. This is to be wondered at above all else: that as many people curiously search for little stones hidden in the bowels of the earth, so accurately do you pursue the celestial splendor of wisdom throughout all nations. For this reason, moved by a certain incredible love toward you, we have undertaken the care of your youths with a devoted mind. And first of all, we have recommended them with singular devotion to a host. We shall give our effort daily so that a field, fertile by nature, may eventually produce a most happy harvest. Therefore, be of good heart, and respond to your princes in our name—

### On the four species of divine madness. Also, true praises for the physician <note>The title plays on the name "Medici," suggesting Lorenzo is a "doctor" of the soul or state.</note> of Lorenzo.

## Marsilio Ficino to Pietro Divizio <note>Pietro Divizi da Bibbiena (1450–1491) was a scholar and influential secretary to Lorenzo de’ Medici.</note>, most distinguished in letters and character.
## Greetings.

Since you have for a long time heard our Plato in the *Symposium* <note>original: "conuiuio." This refers to Plato's dialogue on the nature of love.</note> disputing most extensively about love, and you desired, moreover, a certain brief summary on love: I have given you a booklet to read which we composed in our youth on this subject with outstanding poetic skill for a wandering youth. I recall indeed how wonderfully you delighted in hearing that love itself is not in truth lust, but a certain madness <note>original: "furoreʒ" (furor). In the Platonic sense, this is not "insanity" but a state of divine inspiration that lifts the soul above its ordinary limits.</note> instigated by the divine in excellent minds. Furthermore, that divine madness, as if a single genus, contains four species within itself: Love, Poetry, Prophecy, and Mystery <note>original: "Vaticinium" (prophecy) and "mysterium" (religious ritual/initiation).</note>. And indeed, Love proceeds from Venus, but Poetry from the Muses; Prophecy from Apollo, and Mystery from Dionysius. Finally, it explains by what reasoning different human characters are driven by various madnesses by one or another divinity. 

It remained, most ingenious Pietro, to inquire whether the same talent could be inspired by several gods at once (if I may say so), and thus be stirred by various madnesses. Now, regarding love and poetry, the question does not seem particularly difficult. For we do not doubt that Homer, Pindar, Callimachus, Sappho, and Virgil <note>original: "Maronem," referring to Publius Vergilius Maro.</note> were struck by a poetic and amorous instinct at the same time. Furthermore, Epimenides and the Sibyl were inspired by Prophecy. But beyond these, only those "born of the gods" (as they say) were able to be inspired by Mysteries: such as the gentiles say Orpheus was, and our own people say David was. 

We have known in our own age one most happy in talent, who has obtained these four gifts of madness equally from the four Divinities. Surely, he conceived the poetic and amorous spirit under the Muses and the heavenly Venus long ago in the very flower of his youth; indeed, his most sweet songs and utterly marvelous poems resonate everywhere. But as an adult, he drank Prophecy from Apollo. By this, certainly, through a certain wonderful sagacity of mind divinely implanted, frequently foreseeing future dangers both privately and publicly, he applies a medical hand to the perils, and immediately heals them with Phoebean <note>Referring to Apollo (Phoebus), the god of both prophecy and healing.</note> virtue. 

Finally, now that he is nearly mature, he has happily attained the Mystic madness from Dionysius. The ancient theologians defined Dionysian "drunkenness" as an ecstasy of the mind <note>original: "excessum mentis"</note> separated from mortal things, penetrating the secret mysteries of divinity. Bacchus loves the hills. On the hills of Ambra and the Agnano valley, that Phoebus <note>Referring to Lorenzo de' Medici through the imagery of the sun god.</note> of ours, drunk everywhere on Dionysian nectar, revels in divine frenzy. Then indeed, inspired from on high, he pours out celestial songs with a fluent mouth <note>original: "ore rotundo," a classical idiom for eloquent or polished speech.</note>, the profound meanings of which it is never permitted for anyone to penetrate, unless they are seized by a talent with a similar madness.

<summary>Marsilio Ficino writes to Pietro Divizio summarizing the four types of Platonic "divine madness" (Love, Poetry, Prophecy, and Mystery) and argues that Lorenzo de' Medici possesses all four, elevating him to the status of divinely inspired figures like Orpheus and David.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes a discussion on the Platonic concept of divine inspiration (furor) using the analogy of a magnet, and includes a letter of consolation regarding the death of Cardinal Marco Barbo.</meta>

Indeed, that patron of ours [Lorenzo de' Medici] carries you away with him, along with several others who, at times, listen more attentively and successfully. Upon them, he overflows with an abundance of divine madness <note>original: "furoris." In Ficino's Platonism, "furor" is not insanity, but a state of divine inspiration or "madness" that elevates the human soul to a higher state of consciousness.</note> more than upon others. By what means he himself, struck by the divine power, is able to stir others in a similar way, our Plato teaches in the book titled *Ion*. There, he places a small iron ring beneath a massive Herculean stone <note>original: "Herculeo lapidi," an ancient term for a magnet.</note>, soon to be easily drawn up. To the first ring, he immediately attaches a second; then a third to the second, and a fourth thereafter. He thus forms a chain of rings hanging one from another from the magnet. Through these, the power of attraction is suddenly transferred from the first to the following one in succession. In the same way, he thinks the Muse is moved by Phoebus [Apollo]; the poet is seized by the Muse, and the listeners are similarly seized by the poet. This mystery is perhaps imitated in these verses by Virgil: 

> What the almighty Father foretold to Phoebus, and Phoebus Apollo foretold to me, I, the greatest of the Furies, reveal to you. <note>original: "Quæ phœbo pater omnipotens: mihi phœbus appollo prædíxit Vobis furiarum ego maxima pando." From Virgil’s Aeneid (3.251-252). Ficino uses this to illustrate the chain of transmission, though he immediately clarifies the nature of this "madness."</note>

But I would not wish to name Furies at this time, when we are dealing not with the madness of Furies, but with the madness of the Graces. With which [madness] our patron [Lorenzo], abounding, makes you, happy Pietro, and me alike, and his other observers affected at once. Having affected them, he seizes them. Having seized them, he occupies them. Having occupied them, he soon bathes them in an incomparable pleasure. Therefore, affected by such a great benefit, let us persevere in his most ardent love. In loving him singularly, we receive a divine inspiration <note>original: "instinctum"</note> every day. June 8, 1491.

## True praise of Cardinal Marco [Barbo], a holy man.

Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved Antonio Calderini. Greetings.

Our Pietro Fannio, a learned and upright man, yesterday confirmed your singular goodwill toward me with many testimonies <margin>p</margin>, a goodwill already confirmed for a long time by your many favors toward me. Since indeed I owe you very much for many reasons, Calderini, I certainly owe you the most for this: that you have long since made that holy man, Marco [Barbo] <note>Marco Barbo (1420–1491) was an Italian Cardinal and the Patriarch of Aquileia, known for his piety and patronage of scholars.</note>, Cardinal of San Marco, a friend to us, and at times presented him as a patron in our dangers. We could not help but grieve deeply at his death, unless we hoped that he, from heaven (where he leads a blessed life), will breathe upon us daily with a more certain protection. He certainly (as you well know) seems to have fulfilled that Davidic saying: *My soul is always in my hands* <note>original: "Anĩa mea in manibus meis semp." A reference to Psalm 119:109.</note>, both living and dying. And he seems to have reached that Gospel saying: *I have the power to lay down my soul* <note>original: "potẽtem habeo deponẽdi aiam meã." A reference to John 10:18.</note>. For he foretold the hour so joyfully, and departed from the body as if by his own choice, so that he seemed not to die, but to travel abroad of his own accord—or rather, to return to his desired homeland—ready to give examples of immortal life to mortals and to approach the celestial lights as a new light. Therefore, my Antonio, our friendship is happy for this reason above all: that it was confirmed under the most fortunate of patrons. Farewell happily, and love me (as you usually do) as one who loves you singularly. June 29, 1491.

My singular love for them demands a most exact accounting of each individual, but business prevents it. Therefore, be content with this and fare most happily. July 20, 1491.

### On simplicity and integrity of character.
#### Marsilio Ficino to his fellow Platonist Pierleone <note>Pierleone Leoni of Spoleto, a celebrated physician and philosopher who served Lorenzo de' Medici.</note>: Sends Greetings.

<margin>f</margin>Greetings, Pierleone, most worthy of health; a man of the greatest integrity, or rather, the simplest of all. Indeed, our Plato, in the *Symposium*, thinks that no "whole" <note>original: "integros." Ficino plays on the double meaning of "integrity" as both moral uprightness and "wholeness" or being "undivided."</note> men are born in our age, but only divided ones. In the *Timaeus* and the *Phaedrus*, he asserts that everyone is twofold. Therefore, when I call you "whole" and "simple," I judge you to be a child not of this age, but of another. In that age (as Plato says), men were once born both whole and simple; specifically, as long as a certain divinity reigned within humanity. For the "integrity" of divine beings is the same as their "simplicity." Natural things, however, possess a manifold integrity. Finally, monsters degenerate from both integrity and simplicity at once. But a letter hardly admits these strong mysteries easily. See then, my Pierleone—my other self—how similar a lot we have found in most things: we have the same physician of discipline in the heavens (Saturn, I guest), the same leader (Plato), and again the same patron, Lorenzo de' Medici, the restorer of Platonic disciplines. We have exactly the same friends. As for enemies, we have none; for we love everyone, unless perhaps someone were found who loved only himself. Furthermore, who would not say our characters are alike? For neither of us knows how to feign or hide. Deceivers and pretenders deceive us both alike. But let them deceive us as they wish, again and again; only let them, being false themselves, not eventually make us false as well by changing our character. Fare happily in your integrity and simplicity, even if you are perhaps destined to live in an ungrateful life. August 20, 1491.

->Thanksgiving.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Martin Uranius Prenninger <note>A German jurist and scholar who was one of Ficino's most devoted correspondents in the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, his unique friend: Sends many greetings.

<margin>i</margin> Your Johannes Streller—or rather, by now, our Johannes—read to me today part of your letter to him, which was full of most ardent love toward us. In it, you also indicated that you celebrated our birthday with a gathering of learned men and with magnificent expense. I, therefore, cannot satisfy such great piety toward us unless I love you entirely as much as I love myself. Of my incomparable love toward you, my sweetest Martin, the witnesses will be not only our letters but also certain books to be published by us in the future. Live happily, therefore, my Martin; you are always no less dear to me than my own life. <margin>b</margin> I am sending to you the remainder of our commentary on the *Philebus* <note>One of Plato's dialogues, which Ficino interpreted as being about the "Highest Good."</note>: four quinternions <note>Gatherings of five folded sheets, making 20 pages.</note>. The printing of the books of Plotinus <note>The great Neoplatonist philosopher; Ficino's translation and commentary on Plotinus was a massive undertaking.</note> will be finished (as I believe) this coming March, at the magnificent expense of Lorenzo de' Medici and in royal format. Lorenzo has also decided that our books of Plato are soon to be printed with the same dignity. I will take care, to the best of my ability, that the second edition is more corrected than the first. Furthermore, I will distinguish the individual books into many chapters and small headings. And I will clarify them with very certain titles, as if they were formulas. <margin>i</margin> The books of Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, whose Christian Neoplatonism Ficino was translating.</note>, begun by us long ago, will be finished somewhat later because of such occupations. Farewell. November 24, 1491. Florence.

### On the book *On Life* <term>De vita</term> given as a gift.

### Marsilio Ficino to Mazingus, distinguished physician, his inseparable friend: Sends many greetings.

<margin>f</margin> Greetings, healer of our health (under God's guidance), my friend who is altogether inseparable. First, perhaps you will wonder why I have called you an "inseparable" friend rather than something else. It is clearly because those whom heaven has joined, earth will by no means separate. For in what way can the lowest earth of the world separate our souls through distance of place, when the highest of the planets <note>Saturn, which in Renaissance astrology was associated with deep thought and long-lasting bonds.</note> has joined them in his own dwellings with love? A love, I say, as durable as Saturn himself is stable. Let this book *On Life* <note>original: "vita isthæc." Referring to Ficino's famous medical and astrological work *De vita libri tres* (Three Books on Life).</note> in your possession be a pledge of such firm benevolence. And not without merit do I commit this life to you for approval and for the heavens to see—you, to whom I have long since committed this life of mine and my living for care.

# BOOK ELEVENTH

### Philosophical minds arrive at Christ through Plato, as happened to Aurelius Augustine. <note>St. Augustine (354–430 AD) famously wrote in his *Confessions* that the books of the Platonists helped clear the intellectual path for his conversion to Christianity.</note>

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, his fellow philosopher. Sends Greetings.<-

<margin>f</margin> You write to me, my best of friends—and this is most pleasing to me of all things—that you daily persuade many, and have already persuaded some, to abandon Epicurean impiety <note>Epicureanism was often equated with the belief that the soul is mortal and that pleasure is the highest good.</note> or set aside certain Averroistic opinions <note>Averroism, based on the work of the Muslim philosopher Ibn Rushd, was often criticized by the Church for teaching that there is only one collective human intellect, which seemed to deny individual immortality.</note> in order to follow the pious sentiment of our Plato regarding the soul and God. Through this path, as if by a middle way, they may finally attain Christian piety. 

Hail, therefore, you true fisher of men! For those who persuade common minds seem in reality to be catching mere fish, or rather, little fish; but those who catch the exceptional ones are judged to be "fishers of men." Perhaps the Gospel calls these the "great fish." To ensure the net does not tear while catching them, our net, Mirandola, is now Platonic reason. This net, if it is drawn correctly under the guidance of Christian <note>original: "χpiana", a scribal abbreviation using the Greek letter Chi-Rho for Christ.</note> truth, does not break, but remains whole even as it is filled. You have read that in former times, almost no philosophers except the Platonists accepted the Christian religion. Deservedly, then, you use Platonic matters (so to speak) to fish for the highest minds for Christ. Would that there were at least three such fishers for our religion, so that no great fish would remain lost in the deep sea. But alas, how wretched or rather unfortunate we are: "The harvest is indeed great, but the laborers are few." <note>A reference to Matthew 9:37.</note> Therefore, the fewer we are, my Mirandola, the more frequently and vehemently we must labor. Farewell.

->A Recommendation.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Soderini, Bishop of Volterra. Sends Greetings.<-

<margin>m</margin> Martin Uranius <note>Martin Prenninger, a German scholar and one of Ficino's most devoted disciples in the North.</note> has come from Germany to Rome to carry out the mandates of his prince to the best of his ability; he will succeed, I hope, if you provide your counsel and assistance. I desire this to be granted so vehemently that there is nothing I seek more ardently now. His own wonderful virtue will recommend him to you once you know him. Until then, let him be recommended by our great affection for him. Indeed, he is so dear to me that I cannot express it any other way than to say: he is my "other self" <note>original: "alter ego"</note>. Since I have never recommended any of my friends to you in vain—such is your incredible humanity and kindness—I hope now, or rather I know for certain, that Martin (or should I say, Marsilio) will be successfully recommended to you. April 1, 1492.

->A Recommendation.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to his dear Filippo Valori. Sends many greetings.<-

<margin>m</margin> You remember, my Valori, how ardently our Martin Uranius loves us, so much so that he even named his son Marsilio after me and established that my birthday should be celebrated. I do not doubt, therefore, that you love him vehemently in return. 
<margin>ri.</margin> He will greet you, reveal his plans, and ask for your help. If you remember how often I am accustomed to say of Martin that he is my "other self," I do not doubt that you will find him wonderfully recommended in all things. I have written almost these same words to our venerable Soderini. To him, therefore, recommend Marsilio—who is, as you know, my twin—with redoubled prayers.

Having just discussed the path to Christian piety through Platonic philosophy with Pico della Mirandola, Ficino now turns to personal matters of patronage and the cosmic significance of the death of his great patron, Lorenzo de' Medici, who died on April 8, 1492.</meta>

# BOOK XI

<margin>c</margin> Since doctors consider the fourth degree of medicine to be the highest, and you are indeed the fourth patron to me from the noble "Doctor" family <note>A wordplay on the name "Medici," which means "doctors" or "physicians." Ficino is counting his sequence of patrons within or associated with the Medici family, starting from Cosimo the Elder.</note> since the time of Cosimo, you are undoubtedly the greatest. I see this clearly from this fact: you do not give me things belonging to others, but your own. For a long time now, you have honored me with your canonry <note>A "canonry" is a prestigious administrative position within a cathedral; here, it refers to a post in the Florence Cathedral.</note>; and now, by the gift of the Church of St. Mars <note>original: "Aede martiana." Ficino often associated his name, Marsilio, with the god and planet Mars, viewing this church as a fitting gift for his namesake.</note> granted to you, you have suddenly bestowed it upon me. Therefore, on account of the death of our magnanimous Lorenzo, I am not permitted to bewail my own fortune, since I see myself so greatly commended to such a patron; nor perhaps is it right to pity his fate. We know from many evident arguments that he has been translated to the heavens. 

You have read, I believe, in Hesiod, that thirty thousand beneficial spirits <note>original: "demonum." In the Platonic tradition, these "daemons" are not evil, but intermediary spirits that guard and guide humanity.</note> watch over human affairs throughout the high air. The ancient rulers called them the "observers" of men. Furthermore, it is said that the most excellent princes among men, after their death, migrate to join such rulers, acting as their future colleagues in the governance of human affairs. The Platonists believe that happy souls, flying thither, are congratulated by those spirits. They believe these congratulations provide signs and admirable wonders to men: thunder, lightning, flames, the ruins of structures <note>This refers to the "prodigies" reported in Florence at Lorenzo's death, most notably when lightning struck the lantern of the Cathedral (the Duomo), causing heavy marble stones to fall toward the Medici palace.</note>, oracles, and dreams. These prodigies seem to signify partly the majesty of the migrating soul, partly the loss to the world, and partly the succession of the ancient power to the heirs. They assert without controversy that this happened at the deaths of Romulus and Caesar. And now, at the death of Lorenzo the Magnificent—who was almost a divine figure for Florence—it was manifest to nearly the entire population. Live happily, therefore, my greatest patron, content with the divine will, rejoicing in your father's happiness, and trusting in divine aid. 
April 25, 1492. In the fields of Careggi.

## The Giving of Thanks

Marsilio Ficino to the Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Francesco Soderini, Bishop of Volterra. Many Greetings.

<margin>g</margin> Grammarians indeed have nothing beyond the superlative degree. But orators and poets add something to it. Perhaps that line of Virgil’s points to this: *O three and four times blessed* <note>original: "O ter quaterque beati." From Virgil's *Aeneid*, expressing a state of joy beyond the "most" blessed.</note>. Those who are "three times blessed" are most blessed; but those "four times" are more than most blessed. Thus far, I have clearly perceived myself to be most dear to you, and I never thought I could be dearer. But now I see that I am, without doubt, "more than most dear." For you strip your own closest friends to clothe me. Therefore, I now give you the greatest thanks, just as I have been accustomed to give you great thanks for your many past favors to me. And I confess that I am most devoted to you. Indeed, I owe no small debt to that member of your household who, at your request, I hear has granted our wish with a willing heart. 
April 25, 1492. In the fields of Careggi.

## The causes of the prodigies occurring at the death of a prince.

Marsilio Ficino to Filippo Valori, the Florentine ambassador to the Pope. Greetings.

--- Page 445 ---
<meta>This page continues the correspondence of Marsilio Ficino in Book XI, following the death of Lorenzo de' Medici in April 1492. Having previously touched upon the transition of Lorenzo's soul, Ficino now provides a philosophical and "Platonic" explanation for the supernatural omens that allegedly accompanied the statesman's passing.</meta>

# BOOK ELEVENTH CCXXI

<margin>c</margin> As I consider the causes of the **prodigies** <note>original: "prodigiorum." In the Renaissance, "prodigies" were extraordinary natural events like comets or lightning strikes viewed as divine omens.</note> occurring at the death of excellent men, especially princes, it first comes to mind that these things happen neither by chance—for they follow an orderly pattern—nor by natural processes alone. For these events are diverse among themselves, so they cannot be traced back to a single natural influence following a set path. Indeed, they contain mysteries far superior to nature. Next, it occurs to me that if portents of this kind proceed neither from chance nor nature, they undoubtedly proceed from a certain divinity: that is, from a sublime intelligence that surpasses the forces of nature.

But let us not reduce even the smallest things to the "Primary Mind" <note>A reference to God or the First Cause in Neoplatonic thought.</note> without an intermediate order. These events seem (to speak in the Platonic manner) to be referred to three powers in particular. First, there is the **personal spirit** <note>original: "persona genius." Ficino is bridging the gap between the Classical "daemon" and the Christian "guardian angel."</note>: the familiar spirit of a man, whom our theologians call the **guardian angel**. Second, there is the **spirit of the place**: the guardian of the house, the city, or the kingdom, which they call a **Principality** <note>In the traditional celestial hierarchy, "Principalities" are an order of angels tasked with overseeing nations or large groups.</note>. Furthermore, there is a sublime order and choir of deities, spirits, or angels, into whose number and lot an excellent soul is about to migrate because of its similarity in duty; just as it is about to travel to its own star, it will be a future colleague in that same office.

Therefore, just as there are three authors of prodigies, three types of portents are seen. That **sublime choir** kindles comets <note>original: "crinitas," literally "hairy stars."</note>, stirs the thunder, hurls lightning, and sends flames and falling stars. The **divinity presiding over the province** shakes and destroys structures, pours forth oracles, moves the auguries and omens, and signals through the swelling of the tides. The **familiar guardian**, however, rouses dreams and all sorts of signs, such as the barking of dogs—as if driving away evil spirits from that place.

Furthermore, you seem to me to desire to know the purpose for which these things happen. First, those celestial signs signify that the most excellent souls are not extinguished nor neglected, but after death, they reign with the powers above. Second, they announce the calamity of a people deprived of such a great man, and they warn them to watch for imminent dangers. Third, they both admonish the dying man and indicate to his kin a celestial favor: that although he is dying, he does not truly die, but will watch over his family after his passing. Some **Platonists** add that between these sublime, eternal spirits and short-lived humans, there are certain middle spirits who live for a very long time; they say that more powerful men are commended to the more powerful among these spirits. When one of those spirits dies after many centuries, the great prince commended to it immediately falls ill and departs this life. Then the air is disturbed, and new and marvelous things happen, since the aerial bodies of the great spirits are dissolved, and their friend-spirits take the fate of both the great spirit and the prince poorly. 

Farewell. April 25, 1492.

## On the solitary life: and how much fame should be valued.
### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. Greetings.

<margin>1</margin> Do you ever hope to stay hidden, my Mirandola? Small and obscure things can easily remain hidden; but great and famous things cannot. Indeed, in order to live well, you strive to always "hide well" <note>A reference to the Epicurean maxim "lathe biōsas" or "live unnoticed," which Ficino and Pico often debated.</note>. But meanwhile, the more you become admirable to the people, the more well-known you become. Hence, whatever you attempt, various rumors are immediately stirred up. What then? Will you always look around at the common crowd and look far ahead to see what they might gossip about? Will you be a slave? Or rather [will you be] your own...

### Praises of a friend, namely Bindaccio Ricasoli.

Marsilio Ficino to Filippo Valori, Florentine Ambassador, greetings.
<margin>d</margin>The long illness of Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" died on April 8, 1492.</note>, together with the harshness of the times (as I believe), was the reason I too became seriously ill. But after a long infirmity, I have now recovered quite well, God surely breathing life into me. No one, however, lightened the weariness of my long languor more than our close friend Bindaccio Ricasoli <note>Bindaccio Ricasoli (1448–1521) was a Florentine nobleman and a loyal supporter of the Medici circle.</note>, a man certainly of the most noble nature, most proven virtue, and most diligent in service. Martin Uranius <note>Martin Prenninger (c. 1450–1501), known by the Greek name Uranius, was a German humanist who served as a key intermediary between Ficino and German scholars.</note>, my "other self," having returned to us, told me today how kindly and magnificently you received him. You acted indeed as you are accustomed to do, and you could have done nothing more pleasing to me at this time. June 26, 1492.

### Praises of a legitimate prince.

Marsilio Ficino to Eberhard, Duke of Württemberg <note>original: "Vitebergensi." Eberhard I (1445–1496) was the first Duke of Württemberg and founder of the University of Tübingen.</note> and Lord of Montbéliard <note>original: "montis Peligardi."</note>, greetings.
<margin>m</margin>For a long time now, we have heard from many about the singular excellence of your virtues. We recently received even more from our friend Martin Uranius, a most wealthy witness and guarantor of faith to us, and a most trustworthy herald of your praises among all. Wherefore the immense splendor of your admirable virtues, shining toward us like stars, already ignites an incredible passion in us to love, honor, and above all, revere you. Indeed, I have long desired what our master Plato used to say he wished for: to know a prince in whom, as in Pallas <note>The goddess Athena, representing the union of wisdom and power.</note>, wisdom conspired equally with power. And also, that in him magnanimity should join with clemency, as in Caesar; and gravity should run alongside courtesy, as in Scipio. A prince in whom, furthermore, the justice of Minos <note>A legendary wise king and judge of the underworld.</note> and the religion of Numa <note>Numa Pompilius, the second king of Rome, credited with establishing its sacred laws.</note> would flourish, and under whom that peace of Octavian <note>The Emperor Augustus, whose reign was characterized by the "Pax Romana."</note> would return. One who, finally, would prefer the studies of peace to the business of war, would found temples, and establish public academies <note>original: "Gymnasia," referring to centers of humanist learning or universities.</note> for literature. One whom his subjects might not so much fear as love, observe, and admire. Such is the idea of a legitimate prince, once hoped for by Plato and desired by us above all. And (as constant report now maintains) it is so great in you especially that it is no wonder if I and all my fellow academics are already inflamed by so many rays of your virtues...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s correspondence from Book XI. The first paragraph concludes a letter to Filippo Valori praising Bindaccio Ricasoli. Ficino then writes directly to Bindaccio, warning him against the dangers of predictive astrology—a common theme in Ficino's later years as he sought to distance himself from accusations of magic while maintaining his belief in a divinely ordered cosmos. The page ends with the start of a letter to the German humanist Martin Prenninger (Uranius).</meta>

...honors: to cultivate you like a celestial deity above other princes and to venerate you. But besides this, we are compelled by an incredible love to beseech you (so that you too may love us) as we love you singularly: and that from now on you will always remember (as you already do) that just as all light hangs from above, so the splendor of your virtues depends on God Himself, the Father of lights; so that He, the highest author of all goods, may confirm your integrity together with your happiness for the future, and increase what has been confirmed by His disposition and daily heavenly care, whose sight you consider; may you follow through. 

I certainly approve, my dearest Bindaccio. Yet, if ever you should approach that Astrology by which they promise too certain judgments of future things in vain: I shall not approve of that at all. <note>Ficino distinguishes here between "natural astrology"—studying the heavens as a map of divine order—and "judicial astrology," which attempts to predict specific human fortunes, which he viewed as a dangerous distraction from the present and from God's will.</note> For whom I hold as my most familiar friend, I also desire to be most happy. But we have found that all who gape too curiously at predicting the future are or become the most unfortunate of all. We think the causes of this adversity are either manifest or hidden. The manifest causes are certainly these: that by an infinite and first uncertain study of future things, they are always compelled to neglect all their own affairs. For the most part, either trusting in promised fates or terrified by imminent threats, they do nothing in the meantime concerning their own necessary affairs, hanging entirely from fate. 

But I think the causes of this matter are hidden: because Divine Providence—whom Nature, Fate, and Fortune serve—does not give everything to everyone, but justly dispenses to each their own. Therefore, to those to whom it has granted the future (and these being willing), it rightly denies the present. For since the present, if you compare it with the future, is very little and very small; if you lack such things, provided you possess the future (which is most numerous and greatest), you ought not to complain to Providence about your lot. Perhaps Fortune, which seems at least in this opposed to Fate (since Fate asserts a necessary order of things, while Fortune refuses such an order), is rendered hostile and adverse to the diviners of the future as if they were speakers and assertors of Fate. 

Perhaps also those who boldly anticipate coming things, which the heavenly Father has placed in His own power, insolently usurp for themselves what belongs to God Himself. Enraged at these, Jupiter strikes them down with lightning like those Giants <note>A reference to the Gigantomachy, the mythological battle where the Giants tried to overthrow the Olympian gods and were struck down for their hubris.</note> too highly elated by pride. I will set aside for now the Astrological reasons that occur to me. Namely, that searchers of hidden things far distant from the present immediately fall into [the influence of] Saturn, who holds all the most hidden and remote things. And since Jupiter has granted the present goods of fortune, [one should be] content with future and most secret things. Therefore (to conclude everything briefly), my dearest Bindaccio: since we fall far short regarding the present alone, let us not suffice also for the future; we must always keep in mind with a remembering spirit what Paul of divine wisdom commanded: *Do not seek to know more than what it is appropriate to know, but be wise unto sobriety.* <note>original: "Nolite sapere plus quam oportet sapere. Sed sapere ad sobrietatem." From Romans 12:3.</note> Farewell.

->Opinions should not be rashly spread abroad. Likewise the songs of Orpheus.<-

For as much as it was formerly a concern to the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, known for keeping their philosophical and mathematical discoveries secret from the uninitiated.</note> not to publish divine things to the common people, so much has it always been my concern not to divulge profane things; so much so that I even spared <note>original: "pepercerim" — here meaning he spared the public from them by destroying them.</note> my little commentaries on Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and Epicurean philosopher whose work *De rerum natura* was controversial for its denial of divine intervention in human affairs.</note> which I wrote (I know not how) while still a boy. For a more mature age and a more exquisite examination (as Plato says) often condemns those things which youthful lightness either rashly believed, or at least did not know how to reject (as was fitting). Indeed, it is more dangerous (as Plato also says) to imbibe harmful opinions than to spread the worst poison. For just as the good is more divine the more widely it is spread, so the widest evil is the most pestilential. But I promised to send you certain safer songs of Orpheus. Behold, I send them.

They establish the statue of a man for him because he is the Mind which produces all things by seminal reason <note>original: "seminali ratione"; a Stoic and Neoplatonic concept referring to the generative principles or "seeds" of all things contained within the divine mind</note>. ->He exhorts his friends to favor Plotinus as he goes forth into the world.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved Filippo Carducci. Greetings.<-

<margin>5</margin> Greetings, my dear Carducci, most diligent cultivator of the Academy. See how true that proverb is: "there is a change in all things" <note>original: "omnium rerum vicissitudo est"; a common Latin proverb about the cyclical nature of life</note>. Our divine Plato once gave birth to the great Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism, who saw himself as a successor to Plato</note>. Now Plotinus is in labor with Plato, soon to give birth. Plato gave light to Plotinus; Plotinus will return the light to Plato, when he himself first comes forth into the light. Indeed, he has already been produced by us, but for some reason, he still lingers at the threshold. Arise, come now, Carducci, most ardent of all our circle! Push forward the lingering Plotinus, and exhort all our friends and others to grasp him eagerly with their hands, so that as he steps immediately into the light, he may in turn return the light to all who look upon him. July 12, 1492.

->Regarding the book *On Life* sent to a friend.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved Joannes Cenacius and Bindacio Ricasolani. Hearty greetings.<-

Those among my close associates who possess my mind—and you, certainly the most intimate of all, possess it entirely—are well aware of the purpose I had, and the hope and confidence I relied upon, when I wrote the books *On Life* <note>original: "De Vita"; Ficino's famous three-volume work combining medicine, astrology, and Neoplatonic philosophy</note>. I wrote them to benefit all ingenious men, but among them, even more so my friends, and most especially those citizens who are primarily necessary for the health of our fatherland. Indeed, I did not doubt that I would benefit as many as possible—nay, everyone—if I preserved those who are especially the guardians of the public health. It has been my task thus far to compose those books with this intention and diligence. It is your task, henceforth, to give your constant effort so that my expectation does not perhaps deceive me and I have labored too much in vain. Therefore, as often as you greet our friend Paolo Antonio Soderini <note>A prominent Florentine diplomat and supporter of Ficino</note>—a man most worthy of both frequent greeting and perpetual health—remember to remind him, above all others, to reread and observe the books *On Life*. For we desire for him, above all, a long life and perpetual health. Truly, since he is both most ingenious and most friendly, and since he is no small part of nature, and certainly a very great [patron] to our great physician patrons...

### Catalogue of friends and auditors.
### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Martin Uranius, his unique friend. Greetings.

You could have asked nothing more just of me than what you have already often requested through your kinsman Johann Streler: namely, a catalogue of our friends. I do not mean those who come together through any casual business or shared lodging, but only those who meet in the actual communion of the liberal disciplines <note>original: "liberalium disciplinarum," referring to the classical arts like rhetoric, philosophy, and astronomy</note>. Since I neither ought to be, nor wish to be, anywhere without the presence of my friends—and since I am not only in Italy within myself, but also in you in Germany—I rightly desire my friends here to be present with me there as well. 

Know indeed that they are all proven in character and talent. For I have decided never to have any friends except those whom I judge to have joined letters with honesty of morals, just as if Mercury were joined with Jupiter <note>Mercury represents eloquence and learning, while Jupiter represents wisdom and moral authority</note>. For our Plato says in his letters that the true philosophy is integrity of life; however, he calls letters the external ornament of philosophy. The same author says in his letters that a philosophical communion exists as something more excellent and stable than all other types, not only in benevolence but also in necessity. 

But to come soon to the catalogue: take all these friends, in short, as being thus praised. Yet if I wished to narrate the specific praises of each one individually, I would be undertaking a task far too long. If I should pass over some as not equally praised, it would be utterly invidious. Indeed, it would be altogether absurd if, while I attempt to arrange my friends in order, I should disturb everything with comparisons, ultimately bringing back hatred instead of benevolence. 

By the best right, our patrons, the Medici, claim for themselves the first and highest place among our friends. **Cosimo the Elder**; his two excellent sons, **Piero** and **Giovanni**. The two sons of Piero: **Lorenzo the Magnificent** and the renowned **Giuliano**. The three children of Lorenzo: the magnanimous **Piero**, **Giovanni** (first to be revered as a Cardinal), and **Giuliano**, endowed with an extraordinary nature. And lest I pursue the praises of each at length, I shall embrace all the Medici in one common praise: they are a heroic race. 

Besides our patrons, we have two classes of friends. Some are not exactly "auditors" <note>students who "hear" a master's lectures</note>, nor entirely disciples, but (if I may speak thus) familiar companions in daily life, conversationalists, and mutual communicators of counsel and the liberal disciplines. Others, however, besides what I have said, have listened to us while we were reading or sometimes teaching. And even if these are in some sense disciples, they are not truly...

### Preface to the Compendium of Proclus.

### Marsilio Ficino to Martin Uranius, his unique friend. Greetings.

<margin>p</margin>After your departure from Italy, many books were soon brought from Greece to the magnanimous Piero de' Medici. <note>Piero "the Unfortunate" (1472–1503), who succeeded his father Lorenzo the Magnificent in 1492.</note> These were selected from very many by the collector Lascaris, <note>Janus Lascaris (c. 1445–1535), a Greek scholar who searched for manuscripts for the Medici library.</note> a very elegant Greek, for that royal library established some time ago by the great Lorenzo with such success. Among the many works, I, as is my custom, have always read the Platonic ones first. Among these, the first were the commentaries of Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD), one of the last major Greek philosophers and a head of the Neoplatonic Academy in Athens.</note> on the six books of Plato’s *Republic* and the beginning of the seventh. Therefore, those little flowers which I have gathered here and there by running through these most pleasant meadows—which, above all others, smell of holy religion—I send to you, a man distinguished for your piety.
August 3, 1492.
