| Goodness. | Immutability. | Truth. |
| Goodness. | Power.      | Knowledge. |

<margin>Plato</margin>
Plato, in the *Laws*, defines the very nature of God through three properties: namely, through **goodness**, **power**, and **knowledge**. He also defines it through three similar properties in the *Republic*: namely, through **goodness**, **immortality**, and **truth**. Indeed, immutability is the property of power, while truth is the perfection of knowledge. Moreover, every god is said to be truly good. This is both because no evil is mixed with his good, and because goodness in him is not some attribute <note>original: "habitus"</note> added to his essence, but is his very essence itself. For God does not exist first and then later become good; rather, by his very essence, he is formally both God and Good in equal measure. Thus, every god is said to be good in his own nature, just as the first God is good in himself. Proclus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 412–485 AD) whose "Elements of Theology" heavily influenced Ficino.</note> proves the same in his *Elements of Theology*: that every god is formally a certain essential goodness, just as the first is Goodness itself above all essence. Likewise, he proves that these three things pertain formally to the deity itself: **pure goodness**, **unhindered power**, and **certain knowledge** that is never in doubt.

->God is the cause of no evil: he never changes forms: he deceives no one.<-

<margin>Plato</margin>
Plato, in the *Republic*, sets down three theological dogmas. First: if every god is by his own nature truly good, he is always the cause of good things, but never the cause of any evil. Second: if he is truly powerful, he is entirely immutable <note>unchanging</note>. Third: if immutable power, truth, and goodness all belong to God, he never deceives anyone with any fictions or lies. Regarding the first, it is doubted: from where do evils come, if God does nothing toward evil? Regarding the second: if God is not changed in any way, how do the gods appear of their own accord—sometimes in a specific form and sometimes not? For unless we admit these appearances, we would utterly destroy the entire discipline of sacred rites and the works of the priests, as well as the very visions in which the gods offer themselves of their own accord in various forms. Regarding the third: how is it that oracles sometimes give false responses? For indeed, many lies are discovered in oracles.

The response to the first is: Evil does not have its own process among existing things, neither from God nor from any other primary cause. Nor indeed is it possible to posit an "Idea" <note>the Platonic Form or perfect template</note> of evils, or to say that matter is the cause of evils. For all Ideas are, as it were, certain intellectual and divine species, and they exist as the patterns for both essences and the perfections belonging to essence. Matter, however, was produced by God as something necessary for the world; it is not malicious, especially since it contributes to the generation of the universe. Nor is it "the Good," since it is the lowest of all things, but it holds its place among necessary things. For whatever exists for the sake of something else is of such a kind. Therefore, it is forbidden to posit any specific or material cause of evils. Nor is there one single cause for them. But as he himself says: it must be said that things which are particular and dispersed bring about evil. They are "particular" because none of the universal things—such as the Intellect, the Soul, or the Body—is the cause of evils. They are "dispersed" because...

<sig>f</sig>

<summary>This page explores Platonic theology, defining God through the triad of Goodness, Power, and Knowledge. It addresses the "problem of evil," arguing that since God is perfectly good and immutable, he cannot be the cause of evil, deception, or change.</summary>

<meta>The previous page was identified as Book Twelve, while this page begins Book Ten. # BOOK TEN

There is one certain cause of evils; but (as he himself says) other occasions for evils must be sought. In the body, indeed, evil—that is, in its habits <note>The Latin 'moribus' here refers to the physical constitution or "disposition" of the body rather than moral behavior.</note>—occurs because of certain diverse elements flowing together without mutual proportion between them. While each element strives to overcome the others, evil also occurs in the soul because of the different and contrary species of life fighting amongst themselves. When these fight, evil happens from some to others, with each one doing what is its own.

It was necessary, moreover, for the body to be such—namely, made from contrary and repugnant things—so that there might also be something perishable <term>caducum: things that are subject to decay or falling away from perfection</term> in the world. And thus the world is perfect, being constituted, clearly, out of all things. It was also necessary for souls to have a mixture here, so that these regions of the world would not be devoid of rational beings. Nor should rational lives be planted in bodies without a medium, but they should act and suffer according to the conditions of rational beings, and desire, feel, and imagine such things. For this is necessary for mortals, if they are to remain in these regions for even a brief time. 

Therefore, while any things do what is their own, evils happen incidentally. Nor is it for any other reason except for the sake of the good. The universe uses these contingencies appropriately; and these turn into good through the very power of those who use them. Therefore, there is no "pure evil" anywhere, but it is in some way a participant in the good. And thus evil can even be said to depend on the divine in a certain way, as being in some way good. But meanwhile, from many other particular agents, it happens to fall upon this as something external <term>adventicium: something coming from the outside, not essential to the thing's nature</term>, occurring in many things and in diverse ways. 

Next, we shall respond thus to the doubt concerning apparitions. While the higher beings remain immutable and neither admit nor lose anything, certain divine visions leap forth from there, which take up their generation in the place surrounding us. For since the spectators seem to see them with bodies—while the gods are truly incorporeal—the spectacles emanating from the divine, clearly before those worthy of the sight, have something from the higher beings who produce them, but also something in some way related to the spectators. Therefore they appear; yet not to everyone. And those to whom they appear see only certain shining coverings <note>original: "involucra," likely referring to the "astral body" or vehicle of the soul in Neoplatonic thought</note> of souls. And for this reason, they are frequently seen with closed eyes. 

Insofar, therefore, as they are extended and appear in something else of this kind—that is, in the Air—they become related to the spectators. But insofar as they are filled with divine light and have efficacy, and represent the powers of the gods by an image—through those very clear symbols (that is, signs)—they depend continually, as if suspended, from the divine powers <term>numinibus: the presiding divine wills or spirits</term> producing them. Therefore, even their ineffable sacraments and mysteries are figured through such things, while they offer various forms to those who gaze upon them. The sacred oracles <note>original: "eloquia sacra," likely referring to the Chaldean Oracles, a text highly revered by Ficino</note> bear witness to this, addressing the priest thus: "All divine things are indeed incorporeal. But bodies have been applied to them for your sake. Since you are unable to perceive incorporeal things in an incorporeal way, because of this corporeal nature in which you all exist." This much is said there. These things, therefore, both appear and disappear according to the will of the gods; but they themselves remain hidden, remaining meanwhile as they are by nature, nor do they show anything through these...

# ELEVENTH [BOOK] CCXXVI

...receiving these things, nor losing them. Just as those intellectual species—that is, the **Ideas**—do not become bodily, nor composite, nor formed, even while through them such things are produced; they are, clearly, not at all like the things they create. Thus every god remains unchanged; he is not "formed," even though he may offer himself to be seen in a form. For no such form exists within the god himself, but rather it proceeds from him. This happens because the observer is unable to behold that which is formless without using a form; instead, according to their own capacity, they perceive the unformed under a form.

To the third doubt, we respond in this way: Falsehood is not found in the higher beings who respond, but in those who receive the responses, who, because of their own weakness, receive the oracle perversely. And this very deception does not happen without the will of the divine powers, who wish only the worthy to obtain their desire. There are also some for whom it is not appropriate to know the pure truth that remains with the gods, but who instead must suffer what is appropriate through a deception occurring on their own part. Therefore, the gods are neither ignorant of the truth, nor do they confuse it. Rather, because confusion happens among us due to our own unfitness, it is for our own utility—as the history of oracles itself now testifies. Because of the place, the time, the manner, or some other error of the questioner, a falsehood may occur in the responses.

When **Plato** says in the *Republic* <note>Original: *in repub.* refers to Plato's *Republic* (Book II, 382e), where he argues that the divine is free from all falsehood.</note> that not only every divine being, but also every **demon**, is always truthful and never lies, this must be understood as referring to the *true* and *natural* demon, not to a demonic spirit named so by a certain habit or disposition. The latter undergoes many changes and seduces those to whom it has become a friend. But that which is a demon according to its essence, since it is also rational, is entirely truthful. The irrational kind, however, is itself incapable of truth; it is deceived and deceives as if it were falsehood itself, and is considered a deceitful race. History records that it often deceives, whether it enters into oracles, listens to invocations, or approaches people of its own accord. All of this is not from the nature of demons, but from their disposition.

All religion, the works of priests, history, and common human report agree on this: the gods appear to the senses and offer many forms and various figures. Sometimes they project a light that is unformed, sometimes a formed light; sometimes they appear in a human figure, and sometimes in another. Meanwhile, the divinity remains everywhere unmoved. For the very simplicity of the gods appears manifold to those who look upon them. This is not through any change or deception on the part of the god, but because of the condition of our nature, which defines the properties of the gods according to the modes of those participating in them. 

For although the god who is participated in is himself one and simple, the **intellect** participates in him in one way, and the **intellectual soul** in another. Likewise, the **imagination** perceives him differently than the **senses** do. For the intellect perceives him indivisibly; the intellectual soul, discursively <note>Original: *revolubiliter*, describing how the soul thinks through things step-by-step or in "revolutions," unlike the instant grasp of the higher intellect.</note>; the imagination, through forms; and the sense, passively. That which is participated in is uniform in its substance, but through participation it becomes multiform; it is immutable, but it appears mutable because of our weakness. And although it is in no way heavy, when it fills a person, it seems to weigh them down. Just as the poets record concerning **Pallas** <note>A name for the goddess Athena. This refers to a scene in Homer's *Iliad* where her divine presence causes a chariot to groan and its axle to bend under her "weight."</note>. For that which is received must be (so to speak) such as the receiver is.

# BOOK [XI]

...to appear. Therefore, when some of the gods meet us as if they were guests or in some other way, one must not think that this apparent change exists within them; rather, a varied imagination results from the differing nature of the recipients <note>Original Latin: *indifferentibus susceptaculis*. The "recipients" here are the human minds or souls receiving the divine vision.</note>. And this is the first mode: the way poetry introduces gods who are immutable in themselves, yet seem mutable to us.

There is also a second mode: when the divine itself—which contains many powers within and is full of every kind of form <note>Latin: *specierum*, often translated as "species" or "Ideas" in a Platonic sense.</note>—presents various intelligible sights to those contemplating it. For they say that the divine, containing these powers within itself, transforms that demonstrated variety of powers into various forms. Bringing forth now one form, now another, it is always active according to all its powers; however, it appears as something different to the transitory intelligences of souls because of the multitude of forms it contains within itself. It is in this manner that **Proteus** <note>A sea-god in Greek mythology known for his ability to change shape.</note> is said to change his own form for those watching, appearing as one thing after another.

Therefore, **Proteus**—who is a certain divine intellect full of all powers and forms, and is counted under the order of **Neptune**—is constantly contemplated by particular souls who are called "seals" <note>Original: *phoce*. In the *Odyssey*, Proteus tends to Neptune’s seals. Here, the author treats the seals as an allegory for lower souls following a higher intellect.</note> because they belong to that same order. These souls perceive now some forms, now others; by applying the progression of their own thoughts to **Proteus**, they suspect a change of form within **Proteus** himself. Thus, he seems to become all things to those looking at him—whether they inhabit the earth, the water, the air, or the fire. For as many forms as he contains—or rather, as many forms as he eternally *is*—he seems to become just as many things alternately, because the perception of those watching is constantly alternating.

The third mode of varied appearance occurs when the different visions of a single god do not arise from the perceptions of the subjects, nor from the variety of divine powers, but when the same god proceeds according to different orders. He descends, as it were, to the lowest things, multiplying himself in number and declining into lower orders. Then, in turn, the myths say that the divine is changed into that very form toward which it made its descent from above. For this reason, they say [the gods] made themselves like: **Mercury** to the owl <note>Original: *Nycticorax*, a night-raven or owl.</note> or the garrulous gull; **Apollo**, again, to the hawk. They do this to show the more excellent orders of these gods from which they have proceeded into all things.

For this reason, when they describe divine appearances, they strive to keep them without shape or figure—as when **Pallas** [Athena] revealed herself to **Achilles** alone, and not at all to the army present there. But where they present "angelic" <note>In this Neoplatonic context, "angels" and "daemons" refer to intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily the biblical concepts.</note> appearances, they present the gods clothed in foreign forms, but universal ones. For instance, they sing of a god appearing in a certain human form common to both man and woman, rather than the form of a specific individual. But when they narrate "demonic" processions, they do not fear to describe changes into specific individuals and particulars, or even a descent into irrational beasts. For the lowest of the following orders declare the gods through figures of this kind. Now, it is worth considering how clearly such things agree with the order of reality: for the **Simple** itself befits the Divine; the **Universal** befits the Angelic; and finally, the **Particular** befits the Demonic. To the first belongs the intellectual; to the second, the rational; and to the last, a certain irrational kind...

<margin>Read.</margin> For in the very order of spirits <note>Latin: *demonum*. In this Neoplatonic context, "daemons" or spirits are intermediary beings between gods and humans, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense.</note>, such a life is also intertwined.

### Three Dispositions and States of Separated Souls: Contemplative, Active, and Voluptuous.

<margin>a</margin> The dispositions of souls are different even when they are separated from the body. Similarly, the places in the universe which they inhabit are different. It is necessary, therefore, that souls thus separated from their mortal instruments <note>The "mortal instrument" refers to the physical body.</note> should not have a habit of leaning toward worse things, nor be full of mortal disturbances and trifles. They carry with them their "envelopes" <note>Latin: *involucra*. This refers to the "astral body" or "vehicle" (*ochema*) of the soul, which was believed to be a subtle body that mediates between the immaterial soul and the physical world.</note> which were once bright and pure, as they had been before—neither disturbed by material vapors nor thickened by their earthly nature. However, for those souls not yet perfectly purified through philosophy, but instead inclined by affection toward the thick body and still desiring a life in common with it, it is necessary for those with the power to see to demonstrate that such souls also have their vehicles suspended around them. These are clearly shadowy, material, and falling back due to their weight, carrying with them much of a mortal and solidified nature—a matter which is clearly narrated in the *Phaedo* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the immortality of the soul and its state after death.</note>.

Furthermore, there are many differences among these souls that still incline themselves toward this life. For those who led a more active life <note>Latin: *vitam practicam*, the life of action or politics as opposed to the life of pure contemplation.</note> and have not yet ceased from such a life, they deservedly love the instrument suitable for active deeds. Once separated from this body, they greatly long for its commerce, feeling indignant at the loss. They prefer this life of ours to the separated life, as they are unable to act according to that higher life, being more fit for the active life.

Those, however, who because of a shameful life <note>Latin: *vitam flagitiosam*.</note> cling to the failing body and think that a life with the body differs in no way from a life led within it, it is fitting that they be carried down into the ultimate and dark place of the universe. Just as **Homer** and **Plato** do, one must distinguish the soul from its "idol" <note>Latin: *idolo*, from the Greek *eidolon*, meaning an image, phantom, or shadow-self that remains near the grave or in the underworld while the higher soul moves on.</note>, and the intellect from those things which are proper to the soul. Indeed, it is said that the soul uses the idol, but the intellect is more divine than both. And in a certain way, the idol and the soul are known even in this body, in which (and apart from which) the soul has care and providence for it, and naturally desires it; yet the intellect is not comprehended by our imaginative and shape-forming movements. Furthermore, just as the instruments of souls ascending into heaven emit a harmonic voice and display a graceful movement, so the sound of those descending beneath the earth—who are now less rational—is like a lamentation, carrying only an image of a passionate and imaginative life. Moreover, one must not think that the places of the lower world, the judicial states beneath the earth, and the rivers described by **Homer** and **Plato** are merely vain imaginations and fabulous terrors. Rather, just as many and varied places are distributed there according to merit for souls seeking to return to the heavens, so must it be thought that places are arranged beneath the earth for souls in need of punishment and purification, having various outflows from the elements surrounding the earth. These outflows they have surely called "rivers." Finally, there are different orders of spirits <note>Latin: *demonum*.</note> set over this work, some as victors, some as punishers, and some...

...purgatorial; others, however, are judicial. It is fitting that souls there are terrified by the imagination of the presiding spirits <note>Latin: *demonum*. In this Neoplatonic context, these are intermediary beings or "daemons" who oversee the order of the universe, not necessarily evil "demons" in the modern sense.</note> and by a state determined by their merits and habits—a state that is varied, confused, and cut off from the rays of the sun above.

<margin>Three lives of the soul: divine, human, and beast-like.</margin>
We can summarize the triple life of the soul in this way. The first is indeed the best and most perfect: it joins the soul with the gods. There, it leads a life most closely related to those above, and because of a supreme similarity, it is a life already unified with them. It is no longer under its own law but under that of the gods, while it submits to its own intellect; meanwhile, it awakens the ineffable gift and character <note>Latin: *characterem*. Used here to mean a distinctive spiritual mark or stamp of the divine.</note> of that uniform substance of the higher beings. It joins like to like—namely, its own light to that Light which stands above all essence and life, being most uniform with the essence and life of its own nature. We place the second degree of life where the soul descends from the divine life into itself. It establishes the mind and knowledge as the leader of action, where it unfolds a multitude of reasons, gazes upon the diverse differences of all forms, and gathers within itself both that which it understands and the act of understanding. It represents and, as if through an image, expresses the intellectual essence, grasping the intelligible nature within a certain unity. Finally, we consider the third life to be that which enters into commerce with baser powers. It acts with them and uses imaginations and senses that lack reason, and it is entirely filled with worse things.

<margin>The distinction of things into four kinds. Also concerning images and shadows.</margin>
Plato, in the seventh book of his *Republic* <note>Referring to the famous "Analogy of the Divided Line" in Plato's *Republic*, Book VII, which categorizes different levels of reality and knowledge.</note>, compares the order of things to a line, through a continuous connection of things. This connection proceeds from mutual similarity. Similarity is a certain unity in things that comes from that simple Unity itself, the principle of the universe. This Principle, wishing to make all things as similar to itself as possible—yet not simply one—made them at least as unified as possible. The goodness of the Principle itself also contributes to this union. For since it is the nature of the Good itself to diffuse itself through all things by a process of proceeding, and in turn to call all things back to itself as one through desire, the universe is rightly rendered most unified. According to Plato, the mundane line is divided into two primary parts: namely, into the insensible <note>The "intelligible" or spiritual realm, which cannot be perceived by the physical senses.</note> and the sensible genus. That first part is far larger than the second, containing the second within itself. That first part is divided again into intelligible things and "cogitable" things <note>Latin: *cogitabile*. This refers to things that can be known through the mind’s reasoning, specifically mathematical objects or logical forms.</note>—that is, into divine forms and mathematical forms. This second part, however, is divided into things that are, as it were, substantial and those that are "imaginable." The substantial things are bodies. The imaginable things are the images of bodies and shadows. Indeed, images and reflections of bodies in mirrors require a certain subject possessing three conditions: density, smoothness, and brightness. Density is needed so that the appearing reflection, if it should fall upon a subject that is too thin, does not immediately flow through it; thus, the image does not become one from many outflows. Smoothness is required so that roughness itself—on account of its parts being partly protruding and partly deep—does not cause inequality...

...is suited for the composition of an image. It also possesses a splendid brightness, so that an image which otherwise has slight forms may become conspicuous. For in this way, even the most minute compositions in the air of a house often appear to the eyes in rays of light penetrating through small windows and cracks. Otherwise, they are hidden from us because of their thin nature. We must say, therefore, according to the Platonic opinion in the *Sophist* <note>Plato’s dialogue *The Sophist* explores the nature of being and non-being, including how "images" or "likenesses" can exist.</note>, that appearing images are certain substances fashioned from some demonic <note>Latin: *demonica*. In this Neoplatonic context, "demonic" refers to the work of *daemons*—intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between the divine and the physical—rather than evil spirits.</note> machinery of likenesses. Now truly, even shadows—which he mentions alongside images as if they were related—possess a nature of this kind: for they are themselves images of bodies and figures, and they have a great sympathy—that is, a compassion and consensus—with those very things from which they fall. This is demonstrated by whatever the arts of the magi declare and promise regarding the creation of idols and shadows. But what shall I say of the powers of images and shadows through which many things occur in irrational animals that often surpass all reason? For they say that a hyena, by treading upon the shadow of a dog sitting high up, causes the dog to fall down immediately from its height so that the hyena may devour it. Furthermore, Aristotle says that a woman in the period of her menstrual blood stains a mirror and the image within it with a certain blood <note>A common misconception in ancient and medieval natural philosophy (found in Aristotle's *On Dreams*) regarding the perceived physical influence of the body on external objects.</note>. Finally, Plato confirms that images are indeed certain substances where he says: "As objects of thought are to objects of the intellect, so are objects of the imagination to visible bodies." Objects of thought—that is, Mathematics <note>Latin: *Mathematica*. To Platonists, mathematical truths were the bridge between the physical world and the purely intellectual realm of Forms.</note>—are certain things and species in themselves. Similarly, images, since they are certain natural outflows from natural things, also have their own nature.

## How the Good is above essence: And how it may be known.

Plato, in the sixth book of the *Republic*, compares divine things in this way. He compares the Sun indeed to the Good itself; the Light of the sun he compares to the Truth flowing from the Good. The colors, which depend upon the light, he compares to the formal and ideal reasons <note>Latin: *rationibus*. Here meaning the "rational principles" or blueprints of things.</note> of things, which hang from the Good under the banner of Truth. But the eyes, both generated and illuminated by the sun, he compares to intellects which relate to the Good in a similar fashion. He adds furthermore: just as the sun stands above the generation of lower visible things, so the Good stands above being and essence. Likewise, just as the sun and its light surpass colors and sight, so the Good and the truth of the Good (which is light) are above ideas, beings, and minds. Finally, just as the sun is not only the cause of action and perfection for our visible things and our eyes, but is also the author of their generation, nature, and power, so the Good is the author of all things—both of the things that can be understood and of the intellects that understand them. Therefore, the Good is higher than all these. Since, then, the Good itself is higher than the things of the intellect, the intellect itself, and truth, it cannot be known by the same logic by which intelligible things are known, but by a certain divine intuition and a perception that exceeds intelligence. This, Plato calls the "illumination of the soul." It is then, clearly, that he illuminates divinely after he has separated from the Good (by way of negation) all things that come after the Good, which he has compared quite properly in their turn. By this reasoning, the soul reflects and raises itself into the Good itself, as if having now been turned upward <note>Latin: *resupina*. Literally "lying on one's back," here meaning the soul has turned from looking down at the earth to looking up at the heavens.</note>, whereas until now it had been prone <note>Latin: *prona*. Face-down or leaning toward the material world.</note>. The Sun, among worldly things, seems unbegotten. For it loses nothing of its own, nor does it admit anything foreign in return. All other things, however, always receive new rays from it, while the Sun revolves in its own center. And so the celestial...

...illuminates around and below. The Sun, therefore, is of such a nature for this reason: it rules over all worldly things, insofar as any body or movable thing is subject to another. It is subject to the supreme body, namely the one which is said to have the "circuit of identity" <note>In Platonic cosmology, the "Circle of the Same" or "Identity" refers to the outermost sphere of the fixed stars, which moves with a perfectly uniform motion, representing the eternal and unchanging.</note> in its sphere. For from this source even the sun itself is carried. That sphere, in turn, is referred back to the wisest circuit: that is, the Mind. Among these things, just as in divisible things there is an indivisible moment like a unity or a mathematical point, so in corruptible things, there must be something incorruptible.

### The Triple Good: namely in us; in the idea; above the idea.

<margin>p</margin>Plato considers three degrees of the venerable Good. One indeed exists in all things—namely, a certain state of life properly mixed from intelligence and pleasure. Another exists among the Ideas. Finally, another exists above the Ideas. For among the Ideas, some constitute and define the <term>essences</term> <note>Original: *essentias*. In this context, the "essence" is the core "what-ness" or fundamental nature of a thing.</note> of things, while others apply their perfections to those essences. Furthermore, the first of the former group is <term>Being</term> <note>Original: *ens*. The most basic category of existence.</note> and Essence. This genus applies to all other essential ideas—that is, those which pertain to the constitution of natures, such as the "Animal-itself," "Man-himself," and "Horse-itself" <note>Original: *æquum*. This likely refers to the "Equal-itself," though in medieval and Renaissance Latin lists of Platonic forms, "Horse" (*equum*) is a very common companion to "Man" and "Animal."</note>. Regarding the Ideas pertaining to the perfections of all things: the first is not simply the Good, but the *ideal* Good. This is similarly the genus of all Ideas that relate in any way to the perfections of things, such as the "Beautiful-itself," the "Just-itself," the "Wise," and similar concepts. Therefore, just as the essences of things precede their perfections by a certain origin—for "to be" naturally precedes "to be well"—so Being and Essence in the very series of Ideas precede the "ideal Good" in that same realm. 

But the "Simple Good" itself is finally higher than Being; it is at the same time an unparticipatable Good. For the good found among the Ideas is indeed participatable <note>Original: *participabile*. A Platonic term meaning that lower things can "take part in" or reflect the qualities of the higher form.</note>, but it exists alongside essence or under Being. Finally, the good in us is below essence and is a shared, participatable good. Now truly, the common consensus of all who define the Good—as that for the sake of which all things act and which all things desire—seems to prophesy that the Good itself exists for the sake of nothing else, nor does it desire anything else at all. Therefore, it must be a certain Being <note>The author is refining the definition: the Good is the ultimate end, requiring nothing else.</note>. Nor is it merely some "good thing" within being. For every essence desires the Good—that is, to exist according to its nature, and to maintain itself well and perfectly. The good within an essence is sought for the sake of that very substance, so that it may perfectly follow its nature. Such a thing is not the "Good" simply, but only the good *of* something and *in* something. Finally, to speak briefly: that ideal Good is placed within Being and Essence itself as a part, existing for the sake of the whole. Therefore, the "Simple Good" itself stands above even that.

ELEVENTH [BOOK] 229

# Philosophy is not joined with fortune and riches.

### Marsilio Ficino to Filippo Valori, the Florentine Ambassador to the Pope, sends many greetings. <note>original: "S.D." for *salutem dicit*. Filippo Valori was a close friend of Ficino and a prominent patron who funded the printing of Ficino’s Plato translations.</note>

"A man’s enemies are those of his own household." My own "domestics"—of whom I have many and who are quite troublesome—frequently object to me because they are neither philosophical themselves, nor are they content with a philosopher's lifestyle and possessions. They point out that other <term>clients</term> <note>In the Renaissance, a *cliens* was a dependent or follower of a powerful patron; here, Ficino refers to the various hangers-on of the Medici family.</note> and minor followers of the Medici house have received a great deal within just a few years. Yet I, they say, who am the most intimate friend of this great family and (if I may say so) the most devoted client, have brought home very little after many years. 

But listen for a moment, my dear Valori, to this defense of mine to my people. Other friends of the Medici have not yet received as much as they *wished* for; I, however, have received as much as I *would* have wished, if only I had asked. And I certainly have as much as I want. They often hold things precariously <note>meaning their wealth is dependent on the continued favor or loans from the patron.</note>; I hold mine freely. Likewise, the Medici gave other people things belonging to others; to me, they gave their own. <note>Ficino likely refers to the gift of the villa at Careggi and the deep personal trust of Cosimo and Lorenzo de' Medici, which he viewed as "theirs" in a more essential way than mere political appointments or money.</note> Thus I defend our cause quite well before my household. 

But they—and this is most annoying to me—do not approve. It would have been necessary for either my people to eventually become philosophers along with me, or for me not to have been a philosopher. But it seems fated from the beginning of things: neither will philosophers ever be rich, nor will the rich easily become philosophers. For it is said that Minerva <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom.</note> has no commerce with Juno <note>The goddess of wealth, power, and marriage.</note>. Nor do Jupiter, the Sun, and Venus favor the same people as Mercury and Saturn. <note>In Renaissance astrology, Saturn and Mercury are the planets of deep thought, melancholy, and scholarship, while Jupiter and Venus bring worldly success, joy, and riches.</note> Nor does Fortune, the mistress of affairs, easily agree with Wisdom, the contemplator of things. Furthermore, one thing is necessary: wherever you focus your mind, it prevails. Therefore, the Mind and Fortune have divided rule within us. The Mind rules most over the cultivation of the soul; Fortune rules most over external things. Hence they are called "the goods of fortune." But in the body, perhaps both have equal power. But I must not philosophize any further in this letter, for another business now presses upon me.

# Where there is more fortune, there is less wisdom; and vice versa.

### Marsilio Ficino to Bindaccio Ricasoli, his excellent and most beloved citizen, sends many greetings. <note>original: "S.P.D." for *salutem plurimam dicit*. Bindaccio Ricasoli was a Florentine nobleman and a member of Ficino's Platonic Academy.</note>

That Aristotelian saying—where there is more intelligence, there is less fortune; and conversely, where there is more fortune, there is less intelligence—most people perhaps take it to mean that the wisest men and philosophers are the least fortunate. This is supported by the Pythagorean verses and confirmed by reality itself. Even astronomical reasoning suggests it, considering that philosophy is signified by Mercury and Saturn. These planets have no dealings with Jupiter, the Sun, and Venus, which signify an abundance of worldly things. 

Finally, the legitimate contemplators of truth both neglect the goods of fortune and are themselves neglected by the most "fortunate" people. They please neither princes nor the common crowd. So it is no wonder they have very little fortune. Conversely, the most fortunate people usually neglect wisdom and live mostly in a rash and improvident way, trusting, of course, in the "breath" of fortune. However, although I do not at all reject the above interpretation, I would interpret that Aristotelian saying in a more useful and divine way. For since we have it established that men, by their prudence...

Instead, all things are providently disposed. And in turn, when we see that all celestial and natural things are disposed in a certain order outside the reach of fortune, it is permitted to conclude that a supreme wisdom rules over all these things.

### Preface to the comparison of the sun to God.

Marsilio Ficino to Eberhard, the illustrious Duke of Württemberg and Count of Montbéliard, the Elder, sends many greetings. <note>original: "S.P.D." for *salutem plurimam dicit*. Eberhard I was a key figure in the German Renaissance and a founder of the University of Tübingen.</note>

Our Martinus Uranius <note>Martin Prenninger, a German scholar whose nickname "Uranius" means "the heavenly one" in Greek</note>—that is, "the heavenly one"—and indeed a contemplator of heavenly things, has treated at length in great conversation with me how the sun is among the stars, and how you, beyond our conversation, are such a figure among all the princes of Germany. By which praises indeed, as if inflamed by certain rays of your virtue, I gave you that little letter some time ago; a pledge indeed of our great love for you. But it was not a great pledge (as was fitting). Therefore, so that I may satisfy both your supreme dignity and my own desire somewhat more abundantly, I now send to the "Sun of Germany" himself a Platonic and Dionysian sun <note>referring to his treatise *De Sole*, which blends the philosophy of Plato with the theology of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite</note>; our love for you will be declared everywhere by its splendor. Just as Mercury transfers the gifts of Phoebus <note>Apollo, the sun god</note> to the minds of men, so Johann Streler, acting as if he were another Mercury for us, will carry this gift of Phoebus to you. You will read then happily, O Phoebus-like Prince, those things which partly Plato and Dionysius the Areopagite have treated concerning the comparison of the sun to God, and which I have partly interpreted and commented upon. Live happily in this shadow of life, destined at last to enjoy the perpetual sun after this one. Farewell.

### Praises of our age as if it were a golden one, because of its golden minds.

Marsilio Ficino to Paul of Middelburg, the distinguished physician and astronomer, sends many greetings. <note>Paul of Middelburg was a famous Dutch scientist who later became a bishop and worked on calendar reform.</note>

What the poets once sang concerning the four ages—the leaden, the iron, the silver, and the golden—our Plato, in his books on the *Republic*, transferred to four types of human minds, arguing that in some human minds, lead is naturally implanted; in others iron; in others silver; and in others gold. If, therefore, any age is to be called "golden" by us, it is undoubtedly that which produces golden minds everywhere. Moreover, he who wishes to consider the illustrious inventions of this age will least of all doubt that this age of ours is such. For this age, as if golden, has brought back into the light the liberal disciplines that were almost extinct: Grammar, poetry, oratory, painting, sculpture, architecture, and music. It has restored the ancient singing of songs to the Orphic lyre <note>Ficino was famous for performing "Orphic hymns" on a lyre to promote spiritual health</note>. And it has done this at Florence; a thing which had been venerable among the ancients, but was now nearly destroyed. It has joined wisdom with eloquence, and prudence with the military art. It has declared this most especially in Federico, Duke of Urbino, as if in Pallas <note>The goddess Pallas Athena, representing the union of wisdom and warfare</note>, and has made his son and brother heirs of that virtue. In you also, my Paul, astronomy seems to have reached perfection; furthermore, in Florence, it has recalled the Platonic discipline from the shadows back into the light. In Germany, in our own times, the inventions of printing books...

## Preface of Marsilio Ficino to the Twelfth Book of Letters to Girolamo Rossi, his most beloved.

### Marsilio Ficino to Girolamo Rossi, his most beloved, sends many greetings. <note>original: "S.P.D." for *salutem plurimam dicit*, a standard greeting in Latin letters.</note>

<margin>c</margin>
**W**hen I had put an end to the twelfth book of my letters and was considering to whom primarily I should inscribe this, I judged it would be consistent with reason to dedicate the end of this long work specifically to you, to whom I had already for a long time destined the whole work as if to its goal. Furthermore, so that the whole study of my letters might finally rest in you, I have decreed that whatever letters I shall write hereafter, even at the end, shall belong to this twelfth book, however long it may be, and be contained summarily under the title of Rossi—or rather, Roscius. <note>Ficino often Latinized the names of his friends to sound more classical; here he puns on Rossi's name by linking it to the famous Roman actor Roscius.</note> Read happily, and live most happily; certainly, be happily loved by us.

->No one can completely root out evils and cares.<-

### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Giovanni Vittorio Soderini and Francesco da Diacceto, his fellow philosophers, sends many greetings.

<margin>q</margin>
**Y**ou ask what that Gospel saying means: *It is necessary that scandals come.* <note>original: "Necesse est vt veniant scandala" from Matthew 18:7.</note> It means the very same thing as that Platonic saying: *Evils cannot be completely rooted out.* <note>Ficino refers to a famous passage in Plato's *Theaetetus* (176a) where Socrates argues that evil is a necessary counterpart to good in the mortal realm.</note> Instead, they necessarily revolve around this mortal region. For now, I pass over how many evils Fate, Nature, Fortune, the Elements, Men, and Animals bring upon us; certainly much more serious are those which we imprudently bring upon ourselves. Now indeed, it should not seem surprising that men devoted to a busy life or enslaved to their lusts are oppressed by innumerable evils. For they subject themselves everywhere to fate and fortune, and, as if of their own accord, frequently run into disturbances. This, certainly, is most to be wondered at: that even men who, having neglected the pleasurable and active life, have given themselves entirely to contemplation, are agitated by disturbances. For they seem to have avoided the causes of anxieties, yet they are often troubled by more serious cares than even the pleasure-seekers or the active men. For contemplators, having despised human affairs, turn themselves either to religion and holiness, or to philosophy...

<meta>This page continues the correspondence of Marsilio Ficino. The previous page ended a letter to Girolamo Rossi regarding the completion of the twelfth book of letters. This page concludes a reflection on the hardships of the philosophical life before beginning a new letter to Eberhard, Count of Württemberg, regarding the nature of the Sun and Socrates' famous trances.</meta>

...they say. In both cases, they truly fall into Scylla while desiring to avoid Charybdis <note>This is a classical idiom meaning to fall into one danger while trying to avoid another, much like "between a rock and a hard place."</note>. For the saints, fleeing the delusions and trifles of mortals, fall among tempting demons. For the struggle is not, as the apostle Paul says, against <note>original: "bis" appears to be a printer's error for "nobis," meaning "to us"</note> flesh and blood, but against certain wicked spirits, the tyrants of the dark air. Thus it happens that while God tests the saints, demons harass them. 

But what shall I say of the philosophers? Do they not, in rejecting either the business of Jupiter <note>worldly affairs and governance</note> or the delights of Venus <note>sensual pleasures</note>, often collapse into the weariness and sorrows of Saturn, and into black bile <note>original: "atram bilem," the humor associated with melancholy and intellectual labor</note>? To this great evil, Democritus, Plato, and Aristotle consider all the most gifted men to be subject; they seem to pay those same penalties which Prometheus "the contemplator" <note>Prometheus, who stole fire from heaven, was often seen as a symbol for the philosopher whose heart is "gnawed" by the demands of high thought</note> paid on Mount Caucasus for his celestial theft. Indeed, both types of contemplators <note>both the saints and the philosophers</note> often undergo cares that are as much heavier than those of the clever or the pleasure-seeking as their tormentors are more powerful. 

Wherefore, if men of this kind—who more than all others are thought likely to avoid evils—frequently fall into even heavier evils, surely no one can trust that evils can ever be avoided by mortals. But perhaps this is the difference: that the evils of the former [the worldly] gradually turn into the worst outcomes. These others, however, if they pursue their profession providently and constantly, will at last—with God as the author and permitter—reap in joy what they sowed in tears. *They went out and wept, casting their seeds; but they shall come back with joy, carrying their sheaves.* <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 126:5-6, emphasizing that spiritual struggle leads to ultimate reward.</note> 

I have judged it worthwhile to remind you of these things, my most beloved fellow-philosophers, so that you do not trust that you will taste the sweet flavors of philosophy without some bitterness. Nor again should you despair that even bitterness itself—with God as the author—can sometimes be converted into sweetness, as nature often does in fruit. Farewell, happy ones, and persevere prudently and constantly in your contemplation, just as you have begun. September 27, 1491.

->That the Sun is not to be worshiped as the author of all things.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to the illustrious Eberhard, Count of Württemberg and Lord of Montbéliard, sends greetings.<-

Socrates, while in military camps, often stood under the open sky looking up at the rising sun; he stood astonished in those same tracks, with limbs unmoved and eyes unblinking like a statue, until he might greet the sun rising again <note>This refers to a famous anecdote in Plato's *Symposium* describing Socrates standing in a trance for twenty-four hours at the siege of Potidaea.</note>. Led by these and similar signs, the Platonists might perhaps say that Socrates, guided by a certain Apollonian <note>original: "phoebeo," relating to Phoebus Apollo</note> spirit from his very childhood, was accustomed to venerate the sun itself above all else; and for that same reason, he was judged the wisest of all Greeks by the oracle of Apollo. 

Therefore, what should most be affirmed regarding the spirit of Socrates—whether it be a guiding spirit <note>original: "genio"</note> or an angel—I shall for the present omit. This certainly I would dare to affirm: that Socrates, in that ecstasy of mind, did not admire this physical sun, but another. For since novelty alone is accustomed to bring about admiration, why would the wondering Socrates be so stunned by this one, which he sees daily? Whose motions and powers already for a long time [he has known] through both mathematics and phi...

### TWELFTH 231 ###
->231<-

...comprehended by a philosophical reason. This sun, according to Plato's testimony, he called not the first God, but the son of God. Not, I say, the first son of God, but the second and visible one. For he considers the first son of God not to be this sun manifest to the eyes, but another far superior to it: namely <note>original: "s." abbreviation for "scilicet"</note>, the first Intellect, which can be contemplated by the intellect alone. Socrates, therefore, being sometimes prompted by the celestial sun and divining a supracelestial sun in God, contemplated the majesty of the former with great attention and stood astonished, admiring the incomprehensible goodness of that Sun's father.

The apostle James called him the "Father of Lights" <note>James 1:17</note>—of lights, I say, both more than celestial and celestial—with whom there is no change or shadow of turning <note>original: "transmutatio; neque vicissitudinis obumbratio"</note>. For James believes that even those supracelestial things created are naturally mutable, and he does not doubt that celestial things are overshadowed daily by the turns of night. Wherefore, he judges that "every best gift"—that is, what is naturally implanted in the mind—and "every perfect gift"—namely, that which is added after natural endowments—descends not from this sun and the worldly stars, but from higher up, from the Father of Lights himself. 

For relying on the powers of intelligence as if on certain steps—received not indeed from the heavens but from above—we ascend above the heavens; there we know, love, and worship many things more excellent than the heavens, and we venerate the Architect of heaven <note>original: "caeli fabrum"</note> before all things. Yet we would not be able to understand or love anything incorporeal or better than heaven through intelligence if we possessed intelligence only from the heavens. Now, lest anyone, admiring the sun, moon, and stars too much, should worship them and venerate them as the authors and fathers of intellectual gifts, he prudently warned that this sun is not the Principle of the universe. 

For the moment, I shall set aside the reasons by which we affirm in our theology that the Principle of the universe is neither a body, nor a soul, nor an intellect, but something far more exalted. From this Principle, the celestial sun is indeed very distant, so that it may be judged to be a kind of shadow of it, or rather, an image. However, the reasons which James touches upon here briefly, I shall now briefly summarize. 

Since stillness <note>original: "status"</note>, acting as the principle, ruler, and end of motion, is more perfect than any motion, certainly God himself—the principle, end, and ruler of all—cannot be movable; the sun, however, is constantly in motion. Furthermore, the power of the Principle, being as it were immeasurable, reaches all things powerfully and cannot be restrained anywhere. But the power of the sun, acting through rays, is hindered here and there when its rays are blocked; it suffers an eclipse <note>original: "defectum"</note> when the moon is in the way. It is often confined by clouds. It is repelled by the density of the earth. The sun itself is weakened by the distance of its location; indeed, it is but a very small particle of the world. It is held in a narrow seat. It is pulled. And contrary to the impetus of its own sphere, it is always revolved by a higher sphere. It is hindered by contrary signs <note>the constellations of the Zodiac</note> and stars, and is sometimes weakened by the aspect of evil planets. 

Finally, the Principle of the universe works all things, everywhere, always, and in all things. But the sun neither makes the spheres of the world itself, nor can it by its own power produce anything that is cold, or moist, or dense, or similar things. Nor do similar powers in heaven derive any origin from the sun. Nevertheless, although the sun is very far distant from the Author of the world, all celestial things look toward the sun as their sole ruler, as it were, and measure in heaven...

<summary>Ficino uses the figure of Socrates and the Epistle of James to argue that the physical sun is merely a shadow or "second son" of a higher, divine Intellect. He provides several theological and physical arguments for why the sun cannot be the ultimate Principle of the universe, citing its constant motion and physical limitations.</summary>

### The bond between philosophy and the laws: how happy and noble the philosopher is.

->Marsilio Ficino to Martinus Uranius Prenniger <note>Martin Prenninger (1450–1501), also known as Uranius, was a German humanist and jurist who corresponded frequently with Ficino.</note>, his unique friend, sends greetings.<-

<margin>p</margin> While I have indeed always been a philosopher and never applied myself to the laws, two professors of law are most dear to me. In Italy, Giovanni Vittorio Soderini <note>A prominent Florentine lawyer and statesman.</note>; in Germany, you especially, my excellent Martin. Both of you have joined a remarkable pursuit of wisdom with an outstanding skill in the laws. Someone might therefore ask: What kinship is there between laws and philosophy? It is surely the same relationship that exists between Jupiter, the author of laws, and Saturn, the leader of philosophy—that is, the bond between a son and his father. I will pass over for now the astronomers who assert that when Jupiter is joined with Saturn, he brings forth new laws. This is especially true whenever they join the heads of the triplicity <note>An astrological term referring to groups of three zodiacal signs belonging to the same element; conjunctions of Jupiter and Saturn in these signs were thought to herald major historical shifts.</note> in the very cardinal points of the heaven. Have not the ancient poets and the old theologians imagined Saturn as a contemplator <margin>In</margin> in his retreats, and as one who devises laws and rights after long contemplation? He then hands these <margin>Tr</margin> over to his son Jupiter, the leader of actions, who is to command the citizens to observe them. Homer also says that King Minos, the founder of laws, used to withdraw to the cave of Jupiter for nine years, and there receive the laws from Jupiter. But no one skilled in the ancient mysteries would have dedicated a private cave to Jupiter, who is always public. This, therefore, seems to be nothing other than the dwelling or shrine of Saturn himself <margin>Nu</margin> always added to him. In this shrine, Jupiter, having been established as a colleague with Saturn, instructs King Minos in the laws, which are soon to shape the people.

But having now set aside the duty of laws, let us pursue the study of wisdom. I have indeed exhorted many through my letters to take this up with all their strength. You, however, who are already advanced in this very thing, I will not exhort now, but rather I will confirm you in it. For we either consider ourselves, or we look up to God, or we look around at other men. If perhaps we consider ourselves: wisdom alone makes it so that we finally know ourselves and are able to dwell with ourselves alone, always content with our own riches. If indeed we look to God: wisdom even alone makes us like God and makes us his friends—namely, by assiduously contemplating the things God himself has made, and by venerating him once he is known as the author of all good things. If we look to men: wisdom alone finally establishes the wise man as a king over peoples and kings, and as a divine power <note>original: "numen"</note> to be venerated.

Since, therefore, the pursuit of wisdom makes the soul altogether happy, does it not moreover either make or declare it noble? If one may believe Plato, the race of philosophers is certainly the most noble. For he says it is "golden" and was truly perfected by Jupiter himself, the maker of the whole world. If you give credit to the Stoics, you will recognize the nobility of philosophers from their posterity: for they assert that they alone will be immortal. Finally, it is a sin not to believe the prophet Daniel. Shi[ning...] <note>The text cuts off with the catchword "Ful", likely referring to Daniel 12:3: "Those who are wise shall shine [fulgebunt] like the brightness of the sky."</note>

<summary>Ficino discusses the harmony between legal expertise and philosophical wisdom, using the mythological relationship between Saturn (contemplation) and Jupiter (law-giving) to illustrate how laws should derive from divine meditation. He concludes by praising philosophy for making the soul happy, noble, and god-like.</summary>

--- Page 467 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the divine rewards of the wise, transitioning from the previous page's focus on the "Sun of the Intellect" to a scriptural interpretation of Daniel's prophecy. It then begins a new letter from Marsilio Ficino to Filippo Valori, explaining why Ficino continues to devote his life to ancient Platonic studies through the lens of Saturnian astrology.</meta>

The learned (he says) shall shine like the brightness of the firmament; and those who have instructed many in justice shall be like stars for perpetual eternity. <note>A translation of Daniel 12:3.</note> The firmament <term>firmamentum; the sphere of the fixed stars or the general structure of the heavens</term> indeed seems to signify not only the eighth heaven, but the entire mass of the spheres: the support of all the stars and planets. This firmament also shines in a certain way by its own nature, separate from the stars and planets, but with a rarer, scattered, and white light; for that reason, it is less manifest to our eyes. With a light of this kind, the truly learned and holy men shall shine, both here and in the heavenly homeland, even if they themselves have never taught anyone. But those who have not only contemplated divine things for themselves, but have moreover openly instructed others and given laws for the observance of justice, shall shine with a more manifest brightness than the rest, flashing most clearly like the stars. Nor indeed shall this be for a certain time, but for all time; not only through the duration of the world, but through the very use of a more divine eternity, which is never interrupted, but is utterly perpetual and continuous. For it seems just that those who were authors of a public and divine good should always be of benefit to humanity. And since they did not hide the light given to them from the divine, but brought it forth entirely for the common good, they are gifted by the divine with a certain eternal splendor and goodness.

### Why I always treat the same and ancient things.

-> Marsilio Ficino to Filippo Valori <note>Filippo Valori (1456–1494) was a Florentine diplomat and a close patron of Ficino who funded the printing of his Plato translations.</note>, the Florentine envoy to the Pope, sends greetings. <-

<margin>b</margin> Last evening I had already said farewell to our friend Franco <note>Niccolò Franco, a friend and correspondent of Ficino.</note>; and you shall be to me a letter addressed to our Valori. <note>A play on words: "Valori" being the recipient's name and "valore" meaning value or health.</note> Soon, however (I know not how), I was compelled to add morning letters to those of the evening. Because lovers are often accustomed to doing this, not being content with single letters, the letter to Franco (if I may call it so) will announce my health to you. But as for the reasoning behind our studies, which Franco could not then receive due to his business, this present little letter will report to you. I see you ask what I am doing now. Indeed, my dear Valori, I have been doing the same thing for a long time. I am always revolved back to the same point (by I know not what fate). Saturn, as you know, was the significator for us—I might even say our leader—rising under Aquarius from the beginning. Therefore, we perpetually retract Saturnian and ancient things. Long ago, when Saturn first returned to Aquarius, we translated the ancient works of Plato under the great Cosimo <note>Cosimo de' Medici (1389–1464), Ficino’s first great patron.</note>. Now Saturn has returned again to the same sign. We also return to the same. We are translating Plato again after the "Laurentian Plotinus." <note>Ficino refers to his translation of Plotinus, dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici.</note> But we are explaining a great work (as was fitting) with even greater commentaries. The little commentary on the *Timaeus*, which was composed at your estate in Maiano, is now growing larger for us, as we are similarly about to approach the *Parmenides*. Our great patron, Piero de' Medici <note>Piero di Lorenzo de' Medici (1472–1503), who succeeded his father Lorenzo.</note>, gave us firm hope that he would once more breathe life into the rising Plato. And indeed, he so inspires him that our Plato, who has been wandering until now, is now about to found his Academy upon this "Rock" <note>original: "petrā" — Ficino makes a pun on Piero’s name, Petrus, and the Biblical "upon this rock I will build my church" (Matthew 16:18).</note>. Therefore, when you approach him there at the Pope’s court during your leisure, give him the greatest thanks in our name. Beside this your "Jupiter" [Piero], you will recognize your "Dioscuri" <note>The twins Castor and Pollux in Greek mythology.</note>: the Bibbienas, Castor and Pollux; therefore, after him, you will also commend us to them. But I shall make an end, not (I say) to this little letter, but now to the whole epistle, if I first signify to you that Martian cause—or rather now...

...Saturnian slowness: after medical authority: your work in addition: now being finished. November 7, 1492.

->The Similarity of Mercury with Saturn<-

Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved Filippo Carducci, greetings.
Since all the letters composed by me, which have now been written for you, were almost to be brought to you by the courier, I decided that this "Mercurial" work <note>Ficino often refers to his writings as "Mercurial," relating them to Mercury, the god of messages, eloquence, and intellectual exchange.</note> should be brought to a Mercurial friend under Mercurial auspices. I did this so that if celestial powers have any influence in such matters, the work might reach you more quickly and be read more swiftly. Furthermore, I hoped it might be considered and reread for a very long time. I have added Saturn to Mercury, whether as a companion or a guide. I read again today in the tenth book of the *Republic* <note>original: "x. de repu." Refers to Plato’s *Republic*, specifically the "Myth of Er" which describes the celestial spheres.</note> that Mercury and Saturn "dwell together"—that is, in the light of all the celestial bodies, they are most similar to one another. Thus, it is not surprising that they are also so similar in the light of intelligence: one exhorts us toward wisdom, while the other, with God breathing more deeply, leads us forward. They claim the Sun is the image of God. God himself is the primary author of wisdom; the indicators of wisdom are Mercury and Saturn. As companions of the divine image <note>The Sun</note>, they depart the least of all from the Sun: for while Mercury almost always walks within the Sun’s splendor, Saturn is seen to deviate the least of all from the Sun’s ecliptic path. Astronomers think these two are similar by a certain nature, and that Mercury rejoices in the houses, bounds, and aspects of Saturn. This (in my opinion) is why almost all who begin their journey and profession under Mercury end only in Saturn. I wish that you, Carducci, might also eventually arrive from Mercury even unto Jupiter. <note>In Ficino’s astrology, moving from Mercury to Saturn signifies a transition from cleverness to deep, contemplative wisdom; arriving at Jupiter represents reaching a state of balanced, civic, and joyful leadership.</note> Farewell. November 14, 1492.

->Apology for his book on the Sun and Light<-

Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Filippo Valori, the Florentine Ambassador to the Pope, many greetings.
I was keeping the book about the Sun, intended for the most illustrious Piero de' Medici <note>original: "petro medici." Piero "the Unfortunate" de' Medici, who succeeded Lorenzo the Magnificent.</note>, at home for quite a long time now. Almost impiously, I was hiding the lamp—or rather the Sun—under a bushel, contrary to the Gospel precept. <note>A reference to Matthew 5:15: "Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel."</note> But that "Bright Peter" <note>original: "petrus ille nerus." A pun on the name of Piero Nero, a friend of Ficino whose surname *Nero* means black, but whom Ficino calls *candidissimus* or "most bright/white."</note>, whom we have frequently called "most bright" in our letters, thought it would be a pious act for this light to shine upon as many people as possible, as God commands. And so I most willingly obeyed this most bright man, to whom the care of light and brilliance especially belongs. Beyond the mystery, I allowed the book commended to the magnanimous Piero de' Medici to be openly expressed by the printers through the efforts of Piero Nero. Behold then, my Valori—who are dearer to me than light—this little Sun of mine, however small it may be, is now rising openly. But perhaps it is destined to be struck by rising clouds, or to be troublesome to certain owls and bats. <note>Ficino uses "owls and bats" as metaphors for critics or those who cannot handle the "light" of Neoplatonic philosophy.</note> Winds will immediately scatter the clouds, or the Sun itself, as it rises higher, will thin and dissolve them. As for the bats who grow dim and blind under the light: let them be advised (if they are even capable of advice) not to curse the light which is healthy for others. Rather, let them flee this splendor in their own way, as is fitting for those unworthy of light.

TWELVE CCXXXIII

...they may constantly lie hidden. Indeed, with good hope, I summon my valor to this contest. I say valor, not only against the owls <note>original: "bubones." Ficino frequently uses owls as a metaphor for critics or those who "shun the light" of Platonic truth.</note> but also against empty monsters. Like Hercules, I shall fight most strongly. You are accustomed to frequently having that Boethian saying on your lips, spoken on behalf of Hercules: *The earth, once overcome, grants the stars.* <note>original: "Superata tellus sydera donat." A quote from Boethius’s *Consolation of Philosophy*, Book IV, suggesting that earthly struggles lead to divine rewards.</note> The ancients introduce Hercules as a man fostered by the sun: for the sake of true glory and the splendor of truth, which are the sun's own gifts and duties. He undergoes twelve labors, as if they were the twelve signs of the Zodiac. Go now, my valor, swiftly into battle! For there (I know what I say), you will have at least three invincible champions: I speak of the Herculean Politian <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a brilliant humanist poet and close friend of Ficino.</note>, the Phoebian Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous syncretic philosopher.</note>, and the Amphion-like Landino <note>Cristoforo Landino (1424–1498), known for his commentaries on Dante and Virgil; Amphion was a mythical musician who built walls with his song.</note>. These men have surely fought so vigorously for my life for three years now; they will hereafter fight just as fortunately for this splendor of mine, however great it may be. January 2, 1494.

->Often there are twins in the heavens. Likewise, two suns.<-

Marsilio Ficino to Martin Uranius <note>Martin Prenninger (c. 1450–1501), a German jurist and humanist whom Ficino nicknamed "Uranius" (the Heavenly).</note>, his unique German friend, sends greetings.

<margin>1</margin> It is a joy to treat often of heavenly things with you, my heavenly Uranius. Not only are those Dioscuri <note>The twins Castor and Pollux, who form the constellation Gemini.</note> twins in the firmament, but among the planets there are also brothers. For Mercury is, as it were, a younger brother to Saturn. For they both shine with the light of counsel (as Plato says) and they both preside over geniuses. Bountiful Venus is the sister of Jupiter. So too are Phoebus <note>The Sun</note> and Phoebe <note>The Moon</note> siblings. Mars, however, being somewhat more arrogant and devoid of companionship, does not so much accompany the Sun as emulate him; for besides his own heat, which emulates the Sun, he infuses a certain rival light (I know not what) into the Moon, which has been observed by very few. After these, however, the eternal air, like a second Jupiter, is the brother and husband of the following air, which is Juno. 

But let us return to the Sun. What wonder is it if, since there are twin suns in heaven, twin suns have also been born to me—as it were—the first being the greater and the second the lesser. You yourself, when you were with us in Florence this past summer, saw the lesser Sun—the Orator <note>Likely referring to a specific speech or shorter work dedicated to the Pope.</note>—departing for the Pontiff. It followed you immediately as you left here for Germany, intending to greet your most illustrious Prince Eberhard. But the other Sun—which has now grown larger among my Platonic commentaries—Piero de' Medici <note>Petrus Medices (1472–1503), the son and successor of Lorenzo the Magnificent.</note> rightfully claims for himself; indeed, he rightfully claims all Platonic things for himself, and the light similarly. O my Uranius, a twin light has shone for me among my household gods: a smaller and a larger. The smaller has long since shone for Phoebus Capella <note>Likely a reference to Johannes "Capella" or a similar associate.</note>, but the larger now shines for the most illustrious Piero de' Medici. Therefore, heavenly man, contemplate both fortunately. 

Indeed, you will contemplate them fortunately if, through the likeness of this light, you commit to memory this Platonic mystery concerning divinity which follows. We are accustomed to discerning things that have the least light by no other way than by searching here and there and approaching closer. But when we are about to see the Sun, we are not so much forced to search for the Sun—which meets us of its own accord and is the most obvious of all things—as we are forced to purge our eyes, open them, turn them, and, according to our capacity, adapt them to it. Similarly, we are compelled to investigate the small truths of other things like sparks through arguments. But the Immense...

# BOOK

...indeed, we cannot attain the light of God in this way <note>referring to purely rational or earthly effort</note>, but rather we are prepared for it through a loving conversion of the will and a serenity of mind. That is to say, once we are prepared, that light happily flashes upon us of its own accord. Hence that Platonic saying: *Divine things cannot indeed be taught by words and reasoning in the same way that other things are learned. But from constant familiarity with the divine itself and a shared life, suddenly, like a light flashing forth from a spark of fire, it shines in the soul and then feeds itself.* <note>original: "Diuina qđē verbis rationibufqз doceri nō poflunt..." This is a famous passage from Plato’s *Seventh Letter* (341c), a cornerstone of Ficino’s belief that spiritual truth requires a sudden "spark" of illumination rather than just study.</note>

->Regarding the book on the sun, sent as a gift.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Lorenzo, his fellow philosopher and prelate of the Laurentian house. <note>Lorenzo here likely refers to a member of the Medici family holding an ecclesiastical position in the Basilica of San Lorenzo.</note>

While I was composing a book on the sun and light during these past days—a small work, certainly, but one written with great pleasure—you, in the meantime, though unaware of my current late-night labors, most opportunely discovered through astronomical calculations that our entire study of wisdom pertains chiefly to the sun. This is because that "lot" which the Egyptians call the "part of wisdom" <note>original: "fapientiæ partem." In Hellenistic and Hermetic astrology, "Lots" or "Arabic Parts" are mathematical points on a horoscope. Ficino is noting a synchronicity between his writing and the stars.</note> had reached the Heart of the Lion <note>original: "cor leonis." This refers to the star Regulus, the brightest star in the constellation Leo, traditionally associated with royalty and the sun.</note>, and the sun, being its lord, had taken up a new region of the heavens destined for wisdom. Again, quite opportunely, immediately after the book on the sun and light was finished, you brought your astronomical computation to us yesterday. Therefore, by that same opportunity, I in turn send the book itself to you today. I hope that this light of ours may seem to bring forth not a Moon <note>symbolizing reflected or secondary light</note>, but a Sun. February 18, 1494.

> Love itself, as God, commands that the lover be loved in return.

### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Julian, distinguished professor of theology of the Order of Friars Minor, and no less a friend. Heartfelt greetings.

There is no reason, my dearest Julian, for you to apologize for your silence toward us. For even if you have spoken to us but rarely, you have nevertheless spoken of us frequently. And if anything should be lacking in your words, you compensate for all of it with your immense love toward us. Indeed, I hold this as the greatest proof of your burning love for me: that I, in turn, embrace you while you are absent with a love that grows more ardent by the day. As for that proverb, *If you wish to be loved, love,* I have explained it in many ways in my book *On Love* and in various letters. But the greatest reason of all, which occurs to me just now as I write—unless a sudden opinion deceives me—seems to be this. But so that it might deceive me a little less, let us chat for a moment. 

The ancients used to depict Apollo and Cupid as archers; the latter shooting flames, the former shooting rays of light. Therefore, just as Apollo shoots twin-like rays of light so that by the same light with which I have seen you, you may also see me in return; so Cupid shoots flames so that the same flame by which one person already burns may soon cause the other to burn as well. Truly, that Love is a god is proven by Plato and testified to by all antiquity. Even our own theologians place the Holy Spirit—who is Love—before the Seraphic (that is, the "loving") angels, and they perfect the Seraphic angels everywhere through true loves. Therefore, the divine power of love mu... <note>The text breaks off mid-word "mu-," likely continuing "mutuus" (mutual) on the following page.</note>

# TWELFTH [BOOK] 234
g 2

...friend of your charity and union. When [the Divine] inflames someone with love, he immediately reflects back, as if from a mirror, burning rays from this love into the beloved by a certain hidden and wondrous power; so that the one who is absent or unaware is wonderfully inflamed and loves the lover in turn. For the just divinity, by a heavenly instinct, does not allow a lover who is moved to not be loved back. But enough about love for now. 

Furthermore, you complained in your letter that the books of Plotinus <note>Ficino published his massive Latin translation and commentary on Plotinus in 1492</note> had not reached you at all, almost accusing me of slowness. Indeed, the books themselves were finished by the printers this past May. But those who were commissioned by the Medici <note>original: "medicibus"</note> to distribute them, at least throughout Italy, have been slow until now; and even with me urging them, they are slow. I have not yet published my new interpretation of Plato, though it is now advanced beyond the halfway point. You, above all others, encouraged me most toward this work—perhaps with angels urging us on in whose temple <note>Likely the Basilica of San Lorenzo, the parish church of the Medici</note> you persuaded me to do this during a dinner. At that time, after our declamations there, you were preaching in frequent sermons. I am sending you the little book *On the Sun and Light* recently published by me for you to read; so that where our heat has long been burning, there light may also shine back. February 21, 1494.
