### On the book regarding the Sun.

Marsilio Ficino to Mazingo, the distinguished Physician and his fellow philosopher, sends greetings.

<margin>o</margin> All astronomers (as you well know) believe that the Moon rejoices in the third region of the sky from the ascendant <note>The 3rd House in astrology, associated with short travels</note>, being the leader of a short journey and of small religion; but the Sun in the ninth <note>The 9th House, associated with long journeys and philosophy/religion</note>, as the ruler of a longer journey and of great religion—or, to speak more safely, at least as the signifier. Since, therefore, you are about to undertake a long and religious journey to the House of Loreto <note>The Holy House of Loreto, a major pilgrimage site in Italy</note> very soon, I rightly hand over to you a certain "Sun" recently risen from me. It will be, as I hope, an omen of clear air and an easy journey.

***

### On the book regarding the Sun.

Marsilio Ficino to Giorgio Cyprio, the distinguished physician, sends greetings.

<margin>c</margin> Since everyone agrees that Phoebus <note>Apollo, the god of the Sun and medicine</note> is the author of medicine and the father of physicians, I rightly send to you for reading the "Phoebian" book *On the Sun and Light* <margin>a</margin> recently published by us. You are the long-standing physician of <margin>n</margin> our family; Phoebus, therefore, will be a truthful witness to you of my perpetual love toward you. "The sun will give you signs" (as our Maro <note>The poet Virgil, whose full name was Publius Vergilius Maro</note> says); who would dare call the sun false? June 14, 1494.

***

### Regarding the book on the Sun, sent.

Marsilio Ficino to Baccio Ugolino, sends greetings.

<margin>c</margin> Since Phoebus and Bacchus <note>The gods of the Sun and Wine respectively; Ficino often linked them as symbols of different types of divine frenzy</note> are brothers, one rightly greets the other. But which one approaches the other first? Not Liber <note>Another name for Bacchus</note>, fearing perhaps that he might bring back only words; but Phoebus himself, hoping to bring back Bacchus's own character. June 15, 1494.

Happy omens for philosophy, from Mercury, Saturn, and the Sun.

# BOOK

Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved Niccolò Valori, sends many greetings.
<margin>n</margin> None of our associates began to practice philosophy under more fortunate auspices than you. I will not, for my part, recount at length in this present moment how much you are thought to contribute to the studies of philosophy. That conjunction of Mercury with Saturn in Aquarius was then imminent when I was composing my book *On the Sun and Light* and you were already giving your first efforts to philosophy—and indeed, starting from the Sun itself, truly like a second Orpheus, or rather from Apollo than from the Muses. Therefore, you immediately looked upon this Sun with eagle-like eyes, as was fitting for such great auspices. But following this, you—who rule among celestial things—advanced with a certain wonderful speed toward the higher Sun, the author of the heavens; you have approached *Platonic Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his own major work, *Theologia Platonica*, which sought to prove the immortality of the soul using Platonic philosophy.</note> in a most happy manner. In this work, you truly look into the deepest mysteries daily as clearly as it is permitted for one to discern who observes individual things not under the Moon, but under the Sun itself. Continue, I pray, my Valori, with that same eagerness with which you began: with me as your companion throughout and Apollo as your leader. You shall shortly attain the highest splendor of truth and glory.

->Signs of a legitimate Platonist: and about ideas.<-

Marsilio Ficino to his fellow Platonist Francesco da Diacceto, sends many greetings.
They are entirely in error who think that the Peripatetic <note>original: "peripateticam" – referring to the followers of Aristotle</note> discipline is contrary to the Platonic.
<margin>c</margin> For indeed, the Way cannot be contrary to its Goal. Anyone who considers it rightly will find that the Peripatetic doctrine is the way to Platonic wisdom, for natural things lead us toward divine things. Hence it has come to pass that no one was ever admitted to the more secret mysteries of Plato unless they were first initiated into the Peripatetic disciplines. Of the absolute <note>meaning "perfected" or "complete"</note> Platonist, there are truly three symbols <note>or "marks/tokens"</note> by which his priests are distinguished from other common and enclosed groups: the first is a sublime mind, always turning itself from lower things toward the higher. The second is religion. The third is eloquence—and this specifically of a poetic nature. The first pertains to Saturn, the second to Jupiter, and the third to Apollo. Therefore, only he is a legitimate Platonist who walks the path we have described, endowed with these symbols and commended by these deities (if I may put it so). For this reason, my fellow philosopher Francesco, I congratulate you as a legitimate Platonist and I rejoice for the Academy. 

But as for my response to your question about Ideas <note>The Platonic "Forms" or eternal blueprints of reality</note> in the manner of a letter, receive it briefly thus: You do not think that the proper Ideas of individual things in the First Mind are distinguished from one another absolutely, but rather by a certain relation. I have always judged similarly. Nor do I think this is foreign to the thought of Plotinus, who is now your own. Indeed, I explain this briefly in my commentaries on him. Proclus also, in his commentary on the *Parmenides*, denies that the proper Ideas of individuals are absolutely distinct. This is undoubtedly most consistent with Plato, who says in the *Timaeus* that the Ideal Exemplar is eternal; what is expressed toward it and through it will be everlasting. From this, it is gathered that the species of natural things are expressed from that source inwardly, as being truly everlasting; yet individual things are not equally so, but are distinguished among themselves at the furthest end by the causes that follow in sequence. These distinctions, however...

Hence, in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the universe, which Ficino translated and commented upon extensively.</note>, the "junior gods" and spirits follow the construction of individual things below the Moon, with the architect commanding and arranging them. ## A Clearing of Long Silence

Marsilio Ficino to Filippo Valori, Florentine ambassador to the Supreme Pontiff, sends many greetings. <note>original: "S.P.D." for *Salutem Plurimam Dicit*.</note>

<margin>q</margin> You will perhaps ask the cause of this long silence. This, however, is nothing else—to answer briefly—than an uncertain reason for writing. For what should I write most especially? Perhaps how I am doing? I am always in doubt whether I am doing badly or well. Shall I indicate what I am doing? By Hercules, I am in doubt about this too! Indeed, I know what I want. I know what I am attempting. But what I am achieving, I still do not know. I am even in doubt whether I should think of you as present with us or absent, since the daily companionship of your brother Niccolò, who philosophizes with me, renders you so present to my mind that I did not notice the need for letters. Grateful men are usually accustomed to send at least longer letters after a long silence. I, however, shall be so "ungrateful" now that I trust I can compensate for a very long silence with perhaps a very short letter. Not at all; but rather a great love provides confidence and fulfills the duty. Farewell. 15 June 1494.

## Regarding the Book on the Sun

Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Calderini, sends greetings.

<margin>s</margin> The Sun, the lord among celestial things, excels other causes of natural things most especially in this: that it makes all things by its heat, but reveals them by its light. To me, however, though there is no need to use the heat of the Sun to warm Calderini—whom I have found to be most fervent everywhere in managing and defending my affairs—I nevertheless decided to use the light of the Sun <note>Ficino is referring to his newly completed book, *De Sole* (On the Sun).</note> so that I might now publicly declare to everyone our burning love, already confirmed by many testimonies, with Apollo <note>The god of the sun and wisdom.</note> further as a witness. 15 July 1494.

Light is wonderful, because it is the image of wisdom. Likewise, how wonderful is the bond of wisdom with power.

# BOOK

...[not] perceived this as manifest to the eyes. For he will have noticed that it is nothing other than an image of hidden light—that is, of wisdom itself. For indeed, wisdom is nothing other than the clearest light of intelligence. This is what our Plato <note>Ficino frequently refers to Plato as "our Plato," signaling his role as the leader of the Florentine Platonic Academy.</note> prophesied in the *Phaedrus* <note>A Platonic dialogue concerning the nature of the soul, beauty, and love.</note>: if ever it could be seen with inner eyes, it would excite much more ardent loves than this open light in beautiful bodies is accustomed to incite in lovers daily. Since indeed this light, clear to the sight, has not obtained such grace and admiration among us except from that more secret light of which it is the image—from that light, I say, of divine wisdom. Therefore, divine wisdom has everywhere given preeminence to light as if to its own vicar. Of our body, the eyes alone are the leaders. For they alone among the limbs are participants of light, as if of a certain wisdom. Among all the powers of the soul, the mind alone reigns, shining by the gift of wisdom. Furthermore, among the elements and similar bodies, fire is the master; it alone among these is like something wise, endowed with light. In heaven similarly, the sun itself, the sole source of light, rules over all. Among astronomers, it signifies both power and wisdom, rejoicing in the ninth region <note>In astrology, the "Ninth House" (or region) of the sky governs philosophy, religion, and wisdom.</note> of heaven as if in the temple of Minerva <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom.</note>. By its proximity, Mercury also seems to have obtained the name of "the wise one." What more? Finally, the kingdom of the whole world is claimed not by the violence of any heat or cold, nor by the impulse of certain motions, nor by any crowd of fluctuating bodies or mass of pride. But by the first wisdom: just as it sees all things, so it is powerful over all; just as it provides for each thing everywhere, so it is the mistress of each. This wisdom, therefore, seems to have rightly commanded us to join wisdom with power according to our strength, just as she has clearly joined them in herself and in the universe. Wherefore I believe it was divinely brought about that the light of the sun, which effects all things as if powerful, should similarly demonstrate all things as if wise; indeed, it should help and delight all things as if good. By which we are always reminded to couple with power not only wisdom, but goodness as well. Indeed, the poets sing that such a venerable and blessed union existed once while Saturn was reigning <note>Referring to the mythical "Golden Age" of Saturn, a time of peace and abundance.</note>; and our Plato desired to see this above all others. And we, his followers, desire above all things a man to be loved above others: one who has joined a singular study of wisdom and integrity of character with noble lineage and princely rule. Here, now, the suspicion of flattery and vanity—which is quite foreign to philosophers—forbids me to explain what I feel more extensively. But let it be lawful at least to speak briefly: In Lamberto Malatesta <note>Lamberto Malatesta (1452–1532), a nobleman and patron of letters.</note>, Prince of Sogliano, I already have everything I sought with my whole mind; I love him with my whole mind. And the law of friendship commands me to make all my things common to him.
Just as Venus mixes lovers through Desire <note>original: "cupidinem", referring to Cupid, the god of desire.</note>, friendly Jupiter fuses friends through Mercury.

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains that physical light is a reflection of divine wisdom and argues that a perfect ruler must unite power, wisdom, and goodness. He concludes by praising Lamberto Malatesta as the embodiment of these virtues.</summary>

CCXXXVI
TWELFTH [BOOK]
g 4

# Marsilio Ficino of Florence sends many greetings to the illustrious Lamberto Malatesta, Prince of Sogliano.

<margin>a</margin>The ancient theologians of various nations held friendship in such high esteem that among the other deities—and indeed, often above the others—they worshiped **Jupiter the Friendly** <note>Original: *Iovem amicabilem*. Ficino is referring to *Zeus Philios*, the aspect of Jupiter/Zeus that presides over friendship and hospitality.</note>, who was the protector of reconciling goodwill and friendships everywhere. Among these ancients, just as "nourishing Venus" joined lovers through Desire <note>Original: *cupidinem*.</note> and approaching loves (as I might put it), so "Jupiter the Friendly" brought forth more serious forms of goodwill through **Mercury** and forged friendships. If we are permitted today to name Jupiter and Mercury, we would surely say that our friendship was joined not by any human cause, but by the gift of Jupiter the Friendly—since **Minerva** <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom, said to have been born fully formed from the head of Jupiter.</note> herself, the conciliator of our goodwill, is said to have been born from the very head of Jupiter. But shall we say he achieved this for us through Mercury? Through Mercury, certainly! Not only through that more hidden and celestial Mercury <note>The planet Mercury or the archetypal messenger.</note>, but also through one more familiar to us and human. For indeed, **Piero Martelli** <note>Piero Martelli (1468–1531) was a Florentine politician and scholar close to Ficino's circle.</note>, a most dear friend to both of us who joined us into one, possesses not only a "Mercurial" wit but even seems to display the very image and character of Mercury. Indeed, to speak somewhat from my own prophecy, I intuited this even before examining his horoscope <note>Original: *genesis*.</note>; and having inspected it, I was confirmed in my divination. Therefore, just as he has acted as Mercury under Jupiter in binding friendship between us thus far, so henceforth he shall be our Mercury in signaling and interpreting mutual counsels back and forth. August 4, 1493.

->The Sun: Image and Representative of God<-

# Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to the Father in Christ, Lord Francesco Soderini, Bishop of Volterra.

<margin>l</margin>I am sending to you the *Book on the Sun* <note>Ficino's treatise *De Sole*, published in 1493, which explores the sun as a physical manifestation of God's light.</note>, recently dedicated to the magnanimous **Piero de' Medici**, as it is also necessary for you to read. But so that the entire book may seem inscribed to you as well, my other patron, I dedicate this summary of the whole to you. Theologians attribute three principal qualities to God: **Power, Wisdom, and Goodness**. Therefore, the sun, as the image of God, accomplishes all things among us as one who is **powerful**. Furthermore, it distinguishes and demonstrates individual things to our eyes daily, like one who is **wise**. Finally, it helps and delights us, like one who is **good**. They teach that it is the property of God alone to perform miracles; thus the sun, as God’s representative <note>Original: *vicarius*. Ficino uses this to mean a deputy or physical stand-in for the divine.</note>, appears to perform three most wonderful things. Beneath the heavens, it revives in spring and summer many things that were seemingly dead during winter. In the heavens, however, it illuminates, governs, and covers all celestial bodies. But as for those things which are above the heavens—invisible not only to eyes but even to our minds—the sun itself (so to speak) renders them visible, while it admonishes us to contemplate super-celestial things through the wonderful spectacles of the heavens. Contemplate happily, holy prelate, this sun of ours and this light, you who are most worthy of the nourishing light of the true Sun above all others. September 8, 1493. Florence.

BOOK [XII]

## Preface to the Letters.

**Marsilio Ficino the Florentine sends many greetings <note>Original: *S. D.* abbreviates *salutem dicit*, a standard Latin greeting meaning "gives health" or "sends greetings."</note> to all his letters at once.**

<margin>q</margin> Whenever you, my letters, say "Greetings" to my friends (as I command you), just as often you say "immortal greetings" to your very dear friend Girolamo Rossi <note>Original: *Hyeronimus Rossius*, a Pistoiese physician and friend of Ficino who helped facilitate the printing of his letters.</note>. For I had fathered you as mortal beings, destined soon to die by I know not what fortune; but Girolamo, a man of remarkable devotion, has recently reborn you as (I hope) beings who are now immortal. For you were hidden for a long time, longing for the light, yet until now no one rescued you from the darkness—perhaps because Fate or your guiding spirit <note>Original: *genio*.</note> was not yet willing. But our Rossi—or rather, now even your Roscius <note>Ficino puns on the name "Rossius" and the famous Roman comic actor Quintus Roscius Gallus, implying Rossi has given the letters a grander "stage" through publication.</note>—has followed you now with a certain inherited affection, the same devotion he always showed toward your father Marsilio. With both diligence and labor, he took care that your features, which were just now being suppressed, should be fully expressed <note>Likely a reference to the printing press; *exprimerentur* can mean both to describe/express and to physically press or print.</note>. Therefore, greet this learned and pious restorer of yours—joyfully now, though you were sad before—and give immortal thanks for the great gift of immortality. December 15, 1494. Florence.

---

## Regarding the Book on the Sun: also concerning the Star of the Magi on the solemnity of Epiphany.

**Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to Angelo Niccolini, distinguished citizen and legal consultant.**

<margin>h</margin> Today the Magi (observers of the stars, guided by a wondrous star) greeted Christ, the author of the stars, with three specific gifts: Gold, Myrrh, and Frankincense. Today Christ, with the Holy Spirit flashing down from heaven, is said to have been bathed by John in the water of the Jordan. Today Christ, the creator of water and wine, miraculously changed water into wine at a wedding feast. Therefore, Angelo, a man of remarkable piety, you also solemnly celebrate this day—most famous for these three great miracles—every year with a triple honor: a Banquet, Music, and a Reading. To this sacred reading in your home, I consecrate my *Book on the Sun and Light*, recently composed by me for this reason: so that through the comparison of the Sun and visible light, the minds of readers might be raised, as much as possible, to contemplate the visible light of divinity. I pray that just as a wondrous star led the Magi today to see Christ—both God and man—so today the sun may lead us to the contemplation of God. January 6, 1494.

---

## Regarding the gift of Bacchus. Also that Gospel passage: water made into wine.

**Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to Mazingo <note>Carlo Mazingi, a physician and a member of Ficino's inner circle in Florence.</note>, the distinguished physician <term>physicus</term> <note>In the Renaissance, a *physicus* was both a doctor of medicine and a student of natural philosophy.</note>.**

<margin>m</margin> During the morning readings within the octave of Epiphany <note>The eight-day period of celebration following the feast of Epiphany on January 6th.</note>, being frequently reminded, I was considering within my mind today that Gospel passage: "Wine made from water." I wondered whether, besides the mystical allegory and the moral lesson, it also has a physical sense; for if indeed over a long period of time nature changes water into wine, Christ did so almost in a moment. But the physical sense, which pertains especially to the physician, investigates why Christ wanted this to be the first of his miracles. Perhaps it was to show that wine would be the primary and greatest support of our life. But why "good wine"—that is, strong wine—like the pure wine <note>Original: *merum*, referring to undiluted wine.</note> of Crete and the East, which has been preserved until now? Why did that Master of Life not want to bring out this wine at the first course, but delayed it so much? He wanted, perhaps...

[BOOK] TWELFTH 237

...perhaps to warn. Wine, being vigorous in its power, should by no means be granted to the hot-blooded youth, but rather saved for the recreation of colder old age. Why, then, did He <note>Ficino refers here to Christ at the Wedding at Cana.</note> change not just a part, but absolutely all the water into wine? Clearly so that good wine, and indeed undiluted wine, might be drunk especially in old age. Thus, as I was meditating on these things around noon, I began to long for and seek out wine of such a kind as might comfort both my own old age and my mother's elderly years. For this past autumn, she completed eighty years, while I have now completed sixty. But you, like a prophet, sent wine to me at that very hour: a divine, Apolline <note>referring to Apollo, god of medicine and prophecy</note> medicine indeed, such as my friend Mazinghi <note>Carlo Mazinghi, a Florentine physician and close associate of Ficino.</note> possesses. It suits both prophecy and the gift of Bacchus <note>the god of wine</note>, since Phoebus [Apollo] is called both the first physician and the author of prophecy, being Bacchus's brother and joined in sacred rites. Finally, how highly I value that, together with the choicest gift of Father Liber <note>another name for Bacchus, representing the liberating power of wine</note>, you gave me a Galenic <note>referring to the system of the ancient Greek physician Galen</note> letter providing healthy advice for life, so that you might join counsel with aid in a friendly manner. Therefore, just as much as prognosis is joined with medicine and Bacchus with Phoebus, so truly I am and always shall be joined to you in love. January 13, 1494.

### Regarding the reprinting of the book *On Life*. Also, an immortal omen of friendship.

**Marsilio Ficino the Florentine sends many greetings to Johannes Meuchen, the distinguished priest of Cologne, professor of Canon Law, and secretary to the great Bishop of Cologne.**

¶ On the fifteenth day before the Calends of February <note>January 18th. Roman dates count backward from the start of the next month.</note>, near sunrise, I seemed in my dreams to greet a man previously unknown to me, endowed with an honorable appearance and adorned with fine clothes and companions. After a physical <note>Original: *physicam*, meaning related to natural philosophy or medicine.</note> discussion, he showed me his foot as if it needed treatment. On 그 very same day, you arrived in Florence, about to set out for Rome as the legate of the great Bishop Hermann <note>Hermann von Wied, Archbishop-Elector of Cologne.</note>. Since you could not come to us on account of a bruised foot, you signaled a desire to visit. I came to you, as was not only proper but also fitting. And so, as soon as I looked upon you face-to-face, I immediately recognized the heroic man I had seen in my sleep. After the first greeting, we soon fell into mention of our work *On Life* <note>Original: *De Vita*, Ficino's influential treatise on the health and psychology of scholars.</note>, and we discussed many things together pertaining especially to medicine. During the conversation, so that whatever I had presaged while sleeping might be fulfilled, you showed me your bruised foot. Thus I do not seem to have seen a mere dream, but to have received a divine oracle. It is a certain omen (as I judge) that our friendship will be divine. Since divine things are also immortal, I for my part (as I have just related) sensed the immortal divinity of our friendship. You, meanwhile, devised its future immortality. For you have decided to take care that our books *On Life* be printed again, through which this "Life" of ours might be more widely spread, and posterity may understand from this service of yours toward us how much you loved us, being equally loved by us. And so let this divine friendship of ours become immortal among posterity. Live happily, my Johannes, propagator of our *Life* and most worthy of life itself. Farewell happily. January 17, 1494. Florence.

BOOK EIGHT

# Marsilio Ficino to the Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Francisco Soderini, Bishop of Volterra. Many greetings.

<margin>m</margin> I shall act briefly, for I am about to commend the Monastery of Settimo <note>The Abbey of San Salvatore a Settimo, a significant Cistercian monastery near Florence.</note> to you regarding the case in Modena. I know indeed how much you love those monks, who are quite pious men; I myself not only love them but cherish them. I believe that since they are just men, they are asking for just things; you are a most sharp defender of the law. Whatever service, then, you confer upon them, I shall consider it conferred equally upon me, their devoted observer. The monk there who is the proctor for this case—Justus <note>Latin: *iustus*, meaning "just." Ficino is making a pun on the monk's name and his character.</note> by name and in fact—reports everything to you with diligence. I also commend myself to you most highly. Farewell and be happy. 25 January 1494. <note>In the Florentine calendar, the year began in March; this corresponds to 1495 in the modern calendar.</note> Florence.

->Plato said many things in agreement with Christians. Many Platonists imitated Christian ways.<-

# Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to the Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Jacobo Rodono, Bishop of Rimini. Many greetings.

<margin>f</margin> Brother Santes <note>Likely Sante Pagnini, a famous Dominican linguist and student of Savonarola.</note>, a distinguished professor of theology in the order of Saint Dominic, greeting me in your name, has assured me with many testimonies that I am ardently loved by you. Although this has been clearly known to me for a long time, I nevertheless long desired news of your prosperous health, such as I have now received after a long wait. Philosophy, the mother of all human goods, long ago gave birth to our friendship—which (as Plato says) is to be preferred to every kinship and will not perish with time. But these things are surely too certain to need witnesses or words. 

He reported to us, moreover, that a certain friar (I know not whom) insolently asserted in a public declamation that the divine mystery of the Trinity among Christians exists within Plato himself, and that the first Christians received these familiar things from there. You, however, expect a judgment from me on this matter, as if Platonic matters were my domain. I, therefore, assert beyond controversy: the secret of the Christian Trinity is never found in the books of Plato himself. There are, however, some things similar in words, though not in the same sense. 

Yet things more similar appear in his followers who flourished after Christ: in Numenius, Ammonius, Plotinus, Amelius, Iamblichus, and Proclus <note>These are the major figures of Neoplatonism, a school of thought that flourished from the 3rd to 5th centuries AD.</note>. Since they had all read the Gospel of John, and some moreover the books of Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian once thought to be a convert of St. Paul, but now known as a 5th-century writer who blended Neoplatonism with Christianity.</note>, they willingly adopted some things similar to the Trinity. They even took up the orders and names of angels, as if they were most consistent with their Plato—whom they saw as a follower of Moses <note>The idea that Plato was a "Moses speaking Greek" was a common Renaissance belief used to harmonize Greek philosophy with the Bible.</note>. 

Wherefore Aurelius Augustine, once a Platonist and then deliberating on his Christian profession, when he happened upon these books of the Platonists and recognized that Christian things were approved by them through imitation, gave thanks to God and was rendered more inclined to receive Christian teachings. How much Platonic things are truly similar to Christian things, you will be able to understand briefly from the letter I wrote long ago to Braccio Martelli on this subject. For I am sending a copy of it to you now. Farewell, be happy, and love me as you usually do, as I love you vehemently. 2 February 1494.

BOOK TWELVE

<margin>c</margin>
Since this entire universe, of which we are in a sense parts, is always moving, we certainly can never—nor should we—withdraw ourselves from action and movement. This is especially true because the primary and perpetual motion (as the Platonists believe) is natural to the soul itself, and life is nothing other than the motion and act of the soul; thus, as we live, it is just as necessary—and equally desirable—to move and to act. But am I perhaps being foolish in the meantime? It might have been more appropriate, after such a long silence, to immediately deliver news of our affairs and health to you via letter rather than to philosophize so suddenly. It certainly would have been more fitting, my dear Callimachus <note>Ficino is addressing Filippo Buonaccorsi, an Italian humanist who went by the name "Callimachus Experiens."</note>. Yet the reason I philosophize so out of season is both our long-standing friendship and my guiding Spirit <note>Original: *Genius*. In the Renaissance, this referred to a personal protective spirit or one's inherent nature.</note>. You also are accustomed to philosophizing with us often through letters, but always at the right time and with grace. Let us proceed then for a little while (as we have begun), hopefully not foolishly. 

There are three primary types of motion through space in the universe. Some things revolve perpetually around the same point in the same way. Others continually change their place and position. Still others imitate partly that circular motion and partly this straight one. Men, too, follow different movements. But to speak now of my own motion rather than another’s: it is certainly granted to me that I should always revolve in the same place. What is Marsilio doing today? The same as yesterday. What will he do tomorrow? Again, what he does today. Always (as you see) I am rolled around the same point within the walls of the Academy <note>The Platonic Academy in Florence, centered at the Villa di Careggi.</note>; again and again, I revolve. 

But what I have done, redone, and woven anew during this long circuit, you will understand from the catalog of my books, which I am sending to you to be read along with my book *On the Sun* <note>Original: *De Sole*. One of Ficino's most famous works, blending Neoplatonism with solar symbolism.</note>, so that through the most clear testimony of Apollo’s gift, our most friendly relationship may shine for both present and future generations. Moreover, I am sending a threefold volume of *On the Sun* and *On Light* so that I might not only please you, but that you might also be able to please two of your friends. Therefore, you will learn for yourself from these what we have composed. Indeed, I have heard from your friends Octavian and the Tedaldi that you have already settled your affairs. This news was most welcome to me. Farewell happily. 2 April 1494.

->Wise men are the children of Minerva: She gives birth to philosophy. Philosophy gives birth to philosophers.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved brother, Germain de Ganay. Many greetings.

<margin>m</margin>
The poets celebrate Minerva as a perpetual virgin. Yet she produces grown sons among the gods or men while her perpetual virginity remains meanwhile preserved. If indeed she was born from the head of supreme Jove alone, she similarly gives birth from the head alone; she gives birth, I say, to wise men in place of the fallen giants—that is, to heroes greater than giants. Philosophy too, a perpetual virgin and Wisdom (that is, the daughter of Minerva), gives birth to philosophers from the crown of her head on behalf of the wise. 

Greetings, therefore, once again, my most beloved brother <note>Ficino is playing on his correspondent's name, Germain (Germanus), which in Latin also means "brotherly" or "genuine." Germain de Ganay was a French high official and patron of humanism.</note>, whom our common mother Philosophy truly bore as a brother to me. That pious mother, since she never wished her sons to be divided from one another, drew you (as you write) into a love for me by the light sent there; and in turn, she seized me into a love for you by the heat transmitted here from that very same light. Since, indeed, all things of friends—and especially of brothers—ought to be common...

I have decided that all my things will be shared with you according to your wish. Therefore, I will send to you first the books of Dionysius <note>Likely Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist whom Ficino translated.</note> and of many other Platonists already transcribed for you, which you have requested for a long time. Next, I will send the commentaries on the *Parmenides* <note>Plato's dialogue on the nature of "The One."</note>, which are being copied daily for your sake. These will perhaps be followed by the commentaries on the *Timaeus* and the *Sophist*. Indeed, those on the *Sophist* are hurrying along and are now being transcribed toward the very end. Meanwhile, the letters are also being revised, as are the rest. I had perceived that you already had Plotinus <note>Plotinus was the founder of Neoplatonism; Ficino's translation and commentary on him were monumental works of the Renaissance.</note>, but recently you did not write that you have him. If you wish him to be sent, let me know. Farewell.

->Regarding the book *On the Sun*<-

Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to the Venetian Lord Bernardo Bembo.

<margin>s</margin>Common love is often accustomed to grow cold or be completely destroyed on account of long absence and prolonged silence. But our love, being singular, can neither ever fail nor be blotted out because of these things. Let Apollo <note>Original: *Phoebus*. Ficino uses the sun god as a symbol for the divine light that sustains their friendship.</note> himself be a pledge with his heat and a witness with his light. The 19th day.

->Regarding the book *On the Sun*<-

Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to the Venetian Lord Antonio Cronico.

<margin>i</margin>The ancients used to worship a certain "Friendly Jupiter" <note>Original: *Iuppiter amicabilis*. Jupiter in his aspect as the protector of hospitality and friendship.</note> as the uniter of friends and the preserver of friendship. But in what regions of the world does this Jupiter most inhabit? Perhaps he has placed his dwelling in the sun. Since friendship is named after and derived from love, and love is a certain heat—and the lover’s state proceeds from knowledge and is born from beauty—then Apollo <note>Original: *Apollo*. Here identified with the sun, the source of heat, light (knowledge), and beauty.</note> is, above all others, the author of heat, knowledge, and beauty. Let Friendly Jupiter be the pledge of our friendship in this Apollonian gift <note>Ficino is referring to his book *De Sole* (On the Sun) as an "Apollonian gift."</note>. August 19, 1494.

->What he thinks about Astrology<-

Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Angelo Poliziano <note>A famous Italian humanist, poet, and close friend of Ficino and the Medici family.</note>.

<margin>c</margin>Against many astrologers who, in the manner of giants <note>Referring to the Gigantomachy, the mythological battle where the Giants tried to overthrow the Olympian gods.</note>, strive as vainly as they do impiously to snatch heaven from Jupiter, Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, who wrote a famous attack on "divinatory" astrology.</note>, the foster child of Pallas Athena, and you, a Herculean soldier, often and successfully do battle. For indeed Orpheus sings of Pallas as the expeller of giants, and many poets say that the giant Antaeus was lifted from the earth and from life at the same time by Hercules. And what of me? Certainly, as I am of one mind with you in all of life, I also conspire with you in this study; and if perhaps I do not fight as strenuously, I nevertheless judge just as clearly. Other Platonists indeed mention the celestial images which the astronomers describe when appropriate; they neither reject them nor, on the other hand, strive to prove them. Plotinus, however, laughs at such things beyond controversy. I also, in my commentaries on him, as an interpreter, laugh at them equally—partly relying on his authority, and partly because I have no certain reasoning for such things. Furthermore, in that same place, I bring many rules of the astrologers into controversy by similar reasoning. But in my book *On Life* <note>Original: *De vita*. This refers to his work *De vita libri tres*, which discusses medical and astrological ways to maintain health.</note>, where I profess medicine and the remedies of life, I diligently search everywhere for whatever and however many things I can, and I do not despise...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s defense of his writings on astrology and natural magic, specifically addressing his book "On Obtaining Life from the Heavens" (De Vita Coelitus Comparanda). TWELVE CCXXXIX

...those images; nor do I reject all the rules, even if I do not believe a certain rational principle resides in them. Nevertheless, as a most diligent steward of human medicine, I seek out remedies that are not only certain for the wise but also probable for the many, so that I may accumulate aids from every side that might be of use. In short, I would leave nothing untried that anyone might think could lead to life in any way. However, I intersperse some firmer points and also gather many things here and there which, even if I perhaps have less hope for them, I still desire to be beneficial. 

As for what I seem to say at the beginning of the third book—that images were arranged in the heavens by the older Platonists <note>The followers of Plato, particularly the Neoplatonists like Plotinus and Porphyry, who merged philosophy with mysticism.</note>—that is not truly my intention. For it is not my purpose there to affirm that the Platonists were assertors of celestial images, about which they say either nothing or very little. Rather, it was the opinion of certain Platonists that the **World Soul** <note>original: "mundi animam"; the vital principle that Renaissance philosophers believed animated the entire universe.</note> produced celestial bodies for itself, as well as the stars along with the heavens, and beyond the individual stars—if indeed any such images exist there—it also generated images of this kind. 

I am recounting there that the images of the zodiac signs were arranged not as they are among the Platonists, but as I have observed them among the **astrologers**. Now, indeed, how much I trust in images, whether celestial or made by art, the progression of the book itself declares. Furthermore, in the book *On the Sun*, I teach astronomical notation more so that I may pursue moral allegories through them and seek out **anagogies** <note>term: "anagogies" — interpretations that lead the mind upward from material things to divine spiritual truths.</note> toward divine things. 

Finally, in the books *On Life* as well as *On the Sun* and *On Light*, since you mix poetic things with philosophical ones, I have sometimes wandered quite freely and perhaps too licentiously. I deal more sparingly and severely with Plotinus <note>Plotinus was the 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism; Ficino translated his entire corpus into Latin.</note>, so that in the end it will not be unpleasant to me that the "astrological portents" have been singularly refuted by our **Pico della Mirandola** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Ficino's brilliant colleague, who wrote a famous massive attack on divinatory astrology titled "Disputations Against Divinatory Astrology."</note>. For those things which I never affirm—indeed, which I mock along with Plotinus—I rejoice that they are exploded by Mirandola. I congratulate you, **Poliziano** <note>Angelo Poliziano, a famous poet and scholar in the Medici circle.</note>, that such superstitious vanity is being extinguished by him as if by the arrows of Apollo <note>original: "Phœbo"; Ficino compares Pico to the sun god slaying the monstrous serpent Python.</note> destroying the Pythonic poison. For you have always played the part of **Hercules** in this cause, as you are accustomed to do everywhere. You have for a long time now been accustomed to hunt down these "prodigies" of the astrologers as if they were other monsters, so that you have conquered monsters not only on earth but even in the heavens, like the bravest Hercules. May it be finally that, just as for Hercules, so for you: may the conquered earth grant you the stars. Meanwhile, live long upon the earth. Farewell happily. 

The 20th day of August, 1494.

### Recommendation of a client to the Magistrate

### Marsilio Ficino to Niccolò Benino: endowed with learning and character. Sends Hearty Greetings.

It was surely my duty, from the very beginning of your term in office, in accordance with our no small friendship, to congratulate you in no small measure. Not only because you have been honored with this dignity, but also—and much more so—because you are going to conduct your office in a manner worthy of that dignity. I should also have congratulated my friends and clients, for even if they were innocent, they would be sure to find protection from you; or if they were guilty, they would at least find a certain indulgence and mercy. For I know your character. I know for certain that you—as God himself commands by his own action—will duly join justice with mercy. 

Furthermore, if it is permitted to speak of Jupiter <note>Ficino frequently links the planet Jupiter to the concepts of earthly law, justice, and the "Great King."</note> in this matter, the Hebrews call him *Sedech* <note>original: "sedech"; the Hebrew word *Tzedek* (צדק), meaning 'Justice,' which is the Hebrew name for the planet Jupiter.</note>, that is, "Justice," and astronomers grant to their Jupiter rights and laws. The poets, too, sing of a Jupiter full of indulgence—to say nothing of that poetic license that leans more toward indulgence than law: "Jupiter decreed that whatever helped was pious." <note>original: "Iuppiter eſſe piũ ſtatuít qdcũq; iuuaret"; a quote from Ovid's *Heroides* 4.133, suggesting that for Jupiter, the end justifies the means—a sentiment Ficino here frames as "poetic license."</note> Let it suffice among the astrologers that Jupiter, along with the laws, brings or signifies mercy. In this, indeed, God seems to have warned men from the heavens to mix both equally in their magistracy. But you, in your wisdom (as I believe), know these things well enough already. Farewell happily. Florence, August 31, 1494.

### Giving thanks for the mercy obtained for a client.

### Marsilio Ficino to Niccolò Benino: endowed with learning and character. Sends Hearty Greetings.

Since good and evil are opposed to one another, they consequently take on conditions that are opposite to each other. It certainly seems probable that if good is fertile—whereas evil, on the contrary, is barren—then just as crime is a great evil, so mercy is a great good. It follows that merciful indulgence must be far more fertile than crime and transgression. For this reason, if the offense of my client gave birth to our first letter to you, then your merciful indulgence ought to give birth to a second letter in return—one that is much better and greater. 

Indeed, the first (so to speak) was "Jovian," <note>original: "Iouía"; referring to the qualities of Jupiter: law, justice, and governance.</note> relying on a comparison with Jupiter; the second, therefore, will surpass the first, or at least equal it, if it is "Apollonian." <note>original: "apollínea"; referring to Apollo or the Sun, which Ficino viewed as a higher, more divine light than the planetary power of Jupiter.</note> For only the Sun can surpass Jupiter. Therefore, so that this letter may sufficiently fulfill my duty toward you under Apollonian auspices, I send it to you as a companion of Phoebus <note>A title for Apollo, meaning the "Bright" or "Radiant" one.</note> and a servant of the Sun. Read gladly our book *On the Sun* <note>original: "librũ de ſole"; Ficino’s treatise *De Sole*, which explores the Sun as a physical and spiritual symbol of God.</note>, given to you as a gift, and live happily. September 3, 1494.

### On the friendly Jupiter and Apollo, for the book *On the Sun*.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s correspondence. The previous page discussed the astrological and theological significance of the planet Jupiter (called Sedech in Hebrew) as a symbol of justice, and Ficino was recommending a client to a magistrate.</meta>

<header>BOOK TWELVE</header>

<margin>a</margin> Ancient theologians first, and then the poets, among other deities, worshipped Jupiter as a "friendly" father of pure love and firm friendship. Indeed, he earned this name "friendly" equally from love and friendship. Since our Plato also sometimes mentions this deity, I have often wondered while writing my commentaries what other name I might more clearly call this god. Finally, after long meditation, it came to mind that I should call this most illustrious god especially by the name "Apollo": the source of Light, Heat, Harmony, and Knowledge. For we never love things unknown, nor do we know anything without light, nor are we ever provoked to love without a certain heat. Furthermore, a certain harmonic congruence is necessary for love and friendship. Again, the beauty of the body is often desired for love; for friendship, the beauty of the soul is always desired; yet both beauties seem to be nothing other than a certain splendor. But the author of splendor is Apollo. Therefore, all reasons compel us to name Apollo especially as the source of love and friendship. If we, for the sake of conversation, perhaps accept the number of the gods in the manner of the pagans, we will say he is Phoebus—a certain deity or power perfected by the sun, a king among celestial things. But if we strive instead by more serious reason, we shall assert that Phoebus is the Highest God <note>Ficino often uses "Phoebus" or "Apollo" as a metaphor for the Christian God or the Neo-Platonic "One" in his philosophical poetry.</note>, of whom the celestial sun is the image. Thus, that Phoebus is the author of honorable love and firm friendship, while the sun is the signifier. Since, therefore, I am uniquely inflamed by a certain "Phoebus-like" splendor of your wisdom and virtues, I love you ardently, and I desire that our friendship consist of love; surely I come to you under the auspices of Apollo: Greetings.

### Marsilio Ficino to Germain de Ganay, a man of outstanding virtue. Sends Greetings.

<margin>q</margin> What I had long ago heard from many concerning your excellent virtue and dignity, Cosimo Sassetti and Lorenzo Spinelli <margin>ß</margin> have recently confirmed for me with much testimony; they are noble men and truly most trustworthy witnesses in this matter. <margin>q</margin> They told me, furthermore, how much you value me and how ardently you love me. You will see (as I hope) soon some Platonists coming from here to you. You would also have seen the Areopagite <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian whose works Ficino translated and believed were the peak of Platonic thought.</note>, the summit of Platonists, if he could have arrived now in that dress which became both him and you; but the negligence of the scribe and the bookbinder hindered his arrival. Within a few days (I hope) he will come with the letters. The commentary on the *Parmenides* has already been copied for you. Every day the commentary on the *Timaeus* is being rewritten. Farewell, be happy; and (as you have begun) love your Marsilio, your brother in Plato <note>Ficino puns on the name "Germanus" and the Latin word "germanum" meaning a blood-brother or true kinsman.</note>, who loves you ardently. ### Oration of Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Charles the Great, King of the Gauls. <note>original: "Carolum magnum Gallorũ regem." Your high majesty, King Charles, ever unconquered: it is often said (as many report) that you are sent by divine providence on this expedition. For it is truly likely that the most Christian King of the French <note>original: "Gallorũ," literally "of the Gauls."</note> is sent by Christ, and that Charles, a king distinguished for piety above others, is guided by Christian piety—especially since you have undertaken this journey and work with the intention that you might finally redeem holy Jerusalem, occupied by most cruel barbarians, for the supreme redeemer of the human race. We hope indeed that you will easily redeem that holy kingdom, having first, along the way, received your hereditary kingdom <note>Referring to Charles VIII’s claim to the Kingdom of Naples, which was his primary objective in the Italian campaign.</note>. For if on this journey you follow the footsteps of Christ everywhere with all your strength, Christ, the King of Peace, often promises peace to those who desire it. The same you also, most Christian king, endowed with singular piety, promise (as we hear and as we hope), and truly you will fulfill; and you will in truth do what was once commanded by the father to pious Aeneas and the race of his descendants: "To spare the humble and to cast down the proud." <note>original: "Parcere subiectis & debellare superbos." A famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid (6.853), defining the Roman imperial mission.</note> Wherefore, since you will be the author of peace for all who wish for peace—especially to your own—you will show yourself peaceful to us. You shall visit Florence, your city, with wonderful piety. Florence, named for the flower—that is, the lily—and full of lilies everywhere <note>The lily was the symbol of both the city of Florence (the giglio) and the French monarchy (the fleur-de-lis).</note>. You shall come into your own, and your people will receive you with their whole heart. You, moreover, imitating your leader Christ, shall cry out to the people:

### Why providence permits adversity. Also on prophecies and remedies for evils.

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, sends greetings.<-

It is often asked by the Platonists <term>Platonists: followers of the philosophy of Plato; Ficino was the primary translator and teacher of these ideas in the Renaissance</term> why divine providence always allows men to be shaken by innumerable evils, the just and the unjust alike. He [Plato] is accustomed to respond to these things summarily. First, indeed, that it is unknown to mortals whether these things are truly evils or goods. For human affairs are like shadows, and our thoughts like dreams; this is the point of that prophetic saying: **All is vanity. Every man is a liar.** <note>original: "Omnia vanitas. Omnis homo mendax." Combining Ecclesiastes 1:2 and Psalm 116:11.</note> He responds again that even if it is agreed that what are seen are evils, they are in a way still "evils" only in appearance. Finally, evil is permitted by the highest Good itself only for the sake of the good. For difficult and adverse things purge curable vice, and indeed punish the incurable. In the former, the good of purification shines; in the latter, the good of justice. Moreover, good men are discerned from the wicked in adversity, and they are exercised and proven. Indeed, this testing, progress, and constancy are a good. It is worthwhile, furthermore, to carefully consider that Platonic saying in the *Phaedrus* concerning the sorcerous cunning of the evil demon: a certain demon, right from the beginning, mixed pleasure into as many vices as possible. This is what Socrates says there, warning that the primary aim of evil demons is to detain souls in this exile for a longer time, separated from their heavenly fatherland and forgotten by their celestial Father. They plot long delays using the allurements and delights of the earth, which act like the cups of the sorceress Circe <note>In Greek mythology, Circe used a magical potion to turn Odysseus's men into swine.</note> or the sleep-inducing songs of the Sirens. Charmed by these, souls never, or certainly only very slowly, return to their heavenly fatherland. Conversely, against these demonic traps, the beneficial providence of God has decreed that bitter tastes be mixed back into these sweet and death-bearing flavors. This is so that we are not captured by that kind of pleasure which Timaeus <note>referring to Plato's dialogue "Timaeus"</note> calls "the bait of evils," so that...

<sig>b</sig>

<summary>Ficino praises King Charles VIII as a messianic figure surpassing Caesar and Hercules, then begins a philosophical inquiry into why God permits suffering, arguing that adversity serves to purge vice and test the virtuous.</summary>

--- Page 486 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s philosophical letter to his close friend Giovanni Cavalcanti. Ficino is transitioning from his discussion of King Charles VIII to a broader defense of divine providence, explaining why God allows evil and suffering to exist in the world.</meta>

<header>BOOK TWELVE</header>

...fishes from the hook. This is largely the reason why the Platonists—especially Plotinus and Synesius—think that divine providence willed for souls on earth to be vexed by so many and such great disturbances. To this point tends that Platonic saying in the book *On Science* <note>original: "in libro de scia" referring to Plato's *Theaetetus*.</note>, which is consonant with the Gospel, and which I wrote to you and briefly explained long ago, my dearest Giovanni. It says: "O Theodorus, it is impossible for evils to be utterly uprooted; for it is necessary that there always be something contrary to good. Among the gods above, evils certainly cannot exist; but they necessarily revolve through mortal nature and this lower place. Therefore, we must strive to flee from here to there as quickly as possible. To flee, however, is to make oneself as similar to God as possible, according to one's strength; and justice and holiness joined with prudence make us similar to God." <note>A famous passage from Plato’s *Theaetetus* (176a–b) regarding the "flight from the world."</note>

Thus he spoke. In these words, Plato declares that we meditate on fleeing from here to God chiefly for this reason: so that we may escape the evils that necessarily afflict us here—escaping, that is, from this mortal evil to carry back that eternal good. Indeed, no one unless vexed by diseases recognizes and approaches a physician; nor do sailors admire the pilot’s skill unless they are tossed by waves. Mortals are surely so dull that they do not recognize good from any other source until they compare it with evils; they are so ungrateful that they do not easily worship God, the giver of all good things, unless they are oppressed by evils. Therefore, tortured by frequent diseases and disturbances, they are compelled to flee to God himself as if to a physician and helper. They are also forced to recognize that the earthly province where they are constantly in want and never at rest is not their true homeland, but the heavenly one is.

No more powerful reason can be assigned for why God permits evils and adversities than the Gospel reasoning <note>original: "ratio evangelica"</note>, which teaches that the blind and the maimed are sometimes born so that the admirable power and goodness of God might be declared to men—namely, to miraculously cure those evils incurable by human means. Just as it is not just any diseases or waves, but the most grave ones, that typically testify to a supreme physician or pilot. Often, therefore, men—both privately and publicly—are hemmed in on all sides by such extreme narrows that no exit is open. Let no human safety now be hoped for, but let only divine help be sought. Then divine goodness and power, reaching out a propitious hand from on high to its children praying with a pious mind, declares that God alone is the savior in extreme calamities. And He demonstrates this even more clearly when He predicted through a certain prophet that such great crises were coming long before they arrived.

It is the duty of a human physician, even if he cannot provide health, at least to always provide a prognosis. But the divine physician encompasses both. And although one may bring forth many examples of these things from sacred scripture <note>original: "sacris liris" (literis)</note>, which are ready at hand for everyone, my plan for the present—as it has always been—is to bring to light less known things and to confirm Christian mysteries, as far as I can, with Platonic arguments. Listen, therefore, my Giovanni—who is as much a worshiper of divine things as a student of Platonic ones—to the words with which Socrates, in Plato, confirms the divine plan regarding the remedies of human evils and prophets. For thus he speaks in the *Symposium*: the priestess Diotima, a prophetic woman and expert in divine matters, predicted the plague threatening the Athenians. And so, through sacrifices performed ten years before the plague...

<summary>Ficino explains the necessity of evil and suffering as a means to drive humans back toward God, using Plato’s "flight from the world" and Gospel teachings on divine healing as evidence. He argues that extreme trials allow God to demonstrate His power as the ultimate physician and savior.</summary>
<keywords>divine providence, problem of evil, Plato, Theaetetus, Symposium, Diotima, Giovanni Cavalcanti, spiritual medicine, prophecy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of divine providence and prophecy. Having established that suffering often leads humanity back to God, Ficino now uses Platonic and Islamic philosophy to argue that God sends "divine madness" or inspired prophets to warn cities of impending doom caused by their sins.</meta>

CCXLII
->**TWELVE CCXLII**<-
b 2

...offered a delay of the disease. Likewise, if we were to refer to the *Phaedrus* <note>One of Plato's dialogues, central to Renaissance theories of divine inspiration.</note>, to the Sibyl, and to all others who have used the power of prophecy—those who, by predicting many things, have been of benefit for the future—we would extend our discourse too far and bring forth a matter already manifest to everyone. 

And a little later he says that the ancients testify that prophecy, brought to perfection by a certain **divine madness** <note>original: "vaticinium diuino quodam furore perfectum." Ficino refers to *theia mania*, or "divine frenzy," which he believed lifted the soul toward God.</note>, is infinitely superior to human conjecture and prudence. Indeed, against the most grievous diseases and labors that sometimes threaten mortals because of divine indignation for ancient sins, a divine madness comes to certain nations from elsewhere. By predicting the future, it has miraculously found the remedies that were needed, leading people to take refuge in vows and divine worship. Whence, having attained expiations and propitiations, it restored the possessed person to health; and for both the present and the future, the one who was "rightly mad" <note>The person undergoing divine inspiration.</note> and occupied by the divine obtained a release from present evils.

Besides these things, in the first book of the *Laws*, Plato says thus: Epimenides of Crete, a divine man, ten years before the Persian War, warned by a divine oracle, came to Athens and performed certain sacrifices set forth by the oracle of God. To the Athenians who were dreading the Persian fleet, he predicted that the Persians would not come for ten years, and once they had come, they would depart with their business unfinished. 

Plato certainly judges such a man to be the wisest of all, although among the common people he is often considered the most foolish. Thus, in the *Phaedrus*, he writes something wonderful in this manner: "He who rightly uses divine meditations and is always imbued with the **perfect mysteries** <note>original: "perfectisque mysteriis." In a Platonic context, these are spiritual truths revealed through initiation or inspiration.</note>, alone truly becomes perfect. Separated from human pursuits and clinging to the divine, he is rebuked by the crowd as if he were out of his mind; but he himself, full of God, remains hidden from the crowd." 

After this, when Plato had placed the prophet and the priest occupied with divine things far ahead of human wisdom by a great distance, he describes a certain mind burning with an entirely divine love, undergoing an amorous ecstasy; and he places such madness and alienation not only before human prudence, but before all other divine gifts. Here he clearly confirms that apostolic saying: *The greatest of these is charity* <note>1 Corinthians 13:13. Ficino famously synchronized Plato's "divine love" with Christian "charity" or *caritas*.</note>.

Moreover, regarding the sending of prophets by God and the reason why they are sent, **Avicenna** <note>The 11th-century Persian philosopher Ibn Sina, whose work on the soul and prophecy influenced the Renaissance.</note> also agrees with Plato for many reasons in his *Book of Divine Things*. But now, passing over longer digressions, let us return briefly to our purpose. 

It is certainly worthy of no small consideration that, as Plato said above, because of ancient sins, God in His indignation has in some way destined calamities for men. From this is affirmed that oracle: "Adversities come because of sins"; as well as that Mosaic saying that all adversities have happened to us because of the sin of our first parents <note>A reference to the Fall of Adam and Eve in Genesis.</note>. Where, furthermore, Plato adds that God, as if moved by a certain mercy, frequently inspires prophets who will announce future scourges to us, so that being warned by this, we may take refuge in vows and sacred expiations. Once these are duly performed, we frequently escape unharmed. There, indeed, he seems to confirm all the **mysteries** of our Church. 

Therefore, lest examples of so great a matter be sought from too far away: was not a final destruction threatening this city this autumn because of many sins?

<summary>Ficino argues that God sends divinely inspired prophets (using the examples of the Sibyl and Epimenides) to warn societies of impending disasters caused by sin. He synchronizes Plato's theory of "divine madness" and Avicenna's philosophy with Christian teachings on prophecy and charity.</summary>
<keywords>divine madness, prophecy, Plato, Avicenna, Epimenides, expiation, sin, charity, Athens, Persian War</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s correspondence during the turbulent year of 1494. Following the previous page's discussion on prophecy and "divine madness," Ficino here applies these concepts to the contemporary political crisis in Florence, specifically identifying the friar Girolamo Savonarola as a divinely appointed messenger who saved the city.</meta>

# BOOK

It was absolutely unavoidable by any human virtue: Has not divine mercy, most indulgent toward the Florentines, foretold this to us for a full four years before this autumn? This was done through a man outstanding in holiness and wisdom, Girolamo <note>original: "Hieronimum." Referring to Girolamo Savonarola (1452–1498), the Dominican friar who rose to prominence in Florence as a prophet and reformer.</note> of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans.</note>, chosen by God for this purpose. Have we not—through his fulfillment of divine omens and warnings—wonderfully avoided the certain destruction even now hanging over our heads? This was accomplished by no human virtue of ours, but beyond our hope and expectation. **"This is the Lord’s doing; and it is marvelous in our eyes."** <note>A quotation of Psalm 118:23.</note> It remains, my dear Giovanni, that henceforth, following the healthy advice of such a great man, not only you and I but all Florentines should be grateful to God, who is most merciful to us, and shout with a public voice: **"Confirm, O God, this work which You have performed in us."** <note>A variation of Psalm 68:28.</note> December 12, 1494.

->Congratulation for letters long expected.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved Germain de Ganay <note>Germain de Ganay was a French high-ranking official and a patron of the arts and humanities who met Ficino during the French invasion.</note>, sends greetings.<-

<margin>e</margin> The injustice of this storm <note>Ficino uses "storm" as a metaphor for the political and military upheaval caused by the French invasion of Italy.</note> has intercepted many letters, both from you to me and from me to you. At last, yesterday, devotion conquered the hard journey and granted me your long-awaited letter. Arise now, my present letter! Go now to our honor and enjoy better fates. But what should I write first? Surely what first happened to be most pleasing to me: namely, that I have been commended through your letter to your brother Jean, President of the Parliament of Paris. <note>Jean de Ganay was a prominent French legal official who accompanied King Charles VIII.</note> This was and will be of great value to us. For almost all of Italy—certainly all of Tuscany and especially Florence—is daily agitated by both external and internal tumults. Indeed, I met our Jean here with your exalted King <note>King Charles VIII of France, whose army occupied Florence in November 1494.</note> in recent days; he is a man most worthy of frequent greeting. I rejoiced in his sight not only because of his own brilliance, but I especially congratulated him because in your distinguished brother I seemed to see my own dearest brother. Meanwhile, he was a comfort to me in these present anxieties. Therefore, even if our profession <note>Referring to the life of a philosopher.</note> is a work of a mind at leisure, I nevertheless continue, as much as I can, in my Platonic commentaries amidst these noises, intending to finish them soon (if God breathes upon the work).

->A pious opinion of Plato: Concerning the friends and enemies of God.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to his unique friend Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Giovanni Cavalcanti (1444–1509) was Ficino’s closest friend, student, and the dedicatee of many of his works.</note>, sends many greetings.<-

<margin>c</margin> Yesterday, I discussed with you and your son-in-law, the upright Gerard Jansilatius, what Plato thinks in the *Philebus* <note>One of Plato’s dialogues concerning the nature of pleasure and the highest good.</note> about the friends or enemies of God. It pleased you, therefore, that I should write to you the very words of Plato and our exposition of them in that place. Receive them, then, and read with joy. These are the words of Plato: "Is not the just, pious, and upright man a friend of God? But the unjust and wicked man is an enemy." "He is indeed." Many...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s philosophical correspondence and his reflections on the Platonic tradition. Following the previous entry's focus on the political and spiritual crisis of 1494, Ficino here pivots toward a Neoplatonic psychological analysis of the "good man" versus the "wicked man," before transitioning into introductory letters for his treatise On the Sun (De Sole).</meta>

CCXLIII
# TWELFTH [BOOK] CCXLIII

Indeed, every person is led by hope. For there are certain internal discourses within each of us. Those which we are accustomed to call both opinions and hopes are, furthermore, painted phantasms <note>original: "phantasmata picta." In Neoplatonic thought, these are mental images or "pictures" created by the faculty of imagination that can either lead the soul toward truth or into delusion.</note>. For anyone is permitted to imagine that they possess a massive heap of gold, and, abounding in various delights, to be drenched in every sweetness. Must we not say that opinions and imaginations of this kind frequently turn out to be true for good men, because they are friends of God? But for the wicked, they are frequently false. This must certainly be said: for wicked men, certain pleasures are present, but they are often fabricated and, finally, false. Therefore, the wicked often exult in false pleasures. Good men, however, are always nourished by true joys. Thus far Plato <note>Ficino is summarizing a passage from Plato's dialogue *Philebus*, which examines whether pleasures can be "true" or "false" based on their alignment with reality and the divine.</note>. Our exposition follows: A good man is judged by Plato to be one who is temperate in himself, pious toward God, and just toward men. A soul of this kind, because of its resemblance to the divine, is a friend to God above all others; but the wicked man, because of his dissimilarity, is an enemy. Therefore, since God both moves the soul from within and provides for everything, the opinions, imaginations, and hopes of good men undoubtedly frequently turn out to be true; but those of the wicked are false. Both types devise certain joys, they wish and they hope; for good men, being as it were divine and truth-telling, these joys often come true. For the wicked, they are false. For the wicked, being liars to themselves, just as they are frequently deceived in opinion, so do they more often fabricate false delights. Finally, if hope ought not to succeed for the wicked, since they are in discord with divine truth—even if they often seem to have success in external matters—it follows at least that they do not succeed within. Therefore, they are always troubled and languishing inside, and their pleasures are like the false pleasures of the sick, the dreaming, and the insane. December 20, 1494.

### For the book On the Sun.

->Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to the most worthy Germain de Ganay, President of Paris.<-

Since, because of the crowd of guests in my house and the public tumults <note>Ficino refers to the civil unrest in Florence following the expulsion of the Medici family and the presence of the French army.</note>, I was unable to philosophize there in peace, yet I did not wish to interrupt my perpetual philosophical duty, I withdrew from the city into rural solitude. But before I departed, I often sought out your splendor, which I have long desired. To you, whom I have not yet greeted in person, I send this greeting while absent, by means of a certain gift of Phoebus <note>Phoebus is another name for Apollo, the sun god. Ficino is presenting his book *De Sole* (On the Sun) as a gift from the god of light.</note>. For if Phoebus himself does not perhaps touch us with his physical sphere, he nevertheless reaches everywhere with his rays; indeed, even your splendor reaches me here with its own rays. By that very heat of Phoebus's light, I beseech you, my most splendid Giovanni: love Marsilio, who loves you ardently. Farewell.

### For the book On the Sun.

->Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to Paolo of Verona, a man of distinguished learning.<-

# BOOK TWELVE

I was indeed able to see you in Florence. And that turned out to be quite pleasing to me. It would also have been most pleasing to visit President Parisio <note>Original: "Parisii." Likely referring to Giovanni Parisio, a contemporary legal or ecclesiastical official.</note>, a man most worthy of being seen. And since you two are bound to each other by such love <note>Original: "charitate," referring to *caritas* or Christian brotherly love.</note> (as I judge) that one exists within the other: when I first looked at Paul, in Paul I saw within to John. In the same way, while Phoebus <note>The sun god Apollo. In Ficino’s Neoplatonic philosophy, the sun represents the visible light of God and the source of intellectual illumination.</note> looks from the outside with his brilliance, he meanwhile—so to speak—looks within with his heat. Finally, through this very "gift of Phoebus" <note>Ficino often referred to his treatise *De Sole* (On the Sun) as a "Phoebaean gift."</note> which I am also sending to you, I earnestly entreat you to recommend me often to my "Apollonian" John <note>Referring to Giovanni (John) as a follower of Apollo, the god of light and truth.</note>. Farewell.

->The End of the Twelfth and Final Book of the Familiar Letters of Marsilio Ficino of Florence.<-

Indeed, it was permitted to see you, Florence. Therefore, it was very pleasing to me
